Can one, after all this, fail to recognize that God is the author <note>original: "ingeeber," meaning the one who gave or inspired the text</note> of these books? If they had come solely from men, would they not have flattered human passions? Would they have forbidden mere desire <note>in the sense of internal lust or covetousness</note>, of which Paul said in Romans 7:7, that he *would never have known it was sin, if the law had not said, you shall not covet.*?

One may gather all that is contained in the Laws of a Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta</note>, of a Draco <note>The first legislator of Athens, known for the severity of his laws</note>, and of other wise lawgivers, together with all that the most prominent philosophers of antiquity have written; it is certain that one will find nothing in them that comes close to the excellence and superiority of the Laws of Faith and of the Gospel. Furthermore, let one read through all the best books of piety <note>original: "Godzaligheid"</note> that exist among Christians—those which promote the peace of society and serve most to God’s glory—and one will find that they are all modeled after these Holy Books, and that everything has been drawn from these Fountains. Is this not proof that nothing more perfect or excellent can be made? And must one not necessarily confess that these Books are the work of God’s Spirit?

<margin>Fourth proof, taken from the fact that we learn from them all that we must know to be blessed.</margin>
IV. The fourth thing that convinces us that these Books are Divine is that we learn from them all that we most desire, and all that we must know to be blessed <note>original: "gelukzalig," referring to eternal happiness or salvation</note>, such as God’s essence and His perfections, His providence, and the honor we owe Him; the beginning of the world and of all creatures; the cause of the miseries and punishments to which human nature is subject; the greatness of our condemnation; what we have deserved, and by what means God’s justice is satisfied; the way that leads to bliss, and what must be done to please God; what our soul shall become after our death, and what our bodies shall become after having lain in the dust for some time, and other things of this nature which it is absolutely necessary for us to know. It will perhaps be said that we desire to know many things that these books do not teach us: but one must make two observations here. The first is that we only ask here for things that concern our Salvation <note>original: "Zaligheid"</note>, and not those that concern human

<column-break/>

sciences; the second is that in the matters that concern Salvation itself, it is only a question of what we *must* know; for the Holy Scripture was not given to us to satisfy an idle curiosity.

Furthermore, it is fitting to note that we find five types of things in these books: 1. Historical narratives. 2. Prophecies. 3. Promises and Threats. 4. Commandments. 5. Doctrines. What is more, among the things these books teach, there are some that are known to us by Nature without any revelation, but which these Books teach us more clearly. There are others of which men have had some knowledge, but a weak, uncertain, and confused knowledge. The Holy Scripture does, with respect to these things, the same as a person would do who helps us read the inscription on a commemorative medal <note>original: "gedenkpenning"</note> that is difficult to read. There are others which men could never have invented with all the ingenuity of their spirit. We shall have opportunity to speak of these things more distinctly.

<margin>Fifth proof taken from the harmony of the Holy Scripture.</margin>
V. The wonderful harmony that exists in all parts of Scripture gives us a fifth proof; for there is nothing in it that conflicts, and it gives us an idea of an infinite wisdom, consistent with the proportion that is seen in the whole. And this precise harmony is all the more wonderful because it is found between the Books of the Old and New Testament, even though those who used their pens to write them had no communication among themselves and were separated from each other by a sequence of centuries. This shows that they were all inspired by the same spirit, and that there was a Supreme Lord above them who held the governance and oversight over all this work. It will perhaps be said that there are contradictions in these books; but it is false that there are any essential ones; they are all apparent contradictions; the greatest contradictions that one sees presented regarding some genealogies or some numbers are things of little importance. Furthermore, if it had pleased God’s Spirit to give us more extensive Revelations, or if we had the books that were common among the Jews, we would find that there is no contradiction: there are things that we do not understand, and which the Jews...

Prophets wrote, lived, and understood [their own times] very well, just as there are obscure things in the secular writers which those who lived in the time of those authors understood without difficulty. Finally, one could not bring forward a single passage for which one cannot find various ways to reconcile it with the passage that seems to oppose it. The genealogies of Luke and Matthew seem to conflict to those who do not notice that Luke records the genealogy of Mary, and Matthew that of Joseph. It seems that there is some contradiction in the Books of Kings and Chronicles; however, these are but apparent contradictions <note>original: "schynstryden"</note> which can be resolved, whether by the different ways of counting the years of the Kings—some count only the years in which the Kings reigned alone, others look at the time when the sons reigned with their fathers—or by failing to distinguish the times, etc. In another work we shall perhaps, if God wills, have the opportunity to prove this further. For the rest, this argument—drawn from the wonderful harmony that exists between the Books of the Old and New Testament, and which Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155–220 AD)</note> and Augustine <note>Bishop of Hippo and influential theologian (354–430 AD)</note> used so well in their battle <note>original: "ter acie," a Latin military term for a battle line</note> against the Manicheans <note>Followers of Manichaeism, a dualistic religion that often rejected the Old Testament</note>—serves particularly to convince the Jews.

Sixth proof: that the Holy Books tell us everything that can comfort and sanctify us.
</margin>

VI. I proceed to a sixth proof, consisting in this: that these Books teach us everything that can still the anxieties of our souls and comfort them against the miseries of life, the terrors of death, and the consciousness it has of its sins. That there is now no condemnation for those who are in Jesus Christ and who repent, however great their sins may have been. 3. That the adversities God sends us are Fatherly chastisements by which He brings us back from our wanderings. 4. That God will always give us the strength to be able to endure them. 5. That they cannot last long and are not to be compared with the Glory prepared for the elect. 6. That death is the door to Heaven for believers, and that it is only terrible for the unrepentant. 7. That it will unite them with Him who is the cause of their being and their happiness; and that nothing

<column-break/>

shall ever separate them from that. 8. Finally, that if death lays their bodies in the grave, they shall rise from it in glory. Men could never have discovered such comforting truths for us.

They set before our eyes the holiness of God, of Jesus Christ, and of all the believers who lived under both the old and the new covenant; God's hatred for sin; the judgments He has poured out and will pour out upon sinners; the rewards He promises to those who will live holy, righteous, and godly lives; what Christ had to do to atone for sins, and the death He had to undergo to redeem us. Also, the word contained in these books is of a wonderful power. Paul gives us a description of it.

# THE CHRISTIAN

with excellent promises and terrible threats.

Can one, after all this, fail to acknowledge that God is the author of these books? If they had come solely from men, would they not have flattered human passions? Would they have forbidden mere desire, of which Paul said in Romans 7:7 that he would never have known it was sin if the law had not said, "thou shalt not covet" <note>original: "gy en zult niet begeeren"</note>.

If one gathers all that is contained in the laws of a Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta</note>, of a Draco <note>An Athenian lawmaker known for his exceptionally harsh legal code</note>, and of other wise legislators, along with all that the most prominent philosophers of antiquity have written; it is certain that one will find nothing in them that approaches the excellence and superiority of the laws of Faith and of the Gospel. Let one furthermore read through all the best books of piety <note>original: "Godzaligheid"</note> among Christians—those which promote the peace of society and best serve God’s glory—and one will find that they are all modeled after these Holy Books, and that everything has been drawn from these fountains. Is this not proof that nothing more perfect or excellent can be made? And must one not necessarily confess that these Books are the work of God’s Spirit?

<margin>Fourth proof, taken from the fact that we learn from it all that we must know to be blessed.</margin>

IV. The fourth thing that convinces us that these Books are divine is that we learn from them everything we most desire to know, and all that we must know to be blessed: such as God’s essence and His perfections, His providence, and the honor we owe Him; the beginning of the world and of all creatures; the cause of the miseries and punishments to which human nature is subject; the greatness of our corruption <note>original: "verdoovendheid," referring here to the spiritual numbness or depravity of fallen man</note>; what we have deserved, and by what means God’s justice has been satisfied; the path that leads to happiness, and what must be done to please God; what our soul will become after our death, and what our bodies will become after lying for some time in the dust; and other things of this nature which are absolutely necessary for us to know. It may perhaps be said that we desire to know many things which these books do not teach us: but one must make two observations here. The first is that we only ask here for things concerning our salvation, and not those concerning human 

<column-break/>

sciences; the second is that even in matters concerning salvation, it is only about what we *must* know: for the Holy Scripture was not given to us to satisfy a vain curiosity.

<margin>What one finds in the Holy books?</margin>

Furthermore, it is appropriate to note that we find five types of things in these books: 1. Historical accounts. 2. Prophecies. 3. Promises and Threats. 4. Commandments. 5. Doctrines. Moreover, among the things these books teach, there are those known to us by nature without any revelation, but which these books teach us more clearly. There are others of which men have had some knowledge, but a weak, uncertain, and confused knowledge.

Holy Scripture does, in regard to these things, the same thing a person would do who helps us read the inscription on a commemorative medal <note>original: "gedenkpenning"</note> that is difficult to read. There are others that men could never have invented with all the ingenuity of their minds. We shall have the opportunity to speak of these things more distinctly.

<margin>Fifth proof taken from the harmony of the Holy Scripture.</margin>

V. The wonderful harmony that exists in all parts of the Scripture gives us a fifth proof; for there is nothing in it that conflicts, or that does not give us an idea of an infinite wisdom, perfectly consistent with the proportions seen in the whole. And this precise agreement is all the more wonderful because it is found between the various books of the Old and New Testament, even though those who used their pens to write them had no communication with one another and were separated by a succession of centuries. This shows that they were all inspired by one and the same spirit, and that there was a Supreme Lord above them who had the direction and oversight of all this work. It may perhaps be said that there are contradictions in these books; but it is false that there are any essential ones. They are all apparent contradictions <note>original: "schynstrydigheden"</note>; the greatest contradictions presented concern some genealogies or certain numbers, which are matters of little importance. so much certainty, that one would say, it is much more a narrative of past events, than a prediction of things to come, proceeding from a Spirit to whom all things are present, who sees all things, and reads in the darknesses of the future, because nothing happens except that which He has preordained. Many of the Early Fathers have used this proof, and among others Origen*, Lactantius*, and Tertullian*. This reasoning is within the reach of the common people; for he must be more than blind who does not see that the foretold things have come to pass.

To combat this proof, one will perhaps say that there have been some among the Heathens and the neighboring peoples of Judea who boasted of predicting future things; and that in the writings of the Heathens, certain oracles are found which, according to them, have had their fulfillment.

But I answer thereto:
1. That these same false writers teach us that there have been many false oracles. One also finds a Greek <term>Critic</term> <note>original: Opsgeer</note> named Oenomaus, who wrote against the oracles and struck them down as mere deceptions. Eusebius relates that the Heathen priests, brought to the rack, confessed that they abused the credulity of the people through their pretended oracles; whereas one could not produce a single oracle in the Books of the Old and New Testament that has been found false.

2. I further note that these imagined predictions of the Heathens were only done in secret, and in the presence of a few, and that they were most of the time so ambiguous that they could be interpreted in two completely opposite ways; whereas the Prophets of the Jewish people spoke their oracles in the most solemn assemblies, and they wrote them in books where they could be examined by the entire nation. If some have had some obscurity, there are many that were very clear.

3. Furthermore; these pretended oracles were most of the time given only for the benefit of Princes, who were prepared to give great rewards to the priests, whereas the Prophets spared the Kings no more than their subjects, and set their own interests aside.

I confess that there are some predictions

<column-break/>

that can be made by <term>demons</term> <note>original: Dæmones</note> or evil spirits, because they, through their speed and invisibility, can very quickly know far-off things, and are present at the hidden counsels of men; but there is another sort of prediction that can be attributed to none but God. Such are the predictions of distant outcomes whose preceding causes do not yet exist, and which depend on many circumstances and a sequence of things whose outcomes—if only one were arranged differently—would change the result entirely. Such are those that depend on the uncertainty of the human will, which is very free, and where a choice of things is to be made, where one reason suggests no more cause to choose than the other. Such are the predictions of things that depend on no external circumstances or natural effects, but on God's will alone.

One will perhaps say that the oracles were fabricated after the outcome; thus Porphyry asserted that the Book of Daniel was fabricated; but this <term>Enemy of Christians</term> <note>original: Christenvynd</note> has made himself ridiculous with this saying; for has the authority of the Book of Daniel ever been doubted among the Jews? When they disputed against the Christians, who pressed them with passages from this Prophet, did they ever say that one finds fabrications in it? Josephus relates that the High Priest of the Jews showed Alexander the Great the prophecies of Daniel, which promised him the imperial dominion, and that this Monarch therefore showed the Jews so much kindness. Is the Book of Daniel not translated into Greek with the other Books of the Old Testament, about 300 years before the birth of Christ? Finally, who would dare to say that Jerusalem's final destruction—which was to be carried out by the abominable eagles, that is, by the Roman armies, as Daniel predicts and Christ pointed out from Daniel—was inserted into the writings of this Prophet after the outcome.

These are the strongest proofs of the Divinity of the Holy Scriptures. The <term>Free-thinkers</term> <note>original: Vrygeesten</note>, who bring forth everything that can weaken these proofs, gather all the passages that seem unseemly to Divine Wisdom, such as Exod. XXI. 7, Deut. XXII. 13, XXIII. 19, Exod. XXXII. 23, Ruth II. 20, III. 9, 2 Sam. XII. 8, Hosea I, etc.

I further note / that these supposed predictions of the Heathens were only done in secret / and in the presence of few / and that most of the time they were so ambiguous / that they could be interpreted in two completely opposite ways; whereas the Prophets of the Jewish people spoke their Oracles in the most solemn assemblies / and they wrote them in Books / where they could be verified by the whole people. If some [prophecies] had any obscurity / there are many that were very clear.

3. Furthermore; these pretended Oracles were most of the time only given for the benefit of the Princes / who could give great rewards to the Priests / whereas the Prophets spared the Kings no more than their subjects / and set their own interests aside.

I admit that there are some predictions

<column-break/>

that can be done by *Demons* <note>original: "Dæmones"</note> or evil Spirits / because / through their speed and invisibility / they can very quickly know far-off things / and be present at the hidden councils of men; but there is another kind of prediction / that one can only attribute to God. Such are the predictions of remote outcomes / whose preceding causes do not yet exist and which depend on many circumstances / and a sequence of things / whose outcomes / if only one thing were arranged differently / would change the entire result. Such are those / which depend on the uncertainty of the human will / which is very free / and where a choice of things is to be made / where one [choice] whispers no more reason to choose than the other. Such are the predictions of things / which depend on no external circumstances or natural effects / but on God's will alone.

One will possibly say / that the Oracles were invented after the outcome; thus *Porphyry* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and prominent early critic of Christianity</note> claimed / that the Book of *Daniel* was a fiction / but this enemy of Christians made himself ridiculous with this statement; for has the authority of the Book of *Daniel* ever been doubted among the Jews? When they argued against the Christians / who pressed them with passages from this Prophet / did they ever say that one finds fictions in it? *Josephus* relates / that the High Priest of the Jews showed *Alexander the Great* the prophecies of *Daniel*, which promised him the imperial dominion / and that this Monarch therefore showed the Jews so much courtesy. Was the Book of *Daniel* not translated into Greek with the other Books of the Old Testament / around 300 years before the Birth of Christ? Finally, who would dare to say / that the final destruction of *Jerusalem* / which was to be carried out by the abominable Eagles / that is, by the Roman armies / as *Daniel* foretells / and Christ pointed out from *Daniel* / was inserted into the writings of this Prophet after the outcome.

These are the strongest proofs of the Divinity of the Holy Scriptures. The *Freethinkers* <note>original: "Vrygeesten"</note> / who bring forward everything that can weaken these proofs / gather all the passages / which seem unbefitting of Divine Wisdom / together / such as *Exodus 21:7*, *Deuteronomy 22:13*, *23:19*, *Exodus 32:23*, *Ruth 2:20*, *3:9*, *2 Samuel 12:8*, *Hosea 1*, etc.

# THE CHRISTIAN [RELIGION]

# THE CHRISTIAN

...[authority] the people took or forced through punishments; they were not conquerors who made the world tremble at the sound of their name; no scholars who carried away their listeners through their eloquence or shrewdness. They were poor fishermen, without esteem, without science, eloquence, or friends; without weapons; earthen vessels <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 4:7, "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us."</note>, but in which God had placed his treasures. Can it be that one does not recognize that God worked through their sermons, and that the word they proclaimed was Divine, since it was received so greedily despite the despised appearance of those who proclaimed it? Mahomet <note>A common historical Western spelling for the Prophet Muhammad.</note> introduced his teaching through force and violence; the fear one had for his weapons made everyone bow before him: but the Disciples of the Lord Jesus did nothing but speak. How did it happen that their word converted more people than Mahomet was able to subdue through his armies? No other reason can be given for this than that this Word is the power of God and the scepter of his strength. Mahomet satisfied almost all inclinations of corrupt nature, proposing a fleshly happiness and forbidding the investigation of religion. It is not strange that human causes produce human effects. But the Christian Religion was introduced without human help and power, among enemies, eager and armed to destroy it; it grew up under the suffering and death of those who proclaimed it; it combats natural inclinations and promises no state of happiness until after this life.

3. One will be strengthened in these same thoughts if one considers who they are to whom this word is proclaimed, and what this word teaches. They were people full of prejudices for the religion in which they were born, and who seemed quite healthy in these prejudices. The word proclaimed to them does not flatter their passions; those who proclaim it do not seek to exalt themselves, nor to make themselves valued through healthy rules and feelings that stroke the habit or inclination of the heart; they promise no fleshly pleasures in this life to those who will believe their word; on the contrary, they prepare them for a thousand cruelties and punishments, and they make it known that the founder of their religion was nailed to the Cross between two murderers. How can it be that such a hard word makes such sudden and so great impressions in such prejudiced

<column-break/>

and corrupted minds? Certainly, one must want to be blind not to recognize God's power here; who accompanied his word with the effectiveness of his grace.

<margin>On the preservation of the Holy Books.</margin>
II. The second proof that we can still bring forward for the Divinity of the Books of the Old and New Testament is that they are miraculously preserved, although nothing has been neglected to suppress them. For how does it happen that the Books of the wise men of the Chaldeans, Egyptians, Arabs, and Phoenicians, which handled the mysteries of the Pagan religions, and the Books of the Sibyls <note>The Sibylline Books were a collection of oracular utterances purchased by the last king of Rome; most were lost or destroyed in antiquity.</note> no longer exist, although nothing was done to destroy the memory of them; and that the Books of Scripture exist, although Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, a Hellenistic king who attempted to suppress Jewish customs and burn the Torah.</note> and many Pagan Emperors have done everything in their power to have all the writings of it burned? Where does it come from that the old histories of the mighty world-empires have been lost, and the History of a small people, as the Jewish people were, has been preserved? Let one torment oneself seeking the reason for such a miraculous preservation; one will find none that is completely satisfactory, unless one recognizes that the books which have been preserved with so much care were Divine; and that Providence watched over them in a special way to prevent them from being destroyed.

<margin>On the miracles.</margin>
III. The third proof is taken from the miracles by which those who have proclaimed the Teaching of Holy Scripture confirmed their speeches. These miracles were seen by an innumerable multitude. The Enemies of Christianity have not been able to deny them. The Jews only say that Jesus Christ performed the miracles by the pronunciation of the name Jehovah <note>This refers to the *Shem HaMephorash*; certain Jewish polemical traditions claimed Jesus learned the secret name of God to perform magic.</note>. Julian the Apostate <note>The Roman Emperor Julian (r. 361–363), who converted from Christianity back to Paganism and wrote against the church.</note> admits that Christ healed the blind and the lame, and cast out demons; how can God have performed so many wonders to maintain a false doctrine?

One cannot deny that there are miracles: just as one cannot doubt that God has established an order according to which all things work, so one can also not doubt that he can bend the order of these secondary causes according to his will.

### THEOLOGY. Book I. Chapter XV.

...one would also have to say that things happen that are beyond the power of God.

But it is false that the power of God and the power of what one calls *Nature* are the same power. <note>The author is refuting a pantheistic or naturalist view where God and nature are indistinguishable, likely targeting the ideas of Spinoza or similar rationalists.</note>

It is said that, since miracles are works performed beyond our understanding, one can prove nothing through them; because we can draw no clear conclusion from that which we do not understand.

I answered that it is false that we could conclude nothing clearly from a work that is beyond the reach of our intellect; one can always clearly conclude from it that the cause of the work exceeds our reach.

<margin>
Concerning the miracles in which the Pagans took pride.
</margin>
Someone will perhaps object that this proof is very weak, because the Pagans took pride in miracles performed by the servants of their false Gods: And they have spoken strongly of the pretended miracles of their **Apollonius** of **Tyana**. <note>Apollonius of Tyana (1st century AD) was a Neopythagorean philosopher whose life was often compared to that of Jesus by pagan critics of Christianity.</note> But there is much to be said about that.

1. That there is no comparison between the miracles in which the Pagans took pride and those that **Jesus Christ** and the **Apostles** performed.

2. That most of these imagined miracles were recognized as false even by the Pagans themselves, who openly mocked them.

3. Those who took pride in performing miracles did them in secret, and would not have dared to do them before intelligent people; this was never said of the **Apostles**, who never hid themselves when they performed any miraculous deed.

From this it clearly appears that there is no ground to oppose true miracles with false ones, which even the Pagans themselves sharply joked about and mocked.

<margin>
The History of Apollonius convicted of falsehood. Paris 1705. Chrysostom’s Discourse against the Jews. Augustine, Letters 101 and 138.
</margin>
Regarding **Apollonius** of **Tyana**, it has been very well noted: 1. That many, while he was still alive, opposed him as a deceiver; this was done by a **Corinthian** philosopher named **Bassus**, and the philosopher **Euphrates**. 2. That the wisest men subsequently regarded him in the same way, such as **Lucian** among the Pagans, and among the Christians, **Chrysostom**, **Augustine**, **Photius**, etc. 3. That the wisest among the Pagans noted against the reliable writers that the book of **Philostratus**, which speaks of this **Apollonius**, was full of fictions—something **Photius** had already recognized. One can see

what **Luis Vives**, **Joseph Scaliger**, **Vossius**, and **Casaubon**, **Baronius**, **Le Sueur**, **Godeau**, and **Fleury** say about it.

4. A **New Writer**, who conceals his name, clearly proves in a book he has composed on this subject: 1. That the story of **Apollonius** is devoid of credible witnesses; for **Philostratus** did not write it until more than 120 years after the death of **Apollonius**; it is true, he says he wrote it according to the memoirs of **Daniel** <note>original: "Daniel" — The author likely means Damis (Δάμις), the companion of Apollonius, whose memoirs Philostratus claimed to use. "Daniel" is likely a transcription error or a localized variant in the source text.</note>, companion of **Apollonius**, but who knows if **Philostratus** does not falsely claim this? How is it that **Daniel**, during his life, had not made public his memoirs about such wonderful occurrences? Furthermore, **Philostratus** says that the memoirs of **Daniel** were not written with enough skill. 2. That **Philostratus** wrote only a fiction, as he proves from what is said of the God **Proteus**, who appeared to the mother of **Apollonius**; from the childbirth of this woman; from what **Apollonius** says to the Governor of **Babylon**, and from many other tales that are clearly trifling. 3. That the miracles attributed to **Apollonius** bear visible signs of falsehood, and that there is not one that cannot be attributed to chance or deceit. 4. Finally, that the teaching of **Apollonius** in many things conflicts with reason and understanding.

One will perhaps still say that miracles are no proof of the truth of a doctrine, and that this appears from the Books currently under dispute <note>The Bible.</note>, in which one finds that many false teachers were to arise who would perform miracles.

To that I answer, that one must not judge the truth of a doctrine solely by the miracles that the spirits proclaiming them might do, or which one would believe they did; but that miracles powerfully confirm a doctrine that gives a thousand proofs of truth. God would not tolerate that one give ear to a man who advised serving false gods, even if he did many signs. But He wanted one to recognize as a true Prophet one who taught a good doctrine and confirmed it through miracles.

### IV. *The fourth proof is taken from the great number of Martyrs who have sealed the Doctrine contained in these Books with their own blood: for just as nothing is more precious to humans than life, so it is unthinkable that so many people would have wanted to waste it without having had great reason.*

But, to give this proof more weight, one must observe:

<margin>
*Concerning the Martyrs of false Religions.*

1. ***That these Books have had an innumerable multitude of Blood-witnesses.*** <note>original: "Bloedgetuigen." A literal translation of the Greek "martys," meaning witness.</note>

There have been some deluded spirits who wanted to die to maintain their errors. There have even been those foolish enough to defend atheism <note>original: "ongodistery"</note> in the midst of the flames; but one has never seen so many people die for a doctrine as one has seen *Christians* die. One will possibly say that many despise death for worldly considerations, as one daily sees people who boldly storm [the enemy] and without hesitation place themselves at the front. But it has been very well said that in these cases death appears as if covered with a veil, so that one does not see him in all his terrors; if one goes to battle with the fear of falling, it is also in the hope of returning victorious or coming away fortunately. Furthermore, the variety of objects and the heat of the battle distract the spirit in the middle of the fight and prevent one from attentively contemplating death. It is not so with a person who dies for a Doctrine; he sees death revealed,

<column-break/>

he contemplates it with cold blood; so that there must be something extraordinary that triumphs in him over the prevailing *Passion* that one has for living.

2. ***One must observe that these Blood-witnesses were of all ages, status, and gender.*** It can happen that people whose courage has been hardened by *Philosophical* observations against the terrors of death die steadfastly for a Doctrine which they defend; but the *Christian* Religion has had all kinds of *Martyrs*; there have even been *Women* and *Children* who suffered unheard-of pains, such as the famous *Blandina* and the young *Prodicus*. <note>Blandina was a famous 2nd-century martyr in Lyon who endured extreme torture; 'Prodikus' likely refers to a youth from early accounts of Christian martyrdom.</note>

3. ***One must observe that these Martyrs were not insane:*** for all their conduct was wise, and they suffered, not murmuring, but with joy; not cursing their executioners, but blessing them; not complaining about *Providence*, but praising *God* and glorifying his name that he had called them to suffer for the *Truth*. They died with a wonderful tranquility, unspeakable joy, extraordinary steadfastness, and with a becoming gentleness that amazed all who saw them; their persecutors were astonished by it, and many were so touched that without other proof they recognized the truth of the *Christian Religion* and converted.

# THEOLOGY. BOOK I. CHAPTER XV.

...not to be made of blood; but they preferred to die for Christ, rather than to live by forsaking Him.

Did they suffer out of a principle of vain glory, to be esteemed in the world? But if they had only thought of that, they would have sought to obtain it in another way that would have been less miserable for them, and there would not have been such a great number of them. Is it through a heavy melancholy? But nothing of the kind was noticed in them. Is it through rage, like that of barbaric peoples, who leap from the tops of idols at the sound of musical instruments? <note>The author likely refers to reports of ritual suicides in pagan cultures, contrasted here with the calm demeanor of Christians.</note> But in all their conduct they show a gentle and reasonable spirit. Is it through a strong stubbornness? But they showed themselves to be teachable, and listened attentively to everything presented to them. What then made them so courageous and steadfast, or from where came this joy, which they displayed in the midst of the greatest pains? Certainly one cannot consider the death of so many Christians, the drive of their zeal, the strength of their faith, their rare steadfastness, incomprehensible patience, and the excellent tranquility of their souls, without recognizing that the Lord—who moved them to suffer so much, who produced in them these beautiful and great movements and these virtues, at which even the executioners stood amazed—was necessarily supernatural and Divine.

<margin>
Of the style of the Holy Scripture.
</margin>

V. I draw a fifth proof from the **style** in which these books are written; and this proof is not entirely to be despised.

One sees no adorned affectation in it; one does not notice that the writers of these books are boastful, seeking to display intellect and learning, or that they wish to give greater thoughts of what they do than one ought to have; like Alexander, who, traveling through certain lands, had shields and weapons of excessive size made, so that those who passed by would believe that his soldiers were so many giants. The style of these books is **powerful**, but **simple**; **dignified**, but suited to the reach of men; **clear** in the things that one must necessarily know; **pure** and corresponding with the matters that are treated therein.

It has indeed been said that the Scripture strikes us with wonder through the sublime manner in which it expresses Divine matters; that it induces terror through the vehemence and power of its ex-

<column-break/>

pressions; that it arouses love for virtue and hatred against sin through the vivid imagery it creates of both; that it amazes by the power of its threats; lifts the courage by the sweetness of its comforts; and ignites flames of love by the Divine fire with which it is filled.

If one finds histories in these books, they are written in a simple style, but one which nonetheless has a great majesty; therefore the famous Longinus, <note>Longinus (c. 213–273 AD) was a Greek philosopher and rhetorician. In his work *On the Sublime*, he famously praised the writing of Moses in Genesis as a masterpiece of the "sublime" style.</note> although a pagan, draws examples of true sublimity of oratory from the Books of Moses. If the Greek or Latin historians had had to write of the Incarnation of Christ, His Death, Resurrection, and Ascension, they would have piled up elegant figures of speech to express what the Apostles tell us in two words.

If one finds in these books prophecies of future things: they are described in words corresponding to the excellence of the predicted matters.

Are there threats in it? They are presented in such a way that it appears that the words they use are far below the misfortunes they cause one to fear; and if one finds promises there, one sees that many more things are hidden from us than shown, in order to awaken in us the desire to enjoy them. Majesty is everywhere joined with a noble simplicity.

<margin>
Objections against the manner of writing of the Holy Scripture.
</margin>

Those who do not have much esteem for the Holy Books condemn the style in which they are written; but it is not difficult to refute them. There are those to whom the style of the Holy Scripture is displeasing because they wish the Prophets and writers—who wrote long ago—to write like modern authors, <note>original: "nu schryft"</note> not noticing the distinction between the Hebrew, Syriac, Greek, and our own language; and that every language has its own idioms. There are those who find this style obscure in many places because they do not know what God’s Spirit aims at, not understanding that what now seems obscure to them was very clear to those who lived in the time of the Apostles or Prophets; or perhaps not noting that it was fitting for there to be some obscurity in some places of the Scripture, as we shall show elsewhere. There are those who find that the style sometimes seems "creeping" <note>The "creeping" or "low" style (*kruipende styl*) refers to a plain, unadorned way of writing that lacks the high rhetorical flourishes expected by classical scholars.</note>; but they judge thus either because...

# THE CHRISTIAN

That most people confuse a simple style with a lowly one; either because they do not notice that the expressions, which now seem very lowly, were formerly used by everyone—especially among the Eastern Peoples. Beyond that, it is certain that there is much eloquence in the Song of Moses, in the Book of Job, in the Psalms, the Prophecies of Isaiah, the Lamentations of Jeremiah, the Hymn of Mary and of Zechariah, in the speech of Paul in the midst of the marketplaces <note>The author refers to Paul's speech at the Areopagus in Athens.</note>, and in his excellent Letters. There are those who do not find the matters handled in the same order as they wish, wanting to subject God’s Spirit to the methods of the writers of this Age—which is altogether ridiculous—and not noticing that the Holy Spirit had reason to act so, as those recognize who read the Scripture attentively. There are those who reject the way of writing of the Apostles and Prophets because they do not see the cohesion that exists in the matters they write, or because they do not feel the power of their reasoning. One finds arguments in the writings of Paul that do not convince the Jews now, but which were without excuse <note>Meaning "irrefutable."</note> in respect to the Jews who lived in the time of this Apostle, because he fought them through their own principles and sentiments. There are those who wish to claim that there are many superfluous things in the Scripture, which seems to them to be a great defect. But these people do not notice that there are things which may indeed seem useless to them, but which were not so when they were written: just as there are things that appeared superfluous to those who lived in the time of Moses and the Prophets, the usefulness of which we now recognize. It is said that there are many repetitions in it, and that is true; but it is certain that these repetitions are not as useless as they first appear to us, of which one will be convinced if one pays attention to them. God’s Spirit willed that many writers should say the same thing, so that one would not doubt it; and it happens sometimes that He, repeating the same truths, spreads a new light over them. I end this Article with the words of Origen, who says,

To all these proofs that I have brought forward, one can add the testimony that the Enemies of the truth have given to these books of the Old and New Testament, and the high regard they had for many of the doctrines contained within them.

<margin>The testimony of the Heathens.</margin>
Alexander Severus <note>A Roman Emperor (reigned 222–235 AD) known for his religious tolerance.</note> had a great respect for our Lord Christ, and had some sayings from the Gospel written in public buildings and in his Palace. One even saw there a kind of Chapel where he offered sacrifices in the morning. He had the images of Jesus Christ and of Abraham. He had another Chapel where the image of Christ was placed in the first rank. <margin>original: "περὶ τῆς ἐκ λογίων φιλοσοφίας" <note>Porphyry, *On Philosophy from Oracles*.</note></margin> Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and frequent critic of Christianity.</note> relates the Oracle of the Goddess Hecate, who speaks of Christ as a man renowned for his Piety, whose body was given over to pains, but whose Soul is in Heaven with the Souls of the Blessed. This same Porphyry, according to Eusebius <note>*Demonstratio Evangelica*, Book 3.</note>, says that one must be careful not to offend Jesus, although one should have pity on those who serve him. <margin>original: "πρὸς ἔθνη l. 3." <note>Tertullian, *Ad Nationes* (To the Nations), Book 3.</note></margin> Tertullian says in his defense that Tiberius, upon the reports that came to him from Judea, proposed to the Council to grant Divine honors to Jesus Christ; to say nothing of what Lampridius <note>One of the supposed authors of the *Augustan History*.</note> teaches us, namely, that Hadrian had erected Temples for Christ, which were still seen in the time in which he wrote. All this shows that the Heathens had a high regard for the Christian Religion, for its founder, and its doctrine, although they did not have the strength to embrace it.

When I consider all these proofs together, I confess that I cannot refrain from recognizing that these Books are Divine, especially after having noted that one cannot find all these qualities together in any human Book; this now is what I had set out to prove.

THEOLOGY. Book I. Chapter XVI. Page 77

# CHAPTER XVI.

->On the Inspiration of the Holy Books.<-

Having established the Divinity of the Books of the Old and New Testament, it is not necessary to linger long on proving that they are inspired by God; the matter speaks for itself, and Paul teaches us in 2 Timothy 3:16 that all Scripture is inspired by God <note>The Greek term used by Paul is *theopneustos*, meaning "God-breathed."</note>.

To be convinced of this, one must make several observations.

1. It is certain that one finds in these books infinite Prophecies, which mere men—as the Prophets and Apostles were—could not have invented, and which consequently must have been inspired in them.

2. It is also certain that one finds in these books many histories that would never have been known if He who knows all that happens in the World, and from whom the most hidden thoughts are not concealed, had not revealed them to those who wrote them.

3. One cannot deny that there are in these Writings such excellent and such great truths that they would never have entered into the human understanding, and they carry away those who read them in wonder. What likelihood is there that such exalted truths were invented by poor Fishermen, as most of the Apostles were? Where had these Galileans <note>Galilee was a provincial region; its inhabitants were often dismissed by the elite in Jerusalem as unlearned or rustic.</note> learned the art of writing so well?

4. It appears that these books were written to serve as a Rule for all that we must believe and do, in all times, and to show men the true way of Salvation <term>Zaligheid: a state of eternal happiness and deliverance from sin</term>. But how could they serve as a Rule if they were written without inspiration, or the special guidance of God’s Spirit? What certainty would we have that the Writers had not been deceived?

If these books had not been inspired, the believers in the time of the Apostles could have asked the first Disciples of the Lord Jesus and obtained certain reports of the truth of all that these books contained. But how would Christians, after the death of the Apostles, have been able to know for certain what they had to do, or believe,

<column-break/>

if the books left to them to guide their faith or morals were of no Divine inspiration? One might say it is enough to know that the Writers faithfully recounted what they had learned from our Lord Christ; but how shall one know that, if one is not assured that they were led by God’s Spirit?

5. It is beyond doubt that Jesus Christ, who is the truth itself, promised His Disciples to lead them into all truth through His Spirit, and that He, through this Spirit, would teach them all things and bring to mind all that He had said to them. One only has to read the following passages: John 14:26 and 16:13. Would one dare to say that Christ—the Amen <note>A title for Christ from Revelation 3:14, meaning "the faithful and true."</note>, the Truthful, and whose words are more firm than Heaven and Earth—has not fulfilled His promises?

Jesus Christ fulfilled His other promises made to His Disciples; why would He not have kept this one, which He repeated to them so often, to lead them into all truth?

It is true, then, that the Apostles were led by God’s Spirit when they preached the Gospel, when they wrote it, when they defended themselves before the Authorities, and when they were questioned about matters concerning Religion; and that in all this they acted under the governance of God’s Spirit. Certainly, if the promise of the Savior of the world had to be fulfilled, it was without doubt when the Apostles wrote these books which they have left to us, and which God has so wonderfully preserved to set our faith and conduct by.

6. The Apostles, whom one would not dare to accuse of being deceivers, testify in many places that they are moved by God’s Spirit. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 2:12-13: *Now we have received, not the spirit of the world, but the spirit which is of God; that we might know the things that are freely given to us of God. Which things also we speak, not in the words which man's wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth; comparing spiritual things with spiritual.*

And, after having said in the same Chapter, verse 16: *For who hath known the mind of the Lord, that he may instruct him?* he adds, *But we have the mind of Christ.*

CHRISTIAN [THEOLOGY]

<margin>1 Corinthians 7:40</margin> After having spoken of various things concerning Marriage, he says: *And I think also that I have the Spirit of God.*

One must note here that he maintains this same discourse in the same Chapter, after having said in verse 10: *But to the married I command, yet not I, but the Lord, Let not the wife depart from her husband,* etc. He adds in verse 12: *But to the rest speak I, not the Lord,* so that no one might object to him: "Do you want us to believe a teaching that you have not received from the Lord?" He answers that Christ had indeed not instructed him on the matter he was discussing while He was on Earth before His Ascension; but that, meanwhile, he said nothing that was not given to him by God's Spirit, by which he was led.

<margin>1 Corinthians 14:37</margin> Paul submits himself to the examination of the Prophets and of all who had received the gift of God to discern spirits. *If any man think himself to be a prophet, or spiritual, let him acknowledge that the things that I write unto you are the commandments of the Lord.*

<margin>1 Thessalonians 2:13</margin> He expresses himself in this way: *For this cause also thank we God without ceasing, because, when ye received the word of God which ye heard of us, ye received it not as the word of men, but as it is in truth, the word of God,* &c.

<margin>1 Thessalonians 4:8</margin> He says: *He therefore that despiseth, despiseth not man, but God, who hath also given unto us his holy Spirit.*

But, in order not to be deceived in the matter of the inspiration of the Holy Books, it is appropriate to make a few more observations.

<margin>Whether God's Spirit inspired all the words?</margin>
I. It is not necessary to suppose that God's Spirit always dictated all the words to the Prophets and Apostles which they used, or taught them everything they wrote. It is enough that they wrote nothing except through the immediate guidance of God's Spirit, in such a way that this Spirit never allowed them to err in what they wrote. Agobardus <note>Agobard of Lyon (c. 779–840) was an archbishop known for his critical thinking and opposition to certain superstitions in the early medieval church.</note>, a writer in the 9th Century, says in his answer to Fredegisus: *it is an absurdity to believe that the Holy Spirit inspired the [specific] words and idioms.* It has been very well said: "The Apostles were the instruments of the Holy Spirit"; but

<column-break/>

rational instruments, who used their understanding, judgment, and own language, in such a way that, in the use of their understanding, they were governed by God's Spirit, who did not take away the power to reason <margin>Witsius's *Sacred Miscellanies* <note>Original: "Witsii misc: Sacra." Referring to Herman Witsius (1636–1708), a prominent Dutch theologian of the Further Reformation.</note></margin> which they naturally possessed, but clarified it through His illumination and governed it through His hidden power.

<margin>Objections against the inspiration of the Holy Books.</margin>
II. One cannot deny that the Holy Spirit inspired infinite things which the Holy Writers wrote, such as the Prophecies spread throughout their writings, along with the explanation of these Prophecies, of the Ancient matters of God, and of all the types <note>In theology, a "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament seen as a symbolic foreshadowing of something in the New Testament.</note> of the Old Covenant. Paul teaches us in 1 Timothy 4:1 that *the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith.* The old Prophets said, *the mouth of the Lord hath spoken,* etc.

Those who deny the inspiration of the Books of the New Testament cite as proof that the Apostles do not say, as the Prophets did, "the mouth of the Lord has spoken." But this reasoning is very weak. 1. The Prophets did very well to report that the Lord spoke through their mouths because it was known that they did not always enjoy this advantage; but one was assured that the Holy Spirit always led the Apostles into all truth. 2. The Prophets did not always begin their writings with these words, "the mouth of the Lord has spoken." One only has to read the five books of Moses. 3. When the Apostles predict something, they also say, *the Spirit of the Lord has said it,* 1 Timothy 4:1. To say nothing of what is in the Revelation.

Meanwhile, one must also admit that the Men of God wrote many things that it was not necessary for the Holy Spirit to inspire in them; such as what they had seen, heard, and what concerned their private affairs. One must never invoke miracles without necessity. Why then suppose that God inspired in the Prophets and Apostles that which they already knew?

III. Meanwhile, although all that they wrote was not inspired [word-for-word] into them, they nevertheless wrote nothing without the governance of God's Spirit, so that they wrote nothing except what was very fitting and within the precise rules of truth. It was God's Spirit who drove them to write, who strengthened their memory, who governed their choice of things,

# DIVINE THEOLOGY. BOOK I. CHAPTER XVI.

...which were to come into their work, as the supreme governor suggested; who often made them choose and use one expression over another, because it better conveyed what He wished to say. Finally, it was the Spirit who prevented them from falling into error, even regarding the smallest matters.

<margin>2 Timothy 4:13</margin>
**IV.** After what has been said, one should not be surprised: 1. If the Apostles sometimes speak of things concerning their own affairs, such as when Paul commands that his cloak and parchments be brought to him; 2. If they draw conclusions from the truths that were inspired in them, from the visions they had seen, and from the things they had learned through their senses in another way—as when Peter, comparing the vision of the linen sheet he had received with what 
<margin>Acts 10:34</margin>
Cornelius had seen, says, *Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons.* 3. If they use modes of speech taken from the customs of the nations among whom they lived, and even use common proverbs of their time; 4. Finally, if one notices a modest style in the Holy Books, all this is easily understood as soon as one assumes that the Holy Spirit left to God’s servants the use of their reason and the language of their country.

**V.** But one must always keep in mind what I have established previously. 1. That God’s Spirit inspired in them most of the things they wrote. 2. That He pre-ordained everything they wrote, so that they were infallible in all their writings. One also sees that these Holy Writers agree wonderfully, although they write in different ways, because the same Spirit animated them, as I have shown elsewhere.

<margin>
The Apostles were not without sins and weaknesses.
</margin>
**VI.** One must well observe that I have said the Apostles were only infallible in their doctrine and writings; for in other matters, they were not without sins and weaknesses. It was not necessary that the Holy Men who wrote the Holy Books be perfect, holy, and without flaws; but it was absolutely necessary that they were infallible in their teaching, because God used their ministry to arrange the faith and the morals of the nations. It is therefore not strange that Peter does something 
<margin>Galatians 2:2</margin>
that deserved Paul’s rebuke for breaking off fellowship with the Gentiles 

<column-break/>

by being too compliant toward the Jews.

Before I end this Chapter, I have two more observations to make, which will serve to resolve two difficulties.

The 1st is that the Holy Spirit, who led the Apostles into all truth, did not teach them everything at once, but daily increased their knowledge as they needed it for the building up of the Church. One should then not be too surprised by anything in which it appears that Peter was ignorant of the calling of the Gentiles before the baptism of Cornelius.

The 2nd observation is that the Holy Spirit only revealed to the Holy Writers what they needed to know to instruct others, so that it is not surprising that they sometimes speak tentatively: *I will perhaps stay with you,* says Paul in 1 Corinthians 16:6; and instead of an exact time, they say *about this time*, *about six hours*, *about thirty years*.

# THE CHRISTIAN [THEOLOGY]

<margin>
Objections against the inspiration of the Holy Books
</margin>

...that there are Books in Scripture where the name of God is not even found, such as in the *Song of Songs* and in the Book of *Esther*; but this reasoning proves nothing.

1. Because it is not necessary for God’s name to be present in a Book inspired by God.

2. With regard to the *Song of Songs*, where everything is described in figurative language and Jesus Christ is shown under the symbol of a Bridegroom, it is no wonder that the name of God is not in it. There is more reason for wonder regarding the Book of *Esther*: But there are many things that convince me that this Book was regarded as divine by the Jews, and not without great reason; it is not likely that the Jews would have accepted it as canonical <note>The original Dutch uses "regelmatig," referring to the "rule" or "canon" of accepted scripture.</note> if they had not known for certain that it was written by a Prophet, as they were so sensitive about these matters. And if someone had composed it without inspiration in order to place it among the number of the Canonical Books, he would undoubtedly have spoken of God often, so that people would be more inclined to recognize his book as divine. If I am asked why God's Name is not in it? I confess that I know nothing of it; for the reasons that are brought forward are not satisfying.

II. One will say: if the Holy Spirit had inspired the Apostles in what they wrote, they would have spoken in a different manner. But this objection only affects those who insist that the Holy Spirit dictated every single word. And besides, who does not know that God, to help our weakness, sometimes speaks the language of men?

III. It is objected that it was not necessary for God to inspire things concerning natural truths, because the purpose of Scripture is to instruct us in religion. But I deny that this was not necessary; for it would not have been fitting for God's Spirit to mix falsehoods among truths; the unbelievers would have taken the opportunity from that to doubt everything.

IV. It is said that the Apostles often contradict one another: But this is false; it is easy to reconcile the alleged contradictions that one thinks to find in the books of the Disciples of the Lord Jesus.

V. It is said that the early Church seemed to show more honor to the Gospels

<column-break/>

than to the Epistles: For, it is said, one heard the reading of the Gospels while standing, whereas everyone could sit during the reading of the Epistles; it is added that this distinction would not have been made if it had been believed that the Epistles were inspired just as the Gospels were. But one cannot draw this conclusion from that, since it is certain that the Christians regarded the Epistles as inspired. Of the custom of hearing them read while sitting—the institution of which some have attributed to *Anastasius* <note>Pope Anastasius I, who died in 401 AD.</note>, who died at the beginning of the fifth Century, others to *Siricius*, who passed away in the year 398—I shall say nothing. It seems that the Christians wanted to imitate the Jews, who felt they should show more honor to the Law than to the Prophets, although they did not doubt the inspiration of the Prophets.

VI. It is said that there is not much appearance that *Paul* spoke by inspiration when he treated the High Priest so poorly in *Acts 23:3*. Someone might counter that the Apostles were not infallible in all their speeches, but only in their writings. However, Christ having promised his Disciples in *Matthew 10:19, 20* that He would inspire them with what they had to say,

# CHAPTER XVII.

->In which it is proven that the assistance of God’s Spirit is necessary to well convince us of the Divinity of the Books of the Old and New Testaments.<-

**I**t appears, from what was said in the previous Chapter, that the Books of the Old and New Testaments have many characteristics by which they prove their Divinity.

If sin had not come into the world; if our understanding were not naturally full of prejudices; and our heart enslaved to a thousand irregularities, one would be convinced of the Divinity of Holy Scripture as soon as one read it. If our Spiritual Eye—by which I mean our understanding—were as clear and well-ordered as when God created our first ancestors, it would be enough to present the Holy Books to us to immediately see their beauty: but sin has darkened our eyes and <margin>Part I.</margin>

<column-break/>

made them malicious; the eye of the inner man must then be healed so that it may behold its Sun, as Augustine says, but this cannot happen except through the Holy Spirit. <margin>Augustine</margin>

The necessity of the working <margin>Letter against the Manichaeans, ch. 2 <note original="Epist: contra Manich: c: 2.">A reference to St. Augustine’s writings against the Manichaean heresy.</note></margin> of this Spirit will not be called into doubt when one considers the extreme corruption of the human heart. Certainly, <margin>Certainly</margin> if there were so many who—when Christ was on earth and this Sun of Righteousness spread his light on all sides and performed wonders that had never been seen—nevertheless rejected him as a deceiver, mocked his miracles, and preferred their darkness to his light because their works were evil; how would it be possible that worldly men, without the grace of the Holy Spirit, should receive as Divine those Books in which so many things run contrary to their prejudices and passions, and in which nearly all their deeds are condemned? It is for this reason that David prayed to God, *Open my eyes, that I may see the wonders of your Law.* So too, no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. <margin>Psalm 119:18; Ephesians 1:17, 18. * 1 Corinthians 2:11.</margin>

If one does not establish this principle, namely that the assistance of the Holy Spirit is necessary <margin>1 Corinthians 12:3; 1 John 2:20.</margin> to convince us of the Divinity of Scripture, one would be unable to give a reason why so many, to whom all the proofs of the Divinity of these Books are shown, remain unbelieving in this regard, even though they otherwise have much spirit and insight <note>The original "doorzingendheid" is a likely variant or OCR error for "doordringendheid," meaning intellectual depth or penetration.</note> in the sciences; <margin>Divinity of Holy Scripture.</margin> while others, who have no more spirit or insight, are so convinced of it that they would rather die a thousand times than forsake the doctrine contained in these books. This is the reason why the simple and unlearned are generally more convinced of the Divinity of Holy Scripture than the Learned: because it pleases the Heavenly Father to make his mysteries known to the one and hide them from the others.

To these are added two other reasons. The 1st is the strong impression that the objections and difficulties brought against Scripture make on the minds of those who are sharp enough to understand the problem, but not enough to grasp the solution; whereas the minds of the simple, which do not rise to these objections, cling more strongly to the contemplation of truth. ### XVIII. CHAPTER.

->Concerning the authority of the Holy Scripture, and from whence it derives its authority.<-

<margin>What one understands by the word "authority."</margin>
**A**fter having proven the Divinity of the Holy Scripture, it is easy to demonstrate its authority. One will not doubt this if one considers what this word "authority" signifies. By this word, one understands nothing other than the right that the Holy Books have to obligate all people to believe that which they teach us, and to obey all the commandments that are given to us therein; and this right is grounded upon the excellence and dignity of these Books. As soon as it has been proven that the Books of the Old and New Testament have their inspiration from God, it clearly follows that they must have great weight and authority in our regard; for who can refuse to believe God’s Word and to obey Him from the moment he is convinced that it is truly God’s Word?

The Scripture, then, needs to derive its authority from nowhere else but God, who is its author; and when it testifies of itself, one cannot say that its testimony is not credible: for, just as Jesus Christ answered those who challenged him by saying that his testimony was credible because his works

<column-break/>

clearly demonstrated that he had come from Heaven and the Father was with him, so we can say that the loftiness of the mysteries contained in the Scripture, the holiness of the Commandments, the attractiveness of the promises—in short, this fullness by which it meets all needs (of which all men are fully convinced) and the extraordinary effects it produces to sanctify and comfort people—are marks that show it has come down from Heaven, from the Father of Lights.

<margin>Why one believes the Scripture is Divine.</margin>
So, if one asks why I believe the Scripture is Divine? I answer: it is because of the marks of Divinity which the Holy Spirit—who enlightens my understanding—causes me to observe in this Scripture, such as the greatness of the mysteries, the holiness of the Moral Law, the Prophecies of the Old Testament fulfilled under the new dispensation; the agreement between the truths it teaches and the light of conscience; the wonderful harmony between the revealed law and the natural and innate law. I answer, it is because it feeds, enlightens, and comforts my soul, fills it with an unspeakable and glorious joy, allows me to taste infinite sweetness, and causes me to experience other things of which I have already spoken in the preceding Chapters; in the same way as if one asked me why I believe the Sun is light, Honey is sweet, and the Rose has a pleasant scent. I would answer that I believe it because I see the rays of the Sun, I taste the sweetness of the Honey, and the scent of the Roses affects me pleasantly. These comparisons seem to me most appropriate because God’s Word, contained in the Holy Books, is not only called a light, as David says in *Psalm* 119, but is also compared to Honey and (in *Psalm* 105) to Milk. It is a lamp for our feet (*Psalm* 119), a light for our paths, and a fragrance of life for those who are saved (*2 Corinthians* 2:16).

One cannot object to this reasoning by saying that in *Psalm* 19 and 119 <margin>*Ps.* XIX. *Ps.* CXIX.</margin> it only speaks of God’s Word as proclaimed by a living voice: for it appears by reading these passages that they deal with the Law, which was written at that time. But furthermore, one could give no reason why these passages should apply to God’s preached word and not to the written word, unless one proved that God’s Word lost some of the authority it has

### CHAPTER XVIII.
#### Of the authority of the Holy Scripture, and from whence it derives its authority.

<margin>What is understood by the word authority.</margin>
After having proven the Divinity of the Holy Scripture, it is easy to demonstrate its authority. One will not doubt this if one observes what this word authority means. By this word, nothing else is understood than the right that the Holy Books have to obligate all people to believe what they teach us, and to obey all the commandments given to us therein; and this right is grounded upon the excellence and dignity of these Books. As soon as it has been proven that the Books of the Old and New Testaments have their inspiration from God, it clearly follows that they must have great weight and authority for us; for who can refuse to believe God's Word, and to obey Him, from the moment one is convinced that it is truly God's Word?

The Scripture then needs to derive its authority from nowhere else but from God, who is its inspirer; and when it testifies of itself, one cannot say that its testimony is not credible: for just as Jesus Christ answered those who challenged him, saying that his testimony was credible because his works

<column-break/>

**Right Column:**

clearly showed that he had come from Heaven and the Father was with him, so can we say that the sublimity of the mysteries contained in Scripture, the Holiness of the Commandments, the attractiveness of the promises—in short, this fullness by which it addresses all the needs of which all men are full and convinced—and the extraordinary effects it produces in sanctifying and comforting mankind, are signs that show it has come from Heaven, from the Father of Lights.

<margin>Why one believes that the Scripture is Divine.</margin>
So that, when it is asked, why do I believe that the Scripture is Divine? I answer: it is because of the marks of Divinity which the Holy Spirit, who enlightens my understanding, makes me observe in this Scripture, such as the greatness of the mysteries, the holiness of the Moral Law, the prophecies of the Old Testament fulfilled under the new dispensation, the agreement between the truths it teaches and the light of conscience, the wonderful harmony between the revealed and the natural and innate law; I answer, it is because it feeds, enlightens, and comforts my soul, fills it with an unspeakable and glorious joy, allows it to taste infinite sweetnesses, and makes other things felt of which I have already spoken in the preceding Chapters; in the same way as if one asked why I believe that the Sun is light, Honey sweet, and the Rose of a pleasant scent, I would answer that I believe it because I see the rays of the Sun, that I taste the sweetness of the Honey, and the smell of the roses affects me pleasantly; these comparisons seem to me most appropriate, because God's Word, contained in the Holy Books, is not only called a light, as David says, <margin>Ps. 119:105.</margin> and a light for our paths, and a fragrance of life for those who are saved. <margin>Ps. 19:11.</margin> <margin>2 Cor. 2:16.</margin>

One cannot object against this reasoning that in Psalm 19 and 119 it only speaks of God's Word proclaimed by a living voice: for it appears by the reading of these passages that the Law which was written at that time is being discussed; but furthermore, one could give no reason why these passages would correspond with God's preached word and not with the written word, unless one proved that God's Word loses something of the authority it has

...can lose through being written down; a point that will never be proven. One cannot refute these passages by saying that the Scripture is not a light until after it is recognized and accepted as Divine; for the Scripture is a light that makes itself known for what it is, <margin>Psalm 19:8</margin> and gives wisdom to the simple. If one says that one must have eyes properly functioning to see that light, I will willingly grant that—I have proven it elsewhere; but it does not follow from this that the Scripture does not prove its authority through itself. Everyone agrees that the Sun shows itself to be a body that enlightens the world through itself; meanwhile, to be convinced of its light, it is necessary to have eyes and not be blind. For the rest, the observation we make here shows that it is false to say a thing cannot provide proof of itself. It will perhaps be said that Holy Scripture cannot provide such proof of itself in everything it provides, because there are many things in it that one does not understand; so that it is not the same with the Scripture as with the Sun, which is light from all sides. But it is very easy to answer that one part of Scripture can serve as a proof for the other. For example, one can prove to the Jews the Divinity of the New Testament through the books of the Old Testament. If there are places in the Scripture where our reason cannot penetrate, there is also in the Sun such a fullness of clarity that our weak sight cannot endure it.

<margin>That the Scripture proves itself.</margin>
One can reason about the Scripture, which is the first principle of Faith, as one does with the principles of other sciences, which prove themselves and do not draw their authority from elsewhere; or just as with the Heavens, which prove through themselves that <term>God</term> <note>The author uses the name of the Creator as the ultimate source of authority.</note> made them; or just as with the Laws, which receive all their authority from the Prince who made them, and not from the heralds who proclaim them.

<margin>That it does not have its authority from the Church.</margin>
It appears then that the Scripture does not draw its authority from the Church, by which it is delivered and through which it is proclaimed; which we note against the Roman Catholics, who, when asked why they believe the Scripture, say: because of the testimony of the Church. But some express their opinion here with harsher words than others.

One will not doubt the truth of our sentiment if one makes the following observations.

<margin>First Reason.</margin>
I. If one made the authority of Scripture depend on the testimony of the Church, the authority of <term>God</term> Himself would be subject to that of men, and we would only believe God's word because of the testimony of Men. For one cannot deny that the testimony of the Church is purely human, since the Church consists only of men, who are all subject to deception. But who does not see that subjecting the authority of <term>God</term> to that of Men is the extreme of all extravagances.

# THEOLOGY. BOOK 1. CHAPTER XIX.

### CHAPTER XIX.

#### On the testimony that the Church gives to Holy Scripture.

Although we have proven that the authority of Scripture does not depend on that of the Church, it is not our intention to suggest that this testimony is of no use; on the contrary, we believe that it carries great weight, and we do not doubt that many have been brought to the confession of the truth through it. It is in this way that one must understand the words of Augustine, in the book he wrote against the <margin>Augustine, Book against the Fundamental Epistle, chapter 5.</margin> Fundamental Epistle. <note>original: "Brief van 't Grond Beginzel"; this refers to Augustine’s *Contra Epistulam Fundamenti*, written against the Manicheans.</note> (i) He says: I would not have believed (for according to the African way of speaking <note>The author is likely referring to a grammatical nuance where Augustine uses a form that could be translated as "I would not have" rather than "I did not."</note> one must translate it so) the Gospel, if the authority of the Universal Church had not compelled me to do so. This is evident because one clearly sees that this learned Bishop speaks in this passage of the *means* by which a student is brought to the Faith, or what had moved that Church Father when he was still a Manichean <note>A follower of Manichaeism, a major dualistic religion that competed with Christianity; Augustine was a member for nine years before his conversion.</note> to believe the Gospel. For just before this, he says: *if you find someone who does not yet believe the Gospel, what would you do for him if he said, "I do not believe"? For my part, I would not believe*—that is to say, I would have given no credence to the Gospel—*if the authority of the Universal Church had not compelled me.*

THEOLOGY. Book I. Chapter XIX.

<margin>Augustine, *Against the Epistle of the Foundation*, chapter 5.</margin>
## CHAPTER XIX.
### ->Of the testimony that the Church gives to Holy Scripture.<-

Although we have proven that the authority of Scripture does not depend on that of the Church, it is nonetheless not our opinion that this testimony is of no use; on the contrary, we believe that it carries great weight, and we do not doubt that many have been brought to the confession of the truth through it. In this way, one must understand the words of Augustine in the book he wrote against the *Epistle of the Foundation*. <note>The *Epistula Fundamenti* was a central text of the Manicheans, a group Augustine belonged to before his conversion to Christianity.</note> (i) He says: I would not (for according to the African <note>original: "Afrikaansche," referring to the specific Latin idiom used by North African writers like Augustine</note> way of speaking one must translate it so) have believed the Gospel, if the authority of the Universal Church had not compelled me to do so. This is evident from the fact that one clearly sees that this learned Bishop speaks in this passage of the *means* by which a student is brought to the Faith; or what had moved that Church Father, when he was still a Manichean, to believe the Gospel; for just before this he says, *If you find someone who does not yet believe the Gospel, what would you do for him if he said, "I do not believe"? For my part, I would not believe*—that is to say, I would not have given credit to the Gospel—*if the authority of the Universal Church had not compelled me to do so.*
