# THE CHRISTIAN GOD

...would see error and superstition prevailing in the world. In this sense, <margin>Eusebius, *Church History*, book 5, ch. 1.</margin> the believers of Lyons and Vienne said, speaking of the martyr Attalus, that he had always been the support of their Church. Gregory Nazianzen <margin>\* Oration 19.</margin> <note>Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390 AD) was a prominent Archbishop of Constantinople and a foundational theologian in the early Church.</note> called Basil "the Pillar and Column of the Church, the support of the Faith." Basil <margin>\* Epistle 62.</margin> called the Bishop of Neocaesarea "the Jewel of the Church, the Pillar and Support of the truth." Chrysostom gave this same name to James, and Ignatius called the Apostles "the Pillars of the World."

Paul, through these expressions, may have alluded to the high vault or the bronze platform (k) in the Temple, which was supported by a column that the Jews called the "Royal Column"; upon which Solomon presented himself to the people, as spoken of in 2 Chronicles 6:13 and 2 Kings 23:3. If Paul is making this allusion, he intended to show us the Church as an elevated platform, upon which Truth is seated like a Queen and placed before the sight of mankind. Perhaps <margin>Paul. Athan.</margin> the Apostle, who wrote to Timothy in Ephesus, alluded to the magnificent columns seen in the temples of the Heathens, upon which one could read their supposed oracles and see the images of their false deities or their fictional histories. Against these "pillars of lies and error"—if I may be permitted to call them such—Paul sets the true Church. This Church, appearing openly before the eyes of all people, presents no images of false deities, no fables, nor the ambiguous oracles of the dark Apollo; rather, it presents the oracles of the living and true God: the great "Mystery of Godliness"; Jesus Christ, the image of the invisible God and the imprint of His glory; and all the truths one must know to be saved.

One can also say that Paul is looking toward those columns upon which the decrees of Princes and Governors were posted to be read by everyone; and that he wishes us to understand thereby that the Church teaches the commands and laws of the Supreme Ruler of the world to mankind.

<column-break/>

Theodoret and other Church Fathers <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–457 AD) was an influential theologian and bishop in Syria.</note> understand by this the firmness and permanence of the Church. They say the Church is the pillar that establishes the truth and makes it enduring, in the same sense that Dionysius, Bishop of Alexandria, calls the martyrs "the strong and happy pillars of the Lord." <margin>Eusebius, book 6, ch. 41.</margin>

All that has been said clearly shows that the testimony of the Church is very necessary to teach people to know the Holy Books, to explain them, and to refute those who oppose them. But it is also clear that it does not follow from this that the authority of Scripture depends on the testimony of the Church. The Church performs the same service for us that the Samaritan Woman performed for those of Samaria. She brought them to Jesus Christ and pointed Him out; but once they knew Him, they believed in Him—not because of the testimony of this woman, but because they had heard Him themselves. <margin>John 4:42.</margin> They said: *We no longer believe because of what you said; for we have heard Him ourselves, and know that this is truly the Christ, the Savior of the World.* Upon this, <margin>Augustine, *Tractates on John*, 7 and 15.</margin> Augustine makes this observation: "That the same thing happens to those outside the Church who are not yet Christians. The truth is proclaimed as if this Woman—that is to say, the Church—proclaimed it to them; they come to Christ and believe based on this proclamation, and Christ stays with them 'two days,' and then they believe firmly in Him." Therefore, the Church leads us to the Scripture and places it in our hands; and when we accept the Scripture only on the testimony of the Church, we have only a human faith, or rather a step toward faith. But this is not true faith until we have come to know the Scripture for ourselves; for then we have full assurance. One can understand this through a comparison: the certainty a child has, having learned from parents and teachers that God created this entire Universe and believing such on their authority, is not to be compared with the certainty that same child has when, having grown older, they contemplate all parts of the world in their beauty and order. For then they are certain that God is the cause of all this excellence—

<column-break/>

And the Greek word <note>original: "hedraióma" (ἑδραίωμα)</note> translated by us as "Support" <note>Often translated in English Bibles as "ground" or "buttress" in 1 Timothy 3:15.</note> comes from another word that means "to sit," and literally signifies that which supports us, like a chair or base.

One can reason in the same way about the Scripture and the Church; the testimony that the Church gives to the Scripture brings men to the belief that it is Divine: but while their faith has no other authority than this testimony, they are still merely Pupils, and actually have only an inducement to faith. This is so certain that the Church—should it happen to add to or take away from the Scripture—commits as great a crime as an official clerk would commit by falsifying documents, or a Herald who would proclaim a false command, or a Governor who would forge false letters from his Prince.

It is said: If one does not believe except on the authority of God speaking in the <margin>Mr. the Bishop of Meaux. Confer with Mr. Claude.</margin> <note>This refers to a famous 1678 debate between Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet (Bishop of Meaux) and the Protestant theologian Jean Claude regarding the authority of the Church.</note> Scripture, then there will be some point or other about which a Christian will be in doubt: whether the Scripture is inspired by God; whether the Gospel is a Truth or a fiction; whether Jesus Christ is a deceiver or a Teacher of Truth. Namely, in the time when one has not yet read the Scripture, which is reasonable to think. I answer that this would be reasonable if it followed from our principles that there is a doctrine in Religion among us where every Christian without distinction is bound—by duty and necessity of conscience, on pain of damnation—to doubt the inspiration of the Divine Books, etc. Since there are reasons for and against, nearly equal, which keep the understanding of a Christian in balance: but one cannot draw this consequence from our view; all that can be concluded from it is that there is a time in which a child, and even a man, having been baptized but having nothing of Christianity except Baptism, and having not yet read or heard the Scripture, can exercise no act of faith regarding the Scripture; because he has as yet not the slightest knowledge of it. What causes alarm here? Can anyone exercise an act of faith, by which we are Christians, when the objects—without which such exercise is naturally impossible—have never been presented to his understanding?

But, it is said, is such a person a Christian?

I answer: he has the name of it through his Birth and Baptism: but he is not yet so through an actual faith,

<column-break/>

because a thing that is naturally necessary to exercise faith has been lacking to him until now. <margin>Romans 10:14.</margin> *How shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard?* Moreover, if this man, being able to read or hear the Scripture read, has not done so—either through neglect of his Salvation or by surrendering to all kinds of vices—then he must not be regarded as a Christian. This is because the pretext that he is Baptized, or that Birth and Baptism give the Title of Christian, only applies under the condition that, having come to the use of reason, he will do that which accords with this great name. But if he has had no instruction, solely from a lack of years or the fault of another, then he can be regarded as a Christian by virtue of his Baptism.

Many other things that we would have to say on this subject we shall leave for the treatise on the Church; I will only add a word from Innocent III. He says very well:

This reasoning is almost the same as that of Father Marinier, a <term>Carmelite</term> <note>A member of a Catholic religious order; this likely refers to Jean de la Marinière at the Council of Trent</note> / who / at the Council of Trent, did not think it right that a point of Faith should be made of the necessity of traditions; for / he said, to establish the absolute necessity of traditions, one must state one of two things: either that God forbade the writing of the entire Revelation, or that the Prophets and Apostles wrote their Books by chance, without the intention of setting the revelation in order through writing, and that it resulted from this, that one part of this revelation was written, and the other not. He added to this / that one could not prove the first, namely that God had forbidden it, and that, if one were to prove it, one would also have to say which things were forbidden; And who among those / who have come after the Apostles / has been bold enough to put into writing / that which God had forbidden the Apostles to write?

Someone has very well said / that / if the Apostles had hidden anything / it would have been / either through ignorance / or deceit / or fear / or neglect / or because God had forbidden them; but that one can prove nothing of the sort.

From what has been said / it appears that the Scripture contains all that is necessary for Salvation; but to place this matter in the light of day / one must observe:

1. That there are some things / necessary for Salvation / but known by nature / such as God's existence and the immortality of the Soul, which the Scripture presupposes / without pausing to prove them / although it confirms them / to take away from us all reason for doubt.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the sufficiency of Scripture. The previous page ended with a rhetorical argument that the Apostles would not have left necessary truths unwritten out of ignorance or deceit. This page clarifies what "sufficiency" actually means—specifically that it applies to everything needed for salvation, not every possible piece of information about the universe.</meta>

# THE CHRISTIAN

...to bind those / who are against these errors.

4. We must take good care / that we only speak here of things necessary for <term>Salvation</term> <note>Dutch: 'Zaligheid'; the state of being saved from sin and granted eternal life</note> / so that / under the pretext of the perfection of <term>Scripture</term> <note>The Bible</note> / one does not imagine / that we find everything in it / that humans wish to know. God’s purpose / in giving the Scripture / was not to make us Philosophers / or Mathematicians / or Physicians / but to bring us to Salvation.

5. One must also not place in the category of necessary things / everything that one might desire to know / regarding the mysteries of Religion / everything that has some connection to the Gospel / everything that Jesus Christus and his Apostles said and did: for one cannot deny that we are eager to know many things / regarding the Godhead / the workings of the <term>Holy Spirit</term> / the Resurrection of the Dead / etc. which the Scripture does not teach us; yet of which we can be ignorant / without harm to our Salvation. One also cannot deny that Christ said and did many things / which we do not find in any Book / and that there are many indifferent ceremonies in Religion / which God has left solely to the wisdom of the Teachers. *All the things* (says <term>Cyril of Alexandria</term> <note>A 5th-century Church Father known for his biblical commentaries</note> book 12. on John) *which the Lord has done, are not described, but only those which the Writers judged to be enough, for the doctrines, and for morals.*

6. One must necessarily distinguish the state or age of the Church / according to which God gave more or less breadth to his revelation. As soon as God had his word written / he willed / that it sufficiently contained / according to the era of the Church / everything that could bring people to Salvation / but also / as the Church grew / God gave her greater light; the essence of the matters / which one had to believe / has always been the same / but they are presented more clearly in the Writings of the Apostles / than in those of the Prophets. There were particular matters for each era. For example / the institution of the <term>Sacraments</term> / Baptism and the Lord’s Supper / did not correspond except with the New <term>Dispensation</term> <note>Dutch: 'Huishouding'; the specific way God relates to humanity in a particular era</note>; yet they were the Seals of the same Grace / that the Sacraments of the Old Testament sealed.

This observation is necessary to answer the difficulty / which is raised /

<column-break/>

that one does not find under the Old Testament / that the Sacrifices represented the Sacrifice of the Cross. For regarding the ancient types, we confess / that we owe to the Gospel the knowledge of the truth / which they represented: but it was enough that they under the Old Testament knew these two things (1) That those Sacrifices through themselves could not satisfy God / and therefore were signs of something greater. (2) That the Messiah would come.

7. Finally / one must observe / that the perfection / which we attribute to the Scripture / does not prevent / our needing the ministry of Teachers / and the Grace of the Holy Spirit. These things do not conflict. Those who accuse the Scripture of imperfection / because it requires / that the Teachers proclaim it / and that the Holy Spirit accompanies their sermons with his Grace / have no more ground / than those who would want to claim / that a <term>Rule</term> <note>Dutch: 'Rigtsnoer'; a straightedge or plumb-line used by builders</note> is imperfect / because the hand of the Architect applies it; or that a Testament is imperfect / because one must read it. The Scripture being the Rule of Faith / as we shall prove in what follows / excludes by its perfection all other Rules / but by no means the means / through which this Rule or Standard is applied; such as / the ministry of the Word / the workings of the Holy Spirit / and the attention one must have / in order to read. Everything that the true Servants of Jesus Christus teach / is drawn (as far as the essence of the matter goes) from the books of Scripture / and must be entirely conformed to them. The Holy Spirit imprints the truths / contained in these Books / into the Hearts. *I will give my Spirit within you*, says the LORD, *and I will cause you to walk in my statutes, and do them.* Ezekiel 36:27.

The Ancient Church Teachers acknowledged this <term>Sufficiency</term> <note>The doctrine that the Bible is enough on its own for faith</note> of Scripture. Tertullian, writing against Hermogenes / who wanted all things to be made from a pre-existing matter / says „ I adore the
<margin>See also Tertullian: On Monogamy ch. 4.</margin>
> „ fullness of Scripture, which makes known to me
> „ the maker and the things he has made:
> „ furthermore I find in the Gospel,
> „ that the word was the Servant and
> „ executor of him, who has made
> „ everything; but I have nowhere read,
> „ that all things were created from any
> „ matter; let the shop of Hermogenes
> „ show, where this is written.
<note>Original Latin: "Adoro scripturæ plenitudinem..." Tertullian was a 2nd-century author. Hermogenes was a philosopher who argued that God created the world from eternal matter rather than out of nothing (ex nihilo).</note>

He argues that the need for church teachers and the Holy Spirit does not prove the Bible is imperfect, just as a builder's tool is not imperfect because a hand must hold it.</summary>

It is also not to be believed that the Apostles, writing to the Churches and Believers to teach the Christian Doctrine, would have given them no knowledge of the principal points of their Faith and most essential duties.

<meta>This page continues the theological discussion on the "sufficiency of Scripture," specifically addressing the boundaries of what the Bible is intended to teach. It transitions from citing the Church Fathers to defining the practical limits of biblical perfection—arguing that while the Bible is a complete guide for salvation, it is not intended to be a textbook for worldly sciences or a record of every minor detail of history.</meta>

# THE CHRISTIAN [RELIGION]

...to bind those who are against these errors.

4. One must take good note that we speak here only of things necessary for **Salvation**, so that one—under the pretext of the perfection of the **Scripture**—does not imagine that we find everything in it that men wish to know. God’s purpose in giving the Scripture was not to make us **Philosophers**, or **Mathematicians**, or **Medical Scholars**, but to lead us to Salvation. <note>The author clarifies that the Bible's "perfection" is functional; it is perfect for its specific goal (saving souls), not as an encyclopedia of all human knowledge.</note>

5. One must also not place in the category of necessary things everything one might desire to know regarding the mysteries of Religion, everything that has some relation to the Gospel, or everything that **Jesus Christ** and his **Apostles** said and did: for one cannot deny that we are eager to know many things regarding the Godhead, the workings of the **Holy Spirit**, the Resurrection of the Dead, etc., which the Scripture does not teach us; yet we can remain ignorant of these without harm to our Salvation. One also cannot deny that Christ said and did many things which we find in no Book, and that there are many indifferent ceremonies in Religion which God has left solely to the prudence of the Teachers. All the things (says **Cyril of Alexandria** <note>original: "Cyrillus Alexandrinus lib 12. over Johannes"</note> *in Book 12 on John*) that the Lord did are not described, but only those which the writers judged to be enough for the doctrines and for morals.

6. One must necessarily distinguish the state or age of the Church, according to which God has given more or less breadth to his revelation. As soon as God had his word written down, he willed that it sufficiently contained—according to the era of the Church—everything that could bring men to Salvation; but also, as the Church increased, God gave it greater light. The essence of the things one had to believe has always been the same, but they are presented more clearly in the writings of the Apostles than in those of the Prophets. There have been specific matters for every era. For example, the institution of the **Sacraments**, Baptism and the Lord’s Supper, did not correspond except with the new Dispensation; yet they were the seals of the same Grace that the Sacraments of the Old Testament sealed.

This observation is necessary to answer the difficulty that is raised,

<column-break/>

that one does not find under the Old Testament that the Sacrifices represented the Sacrifice of the Cross. For regarding the ancient examples, we admit that we owe to the Gospel the knowledge of the truth which they represented: but it was enough that they knew these two things under the Old Testament: (1) That those Sacrifices by themselves could not satisfy God, and were therefore examples of something greater. (2) That the **Messiah** would come.

7. Finally, one must observe that the perfection we attribute to the Scripture does not prevent us from needing the ministry of Teachers and the Grace of the Holy Spirit. These things do not conflict. Those who accuse the Scripture of imperfection because it requires Teachers to proclaim it, and that the Holy Spirit accompanies their sermons with his Grace, have no more ground than those who would claim that a <term>Straightedge</term> <note>original: "Rigtsnoer." This refers to a ruler or measuring line used by builders to ensure accuracy.</note> is incomplete because the hand of the Master Builder applies it; or that a Will is imperfect because one must read it. The Scripture being the **Rule of Faith**, as we shall prove in what follows, excludes by its perfection all other Rules, but by no means the means by which this Rule or Straightedge is applied; such as the ministry of the word, the workings of the Holy Spirit, and the attentiveness one must have in reading. Everything that the true Servants of Jesus Christ teach is drawn (regarding the essence of the matter) from the books of Scripture, and must be entirely conformed to them. The Holy Spirit imprints the truths contained in these Books into the Hearts.

> I will put my Spirit within you, says the LORD, and I will cause you to walk in my statutes and do them. **Ezekiel 36:27.**

<margin>See also Tertullian: *On Monogamy*, chapter 4. <note>original: "Tert: de Monog. c. 4."</note></margin>
The Ancient Church Teachers acknowledged this perfection of Scripture. **Tertullian**, writing against **Hermogenes**—who wished that all things were made from a pre-existing matter—says:

> "I adore the fullness of Scripture, which makes known to me the maker and the things he has made: moreover, I find in the Gospel that the Word was the Servant and executor of him who made everything: but I have nowhere read that all things were created from some matter; let the shop of Hermogenes show where this is written."

## CHAPTER XXI.

### Of the Traditions.

<margin>What the word "Tradition" or traditions means? 2 Thess. 2:15.</margin>
**I**n order to handle this subject well, one must explain the word Tradition. It is a Latin word <note>original: "traditio"</note>, coming from one that means to give and to deliver.

One must also observe that in the idiom of the New Testament—which followed the Hebrew language as it was spoken in the time of Christ and His Apostles—the word "giving" signifies teaching, just as the word "receiving" signifies learning. The authors of the ancient paraphrases <note>Likely referring to the Targums, which were Aramaic translations/interpretations of the Hebrew Bible</note> of the Old Testament express themselves in no other way. From the Hebrew word meaning "to receive" <note>Hebrew: *qabal*</note> comes the word <term>Cabbalah; literally "that which is received."</term> The word <term>Massora; literally "handing down" or "tradition"</term> signifies the same.

This word Tradition is sometimes used in a general sense for an Instruction, whether by voice, by writing, or by both; in this sense Paul said in 2 Thessalonians 2:15: *Stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle.* That is, keep the doctrine which you have learned from me, whether through my sermons or through my letters: for Paul had not written everything to the Thessalonians that he could have taught them by mouth; and that which he had not written to them, he wrote to others.

In this sense, the Scripture may very well be called a tradition; and sometimes the first Fathers after the Apostles spoke in this way. Paul called the doctrine of the Lord's Supper, which he had taught the Corinthians orally and subsequently wrote down, a tradition: *For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you.* 1 Corinthians 11:23.

Cyprian said (Epistle 74): if it is commanded in the Gospel, or contained in the epistles or the Acts of the Apostles, let us observe this Divine and Holy tradition;

<margin>*Book 3 against Eunomius.</margin>
> Basil says: the Lord Himself,
> in the tradition of the Savior, 
> regarding Baptism, gave this command, 
> saying: Go ye therefore, and 
> teach all nations, baptizing them in 
> the name of the Father, and of the Son, 
> and of the Holy Ghost. Irenaeus calls the 
> doctrine contained in the

<column-break/>

Scriptures "tradition," which he had also gained knowledge of by voice. He says it is easy for those who wish to give ear to the truth to recognize the tradition of the Apostles, which is proclaimed throughout the whole world in all churches. That he uses the word tradition in this way is evident from the fact that he applies it to the faith,

> that there is one sole Almighty God, 
> Creator of Heaven and Earth, who 
> created Man, sent the flood, 
> called Abraham, drew His people out 
> of Egypt, spoke to Moses, gave 
> the Law, sent the Prophets, and 
> who has prepared the fire for the 
> Devil and his angels; for all these 
> things are contained in the Scripture.

But the word tradition is also sometimes taken for an unwritten instruction. In this sense Christ said, *Why do ye also transgress the commandment of God by your tradition?* 

<margin>traditions Matthew 15:3.</margin>
Matthew 15:3. By an unwritten word, I understand that which is not written in the Holy Books; for it may be in other books.

One distinguishes three types of traditions: those that look upon the things one must believe or do; those that are merely historical; and the third, which concerns the ceremonies of the Church, the order that must be established therein, and the discipline that must be observed.

After explaining the word tradition, it is easy to resolve various disputes on this subject.

1. It appears that one must not reject everything called tradition; for then one would also have to reject the Scripture.
2. That one must not condemn everything taught by the voice; for the things that the Scripture itself teaches were also preached.
3. That one must not reject historical traditions any more than the histories of worldly empires, provided they are examined carefully.
4. That one must have much indulgence for Church traditions regarding things left to the prudence of the Church, such as Liturgies and outward ceremonies. But one must take good heed whether the ceremonies being prescribed do not deviate too much from the simplicity of the Gospel; whether they do not conflict with Good Morals, make the Christian Religion ridiculous, or do violence to the conscience.

It categorizes traditions into doctrinal, historical, and ceremonial types, advising a balanced approach to their acceptance based on their alignment with Gospel simplicity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Traditions from Chapter XXI. Having previously defined what tradition is, the author now shifts to evaluating its utility and its subordinate relationship to Holy Scripture, specifically addressing Roman Catholic arguments for unwritten tradition.</meta>

->### THEOLOGY. Book I. Chapter XXI.<-

<header>THEOLOGY. Book I. Chapter XXI. Chapter.</header>

5. It also appears that Traditions regarding matters of Faith, Morals, and the general state of the Church can be of great use; one can derive much light from them for the explanation of many passages of Scripture that cannot be understood without ancient custom: one can even draw many arguments <note>original: "bespreedene"</note> from them, either for the defense of the truth or for the refutation of errors. But these traditions must always be subjected to the authority of Scripture and viewed as human things. Consequently, one must not accept any that go against Scripture.

For example, since Scripture teaches that there is only one God, one must reject as a godless tradition any tradition that posits many Gods—such as those old Heretics <note>Likely referring to Gnostics or Marcionites</note> who claimed that the God of the Old Testament was different from that of the New Testament.

<margin>
Costerus:
Manual: ch. 1.
Salmeron
Volume:
part: 3.
disp. 8.
Lindanus
Panoplia
on Judgment:
Title:
book 5. ch. 5.
Council of
Trent.
</margin>
But the question is asked whether it is necessary to take refuge in unwritten Traditions to extract from them the things necessary for Salvation—things one must believe or do—as if they were not sufficiently contained in Scripture, and as if we needed another principle of Faith to which Scripture sends us to be more broadly instructed; furthermore, whether one must receive these Traditions with as much reverence as Scripture, and as a Rule of Faith. We do not believe this, and here are the reasons for our view.

<margin>
First
Reason.
</margin>
1. If it is true that everything essential and necessary in Religion, concerning Faith or Morals, is contained in Scripture, then one must admit that there is no need to turn to traditions. Now, we have proven in the preceding Chapter that all the essentials and necessities of Religion are contained in Scripture; it follows then that one does not need to resort to traditions.

One cannot refute this reasoning unless one can show that many things are necessary for Salvation which are not contained in the Books of the Old and New Testaments. But this will never be proven; for when the matter is examined attentively, one will find that what is thought not to be contained in Scripture is either included therein, or that which is not included is not necessary for Salvation, or even conflicts with Scripture.

<column-break/>

I place in the rank of things contained in Scripture: the Immortality of the Soul, the Resurrection of the Body, the Judgment, a future Life, the Creation of Angels; the manner in which Women were Saved who did not receive the <term>Sacrament of Circumcision; a ritual of the Old Covenant only for males</term>, and the children who died before they were circumcised; the manner in which the Heathens who served the true God (though they were not Jews) are Justified; Infant Baptism, Original Sin, the Divinity of the Holy Spirit, the Equality of the Persons of the Trinity, the two Natures of Jesus Christ in the unity of His Person, etc. For we shall prove elsewhere that all these things are contained in Scripture in express words, or can be derived from it by lawful consequence.

I place in the rank of things not necessary for Salvation: what is said of the exorcists in Matthew 12:27; the miracle of the pool of water spoken of in John 5:2; the release of a criminal at the Passover Feast, Matthew 27:15; the ceremony of mixing Water with the Blood of the Covenant, which Paul mentions in Hebrews 9:19; the Dispute of the Archangel with the Devil over the body of Moses, which Jude speaks of, etc. One might say that we only know through Tradition that there are Divine Books: but 1. this Tradition only gives testimony to a written instruction and is the means through which these Books have come to us, just as the public announcement of a Law-book is not the Law itself, and presents nothing other than what is found in the Law-book; so that one must not conclude from this that the authority of Scripture depends on the Tradition of the Church: for Scripture is not made divine by being handed down, but the Church hands it down as Divine because it indeed is so. 2. Tradition points us to the Divine Books, but the marks <note>Internal evidence or "autopistia"</note> they possess prove to us that they are Divine. Other points, such as the sacrifice of the Mass and Purgatory, are contrary to Scripture.

That when all Church Teachers agree in teaching that a tradition is Apostolic—whether they are gathered in a General Council <note>An "Ecumenical Council" representing the whole Christian world, such as the Council of Nicaea.</note> or whether each has testified to it individually—one must believe it to be Apostolic. 5. 1. That it is not possible for simple folk, especially those without letters <note>meaning the illiterate or uneducated</note>, to know whether the entire Church, from the Apostles until now, has steadfastly accepted any particular doctrine, as this requires much research.

2. That one cannot prove that the entire Church, shortly after the death of the Apostles, accepted a doctrine of Faith which is not contained in the Scriptures.

3. That it could have happened that a church, long after the Apostles, established things as Articles of Faith that are not in Scripture; and that one therefore has no right to say that these are Apostolic traditions.

4. That many things have been introduced into the Church that are merely human inventions, which God alone had the right to command, assuming they were meant to be observed.

5. That many things were in use in the first centuries whose origin is unknown to us, yet which are found not to have been introduced by the Apostles.

6. 7. Finally, that many churches boast of being founded by the Apostles; and those that indeed were, have traditions that run contrary to the teaching of the Apostles.

## CHAPTER XXII.

->On the Clarity of Scripture.<-

The Holy Scripture contains all that is necessary for Salvation in such a clear way that no one—except those whom the God of this age <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 4:4, meaning the devil or worldly influences</note> has blinded the senses—finds her obscure.

(k) One finds 5 registers of traditions among the early Church Fathers. Tertullian, having become a Montanist, compiled the 1st in his book *On the Crown*, ch. 3, 4. When Moses speaks of the Laws that God had given to the Israelite people through him, he says: *the commandment that I command you today is not hidden from you, nor is it too far off; it is not in Heaven, to say, who shall go up to Heaven for us? to fetch it for us, and let us hear the same, so that we may do it.* verses 14, 15: *For this word is very near to you, in your mouth, and in your heart, to do it. See, I have set before you today life and good, death and evil.* It is clear that Moses, through these words, wants the people to understand that the word he has proclaimed to them so matches human understanding—in order to bring them to life and deliver them from death—that there is no obstacle other than their own wickedness that can prevent them from following it. When David speaks of this same written word, as the Church of his time possessed it, he says: <margin>* Psalm 119:105. † Psalm 19:8.</margin> * Your word is a lamp for my feet, and a light for my path. † The Law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul; the testimony of the LORD is sure, giving wisdom to the simple; the statutes of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart; the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes.*

One might possibly say that the Scripture enlightens the eyes and gives wisdom only as soon as it is understood, such that this passage does not prove the inherent clarity of the Scripture. But with that same reasoning, one could prove that dark riddles are clear because one understands them only after the explanation; or also, that the sun does not provide light because it does not make one see unless one is illuminated by its light. The Scripture does not only enlighten those who are already enlightened, but it drives away the darkness of the understanding and gives wisdom to those who do not have it.

<margin>2 Peter 1:19.</margin>
Peter is no less explicit in 2 Peter 1:19: *We have,* he says, *the prophetic word which is very sure, and you do well to take heed to it, as to a light shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts.* Add to this 2 Corinthians 4:3, 4: *But if our Gospel be hidden, it is hidden to those who are lost; in whom the god of this world has blinded the minds, so that the light of the Gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, should not shine upon them.* If the Scripture were obscure, it would have been given to us in vain...

But how could the Scripture instruct us if it were obscure? And how could its utterance be a rule for our Faith and Morals if it were not understood?
<margin>Romans 15:4.</margin>

Certainly, one need only consider the things necessary for Salvation <term>Salvation</term> <note>original: "Zaligheid," referring to the state of being saved or eternal happiness in a religious context</note> to see how clearly they are explained in the Scripture. > **Augustine**, the Proud through her height, which they cannot reach. Elsewhere he says, she is like a familiar Friend, who, without Artifice and without Hypocrisy, speaks to the Heart of the learned and the ignorant, and when she hides the truths under hidden expressions, she does not do that through a proud language, capable of frightening humble understandings, and taking away from them the boldness to approach it, just as the poor fear to approach the Rich: but she invites all, through a simple discourse, to come and feed themselves with known truths, and to Exercise themselves, to discover those that are hidden, since she, in both the one and the other, has the same ground of light and wisdom. There are in the Scripture / just like in Nature / three kinds of things. In Nature are things / that everyone sees / like the expanse and beauty of the Heavens. **Irenaeus** uses this comparison. "(Book 2, Chapter 47.) one must," says he / "not be surprised, If there are Spiritual and Heavenly things, that must be revealed to us, since among the things, that are even before our feet, many exceed our understanding."

9. It is said, the Law cannot bring about Sanctification <term>Sanctification: The process of being made holy</term>: but it can teach us all that we must do to be Holy, and that suffices for these subjects we are dealing with.

10. It is said, the Law conflicts with the Gospel; this we deny, and shall prove the contrary elsewhere.

11. It is said, one must not listen to the servants when the Master speaks: but must one not listen to the one whom the Master himself commands to be heard, and whose testimonies he himself brings forward?

# THEOLOGY. BOOK I. CHAPTER XXIV. 111

written to specific people or Churches. That is true; but Providence willed that these books, written for the strengthening of the faith of particular persons and Churches, should also serve for all Christians, because among them there should be but one Faith, one and the same Religion, and one rule for their lives.

Robert Barclay, in his defense of the Enthusiasts <note>original: "Geestdrijvers." This term was often used pejoratively in the 18th century to describe Quakers and other groups who emphasized direct spiritual inspiration over written dogma. Robert Barclay (1648–1690) was a prominent Quaker apologist.</note>, printed in London in the year 1702, has brought forward the following Arguments to prove that Scripture is not a Rule of faith.

<margin>page 79</margin>
**I. Objection.** If it is only through the Spirit, he says, that we come to the true knowledge of God, and if it is through the Spirit that we must be led into all truth and taught in all things; then the Spirit, and not the Scripture, is the ground and origin of all truth and knowledge, and the Rule of faith. This being so, etc.

**Answer.** Mr. Barclay confuses two things: the giver of all light or knowledge that is within us; and the Rule of our faith. The Holy Spirit is the first; the Scripture is the second. I compare the Spirit to the Sun, without which we cannot see, and God’s word to a Rule <note>Here meaning a "ruler" or "measuring stick."</note>, with which we measure all that is presented to us. This writer imagines that they must be merged; he distinguishes the Spirit that is in the believer from that Spirit which speaks through the Scripture, though it is nonetheless the same.

It is certain that, if the Spirit did not enlighten our understanding and instruct us in His Scriptures, we would have no light; but that does not prevent the Scripture from being the rule of faith.

**II. Objection.** The Rule of Christians is not an external written or spoken Law: but an internal and Spiritual letter, so that the Scripture cannot be a Rule.

**Answer.** Mr. Barclay assumes, without any grounds, that there is an internal Law distinct from an external one; whereas they are the same.

**III. Objection.** That which is given to Christians as a Rule must be so perfect that it can instruct them distinctly and teach all things in the cases that may befall them; but, he says, there are infinitely many things for which one finds no Rule in the Scripture. For example, one does not find in the Scripture whether one is fit to be a Teacher, and whether one should accept the Teaching office, and where one should practice the same: one does not find whether one is in the faith. **Answer. 1.** God

<column-break/>

has given us in His Scriptures a sufficient Rule, but at the same time a reason <note>Meaning the faculty of human reasoning.</note> to use this Rule in particular cases. **2.** We do not deny the working of God’s Spirit in our hearts. When the Scripture teaches us what the qualities of a true Teacher are, and the signs of Faith, it is up to us to examine whether we have these qualities and signs; and we must pray to God to make us known to ourselves; and regarding the places where one must exercise his ministry, one has the calling that one obtains to follow, if it appears that it is lawful.

**IV. Objection.** He says that a perfect Rule must be for all; but that the Scripture cannot be for the deaf, for children, and the ignorant; that to make use of the Scripture, one must know the various readings, understand the original Languages, etc.

**I Answer: 1.** When one says that the Scripture is a Rule, we assume that people can use their Reason; likewise, we do not speak of children, or of people who are absolutely without understanding. **2.** Regarding those who are mute, one can make them understand what the scripture teaches; and I have seen some who had much knowledge of Heavenly truths. **3.** The deaf can read the scripture. **4.** Finally, the Languages are not necessary: translations are enough, which will be proven elsewhere.

It is so certain that the scripture is a Rule, that this Writer admits it can be held as a Second Rule.

<header>112 THE CHRISTIAN <note>The header is incomplete, likely "The Christian Religion" or "The Christian Theology."</note></header>

<margin>
Francisco de Corduba, <note>original: "Gordub." Francisco de Corduba (1485–1571) was a Spanish theologian.</note>

<margin>
Reason is no Rule for our faith and morals.
</margin>
It will be said, perhaps, that reason is the Rule of all that we must believe or do. But this is an absurd statement.

1. Because man is so corrupted by sin that he uses his reason poorly; he judges things before he has examined them; he has hundreds of prejudices, and he is blinded by his passions and subjected to many errors; <margin>1 Corinthians 2:14.</margin> he often deceives himself. He does not grasp the things of God and cannot understand them. How could the Reason of such a man be the Rule of Faith and Morals?

2. Because many truths, which are the object of our Faith, are above reason; one cannot discover nor prove them through reason or the light of nature. The Deity is the object of our Faith, and consequently an infinite Being, which transcends a finite reason. If we had nothing to believe but natural things, which are within our reach, there would be some reason to say that it should be the rule of our Faith; but because supernatural things are being dealt with, one cannot claim that reason is the rule of our Faith, <margin>1 Corinthians 2:8, 9.</margin> without striving against reason itself and the Scripture.

It is with our reason as it is with our eye, for reason is the eye of the Soul: but although one can measure nothing without the eye, yet our eye is not our rule; so also, although it is true that one can understand nothing in Religion without reason, nevertheless our reason is not the rule of Religion. These two propositions are very different. *Without reason one can know nothing, nor believe:* And: *reason is the rule of all our knowledge and our Faith.* Just as these two positions are very different: *Without the eye one cannot see, nor know how extensive a thing is in length, breadth, and depth.* And: *the eye is the measure of all things.* But, so that one is not deceived here and understands the true use of reason, it is necessary to make some observations.

<margin>
The Use of Reason.
</margin>
I. It is certain that reason, although it is no rule of our Faith and Morals, is nevertheless of great use. It serves to defend the truth against those

<column-break/>

who will not recognize Revelation; or against those who do accept Revelation and Scripture, but seek to falsify it through perverse interpretations.

It serves to draw conclusions, and to investigate the reasons and agreements that the mysteries <note>original: "verborgendheden." Often refers to theological "mysteries" like the Trinity or the Incarnation.</note> have among one another, along with their coherence and other similarities, which are not discovered except through the use of reason and through the application of generally accepted fundamental laws.

It serves to clarify Heavenly truths, taken from natural things, worldly histories, sciences, Languages, and ancient customs.

It serves to trace the harmony between it <note>Reason</note> and many doctrines of Faith. Therefore the Apostles and Church Teachers have made use of the common ideas of the nations and of the testimony of the Philosophers to support Christian truths and to show that they agree with reason.

It serves to compare what follows with what preceded; the translations with the original Text; the opinions of the Church Teachers with the Scripture; and to distinguish the regular <note>Canonical</note> from the irregular <note>Apocryphal</note> Books.

The Scripture presupposes reason and exhorts us to use it: it wants us to *test all things.* 1 Thessalonians 5:21.

<margin>
Sound Reason and faith never conflict.
</margin>
II. It is also certain, although reason and faith are of different ranks—one natural, the other supernatural—that they are nevertheless never in conflict: these two do not destroy each other because God, who is the cause of both, cannot contradict Himself. We are also assured that whatever runs contrary to the pure and inviolable light of reason, which is common to all men and as such is confirmed by a unanimous and constant experience of all times and places, must not be admitted into Religion; *the carnal mind is enmity against God.* Romans 8:7. But right reason is not. Meanwhile, although one must accept nothing against reason, it does not follow from this that it is the rule of faith.

<margin>
That sin has not entirely extinguished all the light of Reason.
</margin>
III. Furthermore, it remains firm that, although man is corrupted by sin, some knowledge has remained in him as light, which are certain, infallible, and inviolable fundamental principles. As the feel— <note>The text cuts off mid-word "gevoel" (feeling/sense).</note>

<margin>Romans 10:17.</margin>
Faith comes by hearing, as Paul says; but who would dare conclude from this that the sense of hearing is the rule of faith? It will perhaps still be said that if reason is not the rule of faith, one runs the risk of accepting doctrines that are against reason. But this is false; from this, it will only follow that one may embrace doctrines that are unknown to reason, or above reason. This we gladly admit: the Gospel truths—at least most of them—are things that "the eye had not seen, nor the ear heard, and had never entered into the heart of any man." <note>A paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 2:9.</note> One will ask whether a doctrine that reason cannot grasp must be accepted? I answer that it must be accepted if

They also frequently used Philosophy themselves with much benefit. When Paul commands the Colossians (Colossians 2:8) to see to it that no one takes them captive through philosophy, he is looking at the "empty philosophy" of his time. When it does not overstep its proper boundaries, it is very advantageous, and its fundamental rules are not against true Theology. If it says "nothing comes from nothing," <note>original: "ex nihilo nihil fit"</note> it does not conflict with Theology, which teaches that God made everything out of nothing; because Philosophy only speaks of what can happen naturally, and Theology speaks of what God, who is Almighty, has done. But when it seeks to go against Revelation, one must give it no hearing and not let oneself be misled by its false reasonings. These two things are then certain: true philosophy is very useful, but it is not the rule of our faith.

Heraclius, Maximus, Hammonius, Tryphon, Hippolytus, Africanus, Dionysius of Alexandria, and many works of Origen.

2. That there are countless writings falsely attributed to the <term>Church Fathers</term> <note>Early Christian teachers and bishops whose writings are considered foundational after the era of the Apostles.</note>; how many <term>heretics</term> <note>People holding opinions at odds with established religious dogma.</note> have published their books under the names of the most famous Teachers of the Church, and even the Apostles themselves, in order to give weight to their errors. Many copyists have done the same, to better help their books find a buyer; or else through ignorance.

<margin>Jerome, Book on Ecclesiastical Writers, Vol. I.</margin>
How many writings have been brought to light under the name of the Apostles, as Jerome complained about in his day? The *Book of the Trinity* has been attributed to Tertullian, which is actually by Novatian: and to Cyprian, the *Book of the Cardinal Virtues*, which is by Arnold of Bonneval. He has also been credited with the book that Rufinus had written concerning the Articles of Faith of the Apostles; the *Book of a certain Sextus*, a Pythagorean philosopher, has been attributed to Sixtus the Martyr. Similarly, letters have been published under the names of the Popes: Clement, Anacletus, Evaristus, Alexander, Sixtus, Telesphorus, Hyginus, Pius, and Anicetus, up to the year of Christ 385. Those who have provided the identifying marks by which one can recognize false books say they are identifiable: 1. If the book being presented was unknown to those who lived in the time in which it is said to have been made, and even in the time immediately following. 2. If it is not pointed out by Eusebius, nor by Jerome, nor by Gennadius of Marseille, nor by Isidore, nor by Photius. 3. If it was suspected by the ancients among those who had the most interest in claiming it was an authentic scripture. 5. If one finds in the book histories, established ceremonies, emergent opinions, names of authors who lived after the time in which it is supposed to have been written, and phrases that were only used in later times. 6. If one discovers fables in it, unworthy of the authors to whom they are attributed. 7. If the writing

<column-break/>

style is very different from that of the person in whose name it goes. 8. If one encounters opinions there that are contrary to those of these alleged authors, etc.

3. That the true writings of the Church Fathers have been changed and falsified in many ways through ignorance, and often through malice.

<margin>Letter 28 to Lucinus.</margin>
Jerome remarks that the copyists record not what they found, but what they heard. Those who had the general Councils printed in Rome in the year 1608 assure us in the preface to the first book that time and the deceit of heretics are the reasons why the acts of these Councils have not come down to us, neither in their entirety nor in their purity: and they complain that we are deprived of such a precious treasure. Everyone knows how Rufinus mutilated and changed the works of Origen. Louis Vives (commenting on Chapter 24 of the 21st Book of Augustine's *City of God*) remarks that some lines which we now read, and which speak of <term>Purgatory</term> <note>A place or state of suffering inhabited by the souls of sinners who are expiating their sins before going to heaven.</note>, were not in the old manuscripts of Bruges and Cologne; nor in those of Paris. Andreas Masius, Cassander, and others have complained about additions and changes in the old <term>liturgies</term> <note>The customary public worship performed by a religious group.</note>.

<margin>See Council of Chalcedon, Act 16, volume 2 of the Councils.</margin>

## CHAPTER XXV.
### Of the Judge of Controversies.

**A**s it has been proven that the Scripture is the Rule of our faith, one easily perceives that all differences must be decided by it, just as in Republics all disputes are settled by the Laws: the Apostles, therefore, also drew their proof from no other Books than those of the Holy Scripture.

And the Church Fathers did the same when there was a dispute over important Doctrines.

Clement of Alexandria says that we use the Scripture to judge; Basil, in his 80th letter to Eustatius, testifies that the Scripture, inspired by God, judges us; Augustine, in the second book on Marriage, Chapter 33, speaks in this manner: "This dispute requires a Judge; let Jesus Christ then be our Judge." And a little further, that the Apostle [Paul] judges with Christ, for so Christ speaks even through the Apostle; and Chapter 18 of the Book on Grace and Free Will, that the Apostle John be the Judge between us.

> „ Elsewhere he says: we are bre-

> „ he made a Testament <note>Original: *Testament*, referring to the Bible as a legal will or covenant.</note> and there-
> „ upon he died and rose again; one disputes
> „ over the inheritance of the dead, until
> „ the Testament is brought forth; and when

At the opening of the Councils, it was customary to lay the Scripture upon the Table; hence these words, which are often found at the beginning of the Acts of the Councils:

<column-break/>

the Gospels having been brought forward; it is said that the great Constantine, addressing his speech to the Fathers of the Nicene Council <note>The first ecumenical council in 325 AD, which established the core tenets of Christian belief.</note>, showed them that—since the Gospel, the Books of the Apostles, and the Divine things of the Prophets very clearly taught us the sentiments we must have regarding the Godhead—they should set aside all division and contentiousness, and seek in the Scripture the verdict of all their disputes.

<margin>There is no visible Judge on earth.</margin>
One must not seek a visible supreme Judge on earth; for to be a supreme Judge in matters of Religion, one must have at least these two qualities: to be Infallible in judgment, and to be able to decide without a higher appeal. God alone is infallible and, knowing no one above Him, He delivers the supreme sentence, without any possibility of appealing from His Judgment to a higher one; the Scripture speaks of no other supreme Judge.

It is then without foundation that those of the Roman Church maintain that the Pope is the supreme Judge of controversies, or the Councils, or indeed the Pope within the Council.

<margin>Bellarmine: Book 3 on the Word of God, ch. 19. Gregory of Valentia, Book 7.</margin>
One will say that in the Church one must proceed as in Civil States, where, besides the laws, there are supreme Judges who pronounce their Judgment over the parties: but in the Church, it goes differently than in the state. In the state, there can and must be supreme Judges to make an end of disputes, for which it is not necessary to be infallible; the Judges can indeed rob us of some Temporal good through a wrong sentence. But in matters of Religion, where Salvation is at stake, there is but one supreme and infallible Judge, namely, God Himself; and but one Rule, according to which everything must be examined, namely, the Scriptures. It is true that God has, besides this Rule, appointed Teachers <note>Referring to ministers or pastors.</note> who, as subordinate Judges, apply the Rule to the cases brought before them.

One will perhaps say that the Scripture is not the right Means to decide these differences, because they mostly concern the interpretation of the Scripture; but those who make this difficulty do not notice that the Scripture explains itself, and that one must only apply it with attentiveness to understand the true sense of the things it contains.

One will say: the Scripture settles not a single dispute, and the Quarrels are always the same in the World. I admit it: but

### XXV. CHAPTER.
### Of the Judge of Controversies.

**When** it has been proven that the Scripture is the Rule of our faith, one easily understands that all disputes must be decided by it, just as in Republics all disputes are settled by the Laws: the Apostles, therefore, drew their evidence from no other books than those of Holy Scripture.

And the Church Fathers did the same when there was a dispute over fundamental doctrines.

Clement of Alexandria says that we use the Scripture to judge; Basil, in his 80th letter to Eustathius, testifies that the God-inspired Scripture judges us; Augustine, in the second book on Marriage, Chapter 33, speaks in this manner: "This dispute requires a judge; let Jesus Christ then be our Judge." And a little further, "that the Apostle judged with Christ, for so Christ speaks even through the Apostle"; and Chapter 18 of the Book on Grace and Free Will, "that the Apostle John be the judge between us."

At the opening of the Councils, it was customary to lay the Scripture upon the Table; hence these words, which are often found at the beginning of the Acts of the Councils,

<column-break/>

the Gospels having been brought forward; it is said that the great Constantine, addressing his speech to the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea <note>The First Council of Nicaea (325 AD), where the foundational Nicene Creed was formulated.</note>, showed them that, since the Gospel, the Books of the Apostles, and the Oracles of the Prophets taught us very clearly the sentiments we must have regarding the Deity, they should lay aside all division and contentiousness, and seek the resolution of all their disputes in the Scripture.

<margin>There is no visible Judge on earth.</margin>
One must not seek a visible supreme judge on earth; for to be a supreme judge in matters of Religion, one must have at least these two qualities: to be Infallible in judgment, and to be able to decide without higher appeal. God alone is infallible, and, knowing no one above him, he passes the supreme sentence without there being any possibility of appeal from his Judgment to a higher one; the Scripture speaks of no other supreme Judge.

<margin>Bellarmine: Book 3 on the Word of God, Chapter 19. Gregory of Valentia, Book 7.</margin>
It is therefore without foundation that those of the Roman Church maintain that the Pope is the supreme Judge of controversies, or the Councils, or indeed the Pope within the Council.

It will be said that in the Church one must proceed as in Civil States, where, besides the laws, there are supreme Judges who pronounce their Judgment over the parties: but in the Church, it goes differently than in the state, where there can and must be Supreme Judges to make an end of disputes, for which it is not necessary to be infallible; the Judges can indeed deprive us of some Temporal good through a wrong sentence; but in Matters of Religion, where salvation is at stake, there is but one supreme and infallible Judge, namely God himself, and but one Rule, according to which everything must be examined, namely the Scriptures. It is true God has, besides this Rule, appointed Teachers who, as subordinate judges, apply the Rule to the cases brought before them.

It will perhaps be said that the Scripture is not the right means to decide these disputes because they mostly concern the interpretation of Scripture; but those who make this difficulty do not notice that the Scripture explains itself, and that one must only apply it with attentiveness to understand the true sense of the things it contains.

It will be said: the Scripture settles not a single dispute, and the Quarrels are always the same in the World; I admit it: but this

<header>THE CHRISTIAN</header>

It is the fault of the contentious, who will not submit to the pronouncements of Holy Scripture, or are willfully blind. Here one must note that religious disputes are not the same as civil judgments; in the latter, the case ends with the verdict of the Judge, and decisions are immediately put into effect, and the losing party must abide by them. But although the pronouncement of God’s word is clear and sufficient to settle a religious dispute, the opposing party is usually so stubborn that they refuse to hear any conviction.

It will finally be said that the Heretics <note>In this context, "heretics" refers to groups whose beliefs were considered to deviate from established Protestant or Catholic orthodoxy.</note> also make use of Scripture. But this reasoning is absurd; although Satan used Scripture against Jesus Christ, the Savior did not fail to use Scripture against Satan. If one had to throw away all the weapons that the enemies of truth fight with, one would have to abandon all reasoning. Those who have the worst cause often have the impudence to cite the Laws, to falsify them, and to twist them.

<margin>that there are subordinate Judges.</margin>
But although we are certain that Scripture is the only Rule to decide disputes in Religion, and there is no visible [Supreme] Judge on earth, we nevertheless fully acknowledge that there are **Subordinate Judges**; namely, the Shepherds and Teachers, who hear the contending parties, settle the disputes through God's word, refute error, and apply the general commands of Divine Right to specific cases and occasions as they arise. This was done by Moses and Aaron under the Old Testament; they were both subordinate Judges, not Supreme or Sovereign ones; they judged according to God's Law-Book on what was presented to them, or after having asked God for counsel. When the Israelites have a matter, said <margin>EXODUS XVIII. 16.</margin> Moses (to his father-in-law Jethro) they come to me, and I judge between one and another, and make them understand the Statutes and Laws of God. <margin>* DEUTERONOMY XVII. 8. 9</margin> * If a matter be too hard for you, says the LORD, between blood and blood, between plea and plea, and between stroke and stroke, being matters of controversy within your gates; then you shall arise and go up to the place which the LORD your God shall choose; And you shall come to the Levitical Priests and to the Judge who

<column-break/>

shall be in those days, and you shall inquire, and they shall show you the sentence of judgment, etc. Following this, the other Priests—the successors of Aaron—also had to conduct themselves; therefore they are sometimes rebuked for having strayed from the way, for causing many to stumble, and for breaking the covenant of Levi (Malachi 2:8). The Teachers in the Christian Church must also be regarded as subordinate Judges.

This observation serves to refute an Objection; it is said, "Under <margin>Bellarmine, Book 3, On the Word of God, Chapter 3. <note>original: "Bell. l. 3. de verb. Dei: c: 3." refers to Robert Bellarmine, a prominent Catholic theologian who argued for the Pope's role as a visible judge.</note></margin> the Old Covenant there was a supreme Judge, namely Moses." To this one could answer that Moses was an extraordinary Prophet sent by God, and that we no longer have such men. But it will be enough that we note that Moses and Aaron were subordinate Judges who pronounced sentences according to God’s Law, and that the ministers of the Gospel under the New Dispensation <note>term: "Nieuwe Huishouding" (New Dispensation) refers to the era of the Christian church following the coming of Christ.</note> do the same as the Priests of the Old Covenant did: so that we may ask them for counsel in cases of doubt, just as people formerly consulted the Priests under the Law. <margin>Haggai II. 11.</margin> Haggai 2:11, people sought the Law from their mouth; their lips <margin>Malachi II. 7.</margin> preserved knowledge (Malachi 2:7). Some will say that in Ecclesiastes 12:11 <note>The text cites Ecclesiastes 12:13, but the context of the "one Shepherd" is verse 11.</note> it speaks of a single Shepherd or Teacher; but this Teacher is Christ, from whom the words of the wise proceed; so that this passage cannot be applied to any mortal.

These **Subordinate Judges** are not to be believed unless it is found that they perfectly agree with the Scripture; and it is permitted to deviate from their opinion if one notices that they do not teach Apostolic Doctrine: for the Church has no legislative authority in things concerning Faith and Morals.

There is but one Lawgiver (James 4:12). <margin>James IV. 12.</margin> And it is with the Church as it is with <margin>James IV. 12.</margin> ordinary subordinate Judges, who are bound to the Laws, and whose sentences—if against the Laws—are of no value; so that one can always appeal from the judgment of these Judges, as from the pronouncement of the Church, to a higher tribunal <note>In this context, the "higher tribunal" is the Word of God itself.</note>.

Ignatius adds to this—or another writer in the letter to the Philadelphians—as does that which stands in the 2nd book of the *Constitutions* (falsely attributed to Clement), chapter 19; the 23rd letter of Leo I; and the *Decretals*, cause XI, question 3.

Just as these subordinate Judges—whose judgment is nonetheless of great weight—can err, and very often do err, so we believe that everyone in particular is obliged and has the right to examine what the Church says. There is a small treatise in the **Talmud** <note>The Talmud is a central text of Rabbinic Judaism; the author cites it here to show that even ancient Jewish law recognized that high religious authorities could make mistakes.</note> in which it is noted what one must do, and what offerings one must present to God, if it happens that the **Great Council (Sanhedrin)** <note>The Sanhedrin was the supreme judicial and religious council of the Jewish people in ancient times.</note> or the High Priest has not judged rightly, whether one had followed or rejected their pronouncement. II. The purpose for which the Scripture was given to us proves that we are required to read it. It was given to promote the Salvation of Mankind; to set them right from their errors; to teach them to know the God whom they worship, as well as what he has done for them, what service he demands of them, which virtues please him, and which sins he abhors; to bring forth these virtues in them; and to increase them, to strengthen their faith, and to awaken in them the hope of future goods when the goods of the world seem all too alluring to them; and to renew in them the power of Love for what is good. How could the Scripture produce all these healing fruits if one did not read it?

III. All the praises given to the Scripture are so many proofs that one must read it! It is the Testament of our

<column-break/>

Heavenly Father; we must then read it to know and follow his will. It is a Letter from the Creator of the World to his Creature; it is then proper that his creature reads it. It is a light; one must then open the eyes to behold it; a Heavenly Bread to feed our Souls; a fire to warm us; a powerful weapon to protect our Faith against those who oppose it, and to overcome them. This has been the constant practice of the Jewish Church; their Teachers say (m) that every Jew was commanded to write a copy of the Law with his own hand if he could write; or otherwise to have it done.     *   *Section 2 (Objections/Tegenwerpingen):* A numbered list refuting arguments against commoners reading the Bible.
        *   1. "Only the learned should read it." Refutation: Christ spoke to fishermen and tax collectors.
        *   2. "People might misuse it." Refutation: People misuse food/drink, but we don't ban eating. Learned people fall into error too.
        *   3. "Tables of the Law were in the Ark (hidden)." Refutation: They were kept safely, but read to the people.
        *   4. "Scripture is for priests only." Refutation: Law given to all Israel, Psalms for all to worship.
        *   5. "Old Testament was written in unknown languages/letters." Refutation: Never proven.
        *   6. "The Church was without translations for a time." Refutation: Read by those who understood the language.
        *   7. "Philosophers hide their mysteries." Refutation: Christ wants truths proclaimed from rooftops.
        *   8. "Jews had figurative laws and Moses wore a veil." Refutation: Doesn't mean they didn't read it.
        *   9. "Church Fathers restrict youth from certain parts." Refutation: Distinguish between "forbidding" and "advising order of reading" (e.g., Song of Solomon).
        *   10. "Don't give holy things to dogs." Refutation: Christians aren't dogs.

    *   *Section 3 (Specific Historical Conflicts):*
        *   Gregory VII vs. King of Bohemia regarding Slavic language services.
        *   Council of Toulouse (1228) forbidding translations.
        *   Council of Trent / Index of Prohibited Books (Pius IV) Rule IV: Reading Bible in common tongue is more harmful than beneficial.
        *   Cardinal Paceco vs. Cardinal Madruccio: Madruccio's famous line—"Paul II could be mistaken, but the Apostle Paul could not."

    *   *Section 4 (Conclusion/Advice):* How to read Scripture: with respect, adoration, and sincerity.

### THEOLOGY. BOOK I. CHAPTER XXVI. 127

Emperor Conrad IV, in the year 1250. Alfonso, King of Castile, in the year 1280. John Cantacuzenus, Emperor of Constantinople, in the year 1360. Charles V, King of France, in the year 1370. Alfonso V, King of Aragon, who had read the Bible fourteen times along with its marginal notes and explanations, in the year 1450.

<margin>Objections.</margin>
1. It will perhaps be said that for a matter as holy as the Scripture, no one should be admitted except the learned, the wise, and the great intellects. But who does not know that this written Word is the very same that Christ proclaimed to poor fishermen and to tax collectors, etc.

2. People could easily misuse this reading. But if one had to abstain from reading the Scripture because some could make a bad use of it, then one must also not eat or drink, because many exceed themselves in these two things. Moreover, if this reasoning held, then the Scripture should also be forbidden to the learned, because many of them have fallen into grave errors. Finally, if this reasoning took place, one should never preach the Gospel, so as to give no one the opportunity of being lost through the misuse of God's Word.

3. The Tables of the Law were enclosed in the Ark or the Chest of the Covenant. It is true that the Tables which Moses brought down from the Mountain were placed in the Ark to be carefully preserved; but it does not follow from this that the Law was not read to the people: we have proven the contrary.

4. It is an error to believe that the Scripture was only made for the Priests, for the Law was given to all Israel. The Historical Books were written to instruct the people; the Psalms, to teach them to worship and thank God.

5. It is an error to believe that the Books of the Old Testament were written in an uncommon language and in letters unknown to the people; this will never be proven.

6. It will be said that the Church was for some time without a translation, and that Greek and Latin were generally not under-

<column-break/>

stood. But one must at least admit that the Scripture was read by all those who understood the languages.

7. The philosophers hid their mysteries. But Christ wants His truths to be proclaimed to all the world and from the rooftops.

8. The Jews had a figurative Law, and Moses covered his face with a veil. But it does not follow from this that the Jews did not read the Scripture.

9. Some Church Fathers do not think it good that young people read certain passages of the Old Testament before having reached a certain age; but there is a great difference between forbidding the reading of Scripture, which the Fathers never did, and advising not to begin with the Song of Solomon and the final chapters of Ezekiel.

<margin>*Matthew 7:6.*</margin>
10. Christ forbids giving that which is holy to the dogs. But God does not want one to treat the Christian people as dogs.

I shall deal with that in the following chapter: concerning the reading of Scripture, it is further to be noted that in the *Register of Forbidden Books* <note>Known as the Index Librorum Prohibitorum.</note>, drawn up by the Fathers of the Council of Trent, approved and made public by the authority of Pope Pius IV, it is said in Rule IV: *The reading of the Bible in the common tongue, being permitted indifferently, brings more harm than benefit.* It is true that many Roman writers have rejected or softened this rule; according to Pallavicino <note>Sforza Pallavicino, a cardinal and historian of the Council of Trent.</note>, when Cardinal Pacheco wanted the people to be forbidden the Scripture, pointing to what Paul II had done, Cardinal Madruzzo answered: *Paul II could be mistaken, but the Apostle Paul could not.*

->### CHRISTIAN THEOLOGY<-
<page-num>130</page-num>

Consult Hody, printed in Oxford, 1705, regarding point 7: whether we possess the true translation of the so-called <term>Septuagint<note>Original: "LXX." The Septuagint is the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, traditionally said to be the work of seventy-two Jewish scholars.</note></term>. Many other questions are proposed, which we shall pass over.

II. There have been other famous Greek translations.
1. That of **Aquila**, a native of Sinope, a city in the province of Pontus, who lived in the time of Emperor Hadrian, around the year 130. He was a Christian; but because of the great passion he had for astrology, he was excommunicated. Out of spite, he embraced Judaism and was circumcised; he learned Hebrew and set himself to translating the Bible into Greek. He produced two translations, and because he was very intent on translating word-for-word, it is in some places so awkward that one has much difficulty understanding it.
2. The translation of **Theodotion**, who was from Ephesus and is believed to have lived under Emperor Commodus in the year 184. It is said that he had been a disciple of Tatian, later became a Marcionite, and finally converted to Judaism. This writer applied himself more to translating the Scripture according to the sense than according to the letter.
3. The translation of **Symmachus**, who was a Samaritan and, having later become a Christian, fell into the error of the <term>Ebionites<note>A Jewish Christian sect that emphasized the necessity of following Jewish law and often denied the full divinity of Christ.</note></term>; it is believed he made his translation under Emperor Severus, in the year 193.
4. Another translation found at **Jericho** under Caracalla in the year 220, without the name of the translator.
5. Another, called the **Nicopolitan**, because it was found at Nicopolis under Alexander Severus in the year 230.

From all these translations, **Origen** created his four-fold, six-fold, and—if we believe some scholars—his eight-fold translations.

The **four-fold** <note>Original: "viervuldige," referring to the *Tetrapla*.</note> referred to the four translations: the Septuagint, Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus.

The **six-fold** <note>Original: "ses-vuldige," referring to the *Hexapla*.</note> consisted of these four translations joined with the Hebrew text in both Hebrew and Greek letters, making six columns.

The **eight-fold** <note>Original: "agt-vuldige," referring to the *Octapla*.</note> was when two other columns were added to these six, in one of which was the translation from Jericho, and in the other that of Nicopolis. The ancients often call them "six-fold" even when there were up to 9 columns. In the 1st was

<column-break/>

the Hebrew text in Hebrew letters; in the 2nd, the same text in Greek letters. In the 3rd, the translation of **Aquila**. In the 4th, that of **Symmachus**. In the 5th, the translation of the **Septuagint**. In the 6th, that of **Theodotion**. In the 7th, the fifth translation, found at Jericho. In the 8th, that of **Nicopolis**. In the 9th, another translation. But they called it "six-fold" because there were properly only six columns for all the books.

There have been other Greek translations: that of **Lucian the Martyr**, a Priest of Antioch, who died in the year 311; and that of **Hesychius**. All the churches between Antioch and Constantinople used the former; those of Egypt and Alexandria used the second. Following **Jerome** <note>Original: "Hieronimus."</note>, many discerning scholars have believed that Lucian and Hesychius had merely corrected the old Greek translation of the Septuagint, which had become filled with countless errors.

**Apollinarius** had also made a translation, but it was approved by neither the Jews nor the Christians.

I will remain silent regarding a Greek translation of the five Books of Moses which the Samaritans had, of which only a few fragments remain, found in the works of the Early Fathers and some Greek commentators; and regarding yet another in common Greek used by the **Karaite Jews**, printed in Hebrew at Constantinople.

Many Latin translations have also been seen. There was a famous one that **Augustine** calls the **Italic** <note>Original: "Italiaansche."</note>, which was read in the congregations of Italy where Latin was the language of the people. **Julian**, Archbishop of Toledo, who wrote against the Jews at the end of the 7th century, calls it the **Vulgate** <note>Original: "Vulgata."</note>. Little of it has remained to us; what can be found of it in the Latin Church Fathers—chiefly in **Hilary the Deacon**, who lived in the time of **Damasus**, and of which **Nobilius** made an excerpt printed in Rome in 1588—gives us to understand that the maker of this old translation had tried to translate the Greek of the Septuagint word-for-word, and even followed their <term>loanwords<note>Original: "bastaard woorden," referring to Greek words transliterated into Latin rather than translated.</note></term>.

**Jerome**, noticing that this translation had many faults, made two new ones: one based on the Septuagint and one based on the original Hebrew language.
