->### THEOLOGY. BOOK I. CHAPTER XXVII.<-
<page-num>131</page-num>
Sig. ff 2
<meta>catchword: rich.</meta>

It is believed that from the Italian translation, and from that of **Jerome**, the version now called the <term>Vulgate<note>Original: "Vulgata." This refers to the late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible that became the Catholic Church's official promulgated Latin version.</note></term> was later compiled, in which it is claimed many elements from **Theodotion** and **Lucian** are also present. Scholars are not in complete agreement on this: whatever the case may be, it is certain that the Vulgate is not entirely the work of Jerome. **Sixtus V** published a more accurate edition in the year 1589 than previous ones. **Clement VIII** made many further improvements to it in the year 1592; this latter version is used throughout the entire Latin Church. **Father Simon** <note>Referring to Richard Simon, a pioneering 17th-century biblical critic.</note> very effectively refutes **P. Sutor**, a Carthusian monk and theologian from Paris, and others who viewed Jerome’s translation as being of divine inspiration. The same writer notes that the best editions of the Vulgate are those of **Robert Estienne** <note>Original: "R. Stephanus." A famous 16th-century printer.</note> from the years 1540, 1545, and 1546, although they were rejected by the theologians of Paris and Leuven; the latter group published a new edition in the year 1573.

<margin>Critical History of the New Testament, p. 76.</margin>
**Leo Allatius** mentions a decree of the General Assembly of Cardinals from January 17, 1577, which stipulates that one must not deviate by a single syllable or title from the Vulgate; however, this decree was not made public.

1. Besides these translations, there was one in **Syriac**: but one should not imagine, as some Syriac writers do, that the Hebrew Bible was translated into Syriac during the time of **Solomon** at the request of **Hiram**, King of Tyre (at least in part), and the remainder in the time of **Abgar**, King of Edessa: for those are merely Eastern legends.

2. There have been translations in **Arabic**, some made by Jews and others by Christians. It is claimed that **John, Archbishop of Seville** in Spain, compiled one in the year 717 because this language was then the common tongue of that part of Spain. **Rabbi Saadia Gaon**, who lived around the year 900, wrote an expansion upon the entire Bible in Arabic. It is believed that the version printed in the <term>Polyglot Bible<note>A Bible containing the text in several languages side-by-side.</note></term> is later than the **Koran**, as some words are drawn from it, and also later than the translation of Saadia, which it follows in many places. It is based partly on the Hebrew text and partly on the <term>Septuagint<note>Original: "LXX." The early Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note></term>.

3. There was one in **Coptic**,

<column-break/>

which is the ancient Egyptian language, mixed with Greek, Arabic, and Latin.

4. One in **Armenian**, from the time of **John Chrysostom**. Some attribute this translation to this great man; others deny it. An Armenian Bishop named **Uscan** had an Armenian Bible printed in Amsterdam in the year 1664.

5. There was one in the **Dalmatian** language; and it is believed that **Jerome** (who died in the year 420) was the creator of it. This opinion is based on a passage in his letter to Sophronia, but others believe he is speaking there of the Latin language.

6. One in **Samaritan**.

<margin>Homily 2 on John.</margin>
7. One in **Persian** covering the five Books [the Pentateuch], made by a Jew named **Tavose** or **Tavase** in the year 1551. And one can infer from a passage by Chrysostom that such versions already existed in his time.

8. It is said there was one in **Saxon** by **Alfred**, who reigned in England in the 8th century.

9. We have one in the **Slavonic** language by **Methodius** in the 9th century; a complete Bible was printed at Ostrog, which is called the **Muscovite** version because their language is a descendant dialect of Slavonic.

10. In the language of the **Goths**, which is attributed to **Ulfilas**, Bishop of the Goths under the Emperor Constantius.

11. The Jews had one printed in **Spanish** at Ferrara in the year 1553. It corresponds almost word-for-word with the Hebrew text. There is an edition from the year 1559 and one from 1661, besides various others; one by **Cassiodoro de Reina**, printed at Basel in the year 1569. The other by **Cipriano de Valera**, who corrected this translation and had it printed in the years 1602 and 1622. The Jews of Ferrara, in the preface of their Spanish Bible, mentioned a translation in **Catalan**.

12. There are many in **Latin**. **Santes Pagninus**, a Dominican, made one that was printed for the first time at Lyons in the year 1528. **Arias Montanus** also published one, which is in the Polyglots. **Thomas Malvenda**, a Dominican, made one that is very crude. **Sebastian Münster**, a Protestant, had one printed in the year 1534. **Leo Judae** published one covering most of the Old Testament at Zurich.

<header>CHRISTIAN</header>

Consult *Hody*, printed in *Oxford* in 1705, regarding the true translation of the so-called *Septuagint* <note>original: "LXX"; the 3rd-century BCE Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>. Many other questions are proposed that follow from the aforementioned.

II. There have been other famous Greek translations.

1. That of *Aquila*, a native of *Sinope*, a city in the province of *Pontus*, who lived in the time of the Emperor *Hadrian*, around the year 130. He was a Christian; but because of the great passion he had for astrology <note>original: "Sterrekunst"</note>, he was excommunicated. Out of spite, he embraced Judaism and was circumcised; he learned Hebrew and set himself to translating the Bible into Greek. He produced two translations, and, as he was very careful to translate word-for-word, it is in some places so clumsy <note>original: "wankallig"; meaning unstable or faltering in its literalism</note> that one has much difficulty understanding it.

2. The translation of *Theodotion*, who was from *Ephesus*, and who is believed to have lived under the Emperor *Commodus* in the year 184. It is said that he had been a disciple of *Tatian*, and thereafter became a *Marcionite*, and finally converted to Judaism. This writer applied himself more to translating the Scripture according to the sense than according to the letter.

3. The translation of *Symmachus*, who was a *Samaritan*, and having afterwards become a Christian, fell into the error of the *Ebionites*; it is believed that he made his translation under the Emperor *Severus* in the year 193.

4. Another, found at *Jericho* under *Caracalla* in the year 220, without the name of the translator.

5. Another, called the *Nicopolitan*, because it was found at *Nicopolis* under *Alexander Severus* in the year 230.

From all these translations, *Origen* made his four-fold, six-fold, and—as some scholars believe—his eight-fold translations.

The four-fold <note>Known as the *Tetrapla*.</note> referred to the four translations: the *Septuagint*, *Aquila*, *Theodotion*, and *Symmachus*.

The six-fold <note>Known as the *Hexapla*.</note> referred to these four translations joined with the Hebrew text in Hebrew and Greek letters, which made six columns.

The eight-fold <note>Known as the *Octapla*.</note> was when two other columns were added to these six, in one of which was the translation from *Jericho*, and in the other that of *Nicopolis*. The ancients often call them "six-fold" even when there were up to nine columns. In the 1st was

<column-break/>

the Hebrew text in Hebrew letters; in the 2nd, the same text in Greek letters. In the 3rd, the translation of *Aquila*. In the 4th, that of *Symmachus*. In the 5th, the translation of the *Septuagint*. In the 6th, that of *Theodotion*. In the 7th, the fifth translation, found at *Jericho*. In the 8th, that of *Nicopolis*. In the 9th, another translation. But it was called the six-fold because there were strictly only six columns for all the books.

There have been other Greek translations: that of *Lucian* the Martyr, a priest of *Antioch* who died in the year 311; and that of *Hesychius*. All the churches located between *Antioch* and *Constantinople* used the first; those of *Egypt* and *Alexandria* used the second. Many critics have believed, following *Jerome* <note>original: "Hieronimus"</note>, that *Lucian* and *Hesychius* had merely corrected the old Greek translation of the *Septuagint*, which was filled with innumerable errors.

*Apollinarius* had also made a translation; but it was approved by neither the Jews nor the Christians.

I will say nothing of a Greek translation of the five books of Moses which the *Samaritans* had, of which only a few fragments remain, found in the works of the Early Fathers and some Greek commentators; nor of another in common Greek which the *Karaite* Jews use, printed in Hebrew characters at *Constantinople*.

Many Latin translations have also been seen. There was a famous one that *Augustine* calls the *Italian*, which was read in the congregations of *Italy*, where Latin was the language of the people. *Julian*, Archbishop of *Toledo*, who wrote against the Jews at the end of the 7th century, calls this the *Vulgate* <note>original: "Vulgata"; here referring to the "Old Latin" versions used before Jerome's revision became standard.</note>. Little of this has remained to us, and what is found of it in the Latin Early Fathers—principally in *Hilary* the *Dalian* <note>Referring to Hilary of Poitiers or perhaps a specific local variant.</note>, who lived in the time of *Damasus*, and of which *Nobilius* made a neat extract printed in *Rome* in 1588—gives us to understand that the maker of this old translation had tried to translate the Greek of the *Septuagint* word-for-word, even following their hybrid words.

*Jerome*, noticing that this translation had many faults, made two new ones: one based on the *Septuagint* and one based on the Hebrew original language.

# DIVINITY. Book I. Chapter XXVII.

It is believed that the *Vulgate* <note>The standard Latin version of the Bible used by the Roman Catholic Church.</note> was compiled from the earlier Italian translation and from that of *Jerome* <note>original: "Hieronimus." St. Jerome (c. 347–420) was the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note>, and it is claimed that many elements from *Theodotion* and *Lucian* are also present in it. Scholars are not in complete agreement on this: whatever the case may be, it is certain that the *Vulgate* is not entirely the work of *Jerome*. In the year 1589, *Sixtus V* published a more accurate edition than previous ones. *Clement VIII* made many further improvements to it in the year 1592; this latter version is the one used throughout the entire Latin Church. Father *Simon* <note>Richard Simon (1638–1712), a French priest and influential biblical critic.</note> 

<margin>Critical History of the N.T. Page 76.</margin>

very capably refutes Father *Sutor*, a Carthusian monk and theologian from Paris, and others who regarded *Jerome's* translation as being of divine inspiration. The same writer notes that the best editions of the *Vulgate* are those by *R. Stephanus* <note>Robert Estienne (1503–1559), a famous Parisian printer and scholar.</note> in the years 1540, 1545, and 1546. Although these were rejected by the theologians of Paris and Leuven, the latter produced a new edition of their own in the year 1573.

*Leo Allatius* <note>Leone Allacci (c. 1586–1669), a Greek scholar and librarian at the Vatican.</note> mentions a decree from the General Assembly of Cardinals dated January 17, 1577, which dictates that one must not deviate by a single syllable or title from the *Vulgate*, but this decree was never made public.

1. Besides these translations, there was one in Syriac: but one should not imagine, as some Syriac writers do, that the Hebrew Bible was translated into Syriac (at least in part) during the time of *Solomon* at the request of *Hiram*, King of *Tyre*, and the remainder during the time of *Abgarus*, King of *Edessa*; for these are merely Oriental fables.

2. There have been translations in Arabic, some made by Jews and others by Christians. It is claimed that *John*, Archbishop of *Seville* in Spain, prepared one in the year 717 because this language was the common tongue in that part of Spain at the time. *Rabbi Saadia Gaon* <note>original: "R. Zadias Gaön." A prominent Jewish philosopher and exegete (882–942).</note>, who lived around the year 900, wrote an expansion upon the entire Bible in Arabic. It is thought that the version printed in the Polyglot Bible <note>A Bible containing the text in several languages side-by-side.</note> is more recent than the *Alkoran* <note>The Quran.</note>, from which some words were taken, and later than the translation of *Saadia*, which it follows in many places. It is based partly on the Hebrew text and partly on the Septuagint <note>original: "LXX."</note>.

3. There was one in Coptic,

<column-break/>

which is the ancient Egyptian language, mixed with Greek, Arabic, and Latin.

4. One in Armenian, from the time of *John Chrysostom* <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople known for his preaching.</note>. Many attribute this translation to this great man; others deny it. An Armenian Bishop named *Uscan* <note>Oskan Yerevantsi (1614–1674).</note> had an Armenian Bible printed in Amsterdam in the year 1664.

5. There was one in the Dalmatian language, and it is believed that *Jerome*, who died in the year 420, was its creator. This opinion rests on a passage in his letter to *Sophronia*: but others consider that he is speaking there of the Latin language.

6. One in Samaritan.

7. One in Persian, covering the five books <note>The Pentateuch or Torah.</note>, 

<margin>Homily 2 on John.</margin>

made by a Jew named *Tavus* or *Tavafe* in the year 1551. And one can infer from a passage by *Chrysostom* that such translations already existed in his time.

8. It is said that there was one in Saxon by *Alfred* <note>Alfred the Great (r. 871–899).</note>, who reigned in England in the 9th century <note>The text says "VIIIste" (8th), but Alfred reigned in the 9th.</note>.

9. There is one in the Slavonic language by *Methodius* <note>Saint Methodius (c. 815–885), who with his brother Cyril translated the Bible for the Slavs.</note> in the 9th century; a complete Bible was printed at *Ostrovie*, which is called the Muscovite version because their language is a dialect descended from Slavonic.

10. In the language of the Goths, which is attributed to *Ulfilas*, Bishop of the Goths under the Emperor *Constans*.

11. The Jews had a Spanish version printed in *Ferrara* in the year 1553. It corresponds almost word-for-word with the Hebrew text. There is an edition from the year 1559 and one from 1661, besides several others; one by *Cassiodorus de Reina* printed in Basel in the year 1569. The other by *Cyprian de Valera*, who improved this translation and had it printed in the years 1602 and 1622. In the preface of their Spanish Bible, the Jews of Ferrara made mention of a translation in Catalan.

12. There are many in Latin. *Santes Pagnino*, a Dominican, made one that was first printed in Lyons in the year 1528. *Arias Montanus* also published one which is found in the Polyglots. *Thomas Malvenda*, a Dominican, made one that is very "barbarous" <note>In this context, meaning stylistically crude or overly literal to the point of being ungrammatical in Latin.</note>. *Sebastian Münster*, a Protestant, had one printed in the year 1534. *Leo Jud* <note>original: "Leo de Juda." A Swiss Reformer.</note> published one covering the greater part of the Old Testament in Zurich.

# THE CHRISTIAN DIVINITY
### Book I. Chapter XXVII.

<note>original: "rich." likely an abbreviation for "bericht" or "berigt," meaning "account" or "report."</note> in the year 1543. Robert Estienne <note>original: "Robertus Stephanus," a famous Parisian printer and scholar.</note> had it reprinted thereafter with the Vulgate in the year 1545; this is called the Bible of Vatablus <note>François Vatable (d. 1547), a French humanist scholar.</note>. Sebastian Castellio <note>original: "Sebastiaan Castelion of Chatellion."</note> produced one that was printed in Basel in 1551, though without official approval. The best edition is that of 1573. Tremellius and Junius <note>Immanuel Tremellius and Franciscus Junius were influential Protestant Hebraists.</note> also published one.

I shall remain silent regarding those which people have now begun to work upon.

13. The histories of the Waldensians <note>A medieval Christian movement that preceded the Reformation and emphasized the Bible as the sole authority.</note> say that there is an old manuscript of their translation from the year 1228; a Council of Toulouse, assembled against them, made this decree: "We also forbid the laity to have the books of the Old and New Testament, unless perhaps someone out of piety desired to have the Psalter, or the Breviary <note>A book containing the service for each day, to be said by those in orders.</note> of Divine Services, or the Books concerning the Blessed Virgin; but let it not be permitted for them to have the same in their Mother Tongue."

14. There have been several in English. Wycliffe <note>original: "Wicklef." John Wycliffe (c. 1320s–1384), an early reformer.</note> had made one; under the reign of Henry VIII, various editions of it were published in the years 1526, 1530, and 1537. One in 1541. Another in the time of Queen Mary in 1560, and thereafter in 1598. The English now use the one King James had prepared in 1612 <note>The famous King James Version, actually published in 1611.</note>. They have nonetheless retained the old translation of the Psalms which was made under Edward VI.

15. There are several in High German; besides those which are said to have been made in the years 820, 850, 870, 1200, 1250, and 1370. Luther published one; Piscator <note>Johannes Piscator (1546–1625), a German Reformed theologian.</note> another in 1604. Johannes Eck <note>original: "Joh: Eckius."</note>, a Roman Catholic, also had one printed. There is a newer one made by the Protestants. There are also those prepared by the Teachers of the Roman Church: one of the New Testament by Hieronymus Emser, one of the whole Bible by Johannes Dietemberger, and another by Kaspar Ulenberg in the year 1630.

16. There are several in Dutch; the best is that which was published by order of the Synod of Dort <note>original: "Synode van Dordrecht." This refers to the *Statenvertaling* or States Translation, the most influential Dutch Bible.</note>, with notes, in the year 1637.

17. There have been many in Italian; Jacobus de Voragine <note>original: "J. de Voragine."</note>, Archbishop of Genoa, made one around the year 1290. Niccolò Malermi <note>original: "Nicolas Malermi."</note> another. The first printing is from the year 1471. There are two others from 1477. Antonio Bruccioli had one printed in the year 1530; it was dedicated in the year 1540 to the Duchess of Ferrara <note>Renée of France (1510–1574), a supporter of the Reformation.</note>. A New Testament in Lyon,

<column-break/>

dedicated to Francesco de' Medici in 1556. Diodati <note>Giovanni Diodati (1576–1649), a Swiss-born Italian Protestant theologian.</note>, Professor at Geneva, produced one, the first edition of which came to light in the year 1607. The second in 1641. This latter translation is exceptionally well-approved; the added notes by this learned man are of great utility.

<margin>Christian Holt, regarding the various editions of the Bible.</margin>

18. There have been versions in Irish <note>original: "Yersch."</note>, which are attributed to the famous Bedell <note>William Bedell (1571–1642), an Anglican bishop who translated the Old Testament into Irish.</note>; in Icelandic <note>original: "Ylandsch."</note>, which is said to be the old Norwegian or Gothic language; in Finnish or Lappish, printed in 1648; in Polish in 1563, 1572, 1577, 1599; in Danish in 1524; in Swedish by Laurentius Petri, Archbishop of Uppsala, in 1646—he published the translation of the New Testament in the year 1523, etc.

19. Finally, there have been many in French. A portion of the Bible was translated, as is believed, by Nicole Oresme <note>original: "Nicolas Oreme."</note>, who died in the year 1377, under King Charles V. One can still see, in the Library of Geneva, a translation by a Canon named Guyart des Moulins <note>original: "Guyar des Moulins."</note> from the year 1294. The first French Bible was printed by order of Charles VIII, to whom it had been dedicated before the year 1498, being the translation of Guyart. It has also been noted that the first printing of a whole Bible, according to the text of the Vulgate, is that which was published in Antwerp in the year 1530 by Merten de Keyser <note>original: "Martinus de Keyzer."</note> with the privilege of Charles V.

Pierre Robert Olivétan <note>original: "Robbert Olivetanus."</note> had one printed at Neuchâtel in the year 1535. Calvin revised it, and it was reprinted in 1553 by Robert Estienne. Cornelius Bertram, with several Teachers of the Church of Geneva, improved it in the year 1588; and from that time forward, it has been cleared of outdated French words in each new edition.

The theologians of Louvain made a French translation in the year 1557, which was published by Plantin <note>Christophe Plantin (c. 1520–1589), a prominent printer in Antwerp.</note> with two privileges from the King of Spain, at Antwerp in 1578 and at Lyon in 1585.

Sebastian Castellio also had one printed in 1555. And René Benoît, a Doctor in Paris, in 1566, whose translation was favored by the Faculty of Paris and by Gregory XIII by a bull of November 3, 1575. Everyone knows that in our time Mr. de Sacy (whose name is Isaac le Maistre) has brought the Bible to light with observations, which was continued by P. Thomas, Lord of Fossé.

Most of these aforementioned translators, who have translated the Old and New...

# DIVINITY. BOOK I. CHAPTER XXVII.

...have also translated the New Testament; I will therefore only add here those translators who, having made no translations of the Old Testament, have devoted themselves to the translation of the New.

There is a Syriac translation of the New Testament which is considered very old—even by the Evangelist Mark, according to the opinion of the Syrians; though this is without foundation. Others attribute a great antiquity to it and believe it was made not long after the death of the Apostles; others are of the opinion that it is new, which they deduce from certain words; and some are of the mind that it dates from the 5th or 6th century. The first printing was that of Albert Widmanstadt <note>original: "Albert Widmanstad," a German diplomat and Orientalist.</note> in Vienna, 1562, from a manuscript brought by one P. Merdin, sent by Ignatius, Patriarch of the sect of the Jacobites <note>A West Syrian Christian group; "P. Merdin" likely refers to the Patriarch of Mardin.</note>; the second is by Tremellius in Hebrew letters, by H. Estienne in 1569; the third by Martin Trostius, in Syriac, 1621; the fourth by Gilles Gutbier in small format, Hamburg, 1663. Pococke <note>Edward Pococke (1604–1691), an English Orientalist.</note> was the first to publish the four General Epistles in Syriac.

Bede <note>The Venerable Bede (c. 673–735), an English monk and scholar.</note> translated the Gospel of John into the common language of his country.

Sebastian Münster <note>A German cartographer and Hebraist.</note> had a Gospel printed in Hebrew, which Jean du Tillet, Bishop of St. Brieuc, had reprinted in 1555. In the year 1668, the four Evangelists were printed in Rouen, translated into Hebrew by Giovanni Battista Jonas, a well-known Jew who dedicated his work to Pope Clement IX.

Erasmus made a Latin translation of the New Testament in Basel; the first appeared in 1516 and the second in 1518. Theodore Beza published one in 1564, which he dedicated to Queen Elizabeth of England.

Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>A French humanist and theologian.</note> published a new Latin translation of the letters of Paul, Paris, 1531.

There is a Spanish New Testament by Francisco de Enzinas <note>original: "Francois Enzinas," a Protestant reformer also known as Dryander.</note>, 1542; another in Venice, 1556; the translator entirely rejects the reading of the Gospel in a language that the people do not understand.

A New Testament in common Greek <note>Demotic or modern Greek, as opposed to the Koine of the original.</note> was published in Geneva in 1638.

The learned Ussher <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), Archbishop of Armagh.</note> translated one into Persian.

In French, there are many, besides those already mentioned, such as the French Bible of P. Besse, Paris, 1608; that of P. Frison, Canon at Reims, Paris, 1620; and that of J. Corbin, Advocate in the Parliament of Paris, 1641.

Some note that the French, more than 800 years ago, translated their Gospel into their old language, which was then the Teutonic <note>Referring to the Germanic roots of early French culture, specifically Frankish.</note>.

Father Veron published a French translation of the New Testament in the year 1647; Michel de Marolles, Abbot of Villeloin, in the years 1649, 1653, and 1666; Father Amelotte in 1666; Godeau, Bishop of Vence, in 1668. Everyone knows the translation of Mons, 1667 <note>A famous Jansenist translation known for its literary quality.</note>. Monsieur Desmarets also published notes on the Bible in 1669.

Regarding the Arabic translations: Erpenius <note>Thomas Erpenius, a Dutch Orientalist.</note> published one in 1616 from a manuscript written by a Copt in the year 1171; one had already appeared in 1591 through the care of Gabriel Sionita.

There is a translation in Anglo-Saxon or old Gothic by Marshall, at Dordrecht, 1665.

The Muscovites <note>The Russians.</note> have a New Testament printed in their language at Ostrog <note>original: "Ostrovic," likely referring to the Ostrog Bible of 1581.</note>, 1581.

I have made this Register for those who do not possess the books of Father Simon, of Hottinger, and Monsieur Dupin, and of many others <note>The author cites the leading bibliographers and Bible scholars of the 17th century.</note>.

I shall add but a word to this. The translators of Scripture must not take for themselves the same freedom that the translators of secular writings use. For as soon as one exceeds the boundaries here, one makes not a translation but an expansion, wherein one often inserts one's own opinion and gives occasion to wandering spirits <note>i.e., heretics or the misguided.</note> to pervert the Scripture through their false explanations.

To speak now of the authority of translations, one must observe:

1. That no translation should be considered equal to the original text <note>original: "Grondtext"</note>; whether because translations have nothing remarkable that the original text does not have much better, or because the original words were written by the inspiration of God's Spirit, and the translations by men, who can err.

2. All translation must be tested against the original text. The translators have not always understood the Hebrew or Greek well, and often did not grasp the intent of God's Spirit.

3. Nevertheless, their authority is great with respect to the doctrines that are divine and the same as in the original text. I speak of—

<column-break/>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of biblical translations, moving from the history of specific versions like the Syriac and those of Bede or Münster to a theological and practical defense of the use of translations in the Christian faith.</meta>

->### THE CHRISTIAN GOD###<-

...of translations / which contain the essence of the Holy Scripture / concerning what is necessary for salvation. For if they do not provide the true sense in essential matters / they are no longer translations: One must clearly distinguish the sense of the scripture from the words.
<margin>In Galatians, ch. 1</margin>
,, Let us not think, said
,, Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 342–420), the translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note>, that the Gospel consists in the
,, words of the scripture; but in the
,, marrow, not in the leaves of the words,
,, but in the root of the reason. If
then the sense and the marrow are found in the translations / it is enough to guide our faith and morals / and to plant within us / through the powerful cooperation of God's Spirit / the Christian virtues. It is with translations / as with the pipes / through which the waters of a river flow / even if there is some defect in the pipes / that does not prevent us from obtaining through them a living water / springing up into Eternal life. Just as the rays of the Sun shine through some mist or darkness; so it is with the rays of the Sun of Righteousness <note>original: "Zonne der Geregtigheid," a biblical metaphor for Christ/God.</note> / if I may speak so; though they come to us through the darkness of translations / they nonetheless enlighten and warm the heart. Therefore we say / that the translations / in respect to the doctrine they contain / have the same authority / as the original text. Although the translation is human / the doctrine is Divine; the pipes are earthly / but there is an invaluable treasure / in these vessels. There is no translation so bad / if it is made with some sincerity and care / that it does not contain the essential truths / so that the simplest people find enough in it / for the building up of their faith.
<margin>Mestrezat’s treatise on the scripture <note>Jean Mestrezat (1592–1657), a French Protestant theologian.</note></margin>
It is well said / that God’s word is the seed of our rebirth; "But though men, among this seed, mix the weeds of their inventions, as long as it is not so much that it chokes the good seed; there will still be a Harvest for the Lord."

4. Finally, the various translations are useful / to discover the true sense of the original text: the labor of others helps us much. Thus we are convinced / that the translation of the LXX <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> has helped much in making other translations. The Greek of the writers of the New Testament is very similar to that of the LXX. Therefore one can find much in the idioms of the LXX to explain the expressions of the Apostles. We also have much

<column-break/>

reverence for this ancient translation / because the Apostles often used it / and cited the scripture according to this translation; which is why it is also highly regarded by the Church Fathers. Meanwhile, it is not to be equated with the original text / because the LXX are only to be seen as men / and not at all as Prophets; and because we are certain / that they committed errors in many places. Also, the Apostles did not always follow their translation / as can be gathered from Hosea 11:1 compared with Matthew 2:15; Jeremiah 31:15 with Matthew 2:18; Isaiah 53:4 with Matthew 8:17; Zechariah 9:9 and Matthew 21:5; Zechariah 13:7 and Mark 14:27; Psalm 22:1 and Matthew 27:46; Malachi 4:5 and Luke 1:17; Isaiah 63:12 and Mark 15:28; Isaiah 40:4 and Luke 3:5.

They followed them / when they expressed the sense well / at least the hidden sense / to accommodate the Jews and Heathens / whom they served equally; but in many places they abandoned this translation.

It is certain / that the LXX did not translate many places well. See Deuteronomy 29:19; Isaiah 53:10, 11; 63:5; 65:5; Habakkuk 1:11; Psalm 2:12; etc. To which we can add / that it is entirely uncertain / whether we have the correct translation of the LXX. Jerome acknowledged / that we do not have it in its pure form.

I end with these two remarks. 1. One cannot / with any reason / condemn the custom of the Protestants / who / in their public assemblies / read the Bible in a known Language. Father Simon <note>Richard Simon (1638–1712), a French priest and influential biblical critic.</note>, who condemns them in this / because they do not follow the custom of the Western Churches / nonetheless admits / that all Christians in general / in the beginning / read the Bible in a known Language. But is it not better / to follow the authority of the first Christians / which is grounded in reason / than that of the subsequent Christians / which seems so little reasonable? Secondly, it is as difficult / as giving a perfect translation. It is said that Henry III <note>King Henry III of France (1551–1589).</note>, asking Genebrard <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a French Benedictine exegete and Hebraist.</note> how much time and expense would be necessary for a good translation / received as an answer / 30 years, 30 Learned Men, in Languages and in Theology; and over 200,000 crowns for the expenses, and that even then one would still not have a work without defect and entirely perfect.

<summary>This page argues for the spiritual authority of Bible translations, asserting that the "marrow" or meaning of the text is divine even if the "pipes" (translations) are human and flawed. It also discusses the utility and limitations of the Septuagint and defends the Protestant practice of reading the Bible in the vernacular.</summary>

DIVINITY. I. B. XXVIII. Chapter.

## XXVIII. CHAPTER.

### On the Interpretation of the Scriptures.

Following the translations / the Order / requires speaking of the interpretations.
¶ I believe / that I [should mention] here some modes of speaking / that are commonly used / when speaking of the sense of the scripture / to explain it. There is nothing more common / than to hear speaking of the **Literal sense** <term>Literal sense: The direct meaning intended by the author, whether through plain language or metaphors.</term> of a passage: but several descriptions are given of it. The most common is / that the literal sense / is the first / which God’s Spirit had as his objective; whether expressed in proper / or in improper and figurative words. One calls the **hidden sense** / that which is not discovered by the simple reading of the words. For example: Paul teaches us / that the history of Sarah and Hagar signifies the two covenants; that is the hidden sense. Not to bring up here the distinctions of the **Scholastic Theologians** <note>Medieval academics who developed highly structured systems of logic and theology.</note> regarding this / who commonly divide this sense further into an **Allegorical** one, such as the History of Sarah and Hagar in Galatians 4:24. For Paul brings the literal sense to the spiritual / consisting in the signifying of the two covenants; into a **Tropological** one <term>Tropological sense: A moral interpretation that applies the text to human conduct and ethics.</term>, when one applies the words of the scripture / to the improvement of our morals. As Paul in 1 Corinthians 9:9-10 applies to the ministers of the Gospel that which Moses had said / that one must not muzzle a threshing Ox. And an **Anagogical** sense <term>Anagogical sense: A mystical or spiritual interpretation that points toward the future state of glory or eternal life.</term> / when one applies the words of the old Prophets to the future state of happiness. Just as Paul brings home to the eternal rest in Hebrews 4:9 / that which David had said in Psalm 95:11.
1. To succeed well in the interpretation of the holy Books / and to discover the sense of a passage / it is above all necessary / to turn oneself to GOD / and to pray with David /
<margin>Psalm 109:18. <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 119:18.</note></margin>Open my eyes that I may behold the wonders of your law. For the same spirit / that inspired the Writers / must give us the understanding of that which they have put to paper. No one also knows the things of God, except the Spirit of God. 1 Corinthians 2:11.
2. One must strive to clear one's understanding of all prejudices / and propose to oneself only the seeking of truth: for if one is only out / to excel through new opinions / it is not possible / that one succeeds well in the interpretation of the scripture; at

<column-break/>

least / that happens very rarely. It is the same / when one, full of prejudices for the Religion / in which one is born / wishes to find it in God's Word; be it as it may / one must guard against ever making an interpretation / that gives us unbecoming thoughts of God. This was not understood by those **errant spirits** <note>A reference to Anthropomorphites, who believed God possessed a physical body.</note> / who / under the pretext that the scripture speaks of hands / feet / and eyes / attributed to God a body / like ours. This observation is necessary / to explain such passages / where it is said that God rises up / and descends; that he said to Shimei; curse David, and other ways of speaking / which one must explain in a manner becoming of God / as we shall see more broadly elsewhere.
4. One must investigate / what occasion gave the Writers cause for using these modes of speaking: for they have often borrowed their expressions from occurring occasions: Christ
<margin>John 4:10-14.</margin>speaks with the Samaritan Woman of Grace / under the Symbol of Water / because he was by the Well of Jacob. He compares himself to a Heavenly bread / speaking to the Multitudes / for whom he had multiplied the Loaves
<margin>John 6:35.</margin>and after he had dealt with the Manna. Some Scholars believe / that he, on the occasion of the **Feast of Tabernacles** <note>A Jewish festival (Sukkot) involving the ritual drawing of water from the Pool of Siloam.</note>, in which the custom was / to draw Waters from the Fountain of Siloam /
<margin>* John 7:38.</margin>says to the bystanders / * Rivers shall flow from their belly. Seeing the Vineyards, with which Palestine was full /
<margin>† John 15:1.</margin>he calls himself a Vine. † And writing to the Congregations of Ephesus and
<margin>‡ Revelation 2:7 and 11.</margin>Pergamum, ‡ he promises to those who shall overcome / to give to eat of the Tree of Life and the hidden Manna / to set this Heavenly nourishment against that which the **Nicolaitans** <note>An early Christian sect accused of compromise with pagan practices, specifically eating food sacrificed to idols.</note>, who had introduced themselves into these two congregations / taught to bring people to the eating of that which was sacrificed to Idols / in the Feast-meals of the Heathens. This observation is / as one sees / necessary to understand well the sense of a Prophecy / or of an Epistle. One must investigate the state / of those / to whom the Prophets proclaimed God’s Word / to whom the Apostles wrote / what their sentiments and conduct were; and this is also of great importance / for explaining the Parables.
5. One must not give too much extensiveness to the words / nor to God's Spirit

...all that one wishes to make it say, as if the Spirit had two opposite goals at the same time. One must observe what the words naturally signify, without doing them violence.

6. To this end, one must pay attention to what precedes and follows: just as lawyers do regarding their laws; for they say that one must never judge a law without having read it in its entirety.

7. One must not narrow the aim of God's Spirit too strictly, as if there were always only one: for in many places there are several. For example, Isaiah 9:1: *The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light.* Without doubt, this prophecy <note>original: "Godspraak"</note> looks: 1. To the time of the Old Dispensation <term>Old Dispensation: the era of the Old Testament and the law of Moses before the coming of Christ</term>, when the Jewish people were delivered into the Babylonian captivity. 2. To the time of the coming of the Messiah, as Matthew notes in Matthew 4:16. And there is nothing to prevent us from also applying it to the time of the Blessed Resurrection, when the dead shall come forth from the grave. I say the same of the wonderful vision of Ezekiel 37 <note>This refers to the "Vision of the Valley of Dry Bones," which the author suggests can be interpreted as both a national restoration for Israel and a prophecy of the physical resurrection of the dead.</note>.

8. One must not depart from the literal and natural sense without necessity, but only when it cannot be accepted without falling into great absurdities.

Origen <note>Origen (c. 184–253 AD) was an early Christian scholar known for his "allegorical" method of interpretation, looking for hidden spiritual meanings behind every word of the Bible.</note> is unbearable in his allegories; his way of explaining the Creation cannot be sustained. It was somewhat the disease of the early Church Fathers to seek mysteries and allegories everywhere, as Augustine <note>Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential theologians in Western Christianity.</note> often notes. "If," he says, "in God's words, or in those of a Prophet, there is an expression that cannot be understood literally without absurdity, then one must without doubt take it figuratively, as signifying something else. And if it is a command that forbids some evil, or commands something good, such as a benefit, then the presentation is not figurative. But if it appears that it commands some evil or sin, and forbids something good as a benefit, then the presentation is to be taken in a figurative sense. Christ says, *unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you.* It seems that he commands us something sinful and improper. Yet it is a veiled way of speaking, which commands us to have communion in his suffering;

<column-break/>

contemplating for our comfort and benefit that his flesh was crucified and wounded for our sins." Origen adds to this, concerning John 6:53: *Unless you eat my flesh*, etc., "It is a letter that kills," he says, "if taken literally, but taken spiritually, there is a life-giving Spirit in it."

When Christ commands us to pluck out our right eye, to cut off the hand, etc., he does not desire that we be our own executioners, so that this must by no means be taken literally. But when the words include nothing that conflicts with other places of Scripture or the light of sound reason, one need not seek a figurative sense. One should also take good note that when one is required to take a passage of Scripture in a figurative sense, one should not give it an explanation that weakens its meaning. For example, Christ commands us in Matthew 5:29 a duty that is certainly more contrary to the flesh than the loss of an eye, etc. Namely, the killing of our most beloved passions and the forsaking of our dearest idols. When he says in verse 39, *If anyone strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also*, he commands us something incomparably more than merely turning the cheek to the one who wants to strike us; it is the patience that he commends to us, to rather endure all misfortune and insult—so far as one can do with a good conscience—than to defend ourselves with force and violence.

9. One must compare the dark passages with the clear and similar-sounding ones; the one gives light to the other.

10. It is necessary to consult the original text and understand the languages, in order to weigh and consider all the words well.

It is even necessary to investigate the various meanings of the Hebrew words. One is surprised when reading of the Beth-shemites in 1 Samuel 6:19 that God struck seventy men (and) fifty thousand men; so it stands in our translation. But learned men believe that, according to what this history makes known to us, the text can be translated thus: that there were 70 people whom God caused to die, namely 50 out of 1000, and they estimate that there were 1400 criminals, of whom God struck only 70. One is surprised when reading in 1 Kings 4:26 that Solomon had 40,000 stalls for horses, but the learned think...

# THEOLOGY. BOOK I. CHAPTER XXVIII.

...that one can very well translate it as 4,000, which is consistent. People are surprised that during the siege of Samaria 
<margin>2 Kings 6:25</margin>
**Dove’s Dung** was eaten: but one quickly recovers from this surprise when informed by linguists that it was a type of so-called **legume** <note>The author is referring to a long-standing debate where "dove's dung" is interpreted not as animal waste, but as a vernacular name for a plant, such as the Star-of-Bethlehem (Ornithogalum umbellatum) or a type of chickpea.</note>.

Ignorance of the languages has caused many Church Fathers to commit many errors. In translations, there are turns of phrase that seem jarring, but which cause no difficulty in Hebrew. Every language has its particular expressions. One must not skip even the smallest prepositions, but rather investigate the true sense they must have in the specific passage being explained.

For example, Genesis 8:21 has given much trouble to interpreters:
> I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake, says the LORD: **for** the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth.

One cannot understand why God would not want to curse men *because* they are evil, since he had poured out the flood upon them for that very same reason. But the difficulty is removed if one notes that the preposition translated as *for* <note>original Dutch: "want"</note> also means *although* <note>original Dutch: "hoewel"</note>, so that one may translate these words in this way:
> I will no longer curse the earth because of man; **although** the imagination of his heart is evil from his youth.

It is useful to understand the languages that have some similarity to and depend upon Hebrew, such as Chaldean, Syriac, and Arabic. Many words are found only once in the Scriptures, the true sense of which cannot be discovered except through the connection they have with others in different languages, or through the nature of the matter over which there is a dispute.

Thus, it is judged that Job 39:29 <note>In most modern Bibles, this is verse 19.</note> should be translated: *Have you clothed his neck with a mane?* speaking of a horse.

12. One ought to consult the ancient translations, and especially that of the **LXX** <term>LXX: The Septuagint, the oldest Greek translation of the Hebrew Old Testament, traditionally said to be the work of 70 or 72 scholars.</term>, because the writers of the New Testament followed its style closely. The other translations also have their uses.

For example, there is a passage in Genesis 11:26 and 32 that greatly hinders scholars when compared with Acts 7:4. Genesis 11:26 states: *Terah lived 70 years, and begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran:* and verse 32 says *the days of Terah were 205 years.* From this, it appears that Terah was 145

<column-break/>

years old when Abraham took his leave of him, and that he lived for another 60 years after that. For it is said there that Terah was 70 years old when he had Abraham, and Abraham was 75 when he left his father. 70 plus 75 makes 145, which still lacks 60 years before one reaches 205. This now runs contrary to what Stephen testifies in Acts 7:3 and 4, that God made Abraham depart from Haran after the death of Terah. How can one say that Terah was dead if he lived for 60 years after that? Scholars are divided on this. Some believe that Abraham moved out of Haran twice: 1. After his first calling. 2. After the death of Terah. For it is assumed that he came back to Haran to be present at the death of his father and to take his inheritance. They maintain that Stephen speaks of the second departure. But other interpreters believe the difficulty is entirely removed if one follows the Samaritan translation, which explicitly indicates that Terah lived only 145 years. In the Samaritan translation of Exodus 12:40, it says:

<margin>Stillingfleet, Letter to the Deist</margin>
*The time of the dwelling of the children of Israel and of their fathers, in the Land of Canaan and Egypt, was 430 years,* which solves a great difficulty. Namely, that the 430 years spoken of in Exodus 7 <note>The author likely means Exodus 12:40.</note> includes not only the time of Israel's stay in Egypt—which was not 430 years—as the Hebrew text seems to imply.

13. One must always investigate whether the sense given to a passage clashes with the truths clearly contained in Scripture. If it were so, a false sense would follow; for it is certain that the Holy Spirit never contradicts itself.

<margin>Matthew 26:26</margin>
Therefore, we cannot explain the words of Christ, **"This is my body,"** as the Roman Church does; because their explanation is against the nature of the matter in dispute and runs counter to many other passages.

And if it is a commandment that forbids some evil, or commands something good, like a charitable act, then the representation is not figurative. But if it seems that it commands some evil or sin, and forbids something good as a charitable act, then the representation is to be taken in a figurative sense.

<margin>Book 3, On Christian Doctrine</margin>

> “Christ says: *Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you.* It seems that he commands us something sinful and improper. But it is a figurative manner of speaking <term>figurative manner of speaking: an expression where the words are not meant to be taken at face value</term>, which commands us to have communion in his suffering;

<column-break/>

> reflecting for our comfort and benefit that his flesh was crucified and wounded for our sins.” Origen adds to this, concerning John 6:53 <margin>John 6</margin>: *If you do not eat my Flesh, etc.* “It is a letter that kills,” he says, “if taken literally, but taken Spiritually, there is a life-giving Spirit in it.”

When Christ commands us to pluck out our right eye, to cut off the hand, etc., he does not desire that we be our own executioners; thus, this must by no means be taken literally. But if the words include nothing that conflicts with other passages of Scripture or the light of sound reason, one need not seek a figurative sense. One should also take good care that, when one is required to take a Scripture passage in a figurative sense, one does not give it an explanation that weakens its meaning. For example, Christ commands us in Matthew 5:29 a duty that is certainly more contrary to the Flesh <term>the Flesh: a biblical term for human nature's worldly or sinful inclinations</term> than the loss of an Eye, etc. Namely, the killing of our cherished passions and the forsaking of our dearest Idols. When he says in verse 39: *Whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also*, he commands us something incomparably more than simply turning the cheek to one who wants to strike us; it is the patience that he commends to us, to rather endure all injustice and insult—as much as one can do with a good conscience—than to defend ourselves with force and violence.

9. One must compare the dark passages with the clear and similar-sounding ones; one gives light to the other.

10. It is necessary to consult the original text and to understand the languages, in order to properly weigh and consider all the words.

It is even necessary to investigate the various meanings of the Hebrew words. One is amazed when one reads in 1 Samuel 6:19 regarding the people of Beth-shemesh <note>original: "Bethzemiten"</note> that God struck seventy men (and) fifty thousand men; so it stands in our translation. But learned men believe that, according to what this history makes known to us, the text can be translated thus: that there were 70 people whom God caused to die, namely 50 out of 1000; and they estimate that there were 1400 criminals, of whom God struck only 70. One is amazed when one reads in 1 Kings 4:26 that Solomon had 40,000 stalls for horses, but the Scholars believe that...

<margin>2 Kings 6:25.</margin>
"Dove’s Dung" was eaten: but one quickly recovers from this wonder when informed by linguists that it was a type of so-called legume <note>original: "Peul-vrugt." Scholars often identify this as the "Star of Bethlehem" plant (Ornithogalum umbellatum), whose bulbs were sometimes called dove's dung.</note>.

Ignorance of languages has caused many Church Fathers <note>The influential early Christian theologians of the first few centuries.</note> to make many errors. And translations are modes of speech that may seem jarring, but which present no difficulty in the Hebrew. Every language has its particular expressions. One must not skip even the smallest preposition, but investigate the true sense they must have in the passage being explained. For example, Genesis 8:21 has given much trouble to interpreters. *I will no longer curse the earth because of man,* says the LORD: *For the imagination of his heart is evil from his youth.* One cannot understand why God would not want to curse men because they are evil, since he had poured out the flood upon them for that very reason. But the difficulty is removed if one observes that the preposition translated as *for* or *because* <note>The Hebrew word "ki."</note> also means *although*; so that one can translate these words in this way: *I will no longer curse the earth because of man; although the imagination of his heart is evil from his youth.*

It is useful to understand the languages that have some similarity to and depend upon Hebrew: such as Chaldean <term>Chaldean: Also known as Aramaic, the language spoken by Jews after the Babylonian exile.</term>, Syriac, and Arabic. Many words are found only once in the Scriptures <note>These are known as "hapax legomena."</note>, the true meaning of which cannot be discovered except through the connection they have with others in different languages; or through the nature of the matter over which there is a dispute.

Thus, one judges Job 39:29 <note>In most modern English Bibles, this is Job 39:19.</note> should be translated: *Hast thou clothed his neck with a mane?* speaking of a horse.

12. One ought to consult the ancient translations, and especially that of the LXX <term>Septuagint (LXX): The earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Old Testament, frequently quoted by the authors of the New Testament.</term>, because the writers of the New Testament followed its style closely. The other translations also have their utility.

For example, there is a passage in Genesis 11:26 and 32 which greatly encumbers scholars when compared with Acts 7:4. Genesis 11:26 states: *Terah lived 70 years, and begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran:* and verse 32 says *the days of Terah were 205 years.* From this, it appears that Terah was 145 years old when Abraham took his

<column-break/>

leave of him; and that he lived for another 60 years thereafter. For it is said there that Terah was 70 years old when he had Abraham, and Abraham was 75 when he left his father. 70 plus 75 makes 145; there are still 60 years missing before one reaches 205. This now runs contrary to what Stephen testifies in Acts 7:3 and 4, that God made Abraham depart from Haran after the death of Terah. How can one say that Terah was dead if he lived for another 60 years after that? Scholars are divided on this. Some believe that Abraham departed from Haran twice: 1. After his first calling. 2. After the death of Terah. For it is supposed that he returned to Haran to be present at the death of his father and to take his inheritance. They maintain that Stephen speaks of the second departure. But other interpreters believe that the difficulty is entirely removed if one follows the Samaritan translation <term>Samaritan Pentateuch: A version of the first five books of the Bible preserved by the Samaritan community, which often contains different chronological data than the standard Hebrew text.</term>, which explicitly indicates that Terah lived only 145 years. In the Samaritan translation, Exodus 12:40 reads: *The time of the dwelling of the children of Israel*
<margin>Stillingfleet, Letter to a Deist.</margin>
*and of their fathers, in the Land of Canaan and Egypt, was 430 years,* which solves a great difficulty. Namely, that the 430 years spoken of in Exodus 12 includes not only the time of Israel's stay in Egypt—which was not 430 years—as the Hebrew text seems to imply.

13. One must always examine whether the sense one gives to a passage does not conflict with the truths clearly contained in Scripture. If it were so, a false meaning would follow; for it is certain that the Holy Spirit never contradicts Himself. Matthew

<margin>26:26.</margin>

15. To understand the New Testament well, one must compare it with the Old Testament; and to understand the Old Testament well, one must compare it with the New Testament. Most expressions in the New Testament are found in the Old Testament, and the prophecies of the Old Testament are explained in the New.

16. One must know the customs of the Jews: through them, many passages can be explained.

Thus one can explain Matthew 16:19, where Christ speaks of giving the keys of his Kingdom to Peter. This is likely an allusion to the keys given to Jewish Teachers <note>Rabbis</note> to publicly testify that they were recognized as capable of instructing others and explaining mysteries. They were told: *Receive the power of binding and loosing,* or of saying what is forbidden and what is permitted.

<margin>Luke 16:23</margin>
The mention of "Abraham's bosom" in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus is very well explained by the custom of Jewish banquets. There, the guests were placed in such a way that the one to whom they wished to show great honor leaned against the chest or "bosom" of the most prominent person in the company. Thus it is said that John lay in the bosom of Jesus when he held his last supper with his disciples, because Jesus loved him. What is said in Matthew 5:22 about "the judgment," the "Great Council," and "hellfire" is very well explained by the various courts of law that existed among the Jews. But one must be careful to ensure that the customs referenced are not from later times than the era of the Apostles. In the Talmud and the writings of modern Jews, there are many things that were unknown in the time of the Apostles.

17. It is also very useful to know the customs of other nations who were mingled among God’s people and the Church.

When Moses speaks of Egypt in Deuteronomy 11:10, he says it was a land that Israel "watered with its gait"; or, as the Hebrew says, "with its foot," as some translate it. To understand this, one must know that the Egyptians, to moisten their fields and gardens, used a machine into which

<column-break/>

a man climbed, who caused the machine to turn by treading a wheel, in order to bring the water where it needed to be.

<margin>note 7, book IV</margin>
Revelation 3:4 speaks of those who will walk with Christ in white garments. Some have believed this was an allusion to a custom used among the Jews when someone was appointed to the priesthood. According to their teachers, they would investigate the genealogy and other required qualities of the candidate. If he was found unfit, he was sent back in a black garment; but if found fit, he was dressed in white—the priestly attire—in which he joined his companions in processing toward the Temple. However, other scholars believe it is an allusion to the honors shown to victors among the Pagans. They were dressed in radiant garments, their names were recorded in the public records, and a herald went before them proclaiming their praise. This view seems more reasonable than the previous one. The passage reads as follows:

<margin>Revelation 3:5</margin>
> He who overcomes shall be clothed in white garments, and I will by no means blot out his name from the Book of Life; but I will confess his name before my Father and before His angels.

Paul says in 1 Corinthians 4:9: *For I think that God has displayed us, the apostles, last, as men condemned to death.* It is probable that he is referring to those who were brought last into the arenas to fight wild beasts while naked. And when he adds in verse 13, *We have been made as the offscouring of the world and the scrapings of all things,* some scholars believe he refers to those wretches chosen by the Pagans from the most dishonorable dregs of the people to be sacrificed. They believed their sins were wiped away by the death and blood of these men. These people were fed the best food at public expense for a year, and then, after being scourged seven times and loaded with a thousand curses, they were burned alive. Over their ashes, which were cast into the sea, the very words the Apostle uses were spoken: <term>peripsēma hēmōn genou</term> <note>Greek: περίψημα ἡμῶν γένου, meaning "be our offscouring" or "be our purification."</note>.

<margin>Revelation 2:17</margin>
When Revelation 2:17 speaks of the "white stone," it alludes to the manner in which the Greeks cast their votes in capital trials. The white stone was the sign of acquittal and release—

# DIVINE THEOLOGY. BOOK I. CHAPTER XXIX.

success. What Paul says in 1 Corinthians 9:24-25 about those who run in the racecourse, and about the sober lifestyle of the wrestlers <note>original: "wortellaars", here referring to athletes or competitors in the Greek games</note>, is taken from the customs of the Greeks. Without this knowledge, one cannot understand many of the figures of speech in the Scriptures.

<margin>Revelation 16:12</margin>
18. It is therefore also necessary to be experienced in secular <note>original: "ongewyde", meaning non-sacred or profane</note> histories. Revelation 16:12 foretells that the Euphrates will dry up to allow Kings to pass through. This is an allusion to the military ruse by which Cyrus made himself master of Babylon, having cut the Euphrates into many small water channels to drain it.

<margin>1 Corinthians 15:29</margin>
19. One must not imagine that they can always be certain of having hit upon the best meaning. There are many places from which one can determine nothing for certain. For example, one can never know for sure what it means to be "baptized for the dead" in 1 Corinthians 15:29. It is possible that among the many interpretations offered, there is one true one; but which one it is, one cannot precisely determine. Who knows what Paul’s "thorn in the flesh" is? Who is certain that they have resolved all the difficulties found in the genealogies of Christ? How many things remain unresolved regarding the Tabernacle of Moses and Solomon’s Temple? Who can boast of knowing certainly what is to be understood by the struggle of the Archangel Michael with Satan regarding the body of Moses? How many obscurities are there in the visions and prophecies of the Prophets, and of John in particular?

20. One must not think that it is the same with the inspired <note>original: "gedoopte", literally "baptized" but used here to mean sacred or divinely guided</note> writers as it is with secular authors, who do not concern themselves much with the choice of their words, and who use expressions regarding created things that one ought not use except in regard to God.

21. One must ensure that interpretations are not forced or too far-fetched. The conjectures that appear the most learned are not always the best. There are those who, to appear learned, give interpretations that have little in common with the nature of the matter.

<margin>1 Kings 7:23; 2 Chronicles 4:2</margin>
22. Just as Scripture was not given to instruct us in Geometry <note>original: "Meetkunst"</note>, one should not be surprised if there are sometimes things that seem to run contrary to geometric principles; one must not, therefore, immediately accuse Scripture of error. For example, we read that Solomon had a washing vat, or "Brazen Sea" <note>original: "kopere zee"</note>,

<column-break/>

<margin>(See Mr. Bernard Nieuwentijt, who proves this completely by showing that the circle-round shape, being a round, agrees with Geometry.)</margin>
made, measuring 10 cubits in diameter and 30 in circumference. Those among the mathematicians know that the ratio of the circumference to the diameter is more than three to one. Yet one can explain this passage in such a way that it does not contradict the principles of geometry: by saying that the diameter was *almost* 10 cubits, and the circumference *almost* 30; the diameter a little less, and the circumference a little more. In this way, many places regarding the construction of the Temple and other matters of natural science can be clarified.

One could add other remarks and rules here, but these shall suffice. We intend to deal with those in another work, if it pleases God.

It remains for me only to note that all these means I have pointed out are not equally necessary. For I am convinced that a person without learning, who does not understand the original languages and has only a simple translation, will be well able to understand the meaning of Scripture regarding what is necessary for his salvation, and that must be enough for him.

## CHAPTER XXIX.

### Whether any Book of Scripture is lost?

<margin>Socinus, *Sacred Lectures*; Smalcius *against Franz*, disputation 7, *On Good Works*; Volkelius, Book 1, chapter 5; *On Religion*, IV, *On the Word of God*, chapter 4, etc.</margin>
Before we depart from our treatise on the Scriptures, we shall investigate a few more questions.

The first is whether any Book of the scriptures is lost, or whether we have them all?

Before we answer this, it is necessary to note that, even if one granted that some book is lost, Scripture would not, for that reason, be any less a perfect Rule for our faith and morals. This is because the things necessary for salvation are generally so abundantly spread throughout it that the Church could do without many of these Books without harm; in the same way that people can very well abstain from various foods given by God for the maintenance of their lives. Our Heavenly Father has not only provided what is necessary, but he has granted us the necessary in abundance, and made his grace toward us overflow in all wisdom and understanding. Under the Old Testament, the Books of Moses alone were enough for the salvation of the Church. Even if we had the [letter...] <meta>catchword: brief (letter)</meta>

This observation is necessary for many reasons; but particularly to teach us that we must not believe that those who doubted some Books were ignorant of what is necessary for salvation. If they did not learn of the Priesthood of Christ from the Epistle to the Hebrews, they gathered it from the other letters of Paul. If they did not learn of the end of the world and the second coming of Christ from the second letter of Peter, they could have drawn it from Paul’s letters to the Thessalonians.

After this general observation, I say that nothing obliges us to believe that any books have been lost. And it is even unlikely that Providence, which always watches over the salvation of the Church, would have permitted this loss; and that the Church would have been so careless regarding God's word. Everyone knows the zeal the Jews had for these Holy Books, and the care they took that not a single letter was added or taken away. On the other hand, we do not deny that many Books were written by the holy Writers that are no longer found; but one could not prove that these Books were composed by the inspiration of God. mix with fornicators <note>The author is discussing 1 Corinthians 5:9, where Paul says, "I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people."</note>. For although some believe that this letter is distinct from the two others to the Corinthians, I do not see that it is necessary to arrive at this thought, since one can very well say that Paul speaks of the letter he was then writing. I quite approve of the opinion of those who translate the words thus: **I am writing to you by this letter, that you do not mix**, etc.

This translation, however, has two difficulties: 1. In the original text it says, *I have written* <note>original: "Ik heb u geschreeven," referring to the Greek aorist *egrapsa*</note>; 2. It seems that the Apostle in verse 11 contrasts what he is writing now with what he had already written. *But now*, he says, *I am writing to you that you do not mix*. This is easily resolved: for first, besides it being common to use the past tense for the present according to the manner of the Hebrews, it is clear that the word over which the dispute exists must be translated by the present tense. *Now*, he says, *I write to you*; in the Greek, *I have written*. Secondly, nothing prevents us from saying that this word does not signify a different time, as if Paul wrote something other than what he had written before; rather, he only explains what he intended to write. It is as if he had said: *I write to you then*, etc.

Objection: 2 Corinthians 13:1. *This is the third time I am coming to you.* But one can understand this such that he had often prepared himself to come to them, as he had said in Chapter 12:14; or that he spoke to them of the same matter for the third time, namely, that he would not spare them if he came to them.

II. There are books that are believed to have been composed by men inspired by God's Spirit, which were nevertheless not written *by* them, but *to* them. Thus we believe that Colossians 4:16 must be understood, where Paul says: *When this epistle has been read among you, see that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans; and that you likewise read the one written from Laodicea.* This refers to a forged letter to the Laodiceans, which is found in some Bibles of the Anabaptists <term>Anabaptists: A radical Reformation group known for adult baptism; the author suggests they included non-canonical texts</term>.

Some scholars have believed that it was the first letter to Timothy, because the subscription <note>The "subscription" is a postscript found in some ancient manuscripts indicating where a letter was written</note> indicates that it was written from Laodicea. But besides the fact that the subscriptions were not composed by the Apostle, it appears through the letter to the Colossians that the Apostle had not been to Laodicea, or at least

<column-break/>

it seems so from Colossians 2:1. *For I want you to know what a great conflict I have for you and those in Laodicea, and for as many as have not seen my face in the flesh.* Other scholars have believed that it was the letter to the Ephesians, of which they had sent a copy to the Laodiceans, and of which the Laodiceans also had to send one to the Colossians. But I hold with those who believe that it was a letter from the Laodiceans to Paul, which the Apostle desired to be shared with the Colossians for their edification.

It will be said that it appears some books are lost, such as the *Prophecy of Enoch*, Jude 14. But it is not said there that Enoch wrote it down. His prophecy was possibly preserved through the following ages <note>i.e., through oral tradition</note> or revealed to Jude. I say the same of the struggle of Michael with Satan over the body of Moses—unless one prefers to say that Jude alludes to Zechariah 3:2.

<margin>2 Pet. 2:5.</margin> Noah is called the *Preacher of righteousness*, yet it does not follow from this that his sermons have been lost.

It will be said that it is nowhere found among the Prophets that the Messiah should be called a *Nazarene*, Matthew 2:23. But, without bringing up all the opinions of theologians—who believe that Matthew alludes to Genesis 49:26, or to Judges 13:5, or to Isaiah 11:1 <note>The Hebrew word for "Branch" in Isaiah 11:1 is *Netzer*, which sounds like Nazarene</note>—one can very well say that there was a steadfast tradition among the Jews that the Prophets had said that the Messiah would bear the name of Nazarene.

Objection: various passages that are cited in the New Testament are not found in the Old Testament; such as 2 Timothy 3:8, Jude verses 9 and 14, Matthew 2:23 and 27:9, John 7:37, Ephesians 5:14, James 4:5, etc. Which is proof that the books in which these passages were found are lost. But 1. one could only conclude from this that they have been cut out from there, rather than saying that the books themselves are lost. 2. Meanwhile, it is not necessary to come to such an answer; since one can say that these passages, cited in the N.T., *are* in the O.T. <note>meaning they are paraphrased or combined</note>; or that they were things that were perhaps never written, but which were known through tradition, and which were possibly also revealed to the Apostles; just like that of Jannes and Jambres <note>The traditional names of the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses</note>, which is mentioned in the Chaldean paraphrase <note>original: "Chaldeeuwsche uitbreiding," referring to the Targum of Pseudo-Jonathan</note> (Fagius, *Jonathan ad Exodus 7:11*).

## DIVINE THEOLOGY. BOOK I. CHAPTER XXIX.

...associate with the sexually immoral. For although some believe that this letter is distinct from the other two to the Corinthians, I do not see that it is necessary to come to this conclusion, since one can very well say that Paul speaks of the letter he was then writing. I highly approve of the opinion of those who translate the words thus: *I am writing to you by this letter, that you should not associate*, etc. <note>The author is discussing 1 Corinthians 5:9, where Paul says "I wrote to you in my letter." Modern scholars still debate if this refers to a previous "lost" letter or the current one.</note>

This translation, however, faces two difficulties: first, in the original text it says, *I have written to you*; second, it seems that the Apostle in the 2nd verse contrasts what he is writing with what he had already written. *But now*, he says, *I write to you that you should not associate.* This is easily resolved: for regarding the first, besides the fact that it is common to use the past tense for the present, after the manner of the Hebrews <note>original: "naar de wyze der Hebreen"</note>; so it is clear that the word over which the dispute exists must be translated by the present tense. *Now*, he says, *I write to you*, in the Greek <note>original: "ik heb u geschreeven," referring to the Greek *egrapsa*</note>. Secondly, nothing prevents us from saying that this word "now" does not signify a different time, as if Paul wrote something other than what he had previously written; but he merely explains what he intended to write. It is as if he had said: *I write to you then*, etc.

Objection 2. 2 Corinthians 13:1. *This is the third time I am coming to you.* But one can understand this to mean that he had often prepared himself to come to them, as he had said in Chapter 12:14; or that he spoke to them of the same matter for the third time, namely, that he would not spare them if he came to them.

II. There are books which are thought to have been composed by men inspired by God's Spirit, which, however, were not written *by* them, but *to* them. Thus we believe that Colossians 4:16 must be understood, where Paul says: *And when this epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans; and that ye likewise read the epistle from Laodicea.* It is, then, a forged letter to the Laodiceans which is found in some Bibles of the Anabaptists <note>original: "Wederdopers"</note>.

Some scholars have believed that it was the first letter to Timothy, because the subscription indicates that it was written from Laodicea. But besides the fact that the subscriptions were not composed by the Apostle, it appears from the letter to the Colossians that the Apostle had not been to Laodicea, at least

<column-break/>

it seems so from Colossians 2:1. *For I would that ye knew what great conflict I have for you, and for them at Laodicea, and for as many as have not seen my face in the flesh.* Other scholars have believed that it was the letter to the Ephesians, of which they had sent a copy to the Laodiceans, and of which the Laodiceans were also to send one to the Colossians. But I hold with those who believe that it was a letter from the Laodiceans to Paul, which the Apostle desires to be shared with the Colossians for their edification.

It will be said that it appears some books are lost, such as the *Prophecy of Enoch*, Jude 14. But it is not said there that Enoch wrote. His prophecy was possibly preserved through the following ages or revealed to Jude. I say the same regarding the struggle of Michael with Satan over the body of Moses, unless one would rather say that Jude alludes to Zechariah 3:2.

<margin>2 Peter 2:5</margin>
Noah is called the "Preacher of righteousness," yet it does not follow from this that his sermons have been lost.

It will be said that it is found nowhere among the Prophets that the Messiah should be called a Nazarene, Matthew 2:23. But, without bringing up the opinions of theologians who believe that Matthew alludes to Genesis 49:26, or to Judges 13:5, or to Isaiah 11:1 <note>Isaiah 11:1 uses the word *Netser* (branch), which sounds like Nazarene—a common pun or wordplay in ancient interpretation.</note>, one can very well say that there was a steadfast tradition among the Jews that the Prophets had said the Messiah would bear the name of Nazarene.

Objection: several passages cited in the New Testament are not found in the Old Testament; such as 2 Timothy 3:8, Jude verses 9 and 14, Matthew 2:23, and 27:9, John 7:37, Ephesians 5:14, James 4:5, etc. Which is proof that the books in which these passages were found are lost. But 1. one could only conclude from this that they were cut off from there, rather than saying the books themselves are lost. 2. Meanwhile, it is not necessary to come to such an answer, since one can say that these passages, cited in the N.T., are in the O.T.; or that they were things that were perhaps never written, but were known through tradition, and which were possibly also revealed to the Apostles; like that of Jannes and Jambres <note>Jannes and Jambres are the traditional names given to the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses.</note>, mentioned in the Chaldean paraphrase <note>original: "Chaldeeuwsche uitbreiding," referring to the Targum; see Fagius's notes on Jonathan's Targum to Exodus 7:11.</note>.
