**T**he second question is whether the books of the Old Testament were burned in the destruction of Jerusalem when Nebuchadnezzar took that city. What gives rise to this is a passage from 4 Esdras 14:44 <note>In many English Bibles, this book is known as 2 Esdras. It is considered apocryphal—meaning it is not part of the official biblical canon.</note>, where it is said that Ezra, driven by God's Spirit, dictated 204 books word-for-word in 40 days to five assistants, who wrote with great speed from his mouth. It is claimed that in this way the scripture, which had once been consumed by fire, was restored to its original state.

But besides the fact that this book is falsely attributed to Ezra and is apocryphal and full of falsehoods—as we shall prove elsewhere—there are many things that clearly show it was impossible for all copies of the Holy Books to have been burned with the Temple.

I will not speak here of how unlikely it is that not a single Israelite would have taken the holy books with them when the Ten Tribes were carried away into Assyria by Nebuchadnezzar more than 130 years before the burning of the Temple. But I will only note:

1. That many God-fearing Israelites were carried away to Babylon with King Jehoiachin <note>original: "Joachim"</note> before the destruction of Jerusalem; it is beyond all likelihood that none of them would have taken care to bring the Holy Books with them.

2. It is also not probable that Jeremiah, to whom the Babylonians did no harm, would not have preserved the Books of the Law and the Prophets.

<margin>
Dan. IX:
2. and 13.
</margin>

3. It is explicitly said of Daniel that he saw from the books the number of the years of the captivity, in the first year of Darius. It also appears that he had the books of Moses during this captivity.

<column-break/>

<margin>
Bellarmine
on the Word
of God, book 2,
ch. 1.
</margin>

4. In Nehemiah 8:1-2, it is recounted that the people told Ezra to bring out the Book of the Law of Moses, which the Lord had given to the people of Israel. It is not said there that the people requested him to write it anew.

It is therefore false that Ezra rewrote the scripture; he perhaps corrected some errors that had crept into some copies held by the people through the negligence of scribes, and he gathered the books together along with those of the Prophets of that time, such as Daniel, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi.

The third question concerns the falsification of the books.

The question is asked, then: have the books been falsified by the Jews? One cannot answer this better than Origen and Jerome <note>Early Christian scholars (3rd and 4th centuries) who studied the Hebrew texts of the Bible.</note> have done: "If the Hebrews," they say, "had at any time falsified the scripture, it must have been either before or after the coming of Christ. If before, why did Christ and the Apostles never rebuke them, since Christ rebuked them for even lesser sins? Why did Christ say, *Search the scriptures*, etc.? And elsewhere, *The scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses' seat; therefore whatever they tell you, do it.* Who will believe that Jesus invited people to read corrupted scriptures without any warning, or that he commanded them to hear and follow teachers who had ruined the scripture? If after the coming of Christ, how is it that we find in the books we have exactly what Christ and the Apostles quoted, and in the same way? If they were falsified by the Jews neither before nor after, it clearly follows that they were never falsified at all."

To this we could add many other reasons. I could bring up the outstanding zeal of the Jews for the scripture, which Philo, Josephus, and many others mention.

Philo <note>A Jewish philosopher from Alexandria who lived at the same time as Jesus.</note> says that in a period of more than 2,000 years, not a single word in the law of the Hebrews has been changed, and that they would rather die a hundred times than suffer the scripture to be falsified in any part.

...became. Their superstition goes so far in this matter that they reject a copy as soon as a single error is found in it; and where more than four are found in it, they bury it, so that no one may use it. If it happens that the Law <note>The Torah scrolls.</note> falls upon the Earth, they proclaim a public Fast. Is it conceivable that people who preserve the holy Books with so much dread and superstition would have laid their own hands upon them to falsify them?

<margin>Justin, *Dialogue with Trypho* <note>original: "Justin. dial. cum Tryph."</note></margin>
Justin the Martyr introduces the Jew Trypho speaking thus: The Jews were so far from falsifying the scripture that they all believed it would have been a more terrible crime than worshiping the **Golden Calf**, dedicating one’s Children to Idols by making them pass through the fire, and killing the Prophets. This Ancient Father <note>A term for early Christian theologians known as the Church Fathers.</note> only accuses them of having cut off and falsified some passages of the Greek translation. But, not to use this reason, I say that if the Jews had wanted to falsify the scripture out of hatred for the Christians, they would without doubt have erased the principal prophecies and **Oracles** <note>Divine pronouncements or messages from God.</note> that the Christians could use to prove that Jesus, the Son of Mary, is the Messiah. But it is certain that they did not undertake it.

Even if these prophecies, as Cardinal Bellarmine rightly notes, were found to be slightly different in Hebrew than in the Greek and Latin translations, the difference is small, and the Hebrew favors the sentiment of the Christians much more than the translations. A clear proof of the Faithfulness of the Jews!
<margin>Jerome, *Apology 2 against Rufinus* <note>original: "Hier. apolog. 2. adv. Rufin."</note></margin>
Jerome also complains, in his second defense against Rufinus, about the Christians who wanted to exalt their Greek or Latin Bibles above the Hebrew ones of the Jews. Their Books, he says, contain things concerning Jesus Christ that your books do not mention, etc.
<margin>Celsus in Origen, Book 2 *Against Celsus* <note>original: "Cels. ap. Orig. l. 2. adv. Cels."</note></margin>

A New Writer, who claims that the Hebrew Text was corrupted by the Jews, assumes: 1. That the Christians had no knowledge of Hebrew until the conquest of Jerusalem. 2. That the Hebrew Text, after that time, remained among

<column-break/>

the Jews. 3. That there were no Hebrew copies except those from Tiberias <note>A city in Galilee that became a center for Jewish scholarship and the Masoretic text.</note>. 4. That Rabbi Akiba, teacher of Aquila and Disciple of Gamaliel, is the cause of this falsification. 5. That Aquila falsified the Scripture because he followed a corrupted copy from Akiba. 6. That Akiba corrupted the calculation of the lifespan of the Patriarchs in the Hebrew Text. But all these assumptions are groundless. 1. Many Jews who had accepted Christianity would have discovered the fraud of others. 2. Since the Jews were scattered everywhere, there is no probability that there were only copies of the Hebrew Text in Tiberias. 3. What is said of Akiba and Aquila has no basis nor appearance of truth. 4. Finally, Aquila could have falsified the Scripture through malice without having had a corrupted copy.

Furthermore, one cannot understand that God, who gave the Scripture for the instruction of men and to know the Messiah through it, would have permitted the Books written for the **Salvation of the Human Race** to be falsified, His Oracles changed, and thereby become useless for the end for which they were intended. One also does not understand how, even if the Jews had wanted to attempt it, they could have done so: for, being scattered over the whole Earth, they could not have agreed on this change; and even if they had wanted to do it, the Christians, who from the beginning of their conversion had the Old Testament in hand, would have brought this fraud to light and opposed it. We can say the same of the New Testament: Christianity being divided into many sects <note>Groups or denominations.</note> that kept an eye on each other, it is not possible to understand how one could have changed something without the others noticing.

To prove this further, one notes:
1. That the original Writings of the Gospels and Epistles remained for some time in the Churches for which they were written.
2. It seems that in the time of Tertullian they were still there.
3. That copies were undoubtedly made of them, which were spread in all Churches.
4. If these copies had been unfaithful...

### XXX. CHAPTER.
### Whether the Books of the Old Testament were burned with the City of Jerusalem, and whether they have been corrupted and falsified.

<margin>4 Ezra 14:44.</margin>
The second question is whether the books of the Old Testament were burned during the destruction of Jerusalem when Nebuchadnezzar took that city? The reason for this question is a passage in the Fourth Book of Ezra <note>original: "4 Esdras"; an apocalyptic work often considered apocryphal by most traditions.</note> 14:44, where it is said that Ezra, driven by God's Spirit, dictated 204 books word-for-word to five persons in forty days; they wrote with great speed from his mouth. It is claimed that in this way the scripture, which had been entirely consumed by fire, was restored to its original state.

But besides the fact that this book—falsely attributed to Ezra—is apocryphal and full of falsehoods, as we shall prove elsewhere, there are many things that clearly show it is impossible that all copies of the Holy Books were burned with the Temple.

I will not speak here of how unlikely it is that not a single Israelite would have taken the holy books with them when the Ten Tribes were carried away into Assyria by Nebuchadnezzar <note>The author likely means the Assyrian captivity (722 BCE), as Nebuchadnezzar was Babylonian; he acknowledges this happened more than 130 years before the Temple burned.</note> more than 130 years before the burning of the Temple: but I will only note:

1. That many God-fearing Israelites were carried away to Babylon with King Jehoiachin <note>original: "Joachim"</note> before the destruction of Jerusalem; it is beyond all likelihood that none of them would have cared to take the Holy Books with them.

2. It is also not probable that Jeremiah, to whom the Babylonians did no harm, would not have preserved the Books of the Law and the Prophets.

<margin>Dan. 9:2 and 13.</margin>
3. It is clearly said of Daniel that he saw from the books the number of the years of the captivity, in the first year of Darius. It also appears that he had the books of Moses in this captivity.

<column-break/>

<margin>Bellarmine, *On the Word of God*, book 2, chapter 1. <note>original: "Bellarm. de Verbo Dei. lib. 2. c. 1."</note></margin>
4. Nehemiah 8:1-2 recounts that the people told Ezra to bring forth the Book of the Law of Moses, which the Lord had given to the people of Israel. It does not say that the people requested him to write it anew.

It is therefore false that Ezra wrote the scripture again! He perhaps corrected some errors that had crept into some copies held by the people through the negligence of transcribers, and gathered the books together, along with those of the Prophets of that time, such as Daniel, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi.

The third question concerns the falsification of the books.

<margin>Origen on Isaiah & Jerome, book 3 on Isaiah 6.</margin>
<margin>John 5:39.</margin>
<margin>Matt. 23:2, 3.</margin>
It is asked then: have the books been falsified by the Jews? One cannot answer this better than Origen and Jerome have done: If the Hebrews, they say, had at any time falsified the scripture, it was either before or after the coming of Christ. If *before*, why did Christ and the Apostles never rebuke them, since Christ rebuked them for much smaller matters? Why does Christ say, "Search the scriptures," etc.? And elsewhere, "The scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses' seat; therefore all that they tell you, do it." Who will believe that Jesus invited people to read corrupted scriptures without any warning, or that he commanded them to hear and follow Teachers who had corrupted the scripture? If *after* the coming of Christ, how is it that we find in the books we have exactly what Christ and the Apostles quoted, and in the same manner? Since they were falsified by the Jews neither before nor after, it clearly follows they were never falsified by them. Thus Origen and Jerome reason. If Jerome said something to the contrary regarding Galatians 3, on the occasion of Deuteronomy 27, and in his commentary on Micah, it is not his own opinion that he presents there.

<margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 8, chapter 2. <note>original: "Euseb. præp. Evan. c. 2. 1. 8."</note></margin>
To this, we could add many other reasons. I could recount the excellent zeal of the Jews for the scripture, of which Philo, Josephus, and many others speak.

Philo says that in a period of more than 2,000 years, not a single word has been changed in the law of the Hebrews; and that they would rather die a hundred times than suffer the scripture to be falsified in any part.

### THEOLOGY. Book I. Chapter XXX.

...was. Their reverence <note>original: "bygeloof"; literally "superstition," though here referring to extreme scrupulousness</note> goes so far that they reject a copy as soon as a single error is found in it; and where more than four errors are found, they bury it so that no one may use it. If it happens that the Book of the Law falls to the ground, they proclaim a public fast. Is it likely that people who guard the Holy Books with so much trembling and reverence would have laid their own hands upon them to falsify them?

Justin Martyr introduces the Jew Trypho speaking thus: The Jews were so far from falsifying the scripture that they all believed it would have been a more terrible crime than worshiping the Golden Calf, dedicating one's children to idols by passing them through the fire, or killing the Prophets. This Church Father <note>original: "Oud-Vader"</note> only accuses them of having cut out and falsified some passages of the Greek translation <note>The Septuagint</note>. But, even without using this argument, I say that if the Jews had wanted to falsify the scripture out of hatred for the Christians, they would undoubtedly have erased the principal predictions and divine oracles that Christians could use to prove that Jesus, the son of Mary, is the Messiah. But it is certain that they did not attempt it.

<margin><note>original: "Aug al)" likely refers to Saint Augustine.</note> <unclear>Aug. lib.</unclear></margin> Even if these prophecies—as Cardinal Bellarmine rightly observes—were found to be slightly different in the Hebrew than in the Greek and Latin translations, the difference is small, and the Hebrew favors the views of the Christians much more than the translations do. This is clear proof of the faithfulness of the Jews! Jerome <note>original: "Hieronimus"</note> also complains, in his second defense against Rufinus <note>original: "tweede verantwoording tegen Rufinus"</note>, about Christians who wanted to exalt their Greek or Latin Bibles above the Hebrew Bibles of the Jews. "Their books," he says, "contain things concerning Jesus Christ that your books do not mention," etc. Celsus also reproached the Christians for daily changing their Gospels: but Origen <note>original: "Origines"</note> answered him well, saying that Celsus was confusing the old sectarians, such as the Gnostics and Manicheans, with the true believers. A modern writer, who claims that the Hebrew text was corrupted by the Jews, supposes: 1. That Christians had no knowledge of Hebrew until the conquest of Jerusalem. 2. That the Hebrew text, after that time, remained among

<column-break/>

the Jews. 3. That there were no Hebrew copies except those of Tiberias. 4. That Rabbi Akiba, teacher of Aquila and disciple of Gamaliel, is the cause of this falsification. 5. That Aquila falsified the Scripture because he followed a corrupted copy by Akiba. 6. That Akiba corrupted the chronology of the lifespans of the Patriarchs in the Hebrew text. But all these suppositions are groundless. 1. Many Jews who had accepted Christianity would have discovered the fraud of the others. 2. Since the Jews were scattered everywhere, it is not probable that copies of the Hebrew text existed only in Tiberias. 3. What is said of Akiba and Aquila has neither basis nor appearance of truth. 4. Finally, Aquila could have falsified the Scripture through malice without having had a corrupted copy.

Furthermore, one cannot conceive that God, who gave the Scripture for the instruction of men and to make the Messiah known through it, would have permitted the books written for the salvation of the human race to be falsified, His divine oracles changed, and thereby rendered useless for the end for which they were intended. Nor can one conceive that, even if the Jews had wanted to undertake it, they could have done so: for, being scattered over the whole earth, they could not have agreed on this change; and even if they had wanted to do so, the Christians, who from the beginning of their conversion had the Old Testament in their hands, would have brought this fraud to light and opposed it; the same can be said of the New Testament. Christianity being divided into many sects <note>original: "gezintheden"</note> that kept an eye on one another, it is impossible to understand how one could have changed something without the others noticing it.

To prove this further, we also note:

1. That the original writings of the Gospels and Epistles <note>original: "Zend-brieven"</note> remained for some time in the churches for which they were written.

2. It appears that they still existed in the time of Tertullian.

3. That copies were undoubtedly made of them, which were spread throughout all churches.

4. If these copies were unfaithful...

5. That the copyists could not all have agreed with one another to introduce the same falsifications into the text.

Furthermore, while we maintain the integrity or uncorrupted nature of the original text <term>original text; the Hebrew and Greek "ground-text"</term>, we do not deny that some errors have crept into the copies, whether they were drawn from the Old or New Testament. Otherwise, one would have to say that God made the copyists and printers infallible, or that He continually performs miracles on their behalf, which is unlikely; let us further note the following:

1. That the errors found in the copies of the Old and New Testament affect neither the essence of religion, nor faith, nor morals, but only matters of small importance, such as a number, a proper name, the name of a city, and similar trifles; one can be mistaken in these while still retaining their Salvation, and copyists can easily err in such things.

<margin>
See Sim. de Muys, *In Defense of the Hebrew Truth* <note>original: "pro assertione Hebr. verit."</note>; Kellet, *Miscellanies of Divines*; Turretin, *Against Cotta*; Voetius, etc.
</margin>
2. That there is not a single one of these writing errors that cannot be corrected by better copies, by other books of Scripture, by the writings and interpretations of the Ancients, or by old translations.

For example, in 2 Chronicles 22, it is said that Ahaziah was 42 years old when he became King, or began to reign; this is likely a writing error, but easily corrected: 1. By 2 Kings 8:26, where it states that Ahaziah was 22 years old then. 2. By many ancient Greek manuscripts. 3. By the Syriac Bible, which the church of Antioch used from the beginning, as some scholars say. 4. By the Arabic translation, as seen in the work of the learned Archbishop Ussher <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), famous for his biblical chronology</note> in his chronology. Other interpreters offer different solutions.

I add to this that one must be careful, under the pretext of not understanding a passage well, not to immediately say "there is an error" when it appears that the text is the same in all copies and was read in that same way by the first translators and Church Fathers; it is better here to admit one's own ignorance than to reject what one does not understand.

Many have believed that there were errors in the Hebrew and Greek text

<column-break/>

merely because they did not understand the power of the words, the true manner of translation, or the customs of the Jews and other nations. And I am certain that if we had accurate records of the history of the Jews and other peoples, we would perfectly understand many places that seem very dark to us and in which some believe there are errors—just as there are many places in the secular <note>original: "ongewyde" (unconsecrated or non-sacred)</note> writers that learned men think must be corrected because they do not know the history of those times well enough.

I will bring forward some examples. Acts 7:16 states that the Fathers were brought to Shechem and placed in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of money from the sons of Hamor <note>original: "Emmors"</note>, father of Shechem. Some have thought there was an error here because Genesis 23:17-18 says Abraham bought the tomb from Ephron and not from the sons of Hamor, and Genesis 33:19 says it was Jacob who bought a piece of land from the sons of Hamor. To solve this difficulty, many have been of the opinion that "Abraham" was placed there instead of "Jacob," in the same sense as David is placed in the stead of Rehoboam, his grandson, in 1 Kings 12:16. But others consider that it can be translated thus: *the Fathers were moved to Shechem, and by the sons of Hamor, father of Shechem, were placed in the tomb that Abraham had bought with money.* If we knew the reckoning of that time well, we could certainly say whether this translation is correct. Whatever the case may be, these words can be translated this way, and then there is no difficulty. It will possibly be said that we only read of Joseph being placed in this tomb; but although Moses speaks only of Joseph, it nonetheless appears that his brothers were also buried there; at least Jerome repeats that he, having been brought to Shechem,

# DIVINITY. BOOK I. CHAPTER XXXI.

...just as we know that *Jehoiachin* was only 8 years old when he began to reign with the King his father, who, according to the custom of that time, had his son recognized as a partner in the Kingdom and proclaimed King at an early age. But he was 18 years old when he began to reign alone <note>The author is reconciling 2 Kings 24:8 (18 years) with 2 Chronicles 36:9 (8 years) using the concept of a co-regency.</note>. One can bring forward other answers that are also sound.

Some claim there is an error either in *2 Samuel 24:24*, where it is said that *David* bought the threshing floor and oxen from *Araunah* for 50 silver shekels, or in *1 Chronicles 21:25*, where we read that *David* gave *Ornan* 600 gold shekels. But there are great men who prove there is no mistake here; some say that *David* gave 50 shekels for the threshing floor and the oxen, and 600 shekels for the ground of the threshing floor. Others believe that in *Samuel* it refers to gold shekels, and in the *Chronicles* to silver, and they translate the first as: *David gave, in ready money, as payment 50 gold shekels,* and the second as: *David gave the value of 600 silver shekels, in gold.*

It is claimed there is an error either in *2 Samuel 24:13*, where *Gad* <note>Gad was a prophet and seer to King David.</note> proposed seven years of famine to *David*; or in *1 Chronicles 21:12*, where he speaks of only three years. But if we knew everything that happened then, we would find that there is no error. It is possible that *Gad* first proposed seven years to *David*, and that upon the King's prayer, the 7 years were reduced to 3, just as the number of 50 Righteous men was reduced to 10 at the prayer of *Abraham* in *Genesis 18*. It is also possible that when *Gad* proposed this, nearly 4 years of famine had already passed—which God had sent over the land because of the *Gibeonites*—and that the Book of Chronicles speaks only of the three years that were yet to come.

It is claimed there is an error either in *1 Kings 9:28*, where it is said that *Solomon's* servants brought 420 <term>Talents; a large unit of weight or currency</term> of gold from *Ophir*; or in *2 Chronicles 8:18*, where it says 450. But why should one not believe that *Solomon's* servants once brought 420 Talents, and another time 450? Or if this answer is not satisfactory, can one not say that 30 of these Talents were used along the way for the maintenance of the fleet?

Finally, it is alleged that there

<sig>Part I.</sig>

<column-break/>

is an error in *Matthew 27:9*. There, the prophecy of the 30 pieces of silver and the purchased field is attributed to *Jeremiah*, although it is found in *Zechariah 11:12*. 2. That *Jeremiah* is named here because he is the first in the scroll of the Prophets; and the Jews even said that his spirit had passed into *Zechariah*.

3. One can also say that there was possibly an old tradition in the time of the *Apostles* regarding a prophecy by *Jeremiah* that spoke of 30 pieces of silver, which prophecy was written down by *Zechariah*, but was originally attributed to *Jeremiah*.

<margin>Augustine, *Against Faustus*, Book 10, Chapters 3 and 11; Book 32, Chapter 8. <note>original: "Aug. Cont. Faus. l. X. c. 3. en 11 XXXII. c. 8."</note></margin>

It is claimed that there is an error either in 2 Samuel 24:24, where it says that David bought the threshing floor and oxen from Araunah for 50 shekels of silver, or in 1 Chronicles 21:25, where one reads that David gave Ornan 600 shekels of Gold. Others believe that in Samuel it speaks of gold shekels and in Chronicles of silver ones, and translate the first thus: *David gave, in ready money, for payment 50 shekels of gold*, and the second thus: *David gave the value of 600 shekels of silver, in gold.*

3. One can also say that there was possibly an old tradition in the time of the Apostles of a prophecy by Jeremiah that spoke of 30 pieces of silver, which prophecy was written down by Zechariah, but was originally attributed to Jeremiah.

One should not say that the Church Fathers speak of the Jewish Register of Scripture and not that of the Christians: for it appears that they cite the Faith of the Hebrews on this matter as a line of reasoning to justify the Faith of the Christians. From whom else should we receive the books of the Old Testament if not from the Jews, to whom the words of God were entrusted? It is also true that one finds a decree in the Third Council of Carthage, held in the year 397, which places many books—which we consider Apocryphal—among the Canonical ones. It is the same Council that says in Canon 24: "the Bread and the Wine offered in the Eucharist are the Sacraments of the body and of the blood of Christ"; and in Canon 26: "the Bishop of the first see shall not be called Prince of the Priests or Supreme Priest."

->But we note.<-

<column-break/>

1. That the Council of Carthage was only a Provincial Council, whose authority is consequently of no great weight; and there is reason to believe that its acts have been falsified.
2. That this Council, as the reason why it accepted other books as Canonical than those accepted before, brings forward that they were "read in the Church," and it adds that the Martyrdom of the Martyrs was also read on certain days; from which it appears that the Fathers of this Church assembly called the pieces that were read in the Church "Canonical and Divine Scriptures."
3. That the Church Fathers often use the word "Canonical" in a different sense; sometimes they give this name to the books which—although they were not held as a rule of Faith and Morals—were nevertheless worthy to be added to the others, not to prove the doctrines of the Church from them, but for common edification, as Jerome notes; and they were held to be worthier than other human writings.

It is also true that a letter from Innocent I to Exuperius, Bishop of Toulouse, is presented, which is said to have been written in the year 405: but this Letter is so full of absurdities that many scholars have doubted whether it is truly from this Pope.

One also comes forward with a decree from Gelasius in a Council of Rome, held in the year 494. But one may doubt it somewhat; at the very least, it is true that it only became known in the middle of the ninth century. It has also been noted that in this decree only one book of Ezra is mentioned, and one book of the Maccabees, and that in some manuscripts the Book of Job is omitted, and in others the two books of the Maccabees.

But so that one does not believe that we ground our opinion only on the authority of men; here are the reasons for which we accept no other books as Divine than those already mentioned.

# DIVINITY. BOOK I. CHAPTER XXXI.
### T 2
<meta>catchword: There</meta>

1. Because they were written without the inspiration of God. The writer of the *Maccabees* expressly states that there were no prophets in his time; and one could not prove that any of the <term>Apocryphal</term> <note>religious texts not included in the official biblical canon</note> books were written before the time of Malachi, with the exception of *Tobit*. Genebrardus <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a French Benedictine theologian</note> acknowledges, along with the Jewish teachers, that Malachi was the last prophet. It is found in the *Talmud* that after the deaths of Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi—the last of the prophets—the Holy Spirit departed from the Israelites.

2. Because the Jewish Church, to whom the words of God were entrusted, did not receive them as <term>canonical</term> <note>original: "regelmatige," meaning following the "rule" or accepted standard of scripture</note>. One must not claim that the Jews had three different canons: one created by Ezra, which only approved the 24 books of the Old Testament (which we have cited elsewhere); a second established by the sixth Synod of Jerusalem in the time of Eleazar, in the year of the world 3860, which supposedly accepted the books of *Tobit*, *Judith*, *Wisdom*, and *Ecclesiasticus*. It is said that this assembly was held when they were deliberating on sending <term>translators</term> <note>original: "Taalsmannen," likely referring to the seventy-two scholars who translated the Septuagint</note> to Ptolemy Philadelphus. The third is said to have been compiled by the seventh Synod, held in the year 3950 under John Hyrcanus, which added all the Apocryphal books. However, all of this is groundless and without proof.

3. Finally, because many things are found in them that are contrary to historical truth, contrary to godliness, and contrary to the books recognized as divine.

This will become more distinctly apparent when we examine these books individually.

We shall begin with the *Book of Wisdom*, called the *Wisdom of Solomon*. Some have believed that Solomon was its author, based on the ninth chapter where the writer speaks as if he were Solomon.

But the opposite is evident. 1. Because the author says in Chapter XV, verse 14, that the Jewish people were oppressed by their enemies in his time; now, everyone knows that during Solomon's time, no such oppression was known. 2. Because he speaks therein of modes of combat that were not in use in the time of Solomon (Chapter IV, verse 12). Furthermore, most of the ancients attributed this book to a certain Philo—one Philo who lived under the priest Onias, 160 years before
<margin>See Eusebius.</margin>

<column-break/>

Christ. Others attribute it to a Philo who <margin>*Preparation for the Gospel*, book 9.</margin> lived under Caligula <note>The Roman Emperor reigning from 37–41 AD</note>; and we add that he composed this book after he returned from his embassy to Caligula, in order to comfort the Jewish people, who were greatly distressed and plagued by the cruelty of this Emperor.

This last opinion is the most probable. Either because there are many things in this book that can be very well applied to the subject matter Philo wrote about, such as in Chapters XIII and XIV; or because a similarity of style with that of Philo is found therein; compare Chapter VIII, verse 7, with what Philo says in the first book of his *Allegories of the Law*. Some scholars, however, find a difference in the style. Some have believed that these words of Paul in Romans 11:34—*Who has known the mind (or thoughts) of the Lord?* etc.—were taken from the *Book of Wisdom*; but they are from Isaiah 40:13.

In this book are many useful things; but it is written in an overly ornate manner. And although it was written after the coming of Christ, it speaks not a word of the Messiah; which would have served as a great comfort to the Hebrews. This shows that the writer of this work was a Jew and an enemy of Jesus.

Scholars agree that it was written in Greek. The Church Fathers sometimes gave the name "Book of Wisdom" to the *Book of Proverbs*.

<margin>*Ecclesiastical History*, book 4, chapter 21.</margin> Thus Melito, Irenaeus, and many others call it. One must not imagine that they are speaking of the *Book of Wisdom* which is attributed to Philo. Augustine speaks of it distinctly. See *On Christian Doctrine*, book 2, chapter 8; *Retractations*, book 2, chapter 4; and *The City of God*, book 17, chapter 29. In the 8th chapter, verse 20, of the *Book of Wisdom*, Solomon is made to say: *I came into an undefiled body.* David does not speak this way in Psalm 51:5 <note>The original text cites Psalm IX. 7, but the context of "undefiled body" versus "conceived in sin" refers to Psalm 51</note>.

The book *Ecclesiasticus* is called the *Wisdom of Jesus, son of Sirach*, and in the Syriac translation, the *son of Simeon Asir*; therefore, its author was not Solomon. This is also evident from the fact that the author mentions kings who followed Solomon.

It appears that in Chapter XLVIII, verse 10, he alludes to a passage from Malachi; but it is clear that it was made in imitation of the book of *Ecclesiastes*.

In this book are excellent things:

therefore the youth are exhorted in the Apostolic Constitutions <note>original: "Apostolische inzettingen," a 4th-century collection of ecclesiastical law</note> to learn the wisdom of the wise Sirach. The Ancients also gave it a Greek name meaning "all virtue," because there is indeed not a single virtue for which this excellent book does not provide rules of conduct. However, it contains many errors.

1. From chapter XXIV. 8. and 10. it appears that the writer followed the translation of the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>original: "LXX," the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> regarding Proverbs VIII. 26. For he presents Wisdom speaking thus: *He who created me, made my tent to rest; he has created me from the beginning of the world.* <note>The author objects to the idea of Wisdom—often associated with Christ—being "created."</note>

It is true that there are those who interpret the words of the Septuagint and of <term>Ecclesiasticus</term> <note>another name for the Book of Sirach</note> differently.

2. The writer believes that it was the true Samuel who appeared through the conjuring of the sorceress at the request of Saul. Ecclesiasticus XLVI. 22. This contradicts the truth. <note>Protestant theologians generally argued that the "Samuel" seen by the Witch of Endor was a demonic apparition, not the actual prophet.</note>

3. He applies the passage from Malachi to the prophet Elijah: Ecclesiasticus XLVIII. 10. Whereas, according to the explanation of Christ, it must be applied to John the Baptist.

4. He excuses himself in his preface and asks for indulgence if he has committed any error; a proof that he did not write by the Spirit of God.

This book was written in the 38th year of King Euergetes, as the author notes in his preface. This Euergetes is Ptolemy Euergetes II, named <term>Physcon</term> <note>meaning "Potbelly," a king of Egypt who reigned in the 2nd century BCE</note>, who lived in the year of the world 3872, about 132 years before Christ. It is believed that it was written in Greek; whereas the book of his grandfather was in Hebrew.

Jerome <note>original: "Hieronimus," the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate)</note> says, however, that in his time he had seen a Hebrew copy of it under the name of *Parabolon* <note>Proverbs</note>. The book of Tobit bears this name because it concerns the life of Tobit. It is believed that the first 12 chapters were written by Tobit the elder, the following 13 by the younger Tobit, and the rest by someone else. These origins are uncertain.

There are many edifying things in this work, but also very ridiculous ones. 1. In chapter V. 15, the angel Raphael says that he is named Azarias, from the family of

<column-break/>

Ananias. This is a blatant lie. <note>Azarias means "God has helped" and Ananias means "God is gracious"; the author argues an angel should not use a false identity.</note>

One cannot say that these words should be interpreted figuratively, as if the angel meant he was sent by God to assist Tobit and bring many gifts of grace—because Azarias means God's help or assistance, and Ananias means God's grace. Nor should one add that the angel Raphael, having taken the true form of Azarias, son of the great Ananias, could say he was Azarias (just as the angels who visited Abraham were taken for men). To say such things is to try to make us believe that one speaks not in earnest, but only to show off one's intellect; nor do I believe that I will be required to refute such thoughts.

2. In chapter VI. 9, 10, and 20, this angel suggests a ridiculous remedy to drive away the devil using the heart, the liver, and the gall of a fish.

<margin>Estius.</margin>
<note>Willem Hessels van Est (1542–1613), a prominent Catholic commentator</note> One must be very fond of allegories to believe that a figurative sense must still be given to these words, and that the angel wanted to tell Tobit that, to put the devil to flight, his heart must be burning with divine love; that he must moderate the thirst of the senses and concupiscence; that the heart of the fish, placed on coals, signifies the supreme love of Jesus Christ, consumed on the wood of the Cross, which struck terror into all devils; that his blood, represented by the liver, caused a smoke and fragrance of infinite power to rise to Heaven against the rage of evil spirits; and that the bitterness of his suffering, represented by the gall, had the power to heal the blindness of the world; and other things of a similar nature.

<margin>Tobit XII. 15.</margin>
3. He says that he is one of the seven angels who bring the prayers of the saints to God; which the Scripture nowhere teaches us. Tobit says that he was among the number of those who, in the time of Hezekiah, were carried away to Assyria by Shalmaneser around the year of the world 3283 and 721 years before Christ: from which one can conclude when this book was written, or at least when the events recounted therein occurred.

It is believed that it was first written in <term>Chaldean</term> <note>Aramaic</note>; but it is no longer found except in Greek and Latin. Jerome translated it into Latin at the request of two bishops, Chromatius and Heliodorus. It has also been translated into Hebrew.

# THEOLOGY. BOOK I. CHAPTER XXXI.

The Book of Baruch contains several good things; it was also accepted by the Council of Laodicea, by Cyril of Jerusalem, Athanasius, Epiphanius, and Rufinus <note>Early Church Fathers and theologians from the 4th and 5th centuries</note>. It is often cited by the Ancient Fathers under the name of Jeremiah. However, it is easy to see that it is a fabrication and was never composed by Baruch, who was the secretary of Jeremiah.

<margin>
Chapter I.
1-4. etc.

But what likelihood is there that the Babylonians would have permitted all the captive people to gather with their King while he himself was a prisoner? For he was not restored until the 37th year of his captivity.

2. It is stated there that Baruch and Jeremiah were led into Egypt (Jeremiah 43:6). There is no mention of their return.

3. What likelihood is there that Baruch wrote in Greek? Since, in all probability, the language of the Scripture we have in his name is not a foreign one but the original language. Nonetheless, Hebrew idioms are found within it, which has led some to believe it was first composed in Hebrew.

4. In Chapter I:10, an Altar of the Lord is mentioned. But it is certain that there was none. It is true, some say that an Altar was built on the same spot where the Temple had stood, and that the remnants of Judah came there to offer sacrifices after the destruction of Jerusalem; but this is said without proof.

The third Book of Esdras <note>Also known as 1 Esdras in many English Bibles; it contains a variation of the history found in Ezra and Nehemiah</note> is no more canonical than that of Judith: and Esdras is not its author; besides many fictions, there are many things in it that run entirely contrary to the Canonical books. The **Prayer of Manasseh**, being found only in Greek and Latin and not recognized as genuine by the Jewish Church, we are not obliged to accept as canonical scripture. <term>canonical scripture</term> <note>original: "Regelmatig schrift"; referring to books officially accepted as the inspired rule of faith.</note> Furthermore, there is something in this prayer that I do not know if I can approve: for Manasseh is introduced praying to God thus:
<margin>v. 8.</margin>

I proceed to the **Books of the Maccabees**. It is not known who their author is; some say John Hyrcanus, son of Simon Maccabeus; others Josephus. The historical narrative, contained in the first two books and occurring about 167 years before Christ, contains several edifying matters. But there are at the same time entire things in them that indicate to us that they were not inspired by God’s Spirit. Gregory the Great <note>original: "Gregorius le Grand"</note> speaks of them
<margin>Book 19 of the Moralia. <note>original: "Lib. 19. Moral."</note></margin>

Chapter VI relates that Antiochus died in Babylon of heartache, and 2 Macc. 1:15-16 says he was stoned and torn to pieces at Nanea. And ch. IX:28 says he died in the mountains of a terrible disease.

2. He was not stoned in the Temple; but killed by Demetrius, son of Seleucus, and survived his father Antiochus Epiphanes by only two years. 3. Antiochus Sidetes perished in a battle against the Parthians, having been abandoned by his own. Appian says that he took his own life.

# THE CHRISTIAN GOD

These are the books that are called **Apocrypha**, from a Greek word <note>original: "Griechsch woord"</note> that means "hidden." They are so named, according to the opinion of some of the **Church Fathers**—including **Epiphanius**—because they were not kept in the chest of the canonical books. <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 315–403) was a staunch defender of orthodoxy who cataloged numerous heresies and writings.</note> Others believe they bear this name because their authors were hidden <note>meaning anonymous or unknown</note>, which is a poor reason. Others say that in the beginning, they were not read in the Church and were not used to prove the doctrines of faith. Others claim it is because their authority was very uncertain; and still others give different reasons. But so as not to dwell on this, I will note that among the **Hebrews**, there was no such name for the Books of the Bible; those that were poorly copied were buried so that no one would read them.

Besides these books, which we call Apocrypha, there were others that people wanted to pass off as Divine, but which were not written by men inspired by **God’s Spirit**.

1. In this rank is an addition at the end of **Job**, which is found in the Greek translation <note>The Septuagint (LXX)</note> and contains the genealogy of Job and his friends. In it are untrue things, such as that Job is the same person as **Jobab**, that he was King in the Land of Edom, and other such tales. <note>The identification of Job with Jobab, a descendant of Esau mentioned in Genesis 36, was a common ancient tradition but is rejected here as unhistorical.</note>

2. There is another addition to **Job 2:8**, which contains a speech by Job's wife against her husband.

3. In the translation of the **Septuagint (LXX)** is the **151st Psalm**, in which David is introduced speaking of his battle with Goliath. This Psalm has been translated into Syriac, Ethiopic, and Arabic.

4. One finds in the Greek translation a preface to the **Lamentations of Jeremiah** which is not found in the Hebrew and contains a falsehood: namely, that these lamentations were composed after Israel was led into captivity. This is not true.

5. Among these Apocryphal books of the second rank, one places the **4th Book of Maccabees**, which covers a history of 31 years. Some believe it was drawn from the daily records of the priesthood of John.

There have also been Apocryphal books of the **New Testament**, which some wish to defend as canonical books.

1. Under the name of **Christ**, writings have been produced, as **Augustine**

<column-break/>

teaches us (*On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, Book 1, Chapter 9). <note>original: "de conf. Eu lib. 1. c. 9."</note>

2. Specifically, one speaks of his letter to a **King of the Edessenes**, which I have dealt with elsewhere. <note>This refers to the legendary correspondence between Jesus and King Abgar V of Edessa.</note>

3. A letter to **Ignatius** is attributed to the **Virgin Mary**. But no one spoke of it before **Bernard** (*Sermon 7 on Psalm 91*). <note>original: "Serm. 7. in Ps. 9." refers to Bernard of Clairvaux.</note> Also a letter to the Florentines, and one to those of Messina. But these are fabricated letters.

4. **Institutions and Rules** have been attributed to the **Apostles**, but they are not theirs, as the mere reading of these books proves: for they speak of many things that were unknown in the time of the Apostles. <note>Referring to the "Apostolic Constitutions," a 4th-century collection of ecclesiastical law falsely attributed to the Twelve Apostles.</note>

5. The **Articles of Faith** <note>The Apostles' Creed</note> are attributed to them; but they are certainly not their work, although they are taken from their books.

6. A **Liturgy** has been set under the name of **James**, which **Proclus**, Patriarch of Constantinople, recognized as an authentic piece: but it appears it is not from the Apostle James, since it speaks of a **Confessor** <note>original: "Biegt-Vader," literally "Confession-Father"</note>, **consubstantial** <note>original: "medewezend," referring to the term *homoousios*</note>, and the **Trisagion** <note>The "Thrice Holy" hymn (Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal), which entered liturgical use centuries after James.</note>, which are words from the following centuries. One prays there for those enclosed in **Monasteries**, and mention is also made of Temples, Incense, and Altars.

7. A **Liturgy** has been attributed to **Peter**, but it is not from him, since mention is made of **Cornelius** and **Cyprian**; and there are prayers in it for the **Venerable Patriarch**. The entire **Latin Mass** is in it, with other prayers taken from the Sacramentary of **Gregory**.

8. One has been attributed to **Matthew**, which is called the **Ethiopic Mass**, in which one also finds the words **Patriarch** and **Archbishop**. There is also mention of the **Golden Number** <note>A cycle used to determine the date of Easter, devised long after the apostolic age.</note>, of the **Synods of Nicaea, Constantinople, and Ephesus**. # THEOLOGY. BOOK 1. CHAPTER XXXII.

...of Peter and Paul, of John, of Thomas, and of Thecla. <note>These refer to "Acts" of the Apostles which were not included in the Bible, such as the *Acts of Paul and Thecla*.</note> In the *Acts of Peter and Paul*, forged by the Manichaeans, <note>The Manichaeans were a major dualistic religious group that competed with early Christianity.</note> these Apostles are made to say that the souls of humans and of beasts are of the same nature.

11. There is also talk of "Revelations" of Peter and of Paul.

12. To these were added the book of Hermes <note>Generally known as *The Shepherd of Hermas*, an early Christian work once considered for the canon.</note> and others, too many to list. Books that the Christian Church has never recognized as Divine!

I will add these three observations here: 1. That as soon as the Church gradually accepted the translation of Jerome <note>The Latin Vulgate.</note>—who followed the standard <term>Canon</term> of the Hebrews—the Apocryphal books began to lose their authority.

2. That at the Council of Florence, <note>A 15th-century council that attempted to reunite the Eastern and Western churches.</note> matters changed, and the Apocryphal books were restored.

<margin>See Isidore of Seville’s *On Offices*, Book 1, Chapter 12; and the *Glossa Ordinaria*, Preface on the Canonical Books, Volume 1. <note>original Latin: "Siet Isidorus de Seville de Of. l. 1. c. 12. & Glof. ord. Præt. de lib cent. t. I."</note></margin>

3. Finally, that a great dispute arose over this matter at the Council of Trent. <note>The 16th-century council of the Roman Catholic Church which finalized their biblical canon.</note>

Those who cast doubt on the Rule <note>The "Regelmaat" or Canon.</note> of the New Testament bring forward some weak reasons, about which we shall say a word.

1. They object: That the Church Fathers, upon whose authority we received the canon of the New Testament, quoted the Apocryphal and Canonical books indifferently and without distinction; from which one concludes that they must go together.

**Answer 1.** Nothing is more common than for Scripture, the Church Fathers, and sometimes secular writers to be cited together without giving each the same authority. 2. The Church Fathers did not speak of these two types of books without distinction, even though some of them were mistaken regarding certain books.

2. **Objection.** The Church Fathers held the Epistle of Barnabas, the *Shepherd of Hermas*, the Epistles of Clement, and of Polycarp in as high regard as any book of the New Testament. **Answer.** This cannot be proven; and even if a Church Father or two accepted a book as canonical that is not, that cannot in the least harm the general opinion of the Church.

3. They say: It is incomprehensible that one receives the Gospels of Mark and Luke into the canon of Holy Scripture while rejecting the works of Clement and Barnabas.

**Answer.** There is a great difference between these writings; also, the Church has never given the same testimonies to the writings

<sig>Part 1.</sig>

<column-break/>

of Barnabas as to those of Mark. Dodwell <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711), a scholar and theologian.</note> proves through many passages of the Church Fathers that Peter and Paul had given testimony to the Divine inspiration of Mark and Luke.

**Objection.** There is not a single Book of the New Testament that has not been rejected by one or another of the Church Fathers.

**Answer.** That is false. What led to the acceptance of the Apocryphal Books into the Rule of Scripture was likely: 1. Because the Church Fathers cited and praised them. 2. Because they were read in some churches. Therefore, the Council of Carthage placed them in the Canon in the year 397.

Furthermore, instead of these books being called "Apocrypha," the others bear the name of **Canonical**, or Regular—from a word meaning "Rule"—because they are the only ones that must be held as the Rule of Faith and Morals. The register of Holy Books was called the *Canon*; Jerome is one of the first to have used this word in this sense. To these "Rule-books" we must especially hold fast, to exercise ourselves in them and to draw from them the nourishment and comfort of our souls. *Blessed is the man whose delight is in the Law of the Lord, so that he meditates on it day and night!* <note>Psalm 1:1-2.</note> *How blessed are they who walk in this Law, who keep the testimonies of the Lord and seek Him with their whole heart!* <note>Psalm 119:1-2.</note>

There are counted 23,202 verses in the Old Testament and 7,959 in the New Testament.

Answer. Those who pass a false judgment on whatever matter it may be / sin / because they make a bad use of their reason / which God has given them to know the truth / and not / to believe a lie. One thinks that the mistake / which one commits therein / does not mean much / unless it has bad consequences; which one can foresee / but not prevent. But one is mistaken: although the errors / which involve us in sins / and disturb civil society / are a greater evil / than other errors / which are not so bad in their consequences / nevertheless / all error is a moral deformity. The minor consequence of a matter / regarding which one gives a false judgment / does not always diminish the sin; it also weighs it down; when there is no other obligation / to declare ourselves / than the aim we have to satisfy our presumption / and secret pride. One must never pass a judgment / except in proportion to our knowledge. # THE CHRISTIAN <note>This header continues the title "The Christian Divinity" from previous pages.</note>

...plunge into an abyss of error: One can attribute no less wisdom to people who are perfectly righteous and perfectly instructed regarding the use they must make of their reason than corrupt and unrighteous people possess, among whom there are many who are accustomed to suspend their judgment and not to speak as if certain of doubtful things until they see no more reason for doubt.

3. The children, who would not have been in a state to make all these observations, would have been limited and directed by the happy condition of their body and soul—being endowed with **original righteousness** <note>The state of perfection humans were believed to have inhabited before the Fall of Adam.</note>—to not judge unknown things and not to desire what is harmful.

<margin>Volume 2, Supplement, Chapter 18, pages 227, 230, etc.</margin>
6. **Objection.** It is with **heresy** as it is with manslaughter and adultery, which would cease to be so as soon as they are involuntary. That is to say, when one does not know that one is committing manslaughter or adultery: like a hunter who shoots someone hiding in a hedge, or like a woman who gives herself to someone whom she truly believes to be her husband.

<margin>Saurin <note>Jacques Saurin (1677–1730), a famous French Protestant preacher known for his eloquence.</note> page 312, etc.</margin>
**Answer.** Error can never be involuntary in the same way as the acts the writer brings forward. To make an accurate comparison, one must compare heresy to a willful manslayer, but one who commits the act through ignorance of the law. One must suppose that a manslayer convinces himself that manslaughter is no sin, or that killing his enemy in a duel is not manslaughter, but an act of righteousness. In this case, a murderer is no more innocent than a heretic; but it is also true that both are infinitely guilty.

I have been of the opinion that it

<column-break/>

would be pleasing to the reader if I brought him the arguments of a book that has caused a great stir, and the answers that have been given to the same.

I shall end this Chapter and this book after these three observations, which have already been made before me.

<margin>Saurin page 164.</margin>
1. A heretic can never religiously observe God’s laws while he remains in this unhappy state: not having the **true faith**, he also lacks the true love which is the soul and essential form of virtues and good works. He can do things that are good in themselves regarding their essence; but they will always be evil while they have no other principle than a **disguised self-love** which hides itself under the mask of the love of God.

<margin>page 188.</margin>
2. It is often very difficult to distinguish a **tolerable error** from a **deadly one**: since the gap that separates a significant error (though not fundamental) from a fundamental error on the same matter is sometimes so narrow that one cannot perceive or define it. Just as it is difficult to decide the exact moment of the end of the day and the beginning of the night, so it is difficult to distinguish a true Christian—who is subject to great weaknesses and has made little progress in **regeneration** <note>The process of spiritual rebirth and moral renewal in the believer.</note>—from a false Christian who has only moral virtues, which he even mistakes for Christian virtues.

3. One must always take care not to fall into error; and therefore constantly pray to God that He might enlighten us by His Spirit, and powerfully strengthen the truths of His word in our heart and mind.

***

->End of the First Book.<-

### CHAPTER I.

->There is no more than one God.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'W' at the start of the chapter, featuring ornate leaf and scrollwork patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

We have shown in the pre-
ceding Book that
God has primarily
made Himself known to
mankind in the Scriptures;
it now remains for us to 
investigate what they teach us concerning God. They tell us many things about Him, which must be carefully examined.

But, before we come to God’s Essence and Perfections, I will observe that Scripture everywhere establishes this first truth: namely, that there is no more than one God.

<margin>Deut. 6:4. Deut. 4:35. Deut. 32:39. Exod. 20:3. 2 Sam. 22:32. 1 Kings 8:60. Isaiah 44:6.</margin>
Hear, O Israel! The **LORD**, our God, is one **LORD**. Deut. 6:4. <note>This is the "Shema," the central prayer of Jewish life.</note> Which the Jews recite every morning and evening. It was shown to you, that you might know that the **LORD** is God: there is no one else besides Him alone. Deut. 4:35. See now, says God, Deut. 32:39, that I, I am He, and there is no God with me; I kill, and I make alive. And in the first Commandment of His Law: you shall have no other gods before my face. Who is God, except the **LORD**? 2 Sam. 22:32. So that all the peoples of the earth may know that the **LORD** is God; no one else. 1 Kings 8:60. And Isaiah 44:6: *I am the first, and I am the last, and besides me there is no God.*

This same truth is taught to us in the New Testament. Christ, being questioned by a scribe as to which is the first Commandment, answered him: the first of all the Commandments is, Hear, O Israel!

<column-break/>

<margin>Mark 12:29. 1 Cor. 8:4, 5, 6.</margin>
the Lord our God is one Lord. Mark 12:29. Paul says explicitly, 1 Cor. 8:4, 5, 6: *We know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is no other God but one. For though there be those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth (as there be many gods, and many lords), yet for us there is (but) one God.*

One can say that Paul, in this passage, is looking either at the name of "gods" borne by the Angels in Heaven and the Kings and Authorities on Earth, because of some glimmer of likeness between God and them—whether in the holiness and excellence of their being, or in the dignity of their Office—or at the custom of idolaters, who worshipped as gods certain things that were in the heavens, such as the stars, and on the earth, such as their living and deceased Kings, not to speak of other creatures that they served.

<margin>Eph. 4:6. 1 Tim. 2:5.</margin>
The same Apostle says, Eph. 4:6, *there is one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in all.* and 1 Tim. 2:5, *There is one God, and there is also one Mediator.*

<margin>Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, Book 1, Ch. 7. <note>original: "Aug. l. de doct. Christ. c. 7."</note></margin>
Reason confirms what Holy Scripture teaches us; those who have any concept of the Deity understand that by the word "God" one understands a Being that surpasses all others in perfections, and is even the origin of all perfections; the most perfect of all Beings that are, or that can be conceived. Now, one cannot have this concept without at the same time recognizing that there can be only one single God. For if there were many, then one could conceive of a more perfect Being than these gods: namely, a Being that would have no equal,

<meta>This page continues the argument for monotheism (the existence of only one God) that began on the previous page with scriptural proofs. Having established the Biblical basis, the author now turns to logical arguments and the writings of early Church Fathers and pagan philosophers to demonstrate that reason itself points to a single, supreme Deity.</meta>

THE CHRISTIAN

<margin>
Against Marcion, book 1, chapter 3. <note>Marcion of Sinope was an early heretic who believed there were two gods: a harsh creator god of the Old Testament and a loving god of the New Testament.</note>
</margin>
...that [God] alone would possess all the perfections of the others, and upon whom the others would be dependent. Also Bishop Phaebadius <note>A 4th-century bishop of Agen known for his opposition to Arianism.</note> wrote very well against the Arians in the year 359: *God is not God, unless he is alone, and is the true God.* This book is found in the Library of the Ancient Fathers. Tertullian had said almost the same thing: If there were many gods, they would either be equal in power, or one would be more powerful than the other; if equal in power, they would depend upon one another, because one could do nothing except with the consent of the others; and one could not tear down what the other wished to keep standing, so that none of them would have an infinite and unlimited power. Now, God is an absolutely independent being, whose power is infinite. And if one of them had more power than the others, he alone would be God.

Furthermore, if there were many gods, they would either be of the same essence and have the same perfections, and consequently there would be no distinction between them; or the distinction that existed would consist in one having perfections that were not in the other. If there were no distinction, they would not be many gods; and he who did not have all the perfections of the others would not be worthy of the name of God.

It is the most absurd thing in the world to say that there is only one supreme God, but that there can be many other lesser gods. Scripture knows no such distinction; and reason teaches us that whoever names "God" expresses a supreme being who has no one greater than himself.

<margin>
M. Nicole, Christian Instructions. <note>Pierre Nicole was a prominent French Jansenist theologian.</note>
</margin>
If there were many gods, every creature would be obliged to honor the one who had created him, while he could release himself from this honor toward others with whom he had no connection; and thus there would be a god whom one would not be obliged to honor or love, and from whom one would be independent. One must not say here that the works of these gods would be indivisible; for if the beings are divided, their works would be as well. If their union in their works was necessary to bring forth any effect outwardly, each one in particular would not be Almighty, and (consequently) not God. And if this union was not necessary, then why this unnecessary union

<column-break/>

of operation to produce the same effect?
Either a single God is enough, or he is not. If enough, why posit many? If not enough, then he is not God: for he who says "God," says a being who can do all things.

This truth is so certain that the philosophers among the Heathens recognized it, as can be seen from their writings. Lactantius <note>An early Christian author and advisor to Constantine I.</note> testifies that Pythagoras confessed one God, an immaterial Spirit, spread and extended through all of Nature, who gives life and feeling to all that exists. He called God "Unity." It has been believed that Socrates was condemned to death for no other reason than that he recognized only one God and mocked the others.

What can be said with truth is that Socrates recognized a single supreme God, but allowed for lesser deities; and the "godlessness" of which he was accused consisted in his openly condemning all the fables in which the gods were attributed shameful deeds, as one can conclude from Plato’s *Euthyphro*.

<margin>
Caelius Rhodiginus, Antiquities, book 12, chapter 4.
</margin>
<margin>
Plato, Book of Laws.
</margin>
A letter is attributed to Plato, being the 13th to Dionysius, in which these words are found: *You shall know when I write in earnest: then I begin my letters with a single God; but when I write otherwise, I begin them with many gods.* In his discourse to the Citizens of Athens, he addresses them thus: *God, in whom, according to the testimony of the ancients, the beginning, middle, and end of all things resides, for God permeates everything.* Of the same opinion were Apollonius of Tyana, Porphyry, <margin>Iamblichus.</margin> Hierocles, the Emperor Julian, Iamblichus, Proclus, Zoroaster, and Orpheus. Epictetus speaks of only one God. The Phoenicians called the Supreme God by a word <margin>Adad.</margin> that Macrobius explains as meaning "one." Celsus, the enemy of the Christians, acknowledges in the book he published against them under the Emperor Marcus Aurelius—writing in the name of the Heathens for whom he spoke—that there is only one supreme God, <margin>Origen, Against Celsus, book 8.</margin> just as there is only one monarch in the Roman Empire and in that of the Parthians, called Jupiter by the poets.

Tertullian proves in his apology against the Heathens that they naturally had the idea of only one God.

<margin>
chapter 17.
</margin>
"You know," he says, "that despite the constraint your soul suffers in the prison of its body, in the midst

<margin>Causes of the Idolatry of the Pagans.</margin>

## CHAPTER II.

### Concerning the false Deities spoken of in Scripture.

It will without doubt not be unpleasant to see here in a few words the names of the false deities mentioned in Scripture. Many scholars have dealt with this at length, such as Vossius <note>Gerardus Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch classical scholar and theologian.</note>, Seldenus <note>John Selden (1584–1654), an English jurist and polymath who wrote a famous study on Syrian gods.</note>, Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar.</note>, Hottingerus <note>Johann Heinrich Hottinger (1620–1667), a Swiss philologist and theologian.</note>, and Jurieu <note>Pierre Jurieu (1637–1713), a prominent French Protestant theologian.</note> etc.

I. Mention is made of Teraphim in Gen. 31:19, 30, 34, 35; Judges 17:4, 5 and 18:14-20; 1 Sam. 15:23 and 19:13; 2 Kings 23:24; Ezek. 21:21; Hosea 3:4; Zech. 10:2. The Chaldean paraphrasts <note>Translators of the Targums (Aramaic translations of the Hebrew Bible).</note> have translated this word as image, or likeness, or Idol. The LXX <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> sometimes as Idols, Cenotaphs <note>original: "Cenotaphien"; empty tombs or monuments.</note>, or empty burial places; announcers, or tellers of Divine matters, and as speakers, etc. The most probable opinion is that they were human forms, as appears from the history of Micah. 2. Tools for seeking counsel or divining, as seen in Ezek. 21 and Zech. 10. Jurieu believes that they were household and protective Gods, and he proves it by the history of Laban, by the etymology of the word itself—which he derives from a Hebrew word meaning to heal <note>Referring to the Hebrew root 'rapha'.</note>—and by the comparison of the Teraphim with the Lares, or household gods of the Romans. He also believed that in their origin they were human images of their most prominent ancestors, who were honored within households. He subsequently describes the form of the Oracle of the Teraphim, as can be seen in his *History of Church Doctrines* <note>original: "Historie der leerstukken van de Kerk"</note>, Vol. III, p. 462, etc. See also Gregorius Franciscus's Lexicon; Ludovicus de Dieu on Gen. 31:19; Spencer on the Urim, etc.; Hottinger's *Smegma Orientale* Book I, ch. 5; Kircher's *Oedipus* Vol. 1, synt. 4.

II. Mention is made of the Golden Calf, which the Israelites worshipped in the Wilderness, and of which they say that every misfortune that befalls them is an ounce of the Golden Calf <note>A Jewish proverbial idiom suggesting that all subsequent national suffering was a delayed punishment for this original act of idolatry.</note>: Exod. 32:4; Ps. 106:19. Most scholars believe that it was an imitation of the Egyptians,

<column-break/>

to which were added the Calves of Dan and Bethel by Jeroboam. 1 Kings 12:28.

III. Regarding the Baal-Peor of the Moabites and Midianites, see Num. 25:2, 3. The LXX call him Belphegor. Ps. 106:28; Hosea 9:10. It was, according to Seldenus, the Pluto <note>The Roman god of the underworld.</note> of the Heathens; or, according to others, the Priapus <note>A Greek god of fertility.</note> of the Greeks and Romans. The *Miphleseth* <note>An idol or "abominable thing."</note> of Maacha was the same, 1 Kings 15:13; 2 Chron. 15:16, as well as Chemosh <note>original: "Kamos".</note>, Num. 21:29; 1 Kings 11:7; 2 Kings 23:13; Jer. 48:7, 13; Judges 11:24. Nebo was the place where Belphegor gave his oracles. See Isaiah 46:1, where it is taken for the Idol itself.

IV. Regarding the Molech of the Ammonites, see Lev. 20:2; 1 Kings 11:7; 2 Kings 23:10; Jer. 32:35, 7:31, 19:5; 2 Chron. 28:1, 2; Lev. 18:21; Acts 7:43. This Idol was sometimes called Milcom, 1 Kings 11:5, and sometimes also Baal, Jer. 19:5. Adrammelech and Anammelech are the same as Molech, 2 Kings 17:31; these were the Gods of Sepharvaim. It was the Saturn of the Greeks and Romans, and, according to others, the Teutates of the Gauls. Others believe it was Mars. This Molech is the same as Chiun <note>original: "Kyun".</note> and Remphan, Amos 5:26; Acts 7:43. The Egyptians called Saturn "Remphan," and the Phoenicians "Chiun."

V. Regarding Baal, read Num. 22:41; Judges 6:25; 1 Kings 16:30, 32, and ch. 18 and 19; 2 Kings 10 and 11:18, 17:16, 21:3, 23:4, etc. Some have thought that it was Mars; but others consider it the Jupiter of the Heathens, or the Bel of the Babylonians.

VI. Regarding Baal-Berith, see Judges 8:33 and 9:4. Some believe it is the Jupiter who presided over covenants. Others, a goddess named Beroé. Jurieu believes it is Cybele <note>An ancient Anatolian mother goddess.</note>.

VII. Mention is made of Baalzebub, or Beelzebul. 2 Kings 1:2, 3, 6, 16; Matt. 10:25 and 12:24. Some have believed that it was the Baal or Jupiter of the Syrians; others the Pluto of the Greeks.

VIII. Regarding Dagon, see Judges 16:23; 1 Sam. 5:2; 1 Chron. 10:10; 1 Macc. 10:83, 84. It was the God of corn and agriculture <note>original: "Veld-bouw".</note>, according to Bochart. Seldenus believes it is the God Oannes, whom the Babylonians worshipped. Jurieu identifies him as Neptune, the Sea-God.

IX. In 2 Kings 17:30, Nergal is mentioned. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> believed that it was a Goddess who was worshiped among the—

DIVINITY. Book II. Chapter III.

[...the] form of a wild hen <note>The text likely refers to the idol *Nergal*, who in Jewish tradition was often depicted as a cock or hen.</note>, worshipped it. Jurieu <note>Pierre Jurieu (1637–1713), a prominent French Protestant theologian.</note> believes it was the Sun; others, fire.

X. Mention is also made of the idol of the Hamathites, *Aschima* or *Asiama*. *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> believed that it was a Goddess worshipped under the form of a goat. *Jurieu* considers it to be the Sun.

XI. Mention is also made of *Nibkas*, or *Nibchas*, which the Jews believe to have been a dog; just as there was indeed an Egyptian God *Anubis*, who in their symbolism had the form of a dog; but *Jurieu* believes it was the Sun, the God of the Hivites.

XII. <margin>2 Kings 17:31.</margin> *Tartak* was another idol of the Hivites. The Hebrews believe it was a donkey; *Jurieu*, that it was the Sun.

XIII. <margin>2 Kings 5:18, 13;</margin> *Rimmon*. According to some, *Venus*; according to others, the Sun; according to others, *Jupiter*.

XIV. <margin>Isa. 37:38 and 2 Kings 19:37.</margin> The *Nisroch* of Sennacherib is, according to some, *Jupiter Belus*, worshipped by the Assyrians under the form of an eagle; and the Nimrod of Moses.

XV. <margin>Ezek. 8:14.</margin> *Thammus* <note>Tammuz</note> is *Adonis*, the Sun.

XVI. <margin>Judg. 2:13, 3:7, and 10:6. 1 Sam. 7:3, 4, 12:10, and 31:10. 2 Kings 23:13.</margin> *Astharoth*. A Goddess of the Sidonians is the *Astarte* of the Greeks, according to *Bochart*. It is *Venus*, according to *Huet*; *Sephora*, according to *Grotius*. *Cybele* is the same as *Astera* in 2 Kings 21:3. According to *Jurieu*, she is the Moon, and the *Juno* of the Greeks and Romans.

XVII. <margin>2 Kings 17:30.</margin> *Succoth-Benoth* is the *Venus* of the Babylonians, or the *Pleiades*.

XVIII. <margin>Isa. 65:11.</margin> Mention is made of *Gad* and *Meni*. *Gad* is, according to some, the host of heaven; according to others, Fortune; according to others, a constellation and a guardian spirit that ruled over birth. *Meni* is, according to some, a counted and determined number of stars, like the seven wandering stars <note>The seven "wandering stars" or planets known to the ancients: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, the Sun, and the Moon.</note>; according to others, one of the stars and the spirit assigned to it, having influence over the birth of men. Some consider *Gad* and *Meni* to be *Jupiter* and *Venus*; others, *Mars* and *Mercury*. Others consider *Gad* to be the Moon and *Meni* the Sun; others understand *Gad* as the Sun and *Meni* as the Moon.

XIX. <margin>Jer. 25:26 and 51:41.</margin> Mention is made there of *Sesach* <note>Sheshach</note>. Some have believed that *Sesach* signifies *Babel*, or Babylonia, by a scrambling of letters <note>This refers to *Atbash*, a Hebrew reversal cipher where the first letter is replaced by the last, etc. In this system, B-B-L (Babel) becomes Sh-Sh-K (Sheshach).</note>. But it is

<column-break/>

thought that *Sesach* was a deity of the Babylonians, and that the Prophet intended to signify one of their idols by "Babel," which could well be the goddess *Anaitis*, a deity of the Persians who was likely the Moon.

XX. <margin>Daniel 11:38.</margin> *Maüzzim* <note>The "God of Fortresses"</note> is, according to some, the Anti-Christ. According to others, the idol which the Anti-Christ shall serve; according to others, *Mars*; according to others, the *Demones* <note>original: "Demones"</note> of the Heathens, spirits who were mediators between God and men. *Jurieu* believes that it is the Roman Empire, with the Roman Eagles, to which *Antiochus* had to do homage.

XXI. <margin>2 Kings 23:5. Ezek. 8:16.</margin> Mention is also made there of the service of the Sun, Moon, and Stars.

It is with only a word or two that I cite here the primary opinions of the scholars on this matter: I confess frankly that most appear to me as conjectures of little weight, though one seems more probable and ingenious than the other. Our work is not suited to investigating these riddles.

### CHAPTER III.
#### ->Concerning the Names of God.<-

<margin>Gen. 17:1.</margin>
Scripture teaches us not only that there is a God, but it makes Him known under various names.

My intention is not to bring up all these names. There is one which, according to the explanation of some scholars, means "He who is all-sufficient" <note>This refers to the name *El Shaddai*.</note>, to give us to know that all other beings have need of God, but that God needs no one to be perfectly blessed; that He possesses within Himself the beginning of His happiness; that He is all-sufficient to create and bring forth all that He wills, and to fulfill our desires; and that He is the supreme good of the creature. Others translate it as "the Almighty," who can do all things; who, just as He has created all things, can also destroy all things; and before whom everything must yield. There is another name <note>Referring to the Tetragrammaton, *Yahweh*.</note> which means, "I shall be," or "I shall be who I shall be," to express that God is a being that exists necessarily and by Himself. But among all the names given to God in Scripture, <margin>Exod. 3:14.</margin>
