# THE CHRISTIAN [DIVINITY]

...there are three noteworthy [names]: Jehovah, God, and Lord.

<margin>Isaiah 42:8. Revelation 1:4. Isaiah 43:10, 11, 12.</margin>
The First is often found as: *I am the Jehovah, this is my name*, which John explains to us in Revelation 1:4 as *He who is, who was, and who is to come.* One can say that this name includes two things. 1. A Being that exists by Himself, who is eternal, and depends on no other being; from which it follows that He is the cause of all others; for being the first of all beings, He created the others. 2. A being that is unchangeable and steadfast in His promises; therefore God said to Moses:

<margin>Exodus 6:2.</margin>
*By my name Jehovah, I was not known to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.* <note>In traditional translations of Exodus 6:3, God states He appeared to the patriarchs as God Almighty (El Shaddai) but was not known by His name Jehovah. The author is explaining the nuance of "knowing" a name as experiencing its reality.</note> This was because they did not live long enough to see the fulfillment of God’s promises regarding the multiplication of their seed and the leading of their descendants into Canaan. He had made Himself known as the strong and mighty God in the Creation of the World and in the guidance of His providence; but having not yet fulfilled the promises made to the Fathers, it is said: *by my name* (which signifies a being steadfast in His promises) *I was not known to them.*

These words are then poorly translated [in some versions]. *I have not only become known to them by my name Jehovah;* or *have I not become known to them,* etc., as a learned man has very well remarked.
<margin>Gousset.</margin> <note>Jacques Gousset (1635–1704) was a French Protestant theologian and prominent Hebrew scholar who argued for specific nuances in the translation of the Hebrew text.</note>

This name is given only to the adorable Supreme Being. Therefore, Isaiah 42:8 follows: *I will not give my glory to another.*
<margin>Isaiah 42:8.</margin>

It is true that this name is given to an Angel in Genesis 16:13, 18:17, and Exodus 3:4. But we shall see elsewhere that this is no created Angel, but an Angel who is the Creator, who is called the Angel of the Presence <note>original: "d'Engel des aangezigts"</note>, the Angel of the Great Counsel <note>original: "d'Engel van den grooten Raad", a title for the pre-incarnate Christ common in older theology</note>, the God of Vision, and the Judge of all the Earth, who had delivered Jacob from all evil; the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Because it is said in Exodus 17:15 that *Moses built an Altar, and called it 'The Jehovah is my banner'*, one must not imagine that the Lawgiver of the Jews gives this name to the Altar. Rather, these words, *The Jehovah is my banner*, were like the motto of this Altar; in the same way as one writes on a court building, *The LORD is my protector*: from that, it is not to be concluded that one gives the name of

<column-break/>

LORD to the building.

The same applies to Ezekiel 48:35: *the name of the City shall be, The Jehovah is there.* These are two very different things: to say the City shall be named *Jehovah*, or the City shall be named *The Jehovah is there.* The first proposition says that the City has the name of Jehovah; but this is not said. The second only states that the Jehovah dwells in the City; and that is what Ezekiel intends to make known. Jeremiah 33:16.

One must also not believe that the Ark is called *Jehovah*, because the Israelites, turning themselves toward this token or symbol of God’s presence, said, *Arise, Jehovah, and let all your enemies be scattered*, because they spoke to God, and not to the Ark.
<margin>Psalm 68:1.</margin> <note>The Dutch text cites verse 2, following the Hebrew numbering.</note>

Furthermore, it should be noted that the Jews do not dare to pronounce this name, and scholars do not even agree on how it should be read. This name *Jehovah* is the comfort of the Church, which is assured that God will fulfill His promises. Psalm 138:8; Isaiah 50:10; Micah 7:7. This name will also fill the unrepentant and the godless with terror; for if God is constant in the fulfillment of His promises, He is also so in the execution of His threats. The second Name to be noted is that of **Lord**, corresponding in the New Testament to that of **Jehovah** in the Old. In particular, it is applied to our Savior Jesus Christ. It signifies the dominion that God has over us, the Right that He possesses to do with our persons as He pleases; a Right that belongs to Him as our Creator, Sustainer, Benefactor, and Redeemer.

The third name is that of **God**, regarding which some remarks are necessary.

1. This name is sometimes given to creatures. 2 Corinthians 4:4, *the God of this Age*, because he—namely the Devil—exercises an absolute dominion over the corrupt world, which nonetheless belongs to God alone. Rulers are also called **Gods**. *I have said, ye are Gods, and ye are all children of the most High.* This is because there is some comparison between their authority in the world, the elevation they are in, the power they have to command what pleases them and to carry it out, and the authority that God has over His creatures, His infinite elevation above all created things, and His absolute power to do all that He wills.
<margin>Psalm 82:6.</margin>

Lord: A title of dominion and authority, often used for Christ in the New Testament. Moses, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob: The patriarchs of Israel. Gousset: Jacques Gousset, a noted 17th-century Hebrew scholar. Jesus Christ: The Savior. Creator: The maker of all things. Redeemer: One who saves or buys back. will. It is also said of Moses that he was to be a God to Aaron; *Aaron shall speak for you to the people; it shall happen that he shall be a mouth for you, and you shall be a God to him.* That is, you shall do in respect to Aaron what I do in respect to you; you shall make known to him what he shall say to Pharaoh, just as I tell it to you. Finally, the Idols of the Heathen are also called Gods, because the nations held them to be Gods.

When this name is given to creatures, there is always something from which this is apparent: either it is put in the plural, as in Psalm 82:6, *you are Gods*, or something is added, *but you shall die like other men.* Paul says, *the God of this Age* <note>Referring to Satan in 2 Corinthians 4:4.</note>: Or it appears through something that precedes it, as in Exodus 4:16. 3. The name of God implies, in its own meaning, a supreme independent being, on whom all others depend; it is therefore by no means a title of office. The idea that one naturally forms upon hearing this word is that of an excellent and supremely perfect being. This presents itself first to the understanding: therefore, when one wished to convince the Heathen that there was but one God, and to refute the multitude of Gods they had introduced, one always brought them back to this innate idea, and proved that there could be only one first being, on whom all others depend. There is no one who, when asked what he understands by the name of God, does not immediately answer: a being that exists through itself, and that made everything we see. It is true, this name, as has been said, is attributed to men who are elevated in dignity, but it does not follow from this that it signifies only an excellence of dignity: for then it would belong properly, and not figuratively, to the Authorities and Kings of the Earth; which no one would dare to say.

### IV. CHAPTER.

->Of God's Essence, and Perfections<-
->in general.<-

Having considered the Names of God, it follows for us to take His Nature into consideration.

But one must immediately acknowledge here that God, being an infinite being, cannot be perfectly understood by finite beings. The Heathen have confessed that it was impossible for the human understanding to know the Deity; some have said that it is something that is neither to be found nor even to be sought. Everyone knows the case of that Philosopher <note>Simonides of Ceos (c. 556–468 BC), as recounted by Cicero in *On the Nature of the Gods*.</note> who, being asked by the King of Syracuse <note>Hiero I</note> about the Nature of God, first demanded one day to think about it, then two days, then four, and finally confessed that the more he thought about it, the less he understood of it. Among the primary articles of faith of the Brahmins <note>original: "Brachmannen"; early modern term for Hindu priests and scholars.</note>, one finds this proposition: *God has not been known, nor can he be known.* It is no wonder that nations who had not read the Scripture reasoned in this way. But we, who have the Scripture, although we must confess that there are infinite things concerning the Deity that are unknown to us, cannot say that God has entirely hidden His nature from us; on the contrary, we have reason to praise Him that He has made known to us in the Scripture a portion of His adorable perfections: and this we shall now investigate.

<margin>Matthew 5:48.</margin>
Certainly, as often as we think of God, this idea simultaneously arises in us: that God is the most perfect being, and the source of all perfections. This the Scripture confirms. *Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.*

One calls perfection that which places a being in a better state than it would be without the same.

But, besides this general idea, the Scripture describes God's perfections to us in detail. It presents Him to us as a pure Spirit, who has no communion with matter; as an infinite being, infinitely simple, in whom all is essence and pure essence; as an eternal being, without beginning, existing through Himself, absolutely independent of all...

<sig>* 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: all</meta>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of God's essence, specifically focusing on His infinite perfections and the definition of God as a spiritual, non-material being, in opposition to pantheistic views.</meta>

<header>THE CHRISTIAN</header>

all other beings; as being everywhere present, and knowing from all eternity what shall happen / and what is hidden in the abyss of future times; as an almighty being, who does everything by his sole will / whose power extends as much over nothingness / as over existence; and who / having no need for a subject or matter to work upon / produces the subjects / upon which he wishes to work: as an unchangeable being, above all changes of time; the supreme Good, Just, Merciful, Wise, the beginning and end of everything; the source of all Good, and the supreme Good of man; as a being, who has created all others / and through his cooperation sustains / and through his providence governs. Who / whereas he could have destroyed humans / on account of their sins / through his judgments / has appointed for them a Mediator <note>A reference to Jesus Christ as the intercessor between God and humanity.</note> / who instructs them through his word / and Sanctifies through his Spirit / and promises a Blessed immortality. Finally, as a being that necessarily exists, that cannot cease to exist, and is glorified. Beyond these perfections, nothing more can be conceived. God possesses them absolutely: for there is not one perfection / or this supreme being has it in the highest degree of perfection / and one cannot take even one of them away (through thought) / without taking away the Divinity from him. He possesses them all without any imperfection; for he is entirely free from all defect / and can never cease to possess the same / just as he cannot cease to be God.

These perfections are not in conflict with one another / although the effects sometimes seem to run against each other; they are the essence of the Godhead itself.

But let us enter into a particular examination of these perfections / with those firm thoughts / that they all obligate us / to glorify him / who possesses them / and to imitate him to the best of our ability.

## CHAPTER V.
### That God is a Spirit, and Invisible.

The First perfection / that we conceive in God / is / that he is a Spirit; released from all materiality. We know only two sorts of beings / Body and Spirit: there is no one / who does not understand well enough / that a Spirit is more perfect

<column-break/>

than a Body: for that which says Body / says a being / composed of parts / divisible and imperfect / subject to various changes / that cannot move itself / nor once moved can stop; and that / upon the meeting of another Body / loses as much of its movement / as it imparts to the other. Just as the thoughts / that we have of God / exclude all imperfection / and on the contrary make him be regarded as a being / who possesses all perfections / so this idea obliges us to believe / that God is a Spirit / that is / a thinking being: for it would be the greatest absurdity / to attribute any imperfection to a being / that one holds for the most perfect being. One can judge by this / how extravagant the opinion is / of those who have believed / and still believe / that God and extension <note>In philosophical terms, "extension" refers to the physical property of occupying space, which characterizes material bodies.</note> are one and the same thing / and that God and the World make but one being.

<margin>Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book 1.</margin>
The Stoics <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that often identified God with the rational principle of the universe.</note> viewed the whole world and the whole of Nature / composed of Spirits and bodies / as the true God. They fell into gross errors regarding this point / which *Lactantius* refutes. Pliny was of the same thoughts.

<margin>* *Institutes*, book 2. 5. <note>Refers to the *Divine Institutes* by the early Christian author Lactantius.</note></margin>
It is said that one Amaulri <note>Amalric of Bena, a 12th-century theologian whose followers were accused of pantheism.</note>, whose dead corpse was exhumed and burned to Ash / in the Year 1208. had taught / that all things were God / and one single being.

One ascribes the same sentiment to a certain David of Dinant / who may have been the Disciple of this Amaulri. Pietro della Valle <note>A famous 17th-century Italian traveler.</note> speaks of some Mohammedans, who believe / that the four Elements are God / man / and all things; as also of others / who maintain / that all that one sees / all that is in the world / and all that has been created / is God.
This has been / in these times / the opinion of Spinoza; the first / who brought Atheism <note>original: "Ongodistery," a derogatory term for Spinoza’s pantheism, which contemporaries viewed as synonymous with atheism because it denied a personal, transcendent God.</note> to a certain structured doctrine / and dared to defend the most contradictory proposition / running against the clearest knowledge of the human understanding. He posits: 1. That there is but one Substance <note>The underlying reality or essence of things.</note> in the essence of things / and that this Substance is endowed with infinite attributes / and among others / with extension / and thoughts. 2. Indeed one can take no perfection away from him: but one must attribute no imperfection to him / as Spinoza does. 15. One must not wonder that God is shown in scripture as if he had a body, with eyes, ears, arms, etc. It is to accommodate our weak understanding that he describes himself thus; these are figures of speech <note>original: "spreektwyzen"</note> that have less to do with what God is, than with what we are. One must then explain this in a manner worthy of God. It is said that God has **eyes**, because he sees all; **Ears**, because he hears all; **Arms**, because he supports all; **Feet**, because he is everywhere; **Hand**, because he does all. Thus one can explain everything that is said of God, but two observations will be useful here.

1. That scripture ascribes limbs to God which are the most familiar and the origins of our actions, such as the heart, or those that serve us as tools to perform our deeds. It speaks of God’s **heart**, because it is like the beginning of life; of **hands**, because we work with them; of **eyes**, because through them we obtain knowledge of the things we wish to know. **Ears**, because we hear with them those who speak against us; a **mouth**, because through it we make known the feelings of our heart. In short, **feet**, which guide us to all places where we wish to go.

2. When scripture attributes limbs to God, it gives them an infinitely extended power. God sees at the same time all that happens in the world; hears the cry of the heart; reaches from the highest of the Heavens to the deepest of the abysses. He weighs the mountains in a scale, and the hills with a balance. In a word, an infinite power; a proof that these things must not be taken according to the letter.

for no man shall see me, and live. <note>original: "want my zal geen mensche zien, en leeven." A reference to Exodus 33:20.</note>

One must, meanwhile, acknowledge that there are many places where it is said that people have seen God, and shall see Him.

But the meaning of these passages is easy to understand.

<margin>Gen. 32:30.</margin>
I. Some speak of the sight of Christ, who already under the Old Testament allowed Himself to be seen in a human form. Thus Jacob says, having wrestled the whole night with a Man, whom he subsequently realized was God: *I have seen God face to face, and my soul has been delivered.* But Jacob saw only the body that the Son of God had assumed for a time. In this way, one must also explain what is said of Manoah, Samson’s father, who, having seen the human form in which the Son of God had appeared to him—who ascended to Heaven with the flame of his offering—said: <margin>Judges 13:22.</margin> *We shall surely die, because we have seen God.*

<margin>Job 19:25, 27.</margin>
II. Other passages speak of the sight of Christ as a man, as He shall appear on the Day of Judgment. In this way Job said: *I know that my Redeemer lives, and He shall stand at last over the dust; and, after my skin has been thus destroyed, yet in my flesh shall I see God; whom I shall see for myself, and my eyes shall behold, and not a stranger.*

<margin>* Gen. 28:13.</margin>
<margin>† Isa. 6:1.</margin>
<margin>‡ 1 Kings 22:19.</margin>
<margin>Dan. 7:9.</margin>
III. Others mention a sight in dreams, or in ecstasy. Thus it is said that * Jacob saw God in a dream at Bethel. Isaiah saw the Lord, † *sitting upon a high throne, the train of His robe filling the Temple.* Micaiah said: ‡ *I saw JEHOVAH sitting on His throne, and all the host of heaven standing by Him on His right hand and on His left.* So said Daniel: *I watched until thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days took His seat, whose garment was white as snow, and the hair of His head like pure wool.*

IV. It is also said that God has been seen whenever He has given some sign of His presence.

<margin>Num. 12:8.</margin>
V. When it is said of Moses that he saw God face to face, the Scripture intends to inform us that he saw the most glorious signs of His Majesty that God had ever given to

<column-break/>

men, such that no one before had ever beheld such illustrious and evident signs; through this, it also expresses the particular fellowship that this lawgiver <note>The OCR "weigeder" is likely a transcription error for "Wetgever," meaning Lawgiver (Moses).</note> had with God.

VI. When it is said of the Angels that they see God’s face (Matt. 18:10), it is because they are always before God’s throne as <term>attendants</term> <note>original: "Ipstrawanten" (from the Italian *stravante*), meaning guards, satellites, or ceremonial attendants who stand ready to serve a monarch.</note> ready to receive and fulfill His commands. Thus, in the Book of Esther, <margin>Esther 1:14.</margin> mention is made of seven lords of the Persians and Medes who *saw the face of King Ahasuerus*, and held the first places in the kingdom.

VII. Furthermore, one must distinguish between various kinds of "sight." There is a physical sight, and in that regard it is said that no one has ever seen or can see God; there is also a sight of the soul, which is nothing other than knowledge. Regarding this latter sense, it is true that we "see" God because we know Him; <margin>2 Cor. 3:18.</margin> and it is said that in His word, as in a mirror, we *behold with unveiled face the glory of the Lord, and are changed into that same image from glory to glory.*

<margin>1 Cor. 13:12.</margin>
VIII. Finally, when it is said that we shall see God in Heaven, and even "face to face," it is (as we shall show) because we shall know the blessed God as far as a creature is capable of doing so: that we shall have close fellowship with God, and enjoy all the holy blessings that flow from it.

From the invisibility of God’s essence, it follows that we must never undertake to represent Him in images. This is the conclusion we must draw from Deut. 4:15–18, from Isa. 40:18, Acts 17:29, and Rom. 1:23.

<margin>John 4:24.</margin>
From this it also follows: 1. That we must worship Him in spirit and in truth. 2. That purely physical service, if it is not joined with the spiritual, is unworthy of God. 3. That against all physical things, however beautiful and radiant they may be, we must say: "You are not my God." 4. That we are not made for physical things; and finally, that we must withdraw our hearts from them.

# THEOLOGY. BOOK II. CHAPTER VI.

## CHAPTER VI.

### God is a Thinking, Living, and Supremely Blessed Being.

<margin>Isa. 55:8. Jer. 23:20. Ps. 40:6.</margin>
Whenever one speaks of a Spirit, the thought of a being that thinks immediately arises: thus it is easily understood, since God is a Spirit, that thinking belongs to God's essence. The Scriptures often speak of God's thoughts. *For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways,* says the Lord in Isaiah 55:8. *The anger of the Lord shall not turn back, until he has executed the thoughts of his heart,* Jeremiah 23:20. *Your thoughts are very many,* Psalm 40:6. But one must not imagine that God thinks in the same way as angels or humans; certainly, He thinks in a much more perfect manner, which we would not be able to fully explain.

<margin>* Deut. 32:40. † Jer. 10:10. ‡ 2 Cor. 6:16. * 1 Thess. 1:9. † 1 Tim. 4:10. ‡ 1 Tim. 6:17. Acts 14:15.</margin>
Just as all that thinks lives, so the Scriptures also tell us that God lives. * *I live forever.* † *The Lord is the God of truth, he is the living God.* ‡ *You are the temple of the living God.* * *You turned from idols to serve the living God.* † *We hope in the living God, who is the Savior of all men, especially of those who believe.* ‡ *Command those who are rich in this world, that they set their trust in the living God.* Thus the Scriptures distinguish the Creator of Heaven and Earth from the false deities whom the Heathens served, which were either senseless and soulless things—such as the statues in their temples, the stars of heaven, the elements <note>The basic components of nature: earth, air, fire, and water.</note>, rivers, fountains, forests, field crops, herbs, and plants—or wild animals, such as crocodiles, etc., or humans who had lived in former times but lived no longer. Such were the gods of their fables; their Saturn, Jupiter, etc. Therefore, the early Christians used to say that the temples of the Heathens resembled graveyards more than temples.

It is not necessary to prove that we must always regard God as a Living Being; the matter speaks for itself. Life is a perfection; without it, no being can be perfect, and consequently, no God. If the being we worship were not living, it would not be worthy of our worship. What impropriety and unworthiness it would be for a living being,

<column-break/>

such as we are, to subject ourselves to a dead and soulless thing.

<margin>John 5:26.</margin>
But rather than dwelling on this, it is better to note that there is a great difference between the life of God and the life of creatures. God receives His life from no other. He has life in Himself. But all creatures have their life from God. The life of creatures changes every moment; therefore, it is compared to a river, which is never the same for a single moment because its waters are in a continuous flow: wherefore,

<margin>Daillé. You are. <note>original: "Ei", which is the Greek word for "You are" or "Thou art".</note></margin>
As a learned man <note>Likely referring to Jean Daillé (1594–1670), a prominent French Protestant theologian.</note> very well observes, if a philosopher in ancient times said that no one ever stepped into the same river twice, one could also say that one has never seen the same man, animal, or plant twice, since some change has come over them since we last saw them. But it is not the same with the life of God; He never loses anything of what He was and gains nothing that He did not already have. This even led the Heathens to say that, to speak properly, there is nothing but God who *is*. One saw this inscription on Apollo's Temple at Delphi: *You Are* <note>original: "Gy zyt." This refers to the Greek "Εἶ" (Ei) inscribed at the temple.</note>, upon which Plutarch makes this observation:

> "If one looks closely at the matter," he says,
> "we have no part in true being; 
> man is always between being and 
> nothingness; between being born and 
> dying; and of himself would be but 
> a dark appearance, a shadow, a 
> weak and floating idea. If 
> you want to make a strong effort with 
> your thoughts to grasp his being, 
> he escapes you, like water that 
> drips from the hands when one wants 
> to contain it. What is it, then, that is true? It is that which is Eternal. The expressions and words of 'presently,' 'a moment,' and 'now' make us think of time; but that vanishes instantly, and reason cannot lean upon it; it runs immediately toward the future or the past; that is, toward that which is not: and therefore one must conclude that God alone is, that He is without the sequence of time in an Eternal immobility and unchangeability, and that He is not measured by time, and is subject to not the slightest decay; for Him there is neither old, nor new, nor present, nor past; by the presence of His essential existence, He fills eternity; so that nothing but God is truly real."

...therefore, when God is said to Live, it is not only to distinguish Him from the Dead Idols, which Heathendom honored, but also from all Creatures, who have only a borrowed life. Finally, the life of most Creatures is of short duration, but that of God is eternal, as we shall see in the following.

Furthermore, the Scripture says not only that God lives, or * has life in Himself. But also that He is † life itself, ‡ the fountain of Life; * who gives Breath to all; that we live, move, and have our being in Him (y) in a word, that He makes all things alive. 1 Tim. 6:13. That does not only mean that God gives life to all living things, and that they enjoy the breath, power, and life of God; but also that He can give life to the dead, and grant them an immortal life. So that God is the cause of all life; of the life of nature, of Grace, and of Glory <note>In this context, 'Glory' refers to the state of eternal life in heaven.</note>.

Just as God is a living being, so He is always active; the excellence of every being that is capable of acting consists in its action. Therefore, a perfect being is not only capable of acting, but acts by necessity; since that is included in His essence.

God is not only a living and active being, but also supremely blessed <term>blessed: the original 'gelukzalig' combines the concepts of happiness, bliss, and holiness</term>. Some Philosophers have denied that there is a God; but there has not been one who has dared to assert that, if there were a God, He would not be blessed; those who denied providence and removed the governance of the world from God maintained that He was supremely blessed, but that the governance of the Universe would disturb His blessedness. (z) So true is it that one cannot have a thought of God without thinking of a being that enjoys supreme blessedness.

As such, Paul brings God to our attention; for not only speaking of

(y) When it is said that we have life, movement, and being in God, one must not understand it as if we were in Him like God's decrees; for in this sense, we would be God Himself. But this only means that God gives life, breath, and all things.

the Gospel, he says that it is the Gospel of the Glory of the Blessed God, 1 Tim. 1:11. But, after having exhorted Timothy to keep the Commandment, spotless and blameless, until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ, he adds, which in His time the blessed and only potentate Lord, the King of Kings, and Lord of Lords shall show. 1 Tim. 6:14, 15.

How could one not call a being truly blessed that, freed from all evil, possesses in rich abundance all the most perfect goods that one could wish for; who always acts in a profound rest in the noblest and most excellent way; whose glorious essence is unapproachable to sin, ignorance, passion, weakness, sorrow, and lack, and to all that we suffer and fear.

All the happiness of Angels and Men is but a shadow of God's blessedness; they can only have from God what makes them happy: but God has in Himself the riches of His blessedness, without needing to seek it elsewhere; and His blessedness receives no increase. He was as blessed before as after the Creation; and even if He annihilated the Creature, He would be no less blessed.

From this it follows:
1. That one cannot thank God enough for the benefits with which He fills us; without anything more being added to Him thereby.
2. Since God is supremely blessed, it is from Him that the happiness of Creatures depends; and we must seek our state of happiness in Him alone; which consists in knowing, loving, and enjoying God. Ps. 16:11, 33:12, and 73:28.
3. Finally, we shall be assured, if we hold steadfastly to God, that He will make us perfectly blessed.

# THEOLOGY. Book II. Chapter VII.

### CHAPTER VII.
### God is a being who knows all things.

<margin>
Proclus, *Platonic Theology*, Book 1, Ch. 21; Book 4, Ch. 5.
</margin>
**J**ust as God is a perfect being, it is clear that He knows all things. Even the Heathen <note>The author uses "Heathen" to refer to non-Christian classical philosophers, particularly Greeks and Romans.</note> confessed this; it is told that when someone once asked a famous Philosopher whether any crime of men could be hidden from God, he answered that even thoughts are not hidden from Him. Proclus, a famous Platonic Philosopher who lived around the year 500, says, "That all men know this by nature, that God knows all things, even the most hidden thoughts of the Heart." The Stoics were of the same opinion: Epictetus, the Emperor Marcus Aurelius, and many others. The Egyptians represented the Divinity by the "sight" <note>Referring to the 'Eye of Providence' or the Eye of Horus</note>, and dedicated hearing and sight to Her, to express that the Divinity hears and sees everything. The Muslims say, God knows everything that can be known; His knowledge reaches from the end of the earth to the highest heaven: nothing escapes this knowledge, not even the size of an Ant; He knows the movement of a dust mote in the air, as well as the thoughts of the Spirit; not through knowledge acquired over time, but through an eternal knowledge.

Scripture teaches this truth with great clarity.

<margin>
John 21:17.
1 John 3:20.
Heb. 4:13.
</margin>
1. In general, it says that God knows all things. So speak Peter and John. *There is no creature invisible before him, but all things are naked and opened to the eyes of him with whom we have to do.* Heb. 4:13. The expressions of the Apostle are excellent; they are taken from the cutting open of sacrificial animals, which were slaughtered in such a way that all their entrails, and all that was hidden within, were placed before the sight. Paul continues here with the borrowed manner of speaking that he had begun before, having compared God's Word to a two-edged Sword that pierces even to the dividing asunder of Soul, joints, and Marrow; alluding to the Knives that the Priests used to cut the Sacrifices.

<margin>
Matt. 11:27.
</margin>

But this will not be raised as an objection if one considers that nothing happens in the world except what God’s Counsel <term>Gods Raad|The divine plan or sovereign decree of God</term> has determined, as we shall show elsewhere; and when one observes that many things which we think could well happen do not occur because we do not know the connection they have with other things that necessarily take place. Furthermore, if this reasoning held ground, it would follow that God could not have foreseen a single thing, regarded as a matter that might not have happened, and which is therefore called a contingency <term>gebeurlyke|A 'contingency' or 'hap'; an event that is not certain but depends on other factors</term>. But no one has yet dared to maintain this.

It is said: If all future things, of whatever nature they may be, were known to God from eternity, one would have to conclude from that that all things happen by necessity; so that there would be no freedom, nor any Religion.

<margin>Crellius, *On God*, ch. 25. <note original="Crell. de Deo. c. 25.">Johannes Crellius was a prominent Polish-German Socinian theologian.</note></margin> I answer 1. It is true that it follows that whatever happens, happens by necessity; but that does not change the nature of things. 2. That, since God’s foreknowledge and decree do no violence to the will of men, one could not conclude, because God has determined all things, that man has no freedom and that there is no Religion. 3. It is true that it is very difficult to reconcile the freedom of man with God’s foreknowledge; but these two things are nonetheless consistently true: God knows all, and man is free.

It is then certain that God knows all things absolutely, even those which are called <term>contingent</term> <note>Events that happen by chance or through free will, rather than by natural necessity.</note>. We note this against the Socinians, who deny it and follow Cicero in that regard. The Church Fathers teach this truth everywhere. Justin Martyr says it is impossible for anything to be hidden from God—not only what is done, but what is thought. Augustine says, *God sees all.* Among the errors condemned by the <term>Sorbonne</term> <note>The theological faculty of the University of Paris.</note> in the year 1220 is this one: that the First Cause has no knowledge of future contingent events.

Reason agrees wonderfully well with Scripture here; if God did not know everything that can be known, there could be a more perfect being who *would* know everything; and therefore, the God whom we honor and worship would not be God. For, as we have proven elsewhere, to say "God" is to say the most perfect of all beings that are, or can be.

It will be said that, although it is said

<column-break/>

that God is Almighty, it does not follow from this that he can do contradictory things; likewise, although it is said that God knows everything, that only means he knows everything that *can* be known.

**I answer.** Everything that can, and will, happen can be known, since it is eventually known once it occurs. Since contingent things must happen in their own time, and certainly do happen, one must conclude that they cannot be unknown to God.

But, to press this more strongly, I ask whether God will one day know everything that will have happened in the world? No one can deny this; one would then have to say that he will become more perfect than he is now, if it were true that he does not currently know all things.

Let no one imagine that the Divinity humbles itself too much by extending its knowledge to the smallest things; on the contrary, one must be assured of this truth: that God has an infinite knowledge, being himself infinite; and a perfect knowledge, being the most perfect being.

One also need not worry that the knowledge God has of the sins of men defiles his perfectly holy being; one is not stained by the mere knowledge of sins, but only if one approves of them and commits them. That cannot be said of God.

A difficulty is raised about this infinite knowledge of God, which we must examine, consisting of the fact that God sometimes expresses himself in Scripture as if he did not know something; but these expressions should not seem strange to us, any more than when we read that God has limbs, hands, feet, etc., which must not be taken literally. Do not wonder, then, if God is introduced saying: *I will go down and I will see.* Namely, Sodom and Gomorrah. This is 1. to make us understand that he was not driven by blind impulse to punish this shameful people. 2. To make known to us the patience with which he calls sinners to repentance, although he could punish them at the very moment they sin against him. 3. Finally, to teach rulers how they should behave in their judgments, never passing sentence until they have investigated everything.

One does not need to investigate the manner in which God knows all things. It is certain that we cannot understand

# THE CHRISTIAN [THEOLOGY]
<page-num>176</page-num>

<meta>catchword: for</meta>

...how God can know the smallest things, as well as the greatest; the hidden thoughts of the heart, as well as the deeds that fall under the senses. For that reason, a learned Rabbi said that wanting to know the manner in which God knows all things is the same as if one wanted to be God.

One should not think that it is with God as it is with men, who know the same matter sometimes obscurely and sometimes clearly; who often must pay close attention to obtain some knowledge; who have difficulty remembering what they have learned, and usually proceed from known things to the knowledge of unknown things. God knows everything through a single act, most perfectly and distinctly.

Regarding the manner in which God can know future contingent things <note>events that may or may not happen, depending on free will</note>, there are many opinions. 1. Some say that it cannot be explained, such as *Ockham* and *Biel* in book 1, distinction 38. 2. Others say that God knows them in His ideas, such as *Bonaventure*, *Giles of Rome*, and *Alfonso de Mendoza* in *Theological Controversies* <note>original: "contr. Theol."</note>, question 7. But, it is said, ideas come to show that things are possible, and not that they will actually happen. 3. Others say God knows them because they are present to Him from all eternity. This opinion is attributed to *Thomas [Aquinas]*. Many have investigated it, but some do not approve of it. *Molina* in *The Harmony of Free Will [with Divine Grace]* <note>original: "de Concord. Arb. cum praef."</note>, question 14, disputations 48 and 49; *Suárez* in *On the Knowledge of God* <note>original: "de Scientia Dei"</note>, book 1; *Becanus* in *Scholastic Theology* <note>original: "Theol. Sch."</note>, part 1, chapter 10. 4thly, others say God knows them through the efficacy of His foreknowledge, and believe that things are in the future because they are foreseen. But this opinion is contested by many. *Vázquez*, disputation 68, in volume 1. 5thly, others say God knows them because He has determined that they should happen. Such as *Scotus* and the *Scotists* <note>followers of John Duns Scotus, who emphasized God's will and decrees</note>, in book 1, distinction 39, and *Quodlibetal Questions*, 14. See *Bradwardine* in *On the Cause of God* <note>original: "de causa Dei"</note>, book 1, chapter 14; *Durandus*; *Vázquez* in volume 1, disputations 64 and 65; *J. de Rada* in *Controversies between Thomas and Scotus* <note>original: "contr. inter. Thomam & Scot."</note>, part 1, controversies 29 and 30; *Alfonso de Mendoza*, *Theological Controversies*, question 7. 6thly, others say God, through His wisdom, sees which way the free will can turn and what it can do in such circumstances. This is the opinion of the *Jesuits*, etc. The opinion of *Scotus* is the most truthful.

Just as there are two kinds of things—those that are merely possible and those that will necessarily happen—so the theologians distinguish a two-fold know-

<column-break/>

ledge in God; one by which He knows all that is possible; and the other by which He knows what is to happen. They note that God, knowing Himself and His power, thereby knows everything that is possible or not, and that in consideration of His decrees, He knows all that will happen or not happen. From this it appears that God's knowledge is not the cause of the outcomes; the event does not happen because God foresaw it; rather, He foresaw it because it will happen, and it must happen because God determined it. One might possibly say: 1. If God did not know the things that will happen except because He has decided to permit them to happen, one would have no reason to praise God's knowledge so highly. 2. God's knowledge would not differ from that of men, except in that it would extend over more objects. 3. This is to establish Stoicism <note>an ancient philosophy suggesting everything is governed by fate</note>, subjecting God to destiny. 4. This makes all outcomes necessary. 5. Finally, God would not be able to foresee sins. I answer: 1. There is reason to praise God's knowledge, whether for the sake of its infallibility [or otherwise]. 2. These two things elevate God's knowledge infinitely above that of men. 3. Without here investigating what the Stoics believed, no one should wonder that God, after making His decrees, does not change His will, which would be unseemly for Him. 4. All outcomes are indeed necessary with respect to God. 5. Finally, God foresaw sins because He decided to permit them.

It is asked whether there is not also a third [type of] knowledge in God, through which He knows all that *would* happen if this or that thing occurred. <note>This refers to "Middle Knowledge" (Scientia Media), a concept used by Jesuits to explain how God knows what free creatures would do in any given situation.</note> I answer, it is not necessary to posit a third knowledge, since all that one can comprehend is either possible or necessary. Therefore, when it is asked how God knows what would have happened in the event that *Caesar* and *Alexander* had met one another? I answer: God knows it through the infinite knowledge by which He has foreknown all possible things. If one asks how God knew that those of *Keilah* would deliver up *David* (1 Samuel 23:11-12)? I answer: because He knew what was forged in the hearts of the *Keilahites*, just as He knows all the thoughts of all men. If one asks how God knew that *Tyre* and *Sidon* would have repented in the event that as many miracles [had been performed] for them as...

I answer that one must not press these words of Christ too literally, but rather explain them thus: just as when it is said of an immovable man that one could sooner soften the rocks than make him bend, if one could speak to them as to him; it does not follow from this that one knows for a certainty that the rocks will be softened by speaking. It is not to be concluded from this that Christ knew that if the children were silent, the stones would actually speak. See similar expressions in Ezekiel 3:6. But even if one assumed that the peoples of Tyre and Sidon would have converted, one could still say that Christ knew of their conversion through the knowledge of possible things <note>This refers to "simple intelligence," God's knowledge of everything that could potentially happen in any possible world.</note>. Those who support this "middle knowledge" cite other passages as well: Matthew 24:22, Luke 16:31, Jeremiah 38:17, to which the same answer can be given.

<margin>Arminius, *On the Nature of God* <note>original: "Th. de Nat. Dei"</note>. Vorstius, *Disputations on God* <note>original: "Disp. de Deo"</note>. Grevinchovius *Against Amesius* <note>original: "Advers. Amesium"</note>.</margin>
From this, it is easy to determine what one should think of this "middle knowledge" <note>Scientia media: the theory that God knows what any free creature would do in any given set of circumstances.</note>, which [Pedro] Fonseca, Luis Molina, or [Leonardus] Lessius invented, and which the Dominicans and Jansenists strongly oppose. They prove, first, that it is unbefitting of God, since it makes God dependent upon His creature. Second, that this view was only invented to weaken the powerful working of Grace, to rob God of the glory of our conversion and give it to the creature, and to establish the merit of works. Third, finally, that this view does nothing to reconcile human freedom with Grace and predestination, nor to defend God’s Holiness against those who accuse Him of being the cause of Sin. For the inventors of this middle knowledge admit that God knew very well that Adam, in the state he was in, could indeed sin. But we shall have occasion to speak of Sin hereafter. There are teachers who believe in a middle knowledge that differs greatly from the way Molina explained it, such as Gomarus, Robert Baronius, Antonius Walaeus, and Paul Ferry, a teacher at Metz.

This doctrine, that God knows all things, is of great utility in Ethics <note>original: "Zede-Kunde," literally "knowledge of customs/morals"</note>.

Likewise, nothing drives men more strongly toward sin than believing that God does not see it.

...must confess that it is a strong consolation for those who are in this state <note>Likely referring to those being falsely accused or misunderstood by others.</note> to know that the sincerity of their hearts is known to God; and that He will, sooner or later, reveal it. This was the comfort <margin>Job 16:19.</margin> of Job, who cried out: *My witness is in Heaven.* and of Paul, saying: *But <margin>1 Cor. 4:3, 4, 5.</margin> with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you, or by a human judgment: yes, I do not even judge myself: for I know nothing against myself; yet I am not justified by this, but He who judges me is the Lord; therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the things hidden in darkness, and reveal the counsels of the hearts: and then each one will have praise from God.*

Finally, this thought—that God knows everything—ensures that we bring Him our vows, desires, and prayers with certainty, and send our sighs Heavenward, being assured that He hears us, in whatever part of the world we may be, and that the sighs of our souls ascend to Him.

God is not only an omniscient being, but one who is supremely wise. The Scripture speaks of this often. <margin>* Rom. 11:33.</margin> *O the depth of the riches, both of the wisdom and the knowledge of God; how unsearchable are His judgments! and how untraceable His ways!* <margin>† Rom. 16:27.</margin> † To the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, be glory forever. <margin>‡ Job 12:13.</margin> ‡ With Him is wisdom and strength: He has counsel and understanding. Daniel says: <margin>Dan. 2:20, 21.</margin> *Blessed be the name of God from eternity to eternity; for His is the wisdom and the power: for He changes the times and the seasons, and He removes kings, and He establishes kings, He gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding.*

Wisdom is that virtue of God by which He governs all things; He knows all that He will do, and what means He will use to reach His proposed ends; He knows the value of all things, and estimates them at their true price: in a <margin>Wisdom 11:21.</margin> word, He does everything by measure, weight, and number, as the Book of Wisdom says <note>The "Book of Wisdom" refers to the Wisdom of Solomon, a book found in the Apocrypha.</note>. He always works in accordance with His perfections. This wisdom of God is evident daily; it has shown itself in the arrangement of the parts of this Universe; but primarily in the work of redemption and the proclamation of the Gospel. It shines forth in the governance of the world; there

<column-break/>

one sees that He draws light out of darkness; Glory out of shame, and life out of death.

This wisdom is "manifold" in every way, says Paul in Ephesians 3:10, and this variety is seen in all of God’s works; in Nature, where the whole is composed of such diverse parts; in civil society, where one sees the variety of States, Kingdoms, qualities, and social standings of men, and where God raises up and humbles, enriches and impoverishes the inhabitants of the world. Finally, it is seen in Grace, whether one considers the Church—which is now in Egypt, then in the Wilderness, then in Canaan, then in Babylon, then scattered over the whole earth, and whose members have various gifts—or whether one beholds the Head of the Church <note>Referring to Jesus Christ.</note>, who is at one time in humiliation, and at another in Glory.

Paul says, "the only wise God." Because, indeed, all wisdom of <margin>Rom. 16:27. 1 Tim. 1:17.</margin> men and Angels vanishes before the excellence of that of God; just as sunlight extinguishes our candlelight when it shines. Even the Heathens have acknowledged this.

The ways of God's Wisdom are sometimes known to men, but mostly they are hidden, and we must not venture to fathom them. They are as far exalted above us as the Heaven is above the earth. *"It is not for you, O man,"*

The consideration of God's wisdom serves:

1. To restrain our frivolous pride in judging God's works, and to make us wonder in silence at God's counsel, without venturing to criticize it.

# CHAPTER VIII.

## Of God's Will.

Inasmuch as God possesses all perfections that one understands to be in a rational being, it is beyond doubt that He has a Will. Scripture also speaks of this in many places.

But, since God can be considered in these two respects—either as the Supreme Judge of all that happens and Ruler of the world, or as our Lawgiver—it also appears that Scripture attributes two kinds of will to Him: The one, by which He decides to do, to permit, or to produce something; the other, by which He prescribes to man his duty and makes known what pleases Him. David speaks of the first <note>Theologians often call this the "Decrective Will" or "Secret Will."</note> in Psalm 115:13: *God does all that pleases Him.* And in Isaiah 46:10: *My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure.* The second Will is spoken of in various places. Isaiah 65:12: *You have chosen that in which I have no delight.* That is, that which God had forbidden. And Psalm 5:5: *You are not a God who has pleasure in wickedness.* That is, it does not please God; He forbids it. Paul mentions the first Will when he says in Ephesians 1:5: *Having predestined us to adoption as children through Jesus Christ to Himself, according to the good pleasure of His will.* And in 1 Thessalonians 4:3, he says, speaking of the second: *This is the Will of God, your sanctification.*

Through the first, God determines not only what He will do, but also what He will permit: For there are two kinds of things: those that God wills to do, which are indeed good; but there are others which He does not do, and cannot do, because they are evil; which He nevertheless permits, such as sins. Through the second, God commands

<column-break/>

what is good, and forbids what is evil.

I will not bring up all the different names here that scholars give to these two Wills; I will only note the following:

I. Of these Wills, one is for the most part hidden from us, while the other is revealed.

God hides them for many reasons (Proverbs 25:2). And it is certain that all these reasons are appropriate to His wisdom. God often fulfills His counsel through people who are only thinking of themselves; but He also sometimes reveals His secrets to His servants (Amos 3:7).

II. The first is the rule for all outcomes; the second is the rule for all our deeds.

<margin>Romans 9:19.</margin>
III. The things that God wills in the first manner always happen by necessity, and it is not possible that they should not happen. Therefore Paul said, *Who has resisted His will?* If it were otherwise, then there would have to be inconstancy or a lack of power in God, which cannot be said of a perfect being. But it often happens that the things which God commands, and which are pleasing to Him because they agree with His essence, do not happen; therefore God complains that His people have not been obedient to His voice (Psalm 81:12–15).

IV. One can oppose the first will of God without sin when it is completely hidden from us; but the second cannot be transgressed without sin because it has been revealed to us. For example, it is no sin to work toward the healing of a person whose death God has nevertheless decreed, when we do not know what God has determined regarding it; but it is a sin to commit a murder, which God has forbidden.

V. One can sin while fulfilling the first will, but one never sins when doing what God commands. For example: Although God had decreed from eternity that His Son should die, nevertheless Judas, who betrayed Him; Pilate, who condemned Him; and the Jews, who handed Him over, were not for that reason innocent, because their intention was not to fulfill God’s Will, which they did not know. But when one obeys God’s voice and does His commandments, one is completely pleasing to Him, and has everything to expect from His mercy.

While the Hebrews obeyed God's commands, God alone seemed...

...to fight for them and to perform wonders. They were the terror of other nations, the wonder of the Universe, and the masters of Nature, so to speak. But as soon as they rose up against God, they became less than the dust of the Earth, and the prey of their Enemies. One has seen them driven out of their own Land and treated everywhere as Villains or Slaves.

VI. These two wills <note>The author refers to the distinction between God's "Will of Decree"—what He has decided will happen—and His "Will of Command"—what He requires of humans.</note>, however different they may be, are nonetheless not contradictory. Indeed, if God urged men to do what He forbids them by His Law; or if He, after having decided that men should do something, did not want to allow the thing to happen, these would be two contradictory wills: but there is nothing that resembles that. This shall be shown through an example.

God had decided that Abraham should not Sacrifice his Son; meanwhile God commands it of him. It seems that these two wills are contradictory; they are nonetheless not: for God, who had decided that Abraham should not Sacrifice his Son, had also decided to command this Father to slaughter his only Son, with the purpose of testing this Father of the faithful, and subsequently to prevent him from carrying out what He had commanded him. Therefore, these two wills agree very well. God had decided to command Abraham to kill his Son, and indeed commanded it; He had also decided to prevent Abraham from doing what He had commanded him, and He prevented it. Who does not see that there is no contradiction in this?

Meanwhile, to give more light to this matter, which has some obscurity, I shall observe that, properly speaking, there is but one will in God, namely that which directs everything that shall happen in the world: for God has not only decided from eternity what His Creatures shall do, but also to make known to them what pleases Him and what their duty is. In this way, God fulfills but a portion of what He has decided when He commands something. The matter will be tangible through this example. God commands men to believe and to repent, and He does so as a consequence of this act of His will, by which He decided to command them such; if He does not give to all the Repentance and Faith to which He exhorts us, that must not seem a wonder to us, since He only carries out

<column-break/>

what He had decided, namely, not to give these virtues to all men.

One asks whether it is not wanting contradictory things to command repentance to men, and yet not wanting to produce repentance in them? No, without doubt. There would be a contradiction if God at the same time willed repentance and willed not to produce it; but God can have reason to demand repentance from men, and yet not to give the Grace of Conversion to all men; which we shall see in the treatise on the calling <note>The "treatise on the calling" refers to a later section on *vocation*, the theological process of God calling individuals to faith.</note>.

If one asks why God, who commands men to believe, does not give faith to all? I answer, it does not belong to us to judge God’s ways. If God does not give faith to all, it is not from lack of power: He can convert the one as well as the other. It is not with God as it is with men: impotence or passion often restrains our will; but these weaknesses are not in God. It is His wisdom that restrains this favorable movement of His will, for reasons that are always righteous, although inscrutable to us.

Therefore one must confess that in this matter there are depths that no created intellect should seek to fathom: since one cannot find satisfaction except by worshipping God’s guidance with humility and submission.

This will of God never changes, as we shall show more broadly when we speak of God’s immutability.

But it is also supremely free, since God suffers no violence from any being from without, and never does anything except for a wise reason, which is the highest Freedom, as we shall prove in another book.

Freedom being a perfection, God, who is perfect, must be free. One says that God, being an all-wise being, cannot work otherwise than He works, and therefore is not free: But 1. we cannot doubt whether God, whose wisdom is manifold <note>original: "verscheiden"</note>, can work in various ways. 2. ### DIVINITY. BOOK II. CHAPTER IX.

He has pulled us from the depths of nothingness and can cast us back in at any moment; we must always subject ourselves to the same, saying as our Savior <note>A common title for Jesus Christ in Dutch theology of this period.</note> has taught us:
<margin>Luke 22:42.</margin>
> Not my will, but yours be done.

We must never murmur against it.

We must never strive to know that which God wishes to hide from us: but carefully learn to know God's revealed will. We must adore His secret will and regard His revealed will as the infallible rule that we have to follow, and put all our strength and effort into work to fulfill it, so that it does not happen to us as it did to the servant who, knowing the will of the Lord and not doing it, was beaten with many stripes <note>A reference to the parable in Luke 12:47 regarding the responsibility that comes with knowledge of God's commands.</note>.

I believe I should answer two questions here.

1. It is asked: does God will all things in the same way? I answer: there are things that God necessarily wills, and which He could not *not* will. Thus He wills all that corresponds with His essence; and cannot will that one should hate Him. One might say, "If that is so, God would not be an independent being." I answer: God will be no less independent for that, since He depends on no other being. He is no less free than an honest man is free, even though he acts according to the rules of piety <term>Godsvrugt: a term for living a life of active devotion and reverence toward God</term>. But there are other things that depend absolutely on God's choice, such as creating a certain number of beings. God cannot will that sin remains unpunished; but He can determine salvation for one or another; that depends entirely on His good pleasure.

2. It is asked: can one not perceive two opposing wills in God? And does the Scripture not seem to suggest this? When in one place it says:
<margin>* Ezekiel 18:23, 32.</margin>
* God does not desire the death of the sinner. And in another: God rejoices in destroying the sinners (Deut. 28:63). I answer: One cannot perceive two conflicting wills in God without assuming that God contradicts Himself, which cannot be said without absurdity. As for the passages cited, they prove nothing: for these two things can well agree with each other: to have no pleasure in the punishment and death of His creatures, and yet to will their death to satisfy His justice when they have offended it. The first

<column-break/>

passage shows that conversion is highly pleasing to God. The second shows that when men abuse the riches of God's forbearance, it also pleases Him to exercise His justice over them.

Furthermore, we must always recognize God's will as being supremely good and perfect (Rom. 12:2) and accommodate ourselves to it, without ever murmuring (2 Sam. 15:26): "If He should say thus: I have no delight in you; behold, here I am, let Him do to me as seems good in His eyes."

Goodness is one of the most excellent attributes of God; and it is this virtue through which He communicates Himself to the creature. Even the Pagans knew that goodness is an essential perfection of the Godhead; they also said that their Jupiter was "great and good." <note>The author refers to the Roman title *Jupiter Optimus Maximus*, meaning "Jupiter, Best and Greatest."</note>

This will appear through an example.

God had decided / that Abraham should not Sacrifice his Son; meanwhile God commands it of him. It seems that these two wills are contradictory; yet they are not: for God / who had decided that Abraham should not Sacrifice his Son / had also decided to command this Father / to slaughter his only Son / with the purpose of testing this Father of the faithful / and subsequently to prevent / him from fulfilling that which he had commanded. Therefore these two wills agree very well. God had decided to command Abraham to Kill his Son / and did indeed command it; he had also decided to prevent Abraham from doing what he had commanded him / and he prevented it. Who does not see / that there is no contradiction in that?

Meanwhile / to give more light to this matter / which has some obscurity / I will observe that / properly speaking / there is but one will in God / namely that which directs everything / that will happen in the world: for God has not only decided from eternity / what his Creatures shall do; but also to make known to them / what pleases him / and what their duty is. In this way God fulfills only a portion of that which he has decided / when he commands something. The matter will be tangible through this example. God commands men to believe and to repent / and he does it as a result of this act of his will / by which he has decided to command them such things; if he does not give to everyone the Repentance and the Faith / to which he exhorts us / that must not seem strange to us / since he only carries out

One asks if that is not willing contradictory things / to command repentance to men; and to not want to produce repentance in them? No / without doubt. There would be contradiction in it / if God at once willed the repentance / and did not want to produce it; but God can have reason / to require repentance from men / and nonetheless not give the <term>Grace of Conversion</term> <note>The divine influence that enables a person to turn toward God and change their life.</note> to all men; as we shall see in the treatise on the calling.

If one asks / why God / who commands men to believe / does not give faith to all? I answer / it does not belong to us / to judge God's ways. If God does not give faith to all / it is not for lack of power: he can convert the one as well as the other. It is not with God as it is with men: impotence / or passion often restrains our will; but these weaknesses are not in God. It is his wisdom / that restrains this favorable movement of his will / for reasons / which are always just / although for us they are unfathomable.

Therefore one must confess / that in this matter there are depths / that no created understanding should want to sound: since one cannot satisfy oneself / except by adoring God's conduct with humility and submission.

This will of God never changes, as we shall show more broadly / when we speak of God's immutability.

But it is also supremely free, since God suffers no violence from any being from without / and never did anything / but for a wise reason / which is the highest Freedom / as we shall prove in another book.

Freedom being a perfection / God / who is perfect / must be free. # CHAPTER X.

## Of God's Hatred, Desire, Joy, Sorrow, Zeal, Expectation, Repentance, and Wrath.

<margin>Against Crellius, *On God*, chapters 30, 31.</margin> <note>Johannes Crellius (1590–1633) was a prominent Socinian theologian. The author is likely positioning his views against Crellius's more literal interpretation of God's emotions.</note>
Since God is a perfectly blessed being, it is understood well enough that one cannot attribute even the slightest emotion or passion to him: because passions always signify some disturbance, imperfection, and change. Meanwhile, one cannot deny that Scripture sometimes attributes these to him when it speaks of God's Hatred, etc. We shall see what all these expressions are meant to convey.

<margin>Of the Hatred of God. * Ps. 45:8. † Zech. 8:17. ‡ Prov. 6:16–19. Prov. 15:8. * Deut. 12:31.</margin>
To begin with Hatred: it is said there that God * *loves righteousness and hates godlessness.* That God † *hates the false oath, and when one devises evil in his heart against his neighbor.* ‡ *These six the Lord hates, yes, seven are an abomination to His soul: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart that devises wicked thoughts, feet that hasten to run to evil, a false witness who breathes out lies, and one who sows discord among brothers.* *God hates those who serve other gods, and the sacrifice of the godless.

By this, the Scripture intends to make known to us:
1. The will that is in God to punish some.
2. The refusal of the saving Graces which he gives to his beloved.
3. Consequently, it signifies a matter that is contrary to God's perfections and which he condemns.

The most terrible consequence of God's hatred will be the punishment he will bring upon the godless on the last day, when he shall separate them from him forever and cast them down into the dark and ghastly dwelling place of the Devils.

The greatest of all calamities is to be hated by God. To never be exposed to this, one must hate Sin to the highest degree and avoid it carefully: for there is nothing but Sin that is hated by God.

<margin>Of the Wrath of God.</margin>
From hatred I move on to God's Wrath, of which Scripture speaks to us so often.

One should not think that it intends to suggest that God is subject to this violent impulse, which we commonly call by this name,

<column-break/>

but it understands by it the Holy and Righteous will through which he makes sinners feel how much their conduct displeases him. The expression is taken from what commonly happens among men who are carried away by Wrath when they are insulted and wish to avenge it.

God makes the effects of his Wrath felt, sometimes even by his Children and Servants; when they do not answer their calling as they are bound to do, and corrupt themselves with the world. This was experienced by a Moses, a Daniel, a Hezekiah. So it is said that God is angry with his Church, but <margin>† Ps. 30:6. ‡ Isa. 54:7, 8.</margin> † *for a moment,* ‡ *for a small moment I have forsaken you, but with great mercies I will gather you; in a little Wrath I hid my face from you for a moment; but with everlasting kindness I will have mercy on you.* † It is true, this moment seems long to our Flesh <note>In this context, "Flesh" refers to human nature in its fragile and impatient state.</note>, which is naturally impatient and to which an hour of sorrow seems an eternity; but one will nevertheless find that it is but a moment when one considers: 1. That even in the time when God’s Wrath seems most ignited, he gives several signs of Love to his children. 2. That God favors many Believers with many signs of his love, and only lets them feel his indignation for a few moments. 3. That this lifetime must be considered but as a moment. 4. Without doubt, there is only a moment in God’s Wrath regarding the Believers when one compares the time in which God calls them to suffer with the eternal state of happiness he prepares for them after their death.

The Scripture does not speak in the same way regarding God's Wrath toward the godless. It says God's Wrath *remains* on them. *He who is disobedient to the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.* John 3:36. It says that it is a fire that is not quenched, eternal glows; therefore the Sinners and Idolaters are shown to us, thus saying— <margin>* Rev. 6:16, 17.</margin> * *Mountains, fall on us, and hide us from the face of him who sits on the Throne, and from the Wrath of the Lamb; for the great day of his Wrath has come, and who can stand?*

Of these Nahum said: <margin>† Nahum 1:6.</margin> † *Who can stand before the Lord’s indignation? who can endure the heat of his Wrath?*

I will only add one word to this, which is, that Scripture speaks of the *day of God’s wrath*; and by this it sometimes understands the day of Jerusalem's destruction, which was a day of wrath for the Jews; sometimes the day of some extraordinary warning from God: but most often the day of the last judgment, because then God's wrath will be poured out over the godless without end or measure; of this Paul speaks in <margin>Rom. 2:15.</margin> Rom. 2:5 <note>The OCR says II. 15, but the verse cited is Romans 2:5.</note>: *But after your hardness and impenitent heart, you treasure up for yourself wrath as a treasure, in the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God.* Regarding this, a learned man <margin>Claude</margin> <note>Jean Claude (1619–1687) was a highly influential French Reformed theologian.</note> very well said that the judgment of Heavenly Justice remains as if hidden and covered until that day under the cloak of God's long-suffering; that with sins, the punishments accumulate until then, piling up as if in a heap; this is what makes up the "treasure of wrath," which remains under the seal of God's goodness and tolerance. <margin>Of the Desires of God. * Ps. 81:13, 14. Is. 48:18.</margin>
Scripture also speaks of God's desires. * *Oh that my people had listened to me! That Israel had walked in my ways! In a short time I would have subdued their enemies, and turned my hand against their adversaries.* And Is. 48:18: *Oh that you had listened to my commandments! Then your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea.* One must not imagine that Scripture wants us to understand through these expressions that God can have fruitless desires: this clearly contradicts his Wisdom, Power, and Goodness; for one could not attribute such desires to God without assuming either that God does not know what will happen to men, or that he lacks the means to do what he wills, or to prevent what might happen: but one can say nothing resembling that of an omniscient and almighty being. By this, Scripture intends to give us to understand: 1. The propriety of the duty that God demands from his creatures. 2. The pleasure he takes in their conversion. 3. The impropriety of the crime they commit by not doing what they are obligated to do. 4. The inevitable misfortune into which they will fall if they do not fulfill their duty; and 5. The justice of the punishment they must expect.

<margin>Of God's Expectation. Is. 5:4.</margin>
One must reason in almost the same way concerning the Hope or expectation of God, of which Isaiah 5 verse 4 speaks. *What more is there to do to my Vineyard, that I have not done to it? Why, when I expected that it would bring forth good grapes, did it bring forth stinking grapes?* <note>original: "stinkende druiven," often translated as "wild grapes" or "worthless grapes" in English Bibles.</note> This way of speaking has something that seems strange, as if God stood to be deceived in his expectation: like men, who, having very limited knowledge, cannot see far enough to preview everything that can happen, and thus very often find themselves deceived in the expectation they have to pluck the fruits of their labor and care; whereas God, who knows all, sees all, to whom the future is as present as the present itself, and who is moreover the Judge and Lord of all outcomes, cannot be misled, nor fruit-

The blessed God is free from all passions; he always maintains his rest in the high places, said *Job*; as those high mountains are, seeing the clouds beneath their feet and the lightning in the plain, while they enjoy the pure sunlight. Scripture says that something grieves God to express that it is contrary to his virtues; and that men grieve him when they mock his virtues, so that if there were passions in God as in man, those deeds of men would excite this passion in him.

One can also say that Scripture intends to signify thereby what God does when he is offended; just as we withdraw and turn away from what hurts and grieves us, so it is as if God turned away from <margin>Eph. IV. 30. Claude.</margin> those who offend him, and withdrew his graces from them. When believers commit some great sin, Scripture says that they grieve God's Spirit. Not only because they do things that would grieve the Holy Spirit, if he, who is the source of joy, could be grieved; but also because, just as sorrow causes the life-spirits to retreat from the external members toward the heart and enclose themselves there as in their source, so that they no longer perform their usual functions; so it is also with God's Spirit, who goes as if into himself, and remains as if hidden in the soul of the...

Of God’s Repentance.
* Gen. 6:6.
† 1 Sam. 15:11.
‡ Jer. 18:7, 8, 9, 10.
Jonah 3:10.
</margin>
Repentance is a kind of sadness attributed to God in many places. * It repented God that He had made man, † and that He had set up Saul to be King. See here how God speaks through Jeremiah: ‡ "In an instant I shall speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy it. But if that same nation, against whom I have spoken, turns from its evil, then I will repent of the evil that I thought to do unto it," etc. Add to this what is said of the Ninevites <note>The people of Nineveh in the Book of Jonah.</note>, that God repented of the evil He had said He would do to them.

<margin>S. van Til.</margin>
The same Scholar <note>Salomon van Til (1643–1713), a prominent Dutch theologian known for his work on the "Typical" or symbolic interpretation of Scripture.</note> of whom I have spoken believes that one should not translate Genesis 6:6 as "it repented him," but rather that "He was satisfied or content with His work," and points to Genesis 37:35, Ephesians 1:24, and Genesis 5:26 to support his view; but even if one translates it as "Repentance," it is certain that one must reason about it in the same way as about the "sadness" of God. Properly speaking, God has no <term>repentance</term> <note>Original: "Berouw"; in this context, it refers to the human feeling of wishing a past action could be undone.</note>, which is a displeasure arising from something one has done that one wishes had not been done. Those who repent find that they did not foresee what was to happen, or that they lack enough power to carry out the work they started; or it is the result of their inconstancy and lightheadedness. This cannot be said of God. In Him, no sadness takes place; He never does anything that He ought not to have done; He has foreseen the outcomes for all time and can do whatever pleases Him; He is steadfastness itself. Also, the Scripture elsewhere explicitly says that God does not repent. * God is not a man that He should lie, nor a son of man that He should repent. † Also, He who is the Strength of Israel does not lie and does not repent: for He is not a man, that He should repent of anything. ‡ For the gifts of grace and the calling of God are irrevocable <note>Original: "onberouwelyk," meaning without repentance or unable to be taken back.</note>.

<margin>
* Num. 23:19
† 1 Sam. 15:29.
‡ Rom. 11:29.
</margin>
When the Scripture says that God repents, it is because there is much similarity between the act of a man who repents and certain acts of God.

When a man repents, he usually changes what he has done; there-
<meta>catchword: there-</meta>

<column-break/>

-fore, God is said to repent when He behaves differently than before; as when He destroys what He had created. But note here the great difference between the repentance of God and that of men; men repent because they see that their affairs have a different outcome than they had believed. Instead, when it is said that God repents of a matter, it is only because the matter is not as it <italic>seemed</italic> it should be, although it did not happen against the expectation of God. This will be clear from this example: it is said that "it repented God that He had made man," not because He had not foreseen that men would become corrupt, but to say that God wanted to destroy the men who lived otherwise than they were obligated to live.

This repentance does not imply that God changes His will; for God does nothing in time except that which He has previously decided, even from all eternity. Therefore, when God sent the <term>Flood</term> <note>Original: "zondvloed"; the Great Deluge of Noah's time.</note> over the Earth, it is certain that He had decided it before the foundation of the world.

One must distinguish well between these two concepts: "Changing one's will" and "Willing that some change occur in the thing one has made." God never changes His will, as we shall see elsewhere. He wills nothing in the present time that He has not always willed; but He does will that some change should happen in the things He has made, and He sometimes changes His management regarding His <term>creatures</term> <note>Original: "Schepzelen"; all created beings.</note>. By one and the same act of will, God decided to do something and, some time thereafter, to destroy it; and this for wise reasons, even though creatures cannot fathom them.

Furthermore, one can observe that when it is said that God repents in respect to men, it is to teach us: either that they have made themselves unworthy of God’s benefits and deserved to be rooted out because of their sins; or that they have put themselves in a state to appease God’s wrath through their repentance and the improvement of their lives.

<margin>
Of God’s Fear.
* Gen. 3:22.
† Exod. 33:3.
</margin>
It seems that the Scripture also attributes "Fear" to God, as when God said of Adam: * "Now then, lest he reach out his hand," or when He said to His people: † "I will not go up in the midst of you, lest I [consume] you on the way."
