DIVINE THEOLOGY. II. B. XI. Chapter.

<margin>
Deut. XXXII: 26, 27.
</margin>
consume. **But** in particular, Deuteronomy 32:26–27: *I said, I would scatter them into corners, I would make the remembrance of them to cease from among men: were it not that I feared the wrath of the enemy, lest their adversaries should behave themselves strangely, and lest they should say, Our hand is high, and the Lord hath not wrought all this.*

**One** must not believe that fear can truly be found in God; why should He fear, seeing as He has infinite power and knows everything that shall happen? But God only wishes to make known to His People (in Deuteronomy 32) that if He preserves them, it is not because they have deserved it, but to give their enemies no cause for boasting. Fear prevents men from doing something when they foresee that some evil would happen to them; when God then refrains from doing something that He could have done, judging by outward appearances, it is said that He "fears." Likewise, He is introduced as fearing that Adam would eat of the fruit of the Tree of Life, to signify that He did not wish for man to remain any longer in a place where he could have eaten from this Tree. Some add to this that God mocks man with these words, because man imagined that by eating of this Tree, he would have become immortal.

Exodus 33:3. Where God says that He will not go up with His People, lest He consume them, He wishes to give them to understand that He well foresaw that they would not honor His presence with the reverence they were bound to give, and thus provide Him with a righteous cause to destroy them.

<margin>
Of God's Zeal.
<term>Zeal</term> <note>original: "Yver"; in this biblical context, it refers to God's "Jealousy," specifically His intolerance of rivalry or idolatry.</note>
Exod. XX: 5.
</margin>
There remains nothing more for me than to speak of God’s zeal; God is called a "zealous God" in the first commandment of His Law and elsewhere. Everyone knows well enough that zeal <note>or jealousy</note> is that powerful passion with which a husband is affected when the wife whom God has given him violates the marriage vow and gives her affection to others instead of her husband. But one easily understands that God cannot have this violent impulse. The Scripture speaks thus to show us:

<column-break/>

1. By what means our soul is united with Him.

2. That we have obligated ourselves in this union to give God alone the honor and service of our conscience; never to deviate from Him through our own actions toward any other object than God, under whatever pretext it may be.

3. That if we remain faithful to Him, He will cause us to enjoy the effects of the same affection that a husband bears for his wife when she is faithful to him.

4. But also, when we (in whatever way it may be) offer the practice of our religion to any creature and turn the movements of our conscience toward any other object, God will cause us to taste the same wrath that an angered husband makes his adulterous wife feel.

One should then regard the name of the "Zealous God" as being used to make us understand the greatness of the crime of Idolatry; how hateful this sin is to God; with what punishments He will punish it; and that it breaks His communion with the creature, just as adultery tears the marriage bond to pieces.

### XI. CHAPTER.

->Of God’s Holiness and Justice.<-

<margin>
* Isa. VI: 3.

</margin>
Holiness is one of the principal virtues that the Scripture attributes to God. It is the subject that the blessed Angels, in their songs of praise around God’s Throne, exalt there, crying out: * Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of Hosts, the whole Earth is full of His glory. It is also frequently the subject of the faithful in their songs of praise. Moses said in his song: † O Lord! who is like unto thee among the gods? Who is like thee, glorified in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders? And in the Revelation, when the four living creatures give glory to Him who is seated on the throne, they cry day and night: ‡ Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord God Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come. God calls Himself Holy: * You shall be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy.

**Repentance** is a kind of sorrow attributed to God in many places.
* *It repented God that he had made man,*
† *and that he had set up Saul to be King.* See here how God speaks through Jeremiah: ‡ *At what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy it; If that nation, against whom I have pronounced, turn from their evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do unto them, etc.*

<margin>Jonah 3:10.</margin>
Add to this what is said of the Ninevites <note>The inhabitants of Nineveh, who repented after Jonah’s preaching.</note>, that God repented of the evil that He had said He would do to them.

<margin>S. van Til.</margin>
The same Scholar of whom I have spoken <note>Salomon van Til (1643–1713), a prominent Dutch Reformed theologian.</note> believes that in Genesis 6:6, one should not translate it as *it repented him*, but rather that He was *satisfied* or *contented* with His work; he points to Genesis 37:35, Isaiah 1:24 <note>The OCR reads "Ef I. 24," likely a misprint for "Es." (Esaias/Isaiah) 1:24, which discusses God "easing" or "comforting" Himself.</note>, and Genesis 5:29 to support his view. But even if it were translated as "Repentance," it is certain that one must reason about it as one does with the "sorrow" of God: properly speaking, God has no repentance, which is a displeasure arising from something one has done that one wishes one had not done. Those who have repentance find that they did not foresee what was to happen, or that they lack enough power to carry out the work they started; or it is the effect of their inconstancy and lightheartedness. This cannot be said of God. In Him, no sorrow takes place; He never does anything that He ought not to have done; He has foreseen the outcomes for all time, and can do all that pleases Him; He is steadfastness itself. Also, the Scripture elsewhere explicitly says that

<margin>
* Num. 23:19.
† 1 Sam. 15:29.
‡ Rom. 11:29.
</margin>
God has no repentance. * *God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent.* † *And also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent: for he is not a man, that he should repent.* ‡ *For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance.* <note>In modern translations, this is often rendered as "irrevocable."</note>

When the Scripture then says that God repents, it is because there is much similarity between the act of a human who repents and certain acts of God.

When a human repents, he usually changes what he has done; there-

<column-break/>

-fore God is said to repent when He behaves differently than before; as when He was grieved that He had created [man]. But mark here the great difference between the repentance of God and that of men; men repent because they see that their affairs have a different outcome than they had believed; whereas, when it is said that God has repentance of a matter, it is only because the matter is not as it seemed it ought to be, although it did not happen contrary to the expectation of God. This will appear clearly through this example: It is said that it repented God to have made man, not because He had not foreseen that men would become corrupt, but to say that God willed to destroy the men who lived otherwise than they were obliged to live.

This repentance does not imply that God changes His will; for God does nothing in time except that which He has decided beforehand, even from all eternity. Therefore, when God sent the Flood over the Earth, it is certain that He had decided it before the foundation of the World.

One must distinguish well between these two propositions: *Changing one's will*, and *willing that some change should occur in the thing* that one has made. God never changes His will, as we shall see elsewhere. He wills nothing in the present time that He has not always willed; but He does will that some change should occur in the things He has made, and He sometimes changes His governance regarding His creatures. By one and the same act of will, God has decided to do something and, some time thereafter, to destroy it—and that for wise reasons, even though creatures cannot fathom them.

Furthermore, one can note that when it is said that God repents in respect to men, it is to teach us: either that they have made themselves unworthy of God’s blessings and deserved to be rooted out by their sins; or that they have placed themselves in a state to appease God’s wrath through their repentance and the improvement of their lives.

# THEOLOGY. II. B. XI. CHAPTER 189

<columns>

<margin>Deut. 32:26, 27.</margin>
...consume. **But** in particular, consider Deuteronomy 32:26–27: *I said, I would scatter them into all corners, I would make the remembrance of them to cease from among men, were it not that I feared the wrath of the enemy, lest their adversaries should behave themselves strangely, and lest they should say, "Our hand is high, and the Lord has not wrought all this."*

**One** must not believe that fear can truly be found in God; why would He fear, since He possesses infinite power and knows all that shall come to pass? Rather, God wishes to make it known to His people in every way (in Deuteronomy 32) that if He preserves them, it is not because they have deserved it, but to give their enemies no cause for boasting. Fear prevents men from doing something when they foresee that some evil might happen to them; when God refrains from doing something that He could have done—judging by outward appearances—it is said that He "fears." In this way, He is introduced as "fearing" that Adam would eat of the fruit of the Tree of Life, to signify that He did not want man to remain any longer in a place where he would have eaten from this tree. Some add to this that God mocks man with these words, as if because man imagined that by eating from this tree, he would have become immortal.

**Exodus 33:3.** Where God says that He will not go up with His people, *lest He consume them*, He wishes to give them to understand that He well foresaw they would not honor His presence with the reverence they were bound to give, and would thus provide Him with a righteous cause to destroy them.

<margin>Of God’s Zeal. Exod. 20:5.</margin>
**There** is nothing more left for me than to speak of God’s zeal <note>The Dutch *yver* (modern *ijver*) translates here as "zeal" or "jealousy," specifically the "jealousy" of a husband protecting the marriage bond.</note>; God is called a "zealous God" in the first commandment of His Law and elsewhere. Everyone knows well enough that zeal is that powerful passion with which a man is moved when the wife whom God has given him violates her marriage vows and gives her affection to others instead of her husband. But one easily understands that God cannot possess this violent impulse. The Scripture speaks thus to show us:

1. That the covenant He has with mankind through the holy bonds of religion is a "mystical marriage,"

<column-break/>

whereby our souls are united with Him.

2. That we have obligated ourselves in this union to give to God alone the honor and service of our conscience; never to deviate from this by any act toward any other object but God, under whatever pretext it may be.

3. That if we remain faithful to Him, He will allow us to enjoy the effects of that same affection which a husband bears for his wife when she is faithful to him.

4. But also, when we—in whatever way it may be—offer the practices of our religion to any creature, and turn the movements of our conscience toward any other object, God will make us taste that same wrath which an angered husband makes his adulterous wife feel.

**Let** us then regard the name of the "Zealous God" as being used to make us understand the greatness of the crime of idolatry; how hateful this sin is to God; with what punishments He will punish it; and that it breaks His fellowship with the creature, just as adultery tears the marriage bond to pieces.

### THE CHRISTIAN GOD

IT IS not very necessary to expand greatly in order to explain what this Holiness of God consists of. One understands well enough, and one sees clearly, that the Scripture intends for us to understand by this that God is an entirely pure being, free from all failings or imperfections of the creatures; that He loves order and all that is good to the highest degree; that He hates disorder and sin to the highest degree; that He is steadfast in His Decrees, faithful in His promises, righteous in His Commands, just in all His judgments, and perfect in all His ways, and that He wills nothing except that which corresponds with the most perfect of all beings.

<margin>Saurin, *On Divine Love* <note>Jacques Saurin (1677–1730) was a famous French Protestant preacher known for his eloquent sermons.</note>.</margin>
> "Therefore, the Holiness of God is
> "that virtue through which God wills and
> "approves all that belongs to His being,
> "and all that corresponds with the same
> "and all His perfections; and through which
> "He disapproves and rejects all that is
> "contrary to Him; this virtue determines
> "Him to do nothing but that which is
> "becoming to Him, and which the quality
> "of the same virtue and His other perfections

> "Creature than that which has agreement
> "with this attribute—that is, to prevent through
> "His Grace, or to punish through His
> "Justice, that which does not agree
> "with it.

<margin>1 Sam. II: 2.</margin>
But it has been very well noted that the Title of Holy in the Scripture has a more general meaning and includes all of God’s perfections. Just as Holiness, according to the idiom of the Scripture, is a distinction and separation grounded upon dignity and excellence, or that which produces dignity and excellence; in which sense the persons and things dedicated to Divine service under the Old Testament were called Holy. Therefore, when the Scripture gives the name of Holy to God, it attaches to it the idea of an infinite distinction and separation from all that is not God—in short, of a being that has nothing in common with other beings, and in whose sight they are all as nothing. In this way one must understand Exodus XV, as well as that which Hannah, the Mother of Samuel, said when she calls God Holy, to set Him against all false deities, and to show that He alone possesses all the necessary qualities to be the Rock of those who lean upon Him.

Thus one must also explain the Song of Mary

<margin>1 Pet. I: 15. 16.</margin>
God’s perfect Holiness is presented as an example to all men. 1 Pet. I: 15–16: *But as he which hath called you is holy, so be ye holy in all manner of conversation; Because it is written, Be ye holy; for I am holy.* It is true that we can never reach this perfection, but we must exert all our strength and efforts to approach this perfect example as much as shall be possible; we must have it continually before our eyes, so that by beholding it with all the attention of which we are capable, we may be changed into the same image.

# THEOLOGY. BOOK II. CHAPTER XI.

<margin>On God's Justice.</margin>
...constitutes the glory of God / and makes him worthy of the wonder / reverence / esteem / and worship of Angels and Men.

<margin>Deut. XXXII: 4.</margin>
Now God’s Holiness transitions into His Justice, and note immediately / that the scripture sometimes understands the Holiness of God through righteousness / as when Moses says: *God is the Rock, whose work is perfect, for all his ways are judgment; a God of truth, and without iniquity; just and right is he.* <note>Original: "God is de Rottseen, wiens werk volkomen is..."</note> Yet one could note a distinction / between Holiness and Justice. Holiness signifies properly the purity of the Divine being; and Justice signifies the same in relation to the creatures. For God is said to be Just / when He does nothing in respect to other beings / but that which is becoming to a most perfect being.

<margin>* Ps. LI. 16. <br/> † Ps. CXLIII: 1. 2.</margin>
Sometimes the word righteousness is used / to signify God’s Goodness / that is / the will to do us well / His Love and Mercy. In this sense David said: * *Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, thou God of my salvation: and my tongue shall sing aloud of thy righteousness.* <note>Ps. 51:14 in modern English versions.</note> † *Hear me, according to thy truth, according to thy righteousness. And enter not into judgment with thy servant, for in thy sight shall no man living be justified.*

Sometimes that word is taken for that virtue of God / which gives to each what is due to him; which deals out punishments and rewards; which crowns those / who fulfill the conditions of His covenant; and punishes those / who transgress them. Of this Justice Paul speaks in 2 Thess. I: 6, 7: *Seeing it is a righteous thing with God to recompense tribulation to them that trouble you; and to you who are troubled rest with us, when the Lord Jesus shall be revealed from Heaven with his mighty Angels.* And Rom. II, 11: *There is no respect of persons with God.* God’s righteousness looks at that which concerns the state and essence of the matter; and not on the qualities of the persons. It recompenses and gives to each according to his works / namely,

<margin>Rom. II: 6. 7. 8.</margin>
Eternal life to those who steadfastly / by well-doing / seek glory / honor / and immortality; but indignation and wrath to the contentious / who are rebellious against the

that one must not understand God as a
private person, who could waive his right

4. This truth is confirmed, whether
because the conscience instills it in all men,
whether summoned by God’s Judgment Seat
and, after the committed crime,

of the nations, among whom the sentiment
that God is a Just Judge has been
very common. When the Barbarians of the
<margin>Acts 28:4</margin> Island of Malta saw that a viper

that he was a murderer, whom
Divine vengeance would not let live.
From there, the custom arose among the Heathen
of even sacrificing men to
appease the Deity: or through the
multitude of sacrifices, which God
had instituted under the law, to
show us how necessary it was that sins,
in order to satisfy Divine justice,
were atoned for.

This truth is so certain, and so well
established in the scripture and by reason,
that it is easy to answer the
Objections.

1. **Objection.** God being the master of
the order, which he can change according
to his pleasure, it is also up to him
to punish sins or not. I answer
it is false that God can always change
the order of things: for by this
principle I could prove that God
could reward the crimes of men
as if they were virtues; that he

<column-break/>

could release the creature from all obligation,
making it master of itself and
independent; and allow it
to hate and blaspheme God. Indeed, I
confess that this principle makes me shudder.
God was able to change the order he had
instituted under the law regarding
the sacrifices, because this depended
absolutely on his freedom; but an order
grounded upon his essence is unchangeable.

2. **Objection.** It is absurd to think
that there is anything that imposes any
necessity upon God, since he is above all.
I answer, it is true, it would be
absurd, even godless, to use this language
if this necessity were imposed on God
by something outside of God; but
this necessity follows from God’s essence.
Far from it being a lack of perfection in God
to be necessarily what he is, and
to have an unchangeable essence, it is
on the contrary one of his greatest perfections.

3. **Objection.** Assuming that God is the
supreme ruler of the world, it
follows that he can forgive sins unpunished,
just as the Authorities remit the
disorders of the people when
they cannot punish them without
rooting out all their subjects. That the
Authority must indeed exercise justice
when it only concerns some private
persons; because the common wealth
must be placed before the individual,
and the inviolable maintenance of the laws
comes before the maintenance of individuals.
But that this must not happen when it
concerns the ruin of the whole body,
and that the laws would destroy themselves
if they destroyed the common wealth. I
answer that there is a great distinction
between the Authorities of the earth
and God. The Authorities cannot
destroy their states without themselves
perishing, or without losing the
luster of their Majesty, in proportion
to the body of the common wealth
that they would destroy. But, even if God
destroyed all Angels and men, he
would not be any less blessed nor less
perfect; and, if it pleased him,
he could create new creatures.
Add to this, that God did not want to
punish all creatures who have offended him,
but gave them—as we shall
see elsewhere—a mediator.

with Power, or Mercy; all these
Virtues are indeed essential to God: but
it depends on him to exercise them more or less

# DIVINE THEOLOGY. BOOK II. CHAPTER XI.

to exercise, according as He judges it necessary.

I answer that there is a great distinction in God’s virtues regarding their operations. There are perfections in God that are not moved to action by any external object; others act only according to the quality of the objects. God was free to create the world or not; but having created it, He cannot abandon its governance without compromising His wisdom. Whether God exercises His power or not, He will be no less powerful; but it is not so with justice; justice requires that God act whenever an object offends Him. Furthermore, the acts of Mercy are purely voluntary gifts of grace, but the exercises of justice are necessary. When it is therefore impossible to exercise Mercy without doing harm to Justice, God can show no Mercy. I do not answer the objection by saying that, if avenging justice were essential to God, He would necessarily have to exercise it; and yet, it is said, if there had been no sinner, He would never have exercised it. For 1. who does not see that by this reasoning one could prove that Mercy is not essential to God, since if there had been no miserable people, He would not have exercised His Mercy. But even if God had never exercised any of His virtues, it would remain an eternal truth that He is an Almighty, Good, Merciful, and Just being, in the most perfect way, who cannot look upon sin without punishing it.

5. **Objection.** But the Scripture says that God, when He punishes, performs a "strange work"? <note>This refers to Isaiah 28:21, suggesting that judgment is not God's primary desire.</note> I admit it: but that is only said to teach us that to God—who has no pleasure in the death of the sinner—it would be more pleasant if men lived such that they gave no cause for the exercise of His judgments; moreover, that passage speaks of God’s vengeance against His own people; for elsewhere God testifies that He rejoices in the punishment of the godless.
<margin>Deuteronomy 28:63. Isaiah 1:24. Hosea 10:10.</margin>

6. **Objection.** If it were essential to God to punish sins, He would have to punish them always, and as much as He can. But that does not follow. It is enough that sin does not go unpunished and is punished in proportion to the offended Majesty; and therefore God can

<column-break/>

delay the punishment and punish sins in various ways. As we shall see more clearly when we treat of <term>Satisfaction</term> <note>The theological concept that Christ’s suffering paid the "debt" or penalty required by God’s justice.</note>.

7. **Objection.** If avenging justice were not essential to God, He would be no more Merciful than Just, and no more inclined to forgive than to punish, whereas the Scripture nevertheless says that God is slow to anger, and that He shows Mercy to thousands, etc. I answer: God is not more Merciful than Just; but His mercy reveals itself more here below; being infinitely good, He uses the riches of His Mercy before He makes His terrible justice felt: He takes more pleasure in the preservation of His creatures than in their downfall. 2. The Scripture says that God is ready to forgive, slow to anger, particularly toward His <term>Elect</term> <note>Those chosen by God for salvation.</note>, for whom His justice has been satisfied. 3. Finally, the Scripture says that God, most of the time, delays the exercise of His Justice until after this life.

The question is asked: Is God obliged to punish the sin of a person who truly repents and believes in Jesus Christ?

I answer: He is not obliged to do so, because He has received the <term>satisfaction</term> of His justice in Jesus Christ on behalf of the repentant believer. There is no true and God-pleasing repentance except that which the Holy Spirit has produced, who is only given to those for whom God has been satisfied. Therefore, He will not punish the penitent, because another has borne the punishment for their sins.

8. **Objection.** It is not very likely that God watches the deeds of men to punish them, just as a great King does not set his eyes upon a heap of ants.

But 1. This objection can only be made by people who do not recognize the Divinity of the Scripture, for those who do recognize it cannot make this difficulty.

2. God is the creator of men and has made them in His image; but a King is not the creator of the ants.

3. A King cannot attend to all small things, for having a finite understanding, if he let his eye wander over trifling things, no time would remain for matters of importance; but God knows and does everything without any effort or distraction.

endured with much Long-suffering the vessels of Wrath, prepared for destruction. <note>This refers to Romans 9:22, where "vessels of wrath" are those who have made themselves fit for judgment through persistent sin.</note> So He endured the inhabitants of the first world for 120 years; Peter <margin>1 Pet. 3:20.</margin> says in 1 Peter 3:20: "When the Long-suffering of God once waited in the days of Noah, while the Ark was being prepared."

4. It [Scripture] describes to us primarily the Long-suffering of God toward the Jews: a Long-suffering that many centuries did not exhaust, and which a terrible, accumulated heap of Sin did not weary. It [Scripture] desires that we behold this forbearance with wonder.

Indeed, there is nothing more wonderful than to see that an Almighty God—who has no need of any of His creatures and could destroy the entire human race with a glance of His eye—struggles for so long with an ungrateful, rebellious, reckless, and unjust People; enduring the scorn and coldness of some, and the slander and ingratitude of others, without punishing them; even shining His light upon them, watering them with His rain, and satisfying them with His goods and blessings. Wicked men judge God’s Long-suffering very poorly. One imagines that there is no providence; another that God does not know what is happening; another that He cannot do what He wants: but Scripture restrains these godless thoughts and makes us understand that it is not ignorance, impotence, nor weakness that makes God Long-suffering.

Furthermore, these virtues of God teach us:

<margin>Ps. 130:4.</margin> 1. Not to despair of God’s Grace immediately when we have fallen into some Sins. *With You is forgiveness, that You may be feared.* Psalm 130:4.

<margin>Rom. 2:4-5.</margin> 2. Not to despise the Riches of God’s Long-suffering; which is without doubt the greatest of all crimes. The more God goes beyond His common ways, the more He must be honored. Therefore Paul testifies that those who despise these Riches store up for themselves a treasure of Wrath, in the day of Wrath. The Treasure of God's forbearance is followed by the Treasure of His indignation. One gathers blessings for men; the other collects punishments for them. One invites them to repentance; the other casts them into hell.

3. Finally, they teach us how for-

<column-break/>

<margin>Matt. 18:33 Col. 3:12.</margin> bearing we must be toward our Brothers, and how we must assist them.

The consideration of God’s Long-suffering should fill us with gratitude for that which He has shown to us, and prevent us from murmuring about the prosperity of the wicked.

When men despise God’s Long-suffering, they are exposed to His severity. <margin>Rom. 11:22.</margin> Paul speaks of this in Romans 11:22: "Behold then the Goodness and severity of God: against you [who remain], and against those who fell." The word he uses <note>original: *apotomia*</note> means "cutting off" or "hewing down," a metaphorical way of speaking taken from those who cut off the useless branches of Trees.

God exercises this severity sometimes toward an entire nation, sometimes only toward certain individuals.

1. He exercises it over those He has long endured. Just as the inhabitants of the first world were (as has already been said) and <margin>Gen. 18:20 2 Chron. 36:15-16.</margin> the Cities of the Plain [Sodom and Gomorrah], whose cry of sin had ascended to God. He even makes His own people feel it. 2 Chronicles 36:15-16: "The Lord, the God of their fathers, sent to them by the hand of His messengers, rising up early to send them, because He spared His people and His dwelling place; but they mocked the messengers of God and despised His words; they slandered His prophets, until the wrath of the Lord rose against His people, till there was no remedy."

<margin>Acts 12:22.</margin> 2. Over those who dare to exalt themselves as if to His Throne; like Herod, who allowed it to be said of him: "The voice of a god and not of a man." Acts 12:22.

3. Over those who sin immediately after He has bestowed some evident favor upon them. Thus He severely punished Lot’s Wife, because she transgressed His command after she was delivered from the fire of Sodom; and Nadab and Abihu, because they offered strange fire after He had raised them to the dignity of the Priesthood.

4. Over those who have committed sins they could easily have avoided, and which have a deadly consequence. He gives extraordinary signs of His presence and grace. One could bring forward many other causes for God's severity, but there are none for which one may despise the governance of the Supreme Being. It is our duty to see to it that we never bring this severity of God upon ourselves, but that we fear Him, since He is a **consuming fire**; and that we avoid all kinds of sins, however small they may seem to us. For we do not know whether they will also be viewed as light and small by God, since we have certain proof that God has severely punished sins that seem very small to us.

## CHAPTER XIII.

### Of God’s Power and Dominion over the Creatures.

After having spoken of God’s Will, it is time to treat of His **Power**, which is that virtue of God through which He can do all that He wills. It is indeed not distinct from His Will, but the Will of God is called **Power** when the matter has not yet been brought forth, or will not be, even though it is possible and does not conflict with God’s perfections. Therefore, the Scripture distinguishes God’s Will from His Power. <note original: "Esa. XIV. 17. Act. IV. 28. Apoc. XV. 3. Rom IV. 21 Marc. XIV. 36 Matt. III. 9.">Isaiah 14:17, Acts 4:28, Revelation 15:3, Romans 4:21, Mark 14:36, Matthew 3:9.</note> The reason for this distinction is that we do not do things simply by our will, and we are accustomed to judge God as we judge ourselves. But it appears that God’s power is nothing other than His **effectual will**. Because God, being a perfect being, works in the most perfect way. Now, one can conceive of no more perfect way than to work through an act of His will.

This Power of God does not differ from His essence, any more than His other perfections. From this, it is easy to decide what one shall answer to the questions of whether God can communicate His infinite power to

<column-break/>

a creature. No, without doubt, no more than His essence; a finite creature is not capable of infinite power; if the creature were <term>almighty</term> <note>From the Dutch 'Almagtig', meaning possessing all power without limit.</note>, it would be able to resist its creator.

The Scripture speaks everywhere of this Power. *With God nothing is impossible.*
<margin>Luke 1:37.</margin>
Luke 1:37. *All things are possible with God.*
<margin>Mark 10:27.</margin>
Mark 10:27. *But our God is in the Heavens; He does whatever pleases Him.*
<margin>Psalm 115:3.</margin>
Psalm 115:3.

Reason confirms this: to form an idea of a God who is not Almighty is to conceive of no God at all. <note>Pythagoras was an ancient Greek philosopher; the author cites him to show that even "pagans" recognized divine omnipotence as a logical necessity.</note> Pythagoras held those to be insane who denied God’s power.

God's power is infinite, whether in respect to the objects over which it extends, or in respect to the manner of working. There is nothing that God cannot do, if He wills; and that without labor, violence, fatigue, movement, or resistance; at whatever time, place, and manner pleases Him.

It has been manifested in several cases:

1. In this great **Universe**. God had no sooner spoken than matter came out of nothing, the <term>primary elements</term> <note>The "Hoofdstoffen" or elements, traditionally Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> separated from one another, the waters, spread over the surface of the Earth, united themselves in the depths of the Sea, and it was as if Nature hastened to obey the voice of her Creator with greater speed. Oh, how great must the power have been that made all these things!

2. It shone forth in the **Creation of man**, and it shows itself in the **Multitude of Souls** that God creates and unites with the bodies of those who are born daily.

3. It stands out in the **sustenance of the world** and in the governance of <term>providence</term> <note>God's ongoing preservation and timely care for His creation.</note>. *Who upholds all things by the word of His power.*
<margin>Hebrews 1:3.</margin>
Hebrews 1:3.

4. It has appeared in many **miracles** that God has performed. As when God, to deliver His People, changed the water of the Nile into blood, a Staff into a Snake, the dust of Egypt into Lice, etc.; add to this the miracles of Christ.

One cannot deny that God performs miracles; He performs them immediately, whether He uses the action of the Creatures or not, whereby He shows that He is above Nature.

The followers of <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a Dutch philosopher whose rationalist views often led to the denial of supernatural miracles, viewing them as violations of the necessary laws of nature.</note> **Spinoza**, who will acknowledge no miracles, bring forward this reason, as I have said elsewhere,

One must not think that we wish to limit God’s power thereby: for / just as we say / that the object of God’s infinite knowledge is all that can be known; so nothing prevents us from saying / that the object of God’s power is everything / that can be done.

One should not imagine / that everything that comes into our thoughts / is the object of God’s power; for it is certain that we imagine many false things / that are unbecoming of God.

To judge rightly of God’s Omnipotence / one must compare it not only with its object / but also with God’s other perfections / and establish that God’s Power can never conflict with his Wisdom, Holiness, Truth, Goodness, and other virtues; since he does not want / and will never want to do anything / other than what is becoming to him / and corresponds with his Holiness and other perfections. But / besides the infinite extent of the objects of God’s omnipotence / it is clear / how great and infinite it is / from the fact that it / in order to work and bring forth its effects / is not bound to a certain kind of thing / to a certain way of working / to certain objects and their conditions / or to a certain time and place. 1. On the dependence of the Creatures / with respect to their Creator.
2. Judge then how great God’s Sovereignty must be / who is so elevated above all / that there is no proportion between the two: he surpasses them infinitely not only in wisdom / but in all other perfections.

Finally / this Sovereignty is grounded on the countless benefits / with which God fills his Creatures / and fills them daily / and which give him a Just right over them.

The same is absolute / for God is subject to no one’s Judgment / or reproach. Shall the thing formed say to him who formed it, why have you made me thus? **Romans 9:20.**

By virtue of this absolute Right / God has the Right / to do with his Creatures / that which [pleases] him.

## XIV. CHAPTER.

### Of God’s Omnipresence.

<margin>
Ps. 139:7–10.
</margin>
Scripture / which speaks of God’s power / also teaches us that He is present everywhere. Ps. 139:7-10. "Where should I go from Your Spirit, and where should I flee from Your face? If I ascended to Heaven, You are there; or if I made my bed in <note>original: 'de Helle' (the Grave/Sheol)</note> the depths, behold, You are there. If I took the wings of the morning; if I dwelt at the farthest end of the Sea; even there Your hand would lead me, and Your right hand would hold me." <term>Anastasius of Sinai<note>A 7th-century Greek monk and prolific theological writer based at Saint Catherine's Monastery.</note></term> remarks / that the Prophet does not say / "where shall I go, far from Your working?" but "far from Your face," etc.

Note that it is said here / that God is as much in the Grave as in Heaven; now He is in Heaven by His essence / therefore He is also in the Grave by His essence.

<margin>
1 Kings 8:27.
</margin>
Solomon teaches this same truth. 1 Kings 8:27. "Would God indeed dwell on the Earth? Behold, the heavens, yes, the Heaven of Heavens would not contain You; how much less this House that I have built?" Thus he spoke at the dedication of the Temple. The heathens believed that they, through their incantations and prayers, caused the Deity to descend into the Houses they had prepared for that purpose; Solomon will not tolerate the belief that

<column-break/>

the true God descends from Heaven / to confine Himself in the House / that had been built for Him. Therefore he says at the beginning of his prayer / "the Heavens of Heavens cannot contain You." From this it is easy to understand / that God’s essence is not confined to Heaven. For it is without foundation / to say that Solomon intended nothing else by this / than to testify that God’s power was not confined to the Temple. His intention is to show / that God is everywhere / just as He is in Heaven; it is evident that those who dispute God’s omnipresence / believe that He is in Heaven / in respect to His essence. Furthermore / this manner of speaking—"the Heavens cannot contain You"—shows clearly / that He is not speaking of God’s power alone. Let us hear God Himself. Isa. 66:1. "Heaven is My Throne, and the Earth is the Footstool of My feet; where would that House be that you people would build for Me?" God compares Himself here to a King / of such great stature / that He comes with His head in Heaven and His feet on the Earth / by which He makes it known / that He is not confined in Heaven. "Am I a God near at hand, and not from afar?" asks the Lord through Jeremiah, "could anyone hide himself in secret places, that I should not see him, and do I not fill the Heaven and the Earth?" says the Lord. Lest one think / that God indeed sees everything / but from above out of Heaven / as it says in Ps. 14:2 / He says that He fills all things.

<center>THEOLOGY. II. B. XIV. Chapter.</center>

<margin>
<note>original: "Chrifost. hom. 1. de incompt. Dei natura & hom. 5. in Ep. ad Col."</note>
Chrysostom, Homily 1 on the Incomprehensible Nature of God & Homily 5 on the Epistle to the Colossians.
</margin>
The wisest <term>Pagans<note>The original Dutch uses 'Heidenen' (Heathens), commonly referring to non-Christian classical philosophers in this context.</note></term> have acknowledged the same. One of them said: wherever you are, or wherever you flee, you will always be under Jupiter. Xerxes would not allow the Gods to be locked inside Temples; he even overthrew the Temples of the Greeks to punish them for this committed impiety. Pythagoras described the Deity as a spirit / who is dispersed throughout all of nature. <margin><note>original: "Ambr. 1. de fide ad Grar. Alcu. l. II. de Trin. c. 4."</note> Ambrose, Book 1 on the Faith to Gratian. Alcuin, Book II on the Trinity, ch. 4.</margin> Simplicius said / God is at once and always everywhere / with all His virtues. One reads in the Quran that where there are three / God is the fourth / and where there are five / He is the sixth. The Jews called God by a name / that means **Place** / to signify / that He is everywhere. <note>The Hebrew term *HaMakom* (The Place) implies that God is the 'location' of the world, rather than being contained by it.</note>

The reason / for which we must believe that God is everywhere / is / because we must hold the most perfect idea of God. Now it is certain / that / if God were not everywhere / we could conceive of a more perfect being / namely / one present everywhere / and not confined to any place.

It is impossible to explain *how* God is everywhere / and it is also not necessary that one should know it.

1. It is certain / that one must not understand it / as if God’s essence were extended through the whole Universe / like a body; those who understand it thus / have no true idea of God.

2. It is also certain / that God is everywhere / both in regard to His works, and in regard to His power, and in regard to His essence. One cannot doubt / that He is everywhere / in respect to His works: for He works all in all / He gives being to all / He sustains them all / and imparts to each the strength to act. One can likewise not doubt God’s omnipresence / in regard to His power / since He does not act / except through His power; if God then is everywhere through His actions / He is also there through His power. Finally / since God’s power is not distinct from His essence / it is clear / that / if He is everywhere through His power, He is also there through His essence. God cannot work where He is not; because He works through His will and essence.

3. Indeed, one cannot deny that the scripture often says / that God ascends and descends / approaches and withdraws; that He is not with the wicked / but with the believers. But all these ways of speaking do not contradict His omnipresence / and must not be taken literally. It is said that God approaches and descends, when He gives signs of His presence: that He departs and
<sig>Part I.</sig>

<column-break/>

ascends, when He withdraws the visible glimpses of His grace from us / and refuses the tokens of His presence: that He is not with the wicked / because He is not with them in His grace; and is with the believers / because He gives them the feeling of His mercy. <margin>1 Kings XIX. 11. 12.</margin> In 1 Kings XIX. 11. 12. it is said / that God was neither in the wind, nor in the fire / because He did not reveal Himself to Elijah therein.

<margin>Ps. CXXXIX. 2.</margin> The Prophet says in Psalm CXXXIX. 2. that God understands our thoughts from afar; but it is ridiculous to conclude from this / that God is therefore not everywhere: for the meaning is clear / that God discovers and foresees our thoughts / long before we have formed them.

4. One must not think that God’s Majesty is contaminated because He is in contaminated places; a spirit cannot be defiled by bodies.

5. Furthermore / one must not believe / although we say that God is everywhere / that we do not acknowledge Him to be in some places in a special way. # XV. CHAPTER.

### In which it is proven that God is a necessarily existing, independent, and Eternal Being.

Among the perfections of God, one of the most remarkable is that he is a being that necessarily exists.

Existence being a supreme perfection, without which one would have nothing at all, one cannot deny it to the perfect being without taking away the being itself. If God did not necessarily exist, then he could have potentially not existed. But if one supposes this, then it is impossible to understand how he began to exist: for who could have given him existence? Since one cannot conceive of any being as perfect as God, there is no one who could have given him the perfections that they themselves did not possess.

<column-break/>

Indeed, if one could conceive of a most perfect being without a necessary existence, then one could conceive of an even more perfect being; but to say a most perfect being could not exist is a contradiction. It is impossible for God not to be, and for him to cease to be. He is an independent being, upon whom all other beings absolutely depend; most of these are dependent on a countless multitude of other creatures to exist in their being: on the Earth to be supported, on the Air to draw breath, on food to restore the depletion of their bodies; on a thousand remedies to protect themselves against the inconveniences of the seasons. God derives his being from no one; he has no need to be sustained, since he necessarily exists, possessing all things in himself; no one can give him anything, since everything belongs to him. And from this independence of God, which belongs to him alone, one must conclude that no desire is more unseemly than the human desire for independence.

From God’s necessary existence, it follows that he is Eternal. That which necessarily exists must have always existed, and cannot not exist: this is the concept that gives us Eternity; for he who says an Eternal being, says a being that had no beginning and shall have no end.

Reason teaches this: for 1. that which begins or ends is no God, since there could be a more perfect being that would have neither beginning nor end.

2. It is impossible for God to have a beginning: for he would have had to have a cause for his existence, or have given being to himself; one can say neither the one nor the other. One cannot say that he gave himself being, because that involves a contradiction; that God had a cause also cannot be said: for this cause would have been more perfect than he himself, since it would have existed before God, and consequently, he would not be God: for to be God, one must be the most perfect of all beings.

The Pagans have recognized this truth. I speak of the wisest. Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who argued for the eternity of the world and its cause.</note> proved that God is eternal because he exists through himself. Thales <note>The first of the Greek "Seven Sages" (c. 624–545 BC), often considered the first philosopher in the Western tradition.</note> said: God is that which has neither beginning nor end, and he asserted that he existed before all things and was never brought forth. It was a terrible blindness in those nations who [served] Gods...

<meta>The catchword "dien-" at the bottom of the page indicates the next word is "dienden" (served), continuing the critique of pagan polytheism.</meta>

It is true that the Prophets attribute years to God. Daniel calls him the *Ancient of Days*. Job says that *the number of his years cannot be searched out*; but unless one wishes to be blind, one clearly sees that these are infinite ways of speaking through which God wishes to <term>stammer with us</term> <note>A common theological metaphor (often used by Calvin) suggesting God adapts His infinite nature to simple human language, like a parent babbling to a child.</note>. Years are only the measure of created things that are subject to the movement of the Heavens; but it is not so with God.

<margin>Rev. 1:4.</margin>
It is also true that it is said of God that *he was, is, and is to come*; but the Scripture speaks thus because of our weakness, because we cannot understand things otherwise than under these three tenses of time. One must not understand God like the creatures who pass away, where some have been and are no more; others are and have not been; others shall be but are not yet. God has always been, is, and shall always be.

<margin>

Theologians further remark that in eternity there is no sequence of parts. For in Eternity, one understands neither **First** nor **Last**. This is very difficult to understand, I confess; but one must take good care to note that God’s Eternity is God himself; if we could now feel God and understand the Divine essence, we would also understand His Eternity. It is no more difficult to understand a being without a sequence of time than a being without a beginning. If one allows for a sequence of time in Eternity, one cannot fail to recognize a first point in eternity; but this conflicts with the ideas we have of Eternity.

Although Eternity encompasses all time—past, present, and future—it does not follow that these three times exist simultaneously; nor should one believe that Eternity has parts, but only

<column-break/>

various relations to the various parts of time: when one considers it in relation to the past, one says that it *has been*; in relation to the present, that it *is* or exists; in relation to the future, that it *shall be*. Just as Eternity is an indefinite duration, so it is also without parts: for there is never so great a number of parts that one cannot still add some to them; but to the infinite, one can add nothing. For the same reason, time, which has parts, can make no part of Eternity, which is an infinite duration, because the time passed until today—which would be infinite—would be more than infinite by tomorrow.

One must meanwhile confess that Eternity is one of the attributes of God that we understand the least. We cannot, however, doubt it if we reflect well on the fact that God is a most perfect being.

That we have very imperfect and confused ideas of God’s Eternity comes from the fact that our spirit is very limited and our understanding very small.

2. That we attribute the same qualities to God as to created things because we view him as existing with created things. But let us consider him as he was before the world was created, and then we shall understand no sequence of time in his duration.

<margin>Ps. 90:4.</margin>
The Scripture, to come to our aid in this, teaches us that *a thousand years with God are as one day.*

Theologians, in order to explain Eternity in respect to these three parts of time, compare it to a Tower in the middle of a stream or river, washed by various parts of water, of which some have already flowed past long ago, others flow by it now, and others shall soon come flowing by; or to the center point of a circle, which stands equidistant from all parts of the circumference; or to a vertical pillar <note>original: "regtstandigen styl" — referring to a gnomon or sundial</note> on a flat surface, which by the Sun indicates the hours and heights of the celestial signs.

<margin>Plutarch, *Treatise on Isis*, etc.</margin>
The statue of Minerva of Sais <note>Referring to the Egyptian goddess Neith, whom the Greeks identified with Athena/Minerva.</note> had this inscription: *I am all that has been, all that is, and all that ever shall be.*

Furthermore, God’s Eternity must make us understand the infinite distance between this Eternal being and the creatures, who have begun to be and cease to be what they have been, so as to make our soul’s desire stretch out toward a blessed Eternity.

## XVI. CHAPTER.

### Of God’s Simplicity, Immutability, Infinity, and Glory.

<margin>Of God’s Simplicity.</margin> Since we must keep all imperfections far from God, we must beyond doubt consider him as a Most Simple Being. <note>In theology, "simplicity" does not mean "easy to understand," but rather "not composed of parts." A "simple" being is one that cannot be divided or broken down into smaller components.</note>

And certainly, all composition implies a state of dependence; now, that cannot exist in a being that we understand to be absolutely independent.

One cannot conceive of the slightest composition in God; he is not composed of matter and form, like physical bodies: for he is a pure spirit; for the same reason, he is not composed of parts.

If God had parts, he would be divisible into parts, which would either be of the same nature, or different, or equally perfect, or one more perfect than the other; whatever one chooses, one finds a thousand absurdities.

He cannot be composed of accidents <term>accidents: qualities or characteristics that are not essential to a thing's nature, like the color of a coat</term>, as other beings are: for those cannot be in God, God being in himself all that he must be, in order to be perfect.

God’s Simplicity is nothing other than the close union, and even the unity, of the attributes and properties of God. This unity will be realized as soon as one observes that God’s attributes are his very essence, which has various names; this can be proven by this reasoning: if the attributes were different from God’s essence, God’s essence would become more perfect through something that would be essentially distinct from it, which contradicts the highest perfection: moreover, it appears that the attributes are closely united:

1. Because that which we call understanding and will in God is one and the same thing. For it is through a most simple act that God knows and wills all things; and one cannot conceive in God that acts follow one after another.

2. Because most of God’s attributes and virtues are nothing other than the Will of God, which has various names. It is called Holiness when God wills nothing but good and hates evil; Goodness, when God wills to 

<column-break/>

communicate himself to the creature; Love, when God wills to be united with the same; Grace, when God wills to grant his benefits to those who have deserved nothing of the sort; Mercy, when he wills to help the miserable, and does help them; Faithfulness, when God wills to fulfill his promises and fulfills them; Vindicative Justice <note>original: "Wreekende Geregtigheid"</note> and Wrath, when God wills to punish sinners. So it is likewise with the other attributes.

It also appears that God’s attributes and perfections cannot be separated from the Divine Essence, nor one from the other; for if that were possible, God could be deprived of some perfection, which involves a contradiction: for one could not call him perfect if he could be stripped of any of his perfections.

**Obj.** There are three persons. **Ans.** These three are one. 2. **Obj.** There are various relations in God. **Ans.** These relations do not create a composition. 3. **Obj.** If there is a person who generates, and another who is generated, one must necessarily suppose a joining together. **Ans.** This would be true if it were with God as it is with men: but, although the Father generates the Son, there is nonetheless no composition, because the one and the other have the same essence.

<margin>Vorstius <note>Conrad Vorstius (1569–1622) was a controversial Dutch-German theologian whose views on the nature of God were central to the religious debates of the era.</note>.</margin> Scripture makes God’s simplicity known to us when, speaking of him, it calls him Life, Light, Truth, Wisdom.

This property is found in none but God: for in other things, we do not perceive that all properties are united, or at least so united that one cannot exist without the other: but when we think of God’s perfections, we regard them as inseparable properties.

Furthermore, just as God is a most simple being that is not composed, so he also enters into no composition. It is a gross error to believe that all creatures have come forth from God’s essence; as the Manichaeans <note>The Manichaeans were followers of a dualistic religion that taught that the soul was a literal spark of God trapped in the material world.</note> claimed.

Indeed, God is so distinct from the creatures that, being incorruptible as he is, he can come into no composition with them.

<margin>Rom. 11:35. Acts 17:28.</margin> It is true that it is said that all things are from God, and that we are called his offspring: but this is 
there-

God is then a perfectly simple being, although he brings forth an infinite number of different things, and cannot be known by humans except through thoughts whose diversity and multiplicity reveal the imperfection of the creature, as well as the fullness of the Divine essence, which contains everything in its incomprehensible simplicity. We must constantly lift up our Soul to that perfectly simple being, look away from the creatures, and recognize the imperfection of our being in the multiplicity of our thoughts and desires, which divide our understanding and heart.

<margin>Of God's immutability.</margin> From what we have said about the Simple being, it follows that he is also immutable. The immutability of God is a perfection which, if it is permitted to speak so, flows from his unity, from his simplicity, and from his necessary presence.

The Scripture sets this immutability of God before our eyes in many places.

Everything passes away, everything comes to an end, nothing is constant and durable. States and Kingdoms have their fluctuations. We are hardly the same for one day as we were before. Yesterday we were children, today we are young people, tomorrow we shall be old men; then we are strong, then weak, then healthy, then sick, then joyful, then sad. Changeability is itself so natural to man that it is necessary to him. He cannot hold himself to any one thing without change. The Angels themselves, however Spiritual their being may be, are not entirely exempt from change. They can have thoughts that they did not have before. God alone is immutable.

His essence cannot be disturbed: it can receive neither increase nor decrease;
<margin>Aug. of the City of God b. 12. c. 17.</margin>

it can change everything, without changing itself. Augustine says that

<column-break/>

God can work, without ceasing to rest, and through an eternal decree bring forth new works.

Reason clearly teaches us that God is immutable, for he who has all perfections cannot change. If God could change, the change would be for better or for worse; it cannot be for better, because God is perfectly good; it also cannot be for worse, because then he would not have all perfections: for he who, in order to keep himself outside of all change, would not possess them, and by becoming less perfect, he would cease to be God; and to acquire some perfections, equal to those he would have already had, that also cannot be, because it would follow from that that he did not have them all before.

In God no change can fall, neither in respect to his essence, nor in respect to his knowledge, nor in respect to his will; not in respect to his essence, which is Almighty and consequently can be offended or damaged by no being; it also cannot be corrupted, because he is the perfectly simple; it cannot cease to be, because it is eternal.

In God's knowledge no change can come either: for it is perfect and infinite.

In his will it can likewise not fall, because it is so wise that nothing can happen that it has not foreseen, and that nothing can prevent it from carrying out what it has decided. God sometimes changes the order that he has established; for example, the Levitical service <term>Levitical service: the complex system of laws and rituals performed by the tribe of Levi in the Old Testament</term>, which he has abolished: but, therefore he has not changed in will: for to prove that he changes in will, one must show that he willed that all things should always remain in the same state in which he first established them.

If God could change in will, it would be either from lack of power or from lack of wisdom: for those are the two causes that give birth to change. Now, neither one nor the other lack can be in God. No one can

But one must observe: 1. That, as Augustine said, it is the same eternal will of God that brought it about that created things did not exist for an eternity, and that they began to be at the beginning of time. 2. That it is not a "change" when one acquires a new relationship. Change consists in becoming that which one was not.

Now, it is certain that God did not become anything that He was not already before; He only brought forth such works <note>original: "gewrogten," meaning effects or products of labor</note> that gave Him the title of Creator. That new name added nothing to His essence and caused no change within it.

One might say that it is apparent that God often changes His will; for example, He had Hezekiah <note>The Hebrew King Hezekiah (Ezechiäs)</note> informed that he would die, and yet in the meantime He lengthened his days. In many places, one finds that God "repented."

One fails to notice: 1. That the reason why God had Hezekiah informed that he would die was this: that his illness, viewed according to the natural course of things, could be nothing other than fatal; God made this known to him so that he would take his refuge in Him and place himself in a state to receive his healing. 2. One does not notice that when God, for example, makes a promise or a threat, He requires certain conditions from those to whom He promises something: that He does not carry out His threats against those who turn away His wrath through their conversion, just as Hezekiah did. In short, one does not reflect on what I have said elsewhere, namely that when the Scripture says that God "repents," <note>original: "berouw heeft," referring to the concept of divine repentance or changing of mind</note> it is a figurative way of speaking, which one must not insist upon any more than when it ascribes hands and feet to God. It only indicates that God changes His way of acting, and not His will.

One will say that, if it is true—as we shall show in the following—that God has taken on flesh, one

<column-break/>

must confess that some change occurred in that Supreme Being.

When we deal with that subject, it will be very easy to show that the Incarnation of God's Son caused no change in the Divine essence: the Divinity was not changed into humanity, but only united to the human nature, and this union did not change God's nature. One should read the response of Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (Theodoretius), a 5th-century theologian who wrote extensively on the union of natures in Christ</note>, who has written on this in particular.

It is true that some other expressions occur in the Scripture that seem to strike against God's immutability; but one has only to use one's reason to understand their meaning. The changes that seem to be attributed to God are so far below the Majesty and loftiness of His being, and can so little coexist with His other virtues, that one can easily perceive that they must be taken in a figurative sense; whereas, on the contrary, we must understand all the passages that present God to us as perfectly immutable according to the letter, in all the power and extent of their meaning. So closely corresponding is immutability with the perfection and the greatness of the Supreme Being.

Furthermore, one must take note that the immutability of God is the pillar of our faith and of our hope; it teaches us to be immovable and steadfast (1 Cor. 15:58). To place a firm trust in nothing other than God, to long for that happy state in which we shall, in some way, become partakers of this immutability of God, loving Him with an eternal love, and experiencing no more instability in our thoughts. # THEOLOGY. II. B. XVI. Chapter.

<margin>
* Ps. 145:3
† Job 11:7-8.
</margin>
[God's] being is infinite in whatever way one considers it; whether in respect to time, for it is eternal, or in respect to places, for it is everywhere. His power, his wisdom, his goodness, his mercy—in a word, all his virtues are infinite. * The Lord is great and highly to be praised, and his greatness is unsearchable. † Can you fathom the depths of God? Can you find the limits of God? Can you find the perfection of the Almighty? It is as high as the heavens—what can you do? Deeper than hell—what can you know, etc.?

This infinity of God ensures that we cannot perfectly understand the Divine Being; God would be finite if finite beings could know him perfectly.

One asks whether God, being infinite, can produce infinite beings. I answer that it involves a contradiction that an infinite being is produced <note>The author argues that "infinite" implies being uncaused/self-existent; therefore, a "created infinite" is a logical impossibility</note>.

But, although God produces no infinite beings, one cannot help but stand in wonder at what he has done, because he works in an infinite manner.

Furthermore, this infinity of God proves that there is an infinite distance between God and his creatures. But it does not follow from this that all creatures are equally perfect or imperfect; since one must not measure the perfection of creatures by this distance, but by the greater or lesser perfection that they possess.

From God’s infinity, we must conclude that it is an exceeding folly to set one’s heart on limited creatures <note>original: "bepaalde schepzels," referring to finite things with boundaries, as opposed to the boundless God</note>, since we are called to the enjoyment of the infinite being; and God being perfect and having everything within himself, we are not capable of adding anything to his happiness and glory.

<margin>On God's Glory.</margin>
There remains nothing more than to say a word about God’s Glory; by this, one understands three things. Sometimes this word is taken for all the perfections that are in God; sometimes for the exercise of these perfections; sometimes for the knowledge that the creatures have of them; for the honor and service they offer to God; for the wonder with which they are moved upon seeing so many miracles; and for the manner in which they praise God with thoughts, words, and works.

This aligns with the saying of the theologians,

<header>THE CHRISTIAN</header>

When reading scripture, it seems that the praise, honor, service, and worship that Angels and humans give to God are among the ends <note>In theological terms, "ends" refers to the final goals or purposes for which an action is performed.</note> that God sets for Himself in all the wonders He works before their eyes and for their sake. This worship is the fruit and reward He expects from the benefits with which He fills them, and from the eternal blessedness <note>The Dutch "gelukzaligheid" refers to a state of supreme spiritual happiness or salvation.</note> with which He rewards their service and obedience, crowning their godliness, zeal, and virtues.

Meanwhile, some theologians believe that it does not befit the Greatness and Majesty of the true God to work for an end of such little importance to Him as the esteem, approval, praise, and acclaim of a creature <note>The word "creature" here refers to any created being, including humans and angels.</note>. Instead, they argue that God works only to exercise His virtues and to bring forth works that are becoming to Him, since He has nothing to desire nor to seek outside of Himself. Therefore, according to their view, God wills that His creatures show Him reverence and homage as a duty; but He does not expect that as a reward, nor does He propose it to Himself as His end. 

Thus, they say, a man who possesses true and essential virtue acts through the single fundamental principle of the love of virtue and the internal satisfaction he finds in practicing it; but he does not chase after praises. Those who do chase praise are merely "disguised virtuous" people, who push virtue out of its rank by placing it behind that which is merely its shadow. 

For my part, I am certain—along with the learned man whose words I cited above—that all theologians are fundamentally of the same opinion, although they express themselves differently.

3. That the concept and admiration of the greatness of the First Being <note>The "First Being" is a philosophical and theological term for God as the uncaused cause of all things.</note> indeed add nothing to His perfections; but that they are nevertheless the effects, impressions, and images of them. When one reads scripture, it seems that the praise, honor, service, and worship that Angels and men give to God are among the ends that God sets for Himself in all the wonders He performs before their eyes and for their sake. ### CHAPTER I.

->Concerning the Three Persons of the Most Holy Trinity, in General.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'W' featuring foliate scrollwork inside a square border.</image-desc>We have considered God's perfections in the preceding books; now it is necessary to note that there are three to whom these perfections are attributed: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The Scripture, which teaches us that there is no more than one God, nevertheless presents these three together as the principle of our Salvation, and the object of our Faith and Worship. We maintain and defend this against the Jews, Socinians <note>The Socinians were a group that emerged during the Reformation who rejected the traditional doctrine of the Trinity and the divinity of Christ.</note>, and others of whom we shall speak elsewhere.

But so as not to stumble in a matter of such weight, let us hear what the Scripture teaches.

1. One must take note of all the places where God speaks in this manner. Genesis 1:26: *Let us make man in our image.* Genesis 3:22: *Behold, the man has become as one of us, knowing good and evil.* Genesis 11:7: *Come, let us go down, and there confound their speech.* Isaiah 6:8: *Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?* One can clearly see more than one Person here.

<margin>Schlichting against Metinus and Lipman <note>Referring to Jonas Schlichting, a Polish Socinian theologian, writing against traditionalist or Jewish opponents.</note></margin>
One cannot say here that God is speaking to the Angels, for man was not made in the Image of the Angels: and it is beyond all appearance of truth that God would have said to His servants /

<column-break/>

<margin>Nizzachon <note>A Jewish polemical text.</note>; Menasseh ben Israel in *The Conciliator* <note>original: "in Conciliatore"</note>, Folio 38; Eniedinus in *Passages of the Old and New Testament* <note>original Latin: "in Locis Veteris & Novi Testamenti"</note>.</margin>
*man has become as one of us*; it is even more ridiculous to say that God took counsel with Heaven and Earth. One cannot say that God, after the custom of Kings, expresses Himself in the plural. For 1. one cannot prove that the Hebrews spoke in this manner. No King, speaking of himself alone, will say, "one of us." Some places are pointed out from the Old and New Testament where it seems that a single Person speaks of himself in the plural. Such as Laban in Genesis 29:27; Daniel in Daniel 2:36; Jesus Christ in John 3:11. But one need only read those passages to see that Laban speaks of himself, his household, and friends; Daniel of himself and his companions; Jesus Christ of himself, of John the Baptist, and of his disciples—or rather of himself and of his Father, who had sent him; just as he elsewhere adds his testimony to that of his Father, John 8:14, 15, 17, 19. Thus one can explain other passages, such as Job 5:27 and 18:2, etc. Add to this that one does not see the Kings spoken of in the Old Testament speaking of their person in the plural. Neither the King of Sodom, Genesis 14:21; nor Abimelech, Genesis 20:9; nor Pharaoh, Genesis 41:15, 17, 21; nor Nebuchadnezzar, Daniel 2:3, 5, 8 and 3:26 and 4:4; nor Belshazzar, Daniel 5:7, 14, 15; nor Darius the Mede, Daniel 6:26; nor Cyrus, 2 Chronicles 36:23. It is said that those who wish to do something great speak thus after mature deliberation: but that cannot be proven by Scripture, and there are proofs to the contrary. Exodus 3:3, Isaiah 5:1, Jeremiah 5:5, Hosea 2:7.

It is said that God speaks so to give weight to His words.

But regarding the opinion of those who are capable of judging this matter, one sees no variation in style. Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654), an English jurist and scholar of Jewish law.</note> says (in his book *On the Sanhedrins of the Ancient Hebrews* <note>original: "de Syned. vet. The Benedictine Fathers note, in their edition of Jerome, that there is an old manuscript in the library of Colbert—written before the time of **Charles the Bald**, or at least during that time—where this preface is found, and that it is also in three others, 800 years old, which are kept in the library of Saint-Germain.

It is said that the Epistles in the preface are called **Canonical** (*Canonique*), yet Jerome usually calls them **Catholic** (*Catholique*). But this is perhaps a scribal error. Perhaps he said both. Furthermore, even if this preface were not by Jerome, it is certain that it is very old.

It is not easy to discover at what time this passage was obscured.

It is not probable that the **Arians** <note>Followers of Arius, who taught that Jesus was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father.</note> did it. For 1. It is certain that it was in use before Arius appeared. 2. It is unlikely that they would not have been reproached for this, and that **Athanasius** would not have noticed this deception. 3. Finally, it is impossible that they could have corrupted so many manuscripts. The corruption occurred before this time: this is evident 1. from the writings of Epiphanius (Heresy 42) and of Jerome (*Preface to the Epistle to Titus*) that the Cerinthians, Basilians, and Marcionites <note>Early Gnostic and dualist groups labeled as heretics by the early Church.</note> made many changes in the writings of the Apostles. 2. BUT, assuming that this passage was written by John, as we do not doubt, we must confess that we clearly find in it the three Persons and their Unity, and thus it places us beyond the danger of two equally perilous reefs: namely, the error of those who mix the Persons, and the error of those who divide them.

This mystery of Three in a single essence is called the mystery of the **Trinity**.

<margin>Francis Gregory, D.T., *The Doctrine of the Glorious Trinity explained and asserted*. London, 1695.</margin>
One must speak of this with wisdom and moderation, and not venture into investigations that God has willed to hide from us; but one cannot deny this secret without opposing the Scripture, which teaches us these two things everywhere: 1. That there is but one God. 2. That there are three who possess the essence and perfections of the Godhead. We proved the first in the preceding Book; we shall prove the second in what follows.

<margin>1. Socinians and Jews.</margin>
Against this mystery, it is objected: 1. That the Scripture says everywhere that there is but one God.

Answer: All these passages pose no difficulty, because the same Scripture tells us that this one God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; therefore, we must believe both. We shall answer elsewhere the passages that seem to suggest there is only one God, namely the Father.

2. Objection: If there are three, of whom each is God, there will be three Gods.

I answer: There are not three Gods, since each of these three has one and the same essence.

But, it is said, the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God, therefore three Gods. This does not follow; it only follows that, since they all three have but one Divine essence, they are one God. It is said, where there is one and three, that makes four. That is true where there is one essence and three essences: but this cannot be said where there is only one essence and three Persons.

3. Objection: If they have but one and the same essence, then there are not three Persons, but one.

I answer: They have but one essence: but nevertheless, the Scripture says that there are three distinct subjects: therefore, we must believe both.
