<meta>This page continues a theological defense of the Trinity, moving from historical manuscript evidence to philosophical arguments against common objections regarding the nature of the "Three-in-One."</meta>

# CHRISTIAN #

4. Objection: It is contradictory that there is One and Three in God.

I answer: It would be contradictory if we proposed that God is one and three in the same respect: one God and three Gods; one essence and three essences; three Persons, three particular Natures, and yet only one God. But we say there is one single God, one single essence; the three Persons are not three essences, but the one and the same essence.

One asks whether there is nothing in these three other than the Divine essence.

I answer: Without doubt one must note some distinction, since Scripture teaches it, and says of the Father that which it does not say of the Son; this, the theologians call Personhood (Personality), because they have found no more suitable word. But, since Scripture does not explain to us what Personality is, we cannot say anything further about it. Therefore, one must not be troubled by the difficulty that some make in answering. They say: "That which distinguishes the Father from the Son is either a perfection or an imperfection. If it is an imperfection, then the one in whom it resides is not God; if it is a perfection, then one of these Persons has a perfection that the other does not have." We answer: Because we do not know what constitutes this distinction, we cannot speak of it. But of two things we can be certain: that in God there is not the slightest imperfection; and that each Person possesses all perfections.

<margin>Augustine, Book 7, *On the Trinity*, chapter 4.</margin>
When we are asked, said Augustine, what the three Persons are, we try to find some common or specific word to signify these three; and we find none, because the excellence of Divine things exceeds the power of our expressions. For there is more truth in what one thinks of God than in what one says of Him.

5. Objection: It is an incomprehensible thing that there are three, and that these three are one.

I answer: The incomprehensibility of a mystery <note>original: "verborgentheid"</note> must not make us reject it, since we should not be surprised that finite beings, such as we are, cannot comprehend the nature of an infinite being, and that many things are said of this being that are above reason. If there were nothing in the truths of Christianity except that which

<column-break/>

could be easily understood, why would the Scripture call the Gospel a mystery, a great mystery, "things which the eye has not seen, the ear has not heard, and which have not entered into the heart of any man"; things which the Angels do not know; depths which the Angels seek to fathom? One would be as ridiculous to wish to reject a mystery because it is above our reason, as one would be if one claimed that nothing more happens than what we see; for reason is to our Soul what eyes are to our body.

6. Objection: This mystery is not only above, but against reason.

I answer: That cannot be said, because for our reason to use such language, it would have to perfectly understand everything that can be said of the Divinity, but that cannot be said in any way. We often think that there is a contradiction in statements because we do not view the objects from all sides and do not penetrate to the bottom of them. To be certain that there is a contradiction in the mystery of the Trinity, one would have to be certain that there is no Unity that can suffer any distinction, in whatever way it might be.

To receive this mystery with submission, one must note:

1. That in the study of nature (<term>Physics</term> <note>The author refers here to "Physica," the natural sciences, suggesting that even the physical world contains mysteries that baffle the human mind.</note>) there are incomprehensibilities as great and as difficult as those in the mystery of the Trinity that make us stand still in wonder. One might say: "These physical truths are confirmed by experience." I answer: This mystery is not, nor can it indeed be, confirmed by experience; but it is enough that it has been clearly revealed to us and is consistent with other truths of the Gospel.

2. If it had pleased God to explain this mystery of the Trinity more clearly to us, we would see that there is nothing in it against reason; or if we understood the Divine essence better, we would not find so many difficulties here.

3. Our reason must not judge what it does not understand: for one would make a dangerous abuse of the light of reason and change it into darkness. One must not refuse to follow the light, whether of reason or of revelation, when God places this light before us; but one must stand still when the darkness begins.

<meta>The text continues with point 4 of the submission to the mystery.</meta>

The author compares theological mysteries to the unexplained phenomena in the natural sciences (Physics) to justify faith in revelation.</summary>

4. That one must never deny a truth under the pretext that one does not see how it agrees with another known truth; thus, one must not deny the *Trinity* in order to maintain the unity of God.

5. That God's essence is infinite, and that one must therefore hold for certain that Scripture can tell us many things about God that we will never fully comprehend.

6. That we do not understand how the Divine essence is common to several [Persons] because we judge it as if it were a finite being, which cannot be bound in many subjects.

7. That the Divine essence is common to several Persons comes from its own infinity; but following Scripture, we speak of only three who are of one essence.

8. Furthermore, that which must oblige us to believe this mystery—even though we do not understand it—is that it is certainly the principle of all others, and the foundation of the entire system of the *Gospel*, and of the whole *Economy of Grace* <term>Economy of Grace: The historical plan and administration of God’s mercy toward humanity</term>.

One cannot well explain *Redemption*, *Justification*, *Sanctification*, nor *Adoption as children* <note>original: "aanneming tot kinderen"</note> without establishing the mystery of the three Persons.

But the matter will appear more clearly when we deal with all these points in particular, especially when we prove that *Jesus Christ* and the *Holy Spirit* are one and the same God with the *Father*: for, if it is clear through Scripture that there is but one God, and that nevertheless *Jesus Christ is God* and the *Holy Spirit is God*, then it follows that there are three, and that nevertheless these three are a single God; we shall also prove that in this single God—*Father, Son, and Holy Spirit*—we must recognize the perfect cause and the sole principle of that great *Salvation* which was prepared for us before the ages and obtained in the fullness of time, of which we enjoy the firstfruits, pledges, and promises here below, and shall have the full possession in the life to come.

<margin>The Remonstrants in their *Apology*, chapter 3, in Response 3, excerpted edition. Professors of Leiden, pages 38, 39.</margin>
From this it follows that the mystery of the *Trinity* is necessary for *Salvation* and is one of the fundamental articles of Religion. For, if it is true that it is the foundation of the entire system of the *Gospel*, how could one be *Saved* without believing it? In-

<column-break/>

<margin>Episcopius, book 4 of the *Institutes*, chapter 34. <note>Simon Episcopius (1583–1643) was a prominent Dutch theologian and leader of the Remonstrants.</note></margin>
-deed, if all the other *Articles of Faith* depend on this one, how can one be ignorant of it without making oneself guilty? Moreover, if there is a fundamental article, it is that which we must profess in our *Baptism*; from this it appears that one cannot truly be in the *Church of God* without believing this mystery when one has come to years [of maturity] to make an actual profession of one's Faith, and that the denial of this mystery is a renunciation of one's *Baptism*.

But, when I say that one must believe this mystery to be *Saved*, I do not mean thereby that one must know all the distinctions that the theologians have made, and understand all the proposed difficulties; I mean only that everyone must believe in God the *Father, Son, and Holy Spirit*, and that these three are one; a *Faith* that the simplest people can have and profess.

It will be said that the Fathers of the *Old Testament* did not know this mystery.

<margin>Isaiah 9:5 <note>In modern English bibles, this text is found in Isaiah 9:6.</note></margin>
I admit that they did not know it as clearly as we do, who are obliged to have a more distinct Faith in it than they; but they nevertheless knew a single God, and believed in the Son, whom *Isaiah* calls the *Wonderful, the Counselor, the Father of Eternity, and the Mighty God*; they placed their trust in the *Messiah*, who is the *Son of God*, and whom they called *Jehovah our Righteousness*; that was sufficient for the time of the old dispensation.

It will be said that this mystery does not flow into the practice of *Godliness*: but one is mistaken, for if *Christ* is not true *God*, then one should not worship him, and he would not have been able to redeem us.

It will be said: *Paul* wishes to know nothing else but *Jesus Christ*, and him crucified.

I answer: *Jesus Christ* cannot be known without the *Father*; and one cannot know the *Father* and the *Son* without believing in the *Trinity*.

But this material will be explained more clearly when we show that it is absolutely necessary to believe that *Jesus Christ* is the true *God*; which we shall prove after some remarks concerning the first Person.

mystery was known to the Pagans. All that is told of Zoroaster, of Hermes Trismegistus, Plato, Proclus, Orpheus, Numenius, Plotinus, Iamblichus, of the supposed Oracle of Serapis, and of Seneca, proves nothing. <margin>

But here are many weighty observations to be made.
1. When we call God, Father, we do not take this word in the sense / that the wise men of the world have often named him / in consideration that he is the cause and Creator of the Universe / and of all that it comprises / both Heavenly and Earthly things / by some comparison / which in that respect is between God and the Persons, whom men properly call Fathers / being those from whom the household has its origin / and by whose counsel and authority the same is governed. The

<column-break/>

Scripture sometimes uses this manner of speaking / as when Moses said of Israel’s God: Is he not your Father, <margin>Deuteronomy 32:6</margin> who has acquired you, who has made you, and who has established you? Deut. 32:6. Have we not all one Father? and has not one God created us? Mal. 2:10. <margin>Malachi 2:10.</margin> We also do not take this word in the sense / in which God is called the Father of the believers / because he has reborn them unto a living hope; therefore John said, see what great love the Father has given, (namely) that we should be called children of God. 1. <margin>1 John 3:1.</margin> John 3:1. But we call God Father in respect to our Lord Jesus Christ / who generated him from all Eternity / as we shall see in the following.
The Apostles often call him the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, not to distinguish him from another God, as if the Creator of the world / honored / served / and worshipped by the Jews under the Old Testament / was different from the one we serve under the New Testament / and who sent the Lord Jesus / to make us Blessed. This was believed by the Marcionites and Manicheans <note>Early Christian dualist sects deemed heretical for separating the God of the Old Testament from the God of the New Testament</note>, who imagined two principles; one of good and another of evil; that the principle of evil was the God of the Old Testament / strict / and unmerciful: and that the principle of good was the God of the New Testament / the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Godless sentiments! which the Scripture powerfully opposes. The Disciples of the Lord Jesus give this name to the first Person of the Trinity / because he makes himself known particularly in this relationship under the new dispensation. Under the Old Household <note>original: "Oude Huishouding" referring to the Old Covenant or Dispensation</note> one said: Blessed be God the Most High, who <margin>Genesis 14:19.</margin> possesses Heaven and Earth. Thus spoke Melchizedek. Or: Blessed be the God of Israel. But now that this great God has shown himself in the world / in his image and the reflection of his Glory / the Church changes its Language / and says: Blessed be the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. This name also serves / to make known to us / that he is our Father / because we have the honor to be Members and Brothers of Christ. Therefore the Savior said to Mary, when he prepared himself to ascend to Heaven, I <margin>John 20:17.</margin> ascend to my Father, and your Father, and to my God and your God.
II. One must now take note / that our

THEOLOGY. III. B. III. and IV. Chapters.

God the Father is presented to us in the scriptures through attributes that are specifically his own, such as generating his Son and sending him and the Holy Spirit. Of him it is also said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him, but we find nowhere that the Father is generated, or sent, or proceeds from another. It is also not said that he works through another, as is testified of the Son, who does nothing of himself. John 5:19.

III. One must further observe that God the Father is commonly called the First, before the Son and the Holy Spirit. As appears in Matthew 28:19, 1 John 5:7, and elsewhere. But from this, it is not to be concluded that he is "before" the Son and the Holy Spirit in time, dignity, and perfections; for these three adorable Persons are equally eternal, having the same power, Majesty, Glory, and Perfections. The Father is then called the First because he is described as the one who generates the Son, and from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds. This order, however, is not always maintained. See 2 Cor. 13:13 and Gal. 1:1.

IV. Finally, the Father is regarded in the work of Salvation as a Judge who demands satisfaction, who receives it from a Surety <note>original: 'Borg' - a legal term for one who takes responsibility for another's debt; here, Christ paying the debt of sin</note>, who chose us before the Foundation of the world, who appointed a Mediator for us, reconciling the world to himself through his Son; delivering him unto death, raising him up, and granting him a name above all names, and who—to say it in a word—always defends the right of the Deity; and for this reason is sometimes called God pre-eminently <note>original: 'by uitnemendheid' - meaning God in the highest or most distinguished sense</note>.

To this Heavenly Father we must take our refuge through Jesus Christ, his Son, to obtain grace in a timely manner. He is the Father of Christ, who is our head, and at the same time, he is our Father. We must love him as our Father, follow him as beloved children, being Merciful, Holy, and Perfect as he is, so that we may one day have a share in his Inheritance, as co-heirs with Christ, our firstborn Brother, who is not ashamed to call us his Brothers.

### CHAPTER III.

->Of God the Son.<-

<margin>
Socinians <note>A group that denied the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ</note> against Witsius <note>Likely Herman Witsius, an orthodox theologian</note>.
</margin>
Having now spoken of the First Person of the Trinity, we shall 1. Part.

<column-break/>

now deal with the second; This is the Son, Jesus Christ our Lord. The scripture presents him as God and Man; we shall have opportunity in the future to consider his Humanity; it is now most fitting to speak of his Deity, after which we shall deal with his eternal generation <note>The theological concept that the Son is eternally begotten of the Father</note>.

<margin>
Smalcius's treatise on the divinity of Christ and against Franz. Ostorodius. Volkelius. <note>These names refer to prominent Socinian authors who challenged the traditional view of Christ's divinity</note>
</margin>
To present this material clearly, we shall 1. see all that can prove to us that a Person is Divine, and 2. subsequently investigate whether Scripture says of J. Christ what it says of God. 3. After which we shall answer the objections.

1. It is certain that one cannot fail to regard as a Divine Person anyone to whom Scripture gives the name of God and all the attributes of the Deity; to whom it attributes the works of God, which require an infinite power; and to whom it desires that one should offer the honor, service, and worship that belongs to the true God alone.

If a Person, of whom Scripture testifies all these things, is not Divine, then I do not understand what more could be required for it.

2. We shall then investigate whether Scripture attributes the same Names, Perfections, Works, Honor, and Service to J. Christ as it gives to God. For if it does so, then Jesus Christ is without doubt God, and equal with the Father.

Let us then search the Scripture, and to do this accurately, let us follow the order of the Books, yet remembering two things. 1. That one must not expect to find the same clarity in the Oracles of the Old Testament as in the New Testament. 2. That one must seek, in the writings of the Apostles, the explanations of the Oracles of the Old Testament which they quoted or upon which they were inspired.

<margin>Genesis 16:7, 9, 10.</margin>
Genesis 16:7, 9, 10. It is said—when Hagar fled from Sarah, her mistress—that the Angel of the Lord appeared to her; this same Angel is called Jehovah in verse 13, for Hagar called upon the name of the Lord who spoke to her, "You are the God who sees me" <note>original: "God des aanziens"; a translation of the Hebrew 'El Roi'</note>. And it appears that he truly was Jehovah, for he says to Hagar in verse 10: "I will greatly multiply your descendants, so that they shall not be counted for multitude." This cannot be applied to God the Father, for an Angel of the Lord is spoken of here; nor to a created angel, for such a one would not be called Jehovah, nor would an angel have said, "I will multiply Hagar’s descendants."

It will be said that Paul in Hebrews 1:1 testifies that God has only in these last days spoken to us through his Son. But Paul means to say that God in these last days has spoken through his **Incarnate** Son, although he had already spoken through that same Son, who from time to time took on a human form. This observation is enough to answer Hebrews 2:2 and 3.

<margin>Genesis 18:2.</margin>
Genesis 18:2. It is said that Three Men came to Abraham. These are three angels, one of whom is called Jehovah (verses 1, 13, 14, 17, 20, 22). He says that the cry of Sodom has reached him (verse 20), and Abraham calls him the Judge of all the Earth (verse 25). These words are to be understood as coming neither from God the Father, nor from a created angel, but from God the Son, to whom the Father has given all judgment, and who shall be the Judge of the living and the dead.

People say: 1. that it was only three Men whom Abraham saw, and that he ate with them. **Answer:** The Text, which one only has to read, proves the opposite.

2. People say: That one might doubt whether Jesus Christ had truly risen from the dead if an angel had been able to do everything recounted in Genesis 18. **Answer:** There are many irrefutable reasons that prove Christ is risen. What likelihood is there that a good angel would want to deceive people; or that a Devil would want to convince people of a feast <note>original: "gebal" - likely referring to the meal Abraham prepared</note> in a way that utterly overthrows his own cunning?

<margin>Hebrews 13:2.</margin>
3. People say: If one of these three angels had been God, Paul would not have called them merely "angels" in Hebrews 13:2. **Answer:** But why would one

<column-break/>

not want Paul to be alluding to the history of Lot, who indeed hosted only angels; or to the story of the spies of the Promised Land?

4. People say: If one of them had been God, they would have had no need to be guided by Abraham (verse 16). **Answer:** Although it says that Abraham guided them because he accompanied them to show them honor, they did not actually need this guide.

5. People say: God would have made himself known by some sign. **Answer:** He made himself sufficiently known by his names.

<margin>Genesis 31:13.</margin>
Genesis 31:13. Moses relates that an Angel of God said to Jacob: "I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed the pillar and where you made a vow to me; now arise, depart from this land, and return to the land of your kindred." See there an Angel, who can be none other than the Son of God; for he alone can say, "I am the strong God," while calling himself the Angel of the Lord; and it is also to God that Jacob made his vow.

Genesis 32:28. It is recorded that a Man came to wrestle with Jacob. He is called a Man because he appeared in the form of a Man. But Jacob realized that it was a God, and he [the visitor] made himself known to him as a God; when Jacob asked his name, he said, "Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel; for you have behaved princely <note>original: "Vorstelyk gedragen"; implying power or status like a prince</note> with God and with men, and have prevailed." Upon this, Jacob called that place Peniel in verse 30, "for" (he said) "I have seen God face to face." It is said there that Jacob requested his blessing; add to this Hosea 12:4-5 <note>In the Dutch text, cited as verses 5-6</note>, where the Prophet, recounting the case of Jacob, says that he behaved princely with God. Yes, he behaved princely against the Angel, and prevailed over him. He wept and entreated him; at Bethel he found him, and there he spoke with us—namely the LORD, the God of hosts, LORD is his memorial name.

<margin>Hosea 12:4-5.</margin>
To say that this was a Vision, and the power of Jacob’s imagination, which made him move his body so violently that he dislocated his hip <note>original: "ontheupte" - literally 'de-hipped' or dislocated</note>, is the greatest absurdity that can be imagined; the passage in Hosea proves that this was no mere vision.

Add to this Genesis 48:15, 16.

Where Jacob, blessing Joseph, says: **The God, before whose face my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has fed me from my beginning until this day; the Angel who has delivered me from all evil, Bless these children.**

From all these places one sees clearly that, in the time of the Patriarchs, there was an Angel who called himself Jehovah, and consequently cannot be regarded as a created angel; who also cannot be the first Person of the Trinity, from which one must necessarily conclude that it is the second, the Son: for there is no reason to understand this Angel as the Holy Spirit. From this it then appears that the Son, who is Jesus Christ, was called God and Jehovah by Moses and the Patriarchs.

If we pass from the first Book of Moses to the second, Exodus, we shall be strengthened in the same truth.

<margin>Exodus 3:2.</margin>
Exodus 3:2 says Moses, that the Angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a burning bush; and in verse 4 he calls this Angel Jehovah; he adds that God called to him from the midst of the bush and said to him in verse 6: **I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob;** and verse 7: **I have surely seen the oppression of my people,** etc. A created angel would not have dared to speak in this manner; it must then be an uncreated Angel, and this is none other than the Son of God.

<margin>1 Kings 5:3.</margin>
One must not say that this Angel speaks in God's name, just as emissaries speak in the name of their Princes, as is repeated in 1 Kings 5:3, that Solomon sent to Hiram to say to him: **You know that my father David could not build a house for the name of the LORD his God, etc.** For who does not see that these things are very different: when emissaries speak in the name of their masters, they make that known; and among the Eastern peoples it was the custom, as our Master has said, in the same way as the Prophets said, **"Thus says the Lord."** The emissaries of Solomon said, **"our King, and you know,"** etc. But this Angel says here, without any qualification, **I am the God of Abraham.** Is it possible that these blessed spirits, who are so jealous of God's honor, would have

<margin>Acts 7:38.</margin>

That Christ is the Jehovah, the God of Israel, whom the Israelites tempted in the wilderness. 2. That Jesus Christ existed before his conception in the womb of Mary. From the writings of Justin <note>Justin Martyr, a 2nd-century Christian apologist</note>, of Irenaeus, etc., as we shall see elsewhere, it appears that it has generally been believed that God's Son was He whom the sinful Israel tempted in the wilderness. <margin>Exodus 23:20, 21.</margin>
One will say that 1 Corinthians 10:9 should be read as **"let us not tempt God,"** just as this passage is read in a manuscript sent from the East to England. <note>The author is likely referring to the Codex Alexandrinus or similar manuscripts being debated by scholars of his time.</note> But to support this conjecture, one must be very reckless; is it not better to correct one manuscript by all the others, than all the others by one? One has very old manuscripts that read, **"let us not tempt Christ"**; the Latin, Syriac, and Arabic translations read in the same way.

the Greek and Latin Fathers, who have explicitly explained or cited this passage, take it exactly as it stands in our Bible. Among the Greeks, one need only read Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius; and among the Latins, the Interpreter of Paul who published under the name of Ambrose <note>Referring to "Ambrosiaster," a name given by modern scholars to the unknown author of a 4th-century commentary on Paul's epistles</note>, as well as another who explained Paul's letters in the time of Jerome; this latter writer likewise derives the Divinity of the Lord Jesus from this passage. Augustine does the same in a disputation against the Arians. <margin>Against Maximinus the Arian, book 3, chapter 26. Irenaeus, book 4, chapter 45.</margin> Irenaeus reads the same words in the same way. If there are any Ancient Fathers who have cited this passage differently, they place the word *Lord* in place of *Christ*. For instance, Epiphanius and Theodoret, quoting it from memory without having checked it.

It is said that the text reads, *let us not tempt Christ, as some of them also tempted*, and not *tempted him*. But one must wish to be blind not to see that it amounts to the same thing. For example, in John 8:56 it is said: *Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day: and he saw (it).* In the Greek it says, *he saw*. Likewise in Hebrews 3:16, after Paul had brought forward these words of the Psalmist: *Today if you hear his voice, harden not your hearts*, he adds: *for some, when they had heard, did provoke him.* The Greek and Latin text simply has: *some, having heard, provoked to anger.*

It is said that Moses must be understood as "Christ" here. But 1. Scripture has never given the name of Christ to Moses. 2. Nowhere is it said that the Israelites tempted Moses. 3. Even if it were true that Moses was called "Christ" in some places, it is clear that one could not interpret Paul in this way: for here it concerns the Messiah, and not Moses, who had died many centuries before.

It is said that Moses is called "Christ" by way of comparison, in respect to the Israelites, because he was to them what Christ is now to us. But 1. If Paul had had these thoughts, he would have said, *tempt not your Christ*, as some tempted theirs;

<column-break/>

instead of saying, *tempt not Christ, as some have tempted him.* 2. Nowhere is it said that Moses was tempted; it is indeed noted that they spoke against Moses, but not that they tempted him.

It is said that one must explain the words of the Apostle as if someone now in Poland said: "let us not offend our King, as our ancestors have done." Now, it is argued, one must not conclude from this that the King who is now in Poland has been there from the beginning. <note>This "Poland" analogy refers to the Socinians, a group based in Poland who denied the pre-existence of Christ and were the primary targets of this theological defense.</note> But 1. Paul does not say, *let us not tempt our Christ*, but *let us not tempt Christ.* 2. All Princes can be exposed to the slander of their subjects, but it is not so with this "tempting," for Moses was not tempted; that is nowhere said, but rather that God, or that Christ, was tempted. 3. The name of "King" is common to all who have been Kings in Poland, but the name of Christ in the New Testament is given to only one Person.

...before the face of the Lord; before the face of the Lord of the whole Earth. The Heavens declare His righteousness, and all Peoples see His glory; ashamed must be all who serve Images, who boast of Idols; bow down before Him, all you Gods. <note>This is a translation of Psalm 97:5–7.</note>

It cannot be denied that these words are spoken of the supreme God: for He is described in this Psalm by the same attributes with which He is depicted in all other parts of the Scripture; by His name Jehovah, by His Sovereignty over the whole world, and by the signs of His Glory, which are spread throughout all of nature.

Now Paul applies this divine oracle <note>original: "Godspraak"</note> to Christ. In Hebrews 1:6, it says: *And again, when He brings the firstborn into the world, He says: And let all the angels of God worship Him.* From this it follows that the Son is the Supreme God, the God of Israel, the Lord of the whole Earth: for, if He were not, then Paul would have uttered the most terrible blasphemy by applying to Christ a divine oracle that belongs to no one other than the living God; it also follows that the Son was worshipped with the highest degree of adoration.

One might say that the Psalm states, *all you Gods, worship Him*, whereas Paul says that *all Angels worship Him*. But this distinction is of no importance. Besides the fact that Paul followed the <term>LXX</term> <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, which often translates "gods" (Elohim) as "angels" in this context.</note> translators, he has given us the true sense of what must be understood by the "Gods" of whom the Prophet speaks, namely the Angels. It is true that one could also understand it as the Great Men of the Earth, but without excluding the Angels.

One might say that this application by Paul proves nothing to the Jews. I grant that, but the Jews cannot deny that their Fathers have said that the Psalms from 93 to 101 inclusive refer to the <term>Messias</term> <note>Messiah</note>, and that the Kingdom of the Messiah is spoken of as often as the Kingdom of God over the Universe is mentioned; for Christians, this proof is beyond all contradiction.

One might say that those who worship Jesus Christ worship the supreme God because Jesus Christ represents the supreme God in a special way. I answer: that the point here is not to know

<column-break/>

whether one, by worshipping Christ, worships the supreme God; but whether it is not said of Christ that all the Angels of God worship Him; and whether this is not the natural idea that the words of the Writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews must awaken in the mind, and whether they can be explained in any sense other than the one we take.

One might say that the word for worship is often taken for a Civil honor <note>Respect shown to a high-ranking human official rather than divine adoration.</note>; but, even if that were so, it cannot be denied that in this Psalm, a Religious honor is being spoken of.

One might say that Paul speaks of a Firstborn, of whom no mention is made in the Psalm. But Paul speaks of Him, and teaches us that this firstborn is the Jehovah of whom the Prophet speaks.

Furthermore, it is necessary to note what the worship of the Angels consists of. It consists of a deep humiliation before Jesus Christ, whom they confess to be their Lord and God, and before whom they acknowledge themselves to be nothing. Who does not understand from this that Christ is the most high God? It is true that <term>Socinus</term> <note>Fausto Sozzini (1539–1604), a theologian who denied the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ, arguing He was a man granted divine authority.</note> and his followers believe that Christ, as a Man, deserves to be worshipped by the angels; but that is directly contrary to the Scripture, which testifies that God alone must be worshipped. This has been recognized by other Heretics who, while denying the Divinity of Christ along with Socinus, maintained that He must not be worshipped.

<margin>Ps. 102:25–27.</margin>
The fourth passage is taken from Psalm 102:25–27, etc. *Of old You laid the foundation of the Earth, and the Heavens are the work of Your hands. They will perish, but You will endure; they will all wear out like a garment. You will change them like a robe, and they will pass away, but You are the same, and Your years will have no end.*

If this divine oracle is not spoken of the supreme God, then none can be applied to Him. For one must note that God distinguishes Himself here from all other beings through the Act of Creation. *Who has measured the waters in the hollow of His hand?* etc. verse 26. <margin>Isa. 40:26.</margin> *Lift up your eyes on high, and see who has created these things.* and in Isaiah 48:12, 13, God says: <margin>Isa. 48:12, 13.</margin> *I am He; I am the first, I also am the last. My hand laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand...*

DIVINE THEOLOGY. III. B. VI. Chapter 223

...hand has measured the Heavens with a span. <note>This imagery, likely referencing Isaiah 40:12, emphasizes God's immense power in creation.</note> And when he speaks of the false Gods, he describes them as those who have not created the Heavens and the earth.

Paul now applies these words of the Prophet to Jesus Christ in Hebrews 1:10, 11, 12, where the Apostle—in order to exalt Christ above the Angels and all creatures—shows that there is as much difference between Christ and these heavenly spirits as there is between the Creator and the Created.

From this it follows that J. Christ is the Creator of the world, and consequently God, for God alone possesses an infinite power to create everything out of nothing.

It is remarkable that the Apostle, in the preceding verses, had named Christ God, applying Psalm 45 to him. But, because he had described him thereafter as anointed by his Father, from whom he received his Kingdom—which might have made him appear lesser than the Father—he applies to him a divine oracle <note>original: "Godspraak"</note> that places him on equal footing with the Father and attributes the creation to him. Who then can doubt that Christ is God with his Father, to be praised for eternity? Paul had said that God made the Ages through his Son; but, so that one would not believe that this Son had been merely the instrument that God made use of—though in the work of creation no instrument can have a place—he adds that he himself founded the earth and the Heavens.

<margin>Enied.</margin> <note>This likely refers to Marcin Krowicki or more probably Andrzej Wiszowaty’s references to the Socinian theologian Enjedinus, who argued against the Trinity.</note>
It is said that Paul is speaking of the improvement of the world and of the new creation. But who does not see that by such an interpretation the words of the Prophet and the Apostle are twisted?

It is said that Paul applies these words, *you have founded the earth*, not to Christ but to God the Father; that Paul’s intention is only to apply the following words to him: *you are permanent, and you are the same, and your years shall not cease.* And that this means nothing other than that the Son is immortal and unchangeable. However, 1. is this not to contradict Paul to his face, since he testifies that it was said of the Son: *You have founded the earth*? 2. Why insist that the first words are said of the Father and the following of the Son, since it is clear that they both have the same Person as their subject? 3. Why bring these words forward if they only refer to God the Father? Since the

<column-break/>

issue here is not to exalt the Glory of God the Father? The Hebrews had never doubted that. The Apostle is not making a comparison of the Father and the Son with the Angels. Certainly, since the Apostle’s aim is to show that Christ has qualities that exalt him above the Angels, one must admit that he intends to apply the creation of the world to Christ.

To say that Paul is merely adapting himself to the nature of the Jews, and applying to Christ what they believed of the Messiah—even though it does not belong to him—is the most convenient blasphemy: for thus one would suggest that Paul gave the Jews the occasion for this blasphemy; and that he even committed it himself by saying that Christ created Heaven and Earth when he knew the contrary. God save us from such thoughts! Let us then recognize that Paul was fully convinced that Christ is God, that he created the world, and that he is eternal and unchangeable. It is said that Paul would contradict himself if he now said that Christ founded the earth and the Heaven, after he had said that God made the Ages through him. Answer: It is clear that both are true. God the Father created the world through his Son; and the Son also created the world. What gives rise to the error is that people view Christ as a middle-cause <note>A secondary or intermediate cause.</note> or instrument through which God made the world; whereas it is certain and sure that no instrument has a place in creation, as I have already noted.

I pass over other Psalms, which I shall speak of elsewhere.

THE CHRISTIAN

<margin>Prov. VIII. 22. 27. 30.</margin>

> *Prov. VIII. 22-27. and 30.* The Lord possessed me (in) the beginning of his way before his works, from of old. I have been anointed from eternity, from the beginning, from the ancient times of the earth. I was born when the depths were not yet there, when there were no fountains heavy with water. Before the mountains were settled: before the hills was I born. He had not yet made the earth, nor the fields, nor the beginning of the dust of the world. When he prepared the Heavens, I was there, etc. Then I was a nursling <note>original: "voesterling." This term refers to a foster child or a cherished ward, suggesting an intimate, eternal relationship between God and Wisdom.</note> with him, and I was daily (his) delight, playing before his face at all times.

It is clear that by this Wisdom one must understand God’s Son; since nothing is said of the same that is not also taught of *Christ*: just as one will be convinced of this if one reads what Solomon says of wisdom and what the Apostles and Evangelists testify of *Jesus Christ*. If it were only an attribute of God, introduced speaking [figuratively], it would not be necessary for her to describe her eternity to us: for one can doubt the Eternity of God's wisdom as little as the Eternity of God himself; he who was without wisdom would not deserve the name of God; or if it had been necessary for God's wisdom to describe its Eternity to us so cautiously, then one sees no reason why she calls herself his nursling, and rejoices so much that she has been his delight.

One will say that Solomon presents the virtue of Wisdom as a Person through a rhetorical personification <term>Redenkunstige verbeelding: a rhetorical device where an abstract quality is given human characteristics.</term> which presents things in a personal manner. Just as *Paul* makes a personification of love in *1. Cor. XIII.* Answer: 1. It is certain that one finds nothing similar elsewhere where a virtue tells its own history, as in this and in the IXth Chapter. 2. Such a personification can take place when neither the name of the speaker is introduced, nor the saying can correspond with the person; but everyone knows that the name of wisdom is given to *Jesus Christ*. *Luke VII. 35.* and *XI. 49.*

It is said that this Wisdom is presented to us as teaching men; whereas *Christ* did not teach them except in the last times. Answer:

<column-break/>

Although it is true that the Incarnate Wisdom has taught men in these last days, it does not follow from this that she did not do so before her Incarnation. *1. Pet. III. 18. 19.*

Now, if *Jesus Christ* is this Wisdom of which is spoken in the Book of Proverbs, then one cannot doubt his Eternity; for it is signified to us here by the same words with which God's Eternity is described. One need only compare this passage of Solomon with *Psalm XC. 2. 3. CIII. 17.* etc.

I then proceed to the revelations of the Prophet *Isaiah*, who gives us indisputable proofs of the Divinity of *Jesus Christ*.

<margin>*Isa. VI. 1 — 3.*</margin>
I begin with *Isa. VI. 1 — 3.* He says, in the year that King *Uzziah* died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted Throne, and his skirts filled the Temple. The Seraphim stood above him, each one had six wings, with two (each) covered his face, and with two he covered his feet, and with two he flew: and one cried to the other, and said; Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of Hosts; the whole earth is full of his Glory, etc.

<margin>*vs. 9. 10.*</margin>
He adds that the Lord said to him, *vs. 9. 10.* Go and say to this people, hearing hear, but understand not, and seeing see, but perceive not. Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest they see with their eyes, nor hear with their ears, etc.

If there is anywhere a place in scripture that speaks of God, of the *Jehovah* <note>The author uses "Jehovah" here to signify the unique, personal name of the God of Israel.</note>, it is without doubt this one. *John* therefore also applies it to *Christ*, saying in *John XII. 41.* These things said *Isaiah*, when he saw his Glory and spoke of him, that is of *Christ*, as appears from *vs. 37.* and *vs. 42.* He is then the great God whom the Angels worship.

One can bring nothing of any weight against this proof.

It is said that *Isaiah* saw the Glory of *Christ*, not that which he had, but that which he would have. But 1. it will always be true that *John* regards *Christ* as the *Jehovah* whom *Isaiah* had seen sitting on his Throne, and before whom the Seraphim cried out, Holy, Holy, etc. 2. It appears that *Isaiah* saw a present and not a future Glory.

It is argued that the pronoun "him" does not refer to *Jesus Christ*, but to God...

It is said that there is a manuscript in which it is written: "Isaiah saw the Glory of God." **Answer.** But one manuscript cannot outweigh all the others; moreover, since Christ is spoken of here, it would be a new proof that He is God.

It is said that the words of John refer to Isaiah 53, from which this first part that the Apostle quotes—"who has believed our preaching"—is taken.

But why would one want verse 41 to relate more to verse 38 than to verse 40? 1. Everyone knows that the context must always be taken from the words immediately preceding, unless there are great reasons against it. 2. One cannot say that Isaiah saw the Glory of Christ when he wrote the 53rd chapter of his prophecies. For he speaks there of almost nothing else but His humiliation; and one must want to be misled to look for this Glory, of which John speaks, anywhere else but in Isaiah 6, since he had quoted a passage from that very chapter in the verse immediately preceding.

It is said that Isaiah, seeing and describing the Glory of God, also saw and described the Glory of Christ, because the Glory of Christ is included in the Glory of God. But that is ridiculous: I could just as well say that Isaiah saw the glory of all creatures, since God's glory includes that of all creatures, without any exception.

It is said that He is called "the Mighty God," but that there is no <term>article</term> <note>original: "woordlid." An archaic Dutch term for a grammatical article (like "the"). ...beginning? I, the Lord, who am the first, and with the last, I am the same. No one doubts that the most high God is speaking here. Now Christ speaks of himself with these words in Revelation 1:17: *I am the first and the last;* he had said in verse 8 and verse 11: *I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last.* <margin>Isaiah 48:12</margin> Before Christ, this title of honor was given to no one but God; one must then conclude that Christ is truly God, since God testifies that he will not give his honor to any other. One must then necessarily confess that Jesus, who accepts this honor with the consent and authority of his Father, is one and the same God with him.

It is said—but without grounds—that Christ claims this honor for himself in a different sense. For, if that were true, one would have reason to be surprised that Christ did not warn us of it. If he is not God, how can he be the first and the last? And if he is merely a man, then he is not the first, neither in time nor in dignity.

It is said that Jesus Christ calls himself the first and the last in respect to his Church, to signify that he is the first and last of the Believers, the beginning and the end of the Christian Church.

But 1. Christ says, *I am the first and the last*; why limit these words? 2. In Isaiah, to be the first is to be before everything that has existence, and before time had begun to run. In a word, it is to be without beginning and from eternity. And to be the last is to exist after all that is shall have ceased to be. 3. Christ calls himself in this way to signify the power he has over all things, over Hell, over the Devils, and over the Universe <note>original: "’t Geheel-Al"</note>; to prepare his Disciple to believe the great things he would show him. Now, that Christ existed before the Christian Church was gathered by the ministry of the Apostles in no way proves that he has this power; but by saying that he is eternal, without beginning and without end, he clearly proves that he has a supreme power. 4. Everything said in this text about Christ, according to the sense we give to it, is also testified of him elsewhere.

<margin>Isaiah 45:22-23</margin> Isaiah 45:22-23 confirms this truth: *Turn to me, and be saved, all you ends of the Earth: for I am God and no one else; I have sworn by myself, a word of Righteousness has gone out of my mouth, and it shall not return; that to me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear (to me).* It is the great God who speaks; but let us hear Paul. Romans 14:10-11: *But you, why do you judge your Brother? or you, why do you despise your brother? for we shall all be placed before the Judgment Seat of Christ: for it is written, as I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess God.* It appears then, according to Paul, that it is Christ who speaks in Isaiah; or at least that he is the same God whom Isaiah introduces speaking thus, and the object of worship for all Creatures.

<margin>Isaiah 54:5</margin> In Isaiah 54:5, we find a new proof. Note what he says here to the Church: *Your Maker is your Husband; LORD of Hosts is his name, and the Holy One of Israel is your redeemer; he shall be called the God of the whole Earth.* God often calls himself the Bridegroom <note>original: "Bruidegom"</note> of the Church, a name that is absolutely incommunicable <note>meaning a title that God cannot share with a created being</note>. A Bridegroom cannot suffer a companion; God uses this name to obligate the Church to give him her heart undivided; he even attributes to himself the jealousy of a Bridegroom, and depicts the idolatry of Israel and Judah as unfaithfulness and Adultery.

When we now read the Books of the New Testament, we see that Christ is described as the only Bridegroom of the Church, and his union with her is described under the Symbol of a Marriage; we conclude then that Christ is the God of Israel, the Lord of Hosts, the only object of the highest love and worship of the Jewish and Christian Church, which are but one Church, and the same Bride of Christ.

It is said that this refers to the Church of the Old Testament, of which God the Father was the Bridegroom. **Answer.** 1. It speaks of that Church which the Prophet portrays as invisible, which refers to the Church of the New Testament. 2. ## VII. CHAPTER.

->Consequences of the proofs of the Divinity of Jesus Christ, from the Old Testament<-

Jeremiah is the first Prophet whom we shall consult after Isaiah. We shall bring forth only one passage from there.

<margin>Jer. XXIII. v. 6.</margin>
The same is found in Jeremiah 23:5, 6.
> Behold, the days come, says the Lord, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, who shall reign as King, and prosper, and execute judgment and justice in the Earth. In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell safely; and this shall be his name whereby he shall be called: The Lord our Righteousness. <note>original: "de Heere onze Geregtigheid." This refers to the Hebrew name "Yahweh Tsidqenu."</note>

It is clear that this Righteous Branch, who shall rule as King, is called Jehovah our Righteousness. Now this Righteous Branch can be no one other than Jesus Christ, who is the Jehovah our Righteousness—that is, the Jehovah who justifies us.

The Rabbis have also understood this passage as referring to the Messiah. One must wish to resist the truth not to agree with this.

*Socinus* <note>Faustus Socinus (1539–1604) was a theologian who argued against the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ.</note> says that this only means that, at the time of the Messiah’s coming, Jehovah shall become our righteousness, and that He will justify us. Answer: It appears clearly from the New Testament that it is the Messiah himself who is the Jehovah our Righteousness. See 1 Corinthians 1:30 and elsewhere, where his righteousness is frequently spoken of.

<margin>Hos. I. 7.</margin>
From Jeremiah I come to the Prophet Hosea. There God speaks thus, Hosea 1:7:
> I will have mercy upon the house of Judah, and will save them by the Lord their God.

This Chapter is without doubt Prophetic, and God promises there salvation through Christ His Son; therefore, it is very proper to say that Christ is here called Jehovah our God; since he is described to us everywhere as the one who redeems and saves his People.

<column-break/>

The Chaldean paraphraser <note>The "Chaldean paraphraser" refers to the Targums, ancient Aramaic translations of the Hebrew Bible that often used "The Word of the Lord" (Memra) as a title for God's manifestation.</note> has: *I will save them by the Word of the Lord.*

3. Everyone now knows that the Jews gave this name to the Messiah.

Compare this with Genesis 19:24 and Isaiah 10:27, where it is said that the yoke shall be taken away because of the Anointed One; see also Daniel 9:17.

The Prophet Zechariah gives us various proofs of this truth.

<margin>Zech. II. 10. 11.</margin>
Zechariah 2:10, 11:
> Shout and rejoice, O Daughter of Zion, for lo, I come, and I will dwell in the midst of you, says the Lord; and many nations shall be joined to the Lord in that day, and they shall be my people, and I will dwell in the midst of you, and you shall know that the Lord of Hosts has sent me to you.

The Lord who sends is clearly distinguished from the Lord who is sent. Who does not see now that the one sent is Jesus Christ? He is, then, the Lord.

One cannot say with Socinus that the one sent is an Angel, or the Prophet himself; for no created Angel nor Prophet can be called Jehovah.

> If it be good in your eyes, give me my price; and if not, forbear. So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said unto me, Cast them unto the potter: a magnificent price that I was valued at by them.

One sees here that the one who was valued at thirty silver pieces is Jehovah; but who does not know that this very thing happened to Jesus Christ? Matthew 26:15 and 27:9.

# THE CHRISTIAN <note>This header is likely part of the title "The Christian Religion" or a similar work.</note>

...beginning? I the Lord who am the first, and with the last I am the same. And Isaiah 44:6, so says the Lord, the King of Israel, and his redeemer, the Lord of Hosts, I am the first and I am the last, besides me there is no God.

<margin>Isaiah 48:12.</margin>
No one doubts that the Most High God speaks here. Now Christ speaks of himself with these words in Revelation 1:17, "I am the first and the last." He had said in verse 8 and verse 11, "I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last." <note>original: "d'Alpha en d'Omega". These are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, symbolizing eternity.</note> Before Christ, this title of honor was given to no one but God; one must then conclude that Christ is truly God, since God testifies that he will not give his honor to any other. One must then necessarily confess that Jesus, who accepts this honor with the consent and authority of his Father, is one and the same God with him.

It is said, but without basis, that Christ assumes this honor in another sense. For if that were true, there is reason to be surprised that Christ did not warn us of it. If he is not God, how can he be the first and the last? And if he is but a man, then he is not the first, neither in time nor in dignity.

It is said <note>This refers to the arguments of the Socinians, who denied the pre-existence of Christ.</note> that Jesus Christ calls himself the first and the last in respect to his Church, to make it known that he is the first and last of the believers, the beginning and the end of the Christian Church.

But 1. Christ says, "I am the first and the last"—why limit these words? 2. In Isaiah, to be the first is to exist before everything else had being, and before time had begun to run. In a word, it is to be without beginning and from eternity; and to be the last is to exist after all that is shall have ceased to be. 3. Christ calls himself this in order to make known the power he has over all things, over Hell, over the Devils, and over the Universe <note>original: "Geheel-Al"</note>; to prepare his disciple to believe the great things he would show him. Now, that Christ existed before the Christian Church was gathered by the ministry of the Apostles in no way proves that he has this power; but by saying that he is eternal, without beginning and without end, he clearly proves that he has a supreme power. 4. Everything said in this text of Christ, according to the sense we give to it, is also testified of him elsewhere.

<column-break/>

Isaiah 45:22-23 confirms this truth. "Turn to me, and be saved, all you ends of the Earth: for I am God and no one else; I have sworn by myself, a word of Righteousness has gone out of my mouth, and it shall not return; that to me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear (to me)." It is the great God who speaks; but let us hear Paul. Romans 14:10-11: "But you, why do you judge your brother? or also you, why do you despise your brother? for we shall all be set before the judgment seat of Christ: for it is written, 'As I live,' says the Lord, 'every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess God.'" It appears then, according to Paul, that it is Christ who speaks in Isaiah; or at least that he is the same God whom Isaiah introduces as speaking thus, and the object of worship for all creatures.

<margin>Isaiah 54:5.</margin>
In Isaiah 54:5 we find a new proof. Note what he says here to the Church: "Your Maker is your Husband; LORD of Hosts is his name, and the Holy One of Israel is your redeemer, he shall be called the God of the whole Earth." God often calls himself the Bridegroom of the Church, a name that is absolutely incommunicable. A Bridegroom can suffer no companion; God uses this name to obligate the Church to give him her heart undivided; he even attributes to himself the jealousy of a Bridegroom and depicts the idolatry of Israel and Judah as unfaithfulness and adultery.

When we now read the books of the New Testament, we see that Christ is described as the only Bridegroom of the Church, and his union with her is described under the symbol of a marriage; we then conclude that Christ is the God of Israel, the Lord of Hosts, the only object of the highest love and worship of the Jewish and Christian Church, which are but one Church and one and the same Bride of Christ.

It is said that the Church of the Old Testament is spoken of, of which God the Father was the Bridegroom. Answer 1: That Church is spoken of which the Prophet presents as a barren woman, which refers to the Church of the New Testament. 2. If the Church of the Old Testament had God the Father for her Bridegroom, and that of the New Testament had only a single man, as the Socinians <note>The Socinians were a sect that followed the teachings of Laelius and Faustus Socinus, denying the Trinity and the deity of Christ, viewing him as a remarkably gifted man rather than God.</note> would have it,

# VII. CHAPTER.
## Continuation of the proofs of the Divinity of Jesus Christ, from the O.T.

Jeremiah is the first Prophet we shall consult after Isaiah. We shall bring forth only one passage from him.

<margin>Jer. 23:5, 6.</margin> The same is found in Jeremiah 23:5, 6. *Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, that I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, who shall reign as King, and be prosperous, and execute judgment and righteousness on the Earth. In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell safely; and this shall be his name by which he shall be called, the Lord our Righteousness.* It is clear that this righteous Branch <note>The "Branch" (Dutch: "Spruite") is a traditional Messianic title referring to a descendant of King David.</note>, who shall Rule as King, is called Jehovah our Righteousness. Now this Righteous Branch can be no one other than Jesus Christ, who is the Jehovah our Righteousness, that is, the Jehovah who Justifies us.

The Rabbis have also understood this passage as referring to the Messiah. One must wish to resist the truth to not agree with this.

Socinus <note>Fausto Sozzini (1539–1604) was a theologian who argued that Jesus was a remarkable man but not divine. His followers were known as Socinians.</note> says that this only means that, at the time of the Messiah's coming, Jehovah will become our righteousness, and that he will justify us. Answer: It appears clearly from the N.T. that it is the Messiah himself who is the Jehovah our Righteousness. See 1 Corinthians 1:30 and elsewhere, where his righteousness is frequently spoken of.

From Jeremiah I come to the Prophet <margin>Hos. 1:7.</margin> Hoseas. There God speaks thus. Hosea 1:7. *I will have mercy on the House of Judah, and will save them by the Lord their God.* This Chapter is without doubt Prophetic, and God promises there the salvation through Christ his Son; therefore it is very proper to say that Christ is called here the Jehovah our God; since he is described to us everywhere as the one who saves and keeps his People.

<column-break/>

The Chaldean interpreter <note>This refers to the Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary of the Hebrew Bible.</note> has: *I will save them by the Word of the Lord.* Everyone knows now that the Jews gave the Messiah this name.

In Zechariah 12:10, the Lord speaks in this way: *But over the house of David and over the inhabitants of Jerusalem, I will pour out the Spirit of grace and of prayers, and they shall look upon me, whom they have pierced,* etc. John applies this to Christ in John 19:37 and Revelation 1:7.

<margin>Acts 9:4.</margin>
It might be argued that this passage should be interpreted in the same way as when Christ said, *Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?* <note>Acts 9:4; the objection suggests that "piercing" the Lord is merely a metaphor for persecuting his followers.</note> Answer: 1. It is certain that Saul persecuted Christ’s Name, Teachings, and Disciples. 2. In Zechariah, God does not say "they shall look upon me, whom they have persecuted," but "whom they have **pierced**," which indicates the specific crime they committed. It has never been said that Christ was beheaded or pierced simply because his members or Disciples were.

It might be said that there was only one who pierced Christ, and that the text here speaks of many. Answer: If one person did the deed, there were many who consented to it.

We end our proofs of the Divinity of Jesus Christ from the O.T. <note>O.T.: Old Testament</note> with Malachi, the last of the Prophets.
<margin>Mal. 3:1.</margin>
In Malachi 3:1, one reads these words: *Behold, I send my Messenger, who shall prepare the way before my face, and the Lord, whom you seek, shall suddenly come to his Temple; even the Messenger of the Covenant, in whom you delight, behold, he comes, says the Lord of Hosts.*

It is certain that the one for whom John the Baptist came to prepare the way is Jesus Christ, according to the Evangelists. Meanwhile, it is the Lord of Hosts here who says, *Behold, I send my Messenger.* Consequently, Jesus Christ is the Lord of Hosts.

Even if this proof does not seem convincing to some, and even if one made more excuses, one cannot deny that the Messiah—that is, the Christ—is at the very least meant by these words: *The Lord, whom you seek, shall come into his Temple, and the Messenger of the Covenant, whom you seek.* For God alone is the Lord of the Church, who can call the Temple of Jerusalem **his** Temple.

Let us now examine the passages of the N.T. <note>N.T.: New Testament</note>

After having searched the principal passages of the O.T. that prove the Divinity of Jesus Christ, I proceed to those of the N.T. and begin with John—not because there are no proofs of this same truth in the other Evangelists, but because there are not as many, and because I will bring many of those up in connection with these.

<margin>verse 3.</margin>

John says: *Without the same was not any thing made that was made.* These Heretics said that the Son of the highest God was sent into the world (of which they believed he was not the Creator) to rescue men from the service of the Creator of the world.
<margin>verses 10, 11.</margin>

...to prove. But let us enter into a particular investigation, and in order to draw all the consequences that flow from these words, let us first see what John understands by *the Word*. One must not translate it as **Reason**, as if John had only wanted to teach that **reason** was in the beginning and that God made nothing without reason and wisdom: for this was not a truth that people needed to be taught; no one has ever believed that God was without reason. One might say that this means that God had the will from the beginning to make everything with counsel and wisdom, that it is through this will that everything was created, and that nothing was brought forth except what comes from this will; but what appearance of truth does such an explanation have? Would John have expressed himself in the way he did if he intended to say, *In the beginning was Reason, and reason was with God, and Reason was God*? Would he have added to that, that **Reason became flesh**? Certainly, it is clear that our Lord **Jesus Christ** is this **Word**. John teaches us this himself in Revelation 19:13, where he says that his Name is **THE WORD OF GOD**. If one asks why he gives him this Name, opinions on the matter are divided. The Church Fathers gave many reasons for this, and modern writers also bring forth several.

<margin>Gregory of Nazianzus, oration 36. Basil on the beginning of John. Chrysostom, Homily 116. Theodoret, *Compendium of Divine Dogmas*. Theophylact on John ch. 1. Dionysius the Areopagite, ch. 6 *concerning the Divine Names*. Isidore of Pelusium, etc.</margin>
Some are of the opinion that it is an allusion to the **Chaldean paraphrase** <note>original: "Chaldeeuwsche uitbreiding"; refers to the Targums, Aramaic translations/interpretations of the Hebrew Bible used in synagogues.</note> and to the custom of the Hebrews, who, instead of the Name of God, often put **the word of God**, as in Genesis 6:3, 6, 7; 8:1; 9:12, 13, 15, 16; 19:24; 21:20, 22; Deuteronomy 20:1; Numbers 11:22; Exodus 16:8; Deuteronomy 18:19; Psalm 110:1. Instead of what stands in the Hebrew, *the Lord says to my Lord*, the paraphrase has, *the Lord says to his Word, sit at my right hand*, etc. Instead of what stands in the original language in Genesis 3:8, *they heard the voice of the Lord*, the paraphrase has *the voice of the Word of the Lord God walking in the Garden*. The author of the **Book of Wisdom**, which is attributed to **Philo**, uses the same expression in chapter 18:15; he also uses it figuratively in the *Book on Agriculture*, p. 195 of the Paris edition, as also in the *Book on the Confusion of Tongues* p. 341, and elsewhere. He says that **the Word**, the **first-born Son of God**, was appointed by God

<margin>Fagius, Haekspan, Buxtorf.</margin>

<column-break/>

over the government of the world. This opinion is not without ground; but it is nevertheless not entirely sufficient.

<margin>Tertullian, *Apology* ch. 21. Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* book 11. Seneca, Epistle 16. Diogenes Laërtius, book 7, 65. Benoit on the Gospel of John ch. 1.</margin>
Others say that John expressed himself thus to set **the Word**, which was in the beginning, against the "Word" <note>The Greek term *Logos* translates to both "Word" and "Reason," a concept central to Greek philosophy.</note> of which the Pagan writers so often speak, and in particular **Plato**; but it has no appearance of truth that John thought of Plato and the Pagan philosophers, much less that he borrowed this expression from them. How did a fisherman from Bethsaida come to know what Plato had said!

Others look for similarities between Christ and "the Word," of which most are more ingenious than well-founded. There are those who understand **God's Power** by "the Word"; but that is ridiculous: who doubts whether God's Power was in the beginning, and how can one say of the same that it **became Flesh**?

I confess that I am of the opinion that John borrowed this way of speaking neither from **Zoroaster**, nor from **Pythagoras**, nor from **Plato**, nor from the Chaldean paraphrase, nor from the **Kabbalistic writers**, but that it was inspired in him by the **Holy Spirit**, who wished thereby to unfold to us a secret that we would never have discovered; namely, that Jesus Christ is that **Word** through which God created the world. **Moses** had said that everything was brought forth by a Word: *God said, let there be light, and there was light*, etc., etc. We would have forever believed that this only meant that everything was made by God's simple command, or by a single act of his will. But John opens the secret to us, saying, *In the beginning was the Word*, etc. and through the same all things were created. That Word is Christ, for it is of him that the scripture testifies that everything was made by him, and there is also no one but he who **became Flesh**. Add to this that John intended thereby to explain to us who one must understand by "Wisdom" in Proverbs 8.

# THE CHRISTIAN [THEOLOGY] #

Ee 4
<meta>catchword: Evan-</meta>

...in all probability, that John described Christ’s Office <note>original: *Ampt*; referring to his role or mediatorial function</note> before his person and birth. 3. If the Name of (*the Word*) signified the same as that of Prophet, then John would speak of it as a Name that no one knows but Christ himself (Revelation 19:13). If Christ is called the Word because he has made the will of our Heavenly Father known to us, then the Prophets and the Apostles could bear the same name.

Having considered what one must understand by "the Word," let us investigate what John testifies concerning it. He sets down five things that one must well observe.
1. That the Word was in the beginning.
2. That it was in the beginning with God.
3. That it was God.
4. That all things were made through the same; that without the same nothing was made; and that the world was made through the same.
5. That the Word became Flesh.

Each part deserves our observation, in order to extract from them the proofs of Christ’s Divinity.

1. John says first, that the Word was in the beginning, that is, in the beginning of the world, upon which John visibly has his eye. *In the beginning God created Heaven and earth.* (Genesis 1:1).

By this, one cannot understand the "beginning of the Gospel"; there is no reason for such an interpretation.

To begin the Gospel of John thus—*In the beginning of the Gospel of Christ was Christ*—is as ridiculous as if one, describing the history of Moses, said: *in the beginning of the Deliverance of the Children of Israel out of Egypt by Moses, was Moses.* Elsewhere, the word "beginning" signifies the beginning of the world. (Matthew 19:4): *He which made them at the beginning made them male and female.* (John 8:44): *The devil was a murderer from the beginning.* (Hebrews 1:10): *Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast laid the foundation of the earth.* If one understands by the "beginning of the Gospel" the first good news regarding the coming of the Messiah, then Christ did not yet exist, according to the opinion of those who believe that he had no existence until Mary brought him into the world <note>Referring to Socinianism or other non-Trinitarian views that deny Christ's pre-existence</note>. If one understands by the "beginning of the Gospel" the time of Christ’s birth, one makes a person say an absurd thing: *in the beginning of the time of the birth of Christ, was Christ.* If one understands by it the time of the

<column-break/>

birth of John the Baptist, one likewise makes the Evangelist put forward a ridiculous thing: for who doubts whether Christ existed when John Baptized, seeing as they were contemporaries.

It is said that the aim of the Holy Spirit is to respond to a thought that might arise concerning John the Baptist, who came before Christ, as if John were the Messiah and should be placed above Christ. For 1. if John should be placed above Christ for that reason, one must for the same reason place the Prophets, who lived before his time, above him. 2. When John wrote his Gospel, there was no fear that one would place John the Baptist above Christ, because John the Baptist was dead, and Christ had performed many things that highly distinguished him from John the Baptist. 3. Assuming that someone had been so simple-minded as to place John the Baptist above Christ because John came before him, the Evangelist does not satisfy the objection; for he then would only have had to say that John, being the Forerunner of the Messiah, had to appear before him, instead of making him say that Christ was in the beginning of the Preaching of John the Baptist. 4. The following verses are a clear proof that the "beginning of the world" is spoken of here, for it is said therein that all things were made by the Word. 5. There is not the least appearance that by "in the beginning" the start of John’s Preaching must be understood, since the Evangelist mentions nothing of John the Baptist until after he had finished the Eulogy <note>original: *Lofreden*; referring to the poetic Prologue of John 1:1-18</note> of the Word.

From this it follows, then, that Christ was in the beginning of the world, and consequently before all created things, which demonstrates his eternity; for the scripture uses this manner of speaking to express eternity.

One asks, why does John not say "in the beginning of the world," if this is his meaning? I answer with a question: why does the Evangelist not say "in the beginning of the Gospel," if that is his thought? 2. I answer that it was not necessary to express himself more clearly, because it is the natural meaning of the words, and the sequence sufficiently shows in what sense one must take them.

It is said that the creation of the world was not the point. I answer that this is indeed the subject of John...

# THEOLOGY. III. B. VIII. Chapter. 231 #

<margin>Socinus</margin> <note>Followers of Socinianism, a movement that denied the pre-existence and essential divinity of Christ, viewing him as a man who was granted divine status after his resurrection.</note> Gospel is / but that he answers a question / that one might ask / and which one naturally does / if it is true / that the Word / that became Flesh / whose history the Apostle intended to describe / did not exist in essence / when it took on the human form. To this, John answers / that it already existed from the beginning / and that the world was made through the same.

II. John testifies / that the Word was with God. This means:
1. That the Word is a Person / distinct from the Father.
2. That the Son exists with the Father.
3. That he is closely united with the Father.

Those who explain these words as if John intended to say that Christ was known to God alone, distort them; one would then have to say that when our Apostle, in his first Letter (1 John 1:2), testifies that the life was with the Father, these words mean nothing other than that the life was known to God the Father alone. For the same reason, one could say that eternal death, the Antichrist, etc., are with God, because God knows them. In short / it is not true that the Lord Jesus was known only by God when John the Baptist began his ministry / as those who give this meaning to the aforementioned words understand it: for he was known by the Angels / by Joseph, by Zacharias, Elizabeth, Simeon, etc. etc.

III. John adds / that the Word was God. In this way, he answers three questions in one verse. One asks: when did the Word exist? In the beginning. With whom? With God. And who was it? It was God. And in that way, he teaches us that Christ had a Divine nature / before he took on the human one.

<margin>Smalcius</margin> <note>Valentin Smalcius (1572–1622), a prominent Socinian theologian who argued that Christ was "God" only in name due to his authority.</note> One says, that the name of God is not a name / that signifies a nature / but that it is a title of office <note>original: *ampt-naam*; a name referring to a position of authority rather than essence</note> / just as the Rulers are called Gods. (Psalm 82:6).
1. We have already shown elsewhere / that it is false that the idea / that one naturally forms of the word "God" / is an idea of Office or ministry / and that there is no one / who does not understand an Supreme Being by it / a first and independent being; we have also shown / in what sense the Rulers are called Gods. 2. If the word "God" only signified the Office of Christ / the Apostle would have said / that

<column-break/>

the word *became* God, just as he says later / that it became Flesh: but he testifies / that it *was* God.

One says, that Christ is called God / because his ministry was Divine. But for the same reason / Paul, Peter, and the other Apostles could be called God; they revealed life and immortality to us / performed miracles / their ministry was Divine. Meanwhile, one reads nowhere / that the name of God was given to any of them. One will perhaps say, that the Apostles were only Servants / and therefore should not be called Gods: But assuming / that Christ is not God / then one also assumes / that he is a Servant / with respect to God / and indeed in many respects; he then should not be called God / according to the opinion of those who object to this.

**Objection.** He is called God / because through his exaltation he received a Supreme Authority / and was ordained to it from his birth / and in that manner he became a God through his exaltation. But who has ever heard of a *created* God! Is it to be believed / that John and the Apostles would have wanted to deceive people / by taking the word God in a sense / that is so far removed from the thoughts / that it properly and naturally awakens in us?

**Objection.** Christ is called God / because he represented God / and was his ambassador; But who has ever heard / that one gives the name of God itself to such a servant / as one supposes Christ to be. God testifies (Isaiah 42:8 and 48:11): *I am the Jehovah <note>original: Jehova</note>, that is my name, my glory I will give to no other:* Is it not giving his glory to another / to permit / that one's Servant be called by one's own name?

**Objection.** Jesus Christ is God, because he was conceived by the Holy Spirit / and was taught by God: But who does not see / that it is absurd / to call a man / who was conceived in the womb of the Virgin / and who had need of someone to teach him / God? Let us then conclude / that he is called God / because he truly is so.

**Objection.** The word *of* God / is not God himself. **Answer.** He who is the Word / is not the same Person / whom he is the Word of / but he has the same essence.

**Objection.** The word is *with* God; but is not God. **Answer.**
