# THE CHRISTIAN <note>The header "DE CHRISTELYKE" likely refers to "The Christian Theology" or "The Christian Religion," continuing from the previous page.</note> #

*Answer:* The Father and the Son are one. John 10:30 and 1 John 5:7.

*Objection:* He who is not the God of all beings is no God; the Son is not the God of the Father. And so forth. *Answer:* It is enough to be the God of all creatures to truly be God.

<margin>John 1:3</margin>
IV. John continues, saying that *through the Word all things were made.* This repeats the words of Moses <note>Referring to the creation account in Genesis.</note> and at the same time demonstrates the divinity of Christ; for God alone can make all things.

*Objection:* Jesus Christ was merely the instrument <term>instrument|an agent or tool used by a higher power to accomplish a task</term> in this; that is what the word *through* <note>original Greek: *dia*</note> signifies: all things were created through Christ. 1. In the act of Creation, no instrument has a place. We shall prove this in the discourse on Creation. 2. *Through* <note>original Greek: *dia*</note> does not always denote an instrument, but sometimes signifies the principal and first cause. Compare John 5:17, Acts 3:16, Romans 1:5 and 5:2, Galatians 1:1, Hebrews 9:14, 2 Corinthians 1:1, Ephesians 1:1, Colossians 1:1. Scripture uses this word even in reference to the Father. 1 Corinthians 1:9, Hebrews 2:10.

*Objection:* This passage only speaks of things concerning the Gospel <note>The Socinian argument was that John 1:3 referred to the "new creation" of the church, not the physical universe.</note>. But it is ridiculous to try to limit such a universal statement as John’s, especially since Scripture attributes the Creation of all things to Christ, as we have already proven and shall prove again. John confirms this by adding: *the world was made through the Word.* For one cannot say that this refers to a "new world"; if John had intended to speak of a new Creation, he would never have expressed himself in this manner.

V. Finally, he says: *the Word became Flesh.* This shows that there was a time in which this Word was not flesh, and consequently, that He existed before He took on our human nature.

<margin>1 Corinthians 15:45</margin>
It is argued that Paul teaches us that *Adam became a living soul,* but it does not follow that he existed before he had this living soul. It is further added that each of us has "become flesh." I answer: 1. Our proof does not rely solely on the word *become*, but on everything that precedes it. 2. In the proposition *Adam became,* Adam is considered in respect to his body, which was indeed made before it was animated <note>given a soul</note>. 3. Finally, it has been 

<column-break/>

said that every human has become flesh.

*Objection:* One should translate this as: *the Word was flesh.* 1. Because the Greek allows for this. 2. Because it would otherwise seem absurd that John would say the Word became flesh after he had already spoken of John the Baptist and the testimony he gave of Christ. 3. Because one thing cannot become another thing without the one being changed into the other. Now, the Word was not changed into flesh.

*Answer:* It is clear from the phrasing of verse 1 and verse 14 that one cannot translate it as *the Word was flesh.* John would have expressed himself in verse 14 the same way he did in the first. 2. There is no absurdity in our view. John explains immediately when and where the Word existed: what it was and what it became. Having said that the Word was the light of the world, he anticipates an objection; one might ask, "where does it come from that men did not know this light?" He answers: men, being in darkness, could not comprehend this light; and therefore God sent John the Baptist to bear witness to this light, and He sent the Light itself, which came to His own. Subsequently, he shows how it came: *the Word became Flesh.* Regarding the opinion of the Socinians <note>A group that denied the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ.</note>, that is entirely absurd: for they want John to speak of the Office of Christ before he mentions His birth. 3. Finally, it is false to say the Word could not have become flesh without being changed into flesh; He became such when He took on our human nature. We shall speak of this in another place.

Let us follow the Apostle and move on to other chapters of his Gospel.

Chapter 3:13. Christ reasons against Nicodemus in this way: *No one has ascended into Heaven, but He who came down from Heaven, (namely) the Son of Man, who is in Heaven.* We shall have the opportunity to explain these words regarding the Ascension of Christ; for now, we draw two proofs from them. One, to show that Christ did not begin to exist when He took on our human nature

...[them]. 2. To show that he is God, since he is in many places at the same time: for omnipresence <term>omnipresence|the state of being present everywhere at once</term> is an attribute of the Deity.

The 1st proof is taken from what Christ says, that he has descended from Heaven. By this, the Scripture signifies his revelation in the Flesh, and his coming into the World. Consequently, he was in Heaven before he came to Earth. He even says this to his Disciples. John 6:62. *(What then)* if *(you)* should see the Son of Man ascend where he was before? and John 16:28. I came forth from the Father, and have come into the world; again, I leave the world, and go to the Father.

<margin>John 3:31.</margin>
John the Baptist, setting himself or other Prophets against the Lord (Jesus), says: *he who is of the Earth is of the Earth; he who comes from Heaven is above all.* But just as one, saying of someone that he has come from the Earth, intends to convey that the Earth, and not Heaven, is the place where he began to be; even so, by saying that the Son of God has come from Heaven, it is clearly signified that Heaven, and not the Earth, is the place where Christ first was.

It is said <note>This refers to the Socinian argument, a group that denied the Trinity and believed Christ was only a man who was granted divine status.</note> that Christ, some years after his Birth but before the start of his Preaching, had ascended to Heaven; and that he afterwards returned and descended to Earth. But this imagined Ascension is a fantasy, as we shall prove elsewhere.

It is said: Christ is described to us as having descended from Heaven because he was given to us through a special Grace of the Father. But it has never been said of a Person that he descended from Heaven to signify that he was given through a special Grace of God. That can be said of qualities, but not of Persons. John the Baptist was an extraordinary gift of God’s bounty; meanwhile, it is nowhere said that he had descended from Heaven. He says that he has come from the Earth, and that he is of the Earth.

The 2nd proof is taken from the fact that the Son of Man was in Heaven at the same time as he spoke on Earth. For there is no Creature that is not so limited to the place where it is that it is impossible, being there, to be elsewhere. To explain these words as referring to the

Part I.

<column-break/>

knowledge that Christ had received of the secrets of Heaven is to abandon the manner of speaking used in the Scripture. Such a way of speaking has never signified that. Since, then, the Son of Man was in Heaven and on Earth at the same time, one must confess that he is God, and has an infinite being, and consequently is eternal. Add to this Matthew 18:20. *For where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.* And chapter 28:20. *I am with you always, even unto the end of the world.*

The fifth Chapter of John <note>original: "Joh. V."</note> is full of arguments for the Divinity of Christ. The Evangelist relates that the Jews, as soon as Jesus had said, *My Father works until now, and I work (also)* (verse 17), sought to kill him; because he had said that God was his own Father, making himself equal to God (verse 18). If Christ had not been equal to his Father, he would not have failed to better instruct the Jews; but he strengthens them in these thoughts, and answers (verse 19): *Whatever the Father does, that the Son does also.* And verses 21-23: *Just as the Father raises the Dead and makes them alive, so also the Son makes alive whom he will. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.* He continues in verse 26 by saying: *Just as the Father has life in himself, so he has also given to the Son to have Life in himself.*

One only needs to bring forward these words to draw from them the powerful proofs for the Divinity of Christ. If Christ were not equal to his Father, would he say that he does all that the Father does? Would he claim for himself the power to raise the Dead, which requires an infinite power? Would he wish to be honored just like his Father, and boast of having life in himself?

The 8th Chapter teaches us that Christ existed before Abraham: which clearly proves that he was before he was conceived in the womb of Mary.

# THE CHRISTIAN <note>Likely "The Christian Theology"</note>

words: *Before Abraham was, I am.* One cannot say anything more clearly or decisively.

It is said <note>This refers to the arguments of the Socinians, a group that denied the Trinity and argued Jesus did not exist before His birth.</note> that the words must be translated: *Before Abraham becomes, I am.* And that it means: before Abraham becomes the Father of the faithful, and before the Heathens are converted to God. This translation is defended because it says Christ said, "Truly I say to you," and not "I have said"; and because He adds "I am," and not "I have been." But can one bring forth anything more ridiculous? 1. Who can get it into their head that these words—*before Abraham was*—mean: before Abraham became Abraham, that is, before Abraham became the Father of the Faithful? When one says "before the Emperor was Caesar," no one will understand it to mean "before Caesar became Emperor"; but all the world sees that it must be understood as if it were written: "before the Emperor Caesar was in existence," or "before he was in the world." 2. Was it such a great wonder to say that Christ was before the Heathens had become Abraham's children? Since one could say the same of the least person then living, even of Judas and Pilate. Was it worth the effort for Christ to say because of that: *Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am*? 3. As for the rules of grammar brought forward—according to which they claim that because Christ says "I say," "I am," and not "I said," "I have been," one must translate it "before Abraham becomes"—it is a ridiculous observation. In the beginning of Psalm 90, one finds in the Greek translation of the Septuagint <note>original: "LXX"</note> a similar way of speaking, which is taken without contradiction in the same sense as that of Christ. The Prophet addresses God and says: *You are before the Mountains were*. According to the critics who make this objection to us, one would have to translate it: *You are before the mountains become*. But what nonsense would that be?

It is said: Christ was in God’s decree <note>meaning God's plan or foreknowledge</note> before Abraham was; but this excuse is no better than the first. For can one not say of all men who lived after Abraham that they were before him in God’s decree? Would Christ have answered the objection of the Jews with that? They said: *You are not yet fifty years old, and you say that you have seen Abraham?* Was it giving a fitting answer to tell them that He was in the decree of God before Abraham had appeared in the world?

It is said these words must be ex-

<column-break/>

plained like those of Revelation 13:8, where it is said that the Lamb was slain from the foundation of the world. But, besides the fact that many theologians believe these words must be interpreted thus:

> All who dwell on the earth shall worship the image, whose names, from the foundation of the world, are not written in the Book of Life of the slain Lamb.

Even following the common translation, one can give a very good meaning to these words by distinguishing a twofold sacrifice of Christ. One in the Spirit; for He offered Himself to God His Father throughout all the ages, and it is by virtue of this offering that the Father took pleasure in the prayers and sacrifices of the Old Testament. Another in the body, accomplished in the fullness of time. John speaks of the first, following the common translation. But it is impossible to give the same meaning to the words of Christ; since the Savior would not have answered the objection of the Jews. It appears then that Christ existed many centuries before His incarnation. We shall prove by other passages that He has existed from eternity.

<margin>John 10:30</margin>
I pass over to the tenth chapter, verse 30, where Christ says to the Jews: *I and the Father are one.* Nothing more powerful can be said to prove the perfect equality of the Father and the Son.

<margin>vs. 27--30</margin>
To be convinced of this, one need only read that passage and the preceding, verses 27--30.
> My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me: And I give them eternal life; they shall never perish for all eternity, and no one shall snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who gave them to me, is greater than all, and no one can snatch them out of my Father's hand. I and the Father are one.

One cannot apply these words to the unity of consent alone. For Christ reasons thus to prove that no one shall snatch His sheep out of His hand: because He is one with His Father, whose power is so great that no one can snatch them out of His hands. He wants then to show that His power is not less than that of His Father, because He has the same essence <term>essence: the fundamental nature or substance of a thing; here, the divine nature shared by the Trinity</term>.

The Jews understood it thus also: for they wanted to stone Him because He made Himself God.

### DIVINITY. BOOK III. PART B. CHAPTER VIII. 235

It will be said that Christ elsewhere admonishes us to be one with him, just as he is one with his Father; that just as we are one with Christ through unity of agreement and harmony, and in no way through a unity of existence and essence, so we must conclude that Christ is one with his Father through a unity of agreement and not of existence.

I answer. It is evident from the Text itself that the Father and Son are one through unity of power, and consequently of essence; and that this unity is presented to us as an example only of the likeness of the fellowship that we must have with him. Christ is so one with his Father that he says, *he who sees the Son, sees the Father*; which cannot be said of any creature; and it is clear enough that the union of believers with God is not an essential union <note>original: "wezendlyke vereeniging"; a union of the same substance or nature</note>, since Christ requests the same from his Father for them.

**Objection.** 1. Cor. III. 8. *He who plants, and he who waters, are one.* But Paul only intends to say that the one and the other are nothing at all. As he had already said previously.

<margin>John XI. 25. 26.</margin>
In John XI, 25 26, Christ says to Martha, *I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me shall live, even though he has died; and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die.* God alone can be called the resurrection and the life.

<margin>John XIV. 1.</margin>
In the XIV Chapter, verse 1, the Savior desires that his Disciples believe in him; *you believe in God, believe also in me.* If he were merely a creature, would he admonish his Apostles to place their trust in him, since Jeremiah curses those who trust in a man? <note>Referring to Jeremiah 17:5.</note> It is true that in Exod. XIV. 30. 31. it is said the people believed in <term>Jehovah</term> <note>The personal name of God in the Hebrew Bible</note> and in Moses. But it is clear that this means nothing other than that the people believed what God commanded them through the mouth of Moses his servant. It is also true that Jehoshaphat admonished the people to believe in Jehovah and his Prophets. 2 Chron. XX. 20. But to believe the Prophets only means to believe that they speak on God's behalf; but *to believe in Christ* includes that same perfect trust which we place in God. Ps. II. 12.

<margin>John XVII. 5.</margin>
In the High Priestly prayer of Christ, John XVII. 5, he speaks thus: *Glorify me now, O Father, with yourself, with the Glory which I had with you before the world was.* By this it is evident that

<column-break/>

Christ was before the creation of the world, and consequently from eternity: for one cannot say of a person that he had something in a time in which he did not yet exist.

<margin>Schlichtingius against Meisner p. 465.</margin> <note>Jonas Schlichting was a Polish Socinian theologian who argued against the Trinity; Balthasar Meisner was a Lutheran theologian.</note>
**Objection.** God’s Son had a certain Glory in God’s decree <note>In God's pre-determined plan or thought</note> before the creation of the world. **Answer.** One cannot say that Christ had glory before the Foundation of the Ages if one merely intends to indicate that it was ordained for him.

<margin>2. Corint. V. 1.</margin>
**Objection.** It is said there that the believers have an eternal house in the Heavens. That is true, but it is not said there that they have had this before the world and they themselves existed: since it is then said that Christ had this Glory before the creation of the world, one must necessarily conclude that he had his existence before the world was brought forth out of nothing.

<margin>2. Tim. I. 9.</margin>
**Objection.** Grace was given to us in Jesus Christ before the times of the Ages. 2. Tim. I. 9.

**Answer.** There is a great distinction between these two things. One can give to those who do not yet exist; for example, a Father gives by Will to his descendants who are not yet in being; but one cannot say that a person who is not yet, *has* something. If Christ had possessed the Glory only in God’s decree, then there is no true believer who could not also pray that God glorify him with the Glory which He has assigned to him.

The <term>Ethiopian translation</term> <note>The Ge'ez version of the Bible, often cited by scholars of this era to compare linguistic nuances.</note> has: *God has given us the grace in Jesus Christ, who was before the world.*

It will perhaps be said that Christ could not have lost the Glory which he had before the creation of the world, since it was essential to him; and therefore had no need to pray his Father to give it to him. **Answer.** Christ never lost this Glory: but, since it had been obscured, and God had treated his Son as a servant, he prays that his Father treat him in such a manner that corresponds with the Glory which he had had with Him, to be recognized as His well-beloved Son.

It will be said that this Glory consists in the power over all flesh, which was not given to him until after the resurrection.

**Answer.** 1. This Glory is not spoken of here; Christ speaks of a Glori-

### CHRISTIAN THEOLOGY. PAGE 236

...glory that he possessed. 2. One must distinguish the essential glory from the dispensational <note>original: "huishoudelyke," referring to the 'economy' or management of the plan of salvation</note> glory, which concerns the mediatorial office. The first he possessed before the creation of the world; the second in time.

<margin>John 20:28.</margin>
I proceed to the 20th Chapter, and to the answer that Thomas gave when he was convinced of the truth of Christ’s resurrection, verse 28: **My Lord, and my God.** He calls him not only his Lord, to show that he recognized him as the true Christ, the Lord and King of the Church; but he calls him his God. Christ approves this confession, from which one must conclude that he intends and understands that we should regard him as our God.

Those who oppose the divinity of Christ admit that the word *God*, when accompanied by the definite article <note>original: "het vingerwys (de)," referring to the Greek article *ho*</note>, as when one says "the God," always signifies the true God, Jehovah, in the Scripture. Now, in this passage, it is given to Christ along with a pronoun.

<margin>
Servetus, book 1 on the Errors of the Trinity.
Socinus, Epistle to Francis David.
Volkelius, book 5 on Religion, chapter 10, page 413.
</margin>
Some say that Thomas speaks here to God the Father, and not to the Son; but the contrary is evident from the text. For John clearly notes that Thomas said *to him*, that is, to Christ: **My Lord, and my God.** Many enemies of Christ’s divinity acknowledge this, such as Servetus, Theophilus Nicolaïdes, and even Socinus <note>Michael Servetus and Faustus Socinus were famous historical figures who challenged traditional views on the Trinity</note>; it is said that Thomas does not say absolutely "O God," but "my God," which is the excuse of Volkelius. I answer: Thomas here says the same thing to Christ that Christ had said to his Father, "My God, my God," and David in Psalm 22:2.

It is said: Thomas acknowledges that Christ was God through the resurrection, but that the true God cannot rise. I answer that indeed the true God cannot rise, since he is immortal; but that Thomas could know that Christ was the true God because he saw him risen from the grave, since his resurrection was a clear proof that he was the Christ who was to rise; and that he was God, because it was not probable that God would have raised him if he had been a deceiver who called himself God although he was not. Likewise, Paul says in Romans 1:3–4: *Concerning his Son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, and powerfully declared to be the Son of God according to the spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead, namely Jesus Christ our Lord.*

<column-break/>

One would almost have to transcribe the entire Gospel of John if one wished to collect everything therein that can prove the divinity of Christ; I will bring forward only one more passage from the last chapter, verse 17. There, Christ having asked Peter if he loved him, the Apostle answers: **Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you.** 
<margin>John 21:17.</margin>
Of whom can it be said but of God that he knows all things? One cannot say that Peter answers this of his own accord: for what he says is either a truth or a lie; if a truth, then Christ knows all things and he is God: if a lie, then it is a wonder that Christ does not rebuke him, since he had treated him so sharply when he had wanted to prevent him from dying <note>The author refers to Christ’s earlier stern rebuke of Peter—"Get behind me, Satan"—as evidence that Christ would not let a false statement pass uncorrected</note>.

Argument VIII.</margin>In Romans 9:5 he says: *of whom* (namely the Jews) *Christ is, as far as the flesh is concerned, who is God, to be praised above all for eternity.* One cannot speak more clearly or expressly.
It cannot be said that this passage is falsified, for all Greek manuscripts read it this way, as Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus, the famous Renaissance humanist and editor of the Greek New Testament</note> remarks.
It is not a turn of phrase directed toward God the Father: for God the Father is not spoken of there, and the relative word *who* can be applied to no other than to Christ, who immediately precedes it.
Thus also the Arabic, Ethiopian, and Syrian translators have understood it.

...he had to maintain either that Christ was God, or that he should not worship him. Therefore, he says that we *can* certainly worship him, but that we are not *obligated* to do so; and in this, he has been followed by many of his adherents.

**Answer:** Nothing more absurd could be said. For, first: either the Scripture commands us to worship Christ, or it does not. If it commands it, then we must worship him; if it does not command it, then we cannot worship him without committing a crime. This is exactly what Niemojewski <note>Original: "Nomojerius," likely referring to Jan Niemojewski (1526–1598), a Polish theologian and prominent figure in the Socinian movement</note> proposed in his first letter to Socinus in the year 1587. Secondly: although Franken <note>Christian Franken, a theologian who eventually argued that if Christ was not God, worshipping him was idolatry</note> denied the divinity of Christ along with Socinus, he could not tolerate Socinus worshipping him. In a conversation he had with him in the year 1584, he confronted him with the fact that there is such a vast difference between the Creator and the creature that one cannot give to Christ, a creature, what belongs only to the Creator. He added that to worship, serve, or invoke those who are not by nature God is idolatry, citing Galatians 4:8. "Now you believe," he said, "that Christ is not God, so you are an idolater." He also countered him with Matthew 4:10, Jeremiah 17:5, and Revelation 19:10.

<margin>
2 Corinthians 8:9.
</margin>
In 2 Corinthians 8:9, the Apostle says: *For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you through his poverty might become rich.* From this, it appears that Christ existed before he was conceived in the womb of Mary. For the Apostle says that he was rich at the time he made himself poor. Since Christ was poor from the very beginning of the life he led on earth, one must suppose that he had another life before the one he spent in poverty. If Christ had been only a man, it would be true that he, being poor, became rich, since we now see him—after the extreme poverty in which he lived and died—crowned with honor and glory and exalted even to the throne of God. But one could not say that he, being rich, became poor. Since Paul says this, one must conclude that Christ existed before his conception and had another existence before Mary, even before the world—that is, from all eternity.

It is said <note>referring to Socinian arguments</note> that the word the Apostle uses does not mean "to become poor" or "to be made poor," but to live as a poor person, 

<column-break/>

or to behave as if poor. But those who are experienced in the language used in Syria and Palestine <note>Refers to the Semitic linguistic background of the New Testament writers</note>—which the translators of the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament, abbreviated here as LXX</note> and the writers of the New Testament employed—know well that they use the word Paul employs in the very sense we give to it. Similar uses are found in Psalm 79:8 (which is Psalm 78 in the Septuagint), Proverbs 23:21, Judges 6:6 and 14:15, and Psalm 34:11 (which is Psalm 33 in the Septuagint). One can also look at Tobit 4:22. The Syriac and Latin translators also understood it this way. While secular Greek writers commonly use the same word to mean "to beg," that meaning can have no place here.

And he teaches us at the same time that the Galatians, leaving Heathenism and becoming Christians, ceased to serve those who were not gods by nature. How could Paul have reasoned thus if he, while urging them to serve the Lord Jesus, had himself taught them that Christ was not God by nature?

# THEOLOGY. III. B. IX. Chapter.

2. That Paul says that Christ was in the **form of God** before he took on the **form of a servant**; for he does not say that, being in the form of a servant, he took on the form of God. Rather, being in the form of God, he emptied himself, having taken on the form of a servant. <note>This refers to the concept of *Kenosis*, or Christ's self-emptying, as described in Philippians 2:6-7.</note>

3. Just as being in the **form of a servant** means having a human nature with all its attendant weaknesses, so being in the **form of God** means being God—possessing the highest Majesty, enjoying infinite Sovereignty, and exercising the Authority, Right, and Works of God; living and appearing in a manner consistent with this incomprehensible essence.

This must be carefully noted: I understand the **form of God** to mean God’s Majesty united with his essence. It is sometimes said that the "form of God" only means something external that affects the senses. **Answer:** I admit that the word "form" or "appearance" sometimes means this, but it has been proven that even among the secular writers, such as *Aeschylus* and *Phavorinus* <note>Aeschylus was an ancient Greek playwright; Phavorinus likely refers to Varinus Phavorinus, a 16th-century scholar of Greek.</note>, the word "form" is used for the **essence** of things. Thus it must be taken here to mean the Divine essence, united with the radiance or Majesty that surrounds it.

4. One must also take note that Christ could not have had the form of God without being God. It would have been absolutely impossible for a finite subject to have possessed an infinite Glory and Majesty. Besides that, God testifies that he will not give his glory to another.

5. Paul here places the Son as equal with the Father, which indicates a distinction of Persons within the Godhead.

6. He says that this Son did not consider it "robbery" <note>The Dutch "roof" (robbery/prey) translates the Greek *harpagmos*, often debated by scholars as meaning either a "thing to be snatched" or a "thing to be clung to."</note> to be equal to his Father. He did not believe it was an unjust possession. This can mean that Christ, being truly God, judged that he committed no injustice by making himself equal to God—unlike those who steal what does not lawfully belong to them. In this way, our first father <note>Adam</note> presumed to want to become like God. In this way, the fallen angels wanted to claim for themselves by force the honor that belongs only to the sole Ruler of the world; likewise, there have been Roman Emperors who wanted to be regarded as Gods. But

<column-break/>

it is not so with our Lord Jesus Christ: before his humiliation, he enjoyed the form of God; a Glory and a Majesty equal to that of the Father, through the lawful Right of his essence, and not through robbery or any other kind of injustice. But, although the Lord Christ did not consider this equality of essence with God as robbery, and knew that he could lawfully retain it, he nevertheless emptied himself.

<margin>Cameron. Daillé.</margin>
This manner of speaking also indicates, according to some scholars <note>John Cameron (1579–1625) and Jean Daillé (1594–1670) were influential Protestant theologians.</note>, that Christ did not make this equality a matter of triumph or boast about it—just as one does not parade what one possesses naturally. This is in contrast to the conquerors of old, who, having conquered some place or seized something from their enemies—such as weapons or banners—would set them up as a trophy <note>Original: "Zegepraal"</note> or other monuments of their bravery. Thus, the Apostle intended to show that Christ did not wish to appear on Earth with a splendor and Glory worthy of his Divinity, as if he wanted to make a "trophy" of his equality with God, but rather that he emptied himself.

<margin>Alex. Morus.</margin>
This latter explanation does not please other scholars <note>Alexander More (1616–1670), a Franco-Scottish preacher and scholar.</note>; they believe that while the French might speak this way (saying "he made no parade"), the Greeks did not. They judge that Paul is much more likely alluding to the deification of the Emperors. This thought is quite clever, but it seems too subtle to me, as does the thought of a certain learned man, <margin>Steph. le Moyne *Varia Sacra*. p. 276. Grot.</margin> who suggests it is a contrast to what *Alexander the Great* did (whose name was famous among the Philippians), who wanted to be held as the *Son of Jupiter*. <note>Stephen le Moyne and Hugo Grotius were prominent 17th-century scholars.</note>

Whatever the case may be, it is always evident, according to Paul, that Christ possessed equality with his Father.

It will be said that one should not scrutinize these words so literally, and that they do not mean an actual equality, but rather a conformity or likeness—just as one finds an example of this in the *Odyssey* of *Homer*, where it means as much as being "regarded as a God."

But it is absurd to cite pagan books—which are full of blasphemy and godlessness—when the sacred writers distinguish God from the creature infinitely, and never mix the Supreme Being with mortals. It is not probable that

# CHRISTIAN THEOLOGY

...that Paul would have paired the Creator with the creature. Furthermore, one must observe that this is a way of speaking that does not naturally come to mind, and that one must distinguish between being equal to God and being *regarded* as equal to God.

It is said that this is a **hyperbolic** <note>Exaggerated for effect.</note> way of speaking, which magnifies things too much.

**Answer.** Although these modes of speech are sometimes found in the Scriptures, they are never used in a way that harms God’s Glory. Paul, who well knew that God had testified that no one is equal to him—*who is like me?*—would never have said that Christ was equal to the Father if he were not the true God. Especially knowing that Christ was condemned to death because he had made himself equal to God.

It is said that Christ was equal to his Father through agreement and through likeness. But one never expresses oneself this way. If Christ is not equal to his Father, why would Paul say it, since it could give such a bad impression to the minds of his listeners or readers? Must he, in order to exalt Christ, place him as equal with God if he were not?

It is said that to be in the **form of God** means to be worshiped as God; this is how Smalcius <note>Valentinus Smalcius (1572–1622) was a prominent Socinian theologian who denied the Trinity.</note> explains it.

**Answer.** 1. If Christ was worshiped as God, then he was indeed God: for worship belongs to God alone. 2. If he was worshiped before he took on the form of a servant, then he had his existence before he became man.

<margin>Grotius, Schlicting, Crellius, etc.</margin> <note>These are scholars associated with Socinianism or Remonstrant theology who emphasized Christ's humanity.</note>
It is said that to be in the form of God means to perform miracles, to command the winds, to raise the dead, to make the deaf hear, and the mute speak. But 1. If one only had to perform miracles to be in the form of God, one could have said of Moses that he had been in this form. 2. One asks when Christ was in this form, if he is only a man? He performed no miracles until after he was born in a manger; consequently, after having already taken on the form of a servant. 3. One cannot understand what the form

<column-break/>

of a servant consists of if Christ did not take it on as soon as he became man. Since then, according to Paul, Christ was in the form of God before he took on the form of a servant, it follows that he was in that form before he became man.

It is said that the **form of a servant** consists of this: that he surrendered himself to the power of his enemies, letting himself be captured, bound, and crucified.

These are, I confess, the *consequences* of the form of a servant, but the form of a servant can exist without them. Is a slave not in the form of a servant unless someone is beating him, binding him, and dragging him to his death? Are all servants or slaves like this, who are captured and bound by the authority of the government? Certainly, that resembles the form of a criminal more than that of a servant.

Furthermore, one only needs to read Paul to see what must be understood by the "form of a servant." Namely, the **human nature** in a humbled state. This is evident from the following words: *becoming like men.*

**Objection.** These words are not the explanation of what Paul had said: he only means to say that Christ became like common men, and he contrasts this likeness with the form of a servant.

But 1. if he contrasts this likeness with the form of God, it follows that this likeness *is* the form of a servant: for it is clear that the form of a servant and the form of God are placed in opposition to one another. 2. It is certain that this likeness followed the form of God. But Christ became like men as soon as he came into the world. He was therefore in the form of God before he became man. 3. There is a progression <note>A rhetorical "climax" or stepping up of intensity.</note> in the words of Paul; he had said that Christ, being in the form of God, had emptied himself by taking on the form of a servant; but since the Angels are also servants of God, he adds to it: *Christ became like men*, and *became as a man*; he continues and says that in this state he obeyed his Father unto the death of the cross.

A new critic, who believes that only the human nature of Christ is spoken of here, translates the...

# THEOLOGY. III. B. IX. Chapter 241
Hh
<meta>catchword: time</meta>

...Paul’s words in this manner: *Being in the form of God, he did not believe that making himself equal to God was something that could be stolen.* <note>The author is discussing Philippians 2:6. The Dutch text uses "roven" (to rob or steal) to translate the Greek word *harpagmos*, debating whether Christ's divinity was something he "clutched" or something inherently his.</note> But: we have proven that by the "form of God," the Deity and Majesty of Christ must be understood. 2. The original text <note>original: "Grond-text"</note> does not support this translation. The word translated as "a thing that could be stolen" actually means the act of stealing, or the stolen thing itself, and not the possibility of stealing.

**Objection.** If the "form of God" means the divine nature, Paul would not have said that Christ "annihilated" himself <note>The Dutch word is "vernietigt." In modern bibles, this is usually translated as "emptied himself" or "made himself of no reputation" (the concept of Kenosis).</note>, for that implies he laid aside this nature; however, divinity can never be laid aside.

**Answer.** Christ never laid aside the form of God, but hid it during the days of his flesh; and in that, he "annihilated" himself: we shall explain this more broadly in the section regarding the Incarnation. <note>The "Incarnation" refers to the belief in God becoming human in the person of Jesus.</note>

**Objection.** One would never say of a God that he "did not consider it a robbery" to be equal to God; for that assumes that Christ could have considered equality with God a robbery.

**Answer.** This does not follow: if one says that "God does not lie," must one then conclude that God *could* lie?

**Objection.** If Christ were spoken of as God, the Apostle would not say that he has been "exalted"; for divinity cannot be exalted.

**Answer.** Who does not see that Christ is spoken of here as the Mediator <note>A theological title for Jesus as the bridge between God and humanity.</note> who has been exalted? This is either because the Glory of his Divinity was revealed, or because his humanity gained a new luster of Glory. Since Paul says in Acts 20:28 that God purchased his church with his own blood, why could one not say that he has been exalted? That better accords with his Divinity.

**Objection.** If Paul’s thought were what we attribute to him, he would have said, "who being in the form of God, and having no unjust possession, considered etc." instead of what is written: "Who being in the form, did not consider it robbery, etc. But emptied himself."

**Answer.** It amounts to the same thing, and it is as if the Apostle had said, "nevertheless he emptied himself," just as <term>ἀλλὰ</term> <note>Greek: "alla," usually meaning "but," but sometimes used as "nevertheless" to show a contrast.</note> sometimes means. Colossians 2:5.

<margin>Philip. III. 21.</margin> In the same Letter, chapter 3:21, the Son is presented to us as having a power by which he can subject all things to himself.

->Part I.<-

<column-break/>

<margin>Col I. 16. 17.</margin> The [Holy] Spirit also gives us powerful proofs of the Divinity of Christ: *Through him (that is, through Christ) all things were created that are in the Heavens and that are on the earth, the visible and the invisible, whether Thrones, or Dominions, or Principalities, or Powers; all things were created through him and for him; and he is before all things, and all things consist together through him.*

One cannot read these words without finding a strong proof for the Divinity of Christ: Scripture never attributes the act of **Creation** to anyone but God alone, and, as we have noted elsewhere, the title of **Creator** is given to the true God to distinguish Him from created beings; and the infinite power to create the world cannot be found outside of God. Since creation is attributed to Christ, it follows that he is God.

**Objection.** "To create" here means to restore, to improve, or to put things in a better state than they were before; therefore Paul is speaking of the renewal that occurred through the preaching of the Gospel by the Apostles, whom Christ sent to reform the nations.

**Answer.** Although it is true that the world is renewed through the Gospel, and this is the work of a Divine power—so that one can and must call it a "Creation"—it is certain that this passage cannot be understood as this "new creation." 1. Not only because that is spoken of in the following verses, but 2. Because Paul explicitly counts the **Angels** among the things created by Christ, and dwells on them more than all the others. Now, the Angels were not "renewed" or "restored" by Christ, for their essence was not corrupted by sin. They were reconciled with us through Christ, who earned salvation for us; but it has never been said that "creating Angels" means reconciling them with those they once hated. I add to this, that even if these words could be understood as the second creation, they would nevertheless serve as proof that Christ, to whom the same is attributed, is the true eternal God: for the second creation requires no less power than the first.

<margin>Socinus</margin> <note>Faustus Socinus (1539–1604) was an Italian theologian whose followers, the Socinians, denied the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ.</note>
**Objection.** It appears that the second creation is spoken of here. 1. Because Christ is dealt with as a man. Now, it is a fact that the creation of the world preceded the birth of Christ by many centuries. 2. Because Paul had previously spoken of Christ’s Blood. 3. Because he calls him God’s image. Now this praise does not belong to him except in respect to the Gospel that he proclaimed.

**Answer.** It is true that Christ, who is man, is spoken of, but not insofar as he is man; the blood belongs to him as a man: but it is as God that he created all things, and is God’s image, for he is called God’s image in view of the fact that he perfectly possesses all the perfections of the Divinity, so that he who has seen him has seen the Father.

This passage gives yet another proof: Paul says that all things are created for or unto Christ.

God is the final end for which all things are created: since they then are created for the Son, he is consequently the true and eternal God.

This is not yet enough for Paul: he says that Christ is before all things. Not only before Moses and Abraham, but before anything was created—that is, from eternity. For by this way of speaking, the Scripture signifies Eternity.

He adds to this, that all things consist <note>Meaning "are held together" or "endure."</note> through him. To make known that he maintains them through his providence, and that their being, life, and motion depend on him: a new proof that he is the true eternal God, since the maintenance of the universe is one of the works of the Divinity.

<margin>Colossians 2:9</margin>
In Colossians 2:9, our Apostle says that in

<column-break/>

Christ all the fullness of the Divinity dwells bodily. There is none but God who can have the infinite fullness of the Divinity: there is nothing but the infinite that can contain the infinite. He who speaks of the fullness of the Divinity speaks of a rich abundance of the perfections of the Divinity: his life, power, wisdom, goodness, infinity, eternity, and all other attributes: to say that the fullness of the Divinity dwells in Christ is to say that he possesses all perfections of the Divinity, and consequently, that he is the true eternal God.

<margin>Colossians 3:17</margin>
Add to this Colossians 3:17: Whatever you do in word or in deed, (do) it all in the Name of the Lord Jesus; for, if Jesus were not God, it is certain that Paul would not present him as the beginning and end of all the actions of our life.

Here Christ is called God, manifested in the flesh, and taken up into Glory. See there then a fresh proof of his Divinity.

What would be given to this expression: *The mystery of Godliness was taken up into Glory*? They say this means that the Gospel is gloriously exalted because it brought about a much greater Holiness than all the other teachings previously...

DE CHRISTIAN <note>The header is partially cut off; it likely reads "The Christian Religion" or "The Christian Theology."</note>

...means "by means of an instrument." **Answer:** "Through" <note>Original Dutch: *door*, which corresponds to the Greek *dia*.</note> does not always signify an instrument; the contrary is evident in Galatians 1:1, Ephesians 1:1, 1 Corinthians 1:9, Romans 11:36, and Hebrews 2:10.
<margin>Gal. 1:1. Eph. 1:1. 1 Cor. 1:9. Rom. 11:36. Heb. 2:10.</margin>

It is said that here the text speaks not of "ancient ages," but of "future ages"—that is, of the world to come. **Answer:** 1. Elsewhere it is stated that Christ made the world. 2. When the Scripture uses the word "ages" <note>original: *eeuwen*; the author is discussing Hebrews 1:2, where the Greek *aionas* is often translated as "worlds" or "universe."</note> absolutely, without adding anything further, it does not mean the future world. 3. If Paul had spoken of the future world, he would not have said that Christ "had made" <note>past tense</note> it, but that he "is making" or "will make" it.

2. He adds not only that the Son is the **radiance of the Father’s Glory** and the **exact image of his substance** <note>original: *zelfstandigheid*; a 17th-century Dutch theological term for the Greek *hypostasis* or "person/being."</note>, as we shall see in another Chapter, but that he **upholds all things by his Almighty word**: from which we draw two proofs.

**The 1st** is taken from these words: *he upholds all things*. That is, the world with all its parts. Certainly, if it is a Divine work to have created the world, it is also a Divine work to govern, direct, and maintain it—if such maintenance requires an infinite power and wisdom without limits.

**The 2nd** lies in the phrase *the word of his power*, through which he upholds all things. There is no more absolute power than that which needs only a word; now, God alone can work in this manner: for he has only to will and to command to make everything he desires.

One might say that Christ upholds all things by the word of the power *of his Father*. But 1. the power of the Father and that of the Son is the same, as we have proven elsewhere. 2. If Christ is merely a creature <note>original: *Schepzel*; here meaning a created being rather than the Creator.</note>, then one cannot say that he upholds all things by the word of his Father's power: for then one would have to conceive that the Father communicated an infinite power to a creature, which is impossible; for a creature cannot receive infinite power. He, then, to whom God has given a power that can move, direct, and sustain everything, cannot be a creature. He must be of the same essence with God to possess the same attribute and power. One might say that God did not communicate this power to Christ; but then how does Paul say that Christ *upholds all things*?

<column-break/>

<margin>Heb. 3:3--6.</margin>
Hebrews 3:3–6 provides us with a new line of reasoning. *This man was counted worthy of so much more glory than Moses, inasmuch as he who hath builded the house hath more honor than the house: for every house is builded by someone; but he that built all things is God. And Moses verily was faithful in all his house, as a servant, for a testimony of those things which were to be spoken after; but Christ as a Son over his own house; whose house are we, if we hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end.*

From this it follows clearly that Christ is God. Thus Paul reasons: he who builds all things is God; Jesus Christ has built all things, for we are his house; therefore, Jesus Christ is God.

It is inconceivable that the Spirit of Christ could have been in the Prophets without Christ himself existing in the time of the Prophets. Now, Peter clearly says that the Spirit of Christ was in the Prophets; consequently, Christ existed in the time of the Prophets, and did not first begin to exist when he was conceived in the womb of the Blessed Virgin.

It is argued that the Spirit is called the "Spirit of Christ" because he inspired the Prophets with everything regarding Christ—his suffering and his glory—just as he is called the "Spirit of truth" because he teaches the truth. **Answer:** There is a great difference between these two things. ### DIVINITY. III. B. Chapter X.

[God]-head <note>The word "head" completes "Godhead" (Divinity) from the previous page's catchword.</note> is a matter. Furthermore, just as it would be absurd to call the Spirit the "Spirit of Truth" if there were no truth in the time that he is called Spirit of Truth; so it would be equally absurd to say that the Spirit is the "Spirit of Christ" in a time when one maintains that Christ was not present. Moreover, if the Spirit who was in the Prophets were only called the Spirit of Christ because he inspired things that looked forward to Christ, one could also call him the "Spirit of the Apostles," the "Spirit of the Antichrist," or "our Spirit," since the Spirit in the Prophets spoke of things that concern us, the Apostles and their preaching, and even the Antichrist and other adversaries <note>original: "Spanden" - referring to those who oppose or stand against Christ</note> of Christ.

<margin>1 Peter 3:18, 19, 20.</margin>
In **1 Peter 3:18, 19, 20**, we find another proof. He who, having gone, preached through his Spirit to those who lived in the time of Noah, was certainly present in the time of this prophet. Now Peter says that Christ, having gone, preached through his Spirit to those who lived in the time of Noah; therefore, Christ was present in the time of Noah. See the passage here: *For Christ also suffered once for sins, the Just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God; being put to death in the flesh, but made alive by the Spirit; by which also he went and preached to the spirits in prison; who formerly were disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being prepared.* One can object nothing against this passage to distort its true meaning that is not exceptionally forced.

It will be said that by "the Spirit," one must understand the soul of Christ separated from his body, or the Holy Spirit who was poured out upon the Apostles on the day of Pentecost <note>original: "Pinxter-Feest"</note>.

**Answer:** One cannot say that this Spirit is the soul of Christ; for it speaks of a Spirit by which he was "made alive"; now, his soul did not have the power to make his dead body alive—not to mention other reasons we shall present elsewhere. Those who want the soul of Christ to have gone to preach to the godly souls could give no reason

<column-break/>

why it speaks here only of those who were disobedient in the time of Noah.

2. One cannot say that it speaks of the Holy Spirit who was poured out upon the Apostles at Pentecost, for he is set in opposition to "the flesh." Now, "the flesh" signifies the human nature of Christ; "the spirit" then signifies his Divinity. Furthermore, if it spoke of the spirit through which the Apostles preached, Peter would not say that he preached to the "spirits," for one does not call living men such. Besides that, why would Peter speak only of the disobedient, without mentioning the believers to whom they also preached? Finally, why would he say that they were rebellious in the time of Noah? For it is groundless to say that the word "as" <note>suggesting they were "like" the disobedient</note> must be added, <margin>as **Volkelius** <note>Johannes Volkelius (d. 1636) was a prominent Socinian theologian who denied the pre-existence of Christ; the author is refuting his interpretation here.</note> suggests,</margin> when the patience of God waited. There is no necessity to insert this word. It is said that by these "disobedient spirits," the Heathen <note>The Gentiles</note> must be understood, whom Peter regards as a single people composed of a succession of generations, to whom he nevertheless ascribes things that only apply to some among them; such as the rebellion regarding those who lived in Noah’s time, and the conversion regarding those converted by the Apostles.

**Answer:** 1. Since the distinction of nations into Jews and Heathen only began after the Deluge <note>The Great Flood</note>, why would one want those who lived before it to be viewed as a part of these nations, in contrast to the Jews? 2. Those who were disobedient when the Ark was being built all perished; not one of them remained. 3. If those who did not obey the preaching of the Apostles could be called "disobedient ones of Noah's time" because they belonged to the same people, one part of which was rebellious before the Flood, one could also say that they perished [in the Flood], which is absurd.

It is said that this speaks of a matter that followed the Ascension of Christ, or at least his Resurrection, since Peter had spoken of those things previously. **Answer:** The meaning of the Apostle is not understood; it is true he spoke of the Resurrection of Christ by the power...

<header>THE CHRISTIAN [DIVINITY]</header>

...spoken by the power of his **Godhead**; but he wishes to give us to understand that Christ, through that same Godhead by which he was made alive, also preached in the time of Noah; and that it is no wonder if Christ now finds rebellious hearts, since there were already such in the time of the Deluge. It is said that the phrase *having gone*, signifies the Ascension of Christ, as in 1 Pet. III. 22. Acts I. 10. 11. Joh. XIV. 2. 3. 12. 18. and XVI. 7.

**Answer:** This word, when stated simply, has never signified the Ascension, unless something else is added to it.

I come now to the Epistles of John.

Immediately the Apostle confirms in 1 John I. 1. what he had said in his Gospel: that Christ was from the beginning. This proves that he is eternal.

But nothing is more explicit than how he ends his Letter in 1 John V: 20.

<margin>1 John V. 20.</margin>
We know that the Son of God has come, and has given us understanding, that we may know the true one, and we are in the true one, (namely) in his Son Jesus Christ; this is the true God, and eternal life. One sees clearly that these last words refer to Christ.

<margin>Volkelius</margin>
<note>Johannes Volkelius (d. 1618) was a prominent Socinian theologian who argued against the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ.</note>
It is said: That one must translate *And we are in the true one THROUGH his Son Jesus Christ.* But nothing obliges us to translate it thus, nor to understand the same preposition differently within the same discourse; all the more because it is frequently said that we remain in Christ. Socinus <note>Fausto Sozzini, the founder of Socinianism, which denied Christ's pre-existence.</note> confesses that this "true one" is the Son of God; and indeed, if one had to understand the Father here, he would have had to say, *we are in the true one, AND in his Son Jesus Christ*.

All the works of John give us irrefutable proofs of the Divinity of Christ; and we find many in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>.

We have already considered two of these in the preceding chapters, while explaining the Old Testament.

I shall examine only two more of them, which seem to me to exclude all doubt.

<margin>Rev. II. 23.</margin>
The first is Rev. II. 23. where Christ, in the Letter to the Angel of the church in Thyatira, says: > All the churches shall know that I am he who searches the reins and hearts; and I will give to each of you according to your works.

<column-break/>

It is known that searching hearts and reins <note>original: "herten en nieren" - literally hearts and kidneys. In biblical language, this refers to the innermost thoughts and hidden emotions of a person.</note> is an incommunicable attribute <note>A theological term for a quality that belongs to God alone and cannot be shared with created beings.</note> of God, and a quality that the Scripture attributes to God alone. *The Lord searches all hearts.* 1 Chron. XXVIII. 9. and XXIX. 17. Jer. XVII. 10. *I the Lord search the heart, (and) try the reins: and that to give to every man according to his ways.* Since Christ then attributes this quality to himself, is it not an unshakable proof that he is God, to be praised above all for eternity?

One might say: That Christ searches the hearts in a different manner than God. God knows them immediately, and through himself; but Jesus, only because God reveals it to him. Yet, how is it that Christ expresses himself in a way that gives reason to believe that he himself searches them, when he knows that this attribute is given to God, and that all believers regard it as a Title of Honor belonging to the Godhead? How is it that he adds the role of Judge to this quality of "searcher of hearts," just as the Prophets did, who attributed these two qualities to God? 2. If knowing the secrets of hearts through revelation were enough to be called the searcher of hearts, then the Apostles could have claimed this for themselves. 3. He who says "searcher of hearts" implies a being who knows them through himself.

One might say, that Christ had more knowledge than the Apostles and the Prophets. But then there would be no distinction except in "more or less"; therefore, one could say it indifferently of the Prophets and of the Apostles, if knowing hearts through revelation were enough.

This is confirmed by Matt. IX. 4. where it is said, *Jesus seeing their thoughts.* And by Mark II. 8. where it stands that Jesus, knowing in his spirit what the Scribes thought within themselves, said to them, *why do you think such things in your hearts?* And by John II. 24. 25. where the Evangelist remarks that Jesus did not trust the Jews, because he knew them all; and had no need that anyone should testify of man, for he himself knew what was in man.

The second passage from the Apocalypse is chapter V. 13. where John says that he heard all creatures cry out: > to him who sits on the Throne, and to the Lamb, be thanksgiving, honor, strength, glory, and power for all eternity.

## CHAPTER XI.

### Observations on the Preceding Chapters.

From all that has been said, it is evident that **Jesus Christ** is the true God.

We have proven this: 1. Because the name of God is given to him in such a way that it is never so attributed to a creature.

2. Because the perfections of God are attributed to him.

3. Because the Scripture attributes the same works to him as to God.

4. Because it is willed that we bring him the same Honor, Service, and worship <note>The original Dutch uses 'aanbidding', which refers to the act of religious adoration or prostration.</note> as to God.

<margin>Episcopius, *Institutes*, Book IV, Section II, chapter 35. <note>Simon Episcopius (1583–1643) was a prominent Dutch theologian associated with the Remonstrant movement.</note></margin>
One must make no distinction here between the highest and a lower worship—one given to God by reason of his Divine essence, and one given to creatures because God wills it. This distinction is unknown to the Prophets and the Apostles. The Angel did not say to John: "Worship God with the highest worship," <margin>Revelation XXII. 9.</margin> where he says simply, "Worship God."

Furthermore, we have shown that the Son is equal to the Father, which we have proven: 1. By showing that the Apostles apply the divine oracles, which were spoken of the God of Israel by the ancient Prophets, to **Jesus Christ**.

On this, it is Objected that these glorious Titles of Honor do not belong to **Jesus Christ** except as the first servant of the Father.

But, if one compares the passages of the New Testament where Christ is honored with these praises with the Books of the Prophets, which give God the same names and attribute to him the same works, one will find that the Prophets and the Apostles speak of one and the same object.

2. Through the words of Christ himself, who testifies to being one with the Father.

3. Finally, through the testimonies of the Apostles, who teach us that Christ is the great God, and did not consider it robbery to be equal to his Father.

<column-break/>

Add to this that to posit two Gods, one lesser than the other, is to not know what God is: for the concept of God includes the concept of a being that has no other being above it. Therefore, I cannot understand how it is possible that those who profess to believe that Christ is a true God, yet want him to be subordinate and less than the Father, so that the Father is the first in order, in dignity, and in power. For the Father and the Son have either the same or a different essence; if the same, how can there be subordination? <margin>*Theological Institutes*, Bull, etc. <note>Likely referring to George Bull (1634–1710), an English bishop who defended the Nicene Creed.</note></margin> If they have a different essence, then they will be two Gods. As for the Socinians <note>A non-Trinitarian sect that followed the teachings of Fausto Sozzini, denying the pre-existence and full divinity of Christ.</note>, it is certain that their opinion favors the error and idolatry of ancient Heathenism, which posited lesser Gods; Gods, not such by their essence, but made Gods through their supposed deification, to whom they nevertheless gave religious worship and Divine honors. With what shamelessness could the Apostles have taught the world that one must recognize only one single God, if they themselves had simultaneously introduced a God who was not such essentially? Would the Heathens not have had reason to say to them: "Do we recognize many Gods? They are Persons elevated to this Highness through the price of their virtues and heroic deeds"? On the contrary, do we not see that Paul condemns as an ungodly matter, entirely contrary to Religion, the serving of objects that by nature are no Gods?

The Church Fathers <note>The influential early Christian theologians whose writings established the foundations of Christian doctrine.</note>, at least most of them, recognized this equality, as one can be convinced of from their writings: such as Augustine, Athanasius, Ambrose, Cyril of Alexandria, Hilary; of Pope Leo, and of Fulgentius.

<margin>Book 2 on the Trinity, chapter 7.</margin>
Augustine says that there are some passages in the Scripture that signify the Unity and equality of the existence of the Father and of the Son; such as John X. 30 and Philippians II. 6. <margin>John XIV. 28.</margin> Others that indicate that the Son is less than the Father, because of his form as a servant (John XIV. 28). <margin>John V. 26, 30.</margin> Others, which do not say that he is less nor equal to the Father, but only that he is of the Father (John V. 26, 30). Ambrose expressly denies that the Son can be said to be less than the Father with regard to his <margin>Athanasius, *Book on the human nature of the only-begotten...* <note>Original: "l. de hum. ser unig. suf.", referring to Athanasius's Christological writings.</note></margin> Godhead. Cyril of Alexandria says: Christ calls himself less than his Father, for...

<margin>Hilary. Leo, *Sermon III on the Nativity*. Fulgentius, *Response to Donatus*, chapter 6.</margin>
...the reason for His Humanity. Hilary says nearly the same. Leo, in his third Sermon: One cannot deny these truths without impiety; for, just as we must take great care not to call anything "God" that is not God, so it is also, on the contrary, that one could not—without great crime—refuse the name and Divine Honor to Him to whom the Scripture attributes the name and perfections of the Godhead.

<margin>Jurieu, *Tableau of Socinianism*, p. 137.</margin>
It has been very well said that, "To strip Christ of His Divinity is to do Him infinitely more wrong than one would do to a lawfully reigning King by snatching the Crown from his head and placing it upon the head of the most despised of all servants. For it is certain that a creature, after its elevation, can never be so low that the proportion between that creature's former elevation and its humiliation is the same as that found between the height where God is and the lowliness in which the creature resides. If the greatest of the Seraphim <note>The highest order of angels in traditional Christian angelology</note> became the most loathsome of all earthworms, there would not be the same distinction between his first and last state as there is between what God is and the most excellent of all creatures."

One might say: It appears that the Father is more than the Son, since He has generated <note>original: "gegenereert"; refers to the theological doctrine of the "eternal generation" of the Son from the Father</note> Him. Answer: All these arguments assume that it is with God as it is with men; but we have already shown that one must not have these thoughts. One must believe that the Father generates the Son, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from both; but one must also believe that they have one and the same essence and, consequently, that one person is not more excellent than the other. The Scripture teaches it to us; one must remain by that.

We have all the less reason to refuse to recognize Christ as God because God testifies through His Prophet that He gives His glory to no other; so it is not possible that He to whom the name, perfections, and works of God are attributed—in which God’s Glory consists—would not be the true God. It is then an indisputable truth that Jesus Christ is the great God.

<column-break/>

# CHAPTER XII.

## Answer to the Objections against the Divinity of Jesus Christ.

So that no one believes that we hide the Objections because we cannot answer them, let us attentively examine what the Socinians <note>Followers of a 16th-century theological movement that denied the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ</note> and other deniers of the Trinity (Anti-Trinitarians) bring forward to combat this truth.

<margin>Smale, *On the Divinity of Christ against the Socinians*.</margin>
Objection: John XVII. 3. *This is eternal life, that they may know You, the Only True God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent.* It is clear that the Father is called the Only True God here.

<margin>Frantz, *ibid*.</margin>
In response, I say that one could first translate those words in a way according to which the Father alone would not be called the True God: *This is Eternal life, that they know You, O Father, and Him whom You have sent, Jesus Christ, as the only true God.* In that case, this reasoning would prove nothing.

<margin>Wick. Bolswick. Crellius, *On the one God the Father*, etc. Wolzogen. Schlicting.</margin>
But following the common translation, I answer that the Father is called the only true God in contrast to the false Gods of the Heathens, and not in contrast to His Son: for otherwise there would be a contradiction in the Scripture, which teaches us (as is well known) that Jesus Christ is God, and true God, just as the same John says at the end of his first Epistle. One can explain this passage through another of similar sound: 1 Timothy VI. 15, where it speaks of the *blessed and only potentate, the King of Kings, and the Lord of Lords*. Now, Jesus Christ is this King of Kings, and this Lord of Lords. See Revelation XVII. 14 and XIX. 16. Even if it were the Father who must be understood here by the "only potentate," it is not to the exclusion of the Son.

Some interpreters explain these words as referring to the Son Himself, but our reasoning will be no weaker for it; for if the Son is called the Only Potentate, and it is added there that He alone has immortality, it is not to the exclusion of the Father; just as it is not to the exclusion of the Son when the Father is called the only God.

<header>DIVINE THEOLOGY. III. B. XII. Chapter 249</header>

**Objection.** It is clear that the Son is excluded [from the Godhead], since he is distinguished from the Father.

1. I deny this conclusion. In the passage cited, the Father is also distinguished from the Son, yet one cannot say that the Son is excluded.

2. In this passage, Christ is viewed as <term>Mediator</term> <note>The role of Jesus as the bridge or go-between for God and humanity</note>; and that is the reason why he is distinguished from the Father; besides which, it is well known that the Son is a distinct Person from the Person of the Father.

But, it is said, is it not the same to say, "the Father alone is the true God," and "the Father is the only true God"? Just as it is the same to say, "Elijah alone ascended to Heaven in a fiery chariot," or "Elijah was the only one who climbed up to Heaven in a fiery chariot."

I answer. There is a great difference between these two propositions. To say that "the Father alone is the true God" is to exclude all other Persons; but to say that "the Father is the *only true God*" is to say that the Father is the true God, who is the only or sole truthful one [in nature]. The example of Elijah proves nothing. For what is said of Elijah is said of him alone. But what is said of the Father—that he is God—is also testified of the Son. One can clarify this through a clear example. Those who possess the true <term>Bezoar</term> <note>A stone-like mass found in the stomachs of certain animals, highly prized in the 17th century as a universal antidote to poison</note>, holding a piece in their hand, may very well say, "this is the only genuine Bezoar," not meaning that there is no more genuine Bezoar in existence other than what they hold in their hand; but because the Bezoar they have is a species which is the only genuine Bezoar.

It is said: The word *alone* excludes all others. Answer: This adjective does not exclude anything except that which *ought* to be excluded. And one can bring many examples of this. Such as Gen. 42:38, Luke 9:36, and 10:40, John 16:32, Acts 4:12, 1 Cor. 2:11, Matt. 11:27, 1 Macc. 10:70. The word *alone* excludes only those who have an existence distinct [in nature] from the Father.

It is said: "The true God" does not only mean "He who is set against false gods," but "He who is God in the most eminent way." Answer: This answer presupposes that there are greater and lesser Gods, and that one God is more excellent than another, which is false.

2. **Objection.** Various pas—

<sig>Part 1.</sig>

<column-break/>

<margin>1 Cor. 8:6. Eph. 4:6. 1 Tim. 2:5. 1 Cor. 12:4, 5, 6. Rom. 3:30. and 16:27. John 5:44. Jude vs. 4.</margin>
—sages are thrown up where the Father is named God, in distinction from the Son.

I answer the same to all these passages: namely, that the Father is called the only God, not with the exclusion of the Son and the Holy Spirit, but with the exclusion of the false deities of the Heathens.

<margin>1 Cor. 8:6.</margin>
If the Father is called the one or only God in 1 Cor. 8:6, the Son is also called the only Lord; since then Christ is not called the only Lord to the exclusion of the Father, likewise the Father is not called the only God to the exclusion of the Son.

<margin>Matt. 11:27.</margin>
Christ says: "No one knows the Son except the Father; and no one knows the Father except the Son." Who does not see that Christ's aim is not to say that the Son alone knows the Father to the exclusion of the Father himself? One must reason in the same way where the Father is called the only God.

Moreover, one must be mindful that when the Father is called the only God, Jesus Christ is being viewed as Mediator.

<margin>Jude vs. 4.</margin>
Regarding the passage in Jude vs. 4, there is nothing that obliges us to interpret it as referring to the Father; for we can translate it thus: "Denying the only Ruler, Jesus Christ, our God and Lord."

<margin>Dan. 7:9.</margin>
3. **Objection.** In Dan. 7:9, the <term>Ancient of Days</term> <note>A title for God in the Book of Daniel, usually interpreted as the Father in this context</note> is distinguished from the Son of Man; and other similar places in the Revelation.

But that proves nothing against the Divinity of Christ; for we do not deny that the Father is distinguished from the Son, especially where the Father is viewed as the one to whom the Mediator [Christ] relates.

4. **Objection.** There is no one but the Father alone of whom it is not said that he is <term>generated</term> <note>original: "gegenereert"; refers to the Eternal Generation of the Son</note> or that he <term>proceeds</term> <note>original: "uitgaat"; refers to the Procession of the Holy Spirit</note>: consequently, there is no one who is God but the Father.

I answer that this only proves that the Father has something which distinguishes him from the Son and the Holy Spirit, but not that the Son and the Holy Spirit are not God. For it appears from Scripture, as we shall see in the following, that the generation of the Son and the procession of the Holy Spirit do not make these two persons less than the Father.

5. **Objection.** He who calls himself the God of Abraham,

I answer. *Christ* is also named in this way. *Acts 7:32.* For the Angel, who appeared to Moses in the Wilderness, says: *I am the God of your Fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.* <note>The author argues that since the "Angel" (often interpreted as the pre-incarnate Christ) uses this title, it is not exclusive to the Father.</note>

6. **Objection.** It is said only of God the Father that he has chosen us, and it is to him alone that our prayers ascend.

I answer. This occurs because the Father is regarded in the work of our salvation as the one who begins it; the Son as the one who promotes it; and the Holy Spirit as the one who completes it. As for prayer, the Father is not the only one worshiped. *Christ* was called upon by *Stephen*, *Acts 7:59*, and the Apostles pray for his Grace and his Peace at the beginning of their Letters. *Compare 2 Cor. 13:13* and *Rev. 1:5.*

Add to this *1 Cor. 1:2*, where the true believers are described as those who call upon the name of Jesus Christ; and *1 Thess. 3:11, 12.* Where Paul says, *Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus Christ, direct our way to you, and the Lord increase you, and make you abound.*

Furthermore, it is no wonder if the Son is not prayed to as frequently as the Father, since he is regarded as our <term>Mediator: a bridge or go-between who reconciles humanity with God</term> and Advocate, in whose name our Prayers are made.

7. **Objection.** The Son of God is not God. He denies this proposition; the Son is not the first Divine <term>Person: in Trinitarian theology, a "Person" refers to the distinct identities of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit within the one Godhead</term>, I admit that; but he does not therefore cease to be God.

<margin>John 5:19.</margin>
8. **Objection.** *John 5:19.* The Son can do nothing of himself, unless he sees the Father doing it.

I answer. This does not prove that the Son is not God. It is even remarkable that *Christ* gave this answer to the Jews to prove to them that he was not wrong to make himself equal with the Father: therefore he adds, *For whatever the Father does, the Son also does in like manner.*

Moreover, we must observe that if Christ could do nothing of himself through lack of power, we would have reason

<column-break/>

to doubt his Divinity: but it is said that the Son can do nothing of himself unless he sees the Father doing it, in order to make known the excellent harmony between the Father and the Son.

Finally, *Christ* speaks here as Mediator, and in this respect he attributes everything to his Father. He even speaks in a human manner: for, just as one says that children follow the example of their Parents, so *Christ* says that he does nothing except what he has seen his Father do.

<margin>John 7:16, 17.</margin>
9. **Objection.** *John 7:16, 17.* My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me, etc.

I answer. *Christ* is looking at the thoughts of the Jews, who, regarding him as a mere man, mocked his teaching and imagined that it was an invention of his own brain; which necessitated him to counter them: *My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me.*

10. **Objection.** Since *Christ* is sent by the Father, can one believe that he is God?

I answer. If the Son were sent by the Father as a superior sends an inferior, one would have reason to conclude that he is not God: but this is a sending of equals by mutual consent.

<margin>John 5:31.</margin>
11. **Objection.** *John 5:31.* If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true. Is that the language of a God?

I answer. *Christ* offers this as a proverb of the Jews, to the Jews themselves, who believed him to be only a mere man and would not accept his testimony about himself; but for the rest, *Christ* makes his thoughts known when he adds *vs. 34, 35, 36.* I receive no testimony from man, but I say these things so that you might be saved, etc. I have a greater testimony than [that] of John, for the works which the Father has given me to accomplish, the very works that I do, bear witness of me, that the Father has sent me. And *John 8:14.* Even if I bear witness of myself, [yet] my witness is true, etc.

Answer. Who does not see that *Christ* is reasoning against the Jews, who imagined that
