# DIVINITY. Book III. Part B. Chapter XII.

...he had no other aim than to attain a vain honor in the world? Besides the fact that Christ, as <term>mediator</term> <note>A go-between; in Christian theology, the role of Jesus in reconciling humanity with God.</note>, always gives the glory for everything to God the Father.

<margin>John 12:44.</margin>
13. **Objection.** *He who believes in me, believes not in me, but in him who sent me.* John 12:44.

I answer. Christ's aim is not to prevent people from believing in him, for he says to his disciples in chapter 14:1: *You believe in God, believe also in me.* And elsewhere it is often said: *whoever believes in him has eternal life.* Rather, he wants to make known that whoever believes in him, believes not only in him, but also in the one who sent him, just as when he says in Mark 9:37: *Whoever receives me, receives not me, but him who sent me.*

<margin>Volkel, *On Religion*, Book 5, Ch. 11. Matt. 24:36, Mark 13:32.</margin>
14. **Objection.** If Christ were God, he would have known the day of judgment; meanwhile, he testifies that he does not know it:

*But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, but my Father only.* Matthew 24:36. And Mark 13:32: *But of that day and that hour no one knows, neither the angels who are in heaven, nor the Son, but the Father.*

<margin>Cameron</margin>
I answer. <note>The author refers here to John Cameron, a 17th-century Scottish theologian.</note> Christ did not know the day of judgment as a man, though he did as God. For the thoughts of those teachers cannot please me who say that "to know" here only means "to teach," as in 1 Corinthians 2:2: *I determined not to know anything among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.* That is, "to teach." For what is said previously regarding the angels shows that "to know" is used here in its literal sense.

<margin>Crell.</margin>
It is said <note>The author is likely citing Johannes Crellius, a leading Socinian thinker who argued against the Trinity.</note>: If Christ had known the day of Judgment in any respect, he would not have stated so categorically that he did not know it; just as a person does not think to say "I do not eat" simply because his soul does not eat.

I answer. 1. We say every day, "man is mortal," even though his soul is immortal. 2. Christ says, "I do not know the day of Judgment," in respect to his human nature, which was visible so as to be believed; judging only by outward appearance, just as we say we eat and are mortal—even though our soul does not eat and is not mortal—because we are considering that part of ourselves which alone is visible and mortal.

<margin>Matt. 20:23.</margin>
15. **Objection.** *You shall indeed drink my cup, and be baptized with the baptism with which I*

<column-break/>

*am baptized; but to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to give, but it shall be given to those for whom it is prepared by my Father.* Matthew 20:23.

One can answer that Christ wants to make known that in the <term>state of his humiliation</term> <note>The period of Jesus's life on earth where he set aside his divine glory.</note> in which he was when he spoke, it did not belong to him to distribute this glory.

But I also say that Christ answers according to the thoughts of the one speaking to him; that person believed it was up to Christ to give this glory to whomever he pleased, whether the Heavenly Father had ordained it for him or not. Christ answers that he cannot give it except to those for whom the Heavenly Father has prepared it. As in Mark 10:40. For otherwise it is said in Revelation 3:21: *To him who overcomes, I will grant to sit with me on my throne.*

<margin>Matt. 19:17.</margin>
16. The answer is thrown back that Christ gave to the one who called him "Good Master": *Why do you call me good? No one is good but one, namely, God.* Matthew 19:17.

<margin>Vulgate</margin>
Answer. We have shown elsewhere that Christ only wanted to make known to this youth that he should not call him "good" because the youth did not regard him as God. Some read it <note>original: "waarom vraagt gy my, naar 't goede?"</note> as if it said, "Why do you ask me about that which is good?" <note>This refers to a textual variation found in some Greek manuscripts and the Latin Vulgate.</note>

<margin>Matt. 26:39.</margin>
17. **Objection.** If Christ were God, would he have a will different from that of his Father? Yet this appears from what he says in Matthew 26:39: *Not as I will, but as you will.*

I answer. Christ speaks here as a man. Since the Savior has two natures, he also has two wills.

<margin>John 14:28.</margin>
18. It is objected from John 14:28: *I go away to the Father, for my Father is greater than I.*

Answer. It is clear that he speaks here of his human nature, according to which he went to the Father; for in respect to his divine nature, he is one with the Father.

<margin>Matt. 28:18.</margin>
19. It is further objected from Matthew 28:18: *All power is given to me.*

But I answer: That since Christ can be considered as the Son of God or as the mediator, one must also distinguish a twofold power: the one which is essential to him as God, and the other which he has received as Mediator.

20. **Objection.** *Christ* is not God, since God is called "his God." John 20:17, Eph. 1:17, Heb. 1:9, Rev. 3:12.

<margin>Ps. 45 and Heb. 1:8.</margin>
I answer: That the Prophet and the Apostle, who tell us that God the Father is the God of his Son, do not fail to call him God. *O God! your God has anointed you.* <note>original: "O God! uwe God heeft u gezalft." Referring to Psalm 45:7 and Hebrews 1:8-9, where the speaker addresses the Son as "God" even while mentioning "his God."</note> From this it follows only that they are not the same person.

21. **Objection.** *Jesus Christ* being a mediator, cannot be God.

I answer: He is both the one and the other, and he could not have been a mediator if he were not God.

22. **Objection.** If *Christ* were God, he would not have been born of a Virgin, died, and been buried, etc.

But from this one can draw no conclusion other than that *Christ*, according to the nature in which he was born, died, and was buried, is not God. <note>The author is distinguishing between Christ's divine nature and his human nature.</note>

<margin>Col. 1:15.</margin>
23. **Objection.** *Christ* is only the image of God.

I answer: He is the image, and at the same time God. An image that has the same essence as its original, and is one with the Father.

They persist in saying that from this it follows that the Son is his own image. But they do not notice that the Father, whose image *Christ* is, is distinguished from the Son, even though he has the same essence.

They say: *Christ* is God’s image because he revealed his will to us.

<margin>Acts 20:27.</margin>
Answer: If that is true, then Paul would also be God’s image, because he proclaimed to us all the counsel of God.

<column-break/>

<margin>Col. 1:15.</margin>
24. **Objection.** *Christ* is the firstborn of all <term>creatures</term> <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to all created things in the universe.</note>; consequently, he is a creature: for the firstborn is of the same nature as his brothers.

Answer: Some believe that Paul means nothing other than that *Christ* exists before all creatures, which is—according to the style of the scriptures—from eternity.

But I believe that he intends to say here that *Christ* is the Lord and Prince of all creatures, because he adds: *by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth.* It is as if he said, he is the Prince of all creatures because there is not one that he did not create. But furthermore, it is well known that the word "Firstborn" is often taken to mean "Lord." God promised to make David his firstborn son; the highest over the kings of the earth: that is, to make him the first and most prominent of kings.

<margin>
Ps. 89:28.
Job 18:13.
</margin>
Job calls "the firstborn of death" <note>original: "Eerstgeboorenen des doods"</note> the one who has dominion and power over death. This way of speaking is grounded in the <term>sovereignty</term> that the eldest formerly held over their brothers, as heads of the household. Therefore, the right of the "firstborn" of *Christ* here signifies his absolute dominion over the whole universe, and each of its parts in particular: compare this with Heb. 1:2. There the Apostle notes that God has appointed his Son as an Heir of all things; and he adds, *by him he also made the worlds.* He expresses the power and dominion of *Christ* over all creatures through the word "Heir." It was customary for the ancients to use this word to mean Lord and Master, as legal scholars have noted. And subsequently, Paul grounds the dominion of *Christ* on the fact that he is the Creator.

<margin>1 Tim. 2:5.</margin>
25. **Objection.** 1 Tim. 2:5. *There is one mediator, the man Jesus Christ.* But 1. If *Christ* were only a man, Paul would have spoken differently. Who would say that the lawgiver of the Hebrews was "the man Moses"; or the Messiah's forerunner was "the man John the Baptist"? 2. This passage proves that *Christ* is man, but does not deny his Divinity; and the work of salvation itself required that he be God. 3. We shall see why Paul calls him man here in Book IX, Chapter 32.

There are still some other objections made—

...that he would be called God’s Son for that reason, and for that cause alone—that he was conceived by the Holy Spirit: he is so named because of the union of the human nature, which was conceived by the Holy Spirit, with the Divine nature, according to which Christ is the Son of God.

One must then observe that, while the Holy Spirit formed the Body of the Lord Jesus in the womb of Mary, the Son of God personally united Himself with humanity—consisting of Soul and Body—so that the human nature and the Divine nature, making but one Person, this Person was called God’s Son: yet for a different reason than the conception by the Holy Spirit.

Christ being God’s Son and willing to become man, his Body could not be conceived except in perfect Holiness, nor prepared in a manner befitting him except by God’s immediate power.

For the rest, these words are a clear allusion to the cloud that formerly covered the Tabernacle of Moses.

3. One must also not believe that Christ is called God’s Son with respect to his appointment to the office of mediator: that cannot be proven by *John 10:34, 35, 36*, as one will admit if one examines this passage thoroughly.

<margin>John 10:34-36.</margin>
The Jews having accused *J. Christ* of blasphemy because he had made himself God, *J. Christ* refutes them in this way. *Is it not written in your Law, I have said, you are Gods? If (the law) called them Gods to whom the word of God came, and the Scripture cannot be broken; do you say (to me) whom the Father has sanctified and sent into the world, you blaspheme (God) because I said, I am God’s Son?* One sees that the aim of *J. Christ* is to give the Jews to understand that if *Israel’s* Authorities, the Judges of the Great Council <note>Original: *Grooten-raad*, referring to the Sanhedrin, the supreme judicial and ecclesiastical council of ancient Jerusalem.</note>, are called Gods because God had placed them in this dignity, and their exaltation was but a shadow of his, then one could not accuse him of blasphemy because he had said, *I am God’s Son;* him, whom the Father had sanctified for the greatest of all ministries, and sent into the world for the Salvation of men, to satisfy his justice and to uphold the Right of the Deity. There is no one but a God who could acquit himself well in so

<column-break/>

great, so Glorious, and difficult an Office. *Christ’s* reasoning then proceeds from the lesser to the greater; proving his Divinity by the excellence of his ministries: but it does not follow from this that he is only called God because he is honored with the Office of Mediator.

One will say: Christ provides no other reason.

->**Answer.**<- He was not obliged to express himself more clearly.

But I add to this, that he expresses himself sufficiently, for 1. he says in his answer that the Father has sanctified him, which shows that he was already God’s Son before the Father sent him into the world, and that he did not call himself Son of God because he was sanctified and sent, but that he brought this forward as a sufficient proof to stop the mouths of the Jews. 2. The continuation of his reasoning confirms us in these thoughts. *If I do not the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, and if you do not believe me, believe the works; so that you may know and believe that the Father is in me, and I in him.* Therefore (it says) the Jews sought again to seize him. *John 10:37, 38.*

<margin>Smalcius, *On the Son of God*, Chapter 11. <note>Original Latin: *Smalc. de Dei Filio. c. XI.* Valentinus Smalcius was a noted Socinian theologian who argued against the Trinity.</note></margin>
4. One must also not think that *Christ* is called God because the Father has raised him from the Dead to an immortal Life, and that he has been generated as if anew from the womb of the Earth: for it is admitted that he was already God’s Son before his resurrection. We shall answer concerning *Acts 13:32, 33* elsewhere.

5. For the same reason, we say that *Christ* is not called God’s Son because he has been appointed as an Heir of all things and exalted upon the Throne of the Universe; this cannot be proven from *Hebrews 1:2*. The Apostle says that God has spoken to us through his Son, whom he has made an Heir of all things, but he does not say, *Christ* is called Son because he is Heir. It is true, *Paul* adds in verse 4, after he had spoken of *Christ* sitting at God’s right hand, that he has become so much more excellent than the Angels as he has inherited a more excellent name above them. But it does not follow from this that *Christ* is called God’s Son by reason of his exaltation.

# DIVINE THEOLOGY. III. B. XIII. Chapter. 255

Certainly, if one reads the scripture attentively, one will find that the name Son of God was given to him to signify his person, and what he is in himself; for all ages, independent of his offices with which he was clothed, of the works that he has done, of what happened to him in the world, and of the Glory to which he was elevated as mediator. 

Therefore, one sees that Christ is called God’s Son because the Father has generated <note>The author uses the term "genereeren" (to generate or beget) to describe the eternal relationship between the Father and the Son, a central concept in orthodox Trinitarian theology.</note> him. 

This the Holy Scripture teaches us. David introduces God speaking thus to his Son in Psalm 2:7: *You are my Son, today I have begotten you.* Paul, citing this passage, says in Hebrews 1:5: *To which of the Angels has he ever said, you are my Son, today I have begotten you?* 

The second Psalm is a Prophetic Psalm, in which there are several things that could indeed fit David, but fit Christ better; and there are others that only agree with Christ. Christians who have read Acts 4 and 13, Hebrews 1 and 5, and Revelation 2, cannot doubt this; and if one examines Hebrews 1:5, where Paul shows that it was never said to any Angels, *you are my Son, today I have begotten you,* one easily understands that this cannot be said of David. Just as little as the following: *ask of me, I will give the Heathen for your inheritance,* etc. *Kiss the Son,* etc. *Blessed are all they that trust in him.* As for the Jews, they cannot deny that this Psalm was attributed to the Messiah by their ancient Teachers. "Our Masters," they say, "have interpreted this Song as referring to the Messiah; but, because of the Christians, we must interpret it as referring to David."

<margin>
Eniedin. <note>Gyorgy Enjedin (1555–1597), a prominent Unitarian theologian who argued against the Trinity.</note>
Le Cène. <note>Charles Le Cène (1647–1703), a French Protestant known for his controversial views on biblical translation.</note>
</margin>

One cannot weaken the power of the Prophet's expressions; and those who translate these words thus—*you are my Son, I have today placed you upon the Throne*—applying this passage to David, whether when he was anointed by Samuel, or when he was made King after the death of Saul, or when he regained his Kingdom after the death of Absalom, do so without any foundation, oppose the scripture, and cannot justify their opinion. 

It is beyond all appearance of truth that God would have said with such figurative words what he had previously expressed with such clear 

<column-break/>

words: *Yet have I set my King upon Zion, the Hill of my Holiness.* And that he would have used an expression that is never taken in that sense. 

The word translated as "generate" <note>original: "genereeren"</note> never means "to elevate to the Throne"; there is no example of it. Especially when it is joined with the word Son. *You are my Son, today I have begotten you.*

<margin>

</margin>

It is said that Matthew 14:6 and Mark 6:21 speak of the day of Herod's birth; that by that day, the day of his coronation is understood; that it was the style of the Greeks and Latins to call the day of coronation and the election as emperor the "day of birth." 

But 1. It will never be proven that in Matthew 14 or Mark 6, by "the day of Herod's birth," the day of his Coronation must be understood; one cannot show that this is the customary sense of these words, or that it must be taken so in that place. 2. Even if this were so, one could not prove that people spoke this way in David's time. 3. Finally, there is no dispute here over the word "birthday," but over the word "generate," which is never used in that way. 

Hosea 7:5 is brought forward. But in that place, there is mention of neither birth nor generation; but only of "the day of the King," which can indeed be understood as the day of his birth or coronation. But nothing follows from that against our view. 

1 Samuel 13:1 is cited, where it is said, *Saul was a Son of a year.* <note>The Hebrew idiom "son of a year" usually means "one year old." The author is debating whether this refers to his age or the duration of his reign.</note> To say that he had been on the Throne for a year. 

But we do not dispute the word "Son," but the word "Son" joined to that of "generate": for otherwise we agree that the Hebrews use the word Son in many expressions. *Saul was a Son of a year* means nothing other than "Saul had reigned for a year." The word Son then does not signify his elevation; that is signified by the word "Reign," which stands in our translation by way of explanation. 

One can say of a child, according to the style of the Hebrews—whatever kind of child it may be—that is only a year old: "it is a Son of a year." 

<margin>Heb. 5:5.</margin>

Furthermore, Paul applies these words to the Priesthood of Christ, saying in Hebrews...

# THE CHRISTIAN GOD

<margin>Hebrews 5:5</margin>
Christ did not glorify himself to become a High Priest, but he who said to him, *You are my Son, today I have begotten you.* <note>original: "gegenereert"</note>

Answer: It is clear that Paul intends to say nothing else than that Christ did not push himself into the High Priesthood; rather, it was the same One who inaugurated him into this weighty ministry for our salvation and, declaring him to be his Son, showed that he alone could reconcile men with the Deity. That is the meaning of this passage; but it does not follow from this that David's words refer solely to the Priesthood of Christ.

<margin>Acts 2:32, 33</margin>
It is said that Paul applies these words to the resurrection of Christ; consequently, it is argued that no generation <note>The term "generation" here refers to the eternal process of the Son being "brought forth" by the Father.</note> of God’s Son is spoken of there. Acts 13:32, 33: *We declare to you the promise which was made to the fathers, that God has fulfilled the same to us their children, in that he has raised up Jesus; as it is also written in the second Psalm, You are my Son, today I have begotten you.*

<margin>Schlichting on Hebrews 1:4, 5</margin> <note>Jonas Schlichting (1592–1661) was a famous Polish Socinian theologian who argued against the Trinity, suggesting Jesus only became "Son" at his resurrection.</note>
It is ridiculous to say that "to beget" <note>original: "genereeren"</note> means to rise from the dead; never is this word used in such a sense.

But 1. Those who object to this must admit that Christ was God’s Son and born of God before his resurrection. One only needs to read the passage to be convinced that Paul wants to teach us that the Father, by raising his Son and clothing him with Honor and Glory, declared that he held him for his well-beloved Son, whom he had begotten before all ages. Paul gives the explanation of this passage in Romans 1:3, 4, when he says, *concerning his Son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh; and declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead, (namely) Jesus Christ our Lord.* While Christ was on earth, he had called himself God’s Son, which he had confirmed through his miracles; but his word and miracles were so disputed that God, by raising him from the dead, decided the dispute and highly declared him to be his Son: for he would never have raised him if he had been a deceiver.
There is, then, nothing that prevents us from taking the

<column-break/>

words of David in the natural sense, which immediately offers itself to the understanding.

<margin>Proverbs 8:24</margin>
This same truth is confirmed by Proverbs 8:24, where eternal wisdom <note>In Christian tradition, the "Wisdom" mentioned in Proverbs is often identified with the person of Jesus Christ (the Logos).</note> says that she was begotten. The root word carries great weight.

It is said that the term "Son of God" and "Christ" are the same; Matthew 16:16: *You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.* And Luke 9:20: *You are the Christ of God.* But 1. All that one can conclude from this is that the same person who is the Christ is also the Son of God. 2. It appears clearly that these two things are distinguished in Matthew, where it says, *You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.*

Jesus Christ is then God’s Son by his essence, and not by adoption and grace. He is not the Son because God loves him; rather, God loves him because he is his Son.

Felix and Elipandus, who were condemned in the Council of Frankfurt in the year 794, believed that Christ was God’s Son by adoption <note>Felix of Urgel and Elipandus of Toledo were leaders of the "Adoptionist" heresy, which claimed Christ was only "adopted" as God's Son in his human nature.</note> with respect to his human nature.

One asks what this generation of the Son means. That cannot be explained. Gregory Nazianzen says: "One must

### THEOLOGY. III. B. XIII. Chapter.

...to clarify. See also Basil <note>Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379), an influential Greek bishop and theologian.</note> homily 25. "It is enough for us," he says, "to know that the Father has generated his Son. It does not belong to us to seek to discover *how* he has generated him. These are abysses in which reason loses itself, but faith embraces these truths because they have been revealed."

There are those who wish to explain this Generation by saying that God, knowing and contemplating himself, brought forth his Image and his Word, which is his Son. But this is to explain a dark matter with something darker, or at least equally obscure. If the Father brings forth his Image and generates his Son by contemplating himself, why should he not bring forth another Image and generate another Son by contemplating his Image and his Son, and so on?

It is enough that we know:

1. That this Generation is Eternal; many theologians prove this with Psalm 2:7, *Today I have generated you*, believing that the Prophet, through this word "today," intends to signify Eternity. And I confess that, although no time properly corresponds with Eternity—being neither past, nor present, nor future—nevertheless, the present time signified by the word "today" corresponds better with it than any other time, because all things are present before God. But one must admit that this proof is not equally convincing to everyone, and that these words can be interpreted differently.

One can give them this sense: *You are my Son; I have shown today, by anointing you as King of the Church, that you are the one whom I generated before the foundation of the ages.* This follows the idiom of the Scriptures, which says that a thing "has become" when it is revealed or made manifest. Thus Elijah said to the Israelites, 1 Kings 18:24: *The God who answers by fire, he shall be God*, meaning he shall be *recognized* as God. Thus Christ said in Matthew 5:44-45: *Love your enemies... so that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven*, meaning so that it may be *evident* that you are children of God. *Let God be true, but every*

<sig>Part I.</sig>

<column-break/>

*man a liar*, Romans 3:4, meaning let God be *acknowledged* as true. Thus, *Today I have generated you* is to say: I have today made it manifest that I have generated you, namely, from Eternity.

I shall then, in order to prove the Eternity of this Generation, bring forward two other places.

<margin>1 Prov. 8:22-25.</margin>
The 1st place is Proverbs 8:22. *The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old.* (a)

Vs. 23–25. *I was anointed from eternity, from the beginning, from the ancient times of the earth. I was born when the abysses were not yet, when there were no fountains heavy with water. Before the mountains were settled, before the hills, I was born.* All these expressions signify Eternity.

<margin>Micah 5:1 <note>In modern English bibles, this is Micah 5:2.</note></margin>
The 2nd place is Micah 5:1. *Out of you, O Bethlehem, shall come forth to me one who is to be a Ruler in Israel, whose goings forth are from of old, from the days of eternity.* It is clear that the Prophet here describes two "goings forth" of the Messiah: one visible, in time, out of Bethlehem; the other Eternal, from of old, from the days of eternity. Christians cannot understand this divine oracle as referring to anyone other than Christ; <margin>Matt. 2:6.</margin> and the Jews make themselves ridiculous by applying it to Zerubbabel <note>A governor of the Persian province of Judah and a grandson of Jehoiachin, who led the first group of Jews back from Babylonian captivity.</note>. It is an absurdity to say that this only means the Messiah would descend from David; for the lineage of David was not so old in the time of Micah that one could say the Messiah’s "goings forth" were from of old, from the days of Eternity, merely to say he would come from David. Furthermore, it would not be such great praise for the Messiah to say he took his beginning from David, since many others had that same honor. The Prophet uses the very expressions that the Spirit of God employs to signify Eternity. Habakkuk 1:12, Proverbs 8:23.

II. One must note that this Generation does not resemble common births. When one applies human actions to God, one must remove all imperfections from them, and attribute nothing to God but what is perfect. It is a...

# DE CHRISTELYKE #
->Volmaaktheid van de Generatie<- <note>The Perfection of the Generation</note> / that the Father communicates his essence to his Son; in this respect one can understand / that the same can take place in God / and that he / generating his Son / makes him a partaker of his existence and perfections. This seems to be explained to us by Christ in John 5:26, saying / *just as the Father has life in himself, so has he also given to the Son to have life in himself.* But one must not conceive of a Generation in God / that includes a division, separation, inequality, or priority of time. One must not believe / that the Father is earlier than the Son / and the Son distinct from the Father / as takes place among men / where the Father precedes / and the Son has a similar / but not the same essence / since their nature is finite and many [individuals] cannot share the same essence.

I confess / that these are things / which one cannot understand; but who does not easily see / that the finite cannot comprehend the infinite?

<margin>Benoist's Sermons</margin> Paul / speaking of Christ / says in Hebrews 1:3 that he is the radiance <note>original: "afschynzel" — literally a reflection or outshining radiance.</note> of God’s Glory. Some theologians believe / that this expression includes 4 things. 1. That the Son is generated of the Father / essentially / just as a radiance shines from the light. 2. That this Generation is Eternal / just as the radiance is as old as the light itself. 3. That the same is without defect and without weakness / just as the radiance takes nothing away from the light / from which it proceeds / does not disturb it / does not diminish it / nor separate itself from it. 4. That the Father and the Son are of one and the same nature / just as the light / and the radiance. But one must not press these parables too much / because / as the theologians remark / nothing is found in the Creature / that can perfectly show us what is in the Creator; these Symbols are far too imperfect / to express the whole subject / to which they are applied.

To speak plainly / we do not need to know / how the Father generates the Son.

It is enough for us to know:
1. That Christ is God / Eternally to be praised with his Father.
2. That he is the proper / and only Son of God.
3. Generated of his Father.

<column-break/>

4. That he has been before all ages.
5. That he is Eternal just like his Father / because he is God.
6. That he and the Father are one.
7. That he did not consider it robbery / to be equal to the Father. <note>original: "geen roof heeft geagt" — a reference to Philippians 2:6; in modern Bibles often translated as "did not consider equality with God something to be grasped."</note>
8. That he then has the same existence / and the same perfections.
9. That he is nevertheless distinct from the Father / so that the Father is not the Son / nor the Son the Father.
10. That the Father has generated the Son; but that the Son does not generate the Father / and never has generated him.
11. That the Father has given to the Son to have life in himself / but that the Son has not given life to the Father.
12. That the Generation does not only mean / that there is a communion of existence between the Father and the Son / but also a communication of essence <term>mededeeling van wezen: the theological concept that the Father shares his entire divine nature with the Son</term>: for otherwise one could say / that the Son and the Holy Spirit generate the Father / which is found nowhere.
13. That there has been no time / in which the Father was without the Son / and the Son without the Father; and that they both have existed from Eternity.

All of this is found in the Scripture with clear words / or derived from it by necessary consequences.

Why does one wish to know more? Is it not an intolerable pride / to reject what one does not understand? As if for a finite reason nothing should be incomprehensible / which cannot contain an infinity of things / which are nevertheless finite. Our Soul does not understand itself / and yet it wants to understand its Creator! It does not know how it is united with its Body / and how it understands the words and sciences / that it is taught / and it wants to understand all that is in God. What extravagance!

I will not delay here / to refute the objections / since they all spring from common human Generation / whereas we have remarked on the contrary / that one must by no means mix that with this.

I also do not delay to answer the questions / that are made regarding this matter: I take honor in confessing my ignorance / and testify highly that I know nothing at all of it. I have learned to go where the light of God leads—

### THEOLOGY. BOOK III. CHAPTER XIII. ###

I shall say something of the sentiments of the <term>Early Church Fathers</term> <note>original: "Oud-Vaders" — the influential Christian theologians of the first few centuries after Christ.</note> concerning the generation of the Son. It is certain / that the Early Fathers / notwithstanding that they believed the mystery of the Trinity / and the Divinity of the Son and of the Holy Spirit / as we shall see / nevertheless had very strange thoughts regarding the generation of the Son. For / although they recognized the Eternity of the Word / they ascribed to him a certain birth / which had a beginning / and which occurred just before or immediately preceding the creation of the world. This has been shown by Bull, Jurieu, and others from many passages of Athenagoras, of Theophilus of Antioch (Book 2, *To Autolycus* <note>original: "ad Autol."</note>), Hippolytus, Tertullian, etc. For this reason, these learned men believe / that one may conclude / that these Fathers held this opinion: 1. That God was never without his Word. 2. That he eternally had communion with the same; but that he generated it at the beginning of the world / when he wished to create the Universe through the same.

Bull has believed / that one must understand these passages as a metaphorical generation: Jurieu does not believe it. 1. Because one is not aware of metaphorical ways of speaking [here]; but that the Early Fathers proved this sentiment. 2. Because to speak metaphorically against the foundations of the Trinity / would be the extreme of imprudence / and inexcusable grossness. 3. That they would not have brought forth such hard things based on a mere figure of speech.

<margin>
Book 1, *On the Trinity* <note>original: "de Trin."</note> ch. 5. No. 7. 
Huet, 
*Origeniana* <note>original: "Huet. Orig."</note>. 
Schultetus, 
*Marrow of the Fathers* <note>original: "Schult. Medul. Pat."</note>.
</margin>
The Jesuit Petau maintains / that they fell into the sentiment of the <term>Arians</term> <note>Arianism was the belief that Jesus was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father.</note>. Huet seems to have had no better thoughts of it. Schultetus says / after he had cited the words of Theophilus / "what is that other than Arianism?" But Jurieu proves / that one cannot accuse them of either Arianism or <term>Socinianism</term> <note>Socinianism was a 16th/17th-century belief that denied the pre-existence of Christ and the Trinity.</note>; not of Socinianism, for they believed / that Christ existed before the creation of the world; not of Arianism, for those called Christ a mere Creature / having had a beginning / that was made out of nothing; which the Early Fathers never said. He further notes / that according to the Early Fathers / the Son of God existed as *Reason* <note>original: "reden" — likely referring to the Greek *Logos endiathetos* or internal reason.</note> from Eternity in and with the Father / but as *Word* <note>original: "Woord" — likely referring to the Greek *Logos prophorikos* or the uttered word at creation.</note> he had a beginning; that the Son and the

<column-break/>

Holy Spirit were enclosed in the bosom of the Father / like a child / that is enclosed in its Mother's womb with all its members; having life / essence / movement / and operation / but not yet released. Whatever the thoughts of the Early Fathers may have been / which we may have the opportunity to speak of in another work; it appears that by wanting to explain this unspeakable mystery / they brought forth unseemly propositions / to say no more.

I then end this Chapter: but I cannot pass by / without drawing these consequences from it.

1. That one cannot highly enough esteem God's goodness / that for our salvation he sent into the world / not an Angel / or any creature / but his own Son. Therefore the scripture gives us to understand / how infinite God's love has been / in giving us so great a gift of grace; this John presents to us constantly and without ceasing in his Gospel / and in his first epistle; and Christ himself in John 3:16. Where he cries out / *For God so loved the world, that he gave his only-begotten Son.* What obliges me to make this remark / is that / if Christ is not God / then there is no reason to be amazed at God's mercy; for if Christ is merely a man / then the gift of Christ is of less value / than the salvation of the human race.

Why would there be so much reason / to highly esteem the love of Christ / for having been only a mere creature / is he not well rewarded with the commission of dominion over the Universe / for a little suffering?

2. It appears / how great the salvation is / for which God has bestowed his own Son; for there must be a proportion between the work / and the worker.

3. The third consequence is / that our salvation is firm and unshakable / since a God has acquired the same for us.

4. From this it also follows / that we must have a perfect trust in God's love / which is grounded in the love / that he bears toward his Son; and that we may come to approach God's Throne with boldness and assurance / since it is a Throne of Grace / to which God's Son calls us.

### CHAPTER XIV.

#### On the necessity of believing that Jesus Christ is God in order to be saved.

<margin>Simon Episcopius, *Theological Institutes*, book 4, chapter 34.</margin>
<margin>Pierre Jurieu, *Table of Socinianism*, page 154, etc.</margin>
We have proven that Jesus Christ is God and the Son of God; we shall now examine / whether it is necessary to believe this truth in order to be saved.

Two or three remarks will clearly prove it / against those who deny it.

1. It is certain / that one cannot be saved without believing in Christ. All of scripture teaches us this. But it is not having true faith in Christ / to regard him as a mere man / if it is true / that he is God / as we have proven: just as it would not be true faith in Christ / to regard him only as God: for the object of our faith is Jesus Christ / God and man; Jesus Christ died and was raised. <margin>1 John 5:10.</margin> Whoever does not believe the testimony that God has given of his Son, makes him a liar. And whoever makes God a liar / cannot be saved; but God has not only testified that his Son is man / but that he is his own Son / <term>generated<note>The theological term for the Son's eternal origin from the Father.</note></term> before all the ages / and that he is God. One cannot, then, be saved / if one rejects the principal part of this testimony / which declares him to be his eternal Son / and God eternally to be praised.

<margin>1 John 4:3.</margin>
2. John says: *every spirit that does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, that is not of God; but this is (the spirit) of the Antichrist.* 1 John 4:3. To deny the <term>Incarnation<note>Dutch: *Menschwerding*; the doctrine of God becoming human in Jesus.</note></term> / is to be Antichrist. Now, one cannot have the spirit of the Antichrist / and be saved. It should also be noted here / that / according to all probability / and according to the notes of the <term>Early Church Fathers<note>The influential theologians of the first few centuries of Christianity.</note></term> / John here specifically opposes those heretics / who in his time troubled the Church / by denying the Divinity of Christ and his Incarnation

<column-break/>

Nothing of weight can be brought against this proof.

One will perhaps say / that in the common translation it says, *Every spirit that divides and separates Jesus, is not of Christ.* <note>original Latin: *Omnis spiritus qui solvit Jesum*. This was a variant reading found in some Latin manuscripts of 1 John 4:3.</note> But 1. Besides the manuscripts we have / and nearly all printed editions / as we have indicated / which read as it stands in John; one need only look at the preceding verse / to be convinced that it is well translated. <margin>verse 2.</margin> In the preceding verse, the common translation and all Greek copies read unanimously, *Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, is of God.* From this it appears / that in the following verse one must read / *he who does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, is not of God;* It is certain / that to "separate" and "divide" Christ / is to deny and destroy one or the other of his natures <note>Meaning his divine nature and his human nature.</note>.

One will say / that to be Antichrist / is to deny that Christ has come into the world / that is / that he was a man; but from that it does not follow / that to deny his Divinity / is to be Antichrist. But 1. One must note / that to deny that Jesus Christ has come into the world / is to deny his Incarnation; and to deny the Incarnation / is to deny that Christ, being God, became Man / and that the Word / which was God / became Flesh. Furthermore, John is not only speaking against the heretics / who denied that Christ was a true Man; but also against those who denied his Divinity / such as the <term>Cerinthians<note>Followers of Cerinthus, who taught that the "Christ-spirit" descended on the man Jesus at his baptism and left before the crucifixion.</note></term>, and <term>Ebionites<note>An early Jewish Christian sect that regarded Jesus as a non-divine prophet.</note></term>. Finally / I say / if to deny the Humanity is to be Antichrist / it is even more Antichristian to deny his Divinity (if it is true that he is God / as we believe we have irrefragably proven) since the Divine Nature is infinitely more than the Human / and that it is an infinitely greater insult / to rob him of that which he has eternally / than of that which he only assumed in the fullness of time.

One will say, that this refers to the Jews / who denied the Incarnation of God’s Son / and disputed his Messiahship. Answer: But one will find nowhere / that the external enemies of Christianity / whether Jews / or Heathens / have been called Antichrists. It is a name / which / according to the...

# DIVINITY. BOOK III. CHAPTER XIV.

...the consensus of the Ancients <note>The "Ancients" refers to the Early Church Fathers</note>, in the Letter of John, signifies the enemies of our Lord Christ, who had to come from the bosom of Christianity. 1 John 2:18, 19: *they went out from us.*

<margin>1 John 2:23.</margin>
3. 1 John 2:23. *Whosoever denieth the Son, the same hath not the Father.* Now, one cannot deny that he who has not the Father cannot be saved; but to deny the Son is to deny the nature that makes him the Son of God, as we have already proven.

4. One cannot be saved without acknowledging Christ as our Savior, and as the one who has satisfied the justice of God for us. Now, one cannot accept him as such if one regards him only as a Man. The first of these propositions is scattered throughout the entire scripture; therefore Paul, describing the object of Faith, says: 
<margin>Rom. 4:25.</margin>
*Christ died for our sins, and was raised for our justification; God has set forth Christ to be a propitiation through his Blood.* The second proposition will be proven when we shall show that our Mediator had to be God.

5. One cannot be saved while being an Idolater. Now, it is Idolatry to worship Christ while viewing him merely as a man. Those who worship him must believe that he is God. These are two indisputable truths: that Idolaters shall not enter into the Kingdom of Heaven is certain according to scripture; and it is also fixed according to the same scripture that the object of our worship cannot be a creature, and that one must serve and worship God alone.

<margin>Episcopius, *Theological Institutes*, Book IV, 34, 35.</margin>
One cannot say with Episcopius <note>Simon Episcopius (1583–1643) was a prominent Dutch Remonstrant theologian who argued for a more limited requirement of belief for salvation</note> that it is enough, in order to worship Christ, to know that he is the true envoy of his Father, and that the commands he brought regarding faith and the obedience that must be given to him are the commands of God his Father; and [he argues] that it is [not] necessary to know *how* Jesus is the Son of his Father, but only that the Father named him his Son, and that he was sent in the name of his Father to save us, and that we owe him faith, obedience, and worship in this relationship. **Answer:** If one regards Christ only as an envoy, one must not give him Divine Honor until one simultaneously knows that he is God. One has never given

<sig>Kk 3</sig>

<column-break/>

to men such honor—neither to Moses, nor to the Prophets, nor to the Apostles—who were nevertheless envoys of the living God. Paul and Barnabas were moved with a holy indignation against the Lycaonians, who wished to offer sacrifices in their honor, even though they were God’s envoys. And everyone knows that the Angels, who are sent by God to earth to fulfill his commands, have refused to be worshipped.

It will be said that all honor and service due to Christ is, according to the declaration of scripture, an honor and service that is due to him only because the Father, whose envoy he is, has given him the power to receive the honor of worship and Religion. **Answer:** But that is offered as a proof which is still in dispute. The worship given to Christ, the envoy of the Heavenly Father, is given to him because he is God.

The first Christians regarded the belief in the Divinity of Jesus Christ as a doctrine necessary for salvation.

This can be proven:

<margin>Bull, *Defense of the Nicene Faith*, etc.</margin>
1. From what we read in the letters attributed to Ignatius, and in those said to be written by him to the Ephesians; where, speaking of the heretics of his time who contested the two natures of Christ, he says that one must flee from them as from beasts; that they are rabid animals who bite in secret. He condemns them to the unquenchable fire and says that their doctrine is the doctrine of the God of this age <note>Referring to the devil or worldly spirit</note>.

2. One can conclude the same from the writings of Irenaeus, who, dealing with the Heretics who claimed that Christ was only a Man, generated by Joseph, says that they are deprived of eternal life. Book 3, c. 21 and Book 5, c. 1.

<margin>*Prescription against Heretics*, c. 13.</margin>
3. Tertullian offers as a rule of Faith that we must believe there is one God, Creator of the world, who created all things from nothing through his word; that this word is called his Son, who appeared several times to the Patriarchs, who revealed himself to the Prophets, and finally descended into the womb of the Virgin Mary, and therein became Flesh.

He speaks even more strongly in his book *Against Praxeas*, c. 2.

4. Novatian <note>A 3rd-century scholar and priest in Rome</note>, who is believed to be the author of the book *On the Trinity* which is included among the works of Tertullian, condemns in chapter 11 the error of those who deny the Divinity of Christ and who say that he was only a man, a creature. He describes this as a very dangerous error, extremely blasphemous toward God the Father; and in chapter 12, he teaches that those who do not recognize Christ as God cannot be saved.

<margin>
Apology of Pamphilus the Martyr, among the Works of Jerome, Volume 9. Athanasius on the Decrees of the Synod of Nicaea, Volume 1.
</margin>
5. Origen, in a book he wrote on the Letter to Titus (which Pamphilus mentions in his defense), places among the heretics those who say that Jesus was born of Joseph and Mary, such as the Ebionites and the Valentinians. He also includes those who say that he is not the Firstborn and the God of all creation, the Word, and the Wisdom that is the beginning of his ways, etc., and that he is merely a man.

6. Dionysius, Bishop of Rome, calls the heresy of those who say that Jesus Christ was in any way "made with hands" <note>A phrase used to imply that Christ was a created being or an artifact of creation rather than the eternal Creator</note> a great blasphemy.

<margin>
Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers on John.
</margin>
7. If it is true, as Jerome testifies, that the Bishops of Asia requested John to write against Cerinthus and other heretics who said that Christ did not exist before Mary, then it is evident that these Bishops viewed this heresy as very harmful, since they requested an Apostle to refute it.

I speak elsewhere of the curses <note>Anathemas or formal excommunications</note> that the Early Church pronounced against the heretics who held the views that we are now contesting.

But let us hear what can be said against our position—that it is necessary to believe that Jesus Christ is God in order to be saved.

It is said, **1.** That the Early Church did not explicitly demand that Christians believe this truth in the Articles of Faith, which served as the "field-sign" <note>original: "Veldteken," meaning a standard, banner, or password used to distinguish friend from foe—in this context, the Creed used to distinguish believers from non-believers</note> by which Christians were distinguished from unbelievers.

**Answer:** It is evident from the writings of the Early Fathers already cited that they viewed this truth as essential to salvation; and it is not true that the Early Church did not require this confession.

It is said that the oldest Creed (*Symbolum*) in the time of the Apostles, used in the first administration of Baptism,

<column-break/>

consisted of this confession: *I believe in God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.*

**Answer:** This confession has never been regarded as a complete Creed containing all necessary Articles of Faith, but rather as a confession of the first Article of Faith regarding the Trinity.

**2.** It is clear that Christ is regarded as God in this short Creed; for it is the same as saying, "I believe in one God, who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit," as the Greeks explain it: *Into one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.* <note>original Greek: "Εἰς ἕνα Θεὸν, τὸν Πατέρα, τὸν υἱὸν, καὶ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα"</note> Now, that is calling Christ God. Therefore, Tertullian, explaining the common faith of Christians, says: "the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God; and each is God." Therefore, it seems to me that this confession very clearly indicates that the Son and the Holy Spirit are one and the same God with the Father.
<margin>Against Praxeas, chapter 13.</margin>

**3.** Tertullian and Irenaeus, who explained it, clearly show that Christ is God. See Irenaeus, book 1, chapter 19; book 3, chapter 4. Tertullian, *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 13; *Against Praxeas*, chapter 2. See also Cyprian, *Letter to Jubaianus*, who explicitly testifies that no one can be the Temple of Christ who denies that Christ is God.

It is said that the Creed which is called the "Apostles' Creed" makes no mention of the Divinity nor of the Sonship of the Son; there stand only these two words: *I believe in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.*

**Answer: 1.** This Creed was not composed or prescribed by the Apostles; and it is probable that it was first formed as it is now after the fourth century.

<margin>
In the Catechesis of a Bishop said to be John. Also the Jerusalem [Creed], page 276, published in Paris.
</margin>
The Divinity of Christ is clearly signified when he is called God’s "only Son"; for it is only as God that he is so named. And if "Son of God" meant nothing more than that he was born of a Virgin, then one would not see why Scripture exalts God’s love so highly in the giving of his Son. Furthermore, the Son is placed there before <note>or alongside</note> the Holy Spirit, which would not have been done if they had believed that Christ was merely a man.

The ancient Creed of the Jerusalem Church, brought forward by Cyril, Bishop of the same, speaking of Christ...

# DIVINE THEOLOGY. III. B. Chapter XIV.

...recognizing / calls him God's only Son, born of the Father before all ages; and he adds / that Christ is this true God / through whom all things were made.

This Creedal Formula preceded the one from Nicaea <note>The Council of Nicaea in 325 AD, which established the orthodox doctrine of Christ's divinity</note>; and it is very old.

It is probable that Eusebius, Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, had this Formula in mind / when at the Council of Nicaea, he recounted the Confession of Faith / which he had made upon receiving his Baptism / and thus states the Article concerning the Son. I believe in one Lord Jesus Christ, God from God, only Son, born of God the Father before all the ages; through whom all things were made.

2. A passage is presented from Justin Martyr, in the *Dialogue with Trypho*, from which some wish to prove / that in his time the ancient Church did not consider the belief in the Divinity of Christ to be necessary. But one only has to read it without prejudice / to be convinced / that this proves nothing at all.

He means nothing else than / that if he could not prove through the Prophets that the Christ must be God and must be born of a Virgin / (which he had already partly proven / and subsequently proves more extensively) he would therefore not lose his case against the Jews / since according to their own principles they could not deny / that our Lord Jesus / is the Christ. Thus he reasoned from the assumptions of the Jews of his time / who / as Trypho had said / expected nothing but a man / who must be born of a man. If one could prove from this passage of Justin / that it is not necessary to believe / that Christ is God / one could also prove / that it is not necessary to believe / that he was born of a Virgin; and that one can believe / that he was born like other men. One has only to read his writings / to be convinced / that he strongly believed in the Divinity of Christ. It is objected that it is said here / that there were Christians who denied the Divinity of Christ / but that proves nothing else / than that these heretics professed Christianity. It does not follow from this / that Justin held these people to be true members of the Church. Moreover / it is probable / that he wanted to indicate to Trypho / that these heretics were of this Jewish

<column-break/>

nation / and that there is an error in the Text; <term>διὰ τὸν ἡμέτερον γένους</term> <note>original Greek: "through our nation"</note> of our nation instead of <term>ἀπὸ τοῦ ὑμετέρου γένους</term> <note>original Greek: "from your nation"</note> of your nation, as can be shown from many places in this dialogue, and by the preceding page. It is clear that Justin speaks of the Ebionites <note>An early Jewish Christian sect that maintained Jewish Law but denied the full divinity of Jesus</note> / as the learned remark and prove.

<margin>
Epist. I. 4 Inst. Theol. c. 34.
</margin>
3. It is said: Scripture nowhere teaches us that it is necessary to believe / that Christ is God. But / in order to regard a truth as necessary for Salvation / must it be in the Scripture in explicit words / saying: you must believe such a truth on pain of eternal damnation? Is it not enough / that this truth is clearly contained in the Scripture / and that it has the hallmarks of a fundamental truth in Religion? Where is it said that one must believe in a Holy and Just God / to be saved? yet it is absolutely necessary to believe that; where is it said that one must believe in a providence? is it nonetheless not a fundamental truth?

<margin>
John III. 18.
</margin>
Besides that, it is certain / that one can have no true faith in Christ / without regarding him as God; for it is said / that one must believe in him to be saved. John 3:18. *He who believes in him (namely the Son) is not condemned, but he who does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only begotten Son of God.* It is then necessary to believe that Jesus Christ is God. Certainly to believe in the Son / is not only to believe that he is man / that he is the Messiah; it is to believe that he is Eternal God / like his Father / and that he has satisfied Divine Justice for the sins of men.

4. It is said / that it is enough to obtain salvation / that the honor and worship which belong to Jesus Christ / remain intact / without investigating whether Jesus Christ is God. But 1. There is nothing falser than this principle; for one could establish a religion / which would command / to worship God and Christ with the highest honor / and which yet having terrible errors / would be abominable: Manichaeism <note>A dualistic religion that combined elements of Christianity, Gnosticism, and Persian beliefs, often viewed as a major rival to early Christianity</note> is an abominable religion / yet meanwhile the Manichaeans worshiped God and Christ.

2. I do not understand how one can say /

# THE CHRISTIAN

<columns>

...those who deny the Divinity of Christ and regard him only as a creature, do not leave his rightful honor intact; since many deniers of the Trinity (Antitrinitarians) do not worship Jesus Christ.

3. Those who view him as a mere human either give him the same worship as they give to God, or a lesser form of worship. If they give him the same worship, they are idolaters, for they give to a creature what belongs to God alone; if they give a lesser worship, then one cannot say that they leave the worship of Christ intact: for if it is true—as we have established—that Christ is God, then he is robbed of his honor if he is not worshipped as God.

<margin>Bury: *Naked Gospel*. That is, the Gospel opened. <note>Arthur Bury (1624–1713) was an English theologian whose book *The Naked Gospel* was burned for heresy because it argued that complex doctrines like the Trinity were not essential for early Christians.</note></margin>

4. It is argued: One does not need to know the nature of Jesus Christ’s Person in order to enjoy the fruits of his work; any more than a traveler needs to know the physical essence of the Sun to benefit from it on his journey, or than herbs and plants need to understand it to be warmed by it. It is said that the Sun gives light to the world not to gain some faint reflection from a diamond or the praise of a philosopher, or for any other such reason, but solely for the benefit of the world. Likewise, the Dayspring from on high <note>original: *opgang uit de hoogte*; a reference to the "Dayspring" or "Sunrise" in Luke 1:78.</note> visited us for no other reason than to bring us healing under his wings.

Answer: This reasoning is irreligious; for it assumes that a rational creature is no more obligated to know his Creator and Redeemer than plants and herbs (which are soulless things) are to be warmed by the Sun; and that a human is no more bound to know his Savior than a traveler is to know the Sun. Does Christ not say,

<margin>John 17:3.</margin>

John 17:3: *And this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent.*

<margin>Isaiah 53:11.</margin>

And did Isaiah not say (Isaiah 53:11): *By his knowledge my righteous servant shall justify many.*? Does Scripture not demand faith in Christ to participate in the fruits of his death? And does faith not presuppose knowledge? But is knowing Christ merely knowing him as a man? Furthermore, the analogy of the Sun is absurd; the Sun is a soulless creature that knows nothing,

<column-break/>

and understands nothing, having neither intention nor any proposed end. But God is a wise Being, who wishes to be known by humans, and has revealed his will to them with that objective.

5. It is argued: If it were necessary to know that Jesus Christ is God and to understand the entire mystery of the Incarnation <term>Incarnation: The Christian doctrine that God became flesh in the person of Jesus</term>, one would thereby exclude the greatest part of the human race, who cannot grasp these mysteries.

Answer: One must distinguish between *knowing and believing* that Christ is God and that he took on our nature, and knowing *the manner* in which he can be a person distinct from the Father and yet have the same essence as him, or how he was able to assume human nature. If we said that to be saved one must perfectly grasp the mysteries and know how there can be three Persons in a single essence <term>Essence: The fundamental nature or 'being' of God</term> and how Christ became Man, I admit that we would exclude most people—indeed, all people. But we say that it is enough to believe that Jesus Christ is God, that he is the Son whom God begot, that this Son existed before all ages and took on a human nature in Time, without investigating the manner in which the Father begat his Son or how the Son was able to unite himself with a human nature. Now, all simple people can know and believe what we say when they read the Scriptures.

6. It is argued: Since the doctrine of the Trinity, and of the Divinity and Incarnation of God's Son, is a mystery, one should not inquire about it or debate it.

Answer: One would then have to abandon the Gospel, which is "wisdom in a mystery" <note>1 Corinthians 2:7</note> and the "mystery of godliness" <note>1 Timothy 3:16</note>; one would speak no more of the coming of the Savior, nor of the resurrection of the flesh, nor of God's eternity itself—never even asking about any of this because they are mysteries. What godlessness! It is true that one must not intrude into what God has hidden from us, but it does not follow that one must not investigate what he has revealed.

7. It is argued: In the first discourses...

<meta>catchword: the</meta>

</columns>

<summary>This page refutes the idea that belief in Christ's divinity is optional for salvation, arguing against the analogy that one can benefit from Christ without knowing him, just as plants benefit from the sun without understanding it. The author maintains that while the "manner" of the Trinity is a mystery, the "fact" of Christ's divinity is a revealed truth that must be believed.</summary>

DIVINITY. III. B. CHAPTER XV.

...of the Apostles, they did not make an effort to prove that Jesus Christ was God.

**Answer.** One should not have begun with that; one first had to make the Jews understand that Jesus Christ is the promised Messiah; after which the Apostles undeniably proved in their writings that Christ is God, as we have seen elsewhere.

**It is asked.** In the event that those to whom the Apostles preached had died before they were instructed in the mystery of the Incarnation <note>The "Incarnation" refers to the Christian belief that God became human in the person of Jesus.</note>, would they have been saved?

**Answer. 1.** We must not trouble ourselves with this, for we do not know God’s ways. **2.** Others answer that they would have been saved, just like our children who die before they are instructed in the most important truths. **3.** If they were to be saved, God would undoubtedly have inwardly given them all that they had to believe in order to obtain salvation.

For the rest, it will not be useless to note that the teacher Bury <note>Arthur Bury (1624–1713), whose book *The Naked Gospel* caused a scandal for its perceived Arian or Socinian leanings.</note>, whose objections I have cited, was expelled from Exeter College, where he was Rector at Oxford, because of his book, which was burned by the hands of the executioner.

---

# XV. CHAPTER.

### Concerning the Holy Spirit, and first, whether it is a Person.

We shall now deal with the Holy Spirit, the Third Person of the most holy Trinity. But before all things, it is necessary to report: **1.** That the word *Spirit*, in all languages, properly signifies a wind or a breath; it is used to make the Divine nature known, because among all physical things, there is none that teaches us better of the spiritual, nor to express Divine things, none that better represents to us the spiritual being of God, joined with an infinite power and effective operation. It has also been noted that, just as the winds are the least known thing in nature and yet are felt the most, so it is likewise with the Deity, whose influences all rational beings perceive, and whose essence they nevertheless do not know.

<column-break/>

**2.** One must also note that the name of *Spirit* is given to Souls and to Angels.
<margin>
Hebrews 12:9.
Hebrews 1:14.
</margin>

**3.** That this word often signifies the gifts and graces of God’s Spirit. But mostly the Third Person of the adorable Trinity. And in this sense, we take it in this Chapter.

To handle this matter as clearly as such a difficult subject can allow, we shall investigate these five questions:

**1.** Whether the Holy Spirit is a power of God, or a distinct Person from the Father and from the Son.
<margin>Jerome: Letter to Gregory of Nyssa, Paragraph 65.</margin>
Gregory of Nyssa <note>A 4th-century church father and theologian who was central in defining the doctrine of the Trinity.</note> seems to have doubted whether the Holy Spirit had a self-existence?

**2.** Whether it is a Divine Person? That is to say, whether it is a God!

**3.** From whom he proceeds or goes out?

**4.** Why he is named Spirit?

**5.** Why Holy?

In regard to the first question, whether the Spirit is an attribute of God or a Person, it is easy to prove that he is a Person, and a distinct Person from the Father and from the Son.

One only needs to read John 14:16, 17: *I will pray to the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever, (namely) the spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive,* etc. And John 16:13, 14: *When he, (namely) the spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth, for he shall not speak of himself, but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak, and he will show you things to come; he shall glorify me: for he shall receive of mine, and shall show it unto you.* It is not possible that one could think that in those places an attribute is being spoken of, and not a Person.

If the Holy Spirit were only an attribute, would Christ have said to his Disciples, *Go hence, baptize, in the Name of the Holy Spirit*? One cannot say that one is baptized in the name of an attribute.
<margin>Matthew 28:19.</margin>

**Objection.** If it is written that we are baptized in the name of the Holy Spirit, it is also said there that we are baptized *with* the Holy Spirit (Matthew 3:11, Acts 1:5, 1 Corinthians 12:13). Now, that cannot be said of a Person. **Answer 1.** If this reasoning held true, one would have to say that Christ is no Person, because...

DIVINITY. III. B. CHAPTER XVI.

Finally, an objection is raised regarding what Christ did in John 20:22. When He gave His apostles His Spirit, *He breathed on them.* But who does not see that this was merely a symbol of the Spirit that Christ shared with them?

It is then clear that the Holy Spirit is a Person; but we must now see whether He is a Divine Person, or to speak more clearly, whether He is God.

## CHAPTER XVI.
### Whether the Holy Spirit is God.

Many reasons convince us of the divinity of the Holy Spirit; but I will only dwell on those that seem most powerful to me.

<margin>Acts 5:3-4. Epiphanius in *The Anchored One*, p. 498. Athanasius, Vol. 1, p. 141. Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, § 16.</margin>
1. It is evident that the name of God is explicitly given to Him. Acts 5:3-4. There Peter, rebuking the deception of Ananias and Sapphira—who had lied against the Holy Spirit—says, *you have not lied to man, but to God.* The early Church Fathers made use of this passage, most notably <note>Epiphanius (c. 315–403), Athanasius (c. 296–373), and Basil the Great (330–379) were influential early Christian bishops who defended the doctrine of the Trinity.</note> Epiphanius, Athanasius, and Basil.

Against this, it is argued that one should not translate the text to say that Ananias and Sapphira lied *to* the Holy Spirit, but rather that they had *pretended* to have the Holy Spirit, and that this is what the Greek word implies. Answer 1: Those who understand Greek know that the word Luke uses signifies lying against someone in secular authors, as can be proven from <note>These are famous classical Greek poets, historians, and playwrights whose works provide standards for language use.</note> Aristophanes, Sophocles, Euripides, Josephus, and Herodotus. 2. One only needs to read the text to see that Ananias had made no pretense of having the Holy Spirit while withholding the price of his property; Peter says explicitly in verse 9: *How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord?*

<margin><note>original: "Enied: Expl. Loc: V. & N. T." refers to Georg Enjedin, a leader of the Unitarian Church in Transylvania who wrote explanations of difficult biblical passages.</note> Enjedin, *Explanations of Passages in the Old and New Testaments*.</margin>
It is said: From this, no conclusion can be drawn that the Holy Spirit is God, just as one cannot conclude that the Apostles are gods because Paul says in 1 Thessalonians 4:8, *Therefore whoever rejects this, rejects not man, but God,* and because Christ said in Luke 10:16 <note>The original text mistakenly cites John 10:16, but the quote is from Luke.</note> *whoever rejects you, rejects me,* and Matthew 10:40, *whoever receives you, receives me.*

<column-break/>

I answer: One indeed cannot conclude from this that the Apostles are gods; yet it remains clear that the insult directed at the Apostles reflects back on God Himself; just as the lie of Ananias, by which he intended to deceive the Apostles, fell upon the Holy Spirit, from which it is concluded that the Holy Spirit is God. For, if Peter had intended to say that Ananias had lied against the Apostles, through the Apostles against the Holy Spirit, and through the Holy Spirit against God, he would have said, *you have not lied to man, nor to the Holy Spirit, but to God.*

2. One cannot read the Scriptures without noticing everywhere that all the perfections of the Godhead are attributed to Him. I will only bring forward a few; one of the greatest perfections, and that by which God distinguishes Himself from those who are not gods by nature, is that He is everywhere, and that He fills Heaven and Earth. Jer. 23:24. Now this perfection is given to the Holy Spirit. Ps. 139:7: *Where shall I go from your Spirit?* And elsewhere He is described as being present with all the believers in the world, and as dwelling in them. Rom. 8:15. 1 Cor. 3:16.

He who knows the most hidden thoughts in His mind is beyond doubt God. 1 Kings 8:39: *You alone know the hearts of all the children of men.* Now the Holy Spirit knows not only the secrets of the heart, but also all the thoughts of God, 1 Cor. 2:10: *The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God.* Paul then explains his meaning and proves his proposition with an example of the spirit of man. Verse 11: *For who among men knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him? So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God.* From these words, one can draw another new proof for the divinity of the Holy Spirit. The spirit of a man does not know what is in a man except because the spirit of the man is the man himself, and what is in the man is in the spirit of the man. So also the Spirit of God knows what is in God because He is God, and what is in God is in the Spirit of God. One will say: "Since the Spirit searches the things of God, it is proof that He is not God, because He needs to search the depths of God." Answer: But then one would have to conclude that God [knows] the hearts...

<header>THE CHRISTIAN</header>

...does not know it, because it is said that He is the one who searches it. <note>original: "die doorzoekt." See Jeremiah 17:10: "I the Lord search the heart."</note> Jer. XVII. 10.

It may perhaps be said that, just as the spirit of a man is not a distinct Person from the man whose spirit it is, so too God's Spirit is not a distinct Person from the Father. But this does not follow, because there are other explicit passages that teach us this distinction.

Furthermore, the foretelling of future things is always placed among God's attributes. By this, God intends for us to know that the gods worshipped by the heathens are false gods; now Paul ascribes this attribute to the Spirit.

<margin>1 Tim. IV: 1.</margin>
<margin>Ps. CXV: 3.</margin>
<margin>1 Cor. XII: 11.</margin>
1 Tim. IV. 1. The Spirit clearly says that in the latter times, some shall depart from the faith. When the Prophet describes God's Omnipotence, he says, *our God is in heaven, he does whatever pleases him.* Ps. CXV. 3. Paul says almost the same thing regarding the Spirit: *All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one individually, just as he wills.* 1 Cor. XII. 11.

3. If we consider the works that are attributed to God's Spirit, we shall find ourselves confirmed in this same truth.

It is certain that He who created the Heavens is God. Isa. XLIV. 24. *I am the Lord, who makes all things, who stretches out the heavens alone, and who spreads abroad the earth by myself.* Therefore, God is often described as He who created the Heavens and leveled the Earth. This is why the church begins all its <term>worship services<gloss>original: "Godsdienstoeffeningen," referring to formal liturgical gatherings.</gloss></term> with these words: *our help is in the name of God, who made Heaven and Earth.* Now, this Creation is attributed to the Spirit; He is shown to us in Gen. I. 2. as *hovering upon the waters,* and we shall have occasion elsewhere to examine this passage. Job confirms the same: chapter XXVI. 13. and <margin>Job XXXIII. 4.</margin> XXXIII. 4. where he says, *the Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty has given me life.* It is also the Holy Spirit who prepared the body of our Lord Jesus Christ from the flesh of the Virgin Mary.

One sees clearly that the <term>regeneration<gloss>The spiritual "rebirth" or internal transformation of a believer.</gloss></term> and <term>Sanctification<gloss>The process of being made holy or set apart for God.</gloss></term> of believers is a work of God, since it is a new Creation; now this is attributed to the Holy Spirit, as we shall prove in its proper place.

4. I cannot neglect to bring forward as a 

<column-break/>

further proof the oft-mentioned passage of Matt. XXVIII. 19. *Go then, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.* This text proves that the Holy Spirit is a Person, and indeed a Divine Person; for He in whose name we are baptized is regarded as the maker of the <term>Covenant of Grace<gloss>A theological concept describing the relationship where God offers salvation to humanity through faith in Christ.</gloss></term>, who has the power to institute the Sacraments to seal the Covenant, who can promise and give Grace, and to whose service all those in the Covenant are bound—which can be said of no created being. Through our Baptism, we subject ourselves absolutely to God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as to the only true God and the only cause of our salvation; we consecrate ourselves to His service and bind ourselves to glorify Him in body and spirit, which are His. Let us then judge, if we are baptized in the name of the Holy Spirit, whether He is not God.

It is true, 1 Cor. X. 2. says that Israel was *baptized into Moses.* But there is a great difference between these two ways of speaking. When it is said that the Israelites were baptized into Moses, it means that they were accepted and hallowed into the Law and discipline of Moses, to recognize him as their Head, Savior, and Leader; by this confession they made, they bound themselves to follow him into the Sea and to place themselves under his guidance and direction. This passage through the Sea, and this staying in the Cloud, was like a Baptism.

We cannot approve of other interpretations, such as those of the Greeks, who believe this means the Israelites were baptized *with* Moses, or under his guidance; or those of the Arabic and Syriac translators, as if it said the Israelites were baptized *by the ministry* and by the hand of Moses. For the same reason, one could say the Samaritans were baptized into Philip, and the household of Stephanas into Paul; however, this is unheard-of language. Paul testifies that he has a horror of this when he asks the Corinthians: *were you baptized in the name of Paul?*

5. This same truth will carry even more weight if one compares certain passages of the Old Testament with some of the New Testament; for from that it will appear that the Holy Spirit...
