### THEOLOGY. III. Book XVI. Chapter. ###

Spirit is the same God whom the ancient *Israelites* worshipped under the name of *Jehovah*, and whom they recognized as the Creator and sustainer of the universe.

<margin>*Isa. 6:1, 2, etc.; Acts 28:25; John 12:41.*</margin>
One cannot doubt that the one whom *Isaiah* saw in the glorious vision in *Isaiah 6:1, 2* is *Jehovah*, the God of Hosts. Now *Paul* explicitly teaches us in *Acts 28:25* that it was the Holy Spirit who spoke thus through *Isaiah*. One must then conclude that the Holy Spirit is God, just as we have proven that Christ is God, because it appears that *Isaiah* also spoke of Him in this vision; this proves that Christ is the same God as the Holy Spirit and the Father. No one can doubt for a moment that He who instructed, inspired, and sent the Prophets of the Old Testament is the true God, served and worshipped among *Israel*. Now, according to *Peter’s* testimony, the Holy Spirit did this. *2 Peter 1:21*: prophecy was not produced in olden times by the will of man, but the Holy Men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit.

<margin>*Lev. 16:2; Jer. 31:33; Heb. 9:8, 10:15.*</margin>
He who commanded *Moses* in *Leviticus 16:2* that the High Priest should not enter the Sanctuary at all times was undoubtedly *Jehovah*; now *Paul* witnesses in *Hebrews 9:8* that it was the Holy Spirit who prescribed this Law. It is *Jehovah*, the true God of *Israel*, who promises in *Jeremiah 31:33* to make a New Covenant; now *Paul* says that it was the Holy Spirit in *Hebrews 10:15*.

<margin>*Ps. 95:7; Heb. 3:7.*</margin>
It is *Jehovah* who says in *Psalm 95:7*: "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts," and who swears there in His Wrath that those with whom He is angry shall not enter into His rest; now the same Apostle says that the Holy Spirit said this in *Hebrews 3:7*. The Holy Spirit is then truly the God of *Israel*, worshipped by Jews and Christians alike.

<margin>*Rev. 1:4.*</margin>
Furthermore, *Paul* wishes no less for the *Corinthians* in *2 Corinthians 13:13* the fellowship of the Holy Spirit than the Grace of the Lord *Jesus Christ* and the love of God the Father. *John* wishes for the seven churches not only the Grace of Him who is, and who was, and who is to come, but also from the seven Spirits—that is, from the Holy Spirit (*Revelation 1:4*).

It is true that the worship and invocation of the Holy Spirit is seldom mentioned; this is because, in the <term>economy of salvation</term> <note>The "economy of salvation" (Dutch: *huishouding der zaligheid*) refers to the distinct roles the Father, Son, and Spirit play in the historical plan to redeem humanity.</note>, He is regarded as the cause

<column-break/>

of prayers; but from that, it does not follow that the Holy Spirit is any less worthy of worship than the other Persons of the Trinity. Are we not called Temples of the Holy Spirit? (*1 Corinthians 3:16* and *6:19*).

<margin>*Augustine to Maximinus, Letter 65.* <note>original: "Aug: ad Max: Ep: 65." Refers to St. Augustine’s debate with the Arian bishop Maximinus.</note></margin>
(Now a Temple is a House of God.) "If we were commanded," said *Augustine*, "to build a temple of wood and stone for the Holy Spirit, we would immediately conclude from that that He is God. Since this service belongs to God alone, how much more clearly does this appear since it is said that we ourselves must be His Temple?"

These proofs are more than enough to unshakeably prove the Divinity of the Holy Spirit. I will only add this observation: that in the Creeds of the Apostles, and in those of the first centuries, the Son is placed between the Father and the Holy Spirit as proof that the Ancients did not consider the Holy Spirit to be merely a "power" of God (for they would then have placed Him in the second position) and that they viewed the Son as God because they placed Him before the Holy Spirit.

<margin>*John 14:16, 17; John 15:26; John 16:7, 13, 14.*</margin>
It only remains for me to show that the Holy Spirit, who is God, is distinct from the Father and the Son. The passages already cited prove this clearly. *John 14:16, 17*: "I will pray to the Father, and he will give you another Comforter," etc. Verse 26: "The Comforter, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things, and bring to your remembrance all things that I have said to you." And elsewhere, *John 15:26*: "When the Comforter is come, whom I will send to you from the Father, namely the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he shall testify of me." And in another place, *John 16:7*: "If I go away, I will send the Comforter to you." Verse 13: "Whatever he shall hear, that shall he speak, and he will show you things to come." It has never been said that the one who is sent is the same Person as the one who sends him, or that the one who proceeds is the same as the one from whom he proceeds.

<margin>*Socinians, etc.* <note>Socinians were followers of a 16th-century theological movement that denied the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ and the Holy Spirit.</note></margin>
From all that I have presented so far, it follows: 1. That those who believe the Holy Spirit is merely a power of God are in error. 2. One must judge the same of those who say that the Holy Spirit is an <term>accident</term> <note>In 17th-century theology, an "accident" refers to a quality that isn't essential to a being's nature. The author argues God's nature is "simple" and has no such external qualities.</note>, as if there could be "accidents" in God. 3. As also of those who imagine that the Holy Spirit is a creat- <note>The word is cut off at the bottom of the page, likely "schepsel," meaning "creature" or "created being."</note>

<meta>The catchword "Schep-" indicates the next page begins with "Schepsel" (Creature), continuing the list of theological errors regarding the Holy Spirit's nature.</meta>

69. 76.</margin>
creature is / for the service of God's Son; and that he is like a good Angel / whom God uses in matters of the greatest importance: for we have shown / that he is not a Creature / but the Creator.

<margin>Macedonius <note>Macedonius I of Constantinople, whose followers (the Pneumatomachi or "Spirit-fighters") denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit.</note>

Likewise from those who interpret the passage / where the Holy Spirit is spoken of / as if it were dealing with the Christian virtues, with Faith, Hope, Love, or with the gifts of miracles, or with the Gospel; for one must wish to do violence to the scripture / to make such interpretations / and be willfully blind to let them pass.

Nevertheless, to show / that we are well-grounded in believing the Divinity of the Holy Spirit / we wish to examine the reasons / brought forward to contest his Divinity.

**Objection.** He is called the Spirit of the Father and of the Son; therefore he is no God.

I deny this conclusion; from it only follows / that he is neither the Father / nor the Son / although he has the same essence with these adorable Persons.

**Objection.** The Holy Spirit is a Gift of God. I admit it: but Christ is also called the Gift of God / meanwhile we have proven / that he is God.

**Objection.** He would be his own Gift / if he were God.

I answer, 1. That he is the Gift of the Father and the Son / who are two Persons / distinct from the Holy Spirit. 2. That Christ gave himself / and therefore the Holy Spirit can also give himself.

**Objection.** If the Holy Spirit were God / the scripture would command us to worship him. **Answer.** We have pointed out the reason / why the Holy Spirit is seldom spoken of. Namely because he is regarded as the efficient cause <note>The "efficient cause" is a philosophical term for the primary source of a change or action.</note> of our prayers. In this way / more is mentioned of the invocation of the Father / than of that of the Son / because he is regarded / as the one / in whose name we pray.

XVII. 3.</margin>
**Objection.** In the High Priestly prayer of Christ <note>The "High Priestly Prayer" refers to the long prayer of Jesus recorded in John 17.</note> the Holy Spirit is not spoken of: *This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom you have sent.* John XVII. 3.

**Answer.** 1. We have already shown / in what sense the Father is called the only true God; and proven / that it is not

<column-break/>

with the exclusion of the Son and the Holy Spirit. 2. If he is not spoken of in this place / mention is made of him in many others. 3. If one had to make use of what Christ says / to contest the Divinity of the Holy Spirit / it would then also follow / that there is no necessity / to know the Holy Spirit / to be saved / since Christ makes eternal life consist in the knowledge of the Father / and of the Son; but this cannot be said without godlessness.

**Objection.** He who knows neither the Father nor the Son, cannot be called God. Now Christ teaches us, *No one knows the Son but the Father, and no one knows the Father but the Son.* Matt. XI. 27.

**Answer.** It is clear that *Jesus Christ* does not exclude the Holy Spirit; just as his objective was not to say / that the Father does not know himself / by testifying that no one knows the Father but the Son; For *Paul* says / *the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God.* 1 Cor. II. 10.

Many more passages are brought in / where the Holy Spirit is distinguished from the Father and from the Son.

But that proves nothing else / than that the Holy Spirit is a distinct Person.

**Objection.** *Paul* says / 1 Thess. V. 19. *Do not quench the Spirit*; this cannot be said of God.

I answer, that by the Spirit one must understand not the person of the Holy Spirit / but the extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit / which accompanied the first preaching of the Gospel / such as the gifts of miracles / speaking with foreign Tongues / and interpreting these tongues and Prophecies. Therefore *Paul* immediately adds / by way of application / *do not despise Prophecies.*

**Objection.** One cannot hold the Holy Spirit for God / who does not speak of himself. John XVI. 13.

But it is evident / that *Christ* only wishes to say / that the Holy Spirit says nothing else / than what the Father and the Son say / and that there is a wonderful agreement / between what the Holy Spirit has taught / and what the Father has taught us through his Son.

**Objection.** If the Holy Spirit were God / he would have always been / where yet *John* says / *the Spirit was not yet, because Christ was not yet glorified.* John VII. 39.

# THEOLOGY. III. B. XVII. Chapter.

But who does not see / that the meaning of these words is not / that there was not yet a Holy Spirit / before the glorification of the Son; for he already existed / when Christ was baptized; he hovered over the waters in the beginning of the world; he was in the Prophets; therefore it clearly appears / that he was given to us only with that outpouring / which Christ had promised to his Disciples / and which he specifically poured out on the first Christian Pentecost. <note>Pentecost is the Christian festival celebrating the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles, described in Acts 2.</note>

It is objected, Acts 19:2, where some Disciples at Ephesus said / that they did not know / that there was a Holy Spirit; Answer: The ignorance of these Disciples cannot be used as a foundation for a doctrinal opinion.

Objection: It is not probable / that the Holy Spirit would pray / if he were God; and meanwhile Paul says, that he prays to God / for the Saints / with unutterable groanings. Rom. 8:26, 27. <note>original: "onuitspreekelyke zugtingen." This refers to the Spirit's intercession for believers when they do not know how to pray.</note>

Answer: Paul explains himself. Rom. 8:15. When he says / that we pray through the Spirit. Thus it is also said / that the Holy Spirit prays for us / causes our prayers to be heard / to signify / that he moves us to pray / puts the prayers as it were into our mouths / and teaches us how to pray well.

Objection: The Holy Spirit is sent / and that cannot be said of God.

Answer: We have / while dealing with God’s Son / shown / that being sent does not prejudice the Divinity of the one who is sent / since it is not a sending of a greater and a lesser / but a sending / which happens through the mutual consent of equal persons.

Finally, the passages are objected / where the Holy Spirit is compared to Water, Oil, Fire, etc.

But one must willfully be blind not to understand / that one should not press these figures of speech / and that the Holy Spirit is compared to all these things / to signify his various workings.

If some other small difficulties are raised; they can easily / by the principles / which I have established / be resolved.

## XVII. CHAPTER.

->Of the proceeding of the HOLY SPIRIT.<-

We have seen / that the Holy Spirit is a Divine Person / and that he is the true God / whom we must worship / with the Father and the Son: we shall now pass over to what the scripture further witnesses of him.

1. It teaches us / that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. John 15:26.

2. That he is the Spirit of the Son, and the Spirit of Christ. Rom. 8:9, Gal. 4:6, Phil. 1:19, 1 Pet. 1:11.

3. That the Father and the Son send the Spirit. John 15:26 and 16:7, Gal. 4:6, Luke 24:49.

One cannot doubt / whether this proceeding / from the Father / is from eternity / since we have proven / that the Holy Spirit is God; that is, an eternal being.

<margin>
Augustine in
John 11,
homily 9.
</margin>
But it is asked / in what this proceeding or coming forth consists / and how it is distinguished from the generation of the Son. <note>In Trinitarian theology, "generation" (or begetting) refers to the relationship between the Father and the Son, while "procession" refers to the relationship of the Spirit to the Father and Son.</note> That I do not know / and I consider it an honor for myself / to confess my ignorance in this; the Holy Spirit alone searches the depths of God / and knows how he proceeds from the Father. I know that he proceeds / just as I know / that the Son is generated; but I do not know how and in what manner.

Some theologians say / that God / contemplating himself / brings forth his image / which is his wisdom, his word / and his Son; and that he / loving himself / brings forth his love / that is his Spirit. They say then / that the Son is the product of the wisdom of the Father; and the Holy Spirit the product of the will of the Father and the Son; that the Son is generated by way of contemplation / and the production of image and idea; and that the Holy Spirit proceeds by way of movement / and indeed of a reciprocal movement between the Father and the Son. Some of the Early Fathers / and Scholastic Teachers have said the same / but I confess / that I would rather say / I know nothing of it at all. *Augustine, book 3 against Maximinus the Arian, chapter 14. Distinguere inter istam generationem, & hanc processionem nescio, non valeo, non sufficio.* <note>Original Latin translated: "To distinguish between that generation and this proceeding, I do not know [how], I am not able, I am not sufficient."</note> That is / to make a distinction between this generation and that proceeding, I do not understand it, I cannot understand...

I answer, 1. That he is the Gift of the Father and of the Son / who are two Persons / distinct from the Holy Spirit. 2. That Christ gave himself / and therefore the Holy Spirit can also give himself.

**Objection.** If the Holy Spirit were God / the scripture would command us to worship him. **Answer.** We have pointed out the reason / why the Holy Spirit is seldom spoken of. Namely because he is regarded as the efficient cause of our prayers. In this way / more is mentioned of the invocation of the Father / than of that of the Son / because he is regarded / as the one / in whose name we pray.

<margin>John XVII. 3.</margin>
**Objection.** In the <term>High Priestly prayer</term> <note>The prayer offered by Jesus in John 17 before his crucifixion.</note> of Christ, the Holy Spirit is not mentioned: *This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom you have sent.* John XVII. 3.

**Answer.** 1. We have already shown / in what sense the Father is called the only true God; and proven / that it is not

<column-break/>

with the exclusion of the Son and the Holy Spirit. 2. If he is not spoken of in this place / he is mentioned in many others. 3. If one had to use what Christ says / to oppose the Divinity of the Holy Spirit / it would then also follow / that there is no necessity / to know the Holy Spirit / to be saved / since Christ makes eternal life consist in the knowledge of the Father / and of the Son; but this cannot be said without godlessness.

**Objection.** He who knows neither the Father nor the Son, cannot be called God. Now Christ teaches us: *No one knows the Son but the Father, and no one knows the Father but the Son.* Matt. XI. 27.

**Answer.** It is clear that Jesus Christ does not exclude the Holy Spirit; just as his intention was not to say / that the Father does not know himself / nor to testify that no one knows the Father but the Son; For Paul says / *the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God.* 1. Cor. II. 10.

Many more passages are brought in / where the Holy Spirit is distinguished from the Father and from the Son.

But that proves nothing else / than that the Holy Spirit is a distinct Person.

**Objection.** Paul says / 1. Thess. V. 19. *Do not quench the Spirit*; this cannot be said of God.

I answer, that by the Spirit one must understand not the person of the Holy Spirit / but the extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit / which accompanied the first proclamation of the Gospel / such as the gifts of miracles / speaking in foreign Languages / and interpreting these languages and Prophecies. Therefore Paul immediately adds / by way of application / *do not despise prophecies.*

**Objection.** One cannot consider the Holy Spirit as God / who does not speak of himself. John XVI. 13.

But it is apparent / that Christ only wants to say / that the Holy Spirit says nothing else / than what the Father and the Son say / and that there is a wonderful agreement / between what the Holy Spirit has taught / and what the Father has taught us through his Son.

**Objection.** If the Holy Spirit were God / he would have always been / where nonetheless John says / *the Holy Spirit was not yet* / because Christ was not yet glorified. John VII. 39.

DIVINITY. III. B. XVII. Chapter.

But who does not see / that the meaning of these words is not / that there was not yet a Holy Spirit / before the glorification of the Son; for he already existed / when Christ was baptized; he hovered over the waters in the beginning of the world; he was in the Prophets; therefore it clearly appears / that he only wishes to teach us / that the Holy Spirit had not yet been given with that <term>outpouring</term><note>The "outpouring" refers to the dramatic descent of the Spirit upon the apostles at Pentecost.</note> / which Christ had promised to his Disciples / and which he only poured out on the first Christian Pentecost-Feast.

It is objected, Acts 19:2. Where some Disciples at Ephesus said / that they did not know / that there was a Holy Spirit: Answer: The ignorance of these Disciples can be laid as no foundation for a belief.

Objection: It is not probable / that the Holy Spirit would pray / if he were God; and meanwhile Paul says, that he prays to God / for the Saints / with sighs that cannot be expressed. Romans 8:26, 27.

Answer: Paul explains himself. Romans 8:15. When he says / that we pray through the Spirit. So it is also said / that the Holy Spirit prays for us / presents our prayers / to make known / that he moves us to pray / as if putting the prayers into our mouths / and teaching us to pray well.

Objection: The Holy Spirit is sent / and that cannot be said of God.

Answer: We have shown, when dealing with God's Son / that being sent does not prejudice the Divinity of the one who is sent / since it is not a sending of a greater and a lesser / but a sending / which occurs through the mutual consent of equal persons.

Finally, they object to the places / where the Holy Spirit is compared to Water, Oil, Fire, etc.

But one must wish to be blind not to understand / that one must not press too hard on these ways of speaking / and that the Holy Spirit is compared to all these things / to signify his various workings.

If one still raises any other small difficulties; they can easily / through the principles / that I have established / be resolved.

# THE CHRISTIAN

...to, it surpasses my understanding.

It is indeed true that there is a distinction between the Generation of the Son and the proceeding of the Holy Spirit: for it is said that the Son is generated <note>original: "gegenereert"; a theological term for the Son being eternally begotten of the Father</note>, but that is not testified of the Holy Spirit; the Holy Spirit is nowhere called God's Son or his Image. Behold there what we know; but it does not belong to us to investigate what God has hidden from us.

Regarding the difference between the Greeks and the Latins, whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and from the Son (as the Latins, and we with them, believe) or from the Father alone (as the Greeks think); that must not delay us. It appears that the Greeks have mistaken themselves, since the Spirit is named the Spirit of the Son as well as of the Father. If, according to the Confession of the Greeks, the Spirit proceeds from the Father *through* the Son, how can he proceed through the Son, except insofar as he proceeds *from* the Son?

<margin>In *Ancoratus* [The Well-Anchored], Against Heresies, 61.</margin>
Many Greek Church Fathers were of this opinion, such as Epiphanius, who, speaking of Ananias and Sapphira, says the Holy Spirit, whom they had lied to, and who is from the Father and from the Son, is God. <margin>In John 16:13.</margin> And elsewhere, the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. Cyril of Alexandria says the Holy Spirit ultimately proceeds from the existence of the Son. See more testimonies in Bellarmine and Montacutius <margin>Bellarmine, Book II on Christ, chapter 25. Montacutius in the 2nd Epistle of Photius; Theodoret’s Reprimand XII, chapter Cyril’s Anathema IX. Photius Epistle 2. John of Damascus, *On the Orthodox Faith*, Book 1, chapter XI. Metrophanes, *Confession of the Oriental Church*, question I.</margin> But other Greek Fathers were not of this opinion, such as Theodoret, Photius, Damascene, and the modern Greeks, as one can see in Metrophanes Critopulus.

The ecclesiastical historical writings teach us that this was a cause of the schism <note>The Great Schism of 1054, which divided the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic churches</note> between the Greeks and the Latins.

The Latins firmly asserted that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and from the Son. In the beginning, this difference of Faith was not considered much, all the more because the Creed of Constantinople <note>The Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed of 381 AD</note>, confirmed by the Council of Ephesus in the year 431, contained only these words: *the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father.* And Theodoret, one of the most learned and famous Church Fathers, was never punished or placed under a Ban <note>excommunicated</note> for this matter, whatever Leo Allatius may say of it.

In the 6th and 7th centuries, this difference caused more of a stir. In the third Council of Toledo, in the year 589, a ban was pronounced over those who did not believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and from the Son.

<column-break/>

<margin>In Cardinal d'Aguirre, *Councils of Spain*, p. 538.</margin>
In the 4th Council, held by King Sisenand in the year 633, this truth was confirmed in chapter I, as it was also by d'Aguirre in the 6th Council, held in the year 638, chapter I; as well as in the 8th Council of Hispania <note>Spain</note>, year 653, under King Recceswinth, chapter I; also in the 11th in the year 675; and in the 12th and 13th.

<margin>Gregory of Tours, *History*, Book I.</margin>
In England, in the year 679, according to the words of Bede <note>The Venerable Bede, an English monk and scholar</note>, the same doctrine was asserted.

<margin>Alexander, Arist. in Vossius, *On the Three Creeds*. Martial, Miles, Sarazanius, Sirmond.</margin>
And it appears from the Confession of Gregory of Tours that in his time, it had already been added to the Creed of Constantinople that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. Scholars do not agree on this addition. Some have believed that this occurred under Pope Damasus, but there is nothing regarding it in the letters of this Pope that Theodoret would have noted if it had been true.

<margin>To the 6th Council, edition by Labbe.</margin>
In the 8th Century, tempers became more embittered.

<margin>Charles le Cointe, at the year 767, numbers I, II, Vol. V, p. 698.</margin>
In the year 767, a Synod was held in France at Gentilly, where this difference and that of the images <note>The Iconoclasm controversy regarding the use of religious icons</note> were handled; on the occasion of the envoys from Constantine Copronymus, they spoke of what had been added to the Creed.

<margin>Councils, Vol. VII, pp. 991, 994, 999. Le Cointe at the year 795, Vol. VI, p. 540.</margin>
In the year 791, the doctrine of the proceeding of the Holy Spirit was established in a Council.

But in this same century, the Greeks in the 2nd Council of Nicaea, in the year 787, reciting the Creed of Constantinople, confessed only that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father; it is true that some have dared to say that the Easterners added *And from the Son*; and that it was written thus in the Latin translation of this Council, but that is not probable: for it would be found in some Greek copies and in the records of Anastasius the Librarian.

<margin>Synod of Ferrara, Session 6. Laurentius Surius in this Council. Compare Bellarmine, Book II on Christ, chapter 23. Encyclical Letter to the Patriarch, Vol. X. Baronius at the year 863, number 34, etc. Leo Allatius, *On the Perpetual Agreement*, Book II, chapter 6, Vol. VIII, p. 941.</margin>
In the 9th Century, the matter went further. Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople, wrote against the opinion of the Latins and reproached them for having added to the Creed of Constantinople; and in the Council of Constantinople, which the Greeks consider the 8th, they rejected the additions that were supposedly made to the acts of the Councils.

In the Council of Aix, in the year 809, this difference was picked up again by a monk from Jerusalem named John: and it was decided that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and from the Son. To this...

to support this decision, Charlemagne <note>original: "Karel de Groot"</note> wrote a letter to Pope Leo III, in which he confirmed this doctrine with many testimonies from the ancient Church Fathers; he sent Bernarius, Bishop of Worms, and others, to oblige the Pope to ratify and approve this article of faith, so that the Profession of Faith <note>The Nicene Creed</note> would be sung with the addition *Filioque* <note>Latin: "and the Son," referring to the Spirit proceeding from both the Father and the Son</note>.

Finally, the Council of Florence in the year 1438 attempted to dissuade the Greeks from this opinion, but it achieved nothing.

# CHAPTER XVIII.

->Why the third Person of the Holy<-
->Trinity is named SPIRIT? Why HOLY<-
->SPIRIT? and concerning the various<-
->workings of this Spirit.<-

One asks why the third Person of the Trinity is named Spirit?

The Scholastic theologians <note>original: "School God-Geleerden"</note> say it is because he proceeds from the Father and the Son by way of breathing <note>original: "blazen"; a reference to the theological concept of "spiration"</note>; but one asks what this is, and that cannot be said. It is also not to signify that his existence is Spiritual; for the existence of the Father and of the Son is also Spiritual.

It is possible that it is because this adorable Person is presented to us as the power of the Most High, through which the Father brings into effect that which his wisdom has decreed. For one is accustomed to attribute to a Spirit the power to move itself and to set other things in motion.

Secondly: One asks why he is called Holy? Not only because of his infinite purity or Majesty, for the Ancients used the word holiness to signify Majesty. The power of the Roman Tribunes <note>original: "Roomsche gemeens Mannen"; literally 'men of the common people'</note> was called Holy,

<sig>Part I.</sig>

<column-break/>

because they represented the Majesty of the Roman people. Julius Caesar speaks of the Holiness of Kings. It is not because he is Holier than the Father and the Son; for they are equal in Holiness: but because, in the order of Divine works, the Sanctification of believers is attributed to him, just as election is attributed to the Father, and redemption to the Son.

There is then nothing left but to speak of the various workings of the Holy Spirit. I shall only point them out here, and will have the opportunity elsewhere to deal with them more broadly.

The theologians bring these workings into three states: 1. Nature. 2. Human society. 3. The Church.

1. As concerns the workings of the Holy Spirit in nature, Creation and the production of creatures are attributed to him in the scriptures, as we have already noted, as well as the preservation of all things. Ps. 104:30. *You send forth your Spirit, they are created, and you renew the face of the earth:* in a word, all the works of providence.

2. With regard to civil life: 1. From what is related in Exod. 35:31, that God had filled Bezaleel with his Spirit for the building of the Tabernacle, it can be concluded that it is through the power of the Holy Spirit that many excel in arts and sciences.

3. In Num. 11:17 it is written that God <margin>Num. 11:17.</margin> took of the Spirit that was upon Moses and put it upon the 70 Elders of Israel, to bear the burden of the people with him. From this, one can conclude that the wisdom and prudence of civil government is a work of God's Spirit.

4. Without doubt, the heroic deeds of the heathens—the remnants of honesty, decency, friendship, moderation, and justice that were preserved among the idol-worshippers—were a special working of God's Spirit, which moderated the insane movements of human corruption.

5. As for the workings of the Spirit in the Church: it is the Spirit who is the cause of all Holiness that has existed in every dispensation and state of the Church.

It is the Spirit who gave the Patriarchs those illustrious virtues at which one must stand in wonder.

It is He who was given to the Prophets and Apostles, who made them undaunted and gave them a wisdom that no one could withstand.

It is He who, after the Ascension of Christ, filled the first Christians with the gifts of won...

THE CHRISTIAN [DIVINITY]

...fulfilled the works that *Paul* and *Luke* described; these were extraordinary workings of God’s Spirit.

Regarding the common workings of the Spirit, these are manifold.

He produces in the temporary believers <note>original: "Tydgeloovigen"; those whose faith is fleeting and not rooted in true regeneration</note> those good movements that one perceives in them, and which give them the enlightenment of which *Paul* speaks. *Heb. VI. 4.*

He plants in the believers all necessary capacities to transition into the fellowship of Christ, and effectively incorporates them into it.

<margin>*Ps. CXIX. 18. Eph. I. 17. 18. 1. Cor. II. 12.*</margin> He enlightens their eyes to see the wonders of God’s law; to know the hope of their calling and the riches of their inheritance; to know the things that are given to us by God.

He produces in their souls all the habits of Christian virtues: Faith, Hope, Love, etc.

Just as *Christ* is our advocate through his merits, so the Spirit is our advocate <note>original: "voorspraak"</note> through the power with which he fills us to seek God’s assistance.

<margin>*Rom. VIII. 16. Gal. IV. 6. Rom. V. 5. Eph. III. 16. 2. Cor. I. 21. Eph. IV. 30. Rom. VIII. 11. 25. 27.*</margin> He assures us of our adoption as children.

He pours into our hearts the sense of God’s love; and that peace which passes all understanding.

He is the Divine Comforter <note>original: "Trooster"</note> who comforts and gladdens all the sorrowful; who comforted the Apostles over the absence of their Master. He comforts us against the terrors of God’s judgments, death, and the adversities of life; in all states he supports us when we waver; he raises us up from our fall, makes us recover from our errors, and encourages us when we are afraid; in our doubting he is our advisor; in our sickness, our Physician <note>original: "Medicyn-meester"</note>; in our straying, our Guide. Though he does not grant us the light of Prophecy to penetrate future ages, he bestows the light of faith to contemplate the unspeakable goods of Glory. Though he does not give us Samson's strength to tear lions apart, he gives us the strength to overcome the roaring lion <note>A reference to the Devil in 1 Peter 5:8</note>. Though he does not endow us with the gift of miracles to move mountains, heal diseases, or cast out devils, he casts down the mountains of arrogance and rebellion in our hearts, heals our spiritual sicknesses, and drives away the evil spirits of our wicked desires.

He strengthens our inner man, confirms, anoints, and seals us until the day of redemption.

<column-break/>

He is the spirit of prayers and supplications, who teaches us how we ought to pray, and through whom we cry *Abba Father* <note>Aramaic for "Father," used as an intimate address to God</note>.

Finally, he shall make our mortal bodies alive; just as through him we put to death the deeds of the body.

Because of all these effects, he is sometimes compared to water, because he is the principle or cause of our spiritual rebirths, and because he makes us sprout in God’s Paradise, cleanses our souls from the stains of sin, extinguishes the heat of our desires, and refreshes us through his comforts. Sometimes he is compared to a fire that cleanses us, consumes the thickest matter, enlightens us, and ignites us in a true love for God. Sometimes to an anointing, which enables us to combat and overcome the enemies of our salvation, and which instructs us. *1. John II. 27.* Sometimes to a Wind, which knocks down all heights that exalt themselves against the knowledge of God, and which drives away all impurity from our hearts. Sometimes to a pledge <note>original: "onderpand"</note>, to a seal, and to many other things that I will not bring up now.

I end this Chapter with three remarks.

1. That we obtain the graces of God’s Spirit through hearing and contemplating the Gospel, which is called the ministry of the spirit; through prayer (*Luke XI. 13*): If you, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more shall the Heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him? and through strong desires, which the scripture calls hunger and thirst. If anyone thirsts, streams shall flow from his belly. *John VII. 38. Isa. XLIV. 3.*

2. That we feel this spirit through his workings: if we walk according to the spirit, placing our trust in God in adversities; if we feel in our hearts a vivid sorrow that we have offended him and find a delight in God’s Law; if we have a horror of sins; and if we have more sorrow that we have sinned against God than that we have not managed our affairs well. If we have more joy over our progress in Holiness than over wealth; if we are Temperate, Just, Patient, etc. These are the signs (and there are more like them) by which one can know if one has God’s spirit.

3. We retain God’s Spirit through the same means by which we obtain his grace. Namely, through prayer, through the...

### XIX. CHAPTER.

### *Of the sentiment of the Church Fathers regarding the mystery of the Trinity, regarding the Divinity of Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit.*

**A**LTHOUGH we, after having leafed through the Holy Scriptures, have nothing more to wish for the assurance of our faith, it will nonetheless not be useless to show that the Church Fathers of the first four Centuries held our sentiments; although we must admit that they often let slip very dif-

<column-break/>

ficult modes of expression <note>original: "harde manieren van spreeken"; the author acknowledges that early Christian writers sometimes used imprecise language that could be interpreted as unorthodox by later standards.</note> which have caused many to doubt their orthodoxy.

### FIRST CENTURY.

**I**n the first Century, we have little to pursue.

<margin>(b) Those who believe that this Hermes is the Brother of Pope Pius place him in the second Century. I do not determine here who has the better reason, <insert>The author of the Pontificate of Regino.</insert> Damasus. If he is the Hermes of Paul, then he lived in the year 65. But if he was the Brother of Pope Pius, then one must place him in the second Century.</margin>
If Barnabas is the writer of the letter which is said to be by him, then he testifies: *That Jesus Christ is the master of the world; that through him and to him all things are.* He attributes to him these words of Ezekiel: *I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh; and will give you a heart of flesh, etc.* Ezek. XXXVI. 26.

Hermes (b), <note>Commonly known in English as Hermas, the author of "The Shepherd of Hermas."</note> whom some believe to be the same one mentioned by Paul in Rom. XVI. 14, says in the third part of his book, which he calls the *Shepherd*, that God’s Son existed before all creatures, and that he was the Counselor of the Father; and he attributes to him the power of sustaining the world and all creatures.

<margin>(c) I place Ignatius in the First Century, although he died in the year 107.</margin>
If Ignatius (c) <note>Ignatius of Antioch, an early Christian martyr and bishop known for his letters.</note> is the author of the letters, as is claimed, then one finds many weighty matters therein.

The letter to the Ephesians begins thus: *Ignatius, also called Theophorus, to the Church blessing, in the greatness and fullness of God the Father, ordained before the Ages to an enduring Glory, unwavering, united, and chosen in the true suffering, and in the will of the Father and of Jesus Christ our God.*

In this letter he warns the Ephesians to beware of those who present an evil doctrine; and he adds: *There is but one bodily and spiritual Physician, born and eternal, God and man, true life in death, who is from Mary, and from God, passible and impassible.* <note>original: "lydelyk / en onlydelyk"; meaning capable of suffering and incapable of suffering, a common early theological distinction for Christ's dual nature.</note> This passage is understood differently in some Copies. We have: *Physician our Lord Jesus Christ, God, who is before the Ages, only Son, and the word, who thereafter became man.*

In the letter to the Romans, he says: *Let me be a follower of the suffering of Jesus Christ, my God.*

->THE CHRISTIAN<-

One can also bring up his letter to the Magnesians <note>Ignatius of Antioch (c. 35–107 AD), an early Christian writer and bishop.</note>, where he says that Christ was begotten <note>original: "gegenerceert," from the Latin *genitus*, meaning born or produced</note> of the Father before the Ages, and that the Word was God; in his letter to those of Smyrna, he expresses himself thus: what can it benefit me if someone praises me and blasphemes my Lord, not acknowledging that God has clothed himself with Flesh?

In the same letter, he threatens with hellfire those heretics who recognized only one nature in Christ; and to those who did not consider him a true man, he says: Our God Jesus Christ was conceived by Mary, according to the Divine dispensation <term>dispensation: the historical unfolding of God's plan for humanity</term>, from the seed of David, through the Holy Spirit.

From this it appears that Ignatius believed that Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man, and that one cannot be saved without believing this.

Clement of Rome <note>Bishop of Rome in the late 1st century AD.</note> says in his letter to the Corinthians, Jesus Christ is from Abraham according to the Flesh: thus he recognized another nature in him.

### SECOND CENTURY.

<margin>Eusebius, History, Book 4, Chapter 15.</margin>
Polycarp <note>A disciple of the Apostle John and Bishop of Smyrna.</note> spoke these words a few hours before his death:
> “Therefore I praise you for all things, O God, I bless you, I glorify you through the eternal and Heavenly High Priest Jesus Christ, your beloved Son, through whom to you, as to him, in the Holy Spirit, be Glory, now, and in all Eternity. Amen.”

And in a letter attributed to him, he says to the Philippians: God, who is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Son of God himself, Jesus Christ, who is the eternal High Priest, build you up in faith and love.

<margin>Eusebius, History, Book 4, Chapter 3.</margin>
Aristides, a Philosopher of Athens, who offered a defense of the Christian Religion to the Emperor Hadrian, proved in the presence of the Emperor that Jesus Christ is **God**.

Although Athenagoras <note>A 2nd-century Christian apologist.</note> said some things about the Trinity that seem somewhat unrefined <note>original: "rouw" (rough); referring to early theological language that was not yet as precise as later creeds</note>, one nevertheless finds in his defense, published in the Year 166, these words where he speaks of the Son:
> “All things were made through him, and the Father and the Son are one: the Son is in the Father, and the Father is in the Son, through the union and power of the Holy Spirit. And further: Who will not be astonished that we are called Atheists,

<column-break/>

we, who say that there is a God the Father, a Son who is God, and a Holy Spirit, and who demonstrate their power in unity? He stands in wonder at the union and the distinction of the Father, of the Son, and of the Spirit.

One can also look at what Eusebius <note>The "Father of Church History" (c. 260–339 AD).</note> says in Book IV, Chapter 5 regarding the Bishops of Jerusalem until the time of Hadrian, and what one reads in Sulpicius Severus, Book II, Chapter 45, regarding the first Church of Jerusalem.

Justin Martyr <note>An early Christian apologist and philosopher martyred in 165 AD.</note> speaks thus in his first defense from the Year 150:
> “Because we do not worship the Demons <note>original: "Demones"; referring to the Greco-Roman gods</note>, we are called god-forsakers, and we admit that we are so with respect to these gods; but not with respect to the true God, Father of righteousness, of purity, and of all other virtues, without the mixture of any defect; with him we honor and pray to the Son, who came from him and taught us all these truths, and the Prophetic Spirit.”

Furthermore, he says in the same defense,
> “We believe that our teaching must be accepted because it is true, and that it was taught to us by Jesus Christ, who alone is the specifically begotten <note>original: "ge-genercerde"</note> Son of God, being his word, his firstborn, and his power, and became man by his will.”

<margin>P. 96.</margin>
And following:
> “Those who take the Son for the Father show that they do not even know the Father, and do not know that the Father of the Universe has a Son, who being the word, and the first-born of God, is also God, and appeared of old to Moses and other Prophets in the form of fire and an incorporeal Image; and has now under your Empire become man, from a Virgin, according to the will of the Father, for the Salvation of those who believe in him.”

<margin>P. 94.</margin>
On page 94, he speaks of those who are baptized in the name of the Father of all things, and of the Lord God, and our Savior Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit.

In his dialogue with Trypho <note>A famous debate between Justin Martyr and a Jewish interlocutor.</note>, he shows that Christ is no mere man, as the Jews expect him to be, but that being God before all Ages, he became man; he proves his Divinity from many Psalms, especially through XLV, and through the appearances to the Patriarchs and to Moses; he says, it is the Lord of Glory, Psalm XXIV, who with

# DIVINITY. III. B. XIX. Chapter.

...spoke with Moses and said, I am the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

It is objected against Justin <note>Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD), an early Christian apologist and philosopher.</note> that he says in his *Dialogue* that the Father is invisible and the Son visible, etc. But he intended to say nothing else than that the Father has not become known to men except through the Son; and *Irenaeus* says the same. One finds similar expressions in Athanasius <note>Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373 AD), the chief defender of Trinitarianism against the Arian heresy.</note>, whom one cannot suspect of having had wrong views on the Divinity of the Word.

<margin>Oration IV against the Arians.</margin>
Justin, to explain the generation <note>The process by which the Son "comes forth" from the Father.</note> of the Son, uses in his *Dialogue* the simile of a fire that lights another fire without diminishing itself. Tatian <note>A student of Justin Martyr and author of the *Diatessaron*.</note> does the same. But it must be admitted that these similes are very poorly suited.

See the defense of Justin, pages 32, 44, 51, 56, 60, 61, 67, 76, 77, 93, 94, 95, 98; the *Dialogue against Trypho* <note>A famous debate between Justin and a Jewish man named Trypho regarding the Messiah.</note>, pages 201, 255, 256, 267, 270, 285, 355, 358, 359; *Epistle to Diognetus*, page 498.

If the work *Questions and Answers to the Orthodox*, which contains 146 questions that are accurate enough, were by Justin the Martyr, one would find evidence there that he believed in the mystery of the Trinity: But it clearly appears that he is not the author, since Origen is cited in the 82nd and 88th questions, Irenaeus in the 115th, and the Manicheans in the 127th. One finds there the words *Hypostases* <term>Hypostases: the distinct persons of the Trinity</term>, of *Person*, of *consubstantial* <term>consubstantial: of the same substance or essence</term> <note>original: "medewezen (consubstantieel)"</note> in the sense that the Church gave to them in the fifth and sixth centuries, and many other things showing that he did not write this book.

I say the same of his *Exposition of the Faith*.

Irenaeus <note>Bishop of Lugdunum (modern Lyon) and a disciple of Polycarp.</note>, describing the faith that he received from the Apostles (Book 1, Chapter 2), says that it looks to:
> "One God Almighty, and to one Christ, etc., and to the Holy Spirit, etc."
In the same chapter he testifies that:
> "Every knee bows before Jesus Christ our Lord, God, Savior, and King."

In the third book, chapter 6, he says:
> "That neither the Lord nor the Holy Spirit have ever called anyone 'God' absolutely and definitively who is not the true God;"
that God’s Son is truly Lord and God, because in Psalm 45 both are called God: the Son who receives the anointing, and the Father who gives it; he says further that "When the Scripture

<column-break/>

"names any other gods, it adds something indicating that they are not gods."

In the 20th Chapter, he says:
> "that the Word is, and always has been, co-existent <note>original: "medewezig (Coëxistens)"</note> with the Father."

See also the 2nd book, chapter 43:
> "O man! you did not always exist with God, as did His Word."
This proves that he believed that the Word was never created, that it is eternal, and that there is a contrast between the Son and the creatures.

It is objected that he said that the Father is greater than the Son, and that the Son did not know the day of Judgment: But he understood these expressions of John and Mark as referring to Christ's human nature. (Book I, ch. 19; Book II, ch. 18, 43, 48, 56; Book III, ch. 6).

In the 4th book, chapter 8, he says:
> "The Son is the measure of the Father, since He comprehends Him."

He mentions three Persons of the Trinity. (Book I, ch. 2; Book III, ch. 18, 19, 20; Book IV, ch. 25, 37, 75).

In the 4th book, chapter 11, he expresses himself thus:
> "He who spoke to Moses from the burning bush, and who made Himself known as the God of the Fathers, He is the living God; who is the God of the living, if not He who is God above all things, and above whom there is no other God?"
See also chapter 12, 14, Book V, chapter 12. These passages are so clear and explicit that one cannot doubt the orthodoxy of Irenaeus on this matter.

<margin>Book II, pages 194, 200.</margin>
Theophilus, Bishop of Antioch <note>An early Christian writer who was the first to use the specific Greek word for "Trinity."</note>, says in his second book that:
> "The three days which preceded the creation of the Stars are patterns of the Trinity <term>Trinity: the union of three persons in one Godhead</term> of God’s Word, and of His Wisdom."
Understanding by Wisdom the Holy Spirit, who gives it. And this is the first place where we find the name of Trinity among the ancients to signify the distinction of the persons.

Theophilus flourished in the year 168.

It is objected against him that he said that the Word can be in one place while the Father is not. But he says that because, in truth, only the Word became man.

On the other hand, he said that the Word was generated in time. But one must know that the Early Fathers believed that the Word, which was in God from all eternity, went out from God in some way when God created the world...

# THE CHRISTIAN

> “...I ask, of what God shall he be the temple? Is it of the Creator? No, that cannot be: for he has not believed in this God the Creator. Is it of Christ? Not that either; he cannot be the temple of Christ, since he denies that Christ is God. Shall it be of the Holy Spirit? Neither can that be, for these three are one. How could the Holy Spirit be favorable to one who is an enemy of the Father and the Son?”

<margin>Book 2, chapters 5 & 6, *Testimonies against the Jews* <note>original: "Testim. cont. Jud."</note></margin>
Arguing against the Jews, he <note>referring to Cyprian of Carthage, a prominent 3rd-century bishop</note> selects the principal passages from the Old Testament where the Prophets speak of Christ as God. Such as Isaiah 42 and 45.

> “Because God is in you, and there is no other God than you, for you are God, and we did not know it; the Lord our God shall do right, he shall come and save us; I am the Lord your God, that is my name, my glory I will not give to another, nor my praise to graven images.”

He also draws several passages from the New Testament, Romans 9, etc. He died in the year 258.

Gregory of Nyssa relates in the *Life of Gregory*, surnamed *Thaumaturgus* <note>meaning "the Wonderworker"</note>, a Creed <note>original: "Geloofs-Belydenis"</note>; which he claims this holy man received from the Apostle John in a night-vision; and which was still preserved exactly as it had been written by Gregory the Wonderworker. See the Confession here:

<margin>Spon's *Travels* <note>original: "Spon. Itin."</note> part 1, page 154.</margin>
> “There is but one God the Father, who is the Father of the living Word, His wisdom, consisting of the power and the eternally expressed image; perfect Father of a perfect Son; Father of an only Son. There is but one Lord, one from one, God from God, the expression and Image of the Divinity, the powerful word; wisdom, which encompasses the assembly of all things; and power, which made all creatures; true Son of a true Father; invisible Son of an invisible Father; incorruptible Son of an incorruptible Father; immortal Son of an immortal Father; eternal Son of an eternal Father. And there is but one Holy Spirit, who has his being from God, and who appeared to men through the Son; image of the Son, perfect like him, life, cause of the living, Holy source, Holiness who gives holiness, through whom God the Father is revealed, who is above all and in all things, and God the Son, who is over all; Trinity, perfect without division,

<column-break/>

> nor change in His Glory, in His Eternity, and in His Sovereignty.”

Athanasius has preserved these words from Theognostus of Alexandria.

<margin>On the decrees of the Synod of Nicaea <note>original: "De decret. Syn. Nicen."</note></margin>
> “The existence of the Son is not taken from elsewhere, or brought forth from things that were not; but is generated from the essence of the Father, just as the rays of light are born from the Sun, and the vapor from water: for the vapor is not exactly the same thing as the water, and the rays are not the Sun; yet they are of no other essence. So too the Word is an outflowing of the essence of the Father, yet in such a way that the essence of the Father suffers no reduction by the rays that continually go out from Him. Thus, the existence of the Father suffers no reduction by generating His Son, who is His image.”

The same Athanasius has preserved for us the words of two men named Dionysius; one the Bishop of Alexandria, the other the Bishop of Rome, both enemies of the Sabellians <note>followers of Sabellius, who taught that the Father, Son, and Spirit were merely different "modes" or masks of a single person</note> and of Paul of Samosata.

Dionysius of Rome speaks thus: “I am currently going to oppose those who divide, undermine, and overthrow the pure and godly doctrine of the Church, dividing the complete and absolute Unity into certain powers, separate substances, and into three deities; for I understand that there are among us catechists and teachers who present such a doctrine; wherein they are directly opposed to the sentiment of Sabellius, for the blasphemy of this heretic consists in his asserting that the Son is the Father Himself, and that the Father is the same as the Son; but these others, on the contrary, make in a way three Gods, dividing the Holy Unity into three <term>hypostases <note>A technical theological term for the distinct "persons" of the Trinity; here Dionysius warns against seeing them as three separate gods</note></term>, foreign and entirely separated from one another, etc. It is necessary that the Word of God be united with God, the master of all things; and that the Holy Spirit remain and dwell in God; it is also necessary that the Divine Trinity unite itself into one head, namely, in the Almighty, who is the God of all things, etc. For the rest, those are no less to be rejected who say that the Son is a work of God, wishing to claim that the Lord was made like all other things; for the Scripture attributes to him a Generation, which him...”

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the page is ", geen" (not/no), indicating the sentence continues on the next page regarding the unique nature of the Son's generation.</meta>

I think that the Confession of Faith—which goes by the name of *Athanasius* <note>Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373) was a champion of Trinitarianism against Arianism.</note>—should be added here.

There are six Formulas of this confession. The 1st is that of *Gilbert Génébrard*, drawn from a manuscript by *Lazare de Baïf*. # DIVINITY. BOOK III. B. CHAPTER XIX.

[addressed] a letter to those of Antioch, signed by many Bishops who were then in Alexandria, because they had been informed that great disputes had arisen among the orthodox in the Eastern Diocese over the use of the word *Hypostasis* <note>A Greek term meaning 'substance' or 'underlying reality,' which caused confusion because it could mean either a distinct 'person' or the 'divine essence' itself.</note>. See here how Athanasius speaks in his own name and in the name of the other Bishops.

<margin>Athanasius' Works, Epistle 1 to the Antiochians.</margin>

> Therefore, if anyone objects to such or similar things, restrain them and bring them to peace; since we have perceived that they are not possessed by anything but stubbornness and a spirit of contention. For having taken knowledge of this disagreement, we found that some people wanted to count it as a crime that [others] said there were *three Hypostases*, because these words are not found in the Scripture and were therefore suspect; and we advised them to hold to the Nicene confession. Meanwhile, as the heat of the dispute among the parties was great, we asked those who were in favor of the *three Hypostases* whether they intended the *Persons* or *Hypostases* to be substances or existences distinct from one another, according to the heresy of the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who taught that the Son was a created being, lower than the Father.</note>, and whether each *Hypostasis*, according to their thoughts, was separate and existed by itself in the same manner as other creatures or as those born of men; or whether they meant that they were entirely different substances, like gold, silver, and copper; and whether by these words of *three Hypostases* they intended, like the other heretics, to make three principles and three Gods. Thereupon they testified that they had no such thoughts and had never said anything of the kind. We further asked why they then used these words? They answered that they believed in a true and essential Trinity, and not a Trinity of words; a Father who had his existence, a Son truly having his existence, and the Holy Spirit likewise having his existence. But they had never said that there were three Gods and three principles; that they would never tolerate anyone who thought or said that. That they very much desired there to be a Holy Trinity, but nevertheless one single Deity, one single principle; that they recognized a Son, consubstantial <note>original: "medewezig" — meaning sharing the same essence or substance.</note> with the Father, as the Old Fathers had described it; that the Holy Spirit is no

<column-break/>

> creature, and no foreign, but a proper and inseparable being of the essence of the Father and of the Son. We approved of this explanation and examined the others, who had been accused by these [first] ones of recognizing only one *Hypostasis* or Person—namely, whether they said that in the sense of *Sabellius* <note>Sabellius taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were just different 'modes' or masks of one person, rather than three distinct persons.</note>, to separate the Son and the Holy Spirit from the Trinity, and to suggest that the Son had no essence, or the Holy Spirit no *Hypostasis* or existence. These answered that they understood that *Hypostasis* and existence were the same thing, and that they posited one *Hypostasis*, which we hold to be one, both because the Son is of the existence or essence of the Father, and because of the complete identity of nature. For we believe that there is but one Deity, and that this Deity has but one nature, and that the nature of the Father is no other than that of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Thereupon the others, who were accused of having posited *three Hypostases*, agreed with the view of these; as did those who confessed only one *Hypostasis*; they rested in the explanation of the others; and both parties cursed both *Arius* as the enemy of Christ, and *Paul of Samosata* and *Sabellius* as godless, etc.

From this it appears that in the first four centuries, the concern for the Trinity was accepted, and [the Church] was convinced of the Deity of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. I shall only add a word to this. We have two monuments in pagan antiquity from which one can infer what the Christians believed.

<margin>Pliny, Book 10, Epistle 97.</margin>

### IV. CENTURY.

<margin>Epiphanius, *Heresies* 69; Athanasius, Volume 1; Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*; Theodoret, book I, chapter 11, VI; Sozomen, book I, chapter 15; Socrates Scholasticus, book I, chapters 5 & 6.</margin>
IN this Century, Arius <note>Arius (c. 250–336) was a priest in Alexandria whose teachings on the nature of Christ led to the first major schism in the Christian Church.</note>, a teacher in Alexandria, disturbed the Church. One can gather from various writings, and especially from those of Athanasius (who was his opponent), what he and his followers believed:

1. That Christ was God, but lesser than the Father.
2. That he had a beginning and was a creature, created out of nothing before the ages.
3. That he was a "made" God, by the will of his Father.
4. That he is the Son of God through adoption, though like his Father.
5. That the Father created the world through him as an instrument.
6. That the essence of the Father is different from that of the Son; that he is neither co-eternal nor of the same essence <note>original: "medewezen," referring to the Greek term *homoousios*</note> with the Father.
7. That the Holy Spirit is not God, but a creature of the Son.

He had many Bishops of his opinion; the Council of Nicaea, in the year 325, was gathered against him.

<column-break/>

The Arians were divided into many factions.

The first were entirely of the opinion of Arius, whom they call <term>Anomeans</term> <note>From the Greek 'anomoios', meaning 'unlike' or 'dissimilar'.</note>, from a word that in Greek means "dissimilar." <margin>Epiphanius, 76.</margin> This was because they believed that the Son was not similar to his Father; their head was one Aëtius, a Deacon of Antioch; he was called "the Atheist." He had a disciple, Eunomius, and thus they were named Aëtians and Eunomians. He was condemned by the Semi-Arians in the year 358, and in Constantinople in 359 by Constantius, who sent him into exile after having heard the declaration of his faith with horror.

Others said that the Son was similar in essence to the Father, but not <term>consubstantial</term> <note>Meaning 'of one substance'. This group used the term *homoiousios* (similar substance) instead of the Nicene *homoousios* (same substance).</note>; the heads were Basil, Eustathius, etc. They were called <term>Semi-Arians</term>.

<margin>Socrates Scholasticus, book 2, chapter 30.</margin>
Others said that the Son was like the Father; but they did not add "in all things" and "in essence"; the heads <margin>Socrates Scholasticus, book 2, chapter 40.</margin> were one Acacius of Caesarea in Palestine, who subsequently, it is said, accepted the opinion of the orthodox in the year 363. The others rejected all these words and said that the Father was greater than the Son in Honor, in Dignity, and in Divinity. Just as the second Formula of Sirmium states in the year 357, which Hosius <note>Hosius of Corduba, a prominent bishop who presided at Nicaea but was later pressured into signing an Arian creed in his old age.</note> signed.

It would be too long to bring up here all the particular Councils held against and by the Arians.

<margin>Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*; Sulpicius Severus; Vincent of Lérins, book 1, commentary 1; Epiphanius, *Heresies* 74.</margin>
Photinus, Bishop of Sirmium, the capital of Illyria, denied the Trinity; according to him, the Father alone was God, the Holy Spirit was not God, nor a Person of the Trinity; the Christ and Son of God did not exist before Mary, and was not God, but a mere man, though born of a Virgin through the operation of the Holy Spirit. He was condemned by the Councils of Sardis, Milan, and Sirmium.

Macedonius, Patriarch of Constantinople, a Semi-Arian who believed that the Son was like in essence, also maintained that the Holy Spirit was not God, but a creature like the Angels, although of a more exalted rank. His followers were named <term>Pneumatomachi</term>, that is, "Enemies of the Holy Spirit." The Council of Constantinople was held against him under Theodosius the Great in the year 381.

### VI. CENTURY.

<margin>

These sects had their followers in the fifth and sixth Centuries; but it is not necessary to provide their names.

I will only say that a certain *Philoponus* <note>John Philoponus (c. 490–570), an Alexandrian philologist and philosopher.</note>, a philologist <term>Taalgeleerde: a scholar of language and literature, often focusing on classical texts</term> and philosopher of Alexandria, claimed in the sixth Century that there were three Gods. The opinion of *Roscelin*, a cleric of the Church of Compiegne, was condemned in a Council of Soissons in the year 1091, because he taught that the three Persons are three distinct things, like three Angels or three Souls.

In the year 1148, in the 12th Century, *Bernardus* <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux.</note>, at the Council of Reims, had *Gilbert Porreus* <note>Gilbert de la Porrée (c. 1070–1154), Bishop of Poitiers.</note> condemned, who was Bishop of Poitiers and was accused of allowing a quaternity <note>original: "vierheid" — the unorthodox idea that God’s essence is a fourth thing distinct from the three Persons of the Trinity.</note> in God.

In the 16th Century, there were many who contested the Divinity of Christ and the Holy Trinity. Such as *Michael Servetus*, who denied that Christ, before he was born of the Virgin, had any other existence than in the mind of God; *Valentinus Gentilis*, who allowed for three Gods. *Mattheus Gribaldus*, *Pau-*

<column-break/>

*lus Alciatus*, *Georgius Blandrata*, *Petrus Coniza*, *Georgius Paulus*, *François Lismanus*, *Erasmus Joannes*, who was an Arian. *Franciscus Davidis*, *Budneus*, *Christian Francken*, *Bernardus Ochinus*, *Lælius* and *Faustus Socinus* <note>The founders of Socinianism, a rationalist Christian movement that denied the Trinity.</note>, *Andreas Dudithius*, *Valentinus Smalcius*, *Hieronymus Moscorovius*, *Christoffel Ostorodus*, *Georgius Enjedinus*, *Joh. Volkelius*. And in the 17th Century, there have been seen to arise *Theophilus Nicolaus*, *Adam Goslavius*, *Joh. Crellius*, *Joachim Stechmannus*, *Jonas Schlichtingius*, *Wolzogenius*, and others, whose names one finds in the *Antitrinitarian Library* <note>original: "Antitrinitarische Bibliotheek"</note> of *Christopher Sandius*, published in 1684 at Freistadt. They have not all shared the same opinion; but it is not necessary that I describe their views here.

There are those among the *Mahometans* <note>A historical term for Muslims.</note> who say that the world has two Gods: one Eternal, who is God above all things; and a new one, who is Jesus Christ; *Mahomet* said that Jesus was God's Spirit.

To God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God in three Persons, be Honor, Glory, the Kingdom, and Majesty. AMEN.

# THE CHRISTIAN
## THEOLOGY,
### BOOK FOUR.
#### Of God’s Decrees in General.

---

##### CHAPTER I.
###### What is understood by the word Decree,
###### and whether there is such a thing.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'N' depicting a figure walking on a path in a rural landscape with trees and a building in the background.</image-desc>

Now that I have spoken of God’s adorable being, and of the three Persons who possess this being, it is only natural to treat of God’s decrees before I speak of His works. We call a Decree of God that which God has intended, decided, and determined to do or to permit.
The word "Decree" <term>Besluit: in this context, a formal decision or purpose determined by God from eternity</term> is in use in the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to Scholasticism, the method of critical thought and theology dominant in medieval universities and early modern academies.</note> and is taken from the *Vulgate* <note>The Latin translation of the Bible. Original: *vulgata*</note>, as can be seen in Ephesians 2:15 and Colossians 2:14, though often used there in a different sense than we do now.
We cannot doubt God’s decrees; the Scriptures teach us this clearly. Isaiah 46:10: *My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure.* Isaiah 14:24: *The Lord of hosts hath sworn, saying, Surely as I have thought, so shall it come to pass; and as I have purposed, so shall it stand.* Acts 2:23: *Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain.*
Those who 1. explain this passage as referring to the gift and present that God made of His Son to the Jews to deliver them from their sins, do not understand it; for the root word <note>The original Greek word used in the New Testament.</note> signifies giving someone over to the mercy of their enemies, as the linguists remark. 2. It also cannot be translated

<column-break/>

as a revealed or made-known intention (which we have translated as "determinate counsel"); for it is clear that the text speaks here not of a revealed intention, but of a determined intention, and of a declaration made within God’s own counsel.
Acts 4:28: Peter says that Herod and Pilate were gathered together *to do whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined before to be done.* And Paul in Ephesians 1:4-5: *According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world... having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will.* And verse 9: *Having made known unto us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he hath purposed in himself.* And verse 11: *We who were predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will.* And Romans 8:28-29: *We know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to (his) purpose. For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate,* etc.
Reason confirms that God is the all-wise being who knows everything, foresees everything, and sustains everything in existence. Now, it befits a wise being to set an end <note>A final goal or purpose.</note> for Himself in all that He does, to arrange all outcomes or possible things that might relate to this end, and not to allow anything to happen against His will; for if this were not so, one could conceive of a being who surpassed Him in wisdom, and without whose will nothing would happen

<meta>catchword: would;</meta>

# DIVINITY. IV. B. II. Chap.

...would; and such a being alone would be worthy of being called God.

Furthermore, if God knows everything—as we proved in the 2nd Book—not only what is possible, but also what is to come, He must necessarily have determined what shall happen: otherwise He could not know for certain what would occur.

Furthermore, because God is independent, it is simultaneously understood that the creatures are absolutely dependent on God; for if this were not so, one could conceive of a more perfect being—namely, one upon whom all creatures depended, while He depended not on them; who could act without them, while they could not act without Him; and whose gaze would be necessary every moment for the existence and activity of the creatures. Now, this dependence on <term>secondary causes: the created means, such as natural laws or human actions, through which God works His will</term> clearly proves that all outcomes must be arranged according to God's will.

The <note>original: "Heidenen" (Heathens or Pagans)</note> ancient philosophers knew this, as many proofs could be provided for it.

### II. CHAPTER.

->*How one must understand God's decrees; and of their Eternity.*<-

Do not think that God makes decrees like men, who, before they go to work, must make a sketch, and subsequently consider what might happen, and who try to carry out their design—but whose spirits are often uncertain and wavering, not knowing which way they shall turn, who then decide one thing and then another, who first think of an end, and then of the means. One must not have such thoughts about God; He sees everything at once and determines it all through a single act of His will. But Scripture attributes decrees to God to teach us that He does everything with great wisdom, that nothing happens against His will, and nothing exists that He did not foresee and determine to either perform or permit.

<margin>What one must distinguish in God’s decrees.</margin>
In God's decrees, one must distinguish three things. 1. God's will, which determines that a thing shall be. 2. The relationship that this will has to the creature or matter,

<meta>catchword: 1. Part.</meta>

<column-break/>

over which God makes any decree. 3. The decreed matter itself. When we consider the act of God's will in these decrees, we do not distinguish it from His essence: for God’s will and essence are the same, and there is nothing in God but God Himself. God could not have been without a decree, because He cannot be without a will.

Just as all beings who work by counsel also work upon some <term>idea: a mental blueprint or concept</term> that they form, it is asked whether there are ideas in God? The question is more curious than it is useful, and it is better to remain silent than to say something that God has not revealed.

The Theologians note the following regarding this: 1. That there are ideas in God, but they are not stirred up from elsewhere, as happens with men. 2. That things <note>original: "den zynd" (existence or being)</note> take their being according to God's ideas, and His ideas are not made according to things; and thus all things are first in God. 3. That these ideas are God’s very essence, who knows His own perfections and wills that there be some traces of them in the creatures. 4. That, strictly speaking, there is but one idea of all things in God, though we perceive many because of the various relationships this single idea of God has to an infinite number of things that are outside of God. 5. That in this sense it is said that the idea of one thing is not the idea of another. 6. That the idea of all the perfections of the creatures is in God; not of their imperfections. 7. Finally, that God indeed knows all the imperfections of His creatures, but He only knows them through the opposite perfections. They cite many other things as well, especially the <term>Scholastic Theologians: university scholars who used formal logic and philosophy to define Christian doctrine</term>. But one reasons about this matter by groping <note>original: "by den tast" (by touch or blindly)</note>, and one quickly falls into extravagances; one becomes entangled in difficulties from which there is no escape. The safest course, then, is to say that one knows nothing of it.

<margin>Of the Eternity of the decrees.</margin>
The Scripture says that God's decrees are eternal. Matt. XXV. 34. *Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.* Eph. I. 4. *According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world.* 1 Cor. II. 7. *We speak the wisdom of God (consisting) in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom, which God...*

<sig>Ee</sig>
<meta>catchword: before</meta>

<keywords>divine decrees, omniscience, dependency of creatures, secondary causes, divine ideas, scholasticism, predestination, eternity of God's will</keywords>
