<margin>Code concerning Sorcerers and Mathematicians, etc. <note>original: "Cod. de Malet. & Math. &c." Refers to the "Codex de maleficis et mathematicis" in Roman law, where "mathematicians" was a common term for astrologers.</note></margin>
4. The Roman Emperors acted harshly against the astrologers. Augustus banished them from Rome; Tiberius and Claudius from Italy; Vitellius ordered them to be put to death. The Law of Art <note>This likely refers to the "art" of divination or a specific legal article.</note>, which is that of Diocletian and Maximian, says that astrology is an accursed art and is entirely forbidden. Constans and Julian, in the Roman Laws, forbid consulting astrologers, soothsayers, and diviners under penalty of death. Honorius and Theodosius willed that the astrologers be banished from Rome and other cities, and if they do not repent, that they be moved to far-distant places to end their days there. (*On the Jurisdiction of Bishops, Code of Laws.*) <note>original: "L. Mathemat. Cod. de Episcop. Audient."</note>

5. It is a very ridiculous imagination to think that the free will of man depends on any constellations; and to believe that an astronomer, who cannot predict whether it will be heat or cold, or whether the weather will be dry or rainy, could foresee that a Polycrates <note>The tyrant of Samos who was famously crucified.</note> will be crucified; that a Croesus <note>The wealthy king of Lydia who faced execution by Cyrus.</note> will be in the extreme danger of losing his life by a violent death; that a Socrates will die from poisonous hemlock; an Aeschylus from the fall of a tortoise; <note>Legend says the playwright Aeschylus died when an eagle dropped a tortoise on his bald head.</note> an Alexander by poison; another by the sword; that one shall be learned and the other ignorant; that one shall go from being a shepherd to a King, and the other from a King to a schoolmaster; one rich, the other poor.

6. What likelihood is there that a hundred thousand people, possibly born in the same hour and under the same birth sign, share the same fate? And that, although born of parents whose constitution, years, morals, and status are very different, they would have the same inclinations, the same way of life, the same fortunes, and die at the same moment and in the same manner?

7. What likelihood is there that all those who die in a war, in a shipwreck, or from a general plague, would have had the same point of birth? That all the firstborn of the Egyptians, killed by the Angel of Destruction; that all the Egyptians who drowned in the Red Sea; that all the children of Bethlehem whom Herod put to death; that all those Galileans whose blood Pilate mixed with the sacrifices, would have had the same planet or celestial alignment?

But it is enough to have refuted an error whose vanity everyone will experience sooner or later; although astronomers sometimes guess some things by chance, even without following the rules of their art.

<margin>Genesis I: 20, etc. The Works of the fifth Day.</margin>
The work of the fifth day was the production of the water creatures, the fish, and the birds. God willed to make another sort of mechanical bodies, far more excellent than the plants; He willed to create animals which, as well as they, had the power of growing and reproducing; but above that, the power of moving and acting in countless encounters, almost as we do. The composition of these bodies was wonderful, both in terms of the delicacy of the parts of which they had to consist, and because of their number, variety, and perfect union. God began with the creation of the animals with which the air and the water were to be filled.

God then commanded the waters to receive in their womb and to form bodies that had the power of movement within them, in the most imperfect way of all, which consists in gliding and crawling.

At the same time, God commanded the air to be filled with such bodies that also had the power of movement within them; but with a movement as swift and varied as that of the fish was meant to be slow and steady.

<margin>Genesis I: 24. The Works of the sixth day.</margin>
But, since the Earth, which was to be the chief object of the care of her Creator, still had no ornament other than plants, God willed that she, like the air, should also have animals. Therefore, on the sixth day, He commanded her to bring forth an innumerable number of animals, which had as much relation to the Earth as the birds to the air and the fish to the water. <margin>Use of the instruction of Creation.</margin>
This section provides us with excellent lessons.

1. One cannot but highly esteem God's perfections; one sees his **Goodness** manifest in the Creation / his **Wisdom** in the order / his **Fullness** and the **Riches of his Glory**, in the abundance and variety of things / that are in the World / his **constancy** in the duration of what he has brought forth / and his **power**, by which he has drawn all these wonders out of nothing.

2. By observing the Creatures we must elevate ourselves to him / who made them; and not misuse any of them / to the disdain of him who created them for his honor.

3. In our needs and necessities we must observe / that we are Children of him / who created all the goods of the **Universe** / the Riches of Heaven and Earth.

4. Let us think / when we see no human help / nor any second cause remaining for our assistance / that God calls the things / which are not / as if they were.

5. When we are in turmoil and perplexity / let us observe / that God brought forth the **Universe** out of the confusion of the Earthly mass.

6. When we are in the dismal night of adversities / oppressions / and sorrows / we must place our hope and trust in God / who / having drawn the light out of darkness / will make his light shine in our darknesses.

## CHAPTER V.

->Of the Creation of the Angels, and of their Nature.<-

<margin>Were the Angels created by God?</margin>
Since the Scripture often speaks of Angels, it is necessary to know whether they were created by God: for I shall not dwell on proving against the Sadducees that Angels exist. <note>The Sadducees were a Jewish sect during the Second Temple period known for denying the resurrection and the existence of spirits.</note>

In Acts 23:8, it is said that the Sadducees claimed there is neither Angel nor Spirit. It is almost incomprehensible that the Jews, who believed in the Books of Moses and (according to the account of Josephus) <note>Flavius Josephus was a 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> denied all that was written, could deny that there were Angels; this has given scholars cause to investigate what their meaning might have been. Some have said that the Sadducees believed that when the Scripture speaks of Angels, it either means God appearing in a human form, or the good inclinations that God gives to men.

<margin><gloss>Instincts</gloss></margin>
Others have said that the Sadducees did not deny that there were Angels, but only evil Angels. Others say that they only denied that the Angels were immortal beings, but rather were beings that God created and subsequently destroyed.

Whatever opinion the Sadducees may have held regarding the Angels, God's Word—the divinity of which we have proven—is so explicit on this point that it is a wonder there have been Heretics who, while accepting the Scripture, could deny such an established truth: all the more because there is nothing in it that offends reason—to believe in finite beings who are spirits without

<note>(b) We have shown elsewhere that it is ridiculous to understand these words as referring to any creation other than the first.</note>

<column-break/>

bodies; just as there are beings composed of spirit and body, and bodies that are not joined with spirits.

I cannot see how it is possible that people who believe they have a spiritual Soul, and who have thoughts in which they can perceive nothing physical, refuse to recognize spiritual beings who are without a body, nor believe that God often uses the service of these spirits to carry out His commands. No one would dare to say that something which is material does not exist.

Reason and Scripture both teach us that the Angels were created by God. Both teach us that everything which is not God is created, and that Eternity is an incommunicable property of God. Reason says that, however excellent the Angels may be, they are nonetheless finite beings who, consequently not being able to exist of themselves, must necessarily recognize as their origin Him who is the beginning of all things. But the Scripture says expressly in Colossians 1:16: *For by him (namely Christ) were all things created, that are in (b) the Heavens, and that are on the Earth, visible and invisible, whether they be Thrones, or Dominions, or Principalities, or Powers: all things were created by him, and for him.*

<margin>The Angels are not created from any physical matter</margin>
It is easy to understand that the Angels, being Spirits, were not created from any matter like man: for how is it to be understood that Spirits can be drawn from a coarse and extended matter? Therefore, we view as a dream the saying of some Jews that the Angels were made from the primary substances (Elements).

Why Moses does not speak of the Creation of the Angels?
</margin>
It is no wonder that Moses does not mention the Creation of the Angels. His primary objective was to write a historical account of the Church; he speaks of no Angels except when it is necessary to describe what they have done in regard to the believers. Those who write a description of an ornate pleasure-house are not obligated to describe the neighboring peoples; they make mention of them only when it is appropriate and the occasion arises.

This is the true reason for Moses' silence; for it is ridiculous to say that Moses mentions no Angels because of the inclination the Israelites had toward Idolatry, or because they were coarse and not quick-witted enough to understand the nature of Angels. For if these reasons were valid, then Moses should never have spoken of these Heavenly Spirits, yet he does so frequently; and one does not need a more penetrating intellect to grasp that the Angels were created by God than to understand the Creation of other beings.

<margin>
Job XXXVIII. 4--7.
</margin>
It has been believed that the Angels were created on the first day, as it seems can be inferred from Job XXXVIII. 4–7: *Where were you when I laid the foundations of the Earth? Declare, if you have understanding. Who determined its measurements? Surely you know! Or who stretched the line upon it? To what were its foundations fastened? Or who laid its cornerstone, when the morning stars sang together, and all the Children of God shouted for joy?* But this reasoning is not conclusive: it would be valid if it said, "when I founded the Earth, the Children of God praised me," but it does not say that. Thus, we can say that the Angels were created after the foundation of the Earth, shortly before God caused all the waters to gather into their places; which did not happen before the third day, or, as some prefer, on the second day. Meanwhile, I do not oppose the opinion of those who believe that the Angels were possibly created at the same time as the Heavens.

The interpreters are not in agreement regarding what one should understand by the "Host of the Heavens" in Genesis II. 1—whether it means the Angels or the Stars. But even if one understood it to mean the Angels, one could

<column-break/>

not conclude from it with certainty that they were created at the same time as Heaven and Earth.

Consequently, nothing is known for certain regarding the time at which they were created, but one can be assured that they were created in great number, as can be concluded from <margin>Rev. V. 11.</margin> Revelation V. 11: *I heard the voice of many Angels around the Throne, and the Living Creatures, and the Elders; and their number was ten thousand times ten thousand, and thousands of thousands.* And from Daniel VII. 10: <margin>Matt. XXVI. 53.</margin> Matthew XXVI. 53: *A fiery stream issued and came forth from before him; a thousand thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him.*

Regarding the Nature of the Angels, the Scripture teaches us that they are Spirits. <note>Nature</note> Paul places them among the invisible things. <margin>Col. I. 16. Heb. I. 14.</margin> Colossians I. 16. Some of the Church Fathers believed that they had bodies—such as Tatian, Justin, Clement of Alexandria, and Tertullian. The Mahometans <note>An archaic term for Muslims.</note> believe that they are thin bodies created from matter. Voetius <note>Gisbertus Voetius (1589–1676) was a prominent Dutch Reformed theologian.</note> and others also believed this (<note original: "apol. exeg. cap. 7.">Exegetical Apology, chapter 7</note>), <margin>A. Reland, *On the Religion of the Mahometans*.</margin> but they were mistaken.

There are those who excuse those who said the Angels are Corporeal by saying that their objective was only to show that they are true substances, or that they are not spirits as spiritual, simple, and pure as God.

It will perhaps be said that they are compared to the Wind and to a flame of fire. That is true; but if one had to conclude from that that they are corporeal, then one would also have to say that God is corporeal, because he is frequently compared to physical things.

It will be said that the Angels have often made themselves visible to men to carry out God’s commands. I admit it; but one cannot conclude anything else from that than that they assumed bodies, in the same way as the Son of God revealed himself visibly to the Patriarchs.

Furthermore, it would be presumption to determine how and from where they assumed these bodies.

Some say that God created them out of nothing; others that they were made of a substance that had no disposition to become a body, like that with which the Angels appeared; others that they took on the bodies of living men themselves. Others, that these bodies [consisted] of...

It is not very necessary that we trouble ourselves to know what the knowledge and power of angels is; one must confess that we know very little of the matters of spirits.

<margin>
Of the Knowledge of Angels.
</margin>

We are assured that, besides the natural knowledge which these spirits have had since their creation, they acquire more daily, and that God reveals many truths to them which they would not have known by themselves.

It is easy to understand that the knowledge of angels is greater than that of men, since they constantly behold God's face, their hearts are not corrupted, and they have no prejudices.

But we know for certain:

1. That their knowledge is not infinite, and that they do not know many things. Thus Christ says in Matthew 24:36 that they do not know the day of judgment. And Paul teaches us in Ephesians 3:10: "So that now through the church the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places." Peter also teaches us in 1 Peter 1:12 regarding those "things into which angels long to look," even into the depths of the mysteries. God alone, being an infinite being, has infinite wisdom.

Matt. XXIV. 36.

He cites Ephesians 3:10 for this purpose. Isidorus <note>Likely Isidore of Pelusium, a prolific letter writer of the early church.</note> generally denied to the angels the knowledge of all objects that were not present. 3. They know God’s perfections much better than men; but one must not imagine that they know them perfectly, because God being infinite, He cannot be perfectly known by any finite being.

4. The manner in which they know corporeal and visible things cannot be explained.

5. One cannot deny that the angels communicate their thoughts to one another; this can be concluded from many passages; but we do not know how. Possibly God has established this order: that when an angel wants to make something known to another angel, that angel knows it; just as He has established this order: that upon certain thoughts of the soul, certain movements of the body immediately follow: for the one is no more incomprehensible than the other.

The meaning is this: if I were as eloquent as the angels would be, if they had a language or tongue; my eloquence would be like the sound of a ringing metal, if it were not animated by love.

# THE CHRISTIAN <note>The header "DE CHRISTELYKE" likely refers to "The Christian Theology" or "The Christian Religion."</note>

Of the Power of the Angels. Psalm 103:20.
</margin>
7. Regarding the Power of the Angels, it is certainly great; thus they are called "mighty in strength"; and they can do innumerable things that exceed human capabilities; but their power is finite; and it is difficult to comprehend, not to say impossible, how they move physical bodies.

8. We are assured that they cannot perform true miracles, because an infinite power is required for that, and consequently, a Divine power; therefore we do not believe that they can raise the dead or create substances. However, we know that God has often performed miracles in the presence of Angels, which are then attributed to them, even though God alone is the cause of them.

<margin>
2 Sam. 24:15, 16. 2 Kings 19:35. Isaiah 37:36.
</margin>

We cannot say if that is the work of an Angel alone, because we do not know the extent of their power.

<margin>
Of the order of the Angels.
</margin>
<margin>
Colossians 1:16.
</margin>
10. Without doubt, there is some order among the Angels, as is evident from the various names given to them; it is for this reason that Paul, speaking of the Angels, uses the names of various ranks or dignities seen in the States and Kingdoms of the World, where there are **Thrones**, which refers to supreme Rulers and Kings; **Dominions**, which are dignities that, though very high, are nonetheless lower than kings, such as Dukes and Archdukes; **Principalities**, such as Administrators or Governors of Cities and Provinces; and finally **Powers**, which are subordinate Authorities. But we believe it would be reckless to define exactly what the distinction of their order is, and we frankly admit with Augustine that we do not know, without concerning ourselves with all that is brought forward on this matter under the name of the Venerable Dionysius the Areopagite <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite was a 5th-century philosopher whose work *The Celestial Hierarchy* became the standard for angelic rankings in the Middle Ages.</note>.

<margin>
Augustine, *Against the Priscillianists*, chapter 11 <note>original: "contr. Prif. ill. d. 11."</note> & *Enchiridion*, chapter 58.
</margin>
It was the opinion of this Dionysius that there are three Hierarchies of Angels in Heaven, each having three orders, and thus 9 Hierarchies <note>Usually referred to as nine "choirs" or "orders" within three hierarchies.</note>. In the first, one places the **Cherubim**, **Seraphim**, and **Thrones**. In the second, the **Dominions**, the **Principalities**, and **Powers**.

<column-break/>

In the third, the **Virtues** <note>original: "Kragten"</note>, **Archangels**, and **Angels**. It is claimed that these various names are given to them because of the diversity of the properties of their Nature, or because of the various ministries they hold: that some are called **Cherubim** because they surpass the others in Wisdom, which they then teach; others **Seraphim**, because they burn with Divine love and ignite others with the same love; others **Thrones**, because they govern and judge the others. The **Dominions** would assign the Angels their duty; the **Principalities** would manage nations and provinces; the **Powers** would restrain the power of the Devils; the **Virtues** <note>original: "Kragten"</note> would have the authority to perform miracles; the **Archangels** the ministry to announce great matters; and the **Angels** the small ones.

</margin>
The Jews had previously distinguished ten Hierarchies of Angels; of which some are under the Throne of Majesty, having access to God’s Secret Chambers; others interact and speak with men. They say that four stand before God: **Raphael, Gabriel, Uriel, and Michael**; Michael is at the right hand, Gabriel at the left, Uriel in front, and Raphael behind. Others serve. One sees from the *Introduction to the Jewish Excommunication* <note>original: "Voorbericht der Joodsche Kerk-Ban"</note>, cited by Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654), an English jurist and scholar of ancient laws.</note> in *On the Law of Nature and of Nations* <note>original: "de Jure Naturæ & Gentium"</note> book 4, chapter 7, that the Jews believe **Uriel** has the governance of the month of *Nisan* (March); **Zephaniel** of the month of *Iyar* (April); **Amniel** of *Sivan* (May); **Peniel** of *Tammuz* (June); **Barkiel** of *Av* <note>OCR reads "Ahh."</note> (July); **Periel** of *Elul* (August); **Zuriel** of *Tishrei* (September); **Zachariel** of *Marcheshvan* (October); **Adoniel** of *Kislev* (November); **Anael** of *Tevet* (December); **Gabriel** of *Shevat* (January); and **Rumiel** of *Adar* (February). They also believe seven Angels rule over the seven days of the week, and four over the four seasons of the year.

But these are mere trifles. Regarding the Hierarchies: 1. Scripture does not speak of them. 2. It says that all Angels are ministering Spirits. 3. According to this opinion, the Seraphim should never have been sent to Earth, yet the contrary appears in Isaiah 6:6. Moreover, Scripture speaks not of many Archangels, but of only one. All these distinctions seem to be taken from the Philosophy of Plato. (See Iamblichus, *On the Egyptian Mysteries*; Proclus, *Commentary on Plato's Alcibiades*). I do not consider it necessary here to give an account of the names of these Heavenly spirits, and to say why they are named Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones.

One must admit that nothing certain can be said about this; therefore, it will be enough to note that the word Angel means *Envoy* <note>original: "Afgezant"</note>, because God indeed sends them to earth to carry out His commands; therefore they are called ministering spirits (Hebrews 1:14) and God’s servants (Psalm 104:4).

God has no need of servants to do what He desires, since He can execute everything through a single act of His will. But He wishes to grant this honor to His creatures, that He chooses to employ them and use them for His glory. Moreover, God acts thus, either for the adornment of the universe—since nothing contributes more to the beauty of the world than seeing that all the creatures of which it is composed, when put together, have a wonderful correspondence with one another: high, middle, and low—or for the comfort of the believers, who thereby perceive how God cares for them, since He uses the ministry of perfect creatures to promote their salvation.

<margin>Whether the Angels are used for the Government of the world.</margin>

# THEOLOGY. Book 5, Chapter 5.

<margin>
Ps. 91:1, 12.
Gen. 19:12, 13, 15, 16, 17.
2 Kings 6:16.
Dan. 6:22 and 3:28.
Acts 5:19.
Luke 16:19–22.

they are shown to us as carrying the soul of Lazarus into the bosom of Abraham. And at the end of the ages, they shall gather the elect.

See there the ministry of the angels; but we do not believe that they quench the flame of our desires or ignite the flame of Divine love. We do not believe that the enlightenments which sometimes come to us in a moment of distress—which reveal to our understanding the vanity of mortal things—the horror of sin, the perfection of a holy life, the willing resolutions we make in our despairs, those unexpected comforts that precede a good outcome, those premonitions of our disasters, and other things of that nature, are proofs of the assistance of angels. We do not attribute to these Heavenly spirits anything other than what we find God Himself ascribes to them: we give the unblemished honor of our enlightenment and sanctification to the work of the Holy Spirit, as the Scripture teaches us.

Without doubt, God uses the blessed spirits for various effects that are unknown to us; but we believe that one must be careful not to attribute to them such works which the Scripture teaches us are the effects of God's Spirit.

->### Whether everyone has their own Guardian Angel?<-

**O**n the occasion of the ministry of angels, it is natural to investigate whether everyone has their own Guardian Angel? Many Church Fathers believed this, although they explain themselves differently on the matter.

In the Roman Church, there are many teachers who maintain that there are seven angels, acting as Princes of the Heavenly Court, presiding over all the Churches, servants of God, and mediators for men; and here are their names: Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, Uriel, Sealtiel, Jehudiel, Barachiel. <note>Pined. *on the affairs of Solomon* book 5, ch. 15. Corn. à Lapide *on the Apocalypse* 1.</note>

But besides these seven, they believe that everyone has their own Guardian Angel—indeed, even their own evil angel. There is a dispute to know whether everyone has one from their conception and birth, or only from their Baptism?

It is believed that this angel does not leave the person whom he protects until the end of life. They attribute fourteen specific actions to this angel...

<column-break/>

1. To punish, whenever one commits any sins.
2. To untie the bonds of sin.
3. To remove everything that prevents us from doing good.
4. To teach inwardly and to enlighten the understanding.
5. To drive out demons.
6. To reveal mysteries.
7. To comfort the sorrowful.
8. To confirm one in the ways of God.
9. To be our guide on a journey.
10. To humble our enemies.
11. To moderate temptations.
12. To bring prayers to God.
13. To take on the appearance of the one he protects.
14. To chastise. *

When we consult the Scripture on this, we will find nothing that obliges us to believe that God has given each person their own angel.

We find, indeed, that God has sometimes sent one of His angels to the believers. We find also that God commits the care of every believer not to one angel in particular, but to His angels; thus many angels accompanied the Patriarch Jacob on his travels.

We find, moreover, that God sometimes uses a single angel to deliver many of His children. One angel caused the siege of Jerusalem to be broken.

But we read nowhere that God would have given each believer their own angel.

Matthew 18:10 is raised as an objection. There it is said that *the angels of the children in the Heavens always see the face of my Father, who is in the Heavens.*

But from that, one can prove nothing except that God gives the protection of children to the angels, and not that each child has his own specific angel. If one says of all the members of a congregation that has many teachers, that their teachers work without ceasing for their edification and building up, that does not prove that each of them in particular has his own teacher. For the rest, it is impious to say that Christ accommodates Himself to the errors of the Jews—

# CHRISTIAN THEOLOGY
<note>original: "DE CHRISTELYKE [GODGELEERDHEID]"</note>

Some object by citing Acts 12:15. There, the maidservant of Mary’s house, who had heard and seen Peter (though those gathered there still believed him to be in prison) came to announce to them that he was there; whereupon those who heard it said she was raving, but she insisted that it was so, and they said: "It is his Angel."

There is much to answer to this.
1. One can say that it was an error of the Jews of that time, and therefore it proves nothing. The Jews believed that an Angel took on the form and voice of every person of whom he was the protector. 
2. One can also say that the word "Angel"—which in Greek means an Envoy or a Messenger <note>original: "Angelos"</note>—was used by those who gave this answer to the maidservant. They believed that whoever had knocked at the door, having said he came from Peter, was merely Peter's messenger, and that she, upon hearing the name of Peter, had imagined that Peter himself was knocking. How could they have thought that an Angel had come to knock at the door—an Angel who could easily enter anywhere—and that he would have mimicked the voice of Peter? 
3. But in short, even if God had granted Peter an Angel from the time of his calling to the Apostleship to assist him during the course of his ministry, that would not be enough to conclude that He likewise gives a guardian Angel to every believer, good or evil, faithful or unfaithful.

The other passages that are brought forward prove nothing at all, as one will be convinced by simply reading them. (e)

The sentiment that everyone has their own guardian Angel came from the Pagans and the Jews. The Pagans believed that everyone had their own protector-god. Plato said that there were such spirits given to every man, not only to be witnesses of his deeds but also of his thoughts: that the same spirit who had the care of our life leads us to be judged; that he stands by during the preparation of our legal case; that he punishes us if we lie and confirms if we speak the truth; whereupon the Sentence is pronounced according to his testimony. See Plato in *Phædo* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the soul</note> and Apuleius’s *On the God of Socrates* <note>original: "de Deo Socrat."</note>.

<margin>(e) These passages are: Gen. 48:16; Exod. 14:19; Ps. 91:11; Isa. 29 and 38:36; Dan. 10:12; Heb. 1:14; Eccl. 17; Judith 13:20.</margin>

<column-break/>

Menander in Ammianus Marcellinus, Book 29, Chapter 3; Arrian on Epictetus, Book 1, Chapter 14; Maximus of Tyre, Dissertations 26 and 27. Every man, says Theocritus, is accompanied by a Spirit to guide him well, who is the good governor of his life. Hermes, surnamed the Shepherd <note>referring to the early Christian text "The Shepherd of Hermas"</note>, confirmed this sentiment with his authority, and many Church Fathers have defended the same.

Some even held gross errors regarding the Angels. Justin Martyr says in his *First Apology* <note>original: "1ste verantwoording"</note> that God gave the Angels the management of the rest of human affairs under Heaven; but that some of them fell because of their passion for women, and that from this union, spirits <note>referring to the Nephilim or demons</note> were born. Athenagoras says that God created the Angels for the care of human affairs, which are placed under their management in such a way that God indeed keeps an eye over everything in general, but leaves the particular investigation to the Angels whom He has appointed. <margin>Book 6 of the *Stromata*</margin> Clement of Alexandria also considers Angels to be Overseers of men; he believes that every country and possibly every man has his own; that God commanded the care of every city and every nation to the Angels and distributed them among them. Origen reasons thus: just as men who were God-fearing in the world become Angels after their death, so those who are now Angels may formerly have been men. <margin>Homily 10 on Jeremiah</margin> He gave Angels to children and others to adult men. He attributed to the Angels the sub-governance of the Universe. He said that there were many powers within us that had the care of our Souls and Bodies. <margin>In Joshua, Homily 20</margin> He had yet other ridiculous <margin>Homily 23</margin> opinions regarding the guardian Angel.

Furthermore, although we do not believe <margin>In Numbers 20</margin> that God has given everyone their own Angel, we nevertheless believe that we must thank God for giving His Angels charge over us to keep us in all our ways, using the most excellent and noble creatures of the Universe for that purpose.

We also believe it is our duty to do nothing in the presence of these blessed Spirits that would make us unworthy of the protection they wish to undertake for us. The Pagans said that one should always think themselves to be before the eyes of a Socrates or a Cato. But we do not need to think of a Cato or Socrates; we have...

## CHAPTER VI.

->Of the Creation of Man.<-

<margin>Why God created Man last?</margin> We have already noted that man was created by God; it is nevertheless necessary to treat this creation more precisely.

Man was created on the last day; God’s infinite goodness having willed that most of His creatures should be suited for the use of man, it was becoming of His wisdom to complete them all before He made Man, so that he might enter into the world like a Prince making his entrance into his territory, where he finds all cities ready and prepared to receive him gloriously.

It was proper that the Universe—which was to be as the house of man—should be created before the inhabitant, who would himself be like a microcosm <note>original: "kleine wereld," literally "small world," a common Renaissance concept where the human body reflects the structure of the universe</note>, was created.

<margin>In what manner God created Man.</margin> God created man in a special way; He did not say, "let there be man," as He had said, "let there be light"; but "let us make humans in our image" (Gen. 1:26). It appears that God, as it were, rouses Himself, that He reflects and consults. This was not because He had need of advice in this matter, but to show the excellence of His work.

With these words, God does not turn to the Angels, as some Jews have believed; nor to Heaven, nor to the Earth, as others have said: but to His Son, and to the Holy Spirit. The first Christians recognized this. One

<column-break/>

finds in a very old letter—which some say is by Barnabas and others by Polycarp—these words: *Our Savior was willing to suffer for our souls, being the Lord of the world, to whom the Father said: let us make humans.* The three adorable persons of the Trinity converged for the production of man. And we shall see in the following what more they have done for his happiness.

<margin>Gen. 1:26. God is only introduced as "Consulting" when dealing with human affairs.</margin> It is observed that God is not introduced as "taking counsel" <note>original: "raadslaande," referring to the use of the plural "Let us..."</note> except when man is spoken of: (1) When God was about to create him, He said, *let us make humans*, etc. (2) When He wished to create the Woman, He spoke thus: *It is not good that the man should be alone, I will make him a helper (who) shall be as a counterpart to him* (Gen. 2:18). (3) When God wished to drive him out of Paradise, He said: *Behold, the man is become as one of us, knowing good and evil* (Gen. 3:22). (4) When God wished to destroy mankind [in the Flood], He said: *My spirit shall not strive with man forever, because he is also flesh, yet his days shall be 120 years* (Gen. 6:3). (5) When He wished to confound the speech of the builders of the Tower of Babel, He cried: *Come, let us go down and there confound their language* (Gen. 11:7). (6) When the Israelites marched out of Egypt, He said: *Lest the people repent when they see war* (Exod. 13:17). (7) When He wished to destroy Ahab, He said: *Who shall persuade Ahab that he may go up?* (1 Kings 22:20). (8) Anticipating the sending of a Prophet, He said: *Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?* (Isa. 6:8). Thus God always speaks in this manner in the case of man, to teach us: 1. Always to work with counsel. 2. To be assured that God consults even for us when we know no counsel. 3. Finally, never to set ourselves against God, since His counsel is always greater than that of men.

<margin>From what was the body formed?</margin> The body of man was made from dust (Gen. 2:7) (f); not from some heavenly matter or precious metal, but from dust that one treads underfoot. It is not worth the effort here to cite the imaginings of the Jews. It is held that it is because of the earth, where the first man...

### THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION

man was except for this, that he was named Adam <note>The name Adam is traditionally linked to the Hebrew word *adamah*, meaning "ground" or "earth."</note>, although there are scholars who give another reason for this name.

God wanted to create man out of the dust, so that he, mindful of his beginning, would constantly carry with him that which must humble him, and prevent him from ever exalting himself against his Creator.

Although God used the dust to make the body of man, He formed it so wonderfully that this formation is nothing less than a Creation. For, to give such an excellent form to such lowly and coarse matter, and to make a machine of so many wheels <note>The author uses the metaphor of "wheels" to describe the complex mechanics of biological systems, a common 17th-century comparison to clockwork.</note>, required nothing less than an infinite power; indeed, the very same power that God had used in the production of other beings.

One cannot be amazed enough by the manner in which God made the body of man; even the most irreligious are forced to confess that something Divine shines through here.

One notices in it the wisdom, goodness, and power of the Master who made this excellent work.

My aim is not to dissect all its parts here: it will be enough to say here that the body is a microcosm <note>original: "kleine wereld," literally "small world."</note>, all the more wonderful for being smaller; for most parts are so fine and delicate that the strongest sight cannot perceive them; and yet they are so well-arranged that neither their delicacy prevents them from having their necessary strength, nor does their number conflict with the perfect harmony they must have with one another, so that nothing is defective or useless.

God created man with his face turned upward, so that he should learn to despise the earth, and look upon Heaven as his true Fatherland and there behold his Creator; who, although being present everywhere, has placed His throne in the highest of the Heavens.

I pass over the confused trifles of the Jewish Teachers concerning the beauty and stature of Adam.

As soon as God, through His infinite power, had created the body and formed it through His inexpressible wisdom, He animated it with a Soul worthy of its Creator, which He created at the same moment He placed it in the body, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of

<column-break/>

life. Gen. 2:7. This way of speaking indicates: (1) That God gave life to the body by making the air enter into his chest, and by this means giving a beginning of movement to the lungs and the heart, to make the circulation of the blood begin there, to ignite this pure and living flame, and to set in motion what we call animal spirits <note>original: "dierelyke geeſten." In historical medicine, these were believed to be subtle fluids that traveled through the nerves to produce sensation and movement.</note>; in a word, to give life to the body, which it had to have in common with the Animals, and maintain through breathing. (2) That by the word "breath of life" one must understand what we call the rational Soul; that is, 그 essence that is capable of thinking, which has the concept of its own existence, and which, joined together with a mechanical body, makes up what we call man. Thus the Hebrew word is used in Prov. 20:27: *The soul of man is a lamp of the Lord; searching all the inner chambers of the belly*, that is, the deepest things. Furthermore, although it is said that God breathed the breath of life into Adam, one must not take these words literally, or believe that it is only to let us know that it was as easy for God to create a soul as it is for a man to draw a breath from his mouth—which was the opinion of Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–457 AD), a prominent theologian and bishop.</note>. Rather, the Scripture intended to teach us that God did not take the soul from the dust; but that it came immediately from Him, not being of the same nature as the body, which is material and perishable, but that it is spiritual, imperishable, and immortal, like its cause.

<margin>The Heavenly origin of the soul.</margin>
The soul then has a Heavenly origin, and one must judge all Souls the same way; they do not come from the Parents, but from God: Zech. 12:1. *The Lord speaks, who stretches out the Heavens and lays the foundation of the earth, and forms the spirit of man within him.* And Paul calls God the Father of spirits. Heb. 12:9. Solomon says in Eccl. 12:7 <note>The OCR text says XXII (22), but Ecclesiastes has only 12 chapters; the citation refers to 12:7.</note>: *The spirit returns to God, who gave it.*

The soul is then in us not by birth, and we must not think that parents communicate it to their children: then one would have to say that the soul of the Father and the soul of the Mother generated that of the child: they would either have transferred their entire soul to the child, or only a part; neither the one nor the other...

# THEOLOGY. BOOK 5. CHAPTER VI.

And **Augustine** remains in doubt. *Epistles 28 to Jerome; 157 to Optatus; Retractions Book 1, Ch. 1; Book 2, Ch. 56.* The difficulties raised concerning this matter are so slight that they will not hinder a man of understanding who considers the reason and the previously indicated passages. A theologian from Cambridge, named **More** <note>original: "Morus." This refers to Henry More (1614–1687), a famous "Cambridge Platonist."</note>, of whom letters are found among those of **Descartes**, has asserted that souls have their existence before they are united with the body, and that they descend from their dwelling place to be united with the body, enticed by a fine scent wafting from the **small embryo** <note>original: "Petit Embryon."</note>, almost like birds of prey from afar by the scent of their quarry; what extravagance!

Even the Pagans have recognized the heavenly origin of the soul; as the learned have proven through the testimonies of **Zoroaster**, **Aristotle**, and **Cicero**.

To prove that the soul had matter as its origin is a great absurdity; for shall one say that matter thinks? Or shall one say that particles of matter, arranged in a certain way, together make up a thinking being? But how shall indivisible particles or small bodies, which, when separated from one another, do not have the power to think, be able through their joining together to produce a work whose origin is not in them? One might perhaps say that, although one cannot understand how matter could think, one must nonetheless not deny it, because we do not know how far God’s infinite power reaches. But if it were permitted to reason thus, then one could never confirm anything; one would say that there is no absolute contradiction in supposing that a substance that reasons can be a body. I admit, the contradiction is not as obvious as when one would say that a circle is a square; but there is no less impossibility in it, because the ideas we have of the body have nothing in common with thought. Furthermore, from the saying that our souls are from God, it follows that

<column-break/>

God has a special right over the movements of our souls, and that they must all go out toward God. Although Nature and Religion bind us very closely to our parents, the bonds that tie us to God are incomparably stronger, since the soul, which we have from God, is something entirely different from the body, which we have in part from our parents.

It is said that God breathed the **Breath of Life** into man's nostrils, to teach us that Adam began to live as soon as God had created the soul.

It did not stop with the Creation of Soul and Body: God united these two parts in such an excellent way that upon certain thoughts of the soul, certain movements of the body are set in motion; and upon certain movements of the body, certain thoughts in the soul are awakened.

We cannot then believe that the soul is only in the body like a **Pilot in a Ship** <note>This is a critique of the "dualist" view (often associated with Plato or Descartes) which suggests the soul is merely a temporary operator of the body rather than being intrinsically united with it.</note>; for if this were so, the spirit would have no more feeling of sadness when the body was injured than a pilot feels when something on the ship is damaged.

I leave it to the Philosophers to reason more broadly upon this union.

It was not good that Man was alone: otherwise he would have been unhappier than the animals, to whom God had given the power of multiplying and remaining in existence through birth.

<margin>Why God gave a Woman to Man?</margin>
Man was made for society; and he had a strong inclination toward it, both because he was endowed with reason and because he could make his thoughts known through speech, which would have been given to him in vain if he had found no creature like himself in the world with whom he could have had fellowship.

If he had been alone on Earth, why would God have made the Earth bring forth so many herbs and plants? etc.

Therefore God wished to give him a helper: but this was not to be found among the animals; he had need of one to whom he could open his heart, and reveal his thoughts, with whom he could share his goods; and who, for the praise of

<margin>From what was the body of the Woman formed?</margin>
**God** did not wish to make that helpmate from the Earth, but from the Body of the Man, so that there might be as close a union between them as possible; and they, being one body, should be of one heart; and so that the human race, of which they were to be the beginnings, should come from one blood.

**God** took her from the sleeping **Adam**; He willed that **Adam** should be the admirer of His finished work, but did not wish him to be the spectator of it while it was being made. Thus **God** desires that we marvel at His works, but often hides from us the manner in which He performs them.

Furthermore, the sleeping **Adam** is a symbol <note>original: "zinnebeeld," referring to a typological representation where an Old Testament figure foreshadows a New Testament one.</note> of the dying **Christ** on the Cross, from whose side flowed water and blood, which brought forth the **Church**: just as the **Bride** of the first man was a representation of the birth of the **Church**, the **Bride** of the second **Adam** <note>The "second Adam" is a common theological title for Jesus Christ.</note>, who also had to draw her being and life from her Heavenly **Bridegroom** while He was in the deep sleep of death, and in some way come forth from the pierced side of this venerable **Bridegroom** with the blood and water that emerged from it.

I shall not investigate the reasons why she was taken from one rib rather than another.

Everything said regarding that is more clever <note>original: "spitsvindig," meaning overly subtle or sophisticated in a way that lacks substance.</note> than it is sound.

I shall only note two things.

1. That this rib of **Adam** was not enough to make a body of the correct size, and that the **Creator** must have added new matter to it.

2. That as soon as **God** had built the body of the **Woman**, He undoubtedly placed a **Soul** in it, just like that of **Adam**; although this is not recounted in the **Scripture**.

<margin>Isaac La Peyrère. Pre-Adamite Exercises and Systems. <note>original: "De la Peyrere. Præadamit. Exercit. & Syst." refers to the works of Isaac La Peyrère (1596–1676) who argued that humans existed before Adam.</note></margin>
I shall not linger on refuting those who have believed that **Adam** was not the first man. The **Scripture** expressly gives him this name; and all other humans it calls Children

<column-break/>

of **Adam**. Certainly, if there had been humans before **Adam**, then no reason can be given why **God** created him from the dust; the **Scripture** would also not say that he was alone when **God** had created him. It is also incomprehensible why **Adam** had to give the names to the animals, which they undoubtedly would have already had by then.

<margin>Whether there were humans before Adam. 1 Corinthians 15:45, 47. <note>The source text cites "I Cor. V. 45. 47," likely a printer's error for chapter 15 (XV).</note></margin>
We cannot, therefore, believe that **Genesis** 1 and 2 speak of two different men; it deals only with one, whose Creation **Moses** recounts with few words in **Genesis** 1 and more circumstantially in **Genesis** 2.

The objections made against our view are not worthy of our lingering to refute them.

It is ridiculous to ask where the garments of skins came from, which **Adam** and **Eve** wore after their fall, and the tools with which they tilled the **Earth**: one understands well enough that **God** gave our first **Parents** all the intelligence they needed for their necessity.

It is no such wonder that **Cain** fears being killed by those who shall meet him; one must not conclude from this that there were other humans before **Adam**; for since the Creation of the World, more than 90 years had already passed; **Abel** <note>The author likely means Adam or the general population, as Abel was killed without descendants; however, he may be suggesting the expansion of the family tree over nine decades.</note> could have had many children and grandchildren whom **Cain** feared meeting; although no mention is made of this in the **Scripture**.

One objects with **Romans** 5:14, where it is said that until the **Law**, **Sin** was in the **World**, and by this **Law**, one understands the **Law** given to **Adam**. But one is mistaken; the **Law of Moses** is spoken of there. For according to **Paul's** saying, that **Sin** reigned until the **Law**, it means **Sin** reigned until **Moses**. (That is **Paul's** aim.)

It is said that mention is made there of those who have not sinned in the likeness of **Adam's** transgression. But it is clear that by this expression one must understand children, who have committed no actual **Sins** like **Adam** did.

# DIVINITY. V. B. VII. Chapter.

## VII. CHAPTER.

### Of God's Image, according to which man was created.

<margin>Gen. I. 27.</margin>
The Scripture, speaking of the creation of man, teaches us at the same time that God created him in His Image and according to His likeness. We must then investigate wherein this Image consists.

<margin>How Jesus Christ is God's Image. Col. I. 15. XIV. 9. Joh. XII. 45. Apoc. II. 23.</margin>
But we shall first distinguish, according to the Scripture, a twofold Image of God: a perfect and an imperfect Image. Christ is the perfect Image of His Father; Paul says the same in Colossians 1:15. The Savior says in John 14:9: *He who has seen me has seen the Father,* and in John 12:45: *He who sees me, sees Him who sent me.* Indeed, Christ has the same nature and the same perfections as His Father; He is Eternal, Unchangeable, Infinite; He possesses supreme Wisdom and searches hearts and minds <note>original: "beproeft herten en nieren," literally "tests hearts and kidneys," a common biblical idiom for God's ability to examine the innermost thoughts and emotions of a person.</note> just as the Father does. He has with Him all power in Heaven and on Earth. He is the Holy of Holies, before whom the Seraphim cover their faces; all things are made by the Son as well as by the Father; He is thus His perfect Image.

<margin>How is Man God's Image?</margin>
It is not so with man; he is God's Image, but this is an imperfect Image. We must then see what should be understood by this word.

I think it is not necessary to investigate what difference there is between "Image" and "likeness." Some, like Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a prominent Jesuit Cardinal and theologian often cited as a representative of Catholic doctrine during the Reformation.</note>, believe that the word "Image" signifies the essence of the Soul, and "likeness" the faculties or properties with which it is adorned. It is better to say that these two words signify that the first man was created according to God's Image, and that this Image makes him resemble God in some measure.

We must not imagine that man was created according to the Image of the human nature that Christ was to assume in the last days, as some have presumed. It is nowhere said in the Scripture that man was made according to Christ—speaking of Him as a man—but rather that Christ became like us. Furthermore, those who hold this opinion believe that Christ would 

<column-break/>

nonetheless have assumed our nature even if man had not sinned, which is beyond all appearance of truth <note>original: "buiten allen schijn," meaning it lacks any biblical evidence or logical probability.</note>.

<margin>2 Peter I. 4.</margin>
We must also not believe that this Image consists in God having communicated a part of His Divine existence to man; for it is clear that an infinite being is incommunicable <note>In theology, "incommunicable" refers to attributes belonging to God alone—such as infinity or eternity—which cannot be shared with created beings.</note> to a finite one, such as man. It is true, Peter says that we have become partakers of the Divine nature. But it is only to teach us that we are born again, and that the Holy Spirit has produced in us the Christian virtues that make us like God.

We must also not seek this Image in the shape of the body, as those heretics <note>Likely referring to the Anthropomorphites, a group in the early church who believed God possessed a physical human form.</note> wished to do, who attributed limbs to God by taking literally what the Scripture testifies about them. However, we must confess that in the wonderful composition of the body, we see many rays of God's wisdom and power shining forth.

The Socinians <note>Followers of a 16th-century theological movement that denied the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ, often holding more rationalistic views on human nature.</note> believe that this Image actually consists only in the Dominion that God gave to man over the Creatures. <note>original citations refer to: Socinus's dispute against Francesco Pucci and his Prelections ch. 3; Volkel's *On Religion* book 2 ch. 6; and Ostorod's *Institutions* ch. 34.</note> They believe that Adam, before he had transgressed God's commands, was not truly righteous, since he was not sinless; that he had had no opportunity to sin, and that it is not known whether he refrained from sin; but that he was created only in uprightness and innocence. <note>original citations: Smalcius against Frantzius disp. II and against Smiglecius ch. 7; Ostorod, *Institutions* ch. 33.</note>

<margin>Wherein does God's Image consist?</margin>
We believe that this Image consists:
1. In the excellence of the natural faculties of man.
2. In uprightness, Holiness, and Righteousness.
3. In the immortality of his Soul, and in that of his body.
4. In the Dominion that God had given him over the Creatures.

To make this matter more understandable, we must see whether God's Image can consist in these four things. Subsequently, whether all these are found in the first man.

It is easy to prove that God's Image can consist in these four things; for one must seek it in that which can make us like this perfect being; but there-

there is nothing that makes us like God but the **spirituality of the soul**, if I may express my thoughts so freely, **immortality**, **holiness**, **righteousness**, and **authority**.

Thus, it is said of man, even after sin, that he is made in God’s Image (Gen. 9:6; James 3:9), which shows that God’s Image does not consist in holiness and righteousness alone. It might be said that if this were true, one could say a godless man would have the Image of God and of the Devil within himself. I admit that, and it can indeed be said in different respects; even the most wicked of all men is created by God and possesses a spiritual and immortal soul.

One cannot doubt whether man, in his state of nature, was created in that same image which is restored in our souls through grace and shall be made perfect in glory. For Paul says in Colossians 3:10: *And have put on the new man, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of Him who created him.*

<margin>Eph. 4:24.</margin>
Now the image that is restored by grace and perfected in glory consists of knowledge, righteousness, and holiness. The word "renew" implies that the thing being renewed existed before, and that it was as if erased or decayed through age. One might say Paul is speaking of a believer; that is true, but he says that the believer is made according to the original image of Him who created him. One might also say that if God’s Image consisted in holiness, one could say the Angels were also made in God’s Image. I admit this, and it can very well be said, even though Scripture does not use this specific phrasing.

It is mere hairsplitting to say that the "New Creation" is spoken of here and not the "Old"; for it is enough that God’s Image is mentioned. Now, Paul places the existence of this Image in knowledge, etc. It is said that if the "new man" had existed before, he would not be called "new." I answer: He is called "new" in respect to sinners, who are born with the "old man" <note>The "old man" is a Pauline term for the fallen, sinful nature of humanity inherited from Adam.</note>; but he was in Adam when God created him holy and righteous.

In respect to **Dominion** <note>original: "Heerschappye," referring to man's authority over the created world.</note>, one can prove that God’s Image consists in that as well. 1. Because it is said,

<column-break/>

Genesis 1:26: *Let us make man in our Image, after our likeness, and let them have dominion,* etc. Unless we would rather say, with some scholars, that this dominion was a consequence of the Image, translating it thus: *Let us [make man], etc., so that they may have dominion.* 2. It can be proven with 1 Corinthians 11:7, where the man specifically is called the image and glory of God because of the dominion he has over the woman.

Having laid these principles as a foundation, I shall investigate whether these four things in which we have placed the existence of God's Image are found in man: which I shall prove in detail.

**I.** We cannot doubt the excellence of Adam's soul and its powers if we consider that the soul, given by God to our first parent, was a spiritual and thinking being—a rational being that could know the truths presented to it, understand the proportions of things, choose a good end and the proper means to reach it, distinguish good from evil, distinguish an apparent good from a substantial one, and recognize substantial evil hidden under the appearance of good; a being that knew itself and its own state.

It is not necessary to prove at great length that the soul is spiritual; an extended thing <note>A reference to "res extensa" or physical matter, which occupies space.</note> cannot think, and in physical bodies, we understand nothing other than local motion. "There is something in us," said Nicolé <note>Pierre Nicole (1625–1695) was a prominent French Jansenist theologian and philosopher who wrote extensively on the nature of the soul.</note>, "that says, *I think*, and that something is but one." Now, that which thinks cannot have various parts; for if it had parts, like bodies do, then the thought would have to be entirely in every part of this matter, and thus there would be many small thinking matters, each of which would say, *I think*; and dividing this further, one would find thinking beings unto infinity. Or, the thought would have to be partly in one of the matters and partly in another, so that the whole alone could say, *I think*, which is impossible: for a thought cannot be divided, and if it were divided, the whole would not be in every part of the matter. Thus, none of them could say, "I know a man," since they would only know a part of him; meanwhile, there is something in us that grasps the entire object, and that something must neces-

->THEOLOGY. Book V. Chapter VII.<-

...be blessedness without parts, and consequently must be spiritual. If matter produced our thoughts, then we would have no thoughts except regarding physical things, which is false.

There are those who do not wish to assert that matter cannot think; to maintain this, they say that the nature and essence of things are unknown to us. But if this were so, then one would know nothing at all; I could not then assert that a circle is not a square, or that sound is not a color. Certainly, when one sees no connection between two things, and when there is even a clear distinction between them, one is well-grounded in not affirming of the one what is said of the other. Heat and color differ no more than matter and thought. It is said that we understand nothing except under the idea of something material, and that our ideas proceed from our senses. But, first: if we understand spirits as small bodies, it is an error of our imagination. Second: it is certain that we have many ideas of things that are in no way physical, such as virtue, etc. It is true that it often happens that our thoughts correspond with our temperament; <note>The Dutch "gesteltheid" refers to the "four humors" or bodily disposition common in early modern medicine.</note> but that only proves the close union of our body and our soul. One might object regarding the souls of animals; but we do not know their nature.

It is also not my intention to treat the faculties of the soul—the intellect and the will. I leave that to the Philosophers. But I will only say that one cannot wonder enough at these two properties, especially when one considers them as not yet corrupted by sin; for this consideration satisfies our statement that God's Image consists in the excellence of the natural faculties of man.

II. I have said that God’s Image consists in Wisdom, in Holiness, and in Righteousness. We cannot doubt whether holiness was present in the first man, if we consider:

1. That it is said in Genesis 1:31 that everything God had created was good, and indeed with a goodness necessary for the end for which all things were created. Now it is certain that man was created to know, serve, and glorify God; he must then have been created with

<column-break/>

this goodness, which made him capable of fulfilling his duty, and which consequently consisted in Wisdom, Holiness, and Righteousness.

2. That it is said in Ecclesiastes 7:29: *God made man upright*; <note>The Dutch "regt" can mean both straight/upright and just.</note> this means not only that he was created without sin, but also righteous.

3. That man was created to hold Dominion over all Creatures; now he could not exercise this if he had not been endowed with wisdom and righteousness.

4. Finally, that sin could not have been natural to the first man; for if this were so, God, who was the Creator of Adam, would be the cause of sin; this cannot be thought of without actual godlessness.

Adam had, then, righteousness and holiness; his understanding was enlightened, his will holy, his passions were regulated and subject to reason, and reason was subject to God. Adam’s understanding was not occupied with prejudices, nor preoccupied by false principles; he was capable of knowing all truths that would have been distinctly presented to him; and his will was moved by the love of the Supreme Good, <note>Original: "Opperste Goed" (Latin: *Summum Bonum*), the ultimate theological goal of human existence.</note> and by a strong inclination that drove him toward the same. He was free from concupiscence. <note>Original: "begeerlijkheid"—in this context, the disordered desire or lust that theologians believed only entered human nature after the Fall.</note>

<margin>Socinus, *Theological Lectures*, chapter 3</margin>
It is said that a man to whom God had given no Law or commandment could not be called righteous.

I answer: 1. God had given Adam a righteousness with which he could fulfill the commandments that would be given to him. 2. He had imprinted the Law of Nature in his soul. 3. God subsequently forbade him from eating the fruit of the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil.

1. That this righteousness was natural to man, for he had it from the beginning of his creation, and it would have passed down to his descendants. God, who is Holy and righteous, was not necessitated to create man, but in creating him, He had to create him Holy and Upright.

It is then an error to believe that God created man in a state in which he was neither good nor evil, neither righteous nor unrighteous, subject to the first movements...

To suppose that Adam was subject to concupiscence <note>The original Dutch "begeerlykheid" refers to disordered desire or lust, often termed "concupiscence" in theology.</note> is to make God the author of sin.

In the Roman Church, opinions regarding this righteousness are divided. Some believe that it was natural to man in every way, either because he possessed it from his creation, or because it agreed with his nature, or because one contrasts the word "natural" with what is called "supernatural." Medina <note>Michael de Medina (1489–1577), a Spanish Franciscan theologian.</note> in 1. 2. q. 18. art. 2. speaks of many teachers who hold this view, as does Bellarmine. <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a highly influential Jesuit Cardinal and Counter-Reformation figure.</note> But this same view was condemned by Pius V and Gregory XIII, as Bellarmine notes. The most common opinion is that this righteousness was a supernatural grace; like a "golden bridle" <note>original: "gulde toom"</note> that prevented the struggle of the higher part of the soul (as they say) with the lower part, so that the state of man after sin differed from the state before sin no differently than a naked man differs from a man who has been stripped of his clothes. This is the opinion of Bellarmine. Some among them believe that it would have been contrary to God's wisdom and goodness to create man otherwise than with original righteousness. That is the thought of Jansenius <note>Cornelius Jansen (1585–1638), whose work "Augustinus" sparked the Jansenist movement.</note> in his *Augustinus*. Others believe that God could have created man without this righteousness. Among the Protestants, they all agree that this righteousness was natural; they regard the state of "pure nature" <note>The concept of "natura pura," a hypothetical state of man without either sin or supernatural grace.</note> as a mere imagination, in which man could be dragged toward evil by his own desire, for that would be to make God a cause of sin—though the Apostle John explicitly denies this. It is true that Bellarmine says that concupiscence would have arisen from the material matter of the body, contrary to the expectation of God, just as rust comes from steel, which cannot be attributed to the swordsmith who made the blade; but this Cardinal compares two unlike things; the swordsmith did not make the steel from which the rust comes, but God created the matter of our bodies; therefore, God would be the cause of concupiscence

<column-break/>

if man had been created with it. Furthermore, the goal of those in the Roman Church in defending this view is to prove that concupiscence is not sin, as it exists in those who are baptized.

The first: not to make Adam so wise that he would have possessed all sciences and known everything discovered since the Creation. The Scholastic theologians <note>original: "School-God-Geleerden"</note> are ridiculous, speaking of Adam's knowledge as if they had heard him or read books by this first man.

The second pitfall is to regard Adam as an ignorant person, as a "stupid fool" <note>Lelio or Fausto Sozzini (Socinus) and their followers often emphasized man's natural limitations.</note> who knew nothing at all. We must hold the middle way and believe that Adam possessed the wisdom necessary for him in the state in which God had placed him; and that he was capable of acquiring more knowledge, whether through reasoning or through experience. 
<margin>Genesis 2:25, 3:7.</margin>
One might say that Adam must have had very little innate knowledge, since it is said that he did not know he was naked. But one would have to lose all sense of understanding to believe that our first parents were actually like infants in a cradle and did not know they were naked; the meaning of these words is that they began to know, after the loss of their righteousness, the necessity of clothing: for then they felt shame, and possibly they then began to feel the harshness of the air. It is therefore a wandering imagination that Adam was merely an empty vessel because he was new, having received no instruction yet; an empty page on which nothing was written; that he was by nature only inclined to what was necessary for his existence and not to what could make him happy, and that he would have become righteous by acquiring a habit of righteousness through many repeated exercises. # DIVINITY. Vol. 5. Book VII. Chapter.

3. We must also note here that this Righteousness, which we call "original" <note>The term "original righteousness" refers to the state of moral and spiritual perfection that theologians believe Adam possessed at his creation.</note> because Adam possessed it from his very origin, was not unchangeable. With this Righteousness, it could have happened that Adam did not sin; but one could not say that, having this righteousness, he *could not* sin.

Because he could be stripped of this righteousness, it does not follow that it was not natural to him; for one must make a distinction between that which is so natural that nature itself consists of it, and that which is indeed natural but is not nature itself. Those things which are natural in the first way are never lost; but those which do not constitute the very nature of beings—even if they are natural to them—can be lost, as was the righteousness of Adam. Furthermore, the Church Fathers believed that the Image of God consisted in Holiness and Righteousness; see Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, Book III, chapter 37; Ambrose, *Hexameron*, Book 6, chapter 7; Chrysostom, *Homily 16 on Genesis III*; Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, Book II, chapter 12. See also the *Augustinus* of Jansenius and Jodocus Coccius, *Catholic Treasury*, Volume II, Book I, article III.

<margin>The immortality of the soul.</margin>
III. I have said that the Image of God consisted in the immortality of man. This immortality includes both that of the soul and of the body. The soul was immortal by a right that could not be alienated <note>meaning the soul's existence is inherently unending by its very nature</note>, and the body by a privilege that could be lost. The immortality of the soul excluded all mortality, but it was not so with the body, which would not have been immortal except insofar as man remained upright. The immortality of the soul was something inherent to its spiritual nature, but that of the body was dependent on holiness and the prize of integrity; man was immortal according to the soul insofar as it was rational, and according to the body insofar as he remained in the state of uprightness.

<margin>The immortality of the soul.</margin>
The immortality of the soul is proven by Scripture and by reason.

Solomon says in Ecclesiastes 12:7, "The Spirit

->Part 1.<-

<column-break/>

returns to God, who gave it, while the dust returns to the earth." The soul, then, does not die, since it returns to God as its principle, and does so to receive either prepared reward or deserved punishment.

<margin>Matthew 22:32</margin>
The words of the Covenant of Grace, which Christ quotes against the Sadducees—who denied the immortality of the soul and the resurrection of the body—confirm this truth: *I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; God is not a God of the dead, but of the living.* Matthew 22:32. If the soul died with the body, then God would be a God of the dead.

Christ's reasoning is grounded on these three truths: 1. That those with whom God has made a covenant live with respect to some part of themselves; otherwise, God could not give them the promised good. 2. That God's covenant is not for a time, but is eternal. 3. That God made a covenant with the whole man, and not just with the soul. However, we shall clarify this matter in another place.

Paul confirms the immortality of the soul when he says in Philippians 1:23: *I desire to be departed, to be with Christ, for that is far better for me.* And 2 Corinthians 5:8: *We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord.* If the soul died with the body, Paul would never have spoken this way.

1. Moses teaches us that God created man in His image. This is proof that He gave him a spiritual and immortal soul.

### DIVINITY. Vol. B. Book VII. Chapter.

so dies this one, and they all have one and the same breath; and the preeminence of man over the beasts is none, for all are vanity: they all go to one place; they are all from the dust, and they all return again to the dust; who notices that the breath of the children of men ascends upward, and the breath of the beasts descends downward into the earth. <note>original: Ecclesiastes 3:19-21. This passage is famously used by skeptics to suggest that humans and animals share the same fate in death.</note>

It is clear that Solomon intended to say nothing else than that, regarding the body, the state of humans and beasts is identical; that the same fate befalls them, and that, judging by outward appearances, when one sees a man die, it seems that he dies like a beast, and that there is no distinction between them.

One has but to read the Preacher <note>original: "den Prediker," referring to the Book of Ecclesiastes.</note> to be assured of the immortality of the soul. From the beginning of the XII. Chapter onward, he threatens mankind with a future judgment; a threat that would hold little terror if the soul were to die; for what should or must a man fear who is certain that everything dies with him? If Solomon had believed that the soul no longer exists after death, would he have taken such great care to bring men to the fear of God, seeing as the belief in the immortality of the soul is the foundation of virtue and religion? Solomon concludes his book with this: *Fear God, and keep his commandments, for this is the duty of all men.* Eccl. XII. 13. <note>The Dutch text cites verse 12, but in modern English Bibles this is verse 13.</note>

If one were to suggest from this saying of the Preacher—*who notices that the breath of men goes upward; and that of a beast descends downward*—that Solomon did not know what would happen, he would have spoken against his better knowledge, since he clearly says in cap. XII. 7: *The spirit returns to God*; and one would have to believe that he doubted that the soul of beasts descends below.

Certain passages of Scripture are brought as objections where it is said: *the dead shall not praise God.* But it is clear that this must not be understood absolutely, as if those who die ceased to exist entirely; for if this were so, the Scripture would not speak with such glory of those who *die in the Lord.* The meaning of these words is then that the dead cannot praise the Lord on Earth, in the company of the faithful, with whom

<column-break/>

they no longer have communion.

Psalm LXXVIII. 39 is also cited: *He remembered that they were flesh; a wind that passes away, and returns not.* But these words signify only the brevity of the life of men, who pass by like a wind and do not return to Earth to live with men again.

<margin>
John XI. 11.
I Cor. XI. 30.
1. Thess. IV. 15.

It is said that the dead are portrayed as those who Sleep.

But that is said only of their body, and not of their soul; for, regarding their soul, they are with Christ—I speak of the believers.

It is said that what has had a beginning must have an end.

But that cannot be proven; for why will one not admit that God has created beings to be immortal?

It is said that because the soul is closely united with the body, one cannot conceive that the body dies while the soul is immortal.

I answer: That if the soul and the body were of the same nature, one would have reason to object to this; but since they are so distinct, one can easily understand that the soul can exist without the body that it animates, just like the Angels.

It is said that the soul, being unable to have thoughts without the body, cannot exist without it.

But it is false that the soul has no thoughts independent of the body; for example, when it thinks of God, it can work independently of the body.

<margin>(* the Petrine Heresy)</margin>
This immortality was not only denied by the Epicureans among the Heathens and the Sadducees among the Jews, but also by others. In the 3rd century, there was a kind of people in Arabia who firmly maintained that the soul perishes with the body. This was called the Heresy of the Arabians (*and the Stone Heresy) <note>original: "Steene Kettery." The marginal note "l'heresie Petree" refers to Arabia Petraea (Stony Arabia), identifying the sect known as the Thnetopsychites.</note>. Those who deny the immortality of the soul can bring forth not a single reason of any weight; meanwhile, their reasons would have to be much stronger than ours to prove their sentiment, both because the belief in immortality is the safest and most comforting, so that if the reasons on both sides were nearly equal, it would be better to side with immortality rather than the mortality of the soul.

Man was meant to be immortal not only in regards to his soul, but also in regards to his body, as long as he remained in the <term>state of righteousness</term> <note>This refers to the original condition of humanity in Eden before the first sin.</note>.

This is evident because the Scripture teaches us:

1. That death entered the world through sin. Romans 5:12.
2. That death is the wages of sin. Romans 6:23.

<margin>Socinus, *Lectures*, chapter 1.</margin>
Some say that temporal death <note>Physical death in time, as opposed to eternal spiritual death.</note> should not be viewed as the punishment for sin, because Christ, having taken away all punishments for sin, does not deliver us from death.

<margin>Socinus, *Against Pucci*; Ostorod, *Institutes*, chapter 30; Smalcius, *Against Frantzius*, d. 7.</margin>
