# THEOLOGY, VI. B. Chapter III.

Authority was given over the Woman, and to both Man and Woman over the animals. But Satan arranged this work in such a way that the serpent made himself master of the Woman, and the Woman became mistress over the Man.

<margin>Was it a real Serpent? Rev. 12:9. 2 Cor. 11:3. Aben Ezra. Amyraldus, *On the Tempting Serpent*.</margin>
The question is asked: was it a real serpent? Some believe not, but rather that the name is given to the Devil, as in other places of Scripture. This view is not probable, for if there had been no serpent, why would Moses have provided us with a description of the cunning of this animal? And what would be the meaning of the curse that God pronounced over this serpent, consisting of the fact that it would eat dust? To understand all this in an allegorical manner <note>The author argues against treating the story as purely symbolic, insisting on a literal historical event.</note> is to abuse the Scripture.

<margin>To Maimonides' *Guide for the Perplexed*, Part 2, ch. 30. Amyraldus.</margin>
Some Jews, however, maintain this. Rabbi Shem Tov <note>A 14th-century Spanish Jewish philosopher and commentator.</note> says that the serpent is the faculty of the imagination. Isaac de la Peyrère, the author of the *Pre-Adamites* <note>A controversial 17th-century writer who argued humans existed before Adam.</note>, says that the serpent represents the senses, the woman represents reason, etc.

It is said that if it had been a real serpent, Moses would have described its species. This reasoning is very weak, for in the same way I could prove that Moses’ staff did not change into a real serpent because he does not say what species of serpent it was.

It is said that in Hebrew there is a prefix <note>original: "voorstel-woord". This refers to the definite article "the" (*ha*) in Hebrew (*ha-nachash*), which some argued implied a specific, supernatural entity rather than a common animal.</note> before the word for serpent, which indicates that it was no ordinary serpent. But it is certain that such a prefix is found in many places where ordinary serpents are spoken of, such as Numbers 21:9, Ecclesiastes 10:11, and Amos 5:19.

It is said that Moses could not have said that the serpent was the craftiest of all the beasts of the field.

I answer that those who have made it their work to know the cunning of serpents confirm the testimony of Moses. Besides that, one can very well say that the sense of the words simply means that the serpent was a cunning animal.

It is said that Scripture always attributes the temptation to the Devil. That is true, since it was indeed he, under the form of the serpent.

It is said that it is not probable that God would have wanted to speak to the serpent, which understood nothing. I answer that this should not appear any stranger

<column-break/>

than when God said to all the animals, "Increase and multiply," or when Christ cursed the fig tree. See 1 Kings 17:4, 2 Kings 7:13, Amos 9:3, Jonah 2:10, and Isaiah 45:12.

It is said that it was natural for the serpent to crawl, and thus God would not have condemned a real serpent to do so. I answer that it is probable that the serpent previously crawled without difficulty, whereas after the sin, it crawls in a different manner. The Jews say that it had the form of a camel, and that God cut off its legs.

It is certain, then, that there was a real serpent; but it is no less certain that the Devil spoke through this serpent and that he possessed it. It is the work of a spirit to make an animal speak, and that of an evil spirit to make it say such false and wicked things as the serpent brought forth. Furthermore, the Devil is called the "ancient serpent." Paul, in one of the places cited above, fears that the serpent which seduced Eve might turn the Corinthians away from the simplicity of the Gospel.

<margin>2 Cor. 11:3. Talmud, *Sotah* folio 9.2. *Sanhedrin* folio 29.1. Maimonides from the *Midrash*.</margin>
The Jews, who are fertile in their imaginations, say that Sammael <note>In Jewish lore, the main archangel of death and a figure often identified with Satan.</note>, the Angel of Death—who is the Devil—was riding upon a serpent when he attacked our first Mother. It is very probable that the history of the seductive serpent gave rise to the fables that the Pagans have spread about their *Ophioneus* <note>A serpent-deity in Greek mythology who ruled the world before being cast out.</note>, and about their Dragon who guarded the golden apples in the Hesperian gardens.

<margin>Augustine, *City of God*, book 14, ch. 11.</margin>
<margin>Aelian, book 17, ch. 5. Maximus of Tyre, Dissertation 38.</margin>
It is remarkable that the Pagans have worshipped serpents. Under that form, they honored their Asclepius <note>The Greek god of medicine, often symbolized by a snake-entwined staff.</note>. It is told that, not long ago, the peoples of Samogitia <note>A region in modern-day Lithuania, known for being among the last in Europe to convert from paganism.</note> held a serpent as their God. But it is surprising that in the second century there were heretics foolish enough to believe that the serpent who seduced Adam and Eve was Christ, for which reason they worshipped a serpent; these are called Ophites. See Augustine, *On Heresies*, ch. 17, and Epiphanius, *Heresy 37*.

The first trick of the Devil was then to hide himself under a serpent. It is no wonder that Moses does not speak of the Devil, since he acts solely as a historian.

One asks, of what kind was the serpent that Satan used? Some wish...

<meta>This page continues the theological investigation into the serpent's role in the Fall of Man. Having previously argued for a literal interpretation of the serpent (rather than a purely symbolic one), the author now explores the specific tactics used by the Devil to deceive Eve and the physical form the tempter might have taken.</meta>

# THE CHRISTIAN <note>This header is likely a fragment of "The Christian Theology."</note>

<columns>
...others want it to have been a **Basilisk** <note>A legendary reptile reputed to be the king of serpents, said to kill with a single glance.</note>, others a **Lamia** <note>In ancient folklore, a female demon or monster.</note>, others a **Dragon**. I confess that I do not know.

One asks, why did the Devil not take a human form?

I answer, to startle Eve less; for knowing that Adam was the only man in the world, she would have immediately conceived some suspicion of deceit if she had seen another man.

Perhaps the Devil preferred using a serpent over another animal because the form of the serpent in which he appeared resembled a woman, as some have believed. But the matter is quite uncertain. The Devil spoke through the serpent to our first ancestors.

There is no more reason for wonder here than there is regarding the speaking of a **female donkey** <note>A reference to the biblical story of Balaam’s donkey in Numbers 22:28, which was miraculously given the power of speech by God.</note>. Therefore, it is unnecessary to suppose with Josephus <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, a first-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> and others that it was natural for the serpent to speak and walk.

It has some appearance of truth that the Devil made the serpent speak in order to make the Woman believe what he wanted to present to her. She knew that eating the forbidden fruit was deadly. This conviction was based on God’s threat. To take this thought away from her, the Devil countered it with experience; he made the serpent eat the fruit and then speak, so that the Woman—attributing this speech to the power of the fruit—might conclude that if this fruit had the power to make an animal speak and reason, it could well happen that she and her husband would become like **Gods**, knowing good and evil.

<margin>
Why the Woman was not surprised?
</margin>

One asks, why was the Woman not surprised when she heard the serpent speaking, since there is now no one who would not be astonished by it and view it as a miracle?

I answer that our wonder would stem from the knowledge we have that animals do not speak or reason; and this knowledge rests on various experiences and investigations based on them. But the first Woman did not yet have enough experience to judge this. It is then no wonder that the speaking of a serpent did not seem strange to her. Ignorance and doubt do not conflict with the **state of uprightness** <term>state of uprightness: (Latin: *status rectitudinis*) the original condition of human beings before the Fall, characterized by moral innocence and intellectual clarity, though not necessarily exhaustive experience.</term>, but the error of the intellect does.

<column-break/>

<margin>
Why the Serpent first addressed the Woman?
</margin>

One asks, why did the Devil address the Woman first?

I answer, because he believed that the Woman would have less power of resistance, given that God had not made this threat from Genesis 2:16, 17—*In the day that you eat of it, you shall surely die*—directly to her, but to Adam.

<margin>
With what reasoning the Devil tempted Eve?
</margin>

Eve could not have been tempted more cunningly. He spoke to her as if God had forbidden her the use of all the trees of the Garden. Is it also true, he asked, that God said, *You shall not eat from all [the trees] of this Garden?* What appearance of truth is there that God, who has given you dominion over all the creatures of the world, would have forbidden you this beautiful fruit that you see? It would be godless to have such thoughts. This evil spirit did not want to criticize God’s conduct directly, because Eve would then have perceived what this tempting serpent sought. But keeping himself ignorant of what had occurred, he asks if it was really so, that God had forbidden her the use of all trees of the Garden? 2. When the Woman answered this, saying that God had only forbidden her the fruit of the tree that was in the middle of the Garden, and that she would die if she ate of it, Satan contradicted this threat, *You shall not surely die, but God knows, etc.*

<margin>
Gen. III 4. 5.
</margin>

How, he meant to say, would it be possible that such a beautiful fruit would make you die? Thus he tried to make Eve believe <note>original: "diets te maken"</note> either that Adam had not understood God’s meaning well, or that God had not spoken seriously, or that Adam had not told his wife the truth? To remove all doubt, Satan went further. He assured Eve that, far from dying, she and her husband would gain a much greater knowledge if they ate of it, yes, even become as Gods; *God knows, that in the day as you eat of it, your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be as God, knowing good and evil.* From this he let her draw the conclusion that she then should not hesitate to eat of this fruit. He appeals to God—*God knows*—so as not to appear an enemy of God, but he depicts God as being envious that humans would become like Him. Some have believed that the Devil feigned being sent by God to assure her that it was permitted for her to eat of the fruit,

# DIVINITY. VI. B. III. Chapter.

etc. But these thoughts have no basis.

Eve yielded to this temptation, and having observed that the fruit was indeed beautiful, she took from it and involved her husband in the same transgression. Thus the Woman, who was given to the man as a helper like unto himself <note>A reference to the biblical "help meet" from Genesis 2:18.</note>, became the instrument of his ruin.

One cannot say what reasoning she used to convince her husband, whether she recounted the speech of the Tempter to him, or whether she added new reasons of her own. I cannot believe that it was tender love alone, which Adam had for Eve, that moved him—under the hope of forgiveness—to rather scorn his Creator than to displease the Woman, who was a part of himself.

<margin>
Daillé <note>Jean Daillé (1594–1670), a prominent French Huguenot theologian known for his works on the early Church Fathers and biblical commentary.</note> on 1 Tim. II. 14.
</margin>
Whatever the case may be, it is certain that he committed the same sin as Eve. And when Paul says, **1 Tim. II. 14**, *Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived, was in the transgression*, he means nothing else than that Adam was not deceived first, and that he was not deceived in the same manner as Eve. "Eve," to use the words of a learned man, "was created last, but sinned first. She had the audacity to swallow the offered poison. They both drank it, but not at the same time. Eve began, and having tasted it at the suggestion of the Serpent, she became the instrument of the Tempter, etc. Thus she opened the door for Sin and Death, and served as a tool for the Devil to corrupt him who was her Head and the stem of the human Race. They were then both deceived, with this distinction: that Adam had no part in the first transgression of Eve. He did not entice her into evil and error; she enticed him into it. Meanwhile, he was no less guilty than she, and it even seems that he bore more guilt, since he ought to have rebuked the Woman for her disobedience to God's command. Some are of the opinion that Adam did not allow himself to be deceived, but that he sinned against his better knowledge, whereas Eve allowed herself to be taken by surprise."

<margin>
Why the Devil attacked the Woman regarding the prohibition
</margin>
The Devil attacked the Woman regarding the prohibition against eating from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil; for had he tempted her regarding something that ran directly against the law of nature, it would

<column-break/>

<margin>
of eating from the Tree of Knowledge.
</margin>
perhaps have been impossible for him to succeed. The movements of the mind and common knowledge were sufficient to ward off all his deceit: but God's command concerning a matter that was in itself indifferent <note>In theology, "indifferent" (adiaphora) refers to actions that are not inherently moral or immoral, but become so only because they are commanded or forbidden by God.</note>, in which the idea of good and evil was not naturally evident, and which did not demand certain execution by its own nature, made the fallen Angel's undertaking easier.

One asks, what was the first sin of Adam and Eve?

I answer: It is probable,
1. That Eve first doubted whether she had rightly understood God's thought regarding the prohibition.
2. That she, instead of asking the Lord for counsel, found it probable what the Devil had presented to her: namely, that she would not die.
3. That she was subsequently flattered with the vain hope of knowing all things and becoming like God.
4. And finally, that she reached out her hand to the forbidden fruit.

Regarding this, one may then observe:
1. That the beginning of her sin was not paying close attention to God's command; for had she done that, she would not have lent an ear to the Tempter.
2. That she thereafter came to doubt what God had said and gave belief to the words of the Devil.

<margin>
What the cause of man's fall was.
</margin>
One asks, what was the cause of man's fall?

I answer: God cannot be accused of it without blasphemy; for He expressly forbade the eating of the fruit; and to turn man away from it, He threatened him with death if he should partake of it. He gave him the enjoyment of all other trees; He had provided him with all necessary powers to do all that He had commanded; and He did not withdraw any benefit that He had previously bestowed upon him.

3. The Devil must also not be viewed as the true cause of man's fall. He did him no violence; he only made use of the way of persuasion, and his reasons were not so powerful that it would not have been easy to refute them: for Satan spoke against an express command of God. Never would he have conquered man if man had not begun to look upon himself.

One must also not place [the blame] on the tree—

<meta>This page continues the theological examination of the Fall of Man. Having previously discussed the Serpent's role and Eve's initial transgression, the text now focuses on the mechanics of Adam's free will, the nature of his original holiness, and the specific reasons why a perfect being was capable of falling into sin.</meta>

# THE CHRISTIAN <note>Likely part of a larger title such as "The Christian Religion" or "The Christian Theology."</note>

lay. The beauty of the fruit and the desire to gain knowledge by eating from it should not have caused man to waver, nor outweighed God’s command.

Man's will alone was the true cause of his fall, determining itself through its own motion toward an object that his misled understanding presented to him, but which God had forbidden. What caused him to listen to the Devil’s temptation was the natural desire we have to obtain and possess what we do not have. A pagan philosopher <note>Likely a reference to the Platonic or Neoplatonic idea that the soul's self-determination is the origin of moral failing.</note> has acknowledged that the human soul is the sole cause of evil, by reason of man's freedom.

One asks, how is it possible that man, who was upright, allowed himself to be taken in by the false reasoning of the tempter? Is it conceivable, it is said, that a will perfectly holy and pure could, in a single stroke, produce such acts of disobedience and contempt for God’s commands?

I answer that one should not wonder at this so greatly, since man was not so strengthened and confirmed in holiness that he could not lose it. He was holy and righteous, but he could cease to be so. He was oriented toward the good, but this orientation could be changed and overturned through a temptation, combined with some neglect on the man's part, followed by a false judgment and a hasty consent. Thus, man’s fall should seem no more miraculous to us than when we see someone who was standing upright fall, or someone who was at rest move.

Furthermore, one must note that Adam did not yet have experience, and that he did not possess the sciences <note>original: "Wetenschappen." In this context, it refers to systematic knowledge or the wisdom gained through long observation.</note> that we acquire when we view objects from all sides and see them from various perspectives and in different lights. Therefore, it is not strange that he allowed himself to be misled by the Devil, who presented evil to him under the guise of good, and that he passed a judgment contrary to the nature of things by rushing his decision.

One asks whether man was in a state in which he could have protected himself from his fall?

I answer that he could have protected himself from it.

<column-break/>

God had given him a help <note>A reference to the theological concept of "sufficient grace," meaning the innate ability provided by God to resist sin.</note> with which he could have remained steadfast if he had willed it. Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a central figure in the development of Western Christian thought regarding original sin and grace.</note> compares this to the help that food gives to the life of those who wish to consume it; whereas one cannot live on food if one refuses to use it. Adam had only to pray to Him and ask God for counsel. He should have taken time to reflect on the objects that were opposed to those proposed by Satan. Thus, he would easily have discovered the deceits and snares of the tempter.

It is said that the impression which objects make on the understanding is not voluntary, and consequently it is not in our power to suspend it.

I answer that one can always suspend judgment on a proposal made to us.

One asks whether being able to be deceived and being able to fall is a defect?

I answer: Yes, it is a defect, an imperfection of the creature as a creature, and a weakness; but if man is on his guard and does not rush his judgment, this weakness and this imperfection will not lead to sin.

One asks why God did not place man in a state where he would always be holy, without ever ceasing to be so.

I answer in a word: that it was God’s good pleasure <note>original: "welbehagen." This refers to God’s sovereign will, which is considered the ultimate reason for the order of creation, beyond human questioning.</note> to have it so. All other reasons brought forward are not sufficient.

<margin>How God intervened in the fall of Adam</margin>
If one is eager to know how God intervened in the fall of Adam, I answer that it is better to remain silent on this matter than to speak too much of it.

One will not be mistaken in saying:

1. That God incited neither Satan to tempt Adam, nor man to fall away. God preserve us from such thoughts regarding a holy being!

2. That God withdrew nothing from man that He had previously given him, for then He would have punished man before he had sinned. Now, there is no punishment where sin does not precede it. Besides that, if God had taken away any help that was previously given to man, it would seem that He would have been the cause of the sin—much as when the pillars upon which a building rests are removed, it must necessarily fall.

<summary>This page explores the theological reasons for Adam's fall, arguing that while Adam was holy, he was not immutable, and his fall resulted from a hasty judgment and the exercise of free will rather than a lack of divine help. The author emphasizes that God did not cause the sin nor withdraw His grace beforehand, as that would constitute unjust punishment before a crime was committed.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of the Fall of Man. The previous page established that while man’s will was the immediate cause of the Fall, he was created with the capacity to choose but without an inherent necessity to sin. This page addresses the difficult question of God’s sovereignty and foreknowledge in relation to human transgression.</meta>

### THEOLOGY. BOOK VI. CHAPTER III.

3. It is certain that God foresaw man’s fall; otherwise, His knowledge would not be infinite.
4. Nor should one doubt that God decreed from all eternity to permit the fall of man; for otherwise, it could not have been certain that he would sin or not sin. If, according to the testimony of Christ, not a single sparrow <note>A reference to Matthew 10:29: "Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground outside your Father’s care."</note> can fall to the earth without the will of our Heavenly Father, who would not be convinced that a fall—which turned the entire universe upside down and displaced the whole order of nature—did not happen without the will and foreknowledge of God?
5. It cannot be denied that God gave Satan free rein; for if He had restrained him, he would not have tempted our first ancestors.
6. By forbidding the Tree of Knowledge, God provided a harmless occasion for the devil to tempt Adam and Eve.
7. It appears clearly that God did not prevent the fall of Adam, though He was able to prevent it, since nothing is impossible for Him.
8. That God, in the moment of temptation, did not provide him with an additional grace that would have so confirmed him in holiness that he would never have fallen from it, was because He wished to test his obedience and faithfulness.
9. It is also certain that God did not refuse Adam any grace that he had requested of Him.
10. Finally, it is established that God maintained the natural faculties <note>The inherent powers of the mind and soul, such as reason and will.</note> of man.

We must abide by these general observations and henceforth worship God’s ways in silence, recognizing that He always acts with justice and supreme wisdom; so much so, that one could not suspect Him of sin without a heaven-defying godlessness.
One cannot say that God is the cause of sin, either because He foresaw it (for God’s foreknowledge and infinite wisdom are not the cause of the outcomes); or because He had decreed to let the fall happen (for this decree placed no coercive force upon the freedom of man); or because He permitted the temptation of the devil (for He did not give the devil the will to tempt man, nor did He approve of this temptation); or because He

<column-break/>

created man in a state in which he was capable of falling; for He did not create man with any evil inclination; He made him holy and righteous. Nor can it be said He is the cause because He did not give him grace sufficient to prevent his fall; for He had given him enough strength to remain in the state in which he was placed. God was not obligated to give him more. Nor because He had forbidden him the use of the Tree of Knowledge; for Adam could easily have refrained from eating of it. Nor because He had created a Tree which became the occasion of man's fall; for this Tree was a very harmless occasion.

<margin>
Why God permitted the fall of man.
</margin>
If it is asked further why God permitted Satan to tempt man, and why man succumbed to the temptation:
I answer with *Augustine* <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian who wrote extensively on original sin and divine grace.</note> that I adore the depths of God’s counsel, but I do not dare to fathom them.
I only note:
1. That God showed His hatred of sin by punishing it, even in His own Son.
2. That God, on the occasion of sin, poured out the unspeakable riches of His mercy and raised His goodness to an infinite degree.
3. Finally, that sin gave God the occasion to make all His virtues known.

<margin>
The greatness of Adam's fall.
</margin>
Adam’s sin was a heap and entanglement of many sins.
One sees in it a disordered desire for a fruit that was forbidden by his Creator.
A distrust of God’s truth and sincerity.
A doubt regarding God’s love and goodness toward him.
A desire to make himself equal to God, and a most punishable pride.
A desire for independence and excessive self-love; a shameful ingratitude and contempt for God.
One can further judge the greatness of this sin if one takes into consideration:
1. That he who sinned was created without any inclination toward evil.
2. That he was overwhelmed with God’s blessings.
3. That he had just come from the hands of his Maker, and had done almost nothing yet for his Creator.

4. That he sinned in Paradise, where everything preached to him the Power, the Greatness, the Wisdom, and the Goodness of God.
<margin>Augustine, *The City of God*, Book 14, Chapter 15.</margin>
5. That it was very easy to refrain from the Tree of Knowledge in a place where there were so many other fruits, as <note>original: "Augustinus"</note> Augustine remarks. If one cannot sufficiently marvel at the obedience of Abraham—because what God commanded him was very difficult—then one cannot sufficiently condemn the disobedience of Adam, because nothing was easier than to keep what God had commanded him.
6. Finally, that one cannot offend their Creator more than by preferring to believe the word of a Serpent over the word of their God.

If, according to <term>Navarra</term><note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canonist and moral theologian.</note>, <term>Lessius</term><note>Leonardus Lessius (1554–1623), a Flemish Jesuit known for his influential works on justice and law.</note>, and <term>Gregory of Valencia</term><note>A Spanish Jesuit theologian (1550–1603) who was a prominent figure in the Counter-Reformation.</note>, it were a provable opinion that <term>penal laws</term><note>Laws that supposedly only obligate the person to accept the punishment if caught, rather than binding the conscience to avoid the act itself.</note> lay no obligation upon the conscience, then Adam and Eve would have had reason to flatter themselves that by eating from the forbidden tree, they would not sin. But this is a godless opinion.

### CHAPTER IV.

->Concerning the harmful consequences of the first sins, with respect to our first Ancestors.<-

Just as the sin of our first ancestors greatly kindled God’s wrath, so it also had very harmful consequences.
<margin>
Valentin Smalcius's work against Wolfgang Franz, Disputation 7.
Socinus, *Theological Lectures*, Chapter 3.
</margin>
1. One cannot doubt that they lost the most beautiful features of <term>God’s Image</term><note>The *Imago Dei*, the theological concept that humans are created to reflect God's character.</note>, consisting in an unblemished holiness. Indeed, they did not lose the entire Image of God after which they were created. God willed that some remnants of this unhappy loss should remain, so that from them one might know how glorious the Image was before it was defaced, and to erect another beautiful building upon the ruins of this fallen house. It is even certain that God, through His Spirit, prevented the disorder within our first ancestors from bursting out as far as it otherwise would have done. But meanwhile, Adam felt from then on what he had not perceived before: a flesh that rose up against his spirit; a law of the members that strove

<column-break/>

against the law of his mind; passions that set themselves against reason and very often carried it away toward irregular desires; guilty inclinations; thoughts that do not become a creature; and an all too great love for the created and the visible.
2. Just as they were separated by sin from the Prince of Life, who is God, so in this regard the sentence that God had pronounced over them began to be carried out. On the day they ate from the forbidden Tree, they died the death of the soul, which consists in the separation from God through sin.
3. They became the objects of God's wrath, and God would have condemned them to the eternal pains He has prepared for the godless, had He not had compassion on them. Also, God called Adam immediately after he had sinned and said, *Adam, where are you?* <margin>Genesis 3:9.</margin> To summon him, as it were, before His judgment seat so that he might give an account of his conduct; to reproach him for his unbelief, rebelliousness, ingratitude, and pride; and to show him from what a high step of glory and happiness he had fallen into the utmost calamity.
4. Their eyes were opened, and they realized that they were naked, and they were ashamed of it. As soon as their soul was stripped of this garment of holiness, the nakedness of their bodies made them afraid, and they stood ashamed over it.
5. Their conscience was troubled, and in place of that quiet peacefulness which it previously enjoyed, it became disturbed. The voice of God, which was their joy, struck terror into them, and they sought to hide themselves from the One who sees all and whom they had so shamefully offended.
6. They were driven out of Paradise, that place of <term>delight</term><note>The original Dutch *wellust* here refers to "pleasure" or "delight" in the context of Eden's beauty, rather than the modern sense of "lust."</note> which the Almighty had planted and adorned with His hand; they were deprived of its fruits, which they previously had use of.
7. From that moment, they were exposed to all the evils and diseases that thwart and shorten our lives, and they noticed that they would imperceptibly lose the life God had given them and return to dust, from which God had made them, just as they indeed experienced after having lived for some time on earth.

# DIVINITY. Book VI. Chapter V.

8. God condemned the Woman / who had first violated the law of her Sovereign / to two things: 1. To carry and bring children into the world with pain and sorrow. 2. To have her desires depend upon her Husband. He willed / that the gentle and lawful submission / which she owed her Husband by the right of creation / should be so aggravated / that he would henceforth have sole dominion over her. A righteous sentence! that subjected to Adam’s will the one / who had presumed to give him such ruinous counsel / and to draw him away from the service / which he owed to his God.

Although there have been some Ancients / such as <term>Tatian</term><note>A 2nd-century Christian writer who became the leader of an ascetic sect called the Encratites; he notoriously argued that Adam could not be saved.</note>, who believed / that our first Ancestors were condemned to eternal punishments / we cannot, however, give any credit to that. This was also the opinion of the <term>Church Fathers</term> / and in former times a book of Adam's repentance was even seen. But Pope Gelasius ordered the same to be placed among the <term>apocrypha</term><note>original: "onregelmatige," referring to books not accepted into the official biblical canon.</note> / by a decree / which he had made in the Council of Rome: but many scholars doubt the authenticity of this decree.

Most of the Ancients believed / that Adam was buried on the Hill of Calvary / where Christ was crucified in the fullness of time / so that he might be the first to feel the power of His blood / just as he was the first to have sinned. This was believed by Origen, Athanasius, Eusebius, Ambrose, Chrysostom, Augustine, Theophylact, Euthymius, etc. Jerome, however, says / that Adam is buried at Hebron or Arba; he bases this on <term>Joshua 14:15</term><note>The source text cites Jos. XIV 17, but the description of Arba as the city of the "greatest man among the Anakim" (often interpreted by Rabbis as Adam) is found in verse 15.</note>. The ancient Rabbis said the same. Some among them have served up to the world pure fables / regarding Adam's repentance.

<column-break/>

One cannot be sufficiently amazed at God's goodness / that he did not crush these first two sinners with one blow / and that he gave their lives a long course. We do not know / how long Eve lived; but Scripture teaches us that Adam reached 930 years.

It is a mere imagination to believe / that Adam did not live a thousand years / because God had said, *In the day that you eat of this tree, you shall die,* since a thousand years are as a day to God; for Adam was counted as dead / as soon as the sentence of death was pronounced against him.

One also cannot sufficiently praise this goodness / which did not wish to deprive Adam of all the features of God’s Image / which he had shamefully disfigured. But above all, one cannot worthily extol the love of the second Adam <note>A common theological title for Jesus Christ.</note> / who died to earn immortality for the first / and who obtained salvation and life for us.

It is asked, why none of the Holy Writers recount any good deed of Adam / and why Paul says nothing of him in Hebrews 11 <note>A chapter in the New Testament often called the "Hall of Faith," listing righteous figures from the Old Testament.</note>.
One answers, that no mention is made of it / so that he might be regarded solely as the beginning of nature / and the boundary of grace; as the origin of sins / and through sin, death / so as to leave to Christ the honor and thanksgiving for our salvation.

### CHAPTER V.

->Of sin in general; of its consequences and deserved punishments.<-

**B**y the fall of our first Ancestors, sin has come into the world. Romans 5:12.

Before we speak of the harmful consequences of the sin of Adam, with respect to his descendants / it is necessary to deal with sin in general / of its nature / effects / and the punishments / which it deserves.

On the

John describes the nature of sin when he says in 1 John 3:4: "Sin is that which is against the Law." <note>original: "De zonde is, dat tegen de Wet is." Modern translations usually render this as "sin is lawlessness."</note>

<margin>
* This

James 4:12.
</margin>
By "the Law," one understands the Law of God, who is the only Lawgiver who can save and destroy; for human laws do not bind the conscience by their own power, but only because of the Law of God, which commands us to obey our authorities. Therefore, we are not bound to obey men except when they command us in things that do not conflict with God’s Law; otherwise, we must always remember that word of Peter: "It is better to obey God than men."

<margin>
Acts
4:19.
</margin>
To understand this matter well, we must observe that the most perfect rule of goodness is God’s own being—His holiness and His purity—according to which God always acts. He cannot deny Himself, so there are things that would be evil solely because of their contradiction of God’s purity, even if God had not explicitly forbidden them—such as being a slanderer, an unbeliever, etc. Other things are not evil except because God has forbidden them, such as eating from the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil. Such were all the <term>Ceremonial Laws</term><note>Religious laws regarding rituals, sacrifices, and purity which were specific to the Israelites, as opposed to universal Moral Laws.</note> that God had given to His people. Those who have received these Laws are obliged to keep them solely because of God’s authority.

<margin>
2 Tim.
2:13.
</margin>
But regarding the other Laws, which are grounded in God’s essence and holiness, we are bound to obey them even if God had commanded us nothing concerning them. 

It is probable that the Apostle, in 1 John 3:4, uses the word "Law" for the expression of God's holiness (if I may be permitted to speak thus) which we find in the <term>Moral Law</term><note>The universal ethical principles, summarized in the Ten Commandments, which Christians believe apply to all people at all times.</note>, and which Christ explained in His Gospel according to the perfect knowledge He had of His Father’s will and being. Just as God's Law commands some things and forbids others, we oppose this Law either by not doing what it commands or by doing what it forbids. This is called a **sin of commission** and a **sin of omission**. In the latter, one sometimes falls voluntarily, when one does not want to do what one is bound to do; sometimes because one pays no attention to it or does not think of one's duty. Sometimes this omission is joined with deeds that are in them-

<column-break/>

selves good, but which are not so at certain times—for instance, when someone, being too attached to his profession, forgets to pray to God. Sometimes this omission arises from a faulty action, such as when someone, being drunk, has forgotten to do what he was bound to do. Sins of commission happen in many ways: 1. When one does something that one must not do, such as killing someone, etc. 2. When one performs a work that is good in itself but from an evil principle, such as giving alms without love and faith, but out of pride. 3. When one does not bring what one does to God’s glory. 4. When one does certain things at certain times or in certain places where they should not be done. 5. One sins in thoughts, words, and deeds. 

Furthermore, since the Law demands a perfect holiness and sincerity, we go against it when we do not possess the holiness it requires and are inclined toward evil.

<margin>
The es-
sence of
sin.
</margin>
The essence of sin, then, consists in a deprivation of the righteousness and holiness that ought to be in a rational creature, into whose heart God has poured a natural law, and for whom He has prescribed a perfect rule in the Law proclaimed on Sinai. Therefore, to know if something is a sin, one must observe whether it is against the holiness that the Law requires. 

It is not always necessary, therefore, that an act be done voluntarily with premeditation and with an actual knowledge of the malice inherent in it. For, as has been very well noted, if one had to essentially know the wickedness of the act one intended to do in order to make oneself guilty of sin, it would follow that there would be no "sin of surprise" <note>Sins committed suddenly or without thinking.</note>, nor of inattentiveness, nor of ignorance. The sin someone commits while drunk would not be a true sin, nor would the sin of habit or innate inclination—which one commits without notice and in a violent fit of temper. And everyone who, in good faith, assumed a matter was permitted would commit no sin by doing it, and there would be no sin of ignorance.

<margin>
Bellarmine, book 1, *On the Loss of Grace*, ch. 1.
Socinus,
disputation 2,
against

</margin>

CHRISTIAN <note>The header "DE CHRISTELYKE" likely continues from the previous page as "The Christian Divinity" or "The Christian Theology."</note>

One asks whether sin deserves an infinite punishment? I answer, in general, yes; yet I add to this that this punishment cannot be infinite except in duration with respect to the creatures. But that it is enough to atone for it that the Person who suffers for the sin be infinite, as we shall show elsewhere. Meanwhile, one cannot doubt whether sin deserves an infinite punishment if one considers that—although it seems there is no proportion not only between a single sin but all the sins of a life as short as ours and eternal punishments—it is nonetheless just that those who have offended an infinite Majesty should be punished with an infinite punishment and never come into grace with God, unless someone satisfies His justice for them and in their place.

God imposes an infinite punishment in duration, but not in <term>degrees</term><note>The author distinguishes between how long a punishment lasts (duration) and how intense it is (degrees). This allows for the theological idea that some people are punished more severely than others in hell, while all remain there eternally.</note>; since the creature, being finite, could not bear a punishment infinite in degrees; and because there would then be no inequality in the punishments if God, to satisfy His justice, imposed on the creature all the punishments it could bear—which is against the Scripture, which teaches us that one shall be punished less and the other more.

Furthermore, although sinners always deserve punishment, they can nonetheless be delivered from it if someone stands in their place who stills God’s wrath for them.

<margin>Romans 8:1.</margin> This causes Paul to say in Romans 8:1 that there is no condemnation for those who are in Jesus Christ, since Christ has delivered them from it. As for the <term>stain</term><note>In Reformed theology, sin is seen both as "guilt" (a legal debt) and "stain" (a moral corruption of the soul).</note> that sin imprints upon our soul, that is gradually taken away by the power of the Holy Spirit who sanctifies us, but He will not completely purify this stain except in the hour of death, so that we may enter into the Heavenly and holy Jerusalem, where nothing that is defiled shall be allowed to enter.

## CHAPTER VI.

->Of the harmful consequences of the first sin of Adam with respect to his descendants, along with the explanation of Romans 5:12, etc.<-

Adam has made his descendants guilty and punishable through sin. Paul teaches us this in Romans 5, where he places this matter in the light of day.

His purpose was to prove that we are justified through the obedience of Christ; but because there were many who could not understand how the righteousness or obedience of Christ could be <term>imputed</term><note>Imputation is a legal term meaning to "credit" someone with something. Here, it refers to God crediting Christ's perfect life to the believer's "account."</note> to us, he makes a comparison between Adam and Christ. He shows that one should no more be surprised by the imputation of Christ’s righteousness than by the imputation of Adam’s sins to his descendants. He therefore presents Adam and Christ as two "heads"—the first of the human race, the other of the believers; the one who brings death to his descendants, the other who grants salvation and life to his members.

But let us hear Paul himself. Romans 5:12: "Just as," he says, "through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin, and so death passed to all men, in whom all have sinned."

The Apostle begins the comparison in this verse and shows that Adam introduced sin into the world and brought death upon all men because they are all considered to have sinned in him. Now, how are all men considered to have sinned in Adam, except through the imputation of Adam's sin?

One can give no other sense to these words without doing them violence.

It is said that, since it is written that all died in Adam, although Adam's death is not imputed to them, one cannot conclude, because it is said that all have sinned in Adam, that the sin of Adam is imputed to them.

I Answer, that there is a great distinction between the sin and the death of Adam; his death could not be imputed to us, but his sin could indeed.

Certainly, if Adam’s sin were not imputed to his descendants, then one can give no reason why God has permitted that the corruption, which in Adam was the consequence of the first sin, has passed over to his descendants. Consequently, to permit that this corruption passes from the parents to the children is to impose a punishment.

# CHRISTIAN [THEOLOGY]

when this corruption of the Parents communicates itself to the children, even though the children have not sinned; consequently, Adam’s sin is <term>imputed</term><note>Imputation is a legal concept in theology where the guilt or merit of one person is "credited" to another's account. Here, Adam's guilt is credited to all humanity.</note> to them, and God regards them as having a part in the sin of this first Father.

One must not say that this happens in the same manner as we see daily, such as when a leper produces a leper. For who does not see that this is an act of God’s justice? How! What appearance of truth is there that God—who could have prevented the propagation of sin as a matter contrary to His holiness and righteousness—would have willed that all people should come into the world corrupt and unhappy without any reason?

Several difficulties are raised against this matter.

<margin>Socinus, *On the State of the First Man*, ch. 13. *On Preservation*, ch. 8. Curcellaeus, *Book of Decisions*. Remonstrants. La Place.</margin>
**I.** It is incomprehensible, it is said, that God <term>imputes</term> the sin of Adam to his descendants, who were not yet born.

I answer, **1.** That it is even more difficult to understand how God allows Adam’s descendants to come into the world infected with a corruption that followed the first sin of this first Man, if it were true that this first sin is not imputed to them.

**2.** God, having made a <term>covenant</term><note>A 'covenant' is a formal, binding agreement or treaty between God and mankind, often involving promises of life for obedience and death for disobedience.</note> with Adam, was able to enter into it with him under these conditions: that should he violate it, not only would he himself suffer for it, but also his offspring.

<margin>Benoist.</margin>
It is very well noted that in the free gifts of grace, which are offered to someone voluntarily and without obligation, the one who is the giver can set such conditions as he pleases. Now all the covenants that God makes with man are free graces, which He grants him without obligation and through pure loving-kindness. God can then be accused of no injustice if He closed a covenant with Adam under these conditions: that He would follow him and his offspring with His graces, provided they kept His commandments; but that he would lose the same for his descendants, as well as for himself, if he transgressed them.

**3.** One cannot deny that Adam was the Head of the human race, and as the King of all men; it

<column-break/>

is then no wonder that the transgression he committed is imputed to his subjects. A Prince forms but one body with his People.

**4.** But there is more. Adam was the Father of men. They are all his children. Now it is something that nature itself teaches: that children follow the status of their Parents. Whether the Parents are Noble or Slave, Rich or Poor, the children are in the same state. One has always viewed children as a part of the Parents.

<margin>Law: *Regarding those who are guilty of High Treason* <note>original: "L. Quib C. ad Leg. Jul. Majest." referring to the Lex Julia Majestatis in Roman Law.</note></margin>
To prove this, I shall not bring up what is done regarding the children of those found guilty of the crime of <term>Lèse-majesté</term><note>An offense against the dignity of a reigning sovereign or against a state; high treason.</note>. Concerning this, the Emperors Arcadius and Honorius made a Law that condemned the children to always be in shame and misery. One might say that men act unjustly in this case. But we shall see in what follows how God has frequently imputed the sin of the Parents.

<margin>Limborch, *Christian Theology*, p. 184.</margin>
**II.** It is said that no mention is made of this imputation in the threat God made to Adam, nor in the execution of the sentence.

I answer that it does not come down to knowing here whether God spoke to Adam of this imputation or not: but that it is evident that it takes place, just as it can be clearly derived from the cited words of Paul in Romans V, against which nothing of any force can be answered.

**III.** It is said that God having forgiven Adam the sin, it is not probable that He has imputed to his descendants a sin which He had forgiven the one who committed it.

I Answer, **1.** That one must not come forward with "probabilities" when the Scripture speaks explicitly.

**2.** That it is easy to conceive that God was free to act thus. Having made a Covenant with Adam on those conditions, that he and his descendants would be guilty of punishment if he transgressed it, it remained within His freedom to remit the punishment regarding Adam and many of his descendants, and regarding others, not.

**IV.** It is said that a personal sin cannot be imputed except to the one who commits it.

I Answer, That there are personal sins...

# DIVINE THEOLOGY. VI. B. VI. Chapter.

...are [those] that go no further than those who committed them; but there are others that communicate themselves to many, such as the sins of Fathers and of kings. Adam's sin is of this latter kind, because he represented the entire human race. Therefore one also sees that the punishments of Adam and of Eve are spread out over all their children.

**V.** One objects not only to Genesis 18:25, where it is said that God does not make the righteous die with the wicked. But above all, Ezekiel 18:20, where God speaks thus:

> the Soul that sins, it shall die; the Son shall not bear the iniquity of the Father, and the Father shall not bear the iniquity of the Son. The righteousness of the Righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.

One adds to this Deuteronomy 24:16, where it is forbidden to kill the children for the Fathers, and further all the places where, as in Matthew 16:27, Romans 2:6, and 2 Corinthians 5:10, it stands written that God will repay everyone according to his works.

**Answer.** These are weak reasonings. If one must take these passages so strictly, how does it happen that God <term>imputes</term><note>To 'impute' is a legal term meaning to attribute the actions or debts of one person to another. The author argues that God treats humanity as a single legal entity under Adam.</note> the sin of the Fathers to the children, and of kings to the subjects, even that of one Man to a whole people? For Achan's transgression, all the Israelites were punished. Joshua 7:10, 11. Then the Lord said to Joshua,

> Israel has sinned, they have transgressed my covenant, they have also taken of the accursed thing.

It was meanwhile Achan alone who had taken from it.

Because Saul did not keep the word that Joshua had given to the Gibeonites, God struck the people of Israel with a three-year famine. 1 Samuel 21:1. <note>The text cites 1 Samuel 21, but this event is recorded in 2 Samuel 21.</note> In the general Deluge, and in the destruction of Sodom, the children perished with and because of the Parents.

The whole house and lineage of Ham was subjected to the curse that Ham alone had deserved. Genesis 9:25.

Because of Pharaoh's hardening, all the firstborn of Egypt were killed by the destroying Angel. Exodus 11.

Because of the crimes of their Husbands and Fathers, the Women and children of the Canaanites were condemned by God to be rooted out to the ground as cursed ones. Deuteronomy 20:13, 14, 16. God commanded Saul to destroy the Amalekites—

<column-break/>

—because their Fathers four hundred years before had set themselves against the passage of the Israelites. 1 Samuel 15:2, 3.

See here God's threat. Leviticus 26:38, 39.

> You shall perish among the Heathen, and the land of your enemies shall consume you, and those who are left among you shall pine away for their iniquity in the lands of your enemies; yes, also for the iniquity of their Fathers shall they pine away with them.

Christ testifies against the Jews in Matthew 23:35: That he will cause to come upon them all the righteous blood that has been shed on the earth, from the blood of Abel the righteous onward.

<margin>Exodus 20:5.</margin>
God declares in his Law, Exodus 20:5, that he will visit the crime of the Fathers upon the children, unto the third and the fourth generation. Because of the sin of David, consisting in the counting of his subjects, God made seventy thousand people die. These examples show enough that one must not consider it such an unusual thing that God imputes Adam's sin to his offspring.

Against all these Scripture passages one brings in: **1.** That God punishes the children when they follow the sins of their Fathers. **Answer.** This is an absurd answer, because besides the fact that God would then visit the children for their own sins and not for those of their Parents, we have brought forward examples of children killed for their Parents' sake, where one cannot say that they had followed their Parents. Secondly, if it only spoke of children who follow their Parents, then the Lawgiver would not only say that he would visit them until the fourth generation, for he will always visit them. One says, **2.** That God only punishes with temporal punishments. **Answer.** But to deprive someone of his covenant and of all its benefits, as he punished the whole lineage of Ham, is that only a temporal punishment? One says, **3.** It is only until the third or fourth generation. **Answer.** But can one say that Ham's descendants were only cast out of God's covenant until the fourth generation? If there were furthermore any distinction between these examples and that of Adam, one could conclude nothing from that against our opinion.

But, besides this general observation, one must **1.** with respect to Genesis 18:25, take note that the case mentioned there is entirely different from this...

**II.** Regarding Ezekiel 18:20, one must note that the Jews, although they were innocent, complained that they were being punished for their parents; that their fathers had eaten unripe grapes, and that the children's teeth had become blunt. <note>original: "stomp," commonly translated in English Bibles as "set on edge." This refers to the proverb that children suffer for their parents' tastes/sins.</note> The Prophet declares to them on God's behalf that He shall not punish them for the sins of their fathers, as He had the right to do, but for their own sins, and that, consequently, the soul that had sinned should die. This is, therefore, a specific case.

**III.** Deuteronomy 24:16 teaches the Judges how they must deal with criminals, but no conclusion can be drawn from that [regarding God]. God has the right to do many things that He may forbid others from doing, and we have seen how He desired that His people should root out the children of the Canaanites as well as their parents.

<margin>Matthew 16:27; Romans 1:5.</margin>
**IV.** Finally, when it is said that God will repay everyone according to his works, God’s Spirit does not intend to deny in this case that God <term>imputes</term><note>To 'impute' is to legally charge or attribute something to someone's account.</note> the sin of Adam to us (2 Corinthians 5:10), but He only wants to make us understand how closely we must pay attention to our works, since God will demand an account of them from us.

**V.** It is said that if the first sin of Adam were imputed to us, his righteousness would also have been imputed.

**I Answer** that his righteousness would indeed have been imputed to us there, so that we would not be born guilty, but would come into the world in that state in which Adam was created; from which we draw yet another proof for <term>imputation</term>.

It is a fundamental rule, grounded on the purest light of reason, that those who share in the benefits of a <term>covenant</term><note>A legal and spiritual agreement between God and humanity. The author views Adam as the "federal head" or legal representative of all people.</note> must also share in the inconveniences. It follows then that, since Adam's posterity would have shared in the righteousness of the first man if he had remained steadfast in righteousness, they must likewise have shared in his sins.

One raises several other difficulties, but these can easily be resolved by the principles we

<column-break/>

have set down.

It is said that if the first sin of Adam is imputed to us, his other sins must also be imputed to us. I answer that only the first sin must be imputed to us, because by that sin Adam broke the covenant that God had made with him as the head of the human race.

It is said that all his other actions, even the most natural ones, should also be imputed to us. I answer that since we are dealing here with an imputation followed by a punishment, there are no other acts besides moral ones that are imputed, as none but these are punished.

It is said that if sin is imputed to all the descendants of Adam, the same must also be imputed to Christ.

I Answer that this is not a valid conclusion, since it depended upon God to make an exception and to free the Lord Christ from that imputation, whom He sent to make satisfaction for our transgressions. I will not bring other reasons here. <margin>in the Theological Ecclesiastical Epistles 66.</margin> Arminius <note>Jacobus Arminius (1560–1609) was a Dutch theologian whose views led to the formation of the Remonstrant movement. He had a nuanced view of how sin was passed down.</note> asserts in one of his letters that Christ was not in the loins of Adam before he sinned, and thus did not sin in Adam. He proves this: 1. Because he would have to have been there by virtue of this blessing, "increase and multiply," which is not so. 2. Because Christ would then have come from Adam’s loins even if Adam had not sinned, which is not true. But he says that He was in Adam’s loins after his sin, by virtue of the promise, "the seed of the woman," etc.; and that He was in those of Abraham by virtue of this blessing, "in your seed," etc.

It is said that no one ever prayed for the forgiveness of Adam's sin; that is granted, but one must pray to God that He not punish us for this sin.

It is asked whether God would damn a perfectly holy man for the sin of Adam alone?

I answer that where Scripture constrains us, we must decide nothing. Meanwhile, I confess that I do not believe it; but one can conclude nothing from that against the doctrine of imputation.

## VII. CHAPTER.
### Of Original Sin.

**The** sin of our first Father ensures / that we come into the world not only guilty / but corrupted.

From him we have the corruption / which since his fall has clung to human nature / defiled it / and made it worthy of God’s aversion. Cyprian <note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage.</note> calls this the "domestic evil," and Augustine calls it "Original Sin," because we have it from our origin / that is to say / as soon as we begin to exist / and because it is the source-vein of all other sins.

David teaches us this truth in the 51st Psalm, which he left to us as a monument of his repentance; for having pleaded with God in this Song for the forgiveness of his sins / the cause of his tears / he climbs up to the source of his corruption / and confesses that he was corrupt from his conception. *I was born in iniquity, and in sin did my Mother conceive me.* verse 7. Now he who confesses / that he was conceived, made, and born in sin / acknowledges / that he brought corruption and sin into the world from his Mother’s womb / and this is what is called original sin.

It is said, 1. That David here speaks not of Adam, but of his Mother. I answer, that the proof is therefore no less powerful; for we agree / that the sin of Adam is communicated to us by means of our Parents. But he is the first origin of [it].

2. It is said, that he speaks only of his Mother / and of his Mother’s sin / just as one says / that someone is born in adultery. I answer: 1. That it is clear / that David here makes confession of his own sin / and not of that of his Mother / which is not the point here. 2. One cannot object to this / without falsely suggesting / that the Parents of David sinned in the begetting of this Prophet /

<column-break/>

as if he were conceived in an illicit encounter. 3. God's Word clearly shows / that it is spoken here of David, being conceived and formed.

3. It is said, that it is a hyperbolic <term>manner of speaking</term><note>An exaggerated or figurative rhetorical device.</note> / by which David acknowledged / that from his youth / and as soon as reason had begun to teach him to distinguish good from evil / he had been inclined toward sin and impurity / and that consequently this expression signifies nothing else / than a long and old habit of doing evil / in the same sense / as he rebukes his enemies. *The wicked are estranged from the womb; the liars go astray from the (mother's) belly.* Ps. 58:4. And God says against the Israelites in Isa. 48:8. *That they were transgressors from the belly.* Answer. But who does not see / that these and other phrases / which are brought forward / are not like this one / *I was born in iniquity, etc!* for it is clear / that here no actual sin is spoken of / as in the places that are cited: but of a sin / in which one is conceived / and of a corruption / that one has from one's Mother. Why explain David's words / as if he spoke of the time / in which reason taught him to distinguish good from evil / since it clearly appears / that the Prophet speaks of a time / which long precedes the use of reason; besides which, one can very well make use of all the quoted texts / to prove original sin / as many learned men have done.

4. It is said, that / if one must conclude from David's expression / that he was truly conceived in sin / one could also conclude / that many holy Men were born in an original holiness / and that they were free from all corruption / like Job, who says / *From my youth he was brought up with me, as (by) a Father, and from my Mother's womb, I have guided her.* Job 31:18.

David uses the same manner of speaking in Ps. 22:11. *Upon you I was cast from the womb, from my Mother's belly you have been my God.* And Ps. 71:6. *Upon you I have leaned from the belly, from my Mother's womb you are my helper.*

I answer, that / if Job and David had said / that they were conceived in righteousness / just as David says / that he was conceived in sin / one would

5. It is said, that David speaks of himself / but that it does not follow from this / that all men are like David in this / that he was born in the iniquity of his Mother. I answer, that unless one assumes / that David’s Parents committed a crime in the procreation of this Prophet / which cannot be proven / one has no reason / why one could not say of all men / what David testifies of his own conception.

6. It is said, that one must explain the words of David / just as the Jews addressed the man born blind / whom Christ had healed, in John 9:34 <note>original: "Joh. IX. 34."</note> / *you were born entirely in sin, and do you teach us?* This cannot now / it is said, mean original sin / for he would have been able to say / that they themselves were also born in sins.

I answer, 1. That this manner of speaking means not only original sin / but also a very great corruption / revealed through various evil deeds. 2. One must not doubt / that the man born blind could have said the same to the Pharisees / as they said to him / and with more reason: but he did not wish to get himself into trouble.

3. Some are of the opinion / that the Pharisees / who believed in the transmigration of souls <term>metempsychosis: the ancient belief that a soul passes into a new body after death</term> / judged / that this man was born blind / because his soul had committed heavy sins in another body. If that holds true / then it appears / that the Pharisees would have believed / that this man

<column-break/>

was born in corruption / which he / upon coming into the world / had brought with him. It will be said, that we do not hold the view of the transmigration of souls / and that one cannot explain this passage in that sense. I answer, that we do not make use of it either: but that we bring forward David’s testimony / which appears to us clear and explicit.

7. It is said, that / if David spoke here of an original sin / he would thereby be excusing his sin: for it is / they say / as if he were picking himself out <note>meaning: making himself an exception or finding an out</note>; it is true / I have sinned / but the cause of my sin is the corruption / which I brought into the world from my Mother's womb / and in which you, O God, willed / that I should be born.

But who does not see / that this excuse has no place here. David’s aim is to pray to God / that he might blot out his sin / and to that end he humbles himself in his presence; he acknowledges / that God would be righteous / if he punished him: that all that was in him / must bring God's wrath upon him; that he / even as he began to be in his Mother's womb / has been stained with sin / and consequently in a state / that made him abominable before God / but that he called upon his mercy.

8. It is said, that David only wanted to teach us / that his disposition drove him to sin to such an extent / that one could say / that he was born in it. But, if it is permitted to explain the scripture thus / everything will be permitted / and one will make God's spirit / say whatever one wants.

9. It is said, that it is / as if he had expressed himself thus; *I am as one / who has been conceived in sin / that is / as a wicked man / * and that one must consequently insert the word *as*, or *like* here / as in Psalm 51:1, 22:14. <note>original: "Ps. LI. 1. XXII. 14."</note> However, one only has to look up these passages / to see the difference / that exists between them and this one.

I shall not bring up any other excuses / which are weaker.

Christ confirms this truth / when he says to Nicodemus / John 3:6 <note>original: "Joh. is said in **Romans 8:7, 8**. *The carnal mind <note>The Dutch "bedenken des vleesch" refers to the mindset or orientation of the "flesh"—the fallen human nature.</note> is enmity against God: for it does not subject itself to the law of God, nor indeed can it; and those who are in the flesh cannot please God.* In this sense it must be taken here; it is then as if *Christ* said / that all that is born of flesh / as all humans are born / is corrupted / just as that which is born of the spirit / that is, reborn by God’s spirit / cleansed by this spiritual water / purified by this Heavenly fire / partakes in the nature of its origin / in its desires / thoughts / and feelings.

From this reasoning of *Christ* one can easily draw these two consequences.

First, that all who are born as we are / come into the world corrupted: For all that is born of flesh, is flesh. Consequently, we do not corrupt ourselves merely by following evil examples / but that corruption is a poison / with which we are born / that has infected us from the first moment of our lives / and that we bring with us into the world.

Secondly, that (with the exception of *Christ* alone / who is God and Man / conceived by the Holy Spirit) there is no human / but he is born in corruption / because they are all born of flesh.

It is said, that the word flesh should not be taken for corruption: but that it signifies a body / in contrast to a spiritual substance; that it is an answer of *Christ* to the coarse objection of *Nicodemus*, who had said / *how can a man be born, being (now) old, can he also enter a second time into his Mother’s womb and be born? John 3:4.* It is then posited / that *Christ* answers this Teacher / that he was not speaking of a physical and earthly birth / which would have no power at all / to make us enter into God's Kingdom / even if it were repeated a hundred times / since all that comes from flesh / is earthly / mortal / weak and frail / like the flesh / from which it proceeds.

I answer, that one must wish to be blind / not to see / that "flesh" here is taken for corruption. For 1. It is set against the spirit. Now "spirit" is not used here for the soul, as one would have to posit / if "flesh" signified the body. 2. A "flesh" is spoken of here / that needs to be reborn; now

<column-break/>

rebirth presupposes corruption. 3. *Christ* speaks of a flesh, with which one cannot enter into God’s Kingdom / that is / being a member of *Christ's* Church / and having a share in salvation. Now if "flesh" meant nothing other / than an earthly and mortal nature / that does not prevent us from being a member of *Christ*. Corruption alone prevents us from that. 4. Finally, I ask / why that which is born of flesh / is mortal and weak? Is it not because of the sin / that clings to it / and has death as its wages?

Furthermore, what *Christ* says / agrees with that of *Job*. **Job 14:4**. *Who shall bring a clean thing out of an unclean? Not one.*

It is said: 1. That an impurity is spoken of here / that can even be in the Angels / who are not pure before God.

I answer, that *Job* speaks of an impurity / that subjects humans to death / now that is not in the Angels.

It is said: 2. That here not a moral / but a natural impurity must be understood.

I answer, that a moral impurity is spoken of here / because it exposes humans to many evils / and to God’s judgment. One can call it natural / because it is natural to us / and that we come into the world with it; but it is called moral / because it corrupts the heart of man.

We are then born infected / since we draw our origin from an unclean source / and that makes us / by nature children of wrath. **Ephesians 2:3.**

1. It is objected: That *Paul* says / we *were* children of wrath / and not / we *are*; therefore this signifies something / that was no longer in the Ephesians. Now / it is said, those who recognize original sin / are of the opinion / that it is never annihilated / until the hour of death.

I answer, That the phrasing of *Paul* does not weaken the strength of the proof / that theologians draw from this passage. It is true / that we are by nature always corrupted / but the believers / who are converted / though by nature corrupted / are no longer children of wrath / because *Christ* has freed them from his Father’s wrath and from damnation. The grace / that has governed them / does not prevent them from being born with an infected nature / but ensures / that they are protected from the arrows of God’s anger.

I answer, That it is clear / that Paul speaks here of everyone in common / *we were by nature children of wrath, even as the others.* <note>Referencing Ephesians 2:3. The author is arguing that "we" includes Paul himself and all believers, not just the former pagans.</note>

3. It is said, That Paul speaks of sins / that the Ephesians themselves had committed / since he adds / that they had *walked* therein / which indicates an old and pleasant habit / and not a condition of nature.

I answer, That Paul in this place ascends from the streams to their source / from actual sins to original sin. *We have all walked*, see there the actual sins; *we were children of wrath by nature*, see there the original sin.

4. It is said, That to be a child of wrath by nature / does not concern birth / because natural things do not change; now those who were by nature children of God's wrath / become children of His love / through the proclamation of the Gospel and through faith in Christ.

I answer, That it is easy to understand / how those / who from their mother's womb had a corrupt nature / and were thereby exposed to God's wrath / were delivered from the same by the blood of Christ and sanctified by His spirit.

5. It is said, That to be a child of wrath by nature / only means / that one is truly worthy of God's wrath / just as Galatians 2:15: *We are Jews by nature*, that is truly; and Galatians 4:8: *You served those, who by nature were no Gods*, that is / who truly were no Gods.

I answer, That it does not only mean to be worthy of God's wrath / but to be worthy of it through the state of nature; and as for the cited passages / to be a Jew by nature, is to be such by a natural right / and not for any other cause / that grafts someone into the body of the Jews / and lets them share in their privileges. To be no God by nature, is to have no Divine existence / to be not worthy by nature / to be worshipped as God. If being a child of wrath by nature only meant being truly worthy of God's wrath / one could say / that we are by nature children of God / because we truly are; but the scripture does not say that.

<column-break/>

6. It is said, That nature signifies a long habit / that habit is a second nature / and that one thus says / that someone is a thief by nature / to indicate / that he has practiced that trade for a long time.

I answer, 1. That this explanation cannot stand here / for Paul does not only say that we were sinners by our nature / but *children of wrath* / which is the punishment of sin. 2. When one says / that someone is a thief by nature / one does not only mean that he is accustomed to stealing / but that he has a natural inclination toward theft / which signifies a ground of natural corruption.

A third proof for original sin / we take from death / which all of Adam's children must undergo / even those who have not yet come to the use of reason: for / as we have often said / *Death is the wages of sin.* <note>original: "De dood is de bezolding der zonde" (Romans 6:23).</note> Since then the children die / they must necessarily be corrupt. With what fairness / asked Fulgentius, <note>Fulgentius of Ruspe (c. 467–533 AD), a North African bishop and staunch defender of Augustinian theology against Pelagianism.</note> would a child be subject to the wages of sin / if it did not have the stain of sin?

It is said, That from the death of children it does not follow / that they are sinners / since the beasts die. I answer, that it is absurd / not to say something worse / to compare the death of children to that of beasts.

The consequence / that we draw from the dying of children / we cannot pass by / because the scripture teaches it to us.

It is said, That children die / because they have their origin from Adam / who after sin was subjected to death. But why does one insist / that they have more of the death of Adam than the sin / since death is a consequence of sin / if it is true / as those who oppose us in this assert / that the sin of Adam was not imputed to his posterity? why does one want / for them to be subject to death / which Adam was subjected to through sin?

If children are born without the stain of sin / what reason is there that they need a Savior? <term>Zaligmaker</term> <note>Literally "Blessed-maker" or "One who makes whole/blessed," the standard Dutch term for Savior.</note> for where there is no sin / no redemption is necessary.
