### CHAPTER XII.

#### On the Sin against the Holy Spirit.

Since the Sin against the Holy Spirit is the greatest of all sins, and one that is never forgiven, it is necessary to know its nature and essence accurately in order to avoid it. To this end, we arrange this Chapter.

This sin is spoken of in Matthew 12:31, 32. *Therefore I say to you, every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven men, but the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven men. And whoever shall have spoken a (certain) word against the Son of Man, it shall be forgiven him; but whoever shall have spoken against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this age, nor in the one to come.* Mark records Christ speaking thus in Mark 3:28, 29. *Truly I say to you, that all sins shall be forgiven the children of men, and all kinds of blasphemies with which they shall have blasphemed, But whoever shall have blasphemed against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness forever, but he is guilty of eternal judgment.* From which it appears that Matthew is explained by Mark. In verse 30, he adds that Christ said this against the Pharisees because they said of him, *He has an unclean spirit.*

There is therefore no doubt that there is a sin against the Holy Spirit, but we must investigate what it consists of.

I. It is certain that all who sin against the Moral Law do not sin against the Holy Spirit, although one often sins against one's own

1. It is a very uncertain matter whether the Pharisees believed that the miracles of Christ could not be done except by a Divine power, or whether they were of the opinion that the Devil could do such things. the Devil.

# THE CHRISTIAN [THEOLOGY]

<columns>
...fell back into sins; others understand this to refer to the Jews who, after they had been baptized and had received the gift of miracles—which the first Christians received through the laying on of hands—returned to the Synagogue, where they poured out their blasphemies against the Lord Christ.
The majority of those who hold this view explain these words, *it is impossible for those who were once enlightened to be renewed*, as if one must understand "enlightenment" to mean "baptism," according to the style of the Church Fathers <note>The early Greek Fathers often used the term *photismos* (enlightenment) as a synonym for baptism.</note>, and as if Paul meant to say that it was impossible for them to be renewed unto repentance because they could be baptized only once.
But I confess that this reasoning does not please me.
1. Paul never called Baptism an "enlightenment"; it was only long afterward that Baptism was named thus.
2. I also cannot approve of interpreting "to be renewed unto repentance" as "to be rebaptized."
3. Most who favor this explanation imagine that those who could not be rebaptized could no longer have faith or remorse.
These thoughts, it seems to me, have no basis. In my judgment, Paul speaks in those two places <note>Referring to Hebrews 6:4-6 and Hebrews 10:26.</note> of the sin against the Holy Spirit; and here is my proof.
Christ presents to us, in Matthew, the sin against the Holy Spirit as the only sin that is unpardonable. Now the Apostle speaks of a sin from which one cannot return, and for which no further sacrifice remains. From this, it appears to me to follow that Paul speaks of the same sin of which Christ had spoken, and of which the Pharisees had made themselves guilty. This being presupposed, we shall draw from these passages the characteristics of the sin against the Holy Spirit.
The 1st Characteristic is that it is a sin that is not committed except by those who know the truth. Paul notes this when he says: 1. That they were *enlightened*, which means that they have known the true Evangelical Doctrine and that they have been instructed in Religion. 2. That they *have tasted the heavenly gift and the good word of God*, that is, that they have acknowledged that the Gospel was the good word, that they had tasted it, and that they had a reasonably lively feeling of the advantages it contains.

<column-break/>

3. That they have had the *knowledge of the truth*. Heb. X. 26.
The 2nd Characteristic of this sin is that it is committed by those who have received some grace of the Holy Spirit; the Apostle notes this when he says that they have been made *partakers of the Holy Spirit*. For, although one can apply these words to the miraculous gifts of the Holy Spirit—which were then distributed in the first century of the Christian Church and consisted of either the gift of tongues or healing, etc.—nothing prevents us from understanding the same as the internal gifts and grace of the Holy Spirit; for one must observe that it is not the believers alone who have a share in the grace of the Holy Spirit; it is true they alone are those whom the Holy Spirit converts and incorporates into the communion of the Savior; they alone are those whom He sanctifies and fills with perfect consolation; but there are graces of the Holy Spirit that are common to the good and the wicked alike.
For example, it is the Holy Spirit who restrains the obstinate passions of the greatest villains and who keeps them from doing as much evil as they otherwise would. It is the Holy Spirit who curbs them and moves them through the gnawings of their conscience, which He awakens. It is the Holy Spirit who convinces so many people of the truth and sweetness of the Gospel, and who sometimes gives them the strength to embrace the true faith.
Thus, it is easy to understand how those who sin against the Holy Spirit have received some grace of the Holy Spirit; indeed, it is necessary that one presupposes it.
The 3rd Characteristic of this sin is that it must be committed *willfully*. *If we sin willfully*, says the Apostle; that is to say, without being forced to do so, and against the light of the conscience.
There are two ways to do something willfully. The one is when one does it with one's full will; the other, when one does it with a conflicting will that is tossed back and forth by the reasons that present themselves for and against—as in the case of a Merchant who throws his goods into the sea, partly with and partly against his will <note>A classic philosophical example of "mixed" voluntary action: the merchant wants to save his life, but does not want to lose his cargo.</note>. He wills and he wills not. When it is said that those who sin against the Holy Spirit sin "willfully," we do not speak of those who, either terrified by the fear of death or blinded by the glitter of honors and riches, abandon the truth; but of those who the truth...

# THEOLOGY. VI. B. XII. Chapter.
->397<-

...abandoned [the truth] voluntarily in a time in which nothing forced them to do so, but rather several things bound them to hold it fast.

<margin>Heb. X. 29.</margin>
The **IV. Characteristic** is that this sin is a total abandonment of the truth of our Savior, through which one shows that they value the world and its pleasures more than Him. Paul notes this when he says that they *trample the Son of God underfoot*, that they *treat the blood of the Covenant as unholy*, and *insult the Spirit of grace* by opposing the good stirrings that He awakens in their hearts.

<margin>Heb. XII. 16.</margin>
The **V. Characteristic** is that this abandonment of the truth is paired with the contempt of the truth. These words further signify this: *Trampling the Son of God underfoot, treating the blood of the covenant as unholy*; for through these expressions, Paul shows us that such people reject the Savior, esteeming Him less than the goods of the earth, and viewing His blood as a trivial and contemptible thing. The Apostle points this out more closely when he compares those people to those who despised the Law of Moses, and to the *unholy Esau*, who sold his birthright for a dish of lentils. <note>original: "geregt van linzen"</note> Hebr. XII. 16.

The **VI. Characteristic** is that this contempt is often accompanied by **hatred**, when these unfortunate souls see that the Gospel comes to disturb their false joy; the presence of the confessors of the truth disturbs them, because it seems as if they reproach them for their apostasy and cowardice. It also often happens that these God-forgetting people persecute the truth and those who proclaim it, just as the Jews persecuted our Savior and His Disciples. They blaspheme not only the Spirit of grace but also those in whom this Spirit dwells.

Finally, the **VII. Characteristic** is that those who fall into this abominable sin become so hardened in it that they remain in it until the end. This leads Paul to say that *it is impossible for them to be renewed unto repentance*. It appears then that the sin against the Holy Spirit is a malicious rejection and, if I may speak so, a total denial of the truths of the Gospel, which were previously known, accompanied by contempt and hatred, and almost always paired with persecution, but always with final impenitence.

<column-break/>

Several questions are asked regarding this.

I. One asks, how is it possible that there could be a person in the world who, knowing the truth and utility of the Gospel, rejects, despises, hates, and persecutes it? How can anyone be so maddened?

<margin>Claude on this subject.</margin>
<note>This likely refers to Jean Claude (1619–1687), a prominent French Protestant theologian famous for his defenses of the Reformation.</note>
I answer that one should not be surprised by this, because those who fall into this sin embrace the Gospel not so much because they have been moved by the preciousness and excellence of its truths, but because they have been touched by the idea of the good that God promises in His fellowship, and of the blessedness that the Gospel makes us hope for; or because they found some temporal advantage in the profession of Christianity, and believed that they could easily pair Christ with the world, the Gospel with the advantages of this Age and their own passions. 

But when they notice that they cannot profess the truth except by curbing their urges, by giving up their pleasure, by exposing themselves from time to time to various persecutions, by enduring many kinds of temptations, the laying down of their offices, the leaving behind of their goods and the comforts of this life, and the losing of that which is most pleasant and desirable to the flesh—then they find that they have miserably deceived themselves in believing that they could easily reconcile Christ with the world and pair the Gospel with their passions. 

And seeing themselves forced to abandon either one or the other, as they take nothing more to heart than the comforts of this present life, caring little for the future, they reject Christ and His truth, even with fury, reflecting on how narrow an escape they had from losing—for the love of Christ—that which they hold as their highest good: namely, their offices of honor, their prestige, and all those temporal goods which are the **Godhead** they worship. The salvation of Jesus, which seemed so advantageous to them when they thought only of the Glory He has obtained for those who love Him, makes them afraid when they remember with what misery, pain, disdain, and loss the confession of the Gospel is accompanied; and, as has been very well said, the idea of the future good that shines in salvation and gladdens their hope is swallowed up in their soul by the present miseries that befall them.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "unpardonable sin," specifically addressing the psychological progression of the sinner, why it is named after the Holy Spirit, and whether this sin is still possible for people today or for the "elect."</meta>

# THE CHRISTIAN
->398<-

I further answer that one does not fall suddenly into this sin, and that one falls into it when it seems that one ought not to fall into it. It happens sometimes that there are those who abandon the true religion through the transport of their passions. Once the "thirst" <note>Likely referring to the heat of the moment or a temporary craving for worldly things.</note> has passed, they feel remorse for it, but they lack the strength to give the glory to God. They even attempt to adapt themselves to the false religion which they have embraced, and they grow accustomed to its practice against their own conscience. Subsequently, seeing that they can satisfy their passions in this way, they come to despise the true religion which they had left, and they mock it. This contempt is sometimes followed by hatred against those who profess the truth, because they cannot endure their presence without feeling shame; from hatred, they pass over to persecution, and they often die in that state.

II. The question is asked: why is this sin called the sin against the Holy Spirit?

It is not because it only strikes against the third Person of the Holy Trinity, for all sins offend the three adorable Persons; rather, it is because it is committed against the enlightenment of the Holy Spirit, to whom the Scripture, in the **Economy of Salvation** <term>Economy of Salvation: The divine plan or arrangement for the salvation of humanity.</term>, attributes the care of enlightening mankind. A great man has said very well:
<margin>Claude</margin> <note>Jean Claude (1619–1687), a famous French Reformed theologian.</note> "That he who sins against the Law is said to sin against the Father; that he who rejects the Gospel when it is proclaimed to him is said to sin against the Son; but that he who resists the light which he has already received, and who makes for himself a bulwark and shield out of the wickedness of his heart and the deceits of his mind against the inspirations of grace, sins against the Holy Spirit."

III. The question is asked: whether all people can fall into this sin.

I answer, 1. That those who do not know the Gospel can never fall into this sin, but indeed those who are called "temporary believers," who received the Gospel with joy, but who thereafter abandoned it.

I answer, 2. That the elect and the faithful <note>The "elect" refers to those predestined for salvation according to Reformed theology.</note> cannot fall into this sin, as shall clearly appear when we treat the **perseverance of the Saints** <term>Perseverance of the Saints: The doctrine that those truly saved by God will never finally fall away from the faith.</term>. We do not deny that the faithful could commit great sins that would make them worthy of eternal death. We do not deny that it could happen that the faithful,

<column-break/>

terrified by the fear of death, or by the violence of persecution, or by the power of some passions, would leave the true faith. But we maintain that they shall not remain long in that state, because God comes to pull them out of it by His almighty hand. The weakness of their nature yields to the conquering power of grace. Their faith, which was like a fire covered under ashes, begins to ignite and shine forth again; and if they have been unfruitful for some time, like trees in the winter, one sees them bring forth beautiful fruits as soon as the **Sun of Righteousness** <note>A biblical title for Christ (Malachi 4:2).</note> comes to cast its rays upon them again.

IV. The question is asked: whether one finds anyone nowadays who falls into this sin.

Answer: Those who believe that none sin against the Holy Spirit except those who attributed the miracles of Christ to Beelzebub are of the opinion that the Pharisees alone committed this sin. But we are not of that thought. We believe that there are many today who still commit it, since many sin willfully after they have known the truth, and hold the **blood of the covenant** to be unholy.

The sin against the Holy Spirit is regarded as the greatest of all sins, since it is unpardonable. Now, it is certain that the sin of Christians—who abandon, hate, despise, and persecute the truth they know—is a weightier sin than that of the Pharisees, who, blinded by their prejudices and by their envy, judged poorly of Christ's miracles. Those who crucify the Lord Jesus anew, whom they have recognized as the true Messiah, sin much more heavily than those who crucified Him while believing Him to be a deceiver.

A learned English writer named **Daniel Whitby** <note>Daniel Whitby (1638–1726) was an English theologian and biblical commentator.</note> in his commentary on the New Testament, believes that this sin was not committed in the time of our Savior, because the Holy Spirit had not yet been given. This opinion seems more probable to me than the view of those who believe that this sin was only committed by the Pharisees. Meanwhile, we are of the opinion that one can say that the sin against the Holy Spirit was committed by the Pharisees, and is still committed today by many Christians.

# DIVINITY. Book VI. Part B. Chapter XII.

...ed. But we are at the same time of the opinion that there are several kinds of this sin.

Those who, after obtaining knowledge of the Gospel, reach the point where they have no fear of God nor show any regret toward Him, and who view the threats of God's word as trifles, must also be placed in the number of those who sin against the Holy Spirit.

We shall observe ourselves that, although it is certain that this sin is particularly committed under the *New Dispensation* <term>New Dispensation: The era of human history following the coming of Christ, characterized by the "New Covenant" and greater spiritual light.</term> where they have a much greater light (it is also distinguished in Hebrews 2 and 10 from the transgression of the Law), it nonetheless took place in some manner under the *Old Testament* among those who despised the Law of Moses and hardened their hearts against God's voice. Every sacrifice is offered to offended justice, so that it may give place to mercy. ### CHAPTER XIII.

->Of the free will of Man in the state of sin, and of his impotence to do good from and by himself.<-

We have considered the free will of man in the state of righteousness <note>The "state of righteousness" refers to the theological concept of humanity's condition before the Fall, when Adam and Eve were believed to be in perfect harmony with God's will.</note>; we must now see what man's free will is in the state of sin. Elsewhere we have shown that freedom consists in acting with reason, without being forced to do so by another; and we have proven that this freedom is so essential to a rational creature that, in whatever state it may be, it cannot exist without this freedom.

It is certain, then, that sin has not taken this freedom away from man, since man cannot lose it without ceasing to be human.

Spinoza <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a Dutch philosopher who argued for determinism—the idea that humans only believe they are free because they are conscious of their actions but ignorant of the causes that determine them.</note> maintained that we only consider man to be free because we do not know the sequence of causes that make him act. But, although we do not know the sequence of causes that make men act, we nevertheless do not fail to say that man is free, because he does what pleases him. The reasons that incite him to do what he does do not diminish his freedom; for, if he did not find them good, he would not do it.

But one must note that, besides this freedom which is essential to human nature, Adam possessed another in the state of righteousness, consisting in being absolutely free from sin. He lost this second freedom by sinning, but he never lost the first. Therefore, all his children are born free, possessing that first freedom by which we act according to our own discretion; but because they come into the world as sinners, they are by nature slaves to sin, and they misuse the first freedom by applying it to nothing but evil, and without the assistance of God's grace, they can do no good.

<column-break/>

It is true that man, regarding natural things, has the same powers that Adam had; he can do them or not do them according to his will: eat, drink, sleep, etc.

<margin>
Socinus, *Theological Lectures*, ch. 5. Volkel, *On the True Religion*, book V, ch. 18. Bellarmine, *On Grace and Free Will*, book V, ch. 9. All the *Articles of the Hague Conference*, art. 3 <note>The Hague Conference (1611) was a pivotal meeting between Remonstrants (Arminians) and Counter-Remonstrants (Calvinists) in the Dutch Republic.</note>.
</margin>
It is also true that man, regarding matters concerning civil life, still has powers, though one must admit he does not have as many as Adam, because sin has filled his understanding with a false light, and his will often deceives itself regarding what it chooses or rejects. But regarding spiritual goods, we believe that man, being corrupted by nature, can do nothing of himself that is pleasing to God, because he has made himself a slave to sin.

The whole of Scripture teaches us this truth. This appears first from all the places where it is said that man of himself can do nothing. <margin>Grevinchovius <note>Nicolaas Grevinchovius (d. 1632), a prominent Dutch Remonstrant theologian.</note>.</margin> Romans 8:7: *The carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be.* 1 Corinthians 2:14: *The natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God.* John 6:44: *No man can come to me,* says Christ, *except the Father which hath sent me draw him.* Jeremiah 13:23: *Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil.* John 15:5: *Without me,* says Christ, *ye can do nothing.* 2 Corinthians 3:5: *Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God.* Matthew 7:18: *A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit.*

<margin>Limborch, *Christian Theology*, book IV, ch. 14 <note>Philippus van Limborch (1633–1712) was a leading Remonstrant theologian and professor in Amsterdam.</note>.</margin>
1. Regarding these passages, it is commonly said that all these ways of speaking—which establish the total impotence of man to do any good of himself—must not be taken literally, and that they are hyperbolic expressions used by the common people. But if that is so, why is it that they are found everywhere in Scripture? Why is it that all the holy writers use the same language? Why is it that God's Spirit tells us nothing that can reveal the true sense of these words?

2. It is said that these words, *he cannot*, only mean that this does not commonly...

# THE CHRISTIAN

commonly happens, or when it is testified that man can do no good, people want to interpret it as merely saying that he does not do it. But, to be convinced of the contrary, one has only to read these Scripture passages. If one were to give it that meaning, would Paul say that the flesh does not submit, and *cannot* submit? Would Christ say that a bad tree does not bring forth good fruit, and *cannot* bring forth? Does that mean it is not *accustomed* to bringing forth good fruit? Can one explain Jeremiah with any appearance of reason thus: *Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil.* <note>Jeremiah 13:23. The original Dutch uses "Moorman" (Moor), referring to an Ethiopian or person of dark skin, a standard biblical metaphor of the era for unchangeable nature.</note> Does this question and this parable not signify a total impotence to do good?

3. It is also said that these words, *he cannot*, mean *he will not*. I answer that it is true that the impotence of man is voluntary, as we shall see in the following; but the will of man is so corrupt that, unless the grace of God changes it, it always incites man to evil.

<margin>Bellarmine, *On Free Will*, chapter X.</margin>
4. It is said that Paul in Romans 8:7 speaks not of the state of an absolutely unregenerate man, nor of the "higher faculty" of the soul, but of the "lower faculty," which is called the carnal mind. Answer: But, besides that this distinction between higher and lower faculties is imaginary <note>The author argues against the Scholastic view that the human mind is split into a "higher" part (reason) that remains pure and a "lower" part (passions) that is corrupted by sin.</note>, one must note: 1. That the word we have translated as the "carnal mind" in Paul’s language <term>vleesch-gezindheid</term> signifies understanding or prudence, just as the Vulgate <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible.</note> has rendered it. Now, understanding and prudence belong to the faculty called the higher faculty. 2. Scripture includes under the word "flesh" the corruption of all our soul's faculties. Among the works of the flesh Paul places idolatry and heresy (Galatians 5:20), and in John 3:6 he calls everything that must be born again "flesh."

<margin>Limborch, *Christian Theology*, book IV, chapter 14.</margin>
5. It is said that when Christ (Matthew 7:18, 12:33, Luke 6:43) teaches us that a bad tree cannot bring forth good fruit, one must not take these words more literally than when he says a good tree cannot bring forth bad fruit. Now,

<column-break/>

it is said, a good tree sometimes bears bad fruit, or those not entirely ripe, or those infected by worms. Answer: Who does not see that one can never say a good tree bears bad fruit if the fruit it produces does not ripen or is spoiled by some vermin? This does not prevent a good tree from bearing fruit that is good by nature but corrupted by an external cause. On the other hand, there is a great difference between a believer and an unbeliever. A believer is such a good tree that has within itself an evil seed that has not been entirely rooted out. One must not be surprised then that a believer all too often brings forth bad fruit. It is not so with the corrupt man; there is nothing in him that can bear good fruit. It is added here that if one were to explain this passage literally, it would follow that man is good or evil by virtue of a natural necessity, just as a tree is good or evil by virtue of a natural necessity. I answer that we take these words literally only insofar as, just as a bad tree by nature cannot bear good fruit unless it is changed by God’s omnipotence, so man, who is conceived in sin, can do no work by his own strength that is pleasing to God unless he be recreated and wholly renewed by grace.

6. It is said that when Paul testifies that the natural man cannot understand the things of God (1 Corinthians 2:14), these words do not mean he can have no knowledge of God’s word, but they mean he cannot grasp the excellence of spiritual things above fleshly things; that he cannot grasp them so as to give his consent to what the word teaches him and direct his conduct accordingly. I answer: That we demand nothing more, and that this is enough to show the impotence that we attribute to the corrupt man.

7. One objects: That when Paul says we are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything, these words only concern the duties of the Apostleship. If we are not sufficient of ourselves to have one good thought, how much less can we fulfill the duties of the Holy Ministry if God does not give us the capacity for it? The manner in which Paul speaks does not allow us to doubt that he reasons thus: for after he has said in general that all our sufficiency comes from God, he adds, *who also hath made us able ministers of the New Testament.* <margin>2 Corinthians 3:5-6.</margin> If a great Apostle was not ashamed to acknowledge that he had no sufficiency of himself, why should anyone in their own calling be ashamed to make the same confession? ->THE CHRISTIAN<-

that there is a great difference between the manner in which believers are made slaves of righteousness and the manner in which humans are born as slaves of sin. Everyone knows that the grace which has freed the believer from the slavery of sin and subjected them to the gentle rule of righteousness has not sanctified them so completely that no remnants of sin remain in them, which still often cause them to sin. But humans are born entirely under the dominion of sin.

I say secondly: That Paul's aim is not so much to describe the *state* in which believers find themselves, as it is to describe their *obligation*. He wants them to understand that, since they were formerly so subject to sin that they offered all their members as instruments of unrighteousness, they ought now—having been redeemed—to give themselves over entirely to the righteousness to which grace has subjected them.

II. It is said that there is a great difference between physical slavery and the slavery of sin. The first is usually an unwilling state, while the second is a completely willing slavery. I admit this, but it actually strengthens our reasoning: for the sinner is a slave to sin to such an extent that he *wants* to be one; he does not want to leave his prison, he kisses his chains, and he worships his tyrant—whereas other slaves long for their freedom and do everything in their power to obtain it.

III. It is said that the sinner, being a slave of sin, is therefore no less free.

I make a distinction here. He is no less free regarding that freedom which is essential to all rational creatures <note>This refers to "natural liberty," the basic human capacity to think and act, which remains even if the moral direction of those acts is corrupted.</note>; but he is meanwhile so subjected to the dominion of sin that he does nothing except what his tyrant desires. One can compare sin to a person in love. This person is free, for no one forces him to do what he does. However, his passion makes him such a slave to the person he loves that he has no other will than that of his mistress.

IV. It is said that man, through the slavery of sin, has not lost the freedom and power to receive the grace offered to him and to cooperate with it—just as some-

<column-break/>

one, it is said, who has fallen into a well has indeed lost the freedom to walk, but not the freedom to move and to hold onto a rope.

I answer: That the sinner by nature resists and rejects the grace offered to him, far from accepting it. Thus, there is a difference between him and someone who has fallen into a well. The latter wants to get out, but the sinner wants to remain in sin; he takes delight in it; he places his pleasure in it.

To prove the inability of man in the state of sin, we draw a third proof from the fact that humans are shown to us as *blind, and being entirely darkness* (Ephesians 5:8); as having a *deceitful and desperately wicked heart* (Jeremiah 17:9); *a heart where the thoughts are evil every day* (Genesis 6:5); *an uncircumcised heart; a heart harder than diamond* (Zechariah 7:12); and *a heart of stone* (Ezekiel 36:26), in which the heavenly seed can take no root. A heart that is dead and without life, like stone; a heart that resists the hammer of God’s word and will not receive the impression and seal of God. An earthly, unfeeling, stubborn heart. A heart that bears no fruit. From all these expressions, we draw a powerful proof to show that man has no strength—neither in his understanding nor in his will—to pursue spiritual things, and that without grace, he can neither know divine truths nor do good works.

1. It is said: That when sinners are called *blind*, that expression only signifies their ignorance in spiritual matters, but not their inability to be converted and enlightened. **Answer.** We do not deny that they can be enlightened by grace; but we maintain that by nature they cannot comprehend heavenly things, and we prove it not only from the name *blind* which the Scripture gives them, but from various similar expressions.

2. It is said: That Christ testifies in John 9:41 that if the Pharisees were *blind*, they would have committed no sin; but that, according to our view, the state of blindness in a sinner is a state of deficiency.

One only has to read the texts where these expressions occur to feel the distinction between them. *You are dead through your sins and misdeeds*, says Paul in <margin>Ephesians 2:1.</margin> Ephesians 2:1. *The woman who follows her <margin>1 Timothy 5:6.</margin> pleasures is dead while she lives*, 1 Timothy 5:6. See there the first way of speaking. See here the second: <margin>Ezekiel 3:18.</margin> Ezekiel 3:18. *If I say to the wicked, "you shall surely die," and you do not warn him, and do not speak to warn the wicked man of his wicked ways, so that you keep him alive, 그 wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but his blood I will require from your hand.* And in Ezekiel 18:24 God says: *he shall die in his sin.* The same expression will be found in John 8:21, 24.

The second observation is that the word "death" is sometimes taken in the Scriptures to mean <term>oppressions</term> <note>Meaning heavy trials or persecutions.</note>, as in 2 Corinthians 11:23. Sometimes it refers to the mortality of the body, as when Paul says in Romans 8:10 that the body is dead because of sin—which is to say, it is mortal.

However, none of these meanings can apply to the cited texts where it is said that sinners are dead in their misdeeds; one can understand nothing else by this than <term>spiritual death</term> <note>A state of being alive physically but separated from God's grace and spiritual life.</note>, which consists of the separation from God (who is the source of life) and the deprivation of holiness (which is the true life of the soul). It is from this concept that it is said that believers are "born again" when they are converted.

Now, it follows from this that man can no more convert himself by his own power than a dead man can raise himself up.

I know well that there is a great difference between a dead man and a sinner. A dead man has no power to act at all, but a sinner only lacks the power to do good. A dead man no longer has faculties like memory, imagination, etc.; a sinner still has them, but they are corrupted. A dead man is not obligated to rise from his grave; a sinner is commanded to leave the grave of his sins.

But there is always this similarity between the sinner and death: that, just as a dead man is deprived of natural life, of all

<column-break/>

feeling, and of all movement, the sinner is likewise excluded from the <term>life of grace</term> <note>The spiritual vitality granted by God's favor.</note> and from all movement toward that which is truly good.

There is something more here. A sinner should be called "dead" much sooner than those whom we commonly call dead. These latter are only dead with respect to the body; their soul, which makes up the principal part, lives and is perfectly happy, provided it is the soul of a true believer. But the soul of a sinner is dead. One sees sinners moving about like other men, but they do not truly "live."

One should not give the name "life" to anything except that which is spent in the exercise of good works, in accordance with the reason with which God has endowed us, and with the image after which He created us, with the will He revealed to us in His law, and with the glory He promises us therein.

It is said, 1. That although sinners do not live the life of grace, they nonetheless live the <term>life of nature</term>, which enables them to contribute something toward their own quickening <note>Their own "coming to life" or spiritual awakening.</note>. I answer that this is the very point of the dispute: for we have proven up to this point that the state in which sinners exist by nature is the reason why they cannot convert themselves.

It is said, 2. That sinners bear the name of "the dead" because they perform no work that indicates they possess any spiritual life, but that this does not mean they are unable to perform any. Answer: How could they do good, since they do not have the life of faith?

It is said, 3. That although it is testified of believers that they are *dead to sin*, they are nonetheless not so <margin>Limborch, Theology, Book IV, ch. 14. <note>original: "Limb. Theol. IV. c. 14." Refers to the Arminian theologian Philippus van Limborch.</note></margin> dead to it that they no longer sin; likewise, when it is said that sinners are dead in their misdeeds, one must not conclude from this that they are in such a state that they cannot do any good. I answer, 1. That the Scripture, which tells us that believers have died to sin, exhorts them to "put to death" their members; but it portrays sinners as being so dead in their misdeeds that they live for no other purpose than to provoke God. 2. That just as it is said of believers that they have died to sin to signify that they are no longer under its dominion, so it is said of sinners...

If we said / that God demands of man what does not correspond with his nature / and that it is such / that he / even if he wanted to do it / would not be able to do it / like moving mountains / making lightning fall / climbing to heaven / splitting the seas / raising the dead; if we said / that it is impossible for man to repent / just as it is impossible / for thorns and thistles to bring forth figs / or just as it is impossible for a prisoner to leave the prison-house / even though he desired it / the objection would hold; but we say nothing that resembles that.

When we say / that it is impossible for the Sinner to repent / we mean nothing other / than that he does not want to / that he is hardened in his wickedness / that it pleases him to remain in sin / that he delights in sin / that all his thoughts / and all the deliberations of his heart lean toward the side of sin / and favor the same / although he is convinced / that he ought to love God with all his soul / avoid evil / and do good. Is not every man then bound / to do what his conscience prescribes that he has to do / and which he does not do out of mere malice?

Through this one can easily answer what is commonly said / namely / that / if man cannot repent / God can neither condemn nor punish him; for / they add / is one not excusable / when one does not do something / that one cannot do / or that one does something else / to which one is driven by the power of an inviolable necessity?

When the Will is sunk in that state / that it never gives its consent to good nor wants to give it / that is called not being able / although this inability springs from a will / that remains stubborn in evil.

If this reasoning held / it would follow from it / that a rational Creature

<column-break/>

would not be guilty of the evil / that it does / when it would be hardened so as not to be able to do otherwise / and that evil habits would have thus strengthened themselves through a great series of actions / that one would not be able to rid oneself of them. One punishes a thief no less / even though he says / that he is so accustomed to stealing / that he cannot stop it.

Jeremiah does not intend at all / to excuse the Jews / when he reproaches them / that they were so accustomed to evil / that it was as impossible for them to learn to do good / as for an Ethiopian to change his skin <note>Reference to Jeremiah 13:23: "Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? <margin><note>The Remonstrants, also known as Arminians, were a group of Dutch Protestants who challenged strict Calvinist views on predestination and human ability.</note> Remon:</margin> Those who make these objections to us / acknowledge / that there are certain moments / in which man can be nothing but rebellious against grace / and in which God foresees / that he will not repent. Now I ask, whether he is in that moment less guilty / and whether God does not always have the right to punish him? One would not dare to deny it.

If someone / who is overcome by the power of sin / and who can do nothing but evil / is not worthy of punishment / one would have to say by the rule of the contrary / that / if someone possesses virtue in a sufficiently high degree so as not to be able to sin / he deserves no praise nor reward / since he could not act otherwise. From that it would follow / that God ought not to be praised for His holiness / because holiness is so essential to Him / that He cannot forsake it. Who would not shudder at such fundamental propositions?

6. One objects, that / if all men are naturally corrupt / there will be no distinction between them / and they will all be equally evil.

I answer, that there would indeed be no distinction between them / if God himself did not place a distinction between them. He is it / who improves and restrains the natural corruption of some / while He leaves others in it / and He uses various means / to make the one better than the others. He gives to some a happier disposition / and a better upbringing. He presents better examples to some. He works in others through His Spirit. And thus it is / that He makes a distinction between these and those.

7. The following passages are raised in objection: those where it is said that even the wicked love those who love them, that they give alms, etc., as in Luke 6:32-33, and so on.

I answer that all these passages prove nothing other than that the wicked sometimes do things that are *outwardly* good; but they do not prove that they can, by their own strength without God's assistance, perform works that are truly pleasing to God.

Other objections are still made, but we refer them to the treatise on **Calling**, and to the section where we shall speak concerning the virtues of the Heathens.

It now remains only for me to say something about the opinions of the **Church Fathers** on this subject.

I. It is certain that the Fathers, before the time of *Pelagius* <note>Pelagius (c. 354–418 AD) was a monk who taught that humans have the free will to achieve spiritual perfection without divine grace, a view later declared heretical.</note>, expressed many things that conflict with Scripture. A learned man of the *Roman Church* says:
<margin>S. Germain, *Survival of the Roman Church concerning the Predestination of the Saints*, etc.</margin>
> "That one must view them as **Advocates** <note>Lawyers or pleaders in a court.</note> who argue amongst themselves over a point of law that has not yet been formally deliberated. They speak with all the greater freedom because there is as yet no lawsuit, nor any particular reason obliging them to speak with caution. They do not look into the matter fundamentally, according to the principles of Jurisprudence or the laws of the Authorities; they say nothing of it except what their spirit suggests to them on the spot, without giving heed to all the consequences that might be drawn from it in court. But," he adds, "as soon as the lawsuit began with the *Pelagians*, the Advocates considered the dispute more carefully; they diligently examined the writings of the Parties and all the documents of the plea. They viewed the state and the consequences of the matter more closely. They pleaded before the tribunal of the Church. *Augustine* was the **Prosecutor** of the case, and the Advocate for the truth placed the matter in such a light that the Church awarded the judgment to him."

II. It is also certain, as the same writer remarks, that what gave the Fathers occasion to speak as they sometimes did before the rise of the heresy of *Pelagius*, was: 1. That we are all born full of arrogance regarding 

<column-break/>

our own strength. 2. That the Fathers had to contend against the *Manicheans* <note>Followers of Manichaeism, who believed in a radical dualism where evil was an inescapable physical substance, often denying human responsibility.</note> and other heretics who had fallen into a different extreme and a worse opinion than *Pelagius*. 3. That human **Philosophy** had greatly biased them against the Foundations of Theology regarding the matter of grace. 4. That many of them built the doctrines of Christian Theology upon the foundation of Heathen Philosophy. 5. That *Origen* <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) whose work blended Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note>, who followed this method, had gathered a great number of disciples through the fertility of his wit and his shining intellect.

III. It is established that most of the passages from the Church Fathers cited against our doctrine either deal with people in a state of grace (and not in a state of sin), or only prove that man possesses that freedom which is essential to every rational creature, or only grant to man the power to do outward good—or else they run entirely contrary to Holy Scripture.

IV. It is further established that there are passages among the Church Fathers showing they believed that all the good we do comes from God, and that we have no reason to boast of it. 
<margin>Book 3 to Quirinus, ch.</margin>
*Cyprian* <note>original: "Cyprianus," a 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage.</note> teaches this.

V. It is also certain that the opinions of the *Pelagians* and *Semi-Pelagians* were condemned by 
<margin>4th Sermon on the Lord’s Prayer <note>original: "4. Serm. Domi. Orat."</note></margin> 
various Church Councils, of which we shall speak later, on the occasion of **Predestination** and **Calling**.

VI. It is indubitable that those who lived and wrote after the rise of the heresies—especially in those churches where one was most obligated to investigate them—must particularly be heard. This is because those who wrote afterward took more notice of the errors, saw the difficulties, adjusted their expressions, and cautiously refined them. From this it follows, as *Augustine* says, that truths were *investigated* with more care, *fathomed* with more clarity, and *taught* with more diligence.

VII. Finally, it is known to everyone that *Augustine*, who lived when *Pelagius* arose and who carefully tracked the errors of this and other heretics, supported the true Doctrine with power, and that there has always been, in all...

> Gregory I <note>original: "Gregorius de I."</note>, concerning the 7th Penitential Psalm, says: "The free will having corrupted itself in our first Father, we cannot will anything ourselves if grace, which directs all the paths of man, does not help us; for it stands written: 'the will of man is prepared by the Lord'; and the Apostle says, 'God works in you both to will and to do.'"

I cannot neglect, before I finish, to resolve an objection of the freethinkers <note>term: <term>vrygeesten</term> (freethinkers) — individuals in the 17th and 18th centuries who rejected traditional religious dogmas in favor of reason or personal liberty.</note>, who claim that the believer is a slave and the sinner is a freeman; that Christ is a domineering master who leaves no freedom to His disciples, who imposes strict laws on them, who forces them against their will away from what might be called the sweetness of life, who keeps them waiting with an uncertain and doubtful future and necessitates them to lose the present—all that they were reluctant to leave—even to forsake their reason, and to believe that there are pleasures in being bound to the burning stakes and on the wheel <note>Instruments of execution and torture commonly used against religious martyrs.</note>, whereas for them there is nothing that consumes them.

**Answer:** Who is judged to be freer, one who serves a father or one who serves a tyrant? A believer serves God; he is a servant <note>The Dutch "slaaf" here carries the biblical sense of "doulos" or bondservant.</note> of the Lord Christ, I admit it: but God is his Father, Christ is his Redeemer. A worldling serves Satan, who is a tyrant. A believer, by serving Christ, labors for himself and for his own well-being; he secures his freedom. But a sinner serves the devils, for whom he prepares himself not only as a spectator of their miseries through this service, but as a companion in their punishments. Moreover, as soon as someone loves Christ, he finds no difficulty in leaving everything for His sake, and he finds His commandments sweet.

With this, we shall end both this chapter and this treatise on the state of man in sin. We must now observe how providence acts regarding sin. That we shall investigate in the following book, after we have spoken of Providence in general.

### CHAPTER I.

What is generally understood by Providence, and whether there is one.

<margin>Seneca, *On Benefits*, Book VII. 31.</margin>
We have seen in the fifth book of our Theology how God brought forth the whole universe out of nothing, and how He created everything we observe within it with a wonderful wisdom and an infinite power. However, one must not imagine that God is like a Master Builder who, after he has constructed a magnificent palace, leaves it to the one for whom it was built, without further concerning himself with who shall maintain it. This is the false idea that Epicurus <note>A Greek philosopher (341–270 BC) often associated in theological texts with the idea that gods exist but do not intervene in human affairs.</note> had formed of it; and he has had all too many followers. God was not satisfied merely with creating all that we see and do not see; He also has a special care for it. Nothing happens in this great commonwealth of the world—as Augustine and Prosper <note>Likely Prosper of Aquitaine, a disciple of Augustine.</note> said—that is not arranged and determined in the Celestial Court of the Master of the universe. This care is called providence, as some have described it.

It is, says Nemesius <note>A Christian philosopher and Bishop of Emesa, c. 4th century.</note> and after him John of Damascus (*On the Nature of Man*, chapter 24), the care that God has for all things, or the will of God, through which all things are governed in a wonderful order.

Boethius in the fourth book of *The Consolation* <note>original: *De Consolatione Philosophiae*</note> etc., says that providence is the Divine reason of the supreme ruler of the whole universe, which arranges and directs all things. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the medieval Scholastic philosopher.</note> says that it is the reason

<column-break/>

which directs things, disposes them, and brings them to their end.

In this sense, one finds the word Providence in the Book of Wisdom 14:3 and 6:8. Plato made use of it, as Diogenes Laertius notes; and the Church Fathers have used it, such as Augustine, Jerome, and others. The Scripture has other names for it: Genesis 22:8, Psalms 33:14, Deuteronomy 32:11, Hebrews 1:3. We shall see this more closely in what follows.

Before we investigate in detail what providence is, we must consider whether one must indeed acknowledge its existence.

1. There is no reason to doubt it, if one pays attention to the concept that one naturally has of God. One understands God as the most perfect being of all beings that exist or can exist. This is a sound concept; everyone agrees on it. But one cannot hold this concept and simultaneously believe that God neglects His own works, that He keeps Himself locked in Heaven, or that He has no care for what He has created. At the very least, one must agree that if God has no care for His creation, there could exist a being more perfect than God.

Nemesius, Bishop of Emesa, who lived in the year 380 (though others place him in the 5th century), said that it was characteristic of God to make everything well and to take good care of that which was made. Gregory of Nyssa, speaking of providence (chapter 2), and Lactantius in the 4th chapter of *On the Wrath of God* <note>original: *De Ira Dei*</note> and elsewhere, make us understand very well that to deny providence is to deny the Godhead, and that a God who has no care for His creature is no God at all.

One cannot conceive of God without

<summary>This page introduces the doctrine of Providence, defining it as God's active and rational governance of the universe, and argues that denying this care is equivalent to denying God's existence.</summary>

# THEOLOGY. VII. B. I, Chapter.

to understand a being who knows all, sees all, can do all, and upon whom everything depends. But, when one does not wish to accept providence, one assumes that God does not know all that goes on, that He abandons His creatures to themselves, that He lets them act as they desire, and thus that they are independent.

Everything that happens, occurs either with or without the knowledge and will of God. If one says that God knows all that happens, and that nothing happens against His will, one acknowledges a providence. But, if one says that God does not know what happens, or that things happen against His will, then one names God something that is not God. For, how can one call a being "God" who is not omniscient <note>all-knowing</note>, or who cannot prevent what He does not want, or who, being able and willing to prevent it, remains in a lazy idleness? One might say that the management of the world would disturb God’s happy state: but one deceives oneself bluntly by imagining a God who tires Himself with working, whereas He works all things through a single act of His will.

II. If one also observes the creatures, one will recognize a providence: Just as they were created out of nothing, it is certain that they would immediately collapse back into it if the same hand that made them did not constantly carry and support them.

Because they exist in this moment, one cannot conclude that they will exist in the next moment. *If You hide Your face,* says the Prophet in **Ps. CIV. 29.** *they are troubled; if You take away their breath, they die and return to their dust.*

<margin>
Jurieu in his treatise on nature and grace, p. 72. <note>Pierre Jurieu (1637–1713) was a famous French Protestant theologian who wrote extensively on Divine Grace.</note>
</margin>

> "When art or 
> "nature," says a learned man, "brings a 
> "new form into an object, 
> "then I well understand that it is not necessary

> "by which they brought forth this form 
> "in order to maintain it; 
> "for the matter carries and supports the 
> "form. But when the matter is supported by no

When one thinks of God, one thinks of a being that necessarily exists; but when one thinks of creatures, one thinks of beings that could very well not exist.

<column-break/>

One might say that it follows from the existence of creatures that they must always exist, unless some cause destroyed them. But those who make this objection take no notice that there are thousands of things that would destroy us every moment if God did not sustain us, and it is easily understood that there is no moment in which the creature cannot cease to be.

One might say that it is enough that God does not want to destroy His creatures to make them exist, even if He did not think of them Himself. But what does one mean by "not wanting to destroy"? Does one mean to say that it is enough that God has no thought of destroying? If that is so, it is false to say that even if God did not think to destroy the creatures, they would last forever; because time would cause them to perish, and they would destroy themselves. Does one mean to say that God wills that nothing be destroyed, and that consequently the creatures remain in the state in which He created them? If that is the meaning, then one joins our view; for this "will" is providence.

III. A third proof for providence we draw from the wonderful order that we discover in the world.

Who is not convinced that there is a providence when he comes to contemplate that glorious harmony that exists between all the parts of the whole universe?

That connection between Heaven and Earth; the revolutions of the seasons; the procreation and preservation of so many animals in the Air, in the Water, and on the earth; that wonderful variety of plants, where some serve for pleasure, others for food, others for medicine; the production of metals and minerals in the bowels of the Earth; the proper disposition of the Air and Regions; the glory of the Heavens, those azure arches that rotate so magnificently above our heads; those bright-shining spheres that every day change the entire face of the universe twice through their movement; the Sea, which—though it sometimes splashes its waves up to the clouds and threatens to flood the Earth—nevertheless comes to break its waves against the sand without passing the boundaries set for it. In a word, everything visible. Certainly, he who perceives no providence in all these things is not only blind, but insane, since it is one of the highest truths...

<meta>This page continues the logical proofs for Divine Providence, moving from the physical order of the universe to the internal witness of the human conscience, followed by scriptural evidence and testimonies from classical philosophy.</meta>

-> THE CHRISTIAN <-

down to the very center of the earth, there is nothing that does not proclaim a providence. Who could believe that such a great number of creatures, possessing such diverse natures, could remain in the same state without a particular care from the Divinity? Who could imagine that the Stars would have such a well-ordered movement, and that the Seasons would cycle in nearly the same way, and with such regularity, if the wonderful Master-builder <note>original: "Werk-meester," a term often used in this period to describe God as the supreme architect or artisan of the universe</note> who made all things did not have a constant care for them?

One might say that this reasoning certainly proves that God is infinitely wise, and that He has unbounded power and knowledge, but not that He carries a particular care for the world, because He could have placed it in such a state that it would have no need of a guide.

**Answer.** But it clearly appears that God has made His work in such a way that they require the support of His hand, because an infinite number of things could otherwise destroy them. This reasoning can be confirmed by as many instances as occur in the world that prove a providence, such as the overthrows of Empires, the manifold judgments that God has exercised and still exercises in the world, and other such things.

IV. The conscience <note>original: "het Gewisse," referring to the internal moral certainty or witness within a person</note> gives us a fourth proof for a providence: for, if it were true that everything happens without God keeping an eye on events, or if God did not concern Himself in any way with what goes on upon the earth, how does it happen that sinners tremble at the memory of their crimes? That the greatest villains almost die of terror at the slightest thunder they hear in the sky? Certainly, one can give no good reason for these terrors if one does not acknowledge that everyone has an idea of a providence, as we have said elsewhere.

These are the proofs that reason provides us: but the Scripture teaches us this truth in a convincing manner. It says that Christ sustains all things by the word of His power (**Hebrews 1:3**). That God gives to all life, breath, and all things (**Acts 17:25**). For in Him we live, and move, and have our being (**Verse 28**). That God preserves both man and beast

<column-break/>

(**Psalm 36:7**). That He looks down from Heaven upon all the children of men. That He looks out from His fixed dwelling place upon all the inhabitants of the earth (**Psalm 33:13, 14**). That He gives the cattle their food (**Psalm 147:9**). That He gives snow like wool (**Verse 16**). That He takes care of the Lilies and Sparrows (**Matthew 6:26–30**). That He causes the light of day to rise, and brings on the darkness of the night. That He makes Summer and Winter; that He sends and restrains the winds; that He sends the rain and the drought, and whatever else of this nature we shall speak of in what follows.

This truth is so firm that the wisest of the Pagans have acknowledged it. Aristotle condemns those who doubt it to be scourged. Another Pagan proves the existence of a Divinity and a providence through all that we behold, not only through the beautiful order and the well-arranged course of the planets, but also through the observation of the earth.

<margin>Cicero, Book II, *On the Nature of the Gods*.</margin>
> Let us, he said, behold the earth, placed in the middle of the world, clothed with flowers, herbs, trees, and fruits, where the unbelievable multitude is distinguished by such great variety that one never tires of beholding them. Let us add to this the clear Springs, the crystal-like Rivers, the flowered adornment of the Banks, the depth of the valleys, the arches of the caves, the peaks of the rocks, the backs of the Dunes, the crowns of the mountains, and the great expanse of the plains. Let us further add the hidden mineral veins of silver and gold, and 그hat infinite variety of precious Marbles found there. But what is to be said of the humans, who, being housed in the midst of the earth to plow it, do not suffer it to be taken over by wild beasts, nor let the thickness of the wild forests cover it. It is through their care and ingenuity that the Fields, the Islands, and the Rivers are so magnificently adorned with Houses and Cities. Certainly, if we could behold all this with a single glance of the eye, as we see it through the light of the understanding, it would be impossible for us to doubt—

# DIVINE THEOLOGY. VII. B. I. Chapter.

<margin>
Diodorus Siculus, Historical Library, Book II.
Pythagoras in Clement of Alexandria, Exhortation, Book II.
Plato, On the Laws, Book IV.

</margin>
...believe in a Divine providence. Many other Philosophers and wise Heathens <note>original: "Heidenen," referring here to the pre-Christian classical thinkers of Greece and Rome</note> have upheld this truth. If one finds the principles of a generally accepted opinion in self-love, in lust, or in the temporary state of affairs, then one may regard it as a general popular error. But general consent is of great weight when one can discover no other cause for it than the truth of the matter itself, upon which all men agree, especially when it is set against the strongest and most prevailing passions. But, in order not to dwell too long on what the Heathens have said, let us consider what may be brought against this sentiment, which reason teaches and the scripture confirms.

I. It is said that it is not possible to believe that all things are arranged by a wise providence, since one perceives so much disharmony <note>original: "wanschiklykheid," implying a lack of proper arrangement or fitness</note> in the world.

**Answer.** I ask those who object to this whether they are quite certain that what they call disharmony is a true disorder? Have they not often themselves regarded as a disorder that which they afterwards found to be a well-arranged order?

I ask again whether it is not true that they call "disorder" that for which they can give no reason? Is it not then a recklessness to judge so hastily of that which one does not know?

That which causes such poor reasoning is that we do not understand the relationships of things which do not seem well-suited to us, compared to those that seem well-arranged. For if we understood them, we would infallibly recognize a providence. We act like those who would want to judge a choir song by a single tone that sounds very strange in their ears; or like those who, in viewing a painting, would fix their eye only upon the shadows; or like those who would look at bits and pieces here and there in a tapestry that show imperfect and hideous shapes. Augustine explains this very well (Book I, *On Order*, Chapter 1) <note>original: "L. I. de ord. c. 1." referring to St. Augustine’s "De Ordine"</note>: "If someone were so short-sighted that he could see only a small portion of a tessellated floor, he might be tempted to criticize the Master <note>The "Master" or Architect here refers to God as the creator</note> because he could not see the beauty of all the parts, which through their proper arrangement...

<column-break/>

...yield charming images. The same happens," he adds, "to those who do not sufficiently know the beauty of the whole Universe. For, their understanding not being extended enough to grasp with one glance the arrangement and the harmony of all that happens in the world, whenever something strikes them because it goes beyond their comprehension, they imagine that there is a deformity in the things themselves which God has made."

But on the other hand, if various things appear as if in disorder, it is certain that there are infinite others in which one perceives the marks of a wonderful wisdom, which clearly prove a providence to us.

These general answers could already be enough. But let us examine these alleged disharmonies in particular.

These are the Sands of Africa, the Deserts of Arabia, the vast Ocean, the inaccessible Rocks, so many Mountains that are always covered with snow, and others that spew out fire and flame. The rains that fall so unequally, and often in places where they do nothing to make the earth fruitful; the Frost and the Sun, which cause the crops to fail; the Hail, which strikes down the fruits; the Lightning, which fells the trees and falls upon the rocks; a great number of Vermin, of which one sees no use; Fish, snakes, and other venomous beasts; monsters, floods, earthquakes, subterranean fires, and other occurrences that threaten to make the world collapse and perish.

Behold, it is said, great irregularities. Others are added to them; but they would only be irregularities in appearance, as one will agree when one observes:

1. That the variety of objects seen in the world constitutes one of the greatest ornaments of the whole Universe.

One will say, that the ornament of the Universe cannot consist in the variety of useless and hideous objects. I answer, 1. That there are many more pleasant, useful, and wonderful objects than there are hideous and useless ones. 2. That, just as the ornament of a Painting consists in the proper placement of the shadows to make the lights appear more beautiful, so does the ornament of the Universe consist in the shading <note>original: "schakeeren," referring to the contrasting or gradation of colors and elements</note> of the objects...

II. From this it follows that one should not be surprised if God did not willed that all parts of the world should be equal, and that there should be uninhabited lands.

One will say: Since God does nothing uselessly, all places in the world ought to be inhabited.

**Answer:** But what seems useless for one thing can be useful in other respects. On a large panel where one paints a large face, there are many places where there is nothing but shadow. If there are places in the world that were formerly uninhabited, they are inhabited today; and it is not impossible that those now inhabited will one day be found without inhabitants.

III. One must not wonder that rain falls on places where it does not serve to make the earth fruitful, because rain has other uses.

IV. It must further be noted that it

<column-break/>

is not to be wondered at that there are trees that bear no fruit. These are not only useful to man for their fruit, but also for their shade, for their wood, leaves, and branches.

<margin>Augustine, Book 1, *On Order*, Chapter 11. <note>original: "de ord. c. 11." refers to *De Ordine*.</note></margin>
V. One has no more reason to be surprised that rain and lightning fall upon the rocks than one has when one sees that the sun enlightens and warms the wildernesses; because it is the heat of the sun that draws up the vapors and exhalations, which are the "cloud-matter" from which the rain and lightning proceed.

VI. One must not find it strange that the sun enlightens the rocks, etc., because it is a great illuminating body placed in the Universe in such a way that the whole earth is enlightened by it.

VII. God can have many reasons for making hail fall upon the fruits he has allowed to grow, in order to chastise men who only too often abuse his blessings.

VIII. <term>Vermin<note>original: "ongedierte," referring generally to pests or small, lowly creatures like insects.</note></term>, which we so greatly despise, have many uses, although most are unknown to us.

IX. In the most despised fish, nature has hidden the greatest medicines, which serve for the relief of man. In the lowliest shells one finds the most beautiful pearls, and one discovers daily that living in certain regions where one dared not dwell is very pleasant and delightful.

<margin>Arnauld.</margin>
X. The creatures that appear most defective to us, such as <term>monsters<note>original: "gedrogten," meaning biological deformities or anomalies, often viewed in this era as divine signs.</note></term>, are only so in comparison with others that are more perfect. Deformed animals, as someone has very well said, are indeed less perfect than others of their kind that have more symmetry, but they are more perfect than stones. One finds hundreds of wonderful things in the structure of these deformed bodies.

Monsters appear in the ways of Providence as signs of God's Omnipotence, or as wonders that leave men amazed, or as instruments to punish them. God allows monsters to be born so that we might thank him that he did not bring us into the world with a deformed body.

One will say: It is a thing against the laws of nature that monsters are born. I answer that it is much more a suspension than a reversal

Certainly, someone who—being in misery and oppression—triumphs through their faith and hope, who maintains the loyalty they owe to God, and who sings the praises of their Creator at the stake, is a spectacle that commands the admiration of men and Angels.

## CHAPTER II.

### Concerning the Object of Providence.

Faith and reason do not allow us to doubt that everything in general is linked to the chain of Providence: perishable things as well as imperishable; those that seem the lowliest as well as the noblest; the particular things which the philosophers call *individuals* <note>original: "individua", meaning indivisible or particular subjects</note>, as well as their genera and species; the outcomes that depend on the will of man, as well as those in which free creatures have no part.

Species do not exist outside of their subjects, and one cannot care for the species without caring for the subjects; and if all the subjects were to perish, the species would perish as well.

This must be noted to counter the error of those who believed that God did not concern Himself with the things of this lower world, or that He only concerned Himself with the great matters without bothering with the small. There have been many of this opinion among the Pagans, Jews, and Christians. *Aristotle* said that it was more becoming for God to act like the Persian Kings, who in their inner chambers ordered the great affairs of the Realm and left the care of others to their governors.
<margin>Pliny, Balbus in Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book 2. Arrian in *Discourses of Epictetus*, Book 1, chapter 12.</margin>

<margin>Maimonides, *The Guide for the Perplexed*, Part 3, chapter 17.</margin>
<margin>Hobbes.</margin>
But in all denominations, there have also been those who defended the opposite truth. *Socrates* said that even the smallest movement was not unknown to the Deity. *Moses Maimonides*, the wisest of the Jews, refutes those who, believing there is a Providence, said that it only applied to imperishable things or those that always persist in their species, and that as for the individuals of these species, everything happens to them by chance. He says that no one has held this opinion...

Let the Heathens then boast of their "blind Fortune," <note>original: "blinde Fortuin," referring to the Roman goddess Fortuna or the concept of random chance.</note> to which they attribute everything; as for us, we recognize a supreme providence that arranges and governs all things, which establishes and breaks down Kingdoms, which distributes and takes away Crowns, which gives life and causes death, which causes one to ascend the Throne and another to descend into the grave.

Hobbes <note>Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), the English philosopher, who argued in *Leviathan* that God's "Kingdom" only properly extends to those who understand His laws.</note> was of the opinion that inanimate and irrational things are not properly governed by providence (though he admits they are subject to his power) because they do not know God's laws. Can one produce anything more absurd?

Several objections are still made against this doctrine, which we must resolve.

It is said, 1. That it is beneath the Divine Majesty to humble Himself to such insignificant and contemptible objects as vermin.

Answer: why would it not befit God to maintain what he has made, and to take care of that which he created out of nothing? On the contrary, is it not becoming that a perfect being causes all his creatures to exist by his word and supports them by his power? Certainly, if God neglected any of his creatures because they were smaller than others, he would have to abandon them all: for they are all small and contemptible in his presence, and there is none that can add to or take away from his glory. It is certain that the greatest outcomes of matters depend on the smallest occurrences. A small insect can cause the death of a great Commander; the death of a Commander can cause a battle to be lost; and the loss of a battle can be the cause of the destruction of an entire Kingdom. The smallest events have their connection to the greatest upheavals.

This observation serves as an answer to the opinion of those who believe that it is in vain for God to concern himself with all subjects. In a word, if small things were not governed by providence, then there would be something that did not depend on God.

2. It is said, that it is impossible for God to govern and arrange everything.

# DIVINITY. VII. Book III. Chapter III.

Those who raise this objection fail to notice that God's knowledge and power are infinite, and that He has only to will a thing for it to be done and governed. They reason about God as they do about men, whose knowledge and power are so very limited. They believe that God exhausts Himself with work, just as they do, and they do not consider that Isaiah 40:28 states that the eternal God grows neither tired nor weary.

3. They object using Habakkuk 1:14, where the Prophet speaks to God in this way: *Why would you make men like the fish of the sea? Like the crawling creatures that have no ruler?*

Answer: This means nothing other than that the fish and crawling creatures have no ruler among themselves who protects the small against the great. But it does not prove that they are not subject to Providence; on the contrary, that Providence is evident in the fact that all the fish are not swallowed up and that they exist in such great numbers.

4. They object using 1 Corinthians 9:9, where Paul asks, *Does God care for oxen?*

Answer: One only has to read this passage to be convinced that Paul’s sole purpose is to show that when God made this law, found in Deuteronomy 25:4—*You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain*—He was not thinking so much of the survival of the oxen as He was trying to make us understand what is owed to those who faithfully carry out the work of their ministries, and who are much worthier than all the animals. <margin>Psalm 36:7 and 105:14 <note>The author uses Dutch numbering; Psalm 36:6 in English bibles refers to God saving both man and beast.</note></margin> That Paul intends this is clear from the fact that he would otherwise contradict David, who explicitly testifies that God maintains both men and beasts, and that He makes the grass sprout from the earth for the cattle. Thus, this passage indicates that God has more care for men than for beasts, just as He cares more for believers than for unbelievers.

5. They object that, if Providence extends to all things—since it is not to be feared that God would allow someone without a right to win their case, or that He would favor injustice—men would have no need to seek witnesses to assure judges of their rights, as they would only have to cast lots; and they further add that duels would be the holiest

<column-break/>

of all actions to decide legal matters where life is at stake.

Answer: 1. Who does not see that this objection assumes that God will never allow the innocent to be oppressed in this world, or the wicked to be exalted? This contradicts experience; see what we have noted regarding this in the previous Chapter.

<margin>Deuteronomy 19:13; Leviticus 5:1</margin> 2. How can one say that men act poorly when they do what God commands them? Does God not say that a matter shall be established by the mouth of two or three witnesses? And does one not read in Leviticus 5 that anyone who refused to be a witness—when he was certain of a matter that was in dispute, and when it was demanded of him that he give testimony to the truth—made himself guilty of a punishable sin?

3. Finally, how can one call a duel a holy act, since it is forbidden in God’s law?

We shall see in what follows how Providence intervenes in matters that depend on the will of man, without violating their freedom or the holiness of God Himself.

### CHAPTER III.

->Of the Works of Providence.<-

We have seen in general what must be understood by Providence and what its object is. We must now enter further into the treatise of this subject.

And therefore, we should note:

I. That Providence is an act of God’s free will, through which He disposes all things with infinite wisdom.

<margin>Chrysippus in Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book 6, chapter 2. <note>Aulus Gellius was a 2nd-century Roman author; Chrysippus was a Stoic philosopher who wrote extensively on fate.</note></margin> One must not, then, confuse Providence with the "Fate" of the Stoics <term>Fate/Nood-lot: the Stoic belief that all events are predetermined by a rigid chain of causes</term>, if the opinion of those philosophers is indeed as it is attributed to them. For: 1. Providence is an act within God, while Fate is a chain of second causes. 2. Providence is an act of God’s free will, through which He has established a certain order that He maintains and changes as He wills, so that God is not bound to second causes.
