# THE CHRISTIAN #

<margin>
John 12:40. Romans 11:8.
</margin>
"...ears might not hear, and their heart might not be converted. Consequently, although John says that God has blinded their eyes, and Paul says that God has given them a spirit of deep sleep, eyes not to see, and ears not to hear until this very day, etc., one must nevertheless not think that God is the cause of the wickedness and the hardening of sinners. Rather, sinners harden their own hearts through the *very same means* that ought to have brought them to conversion. When an eye that is inflamed looks toward the Sun, it becomes even more fiery. Is the blame for this placed upon the Sun? Not at all; it is attributed to the poor condition of the eye. To explain this further, one must observe:

1. That man is by nature blind, and that he is born blind.

2. That God enlightens the human understanding in various ways. He impresses upon it natural concepts <note>original: "natuurlijke begrippen"</note> which serve to guide him regarding the things of this life. He often gives him great talents to understand the sciences, arts, etc. He causes His law to be proclaimed to him, and He accompanies the proclamation of His Gospel with some grace of His Spirit, which reveals to him the knowledge of salvation. Therefore Paul says, speaking even of the temporary believers <note>original: "tytgeloovigen," referring to those who believe only for a season</note>, that they are enlightened.

<margin>
Hebrews 6:4.
</margin>
3. That the passions blind us. We do not judge things according to what they truly are, but according to the imagination that the passions create for us. Now, the greater and more impulsive these passions are, the greater the blindness.

4. From this it follows that God can blind man in various ways; whether by taking away the light He had given him because he misused it; or by no longer letting him hear the Gospel; or by handing him over to the passions that blind him.

5. That God blinds man by accident <note>original: "by toeval," meaning as an unintended consequence of a good action meeting a corrupt heart</note>, because the Gospel that He causes to be preached to him so stirs up and embitters his passions that they take away all light and all perception from him. Thus it happens that what should have enlightened man blinds him by accident, and what should have driven away his darkness increases it.

6. From all this, one can deduce that there is a threefold blindness in sinners: a natural one; one they inflict upon themselves; and one that is the punishment God imposes on them when He gives them over to themselves.

<column-break/>

It is said that to propose the hardening and blinding of man as an end <note>an intended goal</note> is a wicked end and purpose.

Answer: One must carefully note that God proposes no other end than to punish the men who misuse His grace. Now, such an end is fitting for God. Furthermore, it is sufficiently clear that God has righteous reasons to act as He acts.

After all these observations, it is not difficult to explain the other passages of Scripture, as well as all the expressions that agree in sense and power with these we have explained.

I shall now pass over to those where it is said that God tempts <term>verzoekt|This Dutch word can mean both "to test" for growth or "to tempt" toward sin</term> men. Thus He tempted Abraham.

<margin>
Genesis 22:1. Deuteronomy 18:2.
</margin>
To understand this, one must distinguish between the types of temptation. There is a good and a bad temptation. God tempted the father of the faithful when He commanded him to offer up his son, because by this command He proved <note>original: "beproefde"</note> his faith, just as gold is proven in the crucible. In that sense, all adversities are temptations <note>in the sense of trials</note>. But it does not follow from this that God is the cause of sin, because these temptations are wholesome. There are evil temptations that cannot be attributed to God, because they are enticements to sin. In this regard, Satan is called the Tempter, because he is the master and instigator of all evil temptations; having tempted the Chief Leader of Salvation <note>Jesus Christ</note>, he neglects nothing to tempt His members as well. In this sense, the Scripture calls "temptations" the efforts that men put into work through words, examples, and deeds, to turn us away from the true Religion and to drag us away into sin or error.

<margin>
James 1:14.
</margin>
James says that lust tempts us when it incites us toward the evil that appears pleasing to it. This reveals the true state of the heart regarding good or evil. In the latter, God has no part. Let no one, when he is tempted, say, "I am tempted by God," etc. (James 1:13). There are passages that are more difficult to understand, such as Ezekiel 14:9, where God speaks thus: "And if the prophet be deceived when he hath spoken a thing, I the Lord have deceived <note>original: "overredet," literally "persuaded" or "convinced"</note> that prophet."

### THEOLOGY. BOOK VII. CHAPTER VI. ###

...that is, to mislead, and if he brings a command, would I the Lord have misled that Prophet? On the contrary, I will stretch out my hand against him. But one cannot accept this explanation when one examines the original text <note>original: "Grond-text"</note>.

There are those who believe that the Lord declares here that He will punish the false prophet for his deceit and deprive him of his senses; but this interpretation does not agree with the original words. The word that has been translated as *persuaded* <note>The Dutch word used here is "overreden," likely referring to Ezekiel 14:9</note> actually means to draw or lure toward oneself, whether to good or evil, or to indifferent deeds, through gentle ways, through persuasive expressions, or other flattering manners; whether by giving gifts or by stroking the affections with alluring objects. When someone is lured toward evil through such paths, this enticement is not called mere persuasion, but a deception.

To understand the Prophet's meaning, one must know that God, being justly angered against His people, testifies to them that if they do not abandon their false gods, He will no longer give them an answer when they ask Him for counsel. And if it happens that a false prophet allows himself to be misled by those who come to him for advice—by their persuasions, caresses, promises, and gifts—and thus, being misled, makes a false prophecy, "it is I," says the Lord, "who have misled this prophet," not by breathing in the lies he spreads, but by not revealing my will to him and by giving him over to his passions, which cause him to have a blind devotion to those who ask him for counsel. I will act thus to punish the hypocrisy <note>original: "veinzerye"</note>, idolatry, and sins of my people; but afterward, I will punish both the one who asks for counsel and the one who gives it.

This observation serves to explain another passage from Jeremiah Chapter IV. 10, where the Prophet speaks thus to God: "Ah, Lord God! surely you have greatly deceived this people and Jerusalem, saying, 'You shall have peace,'"
<margin>Jer. IV. 10.</margin>
"whereas the sword reaches even to the soul."

There it is said that God had deceived the people because, through a righteous judgment upon the Jews, He had permitted them to be misled by false prophets, who promised them great prosperity in His name even though the ultimate disasters were hanging over their heads. Others are of the

<column-break/>

opinion that these words can be explained as a question, as if the Prophet said, *is it indeed possible that you have permitted this people to be misled by false prophets, and that you have given such great power to lies?*
<margin>Ps. CV. 25.</margin>
One might object using Psalm CV. 25, where it is said that God turned the heart of the Egyptians so that they hated His people.

The answer is: that is to say, instead of God previously inclining the heart of the Egyptians to their benefit by restraining their impulses, He had now ceased to work upon their minds, so that being left to themselves, they obeyed only their envy and greed, which set them against the Israelites.
<margin>Jud. IX. 23.</margin>
One must explain Judges IX. 23, 24 in almost the same way, where mention is made of an evil spirit that God sent between Abimelech and the citizens of Shechem. This means nothing other than that God permitted discord to arise between those of Shechem and Abimelech, so that they no longer wished to keep the treaty they had made with Abimelech. God, who wished to punish them both, had allowed thoughts to arise in them that made them mistrust one another, which was enough to divide them.
<margin>1 Kings XII. 15.</margin>
One might object using 1 Kings XII. 15, where everything that transpired between Jeroboam and the people is attributed to God.

The answer: This only means that this entire proceeding was directed by providence, which thus carried out what He had said to Jeroboam through Ahijah.

In the Book of Samuel, Chapter II. 25, there is a passage that causes some difficulty. There it is testified of the sons of Eli that they did not listen to the voices of their father, "for the Lord would slay them."
<margin>1 Sam. II. 25.</margin>
Some translate it as, "*Therefore* God wished to slay them," and thus there would be no difficulty; but nothing prevents us from following the common translation and taking the words to mean that the sons of Eli did not obey their father because they were corrupt children, whom God, through a righteous judgment, had given over to their perverse mind, and whom He intended to slay for the sins that had made them unworthy of His grace.
<margin>1 Sam. XVIII. 10. 11.</margin>
One might object using 1 Samuel XVIII. 10, 11, where it is said that an evil spirit from God came upon Saul, which made him cast his spear against David.

The answer: This evil spirit was a disease and a sort of insanity <note>The author interprets Saul's "evil spirit" as a psychological or medical condition rather than a literal demon</note>, which...

# THEOLOGY. VII. Book VI. Chapter.

...that is, to mislead, and that he brings a command, <note>original: "zou ik de Heere dien Profeet verleid hebben?" – this refers to Ezekiel 14:9</note> *should I the Lord have deceived that Prophet?* On the contrary, I will stretch out my hand against him. But one cannot accept this explanation if one looks at the original text.

There are those who believe that the Lord declares here that he will punish the false Prophet for his deceit and deprive him of his senses; but this interpretation does not agree with the root words. That which has been translated as *persuaded* actually means to draw or allure to oneself, whether to good or evil, or to indifferent deeds; whether by gentle ways, by persuasive expressions, or other flattering manners; whether by giving gifts or by stroking the inclinations with alluring objects. To understand the meaning of the Prophet, one must know that God, being justly angered against his people, testifies to them that if they do not abandon their false Gods, he will no longer give them an answer when they ask him for counsel. <margin>1 Sam. II. 25.</margin>
In the 1st Book of Samuel, Chapter II, verse 25, there is a passage that causes some difficulty. There it is testified of the sons of Eli that *they did not hear the voices of their Father, because the Lord wanted to kill them.*

Some translate this as, *Therefore God wanted to kill them*, so there would be no difficulty; but nothing prevents us from following the common translation and taking the words to mean that the sons of Eli did not obey their father because they were corrupt children whom God, through a righteous judgment, had given over to their perverse mind, and whom he intended to kill for the sins that had made them unworthy of his grace.

Answer. This evil spirit was a sickness and a type of insanity <note>The author interprets Saul's "evil spirit" not as a literal demon, but as a psychological or physical ailment—likely what we would call clinical melancholy or mania today.</note> which

> Nathan spoke thus to David. 2 Samuel 12:11, 12. Thus says the Lord: behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house, and I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor <note>In this context, the "neighbor" refers to David’s own son, Absalom.</note>; he shall lie with your wives in the sight of this sun; for you did it in secret, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the Sun.

Who can judge otherwise than that God is the cause of Sin? But that is far from the truth. One must distinguish between what God intended to do and what Absalom was to carry out.

God says that He will give David’s wives into the hands of his neighbor, but He testifies at the same time that Absalom would commit an act of incest <note>original: "bloedschande"</note>, to which he was driven by the counsel of Ahithophel. One must not be surprised that everything is attributed to God. God wished to punish David for his adultery.

To that end, He willed that the dignity of the crown should fall into Absalom’s hands and deprive David of it for a time; it is for this reason that everything this dehumanized son—clothed in royal authority—attempted, and everything God permitted him to undertake to punish David, is attributed to God.

In the same sense, someone who has provided the occasion for something to be done is said to have done it themselves. This is how God attributes the persecutions of the Church to Himself—not because He incites men to persecute the Church, but because, intending to chastise His children or to test their faith and patience, He allows bloodthirsty and godless men to rule, who unfortunately abuse their authority and power to persecute God’s children. It was, then, God who gave David’s wives over to Absalom by a righteous judgment, in order to punish a king who had stolen another man’s wife. God’s act was holy and righteous; but Absalom’s heart being corrupt, he abused his father’s wives through a shameful incest; his conduct was detestable. God did not breathe this crime into him, but He permitted it to be committed. One might say: but surely God knew that by handing these wives over to Absalom, this immoral son would abuse them? I admit this; but God did not drive Absalom to commit this sin; rather, Absalom’s own lust seduced him, and it was Ahitho-

<column-break/>

phel who stirred it up. God had reason to punish David, but He was not bound to prevent Absalom’s sin.

<margin>
2 Sam.
16:10,
12
</margin>
Another passage is raised as an objection, which seems to present more difficulty. 2 Samuel 16:10, 12, David says of Shimei: *let him curse; for the Lord has said to him, curse David.*

It is clear that one must not take these words literally. What likelihood is there that David believed that God—who so strictly forbids in His law the cursing of the princes of His people—would have given a command to Shimei to curse the king? If David had believed it, would he have viewed what Shimei did as a sin? One would much rather have to praise him for obeying God’s command, just as one praises Abraham, who fulfilled the command God gave him to offer up his son. But far from David approving the act of this rebellious subject, he instead charged his son Solomon on his deathbed to punish him for it.

What then does David mean by this expression? To understand it well, one must take into account:

1. That Shimei was a malicious man.
2. That he was a secret enemy of David, for he was of the house of Saul and could not endure that David had succeeded Saul; but he hid his hatred, fearing David’s power.
3. That God caused him to encounter David—whom he hated and feared—in a state where he could heap insults upon him without punishment, because David was stripped of the authority and power of which Shimei had been afraid.
4. That God, who could certainly have prevented this bold courtier from insulting his King, did not wish to prevent it because He had resolved to humble David; therefore He gave free rein to this mad dog. This is what David recognizes; he views this action of Providence—which exposed him to Shimei’s encounter and rage—as if it were a command from God Himself. "It is God who wishes to humble me thus: I must worship His providence, which punishes me through one of my subjects, and has therefore given him over to the disorder of his own heart." This led Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393 – c. 458 AD), an influential theologian and bishop of the early Christian church.</note> to say that David regarded God as the one who chastened him, and Shimei as the rod by which he felt the blow. The holy Prophet, he adds, must not

# THEOLOGY. VII. B. VI. Chapter.

<margin>2 Sam. 24:1</margin> I move now to another passage, found in 2 Samuel 24:1, where it is said that the anger of the Lord was again kindled against Israel, and that he incited David against them, saying, "Go, number Israel and Judah." Thus reads the original text. But when one reads 1 Chronicles 21, where it clearly states that Satan stood up against Israel and incited David to number Israel, one sees clearly that when it is said there that God incited David, etc., it signifies that through His righteous judgment and through the hidden ways of His providence, He had permitted Satan to lead David into this sin, in order to punish Israel and to humble David, who was puffed up by pride at seeing so many people subject to his scepter. There are some interpreters who explain this passage thus: "The anger of the Lord kindled against Israel, so that David was set against them to say, go, number Israel." In that way, there would be no difficulty, for it would only mean that David was driven to the numbering of the people by his own ambition <note>original: "staatzugt"</note>, or by Satan.

Similar manners of speaking are found elsewhere in Matthew 1:23, 5:15, 7:16, 9:17; Luke 6:38, 11:22, 12:11, 20, 48; 14:35, 16:4, 9, 21:16; John 12:40, 15:6; Revelation 16:15.

One encounters an even more difficult passage in 1 Kings 22:19–23, where the Prophet Micaiah speaks thus to Jehoshaphat and Ahab: "I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing beside him on his right hand and on his left. And the Lord said, 'Who will entice Ahab, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?' And one said one thing, and another said another. Then a spirit came forward and stood before the Lord, saying, 'I will entice him.' And the Lord said to him, 'By what means?' And he said, 'I will go out, and will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.' And he said, 'You are to entice him, and you shall succeed; go out and do so.' Now therefore behold, the Lord has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these your prophets; the Lord has spoken evil concerning you."

One has only to read this passage to see that it must not be taken

<column-break/>

literally; for, if it were to be interpreted that way, one would have to say that God needs to take counsel, and that He is uncertain about what He ought to do.

It is clear that Micaiah means nothing other than that God, righteously angered against Ahab, permitted a spirit of error to mislead him and to incite him to a war that would be fatal for him. Indeed, the justice and the wisdom of God—who can neither deceive nor be deceived—nevertheless allows a spirit of error to exercise its power upon men who close their eyes and ears, like this godless king, so as not to see or hear the truth.

But, it is said, the Scripture says that God commanded the Devil to act so. It is true: but Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–458 AD) was an influential theologian and bishop in the early Christian church.</note> rightly observes that this is done to teach us that Satan, with all the will he has to deceive men, can mislead no one unless God permits it. This always implies a righteous judgment that punishes those who are willfully blind.

For since they do not wish to hear God when He exhorts them to their duty, they deserve to be given over to their own darkness and to that of the lying spirit.

<margin>Job 12:16</margin> Some object with Job 12:16: "With him are strength and wisdom; the deceived and the deceiver are his."

These words prove nothing else than that all things are under God’s governance; that if someone errs, or makes another err, such happens with God’s permission; that nothing occurs against His will; and that both the one who misleads and the one who is misled depend absolutely on God.

<margin>Prov. 16:4</margin> Some object with Proverbs 16:4: "The Lord has made all things for himself, or so that they correspond to one another; even the wicked for the day of evil." But Solomon does not mean to say that God is the cause of evil, or that He created man wicked. He made man, who corrupted himself, and He ordains everything toward the righteous punishment which he has deserved.

Some object with Psalm 119:36 and 141:4: "Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to greed; Incline not my heart to any evil thing."

Who does not see that it is as if the Prophet said: "Lord, do not abandon me to my [own heart]..."

# THE CHRISTIAN

passions that would incite me to filthy lucre <term>filthy lucre: shameful or ill-gotten financial gain</term> or other sin.

<margin>Revelation XVII. 13.</margin>
One objects with *Revelation XVII: 13*, where it is said that God put it into the hearts of the Kings to give their kingdom to the beast.

This does not mean that God breathed this intention into them. But rather: 1. That He permitted the Kings, captivated by the splendor of the Beast, to subject themselves to it. 2. That He gave them over to their own passions. 3. That He was able to raise in them such thoughts which, though indifferent <note>meaning neutral or non-moral in themselves</note> in their own nature, provided the occasion by chance for other evil thoughts, which led them to the subjection of their Kingdoms to the Beast.

<margin>Isaiah LXIII. 17.</margin>
One objects with *Isaiah LXIII. 17*, where the Jewish people speak thus to God: *Lord, why do you make us wander from your ways, why do you harden our hearts so that we do not fear you?*

One could say that it is the distress in which the people found themselves that makes them speak this way, and that consequently one should not pay it much heed. But beyond that, it is easy to understand that the people do not wish to accuse God of making them go astray, but that it is a kind of humble question or confession in the form of a question: why have you, Lord, permitted us to wander from your ways? Why have you given us over to our passions? Why have you not made our hardened hearts soft? Why have you not restrained our flesh, which rose up against you? It is true that we have made ourselves unworthy of your grace; but, Lord, return, etc. etc.

<margin>Romans I. 24.</margin>
One objects with *Romans I: 24*: *Therefore God also gave them over in the lusts of their hearts to impurity, to dishonor their bodies among themselves.*

One cannot conclude from this that God is the cause of the sins committed among the Heathen. Paul only wishes to teach us that God, justly angered against the Heathen for their sins, gave them over to themselves. It is true that terrible outrages followed upon this "giving over," but the sole cause of the same is the corruption of the Heathen. The abandonment by God is only the cause by chance, and only insofar as the corrupt-

<column-break/>

ion of man, being no longer held back by any bridle, brings forth all kinds of evil deeds; just like water, when held by nothing, has its free course over the land. God had still preserved some seeds of righteousness among them, but regarding the impurities of the flesh, He had loosened the reins on all their lusts.

Lastly, one objects with *2 Thessalonians II: 11. For this reason God will send them a strong delusion, that they should believe the lie.*

<margin>2 Thessalonians II. 11.</margin>
Everyone sees that Paul wants to teach us here how God acts toward those who reject and abandon the truth, which had been confirmed to them by miracles.

1. God permits a false doctrine to be preached to them, which flatters their desires, and permits it to be confirmed by false miracles. 2. He permits the reasons used to make the lie acceptable to lead them entirely away from the truth. 3. He does not give them His grace, by which they would recover from their errors. 4. He leaves them to themselves and gives them over to their perverse mind; so that, being thus given over to their passions, they believe the lies and the errors that they are taught.

I cannot refrain from noting here that all our churches and Church-Teachers have unanimously acknowledged that God is not the cause of sin. It is true that some have used certain harsh expressions, but it is necessary to note regarding them:

<margin>Zwingli, *On the Providence of God*, ch. 6, p. 366. Calvin, *Institutes*, book 1, ch. 18, § 1; ch. 18, § 4; ch. 6, § 5. In the Notes.</margin>

### CHAPTER VII.

->On the misuse that various people make of the Doctrine of Providence, and on the good use that one must make of it.<-

<margin>
Ezek.
XVIII.
29.
XXXIII.
20.
</margin>
There are many people who misuse the doctrine of Providence, such as:
1. Those who murmur against God and accuse Him of injustice, or complain about Him as if He were unjust, when He gives the wicked an abundance of goods and leaves the good in poverty. Ezekiel speaks of certain godless people of his time who dared to say, *The way of the Lord is not right* (Ezekiel 18:29). Scripture even makes mention of believers who, in their adversities, let some complaints escape them, such as Job, Asaph, etc.

<margin>
Job. XXI.
7. 8. Ps.
LXXIII.
2. 3.
Jer. XII.
1,
</margin>
2. Those who wish to excuse their sins by saying that they could not have done otherwise, and that God willed it so.
3. Those who remain in a punishable idleness and deep anxiety, despising the means that Providence gives them to work out their salvation.
4. Those who recklessly expose themselves to dangers without being called to do so and without necessity, imagining that God will always perform miracles for them.
5. Those who fall into despair in their adversities, as if there were no longer any way

<column-break/>

out, and who take their own lives in that state.
6. Those who are in constant worry regarding what will happen to them, saying: *What shall we eat, what shall we drink, wherewithal shall we be clothed?* (Matthew 6:25).
7. Finally, those who bind themselves too much to <term>secondary causes: the physical or human means through which God works, rather than God Himself</term>, and who trust more in the arm of the flesh than in God.

True believers make a good use of the doctrine of Providence.
1. They worship God as the dispenser of all things, who governs the whole Universe through His wisdom and power; who holds infinite treasures of goods in His hand; who exalts some and humbles others; who creates light and darkness, peace and war, prosperity and adversity; from whose mouth good and evil proceed.
2. They fear Him as one who can arm all creatures against them and do with them according to His pleasure.
3. They take refuge in Him in all their needs, as He who ordains everything, and they thank Him for all good outcomes, without <note>original: "hunne netten te wierooken"</note> "burning incense to their own nets" <note>a biblical metaphor meaning to take credit for one's own success instead of thanking God</note> or attributing anything to their own prudence, conduct, and power.
4. They possess their souls with patience in their misfortunes and say with the Prophet (Psalm 39:9): *I will not open my mouth: for you have done it,* etc.
5. They cast all their worries upon God because He cares for them; knowing that He who feeds the birds of the air, clothes the lilies of the field, makes manna rain from Heaven to feed His people in the Wilderness, and who makes water flow from a dry rock for them to drink, can fulfill all their needs.
6. They are full of confidence in the midst of their cruelest enemies, being assured that not a hair of their heads will fall without His will; that God inclines and bends the hearts of men as it pleases Him. That He reconciles their enemies when their ways are right; that there is nothing that can separate God's children from His love; that He sets limits to the passion of the wicked, just as to the Sea, saying: *Thus far, and no further, shall the turbulence of your waves go.*

<margin>
Job XIII.
15.
</margin>
7. They place their entire trust in God and say with Job, *Even if He were to kill me.*

## CHAPTER ONE.

->Concerning the counsel-decree that God has taken to make men in general blessed, and whether it is necessary to explain the Doctrine of Predestination.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'W' featuring a foliate and scrollwork pattern in a square woodcut frame.</image-desc>

We have spoken in the preced-
ing Books of the fall of man / of
sin / of the various sorts
of sins / of the manner / 
how God allows the same / 
and lastly / what they are wor-

It seems that one should conclude from this / that all men / who have sinned / shall be lost eternally; but the scripture does not indicate that we make such a determination. It teaches us / that God has not willed / that all the children of Adam should be lost / as they are worthy / and that he from all eternity has decided to make some blessed <note>The author uses "zalig," which implies both salvation and a state of eternal happiness.</note> / leaving the rest in their corruption. This we shall hereafter prove through various explicit passages.

It must appear strange to no one / that God has taken decrees regarding the salvation of men / since we have proven in other places that nothing happens in the world / that God has not previously decreed to do or to permit / and that nothing happens against his will / or without it being known to him.

One asks, whether it is necessary / that one treats these matters / and explains the same to the people?

<column-break/>

In the time of <term>Augustine</term> <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), whose writings on grace and election were central to Reformed theology.</note> there were some / who did not find it good / that this Church Father had treated this matter / and in the present day one still finds those / who are of the same opinion. But this is without ground. There is no reason / that obliges us to not speak of this matter / which does not also oblige us to remain silent about the other mysteries: such as the mystery of the Trinity, of that of the <term>Incarnation</term> <note>The doctrine of God becoming human in the person of Jesus Christ.</note>, and of various others / which the ungodly <note>original: "Ongoddisten"; refers to those who live without regard for God or mock religious truths.</note> misuse.

The Apostles have spoken and written of this several times / although they well foresaw the evil use / that the godless would make of it through their objections. Why then should we not speak of it / as they have done?

Is it fair / that we pay more heed to the 
<margin>Luke 10:20.</margin>

<margin>2 Thess. 2:13.</margin>

Also the Lord Christ wills that his Disciples rejoice / not because the spirits were subject to them / but because their names are written in Heaven / and Paul wants the Thessalonians to thank the Lord / that he has called them from the beginning to salvation in the sanctification of the Spirit.

It is true / that in this mystery there are depths / that flesh and blood must not venture to fathom / but one must distinguish what God has wanted to reveal to us / and what he has hidden from us.

We must leave the secret things to God / and only reflect upon those which he has made known to us for our consolation.

9. They do not neglect the means that <term>Providence</term> <note>The protective care of God as a spiritual power.</note> offers them, but they do not place their trust in the flesh <note>The "flesh" here refers to human strength or worldly resources as opposed to spiritual reliance.</note>.

<column-break/>

10. They do not fear dangers when they are exposed to them, but they also do not enter into them without necessity.

11. Just as they know that <term>God</term> sees everything, they live always under His eyes.

13. Finally, they rest in the lap of <term>Providence</term>, and their motto is that of <term>Abraham</term>: The Lord will provide <note>original: "De Heere zal het voorzien." Refers to Genesis 22:8.</note>. <note>The numbering skips from 11 to 13 in the original text.</note>

# THE CHRISTIAN
# THEOLOGY,
## EIGHTH BOOK.
->Concerning what God has decreed regarding the Salvation of Man.<-

---

### FIRST CHAPTER.
->Concerning the decree of counsel that God has made to save men in general, and whether it is necessary to explain the Doctrine of Predestination.<-

<image-desc>Ornate decorative drop cap 'W' at the start of the first column, featuring foliage and scrollwork motifs.</image-desc> We have spoken in the preceding Books of the fall of man, of sin, of the various kinds of sins, of the manner in which God permits them, and finally, what they deserve: namely, an eternal death.

It seems that one should conclude from this that all men who have sinned shall perish eternally; but the Scripture does not allow us to make such a determination. It teaches us that God did not will that all the children of Adam should be lost, as they deserve, and that He has from all eternity decided to save some, leaving the others in their damnation. This we shall prove in the following sections through various explicit passages.

It should seem strange to no one that God has made decrees concerning the salvation of men, since we have proven in other places that nothing happens in the world that God has not previously decided to do or to permit, and that nothing happens against His will, or without it being known to Him.

One asks whether it is necessary to treat these matters and explain them to the people?

<column-break/>

In the time of **Augustine** <note>A 4th-century Church Father whose writings on grace and predestination became foundational for Western theology.</note>, there were some who did not approve of this Church Father treating this subject, and in the present day one still finds those who are of the same opinion. But this is without foundation. There is no reason that obliges us not to speak of this subject that would not also oblige us to remain silent about other mysteries: such as the mystery of the **Trinity**, of the **Incarnation**, and of various others which the Godless <note>original: "Ongoddisten," referring here to atheists or those who reject religious authority.</note> abuse.

The Apostles spoke and wrote of this several times, although they well foresaw the evil use that the wicked would make of it through their objections. Why then should we not speak of it, just as they have done?

<margin>Luke 10:20.</margin>
Is it right that we pay more attention to the unholy and to the free-thinkers <note>original: "vry-geesten," a term used in the 17th and 18th centuries for those who questioned orthodox religious doctrines.</note>, who trample all holy things underfoot, than to the believers, who draw comfort from this doctrine? <margin>2 Thess. 2:13.</margin> Also, the Lord Christ wants His disciples to rejoice—not because the spirits were subject to them, but because their names are written in Heaven; and Paul wants the **Thessalonians** to thank the Lord that He has called them from the beginning to salvation in sanctification of the Spirit.

It is true that in that mystery there are depths which flesh and blood <note>A biblical idiom for human nature or limited human understanding.</note> must not venture to sound; but one must distinguish what God has wished to reveal to us and what He has hidden from us.

We must leave the hidden things to God, and only contemplate those which He has made known to us for our comfort.

<header>THE CHRISTIAN [THEOLOGY]</header>

It is also true that one must use caution in presenting this mystery. This topic should not be taught to those who do not yet know the clearest truths of Christianity, and who have need of milk, and are not yet fit to bear solid food <note>This is a reference to 1 Corinthians 3:2 and Hebrews 5:12, where "milk" represents basic teachings and "solid food" represents complex spiritual mysteries.</note>. One must follow Paul, who, wishing to convert the Jews, first spoke to them of the forgiveness of sins promised to believers and of the resurrection of our Savior; one must follow Christ, who, to convert Nicodemus, contented himself with proposing that he who believes in Him shall not perish, but he who does not believe is already condemned. It is not necessary to entertain the common people with the various opinions of the learned on this subject. It is enough to teach them only what God says, and to that end, one must use the expressions of the Scriptures as much as possible.

It is not a doctrine that one should preach about frequently, but only on certain occasions: 1. for example, when the sequence of the books of Scripture that we are explaining obliges us to do so; 2. when one sees great strife arising in the Church between those who are considered the most zealous and holy; it is on such an occasion that most theologians believe Paul makes mention of this in the second letter to Timothy 2:19, where, having spoken of those who had turned away from the truth, he adds these words: *the foundation of God stands sure, God knows those who are His own.* 3. When we find believers who, in times of persecution, are fearful that they will not be able to withstand the strength of the temptations and that they will be eternally lost. One can comfort them through the explanation of this Article of faith. This, Paul does extensively in Romans 8.

When this doctrine is taught, it is necessary to show:

1. That God had the right to condemn us all to eternal pains.

2. That it is a work of infinite goodness that He did not will that all men should perish.

3. That we must not torment ourselves to know whether we are ordained to salvation from eternity or not; but that we must be convinced that if we have faith and love, we shall be saved; whereas, if we have neither faith

<column-break/>

nor love, we shall be condemned.

4. Finally, that those who are preordained to eternal salvation have no reason at all to exalt themselves above others, as if they had made themselves worthy of such a distinction; and those who are not have no reason to complain, since they have deserved nothing but death.

At the end of this book, we shall consider the use that can be drawn from this doctrine. Meanwhile, to say something more specific about the general decree that God has made regarding the salvation of men, it is necessary to make some observations and take heed:

1. That God has established, regarding all men individually, everything that must happen to them, whether they shall be saved or not; this foresight requires no proof.

2. That these decrees are eternal, as we shall prove in the following.

3. That when God made these decrees, He had already decided to create man and to permit his fall; He viewed all the children of Adam as fallen: for it would be absurd to decree the salvation of men whom one had not yet decided to create, and who would have no need of salvation.

Besides that, it seems to be against God's goodness to create men simply to damn them, and against His justice to condemn to eternal death those who have not yet sinned.

It is a matter much disputed among theologians—namely, how God viewed men when He ordained them to glory.

Those in the Roman Church who believe that predestination is that decree of God by which He established everything concerning men are of the opinion that God viewed them only as "possible" and "capable of being created," as held by *Alfonso Mendoza in "Questions on Predestination" <note>original Latin: "quæst. de Prædest."</note>, Estius in "Book of Sentences," Distinction 40, paragraph 6 <note>original Latin: "in l. Sentent. Dist. 40 parag. 6." Estius was a major Catholic commentator on Peter Lombard's "Sentences."</note>, Giacomo Nacchianti, Albert Pighius, Pietro Galatino, Lancelot Politi, and John Duns Scotus.* But the most common opinion is that when God ordained men to salvation, He viewed them as having fallen in Adam.

# THEOLOGY. VIII. B. I. Chapter.

Church, some have been of the opinion that God viewed humans as *creatable*, or at least as being *capable of falling into sin*. <note>This is the "Supralapsarian" view—the idea that God's decree of election occurred "above" or "before" the decree to allow the Fall of man.</note> This was the opinion of Zanchius, Beza, Piscator, Perkins, Ursinus, Gomarus, Polanus, Voetius, Twisse, etc. etc.
Others believe that God viewed humans as *having fallen in Adam*; this is the opinion of most of our theologians and that which most closely corresponds with the decrees of the Synod of Dordrecht. <note>This is the "Infralapsarian" view—the idea that God viewed humanity as a "corrupt mass" after the Fall when He chose whom to save. The Synod of Dordrecht (1618–1619) was the international gathering that standardized Dutch Reformed doctrine.</note> Others maintain that God viewed humans as *being called to the fellowship of Christ* through the preaching of the Gospel; this is the opinion of Georgius Sohnius, theologian of Heidelberg, of Testard, and of Amyraut. These believe that the first effect of election is the gift of faith. The Arminians <note>Followers of Jacobus Arminius; they argued that election was based on God's foreknowledge of an individual's future faith, rather than an absolute decree.</note> also hold that God viewed humans as *redeemed by Christ*, whether they be believers or unbelievers. Regarding the first view, I confess it seems much more natural to me to say that, when God preordained humans, He had already decided to create them and allow their fall (Salvation and damnation presuppose a being that exists, or is supposed to exist); now, before God decided to create humans, one cannot suppose they exist. Furthermore, if God had only considered humans as *coming to be created* when He decided to save or damn them, He could have established the salvation or destruction of an infinite number of people who were never created and will never be created, but who could have been created if God had willed it. Now there is no one who does not understand that it is unbefitting for a supreme wise being to make unnecessary decrees. Add to this that Salvation presupposes that one is lost; it is therefore necessary to posit that God regarded humans as *lost in Adam* when He decided to make them blessed. Scripture teaches us this when it says that believers are chosen in Christ, Ephesians 1:4: *Just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him in love.* If it is now necessary that we

<column-break/>

be redeemed, it follows that we are viewed as miserable and as lost. But, it is said, when Paul presents God under <margin>Romans 9:21</margin> the image of a Potter who makes from one *lump* a vessel for honor and a vessel for dishonor, does he not make us understand well that God did not view humans as having fallen in Adam when He preordained them? For, it is said, it comes down here to a lump that is not corrupt; but there one deceives oneself, for Paul speaks of a lump from which God makes vessels of wrath and of mercy; now, wrath and mercy presuppose misery and sins. He speaks of a lump from which those who are made from it can be hated, like Esau, and from which Pharaoh was brought forth. One will perhaps say that it appears that a *pure* lump is spoken of here, because a lump is discussed from which children came who had done neither good nor evil (verse 11). But it is clear that when it is said that these children had done no good or evil, it is only to teach us that Jacob had not yet done any good that could have obligated God to choose him over Esau, and that Esau had not yet done any evil that could have moved God to hate him rather than Jacob, and thus the election of Jacob depended solely on God's good pleasure. One will perhaps still say that Paul speaks here of a lump from which one makes vessels for dishonor. That is true, yet by *dishonor* one must not understand sin, but the *punishment* for sin. Vessels for dishonor are the creatures who are preordained to destruction; now, that punishment, as stated, presupposes sin and preceding corruption. One will furthermore say that here a lump is being discussed from which Adam was made: one is mistaken; a lump is spoken of from which God makes *vessels of wrath*. But, it is said, if a corrupt lump were seen here, there would be no more difficulty in this matter. One is mistaken; for one always has reason to ask: why does God choose one rather than the other? But, one will say at last, if this is so, then Adam and Eve will not have been preordained, since they were brought forth from a corrupt lump. <note>The author is posing a potential counter-argument here: if the "lump" is always the fallen human race, how could Adam and Eve, who were created perfect, fit into this decree?</note>

I deny this consequence: it is enough that God regarded Adam and Eve as having fallen into sin, which he had decided to allow, in order to subsequently establish that he would make them blessed <note>The Dutch word *zalig* refers to eternal salvation or being "saved" in a state of heavenly bliss.</note>.

## CHAPTER II.

->Regarding various expressions that the Scripture uses to show us the decree that God has made to save humanity, and regarding their election in particular.<-

The Scripture uses four specific manners of speaking to express the decree that God has taken to save humanity. It says that God **foreknew** us (Romans 8:29, Romans 11:2, 1 Peter 1:2); that he **predestined** <note>Dutch: *te voren verordineerd*</note> us (Ephesians 1:5); that he **chose** us (Ephesians 1:4). Finally, it speaks of the **purpose** of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will (Ephesians 1:11).

The word **Foreknowledge** does not only mean the infinite knowledge of God, by which all things are naked and exposed before him; for in the places where one finds this manner of speaking, it refers to a foreknowledge that concerns believers in particular, whereas the general knowledge of God extends over all creatures, both good and evil. Rather, this expression includes a *knowledge of love*, if I may speak so; and a knowledge that is accompanied by a decree in which God has established to give signs of his love to those whom he has thus known. It is called a foreknowledge to indicate the eternity of God's love, which preceded all ages. Let us here make two observations, which will not be in vain for a proper understanding of some passages of Scripture.

The first concerns the word **Foreknowledge**. Sometimes it is taken to mean both the love of God and his **Election** at the same time. Thus one must understand what Paul says in Romans 8:29: *those whom God foreknew*, that is to say, those whom God has loved from all eternity, before they had anything lovable in them, and

<column-break/>

whom he, by an act of his love, has separated from others in order to share his glory with them. Sometimes the word **Foreknowledge** includes nothing other than love; thus it is taken in 1 Peter 1:2, where the Apostle mentions those who are *elect according to the foreknowledge of God*.

<margin>2 Timothy 2:19.</margin>
The second observation is that the Scripture, which says that God has foreknown people from all eternity, also speaks of another knowledge that God has *in time*. *God knows those who are his*, says Paul in 2 Timothy 2:19; and this knowledge includes the love and the protection with which God favors his children as long as they are in the world. The Scripture even speaks further of a knowledge by which he will recognize us as his own on the Last Day, in contrast to the godless, to whom he shall say: *I do not know you.*

**Predestination** <note>Dutch: *Voorverordineering*</note> specifically includes the arrangement of the means that God has established to bring us to salvation. That is why Paul says that *God predestined us to be conformed to the image of his Son* (Romans 8:29) and that *he predestined us for adoption as children through Jesus Christ in himself, according to the good pleasure of his will* (Ephesians 1:5).

One must only note here that the phrase "to predestine" <note>Dutch: *te voren ordineeren*</note> is a general manner of speaking, which the Scripture also uses on other occasions, such as when it is said in Acts 4:28 that Herod and Pontius Pilate did *whatever your hand and your counsel predestined to occur*. From this it follows that the Church Fathers have used it to express predestination to eternal destruction <note>Often referred to as "reprobation" in theological texts.</note> as well as predestination to eternal salvation.

Thus **Augustine** <note>A 4th-century theologian central to Western Christian thought.</note> takes it in the 42nd and 48th treatises on *John*, in the second book of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, Chapter 18, and in the *Enchiridion* (Handbook) to Laurence, Chapter 100. Also in the book *On the Perfection of Righteousness*, and in the 15th book of *The City of God*, Chapter 1. **Prosper** <note>Prosper of Aquitaine, a disciple of Augustine.</note> uses it in the answer to the objections of the Gauls <note>original: "Gauloisen"</note>, 14th objection. **Fulgentius** <note>Fulgentius of Ruspe, a 6th-century North African bishop.</note> in the book to Monimus, to which one can also add the Church decrees...

<header>THEOLOGY. BOOK VIII. CHAPTER II.</header>

<warning>Left margin contains very faded and partially illegible citations.</warning>

<margin><unclear>Mendoza</unclear></margin>
...of Valence, Langres, and Toul, and the Church of Lyon, to say nothing of Gottschalk <note>Gottschalk of Orbais (c. 800–868) was a Carolingian theologian known for his early and controversial defense of double predestination.</note>.

<margin><unclear>VII. B.</unclear></margin>
<margin><unclear>XI. m.</unclear></margin>
<margin><unclear>T. 1. Cap.</unclear></margin>
<margin><unclear>XII. n.</unclear></margin>
Some scholars of the Roman Church take the word **Predestination** <note>Dutch: *Voorverordineering*</note> to refer only to the decree by which God established the giving of heavenly glory to certain people. Gabriel Biel, Occam (one may consult Gregory of Valence, Volume 1, Disputation 1, Question 23, Point 3), others for the decree that ordains the means to salvation (Becanus, *Summary of Theology*, Volume 1, Chapter 14, Question 2, Conclusion 1). Others take it for the eternal decree through which God has destined certain people for the supernatural enjoyment of salvation through supernatural means, such as Eustachius of Saint Paul, Petrus of Saint Joseph, Gregory of Valence, and Estius. Others, like Jansenius in *On the Grace of God the Savior* <note>Original: *de Grat. Dei Serv.*</note> Book IX, Chapter 3, understand by it the decree through which God has destined some to glory and others to destruction.

Others believe that **Predestination** is the first decree of God, and that all others followed upon it, even that of the creation of the world (Alphonse Mendoza in *Scholastic Questions on Predestination*, Section 6 <note>Original: *quæst. Sch. de prædest.*</note>). Those who hold this view place creation, the permission of sin, etc., among the effects of Predestination.

Regarding the Protestants: some take the word **Predestination** for the decree that destines one to salvation and the other to destruction, such as Zanchius, Beza, Ursinus, Perkins, Polanus, Bucanus, and the Synod of Dordrecht. Others take it for the decree that destines certain people to salvation and to the means that lead to salvation.

The word **will** or **firm purpose** indicates the certainty of the outcome—namely, that the things God has established will certainly happen. Paul uses it in this sense in Ephesians 1:11: *In him,* he says, *in whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will.*

Finally, the word **Election** indicates the choice that God has made of certain persons, to the exclusion of others; but one must take note that the word Election sometimes signifies the choice one makes of someone to be

<column-break/>

raised to a worldly or spiritual office, as in 1 Samuel 10:24, Luke 6:13, Acts 1:2, John 6:70, etc. Sometimes it signifies the choice God made of a certain people to enter into a covenant with them; it is in this sense that the people of Israel are called the "chosen people" (Deuteronomy 4:37, 7:7). Sometimes it refers to the separation that God makes in time, through his efficacious grace, of certain people whom he wishes to lead to glory and to whom he gives faith. In this place, we take it for the eternal decree of God, in the same way that Paul uses it in Ephesians 1:4, when he says that *God has chosen us in Christ before the foundation of the world.*

<margin>Alph. Mendoza, *Scholastic Questions on Predestination*, Section 2. Severus on 1 Peter 1:1.</margin>
In the Roman Church, some take the word **Election** for the decree through which God assigns glory to certain persons. Others understand it as the decree to give grace and glory. Among Protestants, the word Election is taken in the sense we have noted; however, there are some who understand it as the decree to efficaciously call certain people to Christ and to give them a living faith, such as Testard, Louis Cappel, and Moïse Amyraut <note>These theologians were associated with the Academy of Saumur and the "Amyraldian" view, which attempted to soften strict Calvinist predestination with a form of hypothetical universalism.</note>.

But by **Election**, we understand 그 eternal and unchangeable decree of God, through which he established out of pure grace, before the foundation of the ages, to draw some out of the miserable state into which he foresaw that the rebellion and the fall of Adam would cause the human race to collapse, and to provide them with salvation through his Son Jesus Christ, although they were no better nor more excellent than others whom he has left behind.

I. We say, then, that **Election** is an eternal decree; Paul teaches us this when he says that *God has chosen us before the foundation of the world* (Ephesians 1:4), and Christ says that *the Kingdom of Heaven was prepared for the blessed of his Father from before the foundation of the world* (Matthew 25:34).

It is said that Paul, in teaching that God chose us, means to say that he *decided* to choose us.

**Answer.** Besides there being no necessity to accept this interpretation, it would nonetheless always follow that the decree of Election is eternal.

III. We note / that Election is a decree / that God has made regarding certain people / so that one would not believe / that God from all eternity has done nothing else / than to decree in general that He will save the believers / and condemn the unbelievers / etc. : for if that were so / God from eternity would only have determined the qualities of those He wished to make blessed / and not have made it as a general law / whereas one / reading the Scripture / clearly

sees / that God has not only established certain conditions / under which He wished to make men blessed; but also marked those individuals in particular / whom He wished to save /

Those whom God foreknew, He also predestined, says Paul: and in another place he speaks of the vessels of wrath, which He prepared beforehand for damnation, and of the vessels of mercy, prepared for glory. 

<margin>Acts XIII. 48.</margin>
Luke says / that those who were predestined to eternal life, believed, from which it appears / that the number of those who will be saved / is known by God from all eternity / and that the same is certain and determined.

Therefore Scripture speaks of certain people / whose names are written in Heaven in the Book of Life. And of others / whose names are not written in the Lamb's Book of Life.

### IV.
We observe that **Election** concerns only a certain number of people whom God appoints to salvation, so that one does not believe that all people are chosen, as Samuel Huberus <note>Samuel Huberus (1547–1624) was a Swiss Lutheran theologian who controversially argued for "universal election," the idea that God had chosen all of humanity for salvation, though many reject it.</note> believed. The word **Election** [Choosing] itself shows that all people cannot have a part in it: for whoever says "an election" implies that others are passed by. Scripture confirms this truth.

Various passages, which I have already cited, do not allow for doubt on this matter; but one can add several others to them. Just as nothing happens in time that God has not established from eternity, so one can conclude that God has not chosen all people and had no intention to save them all from the fact that Scripture says that God shows mercy to one and that he hardens the other <note>A reference to Romans 9:18: "Therefore God has mercy on whom he wants to have mercy, and he hardens whom he wants to harden."</note>; that he reveals his mysteries to children and hides the same from the wise, etc <note>A reference to Matthew 11:25.</note>. Reason itself teaches us that since God will not grant salvation to everyone, this is proof that he had not pre-destined the same for them all; because if he had destined it for them, he would undoubtedly give it to them. He would also not fail to provide them all with the means to reach it; indeed, one cannot conceive that God, who has all means in his hand, would have decided from all eternity to give salvation to all, on the condition of faith, and yet in the meantime he does not let his word be preached to all, and that he does not give faith to all: for he who sincerely desires the ends must also desire the means leading to them.

It is said that he who desires the ends absolutely, and without any condition, must also desire the means that can bring him to it; but that it is not the same with him who desires the ends only under certain conditions, as it is assumed that God desires the salvation of men.

Answer. This assumes what is in dispute, namely, that there are conditional decrees in God. Besides that, when one desires an end with a serious will, one must also seriously desire the means that lead to it.

It is said that he who desires the end also wants the means, but that in order to

<column-break/>

desire the means, one does not always have to want those to whom they are offered to actually use them; that it can coexist with wanting to offer them in such a way that those to whom they are offered can use them if they desire it; just as it cannot be denied that a Father desires nothing else but that his children live well, since he offers them the means to that through his admonitions and promises, although he cannot make them actually use the means that he proposes to them.

Answer. This does not weaken our proof, for he who sincerely desires the end must also, as much as is in him, desire all the means necessary to arrive there; he must not only offer them, but he must produce them, if it is in his power, as one cannot doubt that such depends on God's power; whereas, on the contrary, it does not depend on a Father to produce good inclinations in the heart of his children.

This truth seems to conflict with some passages of Scripture, but it is very easy to explain them.

Lutherans.

1. When Christ, in John III. 16, speaking to Nicodemus, says:
> For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life,

it is to teach us these three truths. 1. That God, who could justly have let the entire human race perish and condemned them to eternal pains, like the fallen Angels, nevertheless loved them so much that he did not want to deal with them so severely. 2. That he, being able to save no one unless his justice was satisfied, sent his Son into the world for that purpose. 3. And that the means to have a share in salvation is faith. But one cannot conclude from this that God would have had the intention to save all people in particular. One can clarify this with a parable. Suppose two Cities that are rebellious against their Sovereign; that subsequently the angry Prince has decided to entirely raze and destroy one of these Cities; yet not to deal thus with the other. ### DIVINITY. VIII. B. III. Chapter.

...of one rather / than of the other / to fulfill his promises to them / without anyone having reason to pride themselves / or to complain / that God shows this mercy to some / and hardens others / because he so desires. The proof / that we draw from this Chapter <note>Referring to Romans 9.</note> / is therefore of great emphasis.

One will say, that it does not speak of eternal Election, but of an election / which happens in time / through which God converts some and passes others by.

But **I.** One cannot deny / that there are verses in this Chapter / that mention Election and Reprobation / as in particular / vs. 22. and 23.

**2.** Even if one granted / that here it is not seen as the election / which happens in time / the proof would be no less powerful / for / if it is a truth / that God distributes his gifts in time / and converts people / although they have nothing in themselves / that can oblige him to do so / it is an even greater truth / that God has decreed from eternity to give his grace / without foreseen works. If temporal election does not presuppose the foresight of faith and of works / then eternal election presupposes the same much less.

<margin>Rom. VIII. 30.</margin>
**III.** A third proof will set this truth in greater light. The Scripture teaches us / that faith and obedience are the effects of election. Paul says / that those / whom he <term>predestined: or "foreordained" (original: te voren verordineert)</term> / he also called, Rom. VIII. 30. Now it is through the calling / that God produces faith in us / and enables us to do good works; consequently it is not true / that predestination presupposes the foresight of faith and of works.

<margin>Limb. Theol. L. VI. c. 3.</margin> <note>Likely a reference to Philippus van Limborch’s "Theologia Christiana," a major Arminian/Remonstrant work.</note>
One will say, that here is spoken of a calling to the cross and affliction / through which one is made conformable to Christ.

I answer, that it is true / that we are predestined to be conformed to the image of Christ in afflictions / as well as in holiness and glory. But it is not true / that here it is only dealt with the calling / to carry Christ's Cross: for the Apostle speaks of the calling to faith and sanctification / (which was mentioned in the preceding verse)

<column-break/>

and to the glory / of which he speaks in verse 17. <margin>Rom. VIII. 28.</margin> In the 28th verse he had said / that all things turn for the best for those who love God / and these he had described as those / who have been called by an <term>effectual calling: a calling that successfully brings a person to faith (original: kragtadige roeping)</term> according to the decree of election. Now he gives here the reason / why everything turns out for their good / which is because / he says / because those / whom God from all eternity has chosen / to give them to his Son / to make them conformable / and to place them in the possession of an eternal glory / must undoubtedly be blessed. God calls and justifies them; he makes them persevere in the faith; he brings them at last to salvation. It depends here on a calling / that goes before justification / and is inseparable from justification. It is therefore a calling to faith / through which we are justified. Finally, the Apostle looks to a calling / which is an immediate effect of Election, which cannot be said of the calling to the cross alone.

<margin>Eph. I. 3, 4.</margin>
Paul speaks in Eph. I. 3, 4. of Election / as of the origin of all spiritual blessings. *Who has blessed us with all spiritual blessings in the heavens in Christ, even as he has chosen us in him*, etc. Now the first of these spiritual blessings is faith. Election is then the origin of faith, and consequently God has not chosen man / because he foresaw that he would believe / but he gives faith to those he has chosen.

Paul says something more / he has chosen us, he adds to that / so that we should be holy and blameless before him in love. He has then chosen us / not because we were holy / nor because he foresaw that we would be / or that we would have a disposition to become so / but so that we should be.

One says, that here it is dealt with the decree of Election / that must manifest itself in time. But / how can one say that here is not spoken of an eternal Election, since it says / that the same was made before the foundation of the world. Certainly one cannot deny / that here it is seen as an eternal decree / before which God has established / to communicate all kinds of spiritual blessings to certain people /

...them / and subsequently to give them his glory. And this is the decree / that we call Election, Predestination, etc.

It is said, that Paul does not look at election to glory, but to grace.

Answer, 1. From that it would then follow / that election to grace does not presuppose the <term>foresight of faith: the idea that God chooses people because he sees in advance that they will believe (original: voorbeschouwing van het geloof)</term>.
2. Who does not know / that all / whom God has chosen for grace / are at the same time chosen for glory / and that / if one supposes / that there was something between these two Elections / (which we do not believe) one would have to say / that God chose his own for glory sooner than for grace / since one looks at the end / before one thinks of the means.

<margin>Acts XIII. 48.</margin>
To those places one must add / *Acts XIII. 48.* And there believed as many as were ordained to eternal life. Luke does not say / that those believed / or those whom one had foreseen would believe / were previously ordained to Life : but that / those who were previously ordained to it / believed. Faith follows / but does not go before.

<margin>Volkel <note>Johannes Volkel (c. 1565–1618), a leading Socinian theologian who argued against traditional views of predestination.</note> L. V. c. 17. p. 523. Remon. <note>The Remonstrants, or Arminians, who opposed the strict Calvinist doctrine of unconditional election.</note></margin>
It is said, that it does not say / those who were *previously* ordained, but simply those who *were* ordained.
I answer, that this is mere hair-splitting / and that it comes to the same thing / as can be concluded from the phrasing / that Luke uses / which is similar to that used in the same sense / *Rom. IX, 23.*

It is said, That it is not said / that those who were ordained *by God* / believed / but simply those who were ordained.
I answer, that one cannot understand it otherwise : for either they had ordained themselves / which is a pure <term>Pelagian thesis: the belief that humans can take the first step toward salvation without divine grace (original: Pelagiaansche stelling)</term> ; or they were ordained by God.

<margin>Volk: Rem.</margin>
It is said, that by this one must understand those / who were *ready* for eternal life / or who had prepared themselves / through the help of the grace / which they had received / in contrast to the Jews / spoken of in verse 46.
I answer, that this expression is never taken in that sense. Besides that / one cannot say / that one is ready for eternal life / before

<column-break/>

one has faith. One can consult *Rom: XIII, 1, Acts XV. 2. and XXVIII. 23.*

IV. If Election presupposes the foresight of faith / then God foresees faith in those whom he chooses / either as a disposition / that proceeds from them / or as a work of his grace.
<margin>Eph. II. 8.</margin>
One cannot say / that God foresees faith in those whom he chooses / as a matter that depends on them ; for the Scripture says very explicitly / that faith is a gift of God. If he foresaw it as one of his gifts / and as a work of his grace / one must suppose / that he has made a decree / through which he intended to give faith.
This is the decree / that we call Election. Election then does not presuppose the foresight of faith. One can make no substantial objection against this truth.

<margin>Limb. <note>Philippus van Limborch (1633–1712), a prominent Remonstrant theologian.</note> I. C.</margin>
It is said, that the Scripture explicitly teaches / that he who believes / shall be saved / and that he who does not believe / shall be damned / *Mark XVI. 16. John III. 36-16, VI. 40, VIII. 24. Rom. X. 9.*
I answer, that indeed no one shall be saved without faith. I speak of Adults, yet it does not follow from this / that God did not previously designate certain persons for salvation / until after he had foreseen / that they would believe. The only conclusion / that one must draw from this / is / that God having previously designated salvation for some / he also at the same time established to give them faith. All the places / that are brought forward / prove the necessity of faith to be saved / but they do not prove / that the foresight of faith precedes election.

It is said, that / since faith must go before salvation / the same must also go before election / because God makes men saved / just as he had decreed to make them saved.
I answer, that it is true / that God in time makes men saved / in the same way as he has decreed from all eternity to make them saved / and that consequently / just as he in time only makes saved those who believe / so he has also decreed to save no one / except those who shall believe : but from this it follows in no way / that faith is the cause of the pre-destination to salvation. It is the medicine / that a Physician makes a sick person take / which makes the sick person healthy / but it is not the motive / that prompted the Physician / to undertake the healing of the sick person.

3. It is said, *Heb. XI. 6.* For without faith it is impossible to please God, and that God consequently could only have chosen those / in whom he foresaw faith.

I answer, That this passage proves nothing else / than that God can take no pleasure in a creature / that has no faith: but that it does not follow from this / that God cannot love his creature as his creature before it believes; and that this is enough / to understand / that he can ordain it beforehand to salvation. This passage indeed proves / that God cannot give salvation / except to those who believe / but it does not prove / that he cannot destine it to them.

<margin>Rom. VIII. 29.</margin>
4. It is said, that Paul calls election a <term>foreknowledge: the divine knowledge of things before they exist (original: voorkennis)</term> / from which it then consequently appears / that God foresaw something in those whom he has chosen.

<margin>Ps. I. 6. 2. Tim. II. 19.</margin>
I answer, That this foreknowledge indicates nothing else than a knowledge of love / according to the style of the Scripture / which makes use of the word *to know* in the same sense / and that it is as much / as if Paul had said / those whom he loved beforehand, and chose through an act of his love. What is it that God could have foreseen in his Creatures / except what he himself has given them / and that therefore his election follows / which is the source of all saving grace.

<margin>Rom. VIII. 29.</margin>
5. It is said, that God ordained beforehand those who were conformed to the image of his Son, and that the passage of *Rom. VIII. 29.* reads thus.

I answer, that it clearly appears / that one must not translate it so / because we cannot be conformed to the image of Christ / except through the Calling. Now the Calling follows the Pre-ordination. God then ordained beforehand those / whom he foreknew / not because they were conformed to Jesus Christ / but so that they should become so.

6. A passage is cited from James, in which it is said / that God has chosen the poor of this world, (to be) rich (in) faith, and heirs of the Kingdom, *James II. 5.*

But one has only to read the Text / to see / that one can demonstrate nothing there to those / to whom he writes / that they should not despise the poor / and that / however despicable they seemed to them / they nevertheless should have respect for them / 1. Because God had chosen several of them / to give them Heaven. 2. Because / however poor they were in the eyes of the world / they were nonetheless rich in faith. 3. Because they / although they were excluded from earthly inheritances / would nonetheless be heirs of the Kingdom of God. One cannot then say / that God has chosen the poor / because he foresaw / that they would be rich in faith; for then one would also have to say / that he chose them / and prepared salvation for them / because he foresaw that they would be heirs of his Kingdom: but one must say / that God / who has chosen many poor / makes the same rich in faith / and that he will make them heirs of his Kingdom.

It is said, that / if this is the meaning of the words of James / God is a <term>respecter of persons: one who shows favoritism based on external status (original: aannemer des persoons)</term>. But those who reason thus / indicate / that they do not understand what the Scripture intends to say / when it teaches us / that with God there is no respecting of persons / as we shall show elsewhere.

7. It is said, that / since Rejection, which we shall speak of hereafter / must presuppose sin; Election consequently also presupposes faith.

I answer, that there is a very great difference between these two matters / that <term>Rejection: or reprobation, the divine decree to bypass or punish the non-elect (original: Verwerping)</term> is an act of justice / which must presuppose sin; but that Election is an act of mercy / which presupposes nothing but the misery of man / and no good aptitude.

Paul wants to say nothing else / than that a man / who applies himself to cleanse himself from the stains of sin / will indeed be a sanctified vessel / and show that he is a <term>chosen vessel: a person selected by God for a specific holy purpose (original: verkooren vat)</term> / previously suited for glory / in the same sense / as Christ said / love your enemies, so that <margin>Matt. But one is very much mistaken / for / when we say that God has chosen us according to his good pleasure / without having foreseen any quality in us, we add to that / that God will not give salvation / except to the believers / and only to those who will strive to work out their salvation.

10. It is said, that through this the prayers are made useless; for why / it is said, should one prevail upon God through prayers / if it is a truth / that he has established from all eternity all that must happen.

I answer, that God / who has taught us / that he has chosen us before the foundation of the ages / demands from us the <term>obligation: a binding duty or debt (original: schuldigpligtigheid)</term> of our prayers / and that we cannot excuse ourselves from them / without showing him [disrespect]. This we shall examine more closely / when we shall treat of Prayer.

11. It is said, that this doctrine strives against the Gospel; for the Gospel / it is said, commands us to have repentance / whereas this doctrine supposes / that God wants to save men / without having foreseen their repentance / and that he produces this repentance in them.

I answer, 1. That / although the decree of <term>Election: God's sovereign choice of who will be saved (original: Verkiezing)</term> does not follow the foresight of repentance / God has nevertheless decreed to give salvation only to the penitent. 2. That penitence is at once a duty of man / and a gift of God.

12. It is said, that this doctrine strives with what the Scripture teaches us of eternal life / which it portrays to us as the inheritance of God’s children / the reward of their obedience / and the crown of those who shall have fought well / etc.

Answer. One does not notice that we say

<column-break/>

/ that eternal life will not be given / except to the believers / who will remain faithful until death.

13. It is said, that this doctrine causes the Shepherds and Teachers to neglect the duties of their ministry / because the same can be of no benefit / except for those who shall be saved / and who cannot be lost.

I answer, that / since God wants to use their service to bring men to salvation / they must labor therein with zeal / leaving the outcome to <term>Providence: God’s divine guidance and care over the world (original: Voorzienigheid)</term>.

->What we have said / is enough to explain this matter. But notwithstanding / we shall make some further remarks upon it.<-

1. The First is / that God / in the choosing of men / acts as a Merciful Father and a Free Lord, who does what pleases him. Therefore / if one asks / Why has God chosen some persons? one must answer / that it is a work of his infinite mercy toward the human race / which has moved him / not to let all go to ruin / who deserved it. But / if one asks / why has God chosen Peter rather than Paul / since they both deserved death? one must answer / because it so pleased him: like a <term>Potter: a common biblical metaphor for God's creative sovereignty (original: Pottebakker)</term> / who from one lump makes one vessel for honor / and one for dishonor. We have reason, then, to adore God’s mercy toward men / that he was willing to spare some of the human race / although he could punish them all; but we must not esteem the Supreme Power / which he has over them / any less highly.

<summary>This page refutes the charge that predestination implies divine partiality, using the Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard to argue that God may bestow unmerited grace on some without being unjust to others. It further explains that God's decree of election includes both the end (salvation) and the means (Christ's sacrifice and the work of the Holy Spirit).</summary>
