--- Page 619 ---
<meta>This page continues the defense of the doctrine of Election (Predestination) against common objections. The previous page established that God is not "partial" or a "respecter of persons" when He chooses some for salvation, using the analogy of a homeowner and his workers.</meta>

# THE CHRISTIAN

nothing can be concluded against the truth that we have established. **Paul** intends to say nothing else than that a person who applies himself to cleansing himself from the defilements of sin will indeed be a sanctified vessel, and show that he is a chosen vessel, previously destined for glory. This is in the same sense as **Christ** said, *love your enemies, so that*

<margin>Matthew 6:44, 45 <note>The text cites Matthew 6, though these verses are traditionally found in Matthew 5:44-45.</note></margin>
*you may be children of your Father, who is in Heaven;* that is to say, to make it evident that you are children of the Father of mercy.

9. It is said that this doctrine makes man careless and causes the practice of godliness to grow cold.

But one is greatly mistaken; for, when we say that God has chosen us according to His good pleasure, without having foreseen any quality in us, we add to this that God will not give salvation except to believers, and only to those who seek to work out their salvation. <note>The author is balancing the idea of "unconditional election" with the necessity of living a holy life.</note>

10. It is said that by this view, prayers are made useless; for why, it is asked, should one seek to prevail upon God through prayers if it is a truth that He has determined from all eternity everything that must happen?

I answer that God, who has taught us that He chose us before the foundation of the ages, demands from us the duty of our prayers, and that we cannot release ourselves from this without offending Him. We shall examine this more closely when we deal with the subject of Prayer.

11. It is said that this doctrine strives against the Gospel; for the Gospel, it is said, commands us to have repentance, whereas this doctrine supposes that God wants to save men without having foreseen their repentance, and that He produces this repentance in them.

I answer: 1. That although the decree of Election does not follow the foresight of repentance, God has nonetheless resolved to give salvation only to the penitent. 2. That penitence is simultaneously a duty of man and a gift of God.

12. It is said that this doctrine contradicts what the Scripture teaches us of eternal life, which it depicts to us as the inheritance of God’s children, the reward of their obedience, and the crown of those who shall have fought the good fight, etc.

Answer: One fails to notice that we say

<column-break/>

that eternal life will not be given except to the believers who remain faithful until death.

13. It is said that this doctrine causes Pastors and Teachers to neglect the duties of their ministry, because the same can be of no benefit except for those who shall be saved, and who cannot be lost.

I answer that, since God wishes to use their service to bring men to salvation, they must labor therein with zeal, leaving the outcome to Providence.

What we have said is enough to explain this matter. But notwithstanding this, we shall make a few more remarks about it.

1. The first is that God, in choosing men, acts as a Merciful Father and a Sovereign Lord <term>Sovereign Lord: A ruler with absolute, independent authority (original: Vrye Heer)</term>, who does what pleases Him. Therefore, if one asks: Why has God chosen certain persons? one must answer that it is a work of His infinite mercy toward the human race, which moved Him not to let all perish who deserved it. But if one asks: Why did God choose **Peter** rather than **Paul**, since they both deserved death? one must answer: Because it so pleased Him. He is like a Potter who, from one lump of clay, makes one vessel for honor and another for dishonor. <note>This refers to the "Potter and the Clay" analogy found in Romans 9:21.</note> We have reason, then, to adore God's mercy toward men, in that He wished to spare some of the human race, although He could have punished them all; but we must not value the Supreme Power He has over them any less highly.

One must not accuse God of being a respecter of persons <note>original: "Aannemer des perzoons," meaning one who shows favoritism or partiality based on status.</note>, as **Augustine** very well remarks. "One calls it respect of persons," he says, "when someone who must pass judgment on a matter leaves aside the justice of the case and favors one to the detriment of the other, because he finds something in his person that draws his esteem or his compassion. But if someone had two debtors, and he wished to forgive the debt of one and make the other pay his, what could one have to say about that, except that he gives to whom he wills, and harms no one?"

<margin>Book 4 to Boniface, chapter 7 <note>Referring to Augustine's "Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians," written to Pope Boniface.</note></margin>

It concludes by citing Augustine to explain that God's sovereign choice is an act of mercy toward some rather than an act of injustice toward others.</summary>

Thus, partiality only takes place when one must give to each what is due to them by

<column-break/>

right; and in that way it remains certain that with God there is no partiality, because He can do no wrong. But when one gives freely what is owed to no one, there is no partiality in giving to one what is refused to another. One may consult what Fulgentius says <note>original: "Lib. de inc. &. grat. ad Petrum. c. 2." — referring to Saint Fulgentius of Ruspe's 6th-century work *On the Incarnation and Grace, addressed to Peter*, chapter 2.</note> and Thomas [Aquinas] <note>original: "2. 2. q. 63. art. 1. ad. 3. item 1. p. q 23. a. 5. ad. 3." — referring to the *Summa Theologica*, various parts regarding partiality and predestination.</note>.

The second observation is that the eternal decree of God, through which He has chosen men, includes two things: the destiny of the elect to salvation, and the arrangement of the means that lead to salvation. **Augustine** says that predestination is the eternal knowledge and preparation of grace, through which those who are saved are certainly saved. Thus God, in choosing and destining men for glory, simultaneously decided to send His Son to obtain salvation for them, to call them to the knowledge of the truth, to justify them, to sanctify them through His spirit, and to produce in them faith and Christian virtues, to make them persevere to the end, and finally to give the glory He has prepared for them. **Christ** is therefore the first means through which God carries out the decree of election, and this is what **Paul** teaches us in **1 Thessalonians 5:9**, where he says: *God has not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ.*

<margin>
1 Thessalonians 5:9.
</margin>

If one asks how God could assign salvation to men who had angered Him without wounding His justice, one must answer that God, in determining to save them, simultaneously established in His decree to send His Son to satisfy His justice. **Christ** is then the cause and the foundation of our salvation: but the mercy and the good pleasure of God is alone the cause of our election.

<margin>
Arminians: *Conference of The Hague*; *Acts of the Synod*. <note>Refers to the debates between the Remonstrants (Arminians) and the orthodox Calvinists in the early 17th century.</note>
</margin>

It is therefore wrong to charge our doctrine with the accusation that it overthrows the merits of **Christ**.

<margin>
Diego Álvarez, *On Aid*, book 5, disputation 5. Gabriel Vázquez, disputation 91, chapter 1. Francisco Suárez, on part 3, question 19, article 4, disputation 43. <note>These are citations of prominent Catholic theologians and Jesuits to show the breadth of scholarly agreement on these points.</note>
</margin>

When the Apostle says then, in **Ephesians 1:4**, *that we are chosen in Christ*, it is to teach us that God, in choosing men, decided to give them to **Christ**. In the same decree in which He destined men for glory, He also established to give them to **Christ**, and to send **Christ** into the world to [be] for them...

## CHAPTER IV.

### Of the View of the Ancient Church regarding the matter of Predestination.

<margin>
<note>original: "Tom. I. Theol. Dogm. l, IX, c, 5, 6, Aug, de bon, Pers, c, 20, p, 1288. T, VII."</note>
Volume I, Dogmatic Theology, Book IX, chapters 5, 6. Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 20, page 1288, Volume VII.
</margin>
It has been well noted that in the disputes which have been held for a long time over Grace, Election, and Predestination, one must give less weight to the teachings of the Church Fathers who lived before the heresy of Pelagius <note>Pelagius (c. 354–418) was a monk who argued that humans could take the first steps toward salvation by their own free will without divine grace, a view later declared heretical.</note> than to those of the Church Fathers who arose afterward, because the latter investigated these matters with greater precision. This is acknowledged by the Jesuit Petavius. „ Every „ new faction of heretics, says Au- „ gustine, that arises in the Church, gives „ occasion, through the disputes they „ stir up, to explain and protect the „ truths of the Scripture which they „ oppose much more broadly and „ accurately than would have been „ done otherwise.

The Fathers, while disputing with the Manichaeans <note>Followers of Manichaeism, a dualistic religion that taught a radical struggle between good and evil; Augustine famously converted from this faith to Christianity.</note>, set the powers of free will a little too high. Meanwhile, many of them favor the truth that we defend, and they have been of great service in combating the errors that we perhaps oppose.

But, so as not to occupy ourselves with the views of the Church Fathers who lived before Pelagius, let us examine what the Church taught when this heretic arose, and what those who came after him believed.

<margin>
<note>original: "Lib. de Praed. T. VII. f. 19."</note>
Book *On Predestination*, Volume VII, folio 19.
</margin>
From the works of Augustine, it appears that in his time there were three doctrines concerning predestination.

The First was that of Augustine and the Church, which ascribed everything to God. The second was that of Pelagius, who attributed everything to man. The third, that of the Semi-Pelagians <note>A group that sought a middle ground, teaching that God’s grace is necessary but that humans must take the first step toward faith.</note>, who indeed divided the work of grace between God and man, but nonetheless ascribed more to man than to God. The Pelagians based pre-

<column-break/>

<margin>
<note>original: "Aug. lib. de Praed. c. 18."</note>
Augustine, Book *On Predestination*, chapter 18.
</margin>
destination, or rather God's election, upon the foresight of human merits. The Semi-Pelagians, acknowledging that grace is necessary for all good works, ascribed only the beginning of faith to the will, and asserted that Predestination was grounded on the foreknowledge of the merits of this first beginning, which according to them was to be ascribed to man alone. They even said that children who happened to die in their childhood years were predestined according to the life that God foresaw they would have led if they had lived longer.

Prosper of Aquitaine, *Epistle to Augustine* and *Response to the Gallic Chapters*.

They also distinguished two decrees: one general and conditional to make all men blessed, and one particular and absolute to preserve only those whose faith God had foreseen.

But Augustine, maintaining with the whole Church that every good quality in man is a gift from God, from the first principle of faith to perseverance itself—and a gift that springs solely <note>original: "enkellyt," likely a typo for "enkellyk" (purely/solely)</note> from a grace which not only includes all merits but is granted to sinners who are entirely unworthy of it—held fast that predestination is wholly and entirely of grace.

If one examines the works of this ancient Teacher, one will find therein most of the arguments that we have brought forward in the preceding Chapter. He makes use in several places of the Epistle to the Ephesians, Chapter 1, which we have also cited, and uses the same against the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians in his book *On the Predestination of the Saints*. <margin>Volume VII, page 1256.</margin> Chapter 19: „ Perhaps, he says, those „ for whom we write will say that „ it is true that the doctrine of the „ Pelagians is struck to the ground „ by this passage of the Apostle, „ where he says that we are „ predestined in Christ, before the „ foundation of the world, out of „ regard for the love he has borne „ us, so that we should be holy „ and blameless before his eyes; „ since to say, as the heretics do, „ that once we have accepted the „ commandments of the Gospel, „ our free will is what makes us „ holy and blameless through love, „ and that it is through the „ knowledge he had from eternity „ that this must happen so, that he „ has predestined us in Christ „ before the creation of the world, „ is to [contradict] the Apostle in...

*Prosper* <note>Prosper of Aquitaine, a lay theologian and disciple of Augustine.</note> defended the same among the *Gauls*.

In the 8th century by Pope *Adrian I*.

Ratramnus, monk of Corbie, taught the doctrine of <term>Predestination</term> <note>original: "Voorverordineering"</note> through grace in the two books he wrote on this subject and dedicated to Emperor *Charles the Bald*.

This *Prudentius* wrote against *Johannes Scotus Erigena*.

THE CHRISTIAN

## V. CHAPTER.

### Of the firmness and certainty / of Election.
<note>In this context, "Election" refers to the theological belief that God has chosen specific individuals for eternal salvation before the beginning of time.</note>

Until now we have seen / how God / who did not want all people to perish / has chosen some / for whom he has intended eternal glory. One must not doubt / that he will put them in possession of it; for God's election is firm / certain / and unchangeable: and we know no election / that would not be firm. This must be proven.

<margin>Remonstrant Apology chapter XVI. 4. etc. Volkel. Socinus, Prelections chapter 11.</margin> <note>These references point to the theological opponents of the author: the Remonstrants (followers of Arminius) and Socinians, who argued that God's choice was based on human actions and could therefore change.</note>
I. There is no reason / that obliges us to judge the decree of Election differently / than the other decrees of God. Who does not know now / that scripture speaks of them / as so many irrevocable and unchangeable sentences / *My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure, says the Lord through Isaiah Chapter XLVI. 10.* Paul speaks in Hebrews VI. 17. Of the unchangeable firmness of God’s counsel. Since it is written, *that the gifts and the Calling of God are without repentance,* Romans XI. 29. do we then not have reason / to speak and teach the same language / regarding the election of God; if God changed the decree of his election / it would have to be / either because he did not foresee what was to happen / or because he cannot carry out what he had intended / or through inconstancy and lightheadedness. One can say none of these about God. One cannot say / that he did not foresee the outcomes: for he sees everything / and all things are naked and exposed before his eyes. One cannot say / that he does not have the power / to do what he has decided. What is impossible for him who created the world out of nothing? Finally / one cannot, without godlessness / accuse God of inconstancy or lightheadedness,

<margin>Numbers XXIII. 19. Isaiah XLVI. 10. Hebrews VI. 17. Romans XI. 29.</margin>
<margin>James I. 17. Numbers XXIII. 19.</margin>
There is with him no change or shadow of turning James I, 17. God is not a man, that he should lie, nor a son of man, that he should repent; would he say it, and not do it? or speak, and not make it certain? Numbers XXIII. 19.

II. To these general observations one must add several specific thoughts.

<column-break/>

Paul, describing the Divine Chain of Salvation / shows that all the links are so closely attached to each other / that one cannot separate them. *Whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many Brothers. And whom he predestined, these he also called, and whom he called, these he also justified, and whom he justified, these he also glorified.* Romans VIII. 29. 30. Here it appears / that God joins foreknowledge and preordination / which are the two acts of God's eternal election (the one concerns the end / and the other the means) not only with calling and justification / which occur in time / but with the glory / that must follow / to assure us that of all / who were preordained before the foundation of the world / there is no one / who will not certainly / after the completion of the ages / be glorified. If now election were not unchangeable / it could happen / that those whom God foreknew and preordained / would not be glorified. These two things stand firm / that all those / whom God will glorify / will have been justified / called / and preordained / and that all / whom God preordains / justifies / and calls / shall be glorified; whichever way one views preordination, calling, and glorification / they are linked with each other in the closest manner.

> One will say, that God will glorify those whom he foresaw / would believe to the end.

Answer. 1. Those who make this objection / do not notice that Paul places calling / through which God works faith in us / after preordination. One can therefore not say / that God has glorified those whom he foresaw / would believe. 2. God will glorify those / whom he has foreknown / and whom he shall have called / and in whom he shall have produced true faith: but one must not say / that he will glorify those whom he shall have foreseen / would believe until the end.

One says, that God will glorify those / whom he has preordained / If they are steadfast in loving him / and doing their duty.

<vocab>Election: God's sovereign choice of individuals for salvation. Predestination: The doctrine that God has ordained all that will happen, especially concerning salvation. Divine Chain: A theological term for the sequence of salvation steps in Romans 8. Justification: Being declared righteous by God. Remonstrants: Dutch Protestants who opposed the strict Calvinist view of predestination. Socinus: A 16th-century theologian who denied the Trinity and strict predestination.</vocab>

->DIVINITY. VIII. B. V. Chapter.<-

**Answer.** It is without basis to claim that Paul’s reasoning is conditional; for it clearly shows that God himself produces the condition—consisting of faith and perseverance—within the elect.

<margin>Phil. IV. 3.</margin>
**III.** A third proof for the certainty of God’s election lies in the recording of the names of the elect in heaven in the book of life. Paul, speaking of his fellow workers, says in Philippians 4:3, *that their names are written in the book of life.*

<margin>
Heb. XII. 23.
Rev. XIII. 8.
</margin>
In the Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 12:23, he mentions the firstborn who are written in heaven. John, in the Revelation, Chapter 13:8, mentions those whose names are *not* written in the Lamb’s book of life. There are those who make a distinction between the "Book of the Lamb" and the "Book of Life." They say that in the first, the names of those who will remain steadfast in faith and be saved are recorded; and in the second, all believers are recorded, under the condition of perseverance. But it appears clearly enough from the passage itself that it is one and the same book.

It is said that one must distinguish between a double recording. One, made from eternity based on the foresight of perseverance, which is unerring; and another, which happens in time according to the present state of the believers; and they add that this latter one can be erased. But this <unclear>notion</unclear> <note>original: "gebooten"; likely a typo for "gevoelen" meaning "opinion" or "view"</note> offends God’s Majesty, as if His decree depended on the movements of our inconstant will.

<margin>Luke X. 20.</margin>
Christ wants His disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven. Luke 10:20. This is a manner of speaking that indicates the firmness and the certainty of the salvation of the elect children of God, in contrast to those who perish,

<margin>Jer. XVII. 13.</margin>
whose names are marked on the earth and in the sand, where they can easily be wiped out. If Pilate

Why would Christ have exhorted His disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven if this writing could be erased?

Part I.

<column-break/>

One must take good note that Christ says, *rejoice that your names **are** written,* and not that they *shall be* written, as some would wish to distort this passage. It is said that Judas was one of those to whom Christ said that their names are written in heaven. But that does not appear to be the case. Christ, expressing himself thus, was not speaking to the Apostles, but to the seventy disciples. Even if He had spoken to the Apostles, Judas was not included, but excluded: for how could one say of such a traitor that he stands recorded in the Book of Life?

To understand these manners of speaking, which occur often, one must note that the Scripture mentions many "Books of God."

It appears, then / that one must not take these expressions literally / as if God had a physical book / in which the names of those / whom he wishes to save / are written. Some are of the opinion / that / when the Books of God are spoken of / in which the names of the elect are written / it is an allusion to what happens in war / where those who take up service / are written down / as if God wanted to take his elect into his service / to fight for his honor.

The 5th and final observation is / that it is said / that the foundation stands firm; which makes it known / that the elect cannot go lost.

1. It is God / who has established them. What men establish / can be overthrown / but in no way that which God himself establishes and supports. Love often makes us wish for impossible things. <note>The author refers to Moses’ plea in Exodus 32:32, where Moses asks to be blotted out of God's book for the sake of the Israelites; this is viewed as a hyperbolic expression of selfless love rather than a literal possibility.</note>

2. With regard to Psalm 69:29. <note>original: "Psalm LXIX. 29."</note>
One can answer:

1. That / when the Prophet <note>King David</note> wishes that God's enemies were blotted out from His Book / he intends to testify to nothing other / than what he adds thereafter / saying; *that they be not written therein* : for these words explain the preceding ones / as commonly occurs in the Psalms / where the second member explains the first. <term>Parallelism: a poetic structure in Hebrew scripture where the second line of a verse repeats or clarifies the first.</term>

2. That here / as in the wish of Moses, only a temporal destruction <note>physical death or earthly ruin</note> is envisioned. Those who understand this as eternal death / and believe it is Christ / who speaks of the Jews / whom he excludes from eternal life with these words / compare this manner of speaking with that of Christ in Matthew 25:29. *From him who has not, even what he has shall be taken away.* And they note / that one must not conclude from this / that those / whom Christ wishes to be removed from the Book of Life / were previously written therein / because the word *blot out*, just like that of *take away*, must not be pressed too strongly. If it is said / that a name must previously be in a book / before it can be removed from it; it is likewise said / that / to take something from someone / he must have had it beforehand. Meanwhile / Christ says / that from him who has not, that which he has, shall be taken away. Just as Luke explains these words / <margin>Luke 8:18.</margin> which stand in Matthew / thus: *whoever has, to him shall be given, and whoever has not, even what he thinks he has, shall be taken from him*; so one can also say / that the Jews are threatened with the blotting out of their names from the Book of Life; not / because they were truly written therein / but because it was so thought / since they were children of the Kingdom.

3. Regarding the passage from the Revelation <margin>Rev. 22:19.</margin> 22:19 one must explain it thus / as if it stood / if it were possible / that one of those written in the Book of Life / should come to take away anything from the words of this prophecy / God would also blot him out of His book; but it does not follow from this / that the event occurs : just as / when Paul says in Galatians 1:8 / Even

if it were that we, or an Angel from Heaven, preached a Gospel to you other than that which we have preached to you, let him be accursed; one must not conclude / that an Angel / or Paul could preach another Gospel. Others explain it in the same manner / as we have indicated concerning the previous passage of Psalm 69:29.

II. It is said, that / if Election were firm and unchangeable / Peter would not <margin>2 Pet. 1:10.</margin> exhort us / to make the same firm through our good works, 2 Peter 1:10.
I answer, although Election is firm and unchangeable / as well as the effectual Calling <note>The internal work of the Holy Spirit that draws a person to faith.</note> / it is nevertheless with reason / that one is exhorted to make the sense of it firm within us / and to show our neighbors the sincerity of our faith / through our good works. Believers often come to doubt their Election and Calling. It is therefore necessary / that we be exhorted to drive away these doubts / through the practice of good works. It is true that it is the Holy Spirit / who seals them / and bears the name of *Pledge, Seal, Witness,* etc.; but we must also labor at this through our works / by which we not only edify our neighbors / but learn to know ourselves / to know whether we are children of God. <margin>1 John 3:19.</margin> This makes John say: *By this (that is, from love) we know that we are of the truth, and we shall assure our hearts before him,* 1 John 3:19. One has well noted / that good works are the Seals of our Election with respect to ourselves / and that they are the fruits of grace / which calls us. Secondly, one can say in a certain sense / that all the means / serving the execution of the decree of Election / make the same firm. When the believers apply themselves to sanctification / election is carried out / and the exhortations / which God gives them to that end / are the means / through which God works out the election of grace in them. Furthermore / some understand by Election that act of God / through which he actually separates us from other men / and brings us to conversion.

IV. It is said, that it appears / that the elect can be lost / since God allows / that they fall into such heavy sins.

I answer, that the Scripture / which speaks to us of the sins of the Saints / to show their weakness / also makes mention of their preservation / so that we should not doubt God's promises.

It says / that the elect and the righteous fall; but it also says / that the seed of God remains in them. It indeed makes us realize / that the sins of the Elect often make them in truth unworthy of God's love / and that they deserve to be cut off from His communion; but it teaches us at the same time / that God never entirely forsakes them. If He allows them to fall / and if He chastises them / He lifts them up again / and comforts them. This we shall demonstrate more broadly / when we deal with the Perseverance of the Saints. <note>This doctrine, a pillar of Reformed theology, argues that true believers may stumble but will always be restored to faith before death.</note>

Furthermore / when we say it is impossible that the elect perish / we do not mean / that it would not be possible / if the elect were left to themselves / for they are weakness itself; but because God / who has chosen them / preserves them / and that there is nothing / that can separate them from His love / they persevere to the end.

<margin>1 Corinthians 9:27.</margin>
V. One objects with 1 Cor. 9:27. where Paul says / *I discipline my body, and bring it into subjection, lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.* From which one infers / that an Elect person can become a Reprobate. <note>original: "Verwerpeling" — a person rejected by God.</note>

Answer. It is clear / that the Apostle only intended to indicate there the care / which he had to be found a good and noble combatant / by way of a parable / taken from the custom of the ancient combatants <note>Referring to athletes in the Greek games, such as runners or wrestlers.</note> / according to which those who did not live according to the set measure of life / which they had to maintain / and because of their wanton and flighty life had become faint-hearted / were cast out of the race and rejected. From this reasoning, then, nothing else follows / but that Paul, if God left him so far / that he came to fight faint-heartedly for Christ / would make himself worthy at the last

<column-break/>

day; as an evil servant / to be rejected. But it does not follow from this / that he could become a rejection / because it was not possible that God forsook him.

We ought now to deal even more broadly with the certainty / that we have of our election; but because this matter cannot be settled / except by another / namely the certainty, which we have of our faith, we postpone this discussion further / until we speak of faith. We proceed to Reprobation.

One thing we have only to add here / namely / that this Doctrine / that no elect can be lost / has always been the Doctrine of the Church.
<margin>Augustine, Book 18 of *The City of God*, Chapter 25. Fulgentius, *On the True Faith*, to Peter the Deacon, Chapter 51, after Chapter 9.</margin>
Augustine, in Book 18 of *The City of God*, Chapter 25, confirms this in the 25th Chapter of the Book on Faith, dedicated to Peter the Deacon. "Hold," says he / "as a firm
" and indubitable rule of faith, that the grace
" of those whom God has predestined
" to His Kingdom, cannot be lost,
" and that no one whom God
" has not chosen for it, can be saved."

The Church of Lyon, in the writings / which it issued in the 9th Century concerning this subject / made this Doctrine one of the seven rules, which it presented as inescapable; the last of these reads thus: "No Elect can perish, no reprobate can be saved."

This proposition / that the predestined could not be lost, being presented from the pulpit by a Dominican <note>A member of the Roman Catholic Order of Preachers.</note> in a City of the Patriarchate of Aquileia <note>An ancient ecclesiastical territory in Northern Italy.</note> / the same was approved by the Patriarch Grimanus / in a letter / which / being read in the Council of Trent <note>The major 16th-century ecumenical council of the Catholic Church.</note>, was recognized as free from all suspicion of heresy.

# THEOLOGY. VIII. B. CHAPTER VI. 479

It appears that this word first began to be used in the time of <note>Godeschalcus, or Gottschalk of Orbais (c. 800–868), was a Carolingian monk whose teachings on "double predestination"—that God predestines some to hell just as he does others to heaven—caused great controversy in the medieval church.</note> Godeschalcus. It is taken from *Psalm 15:4*, "who looks with contempt upon the <term>reprobate</term><note>The original Dutch uses 'verworpenen,' meaning those who are rejected or cast away. In a theological context, this refers to those not chosen by God for salvation.</note>," etc. thus it stands in the Hebrew; and from *Isaiah 41:9*, "You are my servant, I have chosen you, and have not rejected you." Paul uses a word that has also been translated as "reprobate." *1 Cor. 9:27, 2 Cor. 13:5, 6, 7, 2 Tim. 3:8, Titus 1:16, Heb. 6:8.*

One cannot deny that God has rejected some of His creatures, since He has not chosen them all. Paul speaks in *Romans 9:22* of "vessels of wrath, prepared for destruction." Jude verse 4 speaks of certain men who have crept in, who were "marked out long ago for this condemnation."

One can also not deny that this rejection occurred from all eternity. For there is no reason to judge Rejection any differently than Election. Now we have proven through the Scriptures that Election is eternal. Moreover, the concept that we have of God as the most perfect Being does not allow us to believe that anything happens in time that was not decided from all eternity; nor should we ascribe to Him purposes that were only designed in time and depend upon secondary causes.

Reprobation is then that eternal decree of God, by which, at the same time He decided to give salvation to some (though they deserved nothing but death), He determined to leave others in their corruption; and foreseeing that they would commit countless sins, He decided to punish them eternally for them.

Thus we distinguish two acts in this decree.

1. The first is that by which God—all men being in the same state of corruption—decided to leave many in it without taking pity on them, just as He did for the elect. This must not be understood as if God determined to show them no grace at all; for He preserves them, He fills them with temporal goods; there are infinite numbers to whom He causes His Gospel to be proclaimed, and He enlightens some by the light of His Spirit; for which reason Paul says of the <term>temporary believers</term><note>Those who appear to have faith for a time but do not persevere; a common concept in Reformed theology to explain why some "fall away."</note> in *Hebrews 6:4* that they "have been enlightened." But He has decided not to give them all the same grace that He imparts to the elect, and through which

<column-break/>

He grafts them into the communion of His Son, makes them members of His mystical body, and establishes them as His heirs and co-heirs with Christ.

The second act is that by which God decided to pour out His judgments upon those whom He has left in their corruption, and to punish them eternally; and this because He foresees that they will misuse the light of nature or of the Gospel, and that they will fall into the most abominable sins, which are worthy of all His wrath.

Consequently, God can be viewed in the decree of reprobation as a **Sovereign Lord**, who does all that He wills, like a **Potter** who makes from one lump of clay vessels for honor and for dishonor; and as a **Supreme Judge**, who causes the guilty to suffer the punishment they deserve. When He leaves Peter in his natural corruption and chooses Jacob, He acts as Sovereign Lord; but when He condemns Peter to eternal punishment for his sins, He acts as Supreme Judge. To place this matter in a greater light, one must answer several questions.

1. It is commonly asked, what is the cause of reprobation?

I answer: sin. For if there had been no sin, God would have rejected no one. Augustine says that God would not have been a "venging God" <note>Original: "wreekende God."</note> if man had not sinned.

2. It is asked, why God preferred to leave Anthony rather than John; and why He preferred to choose John rather than Anthony?

To this question one must not answer that sin is the cause; for Anthony and John were both included in the same lump of corruption, and consequently deserved to be treated in the same way; and if God had done so, no one would have had reason to complain. One must then say that it is God’s **good pleasure** alone which moved Him to leave the one and accept the other. Paul puts these words into our mouths: "He has mercy on whom He will have mercy, and He hardens whom He will harden." This He explains through the parable of the potter, which we have cited so often. However one explains these words in *Romans 9:13*, "Jacob I have loved and Esau I have hated," it is certain that one

<center>### THE CHRISTIAN ###</center>

...one can say of all people what Paul says of these two brothers, namely, that before they had done good or evil, God loved the one and hated the other.

People say that here it only speaks of the descendants of Jacob and Esau, and of temporal blessings.

Answer: 1. It is clear that Paul reasons about the persons of Jacob and Esau themselves; for he says explicitly, *before the children had done good or evil*. It is said, etc. 2. To be loved and hated by God means more than being filled with temporal blessings or being deprived of them. 3. It appears that the ungodly Esau possessed more goods than Jacob.

3. One asks, Why does God condemn to eternal punishment those who have lived wickedly?

I answer that their sins are the cause of their damnation. When one pays close attention to these three questions, many difficulties can be solved and many objections answered.

It appears then that it is not the same with <term>reprobering</term><note>Also known as Reprobation; the theological doctrine that God, in His sovereignty, decides to pass over some people, leaving them to the consequences of their sin rather than choosing them for salvation.</note> as it is with <term>election</term><note>God's sovereign choice of individuals for salvation through His grace, independent of their own merit.</note>: election places nothing in the person that deserves being chosen, because it is an act of mercy. But reprobation, which is an act of <term>justice</term><note>In this context, 'justice' refers to God's righteous judgment against sin, which the author argues is the basis for rejection.</note>, necessarily presupposes sin.

Some objections are made here:

1. It is said that this doctrine conflicts with God's justice, since it presupposes that God acts in such an unequal way with people who are all sinners.

I answer that one would be right if we taught that God punishes people and condemns them to death without considering their crimes. But we maintain that God rejects only sinners, who consequently deserve to be punished. Although God treats people—who were equally sinners—in an unequal way, He nevertheless does nothing against His justice. 1. Because He is free to show mercy to whom He will, without anyone being able to take offense; 2. Because if He has destined some to salvation, He has found a way to satisfy His justice in their place through the sending of His Son into the world.

Sinners have no reason to complain, for God was not bound

<column-break/>

to have mercy on them, and the good have no cause to boast, because they have deserved nothing from God. The former must worship His justice. The others must praise His mercy; and we all have reason to cry out, <note>original: "O Diepte der wysheid enz."</note> *O the depth of the wisdom* etc. <note>This is a reference to Romans 11:33, a common refrain in Reformed theology when addressing the mysteries of God's decrees.</note>

2. It is said that if God had rejected some people, He would not have the <term>Gospel</term><note>The 'good news' of salvation through Jesus Christ.</note> proclaimed to them as He does, because to present the promises of salvation to them would be as much as mocking them.

I answer that although God has rejected many, He nevertheless has wise reasons for having the Gospel preached to them, as we shall see in our treatise on <term>The Calling</term><note>Refers to the theological concept of the 'external call' (the preaching of the word to everyone) versus the 'internal call' (the work of the Holy Spirit in the hearts of the elect).</note>.

Even if we did not know any of these reasons, that should cause us no more trouble than so many other decrees and actions of God for which we cannot give a reason, and which exceed the reach of our understanding. It is enough that we believe what the Scripture teaches us:

1. That God does not have mercy on everyone.

2. That consequently God has decided from all eternity not to have mercy on everyone, since nothing happens in time that was not established before the foundation of the world. 3. That meanwhile God has His Gospel proclaimed to many to whom He does not show His mercy.

3. It is said that the doctrine of reprobation opposes God's kindness.

Answer: One would then also have to say that the entire world will be saved because, if it is not saved, God would not have infinite kindness. God is kind, and His kindness is unspeakable, that is true; but He is absolutely free in His actions.

4. It is said that the doctrine of reprobation makes God the cause of sin.

I answer that this is untrue; 1. Because God rejects only those who are already sinners. 2. God drives no one to sin through the decree of reprobation. It is true that God decided not to give converting grace to all people, but He is not obligated to do so.

5. But, it is said, how can God punish people for committing sins which they could not avoid, being abandoned by God?

I answer that God always has just reasons to punish sinners who have willfully committed infinite sins...

**The question is asked**, whether it would not have better suited the wisdom and goodness of God not to give life to those He foresaw would misuse His grace.

**Answer.** It does not befit us to rebuke God's actions; we must adore them and not criticize. If they do not align with our ideas, we must reform our ideas, but not reject God's decree. God, through a wisdom that surpasses our understanding, has judged that it was more fitting to draw good out of evil than to permit no evil at all.

**Secondly, God frequently makes use of the wicked** to nurture the arts and sciences, and to provide His elect with many of the goods they possess. Through their means, God teaches His children what they themselves are and would do, if God had abandoned them as He abandons others. He gives them cause to have more gratitude for the benefits they have received from Him, while He lets the others walk in their own ways; in short, He uses the wicked to test the faith and patience of the pious, and to make their zeal shine forth, and at the same time to make His virtues known. ### In the Roman Church.

1. Some limit Reprobation to that eternal decree by which some are excluded from the Kingdom of Heaven and subjected to eternal punishments. Lombard, book 1, *Sentences*, distinction 40; Durandus, distinction 40, question 2; Molina.

2. Others believe that Reprobation encompasses not only the deprivation of Heavenly Glory but also the permission of sin and the lack of grace. Thomas [Aquinas], Part 1 of the *Summa [Theologica]*, question 23, Article 3. Gregory of Valencia.

3. Some attribute Reprobation only to the surrendering of man to sin and the hardening of the heart—through which God, to punish preceding sins, allows some to fall into much heavier sins. Others include the permission of all kinds of sins. Some believe that Reprobation consists of two positive acts: one concerning the permission of sin and the withholding of grace (which is necessary to avoid sinning), and the other concerning eternal punishments. Gregory of Valencia, *On Reprobation*, part 1. Bañez on the first part of Thomas [Aquinas], question 23, article 2, doubt 2, conclusion 3. Estius on the first book of the *Sentences*, distinction 40, paragraph 16. There are even those who believe that at the same time God ordained some to eternal life, He made a definite decree to exclude others from His Kingdom before He had foreseen any of their sins. Alvarez, book 12, *On the Aids of Divine Grace*, disputation 109, section 51, conclusions 1 & 3. Others distinguish two decrees: one positive and one exclusive, similar to the Reformed teachers. Puteanus, *General Questions on Reprobation*, doubt

<column-break/>

2, conclusion 1. St. Joseph in *The Idea of Speculative Theology*, book 1, chapter 20. Eustachius of St. Paul, *Summary*, treatise 1, disputation 17, question 2.

4. Some believe that man, *before* his fall, is the object of Reprobation. Estius in distinction 40, book 1 of the *Sentences*. Others are of the opinion that it is *fallen* man. As seen in Peter of St. Joseph, *Speculative Theology*, chapter 20, resolution 5. Eustachius of St. Paul, treatise 1, *Summary of Theology*, disputation 17. Others believe it is man considered as dying in sin.

5. Some, who limit Reprobation only to the will to damn certain individuals, believe that the cause of the Reprobation of some is the foreknowledge <note>original: "voorbeschouwing"</note> of their persistence in sin. Others, who include the permission of sin in Reprobation, are of the opinion that there is no cause for it other than the will of God; and those who, with Alvarez, Estius, and Rispolis, believe that the object of Reprobation is man as a "creatable" being <note>original: "schepbaare mensch" — referring to man as a potential creature before the decree of creation</note>, are of the same mind. Others believe that Reprobation—viewed strictly in terms of the "negative act," which consists of the refusal of grace—has the sin of the first man [Adam] as its cause. As seen in Vasquez, volume 1, disputation 95, chapter 3, and Becanus.

Others are of the opinion that original sin <note>original: "erfzonde"</note> must be considered the cause, such as Peter of St. Joseph, *The Idea of Speculative Theology*, book 1, chapter 20, resolution 5.

Others limit Original Sin here to children who die without Baptism, as the sole cause of their Reprobation.

Others believe that it is actual sin <note>Sin committed through one's own actions, rather than inherited sin.</note> in those to whom original sin was forgiven through Baptism.

Others view both inherited and actual sin as the cause, as in the reprobate to whom original sin was never forgiven. Domingo de Soto on Romans 9 and Petrus de Soto.

Others, like Bellarmine, *On Grace and Free Will*, book 2, final chapter, believe that the negative act indeed follows the foreknowledge of Original Sin, but that this sin is not the "meriting cause" of it.

DIVINITY. VIII. B. VII. Chapter.

## CHAPTER VII.

->On the proper use that one should make of<-
->the Doctrine of Election and<-
->Reprobation; and on the<-
->misuse that some<-
->commit regarding this.<-

There are those who, to their own misfortune, misuse the doctrine that we have established, and who take occasion from it to fall into despair <note>The Dutch "wanhoopen" refers here to the spiritual crisis of believing one is eternally rejected by God.</note>, through a false imagination that they are among the number of the reprobate <note>The "reprobate" are those not chosen by God for salvation.</note>, and that they, whatever they might do, cannot be saved.

It is easy to show that they are making a poor use of a holy Doctrine.

1. They are wrong to think that they are reprobate, because it is a matter upon which no one can pass a decisive judgment. God’s decrees are hidden from us, and it is not for us to fathom them. It is indeed certain that there are reprobates and elect, but we do not know with any certainty who the elect are and who the reprobate are. Those who are elect can know that they are so <note>Through the "internal testimony" of faith and the Holy Spirit.</note>, but the reprobate cannot know it, because they do not know whether God will yet convert them. A Sinner can certainly see that he bears the marks of a reprobate, or to put it better, that he lives like a reprobate; but he cannot pronounce with any certainty that he is reprobate, because he does not know what God intends for him. He must not, therefore, draw a certain conclusion from an uncertain principle, saying: "whatever I may do, I shall be damned, so I may as well do whatever I desire."

2. One can demonstrate the extravagance of those who reason thus through two common examples. Suppose that there are many sick people in a hospital <note>original: "gasthuis," an infirmary or guest house for the poor and ill.</note>, to whom an Angel from God has come to say that some of them will recover, but that the others shall die. Would one not regard as insane the man who, after this revelation, would begin to imagine—without reason and without grounds—that he must die, and who in this conviction would refuse to take either food or medicine, or who would kill himself out of despair?

<column-break/>

Consider here another example. Suppose that an Angel at the head of an Army announced that the greater part of the Soldiers of which it consists shall fall in battle, and that only a few will escape; would one not consider him mad who, assuming from this that he will be killed no matter what he does, would—like a Raving man—expose himself to thousands of dangers? One must judge the same of someone who, knowing that there are Elect and Reprobate, would imagine that he is a reprobate, and in that thought live like a reprobate. Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), whose writings on grace and predestination heavily influenced both Catholic and Protestant theology.</note> says very well that one must never despair of the salvation of anyone whom God’s forbearance allows to live, and much less of one’s own. For, although one must not hold oneself certain of election before having found faith and other Christian virtues in one's heart, there are nevertheless many things that should convince someone—to whom God allows His Gospel to be proclaimed and at whose heart He knocks daily—that God has not entirely abandoned him. I confess that this is not enough to prove that one is an elect person, but it is enough to be convinced for oneself that one is also not a reprobate. The converted Thief on the cross <note>referring to the "Penitent Thief" (Dismas) crucified alongside Jesus.</note>, who previously lost himself in all kinds of sins, would have had great misfortune to believe that he was reprobate, since he ended his life so well.

3. Those who say, "If I am reprobate, I shall—whether I believe and dispose myself to virtue or not—be damned," are reasoning entirely illogically <note>original: "gansch buiten den haak," literally "entirely off the hook."</note>. For where has God revealed to us that those who believe and pursue their sanctification shall be lost? <margin>John 3:16.</margin> Does the Scripture not say the opposite? *Whoever believes shall be saved,* John 3:16. <note>original: "die gelooft zal hebben / zal zalig worden."</note>

That the Doctrine of predestination <term>voor-verordineeringe</term> <note>The eternal decree of God by which He has settled the fate of all people.</note> brings man to despair is far from the truth; it is a full fountain of consolations. Everyone knows that the believer is exposed to all kinds of seductions and temptations: but what comforts them therein is that God’s Elect shall not perish. We have already brought up a passage that is very fitting here. Matt. 24:24. *For there shall arise false Christs, and false Prophets, and shall shew great signs and wonders; insomuch that, if it [were possible...]*

(if it were possible) would also deceive the Elect <note>The "Elect" refers to those chosen by God for salvation from before the beginning of time.</note>. From this, the Elect conclude that they will not be dragged into destruction by any deception.

<margin>Matt. 24:21, 22.</margin>
The believers are also exposed to various persecutions; but what comforts them is the doctrine of election. For then, says Christ, there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor ever shall be, etc. but for the sake of the elect, those days will be shortened. Matt. 24:21, 22. <margin>Dan. 12:1.</margin> There will be a time of distress, says Daniel, etc. but at that time your people will be delivered, everyone who is found written in the Book <note>The "Book of Life," a biblical metaphor for the record of those destined for heaven.</note>. Dan. 12:1.

Nothing disturbs believers so much as the apostasy <note>Falling away from the faith.</note> of those who should have stood for the truth. Against this offense, scripture arms us when it teaches us that the foundation of God stands firm, 2 Tim. 2:19.

<margin>Luke 12:32.</margin>
Is there a doctrine more suitable to comfort us than this, which assures us that God loved us before the foundation of the world, and that He will consequently love us to the end; that He who loved us when we deserved His hatred, will love us even more now that we have become His children and are recreated in His image; that He who loved us when we were His enemies, will now, having been reconciled with Him, love us even more. In whatever distress the believer may be, the doctrine of election serves as a wonderful comfort. Fear not, little flock, said Christ, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the Kingdom. Luke 12:32.

There are some who misuse the doctrine of Election in another way; whatever I may do, these say, it does not matter; if I am chosen, I must be saved; I can freely follow the impulses of my passions and the current of the world, and, like others, live in all kinds of pleasures. The virtues that I could practice, or the sins with which I could defile myself, cannot change God’s eternal decree.

Regarding these, I note:

1. That no one but unholy and abandoned villains can reason thus: I am preordained, therefore I am free to live like a castaway <note>Dutch: "verworpeling," referring to one rejected by God.</note>: to say that one is preordained means that God, through

<column-break/>

<margin>Col. 3:12.</margin>
an effect of His grace, which cannot be praised enough, has assigned salvation and glory to us, even though we were worthy of death. How is it now possible that someone who believes God has shown him this grace can say: God loved me so much, and I want to hate Him; He opens heaven to me, and I want to live as if hell were prepared for me; He makes His grace abound where my sins were abounding; I want to make my sins abound where His grace is abundant. One must be a monster of ingratitude to use such language. Paul warns us against it and desires that we, on the contrary, as God’s chosen ones, clothe ourselves in Christian virtues.

<margin>Eph. 2:10.</margin>
2. I note that it is not true that an elect person will be saved regardless of what he may do. For who does not know that the same God who preordained people for salvation also appointed them to the means that lead to salvation, and that these means are faith and holiness, etc. That kind of people reason as ridiculously as someone would to whom God, as to Hezekiah, would say: you shall live another fifteen years, and on that ground would boast and say: I do what I do, whether I eat or not, whether I take care of my life or put it at risk, I shall not die. Certainly, Paul was a chosen vessel, preordained from all eternity; I ask whether he would have been saved if he had continued to persecute Christ and His church, and to constantly blaspheme against God? Although it is true that all the elect will be saved, it is not true that they will be saved while doing and acting as they please and what they please. God, who has chosen them and written their names in the book of life, has also created them in Christ to do good works, which God prepared beforehand so that we should walk in them. Eph. 2:10. And He declares that no one shall see God without sanctification <note>The process of becoming holy through the Holy Spirit.</note>.

3. Finally, I note that although all the elect will be saved, they will only be saved for Christ’s sake, whom they will have embraced through faith and followed through good works.

That the doctrine of Election [leads] the people...

DIVINITY. VIII. B. VIII. Chapter.

...leads to an unrestrained life; instead, it provides us with many motives for the practice of godliness.

1. It ignites our hearts with a holy love toward God: for how could one not love Him who loved us so much and first?

2. It awakens us to the pursuit of sanctification; for God has chosen us, so that we should be holy and blameless before His face.

3. It produces humility in us, by making us understand that we have nothing that we have not received, and that God has distinguished us from others.

4. It fills us with full assurance of salvation, and makes us cry out, Romans 8:31: *If God be for us, who can be against us?* and verse 33: *Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth*, etc.

5. Finally, it instills in us the fear of appearing before Him to whom we owe everything, and spurs us on to work out our salvation with fear and trembling.

<margin>Volume 1, Dogmatic Theology, Book 3, On God, Chapter 15, Article 6.</margin>
Furthermore, the Jesuit <note>Dionysius Petavius (1583–1652), a prominent French Jesuit theologian known for his work on the history of dogma.</note> Petavius rightly notes that all the objections that can be made against the doctrine of gracious predestination apply to all the ways in which this mystery is explained. The doctrine of God’s foreknowledge gives as much cause for all these objections as the doctrine of gracious predestination. For, as Mr. Nicole says in his *Theological Instructions on the Faith*: it is certain 
<margin>page 175.</margin>
that God has not only foreseen the end of every human being, but also all their deeds and all their actions which they will do to reach that end; so that, whether God be the primary cause of good works, or the will of man, the same man will go the same way for a long time and come to his end through the same chain of deeds known to God. Thus also, he adds, whether grace be efficacious of itself and draws the consent of the will infallibly after it; or whether it be not so, except only for those whom God has chosen out of a special love and favored with the gifts of grace to which He foresees they will consent—as most theologians who are called <term>Congruists</term> <note>A group of Jesuit theologians who argued that God offers grace in "congruity" (harmony) with a person's circumstances, knowing they will freely choose to accept it.</note> teach—or whether these gifts of grace to which the will

<column-break/>

consents are not given out of a special love from God, but through certain general laws of Providence, as others teach; it is clear that, according to all these opinions, the effect of grace always proceeds with equal certainty, and that man acts in the same way. "What concerns man," he says, "regarding this doctrine is only the certainty of the outcome; they are only fearful of damnation."

## VIII. CHAPTER.

->On the Election and the Reprobation of Angels.<-

There is nothing left for me to finish this subject but the treatise on the Election and Reprobation <note>"Reprobation" refers to God's decision to leave some to their own sin and its consequences, the opposite of election.</note> of the Angels. Even if Scripture did not speak of it, reason would teach us that there are elect and reprobate angels: for, since (as we have often said) nothing happens, and nothing must happen in time, that is not firmly decided in God’s counsel, it is clear that the glory which the good angels enjoy, and the punishment which the evil ones must suffer and which they already begin to bear, was assigned to them from all eternity.

Scripture does not speak with express words of the Election of Angels, unless one wished to apply this passage from Paul, 1 Timothy 5:21: *I charge thee before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the elect angels.* For nothing prevents us from saying that they are called "elect," not only to distinguish them from the evil angels who are rejected and have left their habitation, and to indicate the excellence of their nature, but also to signify that God has chosen them from all eternity to be vessels of honor forever.

<margin>Matthew 25:41. 2 Peter 2:4. Jude verse 6.</margin>
One can clearly derive the Reprobation of the evil angels from what Christ says in Matthew 25:41, of the *everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels.* 2 Peter 2:4 speaks of the *judgment* for which they are preserved, and Jude verse 6 speaks of the *eternal chains* under which they are kept in darkness until the judgment...

One must argue with caution and moderation regarding this subject, so that we are not accused of meddling in things we have not seen. To say something of it in the meantime, it is very probable:
1. That God did not view all the Angels in the same state, in the same way that He viewed all men in a single <term>mass of corruption</term> <note>A reference to the Augustinian concept of *massa corruptionis*, the idea that all humanity is a "lump of sin" due to the Fall.</note>. 2. That the decree of the election of the good Angels includes two decrees: one to confirm them in their holiness, and another to appoint them to an eternal <term>blessedness</term> <note>In the original Dutch *gelukzaligheid*, referring to the highest state of spiritual joy and peace in God's presence.</note> greater than that which they already possessed.

I say that the decree of the election of the Angels includes the decree to confirm them in holiness. To understand this, one must take into consideration that: 1. When God created all the Angels, He gave them sufficient strength to persevere in the state in which He had placed them. 2. That the good Angels, through the strength God had given them, preserved their Holiness. 3. That, as a reward for their constancy, they received a new grace from God, through which they are so firmly established in their first state that nothing is powerful enough, nor shall ever be, to make them waver.

Some are of the opinion that they were confirmed by the example of the other Angels <note>Meaning the sight of the fallen angels being cast out motivated the good angels to stay faithful.</note>, which affected them to such a degree that it is not possible for them to follow them, and that by doing an infinite number of good works, they became confirmed in goodness. But I do not see why one would not want to give the honor of their confirmation to God. If God had not confirmed them, they would have always remained in their natural and changeable state.

One would then have to say that the Angels are in a state that is

<column-break/>

subject to change, which cannot be said without absurdity.

I say also that the decree of the Election of the Angels includes their appointment to a Glory much greater than that which they possess; for nothing prevents us from judging the election of the Angels in the same way as the election of men, though we can decide nothing certain about it. There is a great appearance that the glory they enjoyed has received a great increase, which God can increase unto infinity.

When we spoke of the election of men, we said that God, in appointing them to salvation, had decided to provide them salvation through Christ, and that we are chosen in Him; but we cannot say the same of the Angels.

I well know that some have been of the opinion that Christ is the Mediator of the Angels, and that through His death He earned for them their confirmation in the happy state in which they exist. But there is no reason that obliges us to enter into that opinion.

<margin>Job 4:18</margin>
1. The Scripture says that Christ came into the world and suffered only to save sinners, and the Angels, who are sinless, are not counted among them. It is true that Job 4 says that *God puts no trust in His servants, and He charges His angels with folly.* <note>Original: "God zich niet vertrouwt op zyn knegten, hoewel hy in zynen Engelen klaarheid gestelt heeft." The Dutch translation used here differs slightly from the King James Version, focusing on God's absolute perfection versus angelic limitation.</note> Job 4:18. But that does not mean that these blessed spirits are stained with sin, or that they, being strictly examined, would be found guilty and in need of forgiveness. Rather, Job’s meaning is either that the right God has over His creatures is so great and so absolute that He is not indebted even to the Angels, however excellent their Holiness may be; the luster of the glory He has given them is a gift of His goodness, and not a reward for their merits; or else that the infinite purity of God's Majesty is so wonderful that the luster of the holiest Spirits is imperfect in comparison to that of God, just as the light of a torch or even the stars disappears before the rays of the Sun.

2. It appears from the Scripture that a Mediator must share the nature of the parties whom He reconciles. Thus Christ, as Mediator between God and

### CHAPTER I.

->The order that will be followed in this Book.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'I' containing floral scrollwork.</image-desc>
In the preceding Book we have seen / that God did not wish / that the entire human race should perish / but that He chose some for Himself before the foundation of the world, that they should be holy and blameless before His face in love, having predestined them, to adopt them as children in Christ, according to the good pleasure of His will, to the praise of the Glory of His grace. Ephesians 1:4, 5, 6.

We have observed / how God / from all eternity / has assigned them Salvation and eternal Glory. Now we must investigate what God has done in time / to regain this salvation for them / consisting in the sending of His Son. We then intend to treat this Son / to consider Him as the Mediator <note>A 'Mediator' is a go-between who reconciles two parties—in this case, God and humanity.</note> of mankind / and to unfold all that He / to obtain for us Salvation and immortality / has suffered.

To lay out this subject with all clarity / we intend to follow this order. **1.** That it was necessary / that God's justice be satisfied <note>original: "voldaan" - in theology, 'satisfaction' refers to the idea that a debt or penalty must be paid to meet the requirements of divine justice.</note> to save mankind. **2.** That it was not absolutely necessary / that the sinners satisfied His justice for themselves.

<column-break/>

**3.** That a Divine Person alone could satisfy for us. **4.** We shall see / how this could happen / since all the Persons of the holy Trinity were equally offended <note>original: "beledigt" - in this context, it refers to the violation of God's holy law and honor by sin.</note>. **5.** Why God did not send His Son immediately after the Fall of Man. **6.** By what prophecies <note>original: "Godspraaken" - literally 'God-speeches' or oracles.</note> this Son was promised, etc. **7.** We shall show / that the Messiah has come / and that Jesus / the Son of Mary / is the true Messiah. **8.** We shall treat the Law / which God gave to His people / and why God willed / that His Law be proclaimed before the coming of His Son. **9.** We shall show what state the ancient Church was in / before Christ came into the world. **10.** Why He assumed human nature; whether there are two Persons in Christ / and how His two natures are united. **11.** What the two states of Christ were <note>This refers to the 'State of Humiliation' (His life and death) and the 'State of Exaltation' (His resurrection and glory).</note>. **12.** We shall treat His conception and birth. **13.** Of the principal things / that one must note in His life. **14.** Of His suffering and death / and of the fruits of His death. **15.** Of His burial and descent into Hell. **16.** Of His Resurrection. **17.** Of His Ascension. **18.** Of His Sitting at the right hand of God. **19.** Of His Mediatorial office. **20.** Of His three Offices <note>These are traditionally the offices of Prophet, Priest, and King.</note>. **21.** Of His Prophetic. **22.** And High-Priestly Office. **23.** Of the Truth of His satisfaction. **24.** And of its perfection. **25.** Of His Intercession. **26.** Of the excellence of His Priesthood above the Levitical one / and of its fruits. **27.** Of His Kingly Office. **28.** How Christ [makes us] part- <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "ge-", likely leading to "gedeeltig" or "deelachtig," meaning "to make us partakers" of His benefits.</note>

## CHAPTER II.

->Whether it was necessary to satisfy God for the sins of mankind.<-

<margin>What the Word 'Satisfy' signifies.</margin>
**I**n order to rightly understand the reason / for which it was necessary / that Christ came into the world to acquire for us the salvation / which God has destined for us / one must prove three things. **1.** That it was absolutely necessary to satisfy Divine justice / and that / without satisfaction / God could not make men blessed. **2.** That it was not necessary / that men satisfied for themselves / and that they were unable to do so. **3.** That a Divine Person must bring about this satisfaction.

The question / which we must then investigate / is / whether it was absolutely necessary / to satisfy Divine justice. But first one must take note / that the word satisfy (a) is taken in this place for paying that which Divine justice demanded from Sinners for their sins. The Scripture does not use this specific expression / but it makes use of many others / which signify the same truth / like the words *Redemption, Reconciliation, price or ransom of Redemption*, and such like.

This being laid down as a foundation / it is easy to establish the necessity of a satisfaction. Many reasons prove the same.

<column-break/>

<margin>Proofs of the necessity of the Satisfaction against the Socinians.</margin>
**I.** Even if there were no other proof / than that taken from the death of Christ / after His Divinity has been proven / it is more than convincing. For is there any shadow of appearance / that God would have exposed His Son to so many indignities and pains / that He would have sent Him into the world / to take on human nature with all its sinless weaknesses / to appear in the likeness of sinful flesh / to nail Him to the cursed wooden cross / and to die as an evildoer / if it were indeed of no absolute necessity to satisfy His justice? Is there the least probability / that He would have thus dealt with His Son / His beloved Son / His perfect Image / in whom He had His good pleasure / if He could have forgiven men their sins without satisfaction / and that it was only necessary / to proclaim salvation to men / to give examples of Holiness and patience / and to seal the truth of God with His blood? Can that enter into a human heart?

(a) The Latins <note>original: "De Latynen" - referring to Latin-speaking authors and legalists.</note> have used this in several senses. **1.** When someone granted another's desire, they said that he satisfied him; and one still says today in the French Language, that someone gives another much satisfaction, to say, that he pleases him. **2.** When someone by his works or words testified, that he repented having offended another, and that he asked for mercy, they said, that he had satisfied. The formula, which they used in this case, reads thus, *I wished not to have done it, I am prepared to swear, that you did not deserve this wrong.* <note>original Latin: "non velle factum, iuraturum se non merito fecisse."</note> The French also take this word in the same sense. **3.** When someone paid his debts, or fulfilled his word, the Latins said that he satisfied. Thus one also speaks in French. **4.** The ancient Fathers <note>Early Christian theologians of the first few centuries.</note> called the acknowledging of sins before God, and the calling upon His grace, to satisfy God. They gave the name of satisfaction to all the works of penitence, such as the confession of sins, and change of life and conduct. In that sense Cyprian <note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage.</note> exhorted the Heathens, *We exhort you, while you have the time, to satisfy God, and to go out from the deep abyss of dark superstition, to follow in the beautiful light of the true Religion.* <note>original Latin from Cyprian's 'Ad Demetrianum': "Hortamur vos... dum locus datur, Deo satisfacere..."</note> **5.** One called 'satisfactions' the public testimonies, which the Sinners gave of their repentance in the Church, for the edification of the believers, and that was called Regular satisfactions. Here the word *satisfaction* is taken for the price, which has been paid to Divine justice for sins.

# THEOLOGY. BOOK IX. CHAPTER II.

II. But besides this reason, there are many others. Certainly, if it is true that God is by nature infinitely Holy and Righteous; that He completely hates and curses sin as something that strives against His justice, it is clear that He cannot fail to punish it, and that He cannot forgive it without having received some satisfaction. Now, we have proven in our *Treatise on God’s Perfections* that He is righteous by nature, that He hates all who commit iniquity, and that His eyes are too pure to behold evil. It follows then that He must necessarily punish sin, and that He cannot forgive it without satisfaction. I do not wish to repeat here what I have said elsewhere. I request my readers to please read the chapter on God’s Justice; they will find there the answers to the strongest objections that can be brought against this point.

I shall add only one here. It is said that, since God can punish those whom He does not hate and whom He loves—as in the case of innocent men—He could also grant forgiveness to those whom He hates. I answer that it is not true that God can punish those whom He does not hate: for that would conflict with His virtues. If He punished *Christ*, it was for the reason that He took the place of the sinners whom He hated <note>In Reformed theology, this refers to 'Penal Substitution,' where Christ legally takes on the guilt and the resulting wrath of God on behalf of the elect.</note>.

One objects with *Job 4:18* and *15:15*, from which one wishes to conclude that God can reject the holy Angels.

Answer: Nothing of the sort can be derived from these passages.

It is not the same with our God as it is with the false deities of the Heathens: the Heathens imagined that their Gods were satisfied with some appearance of satisfaction; they also sometimes offered them painted sacrifices, and they believed that their *Jupiter* allowed himself to be reconciled with the fires that were built in his honor. *Porphyrius* <note>original: "Porphyrius"; a Neoplatonist philosopher who was a prominent critic of early Christianity.</note> writes that *Pythagoras* offered an Ox made of dough; and *Athenæus* <note>original: "Athenæus"; a Greek rhetorician and grammarian.</note> relates that *Empedocles*, a disciple of *Pythagoras*, had an Ox—made of Myrrh, Frankincense, and all kinds of spices—distributed to those present at the Olympic games where he had been crowned. The poor among the Egyptians offered a Pig made of dough to *Bacchus* <note>The Roman name for Dionysus, the god of wine and ritual.</note>. Mr. *Thevenot* <note>Jean de Thévenot (1633–1667), a famous French traveler whose accounts of the East were widely read in the 17th century.</note>, in his *Indian Travelogues*

<column-break/>

Part III, chapter 47, speaking of the *Brahmins* of *Telangana*, a province of *Hindustan*, says that on a certain day of joy they make a cow of dough, which they fill with honey, and thereafter slit its throat and cut it into pieces. He adds that the honey, which drips from all sides, represents the blood of the Cow, and that they eat the dough instead of its flesh.

Our God is a consuming fire, and His justice is so strict that it does not forgive sin where it has not been satisfied. If God did not punish sin, He could just as well not hate it: for when the Scripture ascribes hatred to God, it means by this expression the constant will He has to punish or destroy all that is against His virtues. If it were now possible for God not to hate sin, it would be possible for Him to love it; which is a godless thing to say.

Certainly, if it is not possible for God to leave holiness without reward when He finds it in His creatures, it is even less possible that He leaves their sin without punishment, since the exercise of justice is much more necessary than that of His mercy.

It is a natural knowledge imprinted in the hearts of men that the Deity must punish the insult offered to Him; from this come the terrors of conscience, of which we have dealt elsewhere, and the sacrifices of men that the Heathens offered to their Gods. <margin>Acts 28:4.</margin> The Barbarians of the Island of *Malta* were convinced of this: seeing that a Viper had seized the hand of *Paul*, they said that he was a murderer whom Divine justice would not allow to live.

Those who most oppose the necessity of satisfaction are forced to acknowledge that God cannot leave the impenitent and rebellious unpunished. Now, impenitence is not punishable except insofar as it is an intent to do evil. Impenitence, considered in its essence, is a Perseverance, and perseverance is good or evil according to the various applications one makes of it. It is good in respect to virtue, and evil in respect to vice; from which it follows that perseverance is not actually what God's justice takes as its...

II. It is said, that everyone can waive their rights / and consequently / that God can forgive without satisfaction / since he is the Lord and Master of all men.

I answer, that it is true / that there are certain rights / which one can surrender / for example / a creditor can cancel a debt; someone who is insulted / can choose not to demand satisfaction; a Master can do with his servants as he wills. But I add to this, that the high Authority cannot allow / the laws of the State to be violated with impunity. Now, in this matter, God cannot be viewed as a privately insulted Person / or as a private creditor / but as the supreme Judge and Master of the world / and consequently he cannot leave the transgression of his commandments unpunished.

<margin>Socinus, *Theological Lectures*, chapter 16.</margin>
III. It is said, that sins are depicted to us as debts, and that God therefore must be viewed as a creditor. But one pays no heed to the reason / for which sins are portrayed as debts. This is done to teach us two truths. 1. That our sins give God the same right to punish us / as the debts / that one has made / give a right to a creditor to act against his debtor. 2. That / just as a creditor no longer has a right to act against his debtor / once he has canceled his debt / one also has no need to fear Divine justice / when God has forgiven us our sins; but one must not conclude from this / that it is as easy for God to forgive sins without satisfaction / as it is for a creditor / to cancel a debt; for by canceling what is owed to us / one does not wrong the Law; but one cannot leave the transgression of laws unpunished / without overturning the laws themselves.

Certainly / if one had to conclude from the fact that sins are called debts / that—
