God can forgive them without satisfaction / it would also follow / that God could release us from showing him obedience / which is also called a debt. One could likewise conclude / that God could forgive us / even if we lived in impenitence / something which the deniers of the necessity of satisfaction would not wish to grant.

IV. It is said, that Princes and Authorities often show mercy to those who have violated the laws of the State.
I answer, 1. That Princes sometimes forgive the violation of the Laws of the State / because they can act in no other way. But it is not so with God / who is neither bound nor forced to show mercy. 2. That Princes many times do what they ought not to do / and that their actions are not always as they should be. They sometimes imagine / that they are above the laws / and that they can release others from them / instead of keeping in mind what one reads in the fourth Book of the Laws of **Theodosius** <note>Theodosius II (401–450 AD) was a Roman Emperor; his legal code, the *Codex Theodosianus*, was a primary source of Roman law in the West.</note> / that the Prince is bound to the laws.

<margin>Twisse in *A Vindication of Grace*.</margin>

<margin>Twisse, *Vindication of Grace*. <note>original: "Twiss. Vind. Grat." refers to William Twisse (1578–1646), a prominent English theologian and Prolocutor of the Westminster Assembly.</note></margin>

I answer, that it is / because God can never act against his perfections / and by consequence against his justice ; and that it follows / that God / who is a righteous being / does not go against his justice.

**XI.** It is said, that / if God must necessarily punish sin / it would be / either with a temporal punishment / and then it would follow from that / that sin deserves no eternal punishment / or with an eternal punishment / and then the sinner would have to exist eternally / without God being able to <term>annihilate</term> <note>Annihilate: to completely destroy or reduce to nothing. We have much more reason to believe / that it is only eternal punishments / which are proportional to the sins / that we have committed.

**XII.** It is said, that God would do no one wrong / if he forgave without satisfaction.

I answer, 1. That God would deny himself and his perfections.
2. That one could say by the same way of reasoning / that God could forgive the sins of the impenitent / because he would [do no one] wrong therewith...

## CHAPTER III.

### Whether it is necessary that the sinners themselves satisfy Divine justice.

From what has been said / it appears that it was necessary to satisfy Divine justice for the sins of men. A second problem is proposed / and it is asked whether it was necessary / that the sinners themselves should satisfy it.

To answer this / we say three things.

1. That all sinners deserve to be punished / and that their punishment itself is very consistent with the nature of the matter and with order.

2. That, therefore, Divine justice could have demanded / that the sinners themselves suffered for their sin / without having reason to complain about its severity.

3. That, meanwhile, Justice has been able to step away from some of its severity / and allow another to suffer for mankind in their place.

To understand this truth / one must observe that these are two very distinct matters: not punishing the sin / or not punishing the sinner. The justice and holiness of God do not allow him / to leave the sin unpunished / but they do not oppose the forgiveness of sinners. God / as holy and righteous / cannot refrain from hating sin / and he cannot hate it without punishing it / because / as we have proven elsewhere / to hate in God / means to will to punish. It would then run against his Justice and Holiness if the sin remained unpunished / but these are by no means offended if God / having punished the sin / forgives the sinner / because he / by the punishing of the sins / has satisfied his justice. This way of punishing the sin / and leaving the sinner free / suits God's wisdom: for thus he has found the means / to reconcile his mercy with his justice. If all men had been required to satisfy Divine justice /

<column-break/>

they would all have been subject to eternal death / and there would have been no place for the exercise of mercy: but / another having been placed in the stead of the sinners / justice has enjoyed that which it desired / and mercy has been able to have its course.

Justice has punished the sin / and received the <term>satisfaction</term> <note>Satisfaction: the legal fulfillment of a debt or penalty.</note> for the sinners: but mercy has acquitted the sinner of what he owed / because of the satisfaction of the one who placed himself in his stead and satisfied the debt; consequently, these two things are not contradictory in this matter / satisfaction and forgiveness: the <term>surety</term> <note>Surety: a person who takes legal responsibility for another's debt or behavior.</note> and the mediator of men has satisfied for them / and God forgives them the crimes / for which he had the right to punish them in their own persons.

But / it is said, is it not against God's justice to punish an innocent person for the guilty?

I answer, that this does not conflict with justice / when these conditions are observed.

<margin>
Under what conditions an innocent person can be <unclear>substituted</unclear> for a guilty person.
</margin>
1. That the sin be punished / and that with a punishment proportionate to the greatness of the love / that God has for holiness / and of the hatred / that he has against sin.

2. That the innocent person / who offers himself to suffer / suffers willingly / and that no violence is done to him.

3. That this innocent person be master of his own life / to do with it what he desires.

4. That he can perfectly satisfy for those / for whom he offers himself.

5. That he can deliver himself from death by his own power / and thus the commonwealth <note>The author uses 'gemeenebest' (commonwealth) to imply the moral order of the universe or society, which should not suffer the permanent loss of a righteous person.</note> comes to suffer nothing through the loss of an honorable man.

6. That God be more glorified thereby / than he would be through the punishment of the guilty themselves.

7. That God approves / that an innocent person places himself in the stead of the sinners.

8. That the innocent person has the same nature as the guilty / so that the sin may be punished in the same nature / in which it was committed.

When these conditions are met / one sees / that justice is in no way compromised.

And that Scripture teaches us / in Genesis 9:25 / that Canaan was cursed for the sin of Ham; the children of Achan for their father; the children of Saul for what this King had done; and that Christ threatens the Jews / that he will bring upon them all the righteous blood shed on the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel, to the blood of Zechariah, the son of Berechiah. Matt. 23:35.

I could subsequently make some specific remarks regarding these two scripture passages; but / since I have already explained them elsewhere / I will be content to say / that they do not contradict the truth / that I maintain; for there, it speaks of sinners / who might have been punished for others / and indeed against their will / whereas here we speak of an innocent / who willingly offers himself for the guilty. Secondly, it is certain / that God in all these places does not establish a general law / that allows no exception / and could allow none / especially when one establishes the conditions / that I have cited.

I will add to that / that God did not want men to be ignorant / that there would be a sacrifice / who would take the place of sinners / and bear their punishment. This he made known through the offering / which he willed to be offered to him under the Law / and through the custom / that they had of laying hands on the sacrificial animals / just as the High Priest did on the head of the goat Azazel <note>original: *Hazazel*</note> on the Day of Atonement / confessing over it all the iniquities of the children of Israel, Lev. 16:21, 22. For what purpose did this laying on of hands on the sacrificial animal serve / and the confession of the sins of Israel over the same / except

<column-break/>

to make known / that it took the place of the sinners / and to signify that excellent sacrifice / which was to be established therein in the fullness of time.

It is said, that one does not see such exchanges among men / and that it was forbidden by the Romans / to stand in for another / when it came to death.

I answer: 1. That it is not a matter without precedent / that certain people have offered themselves to die for others / or to undergo some other punishment. The Lawgiver of the Locrians <note>Zaleucus (7th century BCE), a legendary Greek lawmaker</note> has never been blamed / who / to satisfy his law / which commanded that both eyes of an adulterer be put out / had one of his own eyes and one of his son's eyes put out / as his son had fallen into the same sin / transferring in that manner a part of the punishment of the guilty onto the innocent / and that to satisfy justice / and at the same time show mercy.

Nothing was more common among the Pagans / than to make some suffer / what others had deserved. Certain persons were surrendered / even from among the most innocent, for the common welfare. In the cities of Greece, it was the custom / to put the children of Tyrants to death along with the Tyrants. Among the Macedonians / they proceeded with great severity against those who were guilty of the crime of injured majesty <note>original: *gequetste Majesteit*, referring to high treason or *laesa majestas*</note>. Among all nations, the hostages pay for those / whose place they occupy.

Just as one now concludes legitimately from the multitude of deities / that the Pagans worshipped / that all nations have had a hidden conviction / that there is a God / so can one deduce from the customs of the idolatrous nations / however evil / that they have had an idea / that one could be put in the place of another / when one wished to appease the Deity.

# THE CHRISTIAN GOD

<meta>catchword: if</meta>

One understands without difficulty that he must be innocent; for, if he himself had committed any crime, he would have needed another to satisfy the debt for him.

We have seen, and shall consider even more closely, that he had to be human so that humanity could have fellowship with him.

But we must now investigate whether it was necessary for the **Surety** <term>Borg: A legal term for a guarantor who takes responsibility for another's debt</term> of humanity to be a **Divine Person**.

There have been ancient Teachers who did not recognize this absolute necessity of satisfying Divine justice through the incarnation of God’s Son. Among them was **Augustine** in his *Sermon on the Annunciation of the Lord* <note>original: "Serm. de Annunt. Dom."</note>, who says that those who claim God’s Wisdom could devise no other means of redemption than the incarnation are ignorant. Others include **Leo I** in his *Second Sermon on the Incarnation* <note>original: "Serm. II. de Incarn."</note>, and **Bonaventure** <note>original: "in 3. Sent. dist. XX. q. 6."</note>. However, several others have recognized this necessity, such as **Athanasius** in *On the Incarnation of the Word* <note>original: "de Verb. Incar."</note>, **Anselm** in his book *Why God Became Man* <note>original: "cur Deus hom."</note>, **Basil** on Psalm 28, **Ambrose** on Hebrews 9, and **Thomas Aquinas** in *Against the Gentiles* <note>original: "contr. Gentil."</note>.

We shall not doubt this necessity if we consider that sin deserves an infinite punishment—as we have proven elsewhere—because it is committed against an **infinite Majesty**. From this, it follows that a satisfaction of infinite value was required; and consequently, the one who would satisfy this debt had to be God, since there is nothing infinite but God.

But here a great difficulty arises: how is it possible for a Divine Person to have provided satisfaction, since all three Persons of the Trinity were equally offended? For it seems absurd to say that a Person provides satisfaction to themselves.

To this, I have two answers to give.

I. While it is indeed absurd in some cases for a person to satisfy themselves, it is not so in all. For example, if someone who was owed money by another paid themselves, or if someone who was wronged by another came to ask themselves for forgiveness, that would be absurd. But when it concerns a wrong that affects the **common good**, and a satisfaction owed to the **Authority** as Authority, nothing prevents the Authority—assuming the person of the offender—

<column-break/>

from paying on their behalf, and thus satisfying itself. <margin>Titus Livius, *History*, Book II.</margin> The history of **Menenius Agrippa** <note>A Roman consul famous for using a fable to reconcile the commoners and the nobles</note> is well known. There are other cases where one can satisfy oneself. For example, it can happen that the Authority itself breaks the Laws; in this case, if it undergoes the punishment commanded by the laws, it satisfies itself in its capacity as **Judge** and **Authority**.

Thus, a Divine Person can satisfy himself because God must not be viewed here as a private Person, but as a **public Person**: as the Lord and Judge of the World, the Governor of the universe, who is obliged to uphold the rights of the Godhead and not leave the violation of his laws unpunished.

II. One must observe that being an offended Person and being a **Mediator** are not contradictory qualities, except when the offended Person demands the total destruction of the offender. In that case, it involves a contradiction to say that a Person simultaneously demands the destruction and the preservation of someone. But when the offended party requires nothing more than satisfaction for the wrong done, they can serve the office of Mediator and even provide a means themselves by which the crime is punished and the wrong satisfied, while the guilty party remains unpunished. Now, God required nothing else than that satisfaction be made for the wrong done to the **Divine Majesty**.

It was therefore quite possible for one of the Divine Persons, though offended, to place himself between the offended Godhead and the humans who had insulted it.

Furthermore, it has been noted that in the case of the sins for which Christ acted as Mediator, the Son was offended in common with the Father and the Holy Spirit; for one cannot say that the Son was insulted specifically in contrast to the other two Persons. Now, in the **economy of our Salvation**, this common interest of the three Persons has been placed, as it were, into the hands of the Father alone. Thus, one can say that the Son here does not strictly act as an offended Person, and consequently, nothing prevents him from working as a Mediator.

The first of these observations serves to refute an objection commonly made. It is said that if...

# THEOLOGY. IX. B. V. Chapter.

if a Divine Person could satisfy himself, he would be at once angry and reconciled. I answer, that this objection seems to assume that something happens in God similar to what happens in us when we are disturbed and angry; whereas it is certain that God is not subject to **passions** <term>hertstogten: In classical theology, this refers to emotions or internal changes. God is considered "impassible," meaning He does not experience shifting moods or suffering like humans do.</term>. To solve the difficulty, one must ask whether it is possible for a Divine Person to will to punish sin, and at the same time to find the means to forgive the sinner. We see no impossibility or contradiction in that. Nothing prevents a **Ruler** <note>original: "Overheid"</note> from being offended by those who break the laws, and meanwhile providing satisfaction himself. He is angry as the Ruler, but satisfies as a private Person.

One will ask whether it was necessary that the second Divine Person satisfied for sinners.

I answer, that we do not know whether another Person could have satisfied; we know for certain that it was consistent with God's wisdom that the Son was sent by the Father, and that the Holy Spirit applied to us the salvation that the Son has earned. There are theologians who give various reasons for this, some of which are more ingenious than substantial. They say that it was fitting that He who held the middle place between the Father and the Holy Spirit should become the Mediator between God and men; that He who is Son by nature made us children of God by grace, to be His fellow heirs; that the one through whom God prepared the ages should re-create us; that He who is the **Image of the invisible God** should reshape us into God’s image; that He in whom God was well pleased should reconcile us with the Father. But it is better to remain silent than to try to fathom what God has hidden from us.

<column-break/>

### V. CHAPTER.

->How one must understand that the Father has sent His Son; by what principle He sent Him; and for what reason He did not send Him immediately after the Fall.<-

WE have seen that it was necessary for a Divine Person to satisfy for mankind, and we have stated alongside this that the second Person of the Holy Trinity placed Himself in their stead, who is therefore described to us as our **Savior**, our **Redeemer**, our **Mediator**, which we shall explain more broadly in what follows.

<margin>How one must understand that the Father sent the Son. Rom. 8:3. Gal. 4:4.</margin>
Now we have three things to consider.
I. That it is the Father who sent the Son. *God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh.* Romans 8:3. *God sent forth his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law.* Galatians 4:4. If it is now true, as we have shown, that the Persons of the adorable Trinity are equal, how can one have the authority to send the other?

I answer, that these expressions do not indicate any inequality between the Persons, but only that in the work of our salvation these adorable Persons agreed among themselves that the Father would occupy the position of the first founder of the Church, of Sovereign of the world, of Protector and avenger of the Laws, and of the first director of the work of our **Redemption** <note>original: "Verlossinge"</note>. The Son that of Mediator between God and men; and the Holy Spirit that of Comforter and Sanctifier of the believers. This is what the Scripture wants to teach us when it says that the Father has sent the Son and the Spirit. Besides that, it is not always a sign of inequality to be sent, when this sending occurs by mutual consent. Finally, one must take into consideration that as soon as the Son offered Himself to the Father to serve the office of Mediator between God and men, and to die for them, He became in that respect less than the Father...

<margin>By what principle God sent his Son into the world</margin>
II. The second matter that we must investigate is by what principle God sent his Son into the world. I answer that the Scripture says that God gave his Son out of a principle of love. *John 3:16:* <note>original: "Joh. III. 16"</note> it is difficult to conceive that God loved the world when he gave his Son, since he gave him to satisfy his justice and wrath. I answer that one can easily understand that God was able to love humans as his creatures, even though they were the objects of his justice; he loved them so much that he provided them with the means to be reconciled with him and to obtain the forgiveness of the sins they had committed. This truly causes us to stand amazed at God’s infinite love, that he willed to give us a **Mediator** <term>Middelaar: A go-between or advocate; in this context, Jesus Christ acting as the bridge between humanity and God.</term> himself, while we were worthy of nothing else than to bear the righteous punishment of his wrath.

<margin>Why God did not send his Son immediately after the Fall.</margin>
III. But, it is asked, why is it that God did not send his Son immediately after the Fall?

Answer. One might be satisfied with saying that it so pleased God, and that his good pleasure sets limits to our curiosity. But one can give several reasons for this action of God.

1. It was fitting that a work of such great importance as that of our **Redemption** <term>Verlossing: The act of being saved or "bought back" from the debt of sin.</term> should be expected for a long time, to make its importance known and to warn people of it many centuries in advance.

2. It was good that humans saw for many centuries what they could do by themselves, so they might recognize the futility of their own attempts at reconciliation and be made to confess that they would never have discovered the true means to satisfy Divine justice.

3. If sin had been reconciled immediately after it was committed, it might have been viewed as a trivial matter that passes in a moment.

4. It seems it was not appropriate for the Son of God to come during the time of the "infancy" of the Church, because he had to bring with him a perfect knowledge of the secrets

<column-break/>

of the Kingdom of Heaven. Now, the church in her infancy required that she be given the first and weak principles, and that she be kept under the discipline of the law.

# CHAPTER VI.
## Concerning the Divine Oracles that foretold the coming of the Messiah.

**GOD**, who did not wish to send his Son into the world immediately after the fall, nevertheless desired to warn mankind of his coming and to foretell all the circumstances of it, so that they might know him, and so that their faith and hope might be nourished and strengthened by these predictions. It was indeed fitting that such a matter should be foretold, and that God—who has marked in his word the extraordinary purposes of his wisdom, the judgments of his justice, and other changes that occur in the world—likewise revealed this great work of grace therein.

Furthermore, all believers under the Old Testament were bound to believe in the Messiah, not only because it is a truth revealed to them, but also because it is the most important of all truths and the source of all consolation.

But, before we bring forward these **Divine Oracles** <term>Godspraaken: Literally "God-speeches," referring to the prophetic utterances or revelations found in the Bible.</term>, it is necessary to make some general observations.

The 1st is that there are Oracles that belong to no one but the Messiah; and there are those that seem to fit another subject, but which cannot be applied perfectly and in all their extent to any subject other than the Messiah.

The 2nd is that the oldest Oracles are contained in the most general terms, which were presented much more distinctly and clearly as the time approached in which the Messiah was to come into the world.

The 3rd is that the Oracles that foretold the Messiah are sometimes mixed with other things that seem to have no relation to his coming; which may have happened because...

### DIVINITY. IX. B. VI. Chapter.

...that the prophecies of one and the same Prophet are joined together, even though they were spoken at different times.

The 4th point is that most of the divine oracles concerning the Messiah are joined with other prophecies that concerned the temporal deliverance and preservation of the Jewish people, because these were the necessary means to fulfill the promise of the Messiah and to carry out God’s great purpose.

The 5th point is that, since the Messiah is described to us as one who would unite the glory of the Godhead with the weakness and humility of human nature in his Person, and would pass through various states, one must not set what the Prophets give as something great in their prophetic descriptions of the Messiah against the idea they give of his humiliation and of his suffering, as if they were contradictory things; rather, they were meant to converge in his person and in his various states.

The 6th and final observation is that some divine oracles characterize the time of his coming, and others his Person.

We shall begin with the first.

<margin>Gen. 49:10</margin>
The first divine oracle that mentions the time of the coming of the Messiah is contained in the words of the dying Jacob, Gen. 49:10. *The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the Lawgiver from between his feet (or from among his citizens, as some translate) until Shiloh comes; and to him shall the obedience of the peoples be.* <note>original: "tot dat de Scilo komt"</note> This divine oracle is applied by the Jews themselves to the Messiah, although some of them attribute it to Moses, others to David, others to Jeroboam, and others to other Kings of Judah.

<margin>See further Sanhedrin c. 11; Bereshit Rabbah; R. Bechai; R. M. Gerundensis; R. Joel Ben Sueb; Abrabanel in Manasseh’s Conciliator.</margin>
The Chaldean Paraphrast <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note> named Onkelos, the Jerusalem Targum, Jonathan Uziel, and Rabbi Solomon <note>Known as Rashi, a famous medieval commentator who lived around 1100.</note> have all assigned this prophecy to the Messiah. There are even those who, through the **Kabbalah of Numbers** <term>Gematria: A Jewish system of assigning numerical values to Hebrew letters to find hidden meanings in words.</term> <note>original: "La Cabale des Nombres"</note>, have found in two words of this prophecy the same numerical value found in the word that means *Messiah*. Others bring these words of Jacob home to Moses, because the name of Moses and that of Shiloh in Hebrew both amount to 345.

<column-break/>

But what Scepter did Judah have until the coming of Moses? And how can it be said of Moses that he was the expectation of the nations and the object of their hope? What is drawn from the hidden art of numbers is ridiculous; by that method, one could also find the word *Messiah* and the name *Jesus* in these prophecies. Others apply the same to Saul because, they say, he was anointed at Shiloh. But 1. Saul was not anointed at Shiloh, but at Ramah. 2. Before Saul, the Scepter had not been in the Tribe of Judah. 3. Finally, it was during the life of Saul that the Scepter was transferred to the Tribe of Judah, far from departing from it.

Others have assigned it to David. But, far from the Scepter of Judah departing in the time of David, it can be said that this Tribe then only first began to reign; although one cannot deny that before this time it had some precedence over the other Tribes in certain cases. Others refer it to the place called Shiloh, where the Tabernacle stood in the beginning, and translate the text thus: *until the Tabernacle of Shiloh shall be destroyed.*

But this opinion is no less ridiculous than that of those who assign it to Ahijah the Shilonite. They do not deserve to be refuted. Others attribute it to Jeroboam, whom they claim was crowned at Shiloh; but he was crowned at Shechem, 1 Kings 12, and the Scepter did not then depart from Judah. Others assign it to Nebuchadnezzar; but it is clear that Jacob here foretells the advantages of the Tribe of Judah, and in no way its calamities. Now everyone knows that this godless Prince brought one of the greatest calamities to this Tribe that it ever suffered. This is enough to refute those who believe that *Shiloh* is not a person, nor a beneficial thing, but a disastrous one—namely, the destruction of the Royal Dignity and Scepter of Judah—and thus translate the Hebrew: *The scepter or the government shall not depart, until it shall end forever, whether the tribe or the government.*

One is blind if one does not see the inappropriateness of this interpretation. It is said that *Shiloh* can be derived from a Chaldean verb meaning *to cease* or *to end*; or from an Arabic one meaning *he has failed* or *he has stopped*

# THE CHRISTIAN

...to be, signifies. But a clever 
<margin>Gusset <note>James Gusset (1636–1704) was a French Hebrew scholar often cited in these theological debates.</note></margin>
man observes: 1. That one sees no reason why one would wish to make Jacob speak Chaldean <note>A term often used for Aramaic.</note> or Arabic in a Hebrew discourse. 2. That neither Daniel nor Ezra <note>original: "Esdras"</note> ever used this word to mean "to cease"; and that consequently, one has reason to doubt that the word itself—or the word it is derived from—meant "to cease" in the Old Chaldean language; although one cannot deny that it is used in the Chaldean paraphrases <note>The Targums: Aramaic translations/interpretations of the Hebrew Bible.</note> in the sense of "destruction": but there is little appearance that it was taken in that sense in the time of Jacob. 3. That one finds in no Arabic dictionary that this word means "he has failed" or "he has ceased to be." But in order not to occupy ourselves with all these bitterness-inducing details, it will be enough to observe that those who translate and expand upon this passage in such a way completely miss the objective of Jacob. To make him say that the Tribe of Judah shall not end until it ends is to make him speak an unripened language that has no meaning.

<margin>Menasseh, Question 65 on Genesis. <note>Referring to Menasseh ben Israel (1604–1657), a famous Portuguese Rabbi in Amsterdam.</note></margin>
There are those who translate: *The scepter shall never depart from Judah, even when the Messiah shall have come.* But it is certain that the Hebrew word which these interpreters translate as "never" or "eternally" does not mean that, except when it concludes a sentence entirely; and then it is usually either repeated with the same word or paired with another that signifies eternity. Now, in this place, it is joined with a word that commonly means "until." It is not true that the accent-mark <note>original: "toon-stip," referring to the Hebrew cantillation marks (trope) that guide the reading and logic of the verse.</note> which stands above this word divides the sentence. The contrary appears through the following verse.

Others say that these words amount to this sense: that when there shall be Kings in Israel, they shall all be of the Tribe of Judah. But this has not been proven; for the ten tribes had Kings from other Tribes.

In order to properly understand the oracle <note>original: "Godspraak"</note> of Jacob, one must make the following observations:

1. That the same is a prophecy for the benefit of the Tribe of Judah in particular, just as every oracle that precedes or follows this one concerns each individual Tribe.

2. That by the word "scepter" one 

<column-break/>

must understand the Royal dignity to which this Tribe would be elevated, Zechariah 10:11.

The Jews translate it as "rod," <note>Implying a rod of punishment or affliction.</note> but they are mistaken. 1. For Jacob does not present a threat to Judah here, but a promise. 2. It is untrue that the rod never departed from the back of Judah before the coming of the Messiah. 3. The Tribe of Judah has not been more chastised than the others. Finally, the fact that something is added regarding the Lawgiver shows that we are not speaking here of a rod of chastisement, but of a scepter of government. The translations of the Septuagint <note>original: "LXX," the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, of Aquila, Symmachus, and the Chaldean paraphrases favor our interpretation. There are Jews who say that this oracle means that the Jews will never lack support in their oppressions (Menasseh, *Conciliator* Question 65 on Genesis, page 89). But 1. if this had been the meaning of Jacob, he would have expressed himself differently. 2. The root word, when stated absolutely like this, does not mean "support," unless it were paired with something else, as in Psalm 23. Furthermore, Jacob would not have limited this promise to the Tribe of Judah alone. Finally, it is ridiculous to explain these last words thus: "and to him shall be the oppression of the Heathens."

There are scholars who believe that one should translate: "and the tribe shall not depart from Judah," to say that this tribe would always remain distinct from the other tribes until the coming of the Messiah, after which they would be mixed with the others. But it seems to me that the common explanation is the most natural, although this latter one can indeed be defended. One can even say that through this explanation, one more easily solves some difficulties that are raised, and of which I shall speak in what follows.

3. That it appears through this oracle that the tribe of Judah would ascend the Throne.

The same has always had some precedence; God commanded that it should be the first to set out, Numbers 2:3, 10:14. Their leaders offered the first gifts, Numbers 7:11, 12. In the time of Joshua, this tribe took its inheritance without drawing lots. After Joshua, God commanded that Judah should hold the supreme command to take the remainder of the promised land. This tribe has given its name to the others. <note>Referring to how the term "Jew" is derived from "Judah."</note>

4. That...

### THEOLOGY. IX. BOOK VI. CHAPTER.

4. That the same tribe would reign for a considerable time; indeed, there were Kings from this tribe until the taking of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar <note>The Babylonian king who destroyed the first Temple in 586 BCE.</note>.

1. There are Jews who explain Jacob's words thus: *The scepter and the lawgiver from the blood of Judah shall not depart forever, since the Shiloh <note>A title traditionally interpreted by both Jews and Christians as referring to the Messiah.</note> shall come,* and the reason they give for this is that the temporal scepter did not remain with Judah until the coming of the Messiah. But 1. We have already shown that the text cannot be translated in that way. 2. It is not true that the scepter and the Lawgiver entirely departed before the coming of the Messiah. 3. The rebellion of Jeroboam <note>The first king of the breakaway Northern Kingdom of Israel.</note> did not cause the scepter of Judah to depart. 4. This happened through the Babylonian captivity. But the Jews later obtained rulers from this tribe. If one had to translate this <term>oracle</term> <note>original: "Godspraak," referring to a divine prophecy.</note> in such a way, it would conflict with that of Daniel, who says that after the coming of the Messiah, the people of the Prince shall come, who shall destroy the City and the Temple.

5. That this tribe, in the course of time, would come to lose some of its dignity; and therefore the Lawgiver is spoken of after the Scepter.

This happened by degrees. Under David's grandson <note>Rehoboam, whose reign saw the ten northern tribes secede.</note>, ten tribes fell away, who no longer wished to subject themselves to the scepter of Judah. The kings who followed Rehoboam became tributary to neighboring Kings, whereas David had extended the borders of his kingdom to the gates of Babylon. The Babylonians brought the Jews under subjection and took from the Kings of Judah the authority they had. Then the scepter departed. But then came Lawgivers; Zerubbabel <note>The grandson of King Jehoiachin and a leader of the Jewish people returning from Babylonian exile.</note> was the head of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. Since his time, the tribe of Judah has had heads of the Jewish Nation, although they were not always of the tribe of Judah, which was not necessary for the fulfillment of the Prophecy. For it is not always true that Kings must be of the same nation as their subjects; just as Poland has had French Kings. The Hasmoneans <note>The dynasty of the Maccabees who ruled Judea in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE.</note> always maintained authority in this tribe, until it was stripped of it by the Romans, which also happened gradually and by degrees: 1. Under Pompey <note>The Roman general who captured Jerusalem in 63 BCE.</note>, 60 years before the birth of Christ. 2. When Judea became a province of the Roman Empire. 3. Under Titus,

<column-break/>

when the Temple and City were destroyed. Yet it appears that there were always either Kings or Lawgivers until the coming of the Messiah.

6. Finally, the prophecy indicates that the tribe of Judah would remain in possession of at least some form of government until the coming of the Messiah, so that one must conclude that this prophecy here, as a sign of the time of Christ’s coming, gives the time of the downfall of the power and authority which the tribe of Judah had still retained in some measure after the Babylonian captivity. Furthermore, one should not be surprised that the scripture teaches us that the scepter and the lawgiver shall not depart before the coming of the Messiah; for, since the Messiah had to be born from the tribe of Judah, he had to come before the Jewish commonwealth had perished and the tribes were mixed together.

The Second Prophecy, in which the coming of the Messiah is predicted, is taken not only from the 2nd Chapter of Daniel, where the Empire under which he would appear is pointed out, but specifically from the 9th Chapter of that Prophet, which marks the time of his coming and of his death.

To understand this <term>prophecy</term> <note>original: "Godspraak," referring to a divine oracle or word from God.</note>, one must observe:

1. That by the "Weeks" of which Daniel speaks, one must understand seven years <note>The "day-year principle," where each day in a prophetic week represents one calendar year.</note>, each day for a year, according to the Hebrew style, *Ezekiel 4:6, Leviticus 25:8.* Thus, 70 weeks make 490 years. For, if one spoke here of weeks properly named of 7 days, they would make only one and a half years, in which nothing of what the Angel had foretold occurred. To imagine that this refers to weeks of 10 years, as *Origen* <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 CE).</note> believed—who calculated that the 70 weeks from *Adam* made 4900 years until *Christ*—or to weeks of Jubilee years, so that 70 weeks yield 3430 years, is without the slightest basis; never is the word "Week" taken for a week of 10 years. Daniel places the coming of the *Messiah* before the destruction of the Temple. But if one had to take Daniel's weeks as weeks of 10 years or Jubilee years, the destruction of the Temple would have preceded the coming of the *Messiah*.

2. One must observe that the years of the Chaldeans <note>The Babylonians.</note> were of 360 days, from which one can deduce that 1260 days make three and a half years.

### DIVINE LEARNING. IX. B. VI. Chapter. ###

books [state] that the Prophet has determined the time that would pass from the destruction of the first Temple under **Zedekiah** <note>The last king of Judah before the Babylonian captivity.</note> until that of the second Temple by the **Romeinen** <note>The Romans, who destroyed the Temple in 70 CE.</note>; and they maintain that this calculation is correct, since exactly 490 years passed from the first to the second destruction. But **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the Greco-Egyptian astronomer and geographer whose "Canon of Kings" is a standard for ancient chronology.</note>, who cannot be held under suspicion here, places 650 years from the destruction of the first Temple until the campaign of **Vespasian**. **Josephus** <note>A first-century Jewish historian.</note> testifies that the second Temple lasted 639 years. However, the Jews are poor chronologists <note>The author likely refers to the *Seder Olam Rabbah*, a traditional Jewish chronology that significantly shortens the Persian period.</note>.

There are Jews, and Christians as well, who are of the opinion that by **Messiah the Prince** one must understand someone other than He who is absolutely called the **Messiah**; they argue that it is said that one shall come after the 7 weeks, and the other shall be cut off after the 62 weeks.

But 1. the difficulty in which they find themselves to say who this **Messiah the Prince**, as distinct from the **Messiah**, actually is, shows the groundlessness of their opinion. 2. One must join the two numbers of 7 and 62 together; it is not strange to see numbers noted separately, as in **Ezekiel 45:12, etc.**

**Marsham** <note>Sir John Marsham (1602–1685), an English chronicler known for his work *Canon Chronicus*.</note>, who separates these two numbers and believes that the first concerns the times of **Cyrus** and the second those of **Antiochus Epiphanes**, presents his view as follows. He lays down as a foundation that the prayer of **Daniel** and the words of the **Angel** were spoken in the 21st year of the captivity, and he tries to prove from this that **Daniel** had this vision after his prayer and fasting, **Dan. 9:3, 4.** Now, he claims that the fasting of **Daniel** lasted 21 years, because it is said that he mourned for 3 weeks, **Dan. 10:3, 4.**

Answer. But 1. there is no appearance that these three weeks signify 21 years: for, besides many reasons that could be brought against this opinion, **Daniel** says that he speaks of "weeks of days," <note>Daniel 10:2-3 specifically uses the Hebrew term *shabuim yamim* to distinguish them from the prophetic "weeks of years."</note> and consequently not of 21 years, but of 21 days or three weeks. It in no way appears that the vision in **Dan. 10:3**, which happened in the 3rd year of **Cyrus**, is the same as **Dan. 9:3, 4**, which he saw in the first year of **Darius the Mede**—which one would nevertheless have to suppose to make the opinion of

<column-break/>

**Marsham** valid. 2. If the first 7 weeks of **Daniel** end with **Cyrus**, as **Marsham** desires, and the 62 and a half weeks—that is, 444 and a half years—end with **Antiochus**, one would have to posit that 444 and a half years elapsed from **Cyrus** to **Antiochus**. Now, **Marsham** himself does not believe this. To make his calculation fit, he made other additions, according to which one would have to say that only 60 weeks were determined for the Jewish People, instead of 70, as the **Angel** testifies.

<margin>Haggai 2:7, 8, 9.</margin>

> Yet once, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens and the earth, and the sea and the dry land. 1. It appears that this prophecy does not concern the deliverance from **Babylon**, which had already occurred; nor the building of the second Temple, which was already finished.

3. That the **Prophet** here predicts a great change, which he portrays as a new movement of Heaven and earth; wherein it is clear to see that he alludes to that time in which **God** truly moved Heaven and Earth, when He delivered His people out of **Egypt**, gave His law on **Sinai**, and brought them into the possession of the Promised Land.

4. That **God** declares this will happen in a little time, by which it is made known that this prophecy will have its fulfillment a few centuries after that of the **Prophet**.

5. That he says the glory of the second house shall be much greater than that of the first. Now, one cannot understand wherein this greater glory would lie, except in this: that the **Messiah** would [fill] it with His presence.

### THEOLOGY. BOOK IX. SECTION B. CHAPTER VI. ###

On the contrary, one observes that most nations have enslaved themselves to him, so that one could much sooner say that *Satan* crushes the heads of most men. To say that *God* intended nothing more by this than the aversion and hatred that exists between humans and snakes is the height of absurdity. For would it be fitting for *God* to signify such a minor matter with such elevated and meaningful words? Especially in a solemn judgment pronounced after a great crime, in which not only the human race but all creatures had an interest. Nor can one understand it to mean the descendants of *Abraham*, for why give them this name rather than other people?

It appears from this Prophecy that the *Messiah* would be born of a Woman, since he is called the seed of the Woman, and that he would be a true human. Some even rightly conclude from this that he would be born of a Woman without the involvement of a Man <note>This refers to the doctrine of the Virgin Birth.</note>.

2. That the *Messiah* would break the power of *Satan*, for that is what the crushing of the Serpent’s head signifies; and thus the *Messiah* would be more than a mere human. *God* wished to put *Satan* to shame through the weakness of the female sex, which *Satan* had used to corrupt the work of *God*.

3. That the *Messiah*, however, would receive a mortal wound from *Satan's* side, although he would only strike his heel—that is to say, his least noble part—and that the *Messiah* would have a nature that could be wounded.

4. That the *Messiah* would have infinite power; for what power is not required to bring down the Kingdom of *Satan*, to overthrow his Throne, and to annihilate that tyrannical authority which he had obtained by force over the human race? Now, such a power can be found in *God* alone. We shall see in the following sections to whom all these sayings apply.

<margin>Gen. XXII. 18. etc.</margin>
The second Prophecy is *Gen. 22:18*, where *God* says to *Abraham*, *In your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed.*

This Prophecy teaches us something more than the first, namely:

<column-break/>

1. That the *Messiah* would spring from *Abraham's* descendants.

In deed, this refers to the *Messiah* and not to the *Jews*, although they are the seed of *Abraham*. 1. The nations have not embraced the Jewish faith, although the *Jews* have often followed the superstitions and idolatry of the nations. 2. It never happened in those times that all the nations of the earth entered into communion with the seed of *Abraham*. 3. Finally, it appears that *God*, for the sake of the *Israelites*, abandoned all other nations; but one reads nowhere that *God* blessed the other nations solely for their sake. One must be careful not to believe that what *God* says to *Abraham* here only means that his descendants will be so happy that if one wanted to bless someone or wish them well, one would cite them as an example of Heaven's favor, as in *Gen. 48:20*. *Paul* teaches us otherwise when he consistently applies this Prophecy to the *Messiah* in his letters. *Abraham* had understood it in that same sense. Also, *Christ* says that he saw his day and rejoiced in it, *John 8:56*.

2. This Prophecy further indicates that the *Messiah* would be the fountainhead of all blessings.

# THE CHRISTIAN GOD

...to be the foundation and the support of the Church, verse 22: *The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.* <note>original: "hooft des hoeks"</note>

<margin>
Psalm 132 and 89.

The 132nd Psalm teaches us, as well as the 89th, that the *Messiah* would spring from the house of *David*.

<margin>
Isaiah 7:14.
</margin>
The Book of *Isaiah* is full of prophecies of the *Messiah*. I will only bring up a few. According to Isaiah 7:14, he was to be born of a virgin; *behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name IMMANUEL.* To understand this oracle <note>original: "Godspraak"</note> fundamentally, one would have to bring many matters to the table; but since they would lead me too far astray, and I must still speak of it in the 18th Chapter, I will content myself for the present by making the following remarks.

I. That the Prophet presents this birth as a miracle and an unheard-of thing, which certainly would not be so highly exalted if it spoke only of an ordinary childbirth of a married woman, according to the opinion of the Jews.

<margin>
Exodus 3:12.
1 Samuel 2:34.
1 Kings 22:25.
2 Kings 8:2.
Jeremiah 44:29.
</margin>
II. That the Prophet gives this promise of the *Messiah* to *Ahaz* in order to confirm to this King, and to the Jews, the promises he made to them at that time—that they would be delivered from the violence of their enemies who were besieging *Jerusalem*. This should seem strange to no one:
1. Because as a sign of things yet to happen, one can give other things that will not occur until after the promised or predicted matter has taken place.
2. Because all the promises God made to the Jews rested upon the *Messiah*.
3. Finally, because if it were true, as *Ahaz* feared, that the entire nation was about to perish, God would not have sent the *Messiah*; thus, by assuring them that he will send them the *Messiah*, God assured them at the same time that he would provide all the deliverances he deemed necessary for that end. Furthermore, one should not be surprised that it seems the following words refer to another object than the *Messiah*; for in all appearance the Prophet gave two signs to *Ahaz*: one taken from the coming of the *Messiah*, and another of a child he had with him and pointed to with his finger. The first sign was a future matter, and the second a present one.

<column-break/>

III. That the son of the virgin, named *Immanuel*, is depicted in the following 8th Chapter as the Lord of the whole earth, verse 8.

Indeed, when this oracle was spoken, *Hezekiah* <note>King Hezekiah of Judah.</note> was nine years old. Therefore, *Isaiah*, speaking of *Hezekiah*, could not say, *behold, a virgin shall conceive.* Some say that since *Hezekiah*, no *Messiah* was to be expected. But can a greater absurdity be thought of?

<margin>
Isaiah 9:5. The Chaldean Paraphrase <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary.</note> applies this passage to the Messiah.
</margin>
The 9th Chapter also contains a glorious description of the *Messiah*, verse 5: *A child is born to us, a son is given to us, and the government is upon his shoulder, and his name is called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of Eternity, Prince of Peace.*

To apply this oracle to *Hezekiah* is also to blind oneself; for is there anyone of sound mind and reason who would dare to attribute to a mortal Prince all that the Prophet states here? These words also cannot be applied to God the Father, as if *Isaiah* had only meant to say that God the Father, who is the *Wonderful One*, etc., would call this child the *Prince of Peace*. For what reason would the Prophet have heaped so many titles of honor upon one another to signify God the Father, when it clearly appears that his aim is to speak of the Son, and not of the Father? Also, the name of *Counselor* <note>original: "Raad"</note> does not belong to the Father.

Isaiah 11:1 etc.
</margin>

One also sees there with what gifts of the spirit the *Messiah* would be endowed; the peace of his kingdom, and the calling of the Gentiles.

In the Book of the Prophet Daniel, there are many glorious Prophecies.

<margin>Daniel 2:44</margin>
Daniel 2:44. In the days of those kings, the God of Heaven shall set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed; and that kingdom shall not be left to another people: it shall break in pieces and consume all those kingdoms, but it shall itself stand for all eternity.

<margin>verse 34</margin>
The Prophet had, in the same chapter, described the Messiah as a small stone, cut out without hands, which had shattered the image and had become a great mountain. The cutting of this stone without hands indicated that the Messiah would come into the world directly through God’s power; the smallness of the stone signified his humble beginnings; but that the same became a great mountain was a sign of his exaltation.

To his Kingdom, he gives four qualities, which are set against the four weaknesses of other Realms, which can be brought down by the weapons of enemies, transferred to strangers without war and without violence, held in balance by others, and destroyed by time.

<margin>Daniel 7:13</margin>
In the 7th Chapter, Daniel says in verse 13: Furthermore, I saw in the night visions, and behold, one like a son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and he came to the Ancient of Days, and they brought him near before him, etc.

Here the Messiah is called the Son of Man to show that he would be human; but by adding "like a son of man," this possibly serves to teach that the Messiah would not be a mere human, but also the Son of God, appearing in a human form.

<margin>Micah 5:1</margin>
The Prophecy <note>original: "Godspraak"</note> of Micah deserves our attention, Micah 5:1. And you, Bethlehem Ephratha, though you are small among the thousands of Judah, out of you shall come forth to me one who is to be a Ruler in Israel, and whose goings forth are from of old, from the days of eternity.

Here the Prophet notes:

The place of the birth of the Messiah, namely Bethlehem, which he calls Ephratha <note>Ephratha was the ancient name for Bethlehem, used here to specify the exact town in the territory of Judah.</note>, where the lineage of David originated, to distinguish it from another Bethlehem situated in a different Tribe.

2. The reason for which the Messiah would come: to be a ruler in Israel.

3. His Divine nature; his goings forth are from the days of eternity.

4. Subsequently, Micah speaks of the stability and vastness of his Kingdom.

The Jews also apply this passage to the Messiah, such as the Chaldean Paraphrast <note>A reference to the Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, Rabbi Salomon Jarchi <note>Also known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval French rabbi and author.</note>, Kimchi <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a medieval rabbi and biblical grammarian.</note>, and Rabbi Eliezer. This application appears clearly from Matthew 2:5-6. There are Jews who say that Bethlehem was counted among the thousands of Judah because David was to come forth from it, and the Messiah from David; but if these words were to be taken thus, Micah would say, "out of you *has* come forth," and not "*shall* come forth the Ruler in Israel." By this Ruler, Zerubbabel <note>A governor of the Persian Province of Judah and grandson of King Jehoiachin; some skeptics argued the prophecy referred to him instead of Jesus.</note> cannot be understood, for he was not born in Bethlehem.

Even one of their most famous Rabbis acknowledges that they sit without a King or Prince of their own nation, and that they are under the power of the Gentiles. For to say that they have Kings in Babylon or elsewhere who are of the House of David, as one of their <margin>Benjamin in his Itinerary</margin> writers <note>Likely Benjamin of Tudela, a 12th-century Jewish traveler.</note> would claim, is a mere fiction, the falsehood of which the Jews themselves know; for if this were so, they would not fail to go to that place with hope, where they could be subject to their own Kings. One must not say that this is merely a temporary suspension of the acts of government, such as happened to them during the Babylonian captivity. For between that captivity, which lasted only 70 years, and the miserable state in which they have been for 1600 years, there is a great difference.

II. Moreover, it is certain that the 70 weeks of Daniel have expired, whether one begins counting them from the 2nd year of Darius Nothus, or from the 20th of Artaxerxes, or from another point in time that we have cited in the preceding chapters. The Messiah, who was to come then and be cut off after the end of 69 weeks, has come.

III. This observation is confirmed by the following. The Messiah had to come while the Second Temple stood; he has therefore come, since this Second Temple was destroyed and laid in ashes by the Romans.

To these reasons, which we draw from scripture, we can add several others that confirm the same truth.

The wretched state of the Jews, the confusion of their tribes, the futile efforts they have made to restore themselves, are proofs that place the coming of Christ beyond dispute. In the year 135, Emperor Hadrian forbade them from even turning their eyes toward Judea. <margin>Apology, chapter 21</margin> Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage, writing around 200 AD.</note> recounts how in his time they

The Emperor Honorius deprived them of the right to appoint Patriarchs and to pay them the tribute money; Julian the Apostate, having permitted them to rebuild the Temple in the year 363 and having given the management thereof to Alypius of Antioch, who had previously been the Governor in Britain, it happened, <margin>Book 23. Now everyone knows how greatly their tribes and genealogical registers are confused, and that the House of David is entirely unknown among them; who then can doubt that the Messiah has come?

The calling of the Gentiles, which was to follow the coming of the Messiah, also proves as clear as day that he has come.

Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note>, in the letter cited by Vossius, brings forward a tradition which says that the Messiah was to come in the year 4976.

I. They say that the Messiah indeed should have come at the time we specify, but that their sins have prevented his appearance, and that he awaits Israel’s conversion.

**Answer 1.** Let them tell us what this great sin is that has delayed the coming of the Messiah. They acknowledge that their first Temple was destroyed because of their idolatry, their licentiousness, and their murders. Yet, they remained in captivity in Babylon for no longer than 70 years, and they had Prophets who comforted them. How is it that God has kept them in this miserable state now for more than 1,600 years, even though during this time they have guarded themselves against all idolatry? It is true that they already had a great aversion to it under the second Temple, preferring to suffer anything rather than allow the Image of the Emperor or the Roman Eagle to be erected in the Temple. Certainly, the Jews can point to no cause for their long-lasting dispersion, unless they consider that it is because they put the Messiah to death. Therefore, the Messiah has come.

The Jews will say that the death of Christ is a crime that cannot be blamed on the Judges of that time. But 1. It was the crime of the Great Council, which represented the entire people. 2. One must well note that they cried out, *His blood be upon us and upon our children.* 3. Today’s Jews, through their stubbornness, approve the verdict of the ancients.

2. How can they prove that the coming of the Messiah is conditional? Where has God said, "if they should convert"? And how is it that we have seen, and still see, that everything which according to the Prophets was to happen after the coming of the Messiah has indeed occurred, if he has not come? They themselves distinguish between two ages: the present and the future. They call the present the time in which the Prophets prophesied, and the future the time of the coming of the Messiah. Why then can one not say that the Messiah was to come at the end of the age which they themselves call the present age? One must not always press too hard on the word "end"; compare in this regard <term>Job XLII. 12.</term> with verse 16.

# THE CHRISTIAN <note>This header likely continues from the previous page as "THE CHRISTIAN THEOLOGY" or "RELIGION".</note>

just as he has crushed the head of the Serpent, so has the Serpent wounded his heels—that is, his human nature—so that he died, but only for a few days.

He is the Seed of Abraham, sprouted from the loins of this Patriarch, in whom all nations should be blessed; which blessing includes our justification (Galatians 3:7, 8, 13, 14), our adoption as children (Galatians 3:29, 4:28), the gifts of the Holy Spirit (Galatians 3:14), and the Salvation that is represented to us by sitting at the table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

To him belongs the Scepter; and he is consequently the Shiloh <note>A title for the Messiah from Genesis 49:10, often interpreted as "he to whom it belongs" or "Prince of Peace."</note> and the Star that would come forth from Jacob.

He is that great Prophet, like Moses, who delivered God’s people from a much more cruel slavery than that of Egypt and led them into the Heavenly Canaan <note>The Promised Land, here used as a metaphor for Heaven.</note>, which Moses could not have done; who is the Mediator of the New Covenant, the Head and the Founder of the Church.

He is that Redeemer <note>Original Dutch: *Losser*, a term referring to a "Kinsman-Redeemer" who buys back family land or freedom.</note> of whom Job spoke, who died but lives; of whom David makes mention, saying that the Father has begotten him; to whom all the kings of the earth must do homage; who was given gall and vinegar to drink; who indeed descended into the grave, but without seeing corruption.

It is he who drank from the brook along the way, but thereafter lifted up his head, taking his place at the right hand of God in the highest Heavens.

He is that Wonderful [Counselor], Counselor, Prince of Peace, Father of Eternity, Mighty God, the Lord Our Righteousness, the Angel of the Covenant; in short, the Messiah, whose Kingdom shall have no end; who came to reconcile the transgression, to seal up sin, and to bring in everlasting righteousness. He is our true Emmanuel, "God with us," just as Isaiah 7:14 had predicted.

The Jews cannot bear our confession that Jesus, the Son of Mary, is the Messiah, because they imagine a triumphant Messiah who must appear in the world as a Conqueror. But one has only to read the aforementioned oracles <note>Prophetic utterances or divine communications.</note> to be convinced that they have a false conception of the Messiah.

Furthermore, they suppose that the

<column-break/>

Messiah will deliver them from their enemies, restore his temporal Kingdom, and appear in a glorious form. But they must well know that they have more formidable enemies to overcome than the Romans and other visible adversaries, namely: sin and the devils.

They say that our Savior himself said, *I did not come to bring peace on the earth, but the sword* (Matthew 10:34); and that if Jesus were the Messiah, one would see no wars nor idolatries in the world.

I answer: 1. That Christ intended to teach us by these words what the preaching of his Gospel would effect in the world because of the perversity of men; and the Prophets had foretold this, namely, that he would be a stone of stumbling and offense. 2. That the wars that are in the world are not caused by the teaching of Christ, which brings men to peace, but by the corruption of those who will not submit to it. 3. That the oracles which foretold that idols would be destroyed in the time of the Messiah did not have to receive their fulfillment all at once, but by degrees; that furthermore, the Christian Religion condemns all sorts of idolatry; and that idolatry is banished from all places and communities where the true Gospel is confessed in its purity; and that if there is still a Church that gives itself the name of "Christian Church" and is nonetheless defiled with idolatry, it must be regarded as an Antichristian Church.

They say that the Messiah was to bring the Jewish people back into the land of Canaan (Isaiah 11:11, 12, 13; Ezekiel 37:25, 28; Zechariah 2:10, 11, etc.) and that, on the contrary, the people were driven out of it shortly after the death of Christ.

Answer: 1. These passages, for the most part, refer to the time of the Babylonian captivity. 2. It is true that there are some that cannot be taken according to the letter. Is it likely that the Messiah, who is sent by God to be King over all nations, was intended only to bring the Israelites back into their Land?

They say that the Gospel differs so much from the law which God has instituted, that one cannot regard the maker of the Gospel as the Messiah.

I answer that the Law contains two kinds of commandments, of which some are so consistent with God's holiness that one cannot release oneself from the obligation one has to maintain them. Others depend so much on His will that He himself could release men from them whenever He judged it good. If the Gospel opposed the first kind of commandments, there would be reason to regard it as a false doctrine, and not to recognize its giver as the Messiah; but far from opposing these commandments, it confirms them. They say that Christ caused himself to be worshipped as God.

### VIII. CHAPTER.

->Of the Law.<-

Before God sent his Son into the world, he wished to give his Law to mankind. We shall see in the following why he acted in this manner; now we must investigate what the Law is that God has given. But, before we come to the investigation of this matter, it is necessary to make two or three observations.

1. That one must generally understand the **Law** as a standard <note>original: "rigtsnoer," meaning a rule or plumb-line</note> that binds the people to whom it is given.
2. That, from the beginning of Creation, God imprinted a natural Law in the heart of man to be a rule for his duties.
3. That all people find this Law written in their hearts, the principles of which are these: that one must worship God, that one must honor one's parents, that one must do to another what one
<sig>Part I.</sig>

<column-break/>

wishes to be done to oneself, etc.

Holy Scripture does not allow us to doubt that there is such a natural Law. Paul speaks of it expressly, Rom. II, 14, saying that the Heathens are a Law unto themselves. We have dealt with that in Book I of our work.

This is confirmed by the unanimous consent of nations, among whom one finds these first seeds of knowledge and these first principles, of which we have spoken elsewhere.

It is true that there are nations that have even established godless Laws: but it is because they misused the reason that God had given them, and took no heed of the principles of Natural Law that were within them.

The Heathens then recognized the Natural Law. Cicero, speaking of the efforts one makes to protect one's life, says that it is a Law which is not written, but born with us, which we have not learned, received, nor read, but have accepted and sucked in from nature, for which we were not fashioned or taught, but for which we were made and imbued. <note>original: "non scripta, sed nata lex" - a famous quote from Cicero’s defense of Milo, arguing that self-defense is a natural right.</note>

This Natural Law can neither be abolished nor destroyed. It is the same in Rome, in Athens, everywhere.

God has had the same Law proclaimed to mankind, and then it is called the Moral Law <term>Moral Law: "Zede-Wet," referring to the divinely revealed ethical commandments, such as the Ten Commandments, as opposed to ritual or civil laws</term>. This he has done: 1. To confirm the Natural Law which he had engraved in the hearts of all men. 2. To prevent the natural knowledge one has of good and evil from being erased by the corruption of mankind. 3. To prevent this knowledge from being taken for a mere human invention. 4. To place people’s duty more clearly before their eyes. 5. To restore the Natural Law, as it has suffered through sin, and to renew the ideas that had perished. There are other reasons to be given for this, which we shall cite in the following.

There is, then, no essential difference between the Natural and the Moral Law. Both prescribe the same duties, both toward God and toward our neighbor.

The difference is further minor. The proclaimed Law explains the duties of man more clearly than the Natural Law, not to mention that the one is written on stone, and the other on the fleshy tables of
<sig>D d d</sig>

# THE CHRISTIAN...

...had been written on the heart; that the one is common to all, and the other was made known only to those who have the Law of Moses.

<margin>Acts VII. 38.</margin>
From the sermon of Stephen, it appears that it was the Son of God who gave the Law, and that Moses received it from him. Acts VII. 38. *This is he who was in the congregation (of the people) in the wilderness with the Angel, who spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and (with) our Fathers, who received the living words to give to us.* This same Angel appeared to Moses in the burning bush, verse 35, and called himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, verse 32, which belongs to none but Christ, who is the Angel of the Covenant <note>This identifies the "Angel of the Lord" in the Old Testament as the pre-incarnate Christ.</note>.

<margin>Acts VII. 53. Gal. III. 19. Heb. II. 2.</margin>
The Angels appeared at the giving of the Law as God’s servants, as Stephen testifies in Acts VII. 53, saying that the Jews had received the Law through the "dispositions" <note>original: *bestellingen*; referring to the administrative ordering or ranks of angels</note>, or multitude of the Angels. Paul says, Gal. III. 19, that it was ordained by the hand of Angels, and calls it in Heb. II. 2 a word spoken through Angels.

Mount Sinai or Horeb, situated in the deserts of Arabia, was the place where God proclaimed his Law.

The Ancients sought many mysteries in the giving of the Law on a mountain, and particularly on Mount Sinai. Their thoughts are more ingenious than substantial, except for those based on the explanations of Paul.

They said that the Law was given on a mountain so that man might take heed of how far God is exalted above him, and that this small elevation might bring to mind the infinite distance between the Creator and the creatures. 2. To signify how far the Law that he gave his people is exalted above all human laws. 3. To teach us that, however much God might descend to us, we still have high to climb, and we shall never reach his height. They added that God chose Mount Sinai over other mountains because there is none that better represents the nature of the Law. Sinai was a barren mountain, and so full of sharp rocks that one shuddered just to look at it. Moreover, Sinai is the same as Hagar, according to Paul in Gal. IV. 24, who signifies

<column-break/>

servitude—a beautiful example of the Law, which is barren and bears no children to God, but makes slaves <note>In Galatians, Paul uses the allegory of Hagar and Sarah to contrast the "slavery" of the Law with the "freedom" of the Gospel.</note>.

The time at which God gave the Law was the fiftieth day after the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt; therefore it is called Pentecost <note>original: *Pinksterdag*; literally "fiftieth day," referring to the feast of Shavuot or Pentecost</note>, and it is Moses to whom God gave it.

When God gave the Law, the mountain was entirely in fire and flame; it lightened and thundered from all sides; and there were barriers set around the foot of the mountain to prevent the people from approaching, Heb. XII. 18, 19, 20, 21. *You are not come unto the mount that might be touched,* says Paul, *and the burning fire, and blackness, and darkness, and tempest, and the sound of a trumpet, and the voice of words; which they that heard entreated that the word should not be spoken to them any more; for they could not endure that which was commanded. And if so much as a beast touch the mountain, it shall be stoned, or thrust through with a dart; and Moses (so terrible was the sight) said, I exceedingly fear and quake.*

One must not doubt that God used this terrible display to compel the Israelites to receive his Law with fear and trembling. Through this, he also wished to signify the effects that the Law would produce.

If we read the ancient and modern commentators, they will tell us:

1. That God appeared in the midst of the fire to show that he is a consuming fire to those who transgress his commandments; and that his Law itself is a fire that shows us the thistles of man's sins but does not consume them; which burns the conscience but neither softens nor gladdens it.

2. That there was darkness to represent the darkness of the old dispensation <note>original: *Huishouding*; literally "household management," used here for the theological concept of a divine "economy" or era.</note>.

3. That there were storms and whirlwinds to signify what the Law is; it is like a whirlwind that rustles the soul, overturns it, and sometimes brings it to despair by showing it the abyss of Hell.

4. If it is said that all were spectators and witnesses of this terrible display, so amazed...

This Law was written down, and God willed to write it Himself upon stone tablets so that it would not be forgotten. Theologians give various reasons for this; those of the Jewish Masters <note>A reference to Rabbinic scholars or commentators.</note> are full of clever subtlety.

It is said that God willed to describe the Law with His own finger, that is to say, immediately and by Himself,
<margin>Exodus 31:18. 32:16.</margin>
1. To show the excellence of His Law above all human laws, and above the other laws that He subsequently gave to Moses. 2. To teach us that God alone can write His law in our hearts. That it was written on stone tablets indicated: 1. That the same should always be the rule of our deeds; that which is engraved in stone or steel is not easily erased. 2. That the heart by nature is a heart of stone. These tablets were written on both sides, so that one would neither add to nor take away from them.

Moses gave three laws to the people. The **Moral Law**, divided into two tablets, which teaches us what we owe to God and our neighbor. The **Ceremonial Law**, which deals with the rites of the Levitical Service. The **Civil Law**, which concerned the governance of Israel's State.

The **Moral Law** regards the people of Israel as a gathering of men who must be obedient to their Creator. The **Ceremonial Law**, as a

<column-break/>

church that expected the Messiah who had been promised to her. The **Civil Law**, as a people and commonwealth set apart from all others. The Ceremonial Law looks directly toward God; the Civil Law toward our fellow man; and the Moral Law toward what we owe to both.

These Laws are very different from one another. The **Moral Law** has been impressed upon the heart of man since the beginning of creation. The other two were given in the time of Moses. The Moral Law is a universal rule that obligates all men. The others obligate the Israelites alone.

The Moral Law is almost entirely grounded in <term>natural law</term> <note>Law believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason.</note>. By natural law, one understands that which rests upon God’s holy and righteous being. For example, the commandment that makes up the summary of the Law—*Thou shalt love the Lord thy God*—is grounded in God’s nature, and it is an unbreakable command; otherwise, one would have to say that God could command that one hate Him, which is a godless thought. But the other Laws are grounded in a <term>positive and arbitrary law</term> <note>Laws based on specific decrees or the will of a legislator rather than inherent nature.</note>. By positive and arbitrary law, one understands that which depends entirely upon God’s will and pleasure, such that God could have chosen not to prescribe it to men without offending any of His perfections. One of the most learned Jews who lived in recent centuries <note>Likely referring to Maimonides or a similar Sephardic scholar.</note> said that the Moral Law, if it were not written, would have to be written; but that if God had not seen fit to give the others, one could do things entirely contrary to them without sinning. The Moral Law is naturally known. The Heathens have not been ignorant of it, even though they did not have it written on stone tablets and had greatly corrupted it through their conduct of life. The Ceremonial Law does not naturally occur to man's thoughts; and regarding the Civil Law, although it rests upon sound reason in its general commands, it is nevertheless certain that, regarding its specific decrees, it depends solely upon God. The Moral Law is immutable and must last forever, although not all the commandments of this Law are equally unchangeable; for there are those which are founded absolutely upon God’s being and His holiness, so that God could not command that

Thus, God cannot command that one serve other Gods, that one use His name in vain, that one lie, etc. etc. But there are other commandments of the **Moral Law** which are grounded in the nature of things in the state wherein God has placed them. Men must never transgress these commandments on their own authority; but God has the power to command such in certain cases. For example, God can command one to kill, and to take a neighbor’s property, just as He commanded **Abraham** to offer up his son, and the **Israelites** to take the vessels of the **Egyptians** with them. <note>Referencing Genesis 22 and Exodus 11:2, where God gives specific commands that seem to contradict the general Moral Law against killing and theft.</note> Although the Law commands that we shall be obedient to our Parents, God nevertheless forbids us to obey them if they demand anything of us that runs against His will.

Regarding the determination of the **seventh day**, which we, according to the precept of the Moral Law, must hallow to God, it is clear that this commandment could be revoked and abolished by God Himself, since it rests upon a <term>positive law</term> <note>The original Dutch "willekeurig regt" refers to laws established by God's choice or decree (positive law), rather than laws inherent to His moral nature (natural law).</note>; so that God, if it had pleased Him, could have required of men the celebration of the first day of the week as well as the last. It appears, therefore, that the Moral Law, in respect of most commandments, is unchangeable, but that the **Ceremonial** and **Civil** laws could be abolished, as we shall see in the following that they have been abolished. It is more difficult for man to keep the commandments of the Moral Law than those of the Ceremonial, because he must struggle against his passions and resist his natural inclinations.
<margin>Ephesians 2:15.</margin>
The Moral Law is called the **Ten Commandments** or Words, because it consists of ten commandments. Paul calls the Ceremonial Law, in Ephesians 2:15, the *Law consisting of ordinances*; and the Civil Law is often expressed in Scripture by the word *Judgment*.

We shall have opportunity to speak more broadly of the Moral Law when we deal with the work of **Sanctification**: for it is the perfect rule of our works and morals.
