### CHAPTER XXVI.

->Of Christ's descent into Hell.<-

<margin>Bellarmine, book IV, chapter 16. Catechism of Trent. Lutheran: Brochmand, Section 9, 6, 7. Book of Concord.</margin> Since the Apostles' Creed adds his descent into hell to the burial of **Christ** / we cannot pass over the same.

We have two matters to investigate.
1. Did **Christ** descend into hell?
2. What is the true sense of this article of faith?

Regarding the first / whether **Christ** descended into hell? Some have believed / and still believe / that **Christ** after his death essentially descended into hell / to triumph over the Devil / and to show himself as a conqueror / as also to preach to the damned / and that he in fact converted many of them through his preaching / and delivered them from eternal pains.

<column-break/>

This has been the opinion of many Fathers <note>The "Church Fathers" were influential Christian theologians and leaders in the early centuries of the church.</note>.

<margin>Justin in *Dialogue with Trypho*, page 298. Clement, *Miscellanies*, Book VI, page 637. Irenaeus, Book V, chapter 31. Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book II. Eusebius, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, Book IV, chapter 12.</margin> **Justin Martyr** in his dialogue with **Trypho** says / that **Christ** after his death descended into hell / that he went there to preach to the Spirits / and to proclaim Salvation to them: he fixes both one and the other proposition with the authority of the Prophet **Jeremiah**, and accuses the Jews of having cut away the words of his prophecy.

**Clement of Alexandria** (**Miscellanies, Book VI, page 637. etc.**) says / that it would not be just / that those who lived and died before the coming of **Christ** / should be excluded from salvation / if one had not indeed made known to them the mysteries of the Gospel / and the Savior had not clearly offered them his grace and salvation; he said / that **Christ** had to preach to the spirits / who were separated from the body / and whose Judgment was still suspended / until they had embraced or rejected salvation: and he confirms this with the authority of an irregular book <note>Meaning an apocryphal or non-canonical work.</note> / that has the title the *Preachings of Peter*.

**Irenaeus** (**Book V, chapter 31.**) **Origen** (**Against Celsus, sermon on Genesis**) **Eusebius** (**Demonstration of the Gospel, Book IV, chapter 12.**) maintain the same matter. They say / that the purpose of the descent of our Savior into Hell was / to draw the first humans and their descendants out of the uncertain and dark state / in which they were until the coming of the Savior of the world / to destroy death and the hellish powers / which had raised themselves against the Savior / and to deliver the Souls / who for many Centuries had expected his coming.

Some Fathers maintain / that **Christ** descended / to save all those / who had died before him; and others claim / that he only descended there / for those who would believe in him / after they had heard the Preaching of his Gospel.

<margin>Estius on the 3rd book of Sentences, distinction 22, paragraph 1</margin> **Bellarmine, Book IV, Chapter 16.** believed that **Christ** descended into hell / but he later recanted this opinion: the Schoolmen <note>Medieval university theologians who used logical analysis to study Christian doctrine.</note> dispute among themselves / whether **Christ** / descending into hell / delivered all the Souls / who were in Purgatory / as **Soto**, **Catharinus**, and **Estius** believed; or only some. DIVINE THEOLOGY. BOOK IX. CHAPTER XXVI.

<margin>1 Peter 4:6.</margin>
When it says "the gospel was preached to those who are dead," <note>original: "gelie aan de dooden is verkondigt"</note> he intends to signify that it was preached to those who are now dead, but who were alive at the time it was preached to them.

To say that Christ went to triumph over the Devils and make his victory known to them is incorrect because: 1. It mixes the state of Christ’s humiliation with his glories, for the descent of Christ into Hell is considered a part of his humiliation. 2. It was not necessary for Christ to go and inform the Devils of what he had done; they could not have been ignorant of it. 3. In short, Hell is not a place of triumph.

We also do not believe that Christ went to preach to the souls of the Believers of the Old Testament who were confined in the forecourt of Hell <note>This refers to the *Limbus Patrum* or Limbo of the Patriarchs, a conceptual place where holy people who died before Christ's resurrection were thought to wait.</note>.

1. We do not know what is meant by the word "forecourt"; the Scripture mentions nothing of it.

2. The cited passages which prove that he did not descend into Hell likewise prove that he did not enter into the Forecourt of Hell.

3. We shall show in another place that the souls of the Believers of the Old Testament were received into Heaven and were not sent to subterranean places. Enoch and Elijah were taken up into Heaven.

Finally, we believe it should not be said that Christ descended into Hell with a "descent of power," as if something tangible occurred in Hell following Christ's death. The Scripture does not speak of this. In any case, it would be more appropriate to attribute this appearance of triumph to the day of Christ's resurrection, with which his victory truly began.

It is objected that it is written in Matthew 12:40: *Just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the fish, so shall the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.*

<margin>Matthew 12:40.</margin>
Answer: This is a figure of speech which signifies only that Christ was in the grave and in the earth, just as it is written in Psalm 46:2: *We will not fear, though the earth should change (its place) and though the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea,* that is to say, into the sea. Ezekiel, speaking of Tyre, says in chapter 27:4: *Your borders are in the heart of the sea,* although it was built at the entrance of the sea, as the Prophet himself had said; it was so near to the shore that, after the time of Ezekiel, Alexander the Great joined it to the mainland, having had the water that lay between them filled in. It is in this sense that Moses says in Deuteronomy 4:11: *That the fire of Mount Sinai burned even to the midst of Heaven* <note>original: "midden des Hemels," literally "middle of heaven" or "heart of heaven."</note>, not that the fire itself rose above the first region of the air, much less that it penetrated through the center of the heavens.

One must also explain in much the same way what is read in Ephesians 4:9, where Paul says of Christ that he descended into the lower parts of the earth. It is very clear that the Apostle intended to show nothing other than the humiliation of Christ—his manifestation in the flesh or his burial. The parts of the earth are not being compared with one another here, but rather the parts of the world: namely, Heaven and the earth. It is as if Paul wanted to say that Christ descended to the earth, which constitutes the lower part of the world. One finds the same expression in Psalm 139:15: *My bones,* says the Prophet, *were not hidden from you, when I was made in secret, and wrought like embroidery in the lowest parts of the earth.* That is to say, on the earth, which is the lowest place of the whole Universe.

Now that we have proven that Christ did not descend into Hell <note>In the sense of a place of punishment or the underworld.</note>, we must examine the true meaning of the words of our Creed; but first, one must note:

3. That it may very well have happened that these Articles were joined together in this way: that when one of them was used in the text, the other was placed in the margin as a synonym, and that they were finally both introduced into the text and taken for distinct articles.

4. That it may also be that those who added the Article of the Descent into Hell were of the opinion of those Fathers of whom we spoke at the beginning of this Chapter.

## XXVII. CHAPTER.

### Of the Resurrection of Christ.

**U**ntil now we have traced the humiliation of the Lord Jesus Christ / which includes his birth, life, and burial; now we must transition to his exaltation / which contains his Resurrection, Ascension, and sitting at the right hand of God the Father; we begin with his Resurrection.

One cannot cast any doubt on the importance of this Article of Faith. The resurrection of Christ is the principal foundation of our hope / the cause of our joy / the certainty of our salvation / the triumph of a Christian / and the source of his comforts. It has fully shown us / that neither the power of the world / nor the violence of the Devil / can prevent the members of Christ from reaching blessed immortality / nor rob them of the fruits of their faith in the struggle. Paul also exhorts his 
<margin>2 Timothy 2:8</margin>
beloved son Timothy to remember the Resurrection of Christ.

In order to handle this subject with order / we shall investigate:
1. Whether Christ has risen?
2. Whether his Resurrection was foretold in the Old Testament?
3. Why he had to rise?
4. Who raised him up?
5. How he was raised up?
6. What life he took up through his resurrection?
7. What the fruits and consequences thereof are?
8. Finally / to whom Christ made himself known after his resurrection?
<margin>Whether Christ has risen.</margin>
Concerning the first point / which regards the truth of Christ's resurrection / [it is certain that he] has risen.

### THEOLOGY. BOOK IX. CHAPTER XXVII. ###

<margin>
Why Christ has risen
</margin>
The third part concerns the reasons why Christ had to rise.

It was not possible for the Divinity of Christ to allow the flesh, which was united with it, to be swallowed up under the power of death, nor for the Temple of His body—in which the Divinity dwelt in such a singular manner—to remain broken and lying forever in the dust of the earth.

It was not possible for God’s Justice, having received the satisfaction <note>The theological concept that Christ's death "satisfied" the debt of sin owed to God's justice.</note> by which our sins were reconciled, to leave without reward the One who had endured so much labor to restore His honor. His Wisdom demanded that things be restored to their original order, and that His Son be raised up again into the glory of His first state.

His Goodness, which cannot pass by a holy creature without showing it His love, did not allow Him to leave His holy child Jesus in corruption; for He had not tasted death, nor descended into the grave, except to defend the rights of the Divinity.

Just as sin and death are naturally inseparable, so life and innocence must naturally go together. Consequently, while the Lord Christ bore our sins in His body, He had to die; but after He had borne and reconciled our sins, He had to rise.

As a **Prophet**, He had to rise. The teaching in which men were to be instructed was included in this: that Christ was delivered for our sins, and that He was raised for our justification. <margin>Rom. 4:25.</margin> Romans 4:25. He also had to share His Spirit with us to convince us of His teaching. Now, He could not grant us the same without rising and ascending to Heaven. During His stay on earth, He had said that He was the Son of God. Now, there was nothing that could better convince the world of this truth than His Resurrection. This led Paul to say that He is declared to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead. <margin>Rom. 1:4.</margin> Romans 1:4.

As a **High Priest**, He also had to rise. <margin>Rom. 1:4.</margin> It was indeed necessary that He be slaughtered and undergo death, but He also had to present Himself alive again to God and pray for us in the same way as the High Priest of old entered into the Holy of Holies with the blood of the sacrifice, after he had slaughtered it outside.

<column-break/>

Finally, as a **King**, He had to rise: how would He have ruled if He had not become alive again? And what glory would He have possessed if He had remained in the grave? Moreover, it is specifically in and through His resurrection that He is glorified.

*If Christ is not raised, then your faith is in vain.* <margin>1 Cor. 15:17.</margin> 1 Corinthians 15:17. How could the death of Christ be viewed as the ransom for our sins if He Himself had remained under the power of death? And what certainty would we have had that Divine justice was satisfied? On what ground would Christ have caused us to hope that we shall rise, if He Himself had not risen? We would have viewed His death as an empty sacrifice in which God took no pleasure, and as the punishment of a reckless man who allowed himself to be led to the death of the cross without reason.

The resurrection of Christ then assures us of His Divinity, of the merits of His death, of the perfection of His sacrifice, and of the certainty of our own resurrection.

<margin>
Who raised Christ?
</margin>
In the fourth place, it is asked: who raised Christ?

The Scripture attributes this sometimes to the **Father**, and sometimes to the **Son**, whom we <margin>John 10:18. John 2:19, 21.</margin> hear saying in John 10:18: *I lay down my life of myself, I have power to lay it down, and have power to take it up again.* John 2:19, 21: *Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.* Peter says in <margin>1 Pet. 3:18.</margin> 1 Peter 3:18: *Christ being put to death in the flesh, but made alive by the Spirit,* that is, by His Divinity. <margin>Racovian Catechism, 2nd part, on the office of Christ. Socinus, Disputation on the existence of the only Son of God. Rom. 6:4. Heb. 13:20.</margin> <note>The author is refuting the Socinians, a group who denied the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ; the author argues that Christ’s ability to raise Himself proves His inherent Divinity.</note> This we note particularly against the Socinians. Elsewhere, Paul says in Romans 6:4 that Christ was raised by the glory of the Father, that is, by His glorious power. And Hebrews 13:20: *Now the God of peace, who brought again from the dead the great Shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the everlasting covenant.*

These passages of Scripture do not contradict one another, because the Divine Omnipotence by which Christ was raised is common to both the Father and the Son. But most often, the resurrection of Jesus is attributed to the Father, because in the work of Salvation He is viewed as the one who issues the commands and sends the Son into the world

<meta>The catchword "zend/" (sends) indicates the sentence will continue on the next page describing the Father's role in the mission of the Son.</meta>

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of Christ’s Resurrection, moving from the necessity of the event to the specific manner and nature of His rising, specifically addressing the "how" and the "state" of His glorified body.</meta>

### CHRISTIAN THEOLOGY ###

<note>This is a continuation of a sentence from the previous page, likely referring to God the Father.</note> ...sent / receives the satisfaction for our sins from his hands / and who had to give this first sign of his reconciliation.

<margin>How Christ has risen.</margin>
In the fifth place, we must examine: how did *Christ* rise?

1. *Christ* rose on the third day, just as he had said; he was in the grave for approximately forty hours. He did not wish to remain there any longer, so that people would not believe that he had felt the beginning of corruption <note>original: "verderbing"; the decomposition of the body</note>; and he did not wish to remain there for a shorter time, so that people would not doubt his death.

2. He arose on the first day of the week, and at a time when all things are renewed. Various ancient and contemporary teachers have sought mysteries in this, saying it was to teach us: 1. That the old things had passed away, and that all things had become new. 2. That *Christ's* resurrection caused the church to pass from an old state into a new state. 3. That the Sun of Righteousness began its course.

3. It is noted that the earth shook to show with what strength and omnipotence the Lord would overcome all the obstacles that might be raised against his Kingdom, as well as the power with which he will one day cause the earth to shake and tremble to make our bodies rise from it.

One must not believe that *Christ*, when he rose, passed through the stone that closed the Grave: for bodies cannot penetrate one another. But the creature gave way for the Creator; the Lord used the service of Angels to roll the stone <note>original: "sark"; a stone slab or lid</note> from the entrance of the grave, as is indicated in *Matthew* 28:2.

<margin>In what state Christ has risen.</margin>
The same question concerns the state in which *Christ* rose, and the life that he assumed.

It is certain that he did not take back the life that he had assumed through his birth, but a much nobler and much more glorious life. That which he had assumed when coming into the world was subject to the necessity of rest after labor, of sleep after waking, and of the use of food to restore the body's strength. It was a mortal life that soon had to end through death on the cross. But the life that he took back was freed from all these weaknesses; it was an immortal life. His body became incorruptible, translucent,

<column-break/>

and agile. It is probable that all those who were raised before him had assumed a mortal life once again, only to lay it down once more, but *Christ* can die no more. At his birth, it was said that he who was in the form of God had taken on the form of a servant: but at his resurrection, one could change the language and say that he who had the form of a servant had taken on the form of God.

It is true that he ate with his Disciples after his resurrection, but it was without necessity. He did this to assure them that he had truly risen, and not to nourish himself; to prove to them the truth of his humanity, and not to sustain it thereby.

Thus one can contrast *Christ* with *Lazarus* and others who took back the life they had laid down and who underwent death once more; but *Christ*, having been raised <margin>*Romans* 6:9.</margin> from the dead, dies no more; death no longer has dominion over him. *Christ* is called the firstborn from the dead because no one before him was raised in such a state.

<margin>*Romans* 6:9.</margin>
<margin>*Colossians* 1:18.</margin>
<margin>*1 Corinthians* 15:23.</margin>
When he is called the firstfruits of those who sleep, <note>original: "eerstelingen der geener die slaapen"</note> *1 Corinthians* 15:23, it is not only to tell us that he was the first who awoke from the sleep of death to take on an immortal life, but also to make known to us that his resurrection will be followed by that of many others, like the firstfruits of the entire harvest; that our resurrection will be like that of *Jesus*, just as the harvest resembles the firstfruits; and that we shall rise through the power of *Christ*, just as it was by the power of the Blessing over the firstfruits under the [Mosaic] law that the abundance and prosperity of the harvest sprouted.

Furthermore, we must take note:

1. That the body with which *Christ* rose was the same in terms of substance as that which he had before, although in terms of qualities it was not the same. It was no new body, nor a body of air, as some Heretics <note>original: "Ketters"; likely referring to Gnostic or Docetic beliefs that Christ only appeared to have a physical body</note> argued in ancient times, but a true human body; the body that was formed from the substance of the virgin, composed of solid parts, extended, tangible, visible, and clothed with all the properties that are inseparable from the human body.

<summary>This page explains the timing and nature of Christ's Resurrection, emphasizing that He rose with a glorified, immortal body that remains physically human but is no longer subject to mortal needs or decay.</summary>

# DIVINE THEOLOGY. BOOK IX. CHAPTER XXVII. #

...be manifest. It was freed from all the imperfections that sin had introduced into the world, and to which Christ had previously submitted Himself. "Behold me," He said to
<margin>Luke 24:39.</margin>
His Apostles, Luke 24:39, "handle me, for a spirit has neither flesh nor bones, as you see that I have." Yet, it had become an incorruptible and glorious body.

2. It is probable that His body did not yet possess the same radiance that it has in heaven. He wished to accommodate Himself to the weakness of His Apostles, who would have been far less able to behold the glitter of His countenance than the Israelites were to behold that of Moses. 2 Cor. 3:7.

### I come to the fruits that spring from Christ’s resurrection. ###

<margin>
Of the
Fruits
of Christ’s resurrection.
</margin>
<margin>Rom. 1:4.</margin>
1. His resurrection assures us completely that He is God’s Son, just as Paul draws this proof in Romans 1:4. One might say that either Christ raised Himself, or the Father raised Him; for if He raised Himself, He is undoubtedly God, since God alone can raise the dead. Indeed, when one sees the Savior raising Himself from the grave by His own power, breaking the bonds of death, crushing death and Hell under His feet, and standing upon the dust of the earth as a victorious and triumphant Prince—setting up His trophies on the battlefield after defeating His enemies—who could doubt His Divinity? And if it is said that the Father raised Him, then the Father must have recognized Him as His Son; for had He taken this title without basis or right, is it believable that God would have lent His omnipotence to uphold a lie?

2. This resurrection also convinces us that He has perfectly satisfied Divine justice, and that He has truly atoned for our sin. As long as a judge keeps a prisoner in
<margin>Rom. 4:25.</margin>
shackles, it is a sign that justice has not yet been satisfied. Therefore, Paul says that Christ was raised for our justification <note>original: "regtveerdigmaking"; the act of being declared righteous before God</note>, Romans 4:25. This does not mean that Christ’s resurrection earned our justification—His death accomplished that—but rather that His resurrection assures us of the reconciliation of our sins. The death of Christ was the ransom for our sins, and His resurrection is the receipt <note>original: "quitancie"; a formal discharge of debt</note> that the Father has publicly given for it.
Part I.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, just as we are justified through faith, so does faith itself depend upon Jesus’ resurrection.

3. The resurrection of Christ is the principle of our rebirth <note>original: "wedergeboorte"; spiritual regeneration</note>; for it was necessary that the life which Christ had earned to share with His spiritual body <note>the Church</note> was first in Him, so that He might be the source of it and subsequently share it with His members. The Spirit of life was given to Christ in His resurrection,
<margin>Rom. 8:2.</margin>
so that He might pour it out into all His members. "The spirit of life, which is in Christ," says the Apostle in Romans 8:2, "has made me free from the law of
<margin>Col. 2:12.</margin>
sin and death." Colossians 2:12: "We are raised through faith in the working of God, who raised Him from the dead."

4. The resurrection of Christ is the pattern for our sanctification <note>original: "heiligmaaking"; the process of becoming holy</note>. The life that Christ took up again was freed from all the weaknesses of animal life; it was a heavenly life. Therefore, having been raised with Christ, we must not contemplate earthly things, but heavenly ones. Christ rose from the dead by the power of the Spirit that was in Him; it is also through the Spirit of Christ that we must put to death the works of the body. Meanwhile, there is a great difference between the resurrection of Christ and our spiritual resurrection. The life that Christ took up was a perfect life, but here on earth, our sanctification has its flaws, and we must strive for perfection every day.

5. The resurrection of Christ assures us of our own resurrection, and produces
<margin>1 Pet. 1:3.</margin>
the hope within us that we too shall one day rise. Peter says in 1 Peter 1:3 that God has birthed us again into a living hope through the resurrection of Christ from the dead. If the Chief Leader of Salvation and our Head had remained in death, how could we have promised ourselves immortality? But seeing the Savior rise from the grave makes us hope, through the union we have with Him, that we shall also rise from our graves; and that death, which could not
<margin>John 14:19.</margin>
hold Him there, will not prevent us from rising out of it either, according to His promise: "Because I live, you shall live also." Therefore Paul says that we are raised with Christ. In Ephesians 2, he suggests that if someone is in the water and lifts his head out of it...

# XXVIII. CHAPTER.

->On the Ascension of Christ.<-

The second stage of Christ’s exaltation is his Ascension, regarding which we have several questions to investigate.
1. Whether Christ ascended to Heaven before he began his ministry.
2. Whether he truly ascended after his resurrection, or whether he merely made his body invisible.
3. Whether his Ascension was foretold.
4. What the circumstances of it were.
5. Why he ascended to Heaven.
6. What fruits come to us from it.

<margin>
Whether Christ ascended to Heaven before he entered into his Ministry. Smalcius, *On the Divinity of Christ*, ch. 4. Ostorodt, *Institutes*, ch. 16. Racovian Catechism, *On the Prophetic Office of Christ*. Socinus in the *Catechism*, p. 127. & in the *Short Discourse on the Office of Christ*, p. 27. Eniedinus. <note>These citations refer to major Socinian authors who argued for a "pre-ministry" ascension.</note>
</margin>

I. Regarding the first question, there have been those who believed (and such people still exist) that Christ ascended to Heaven after his Baptism to learn the will of the Father there, and that he subsequently descended from there to proclaim the same; and they are of the opinion that this occurred during the time in which he fasted for 40 days in the Wilderness.

But this is a fable. Where does one read in Scripture that Christ ascended to Heaven twice? Which of the Evangelists and Apostles has spoken of a first Ascension? How is it that they remained silent on such a remarkable matter? They relate the conversation that Christ had in his twelfth year with the Teachers in Jerusalem; they relate his Baptism, his being led by the Spirit into the Wilderness, his forty-day fast, his temptation by Satan—why do they mention nothing of this Ascension? How is it that the Christian Church did not know of it for so many centuries? How is it that Scripture itself explicitly says that Christ entered into the Holy of Holies <note>A reference to the inner sanctuary of the Temple, used here as a metaphor for Heaven.</note> once?

<column-break/>

It will be said that this Ascension happened in secret; but how is it that other secret things are related—for example, the Transfiguration of Christ, his temptation—and yet nothing is mentioned of his Ascension? And how does one know of it, if the matter was secret? Paul, speaking of Christ’s Ascension, concludes that his previous descent to earth followed from it, <margin>Eph. IV. 9.</margin> *Now this*, he says, *that he ascended, what is it but that he also first descended.* But those with whom we dispute on this point maintain that his Ascension preceded his Descent.

Why would Christ have needed to ascend to Heaven—he who knew all things and had received the Spirit without measure? Moses had to receive the commands of God on the mountain, and Paul had to be taken up into the third heaven, but Christ had no need of this.

It is true that it is said that Christ descended from Heaven and came forth from his Father, but this does not establish that he had previously ascended there. He was in Heaven, but he had not ascended there. He was there as God, and he is said to have descended to make known his revelation in the flesh.

<margin>
Socinus, *Catechism*. Ostorodt *against Tradelius*. <note>Refers to Christoph Ostorodt's polemics.</note> Smalcius, *On the Divinity of Christ*, ch. 4.
</margin>

The Socinians <note>A group of 16th and 17th-century theologians who denied the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ, viewing him as a man uniquely chosen by God.</note> object using John III. 13: *No one has ascended to heaven, but he who came down from heaven*, and verse 31: *I have come down from heaven*. John VI. 38. But we have shown in another place how this "descent" must be understood. The Son of God descended from Heaven when he took on our nature. They also object that Moses and Paul were taken up into Heaven. Answer: It does not follow that Christ also had to be drawn up there, because there was no necessity that required it.

<margin>Whether Christ truly ascended to Heaven.</margin>

II. It is asked whether Christ truly ascended to Heaven? One cannot doubt it: and one must apply here what we said in the previous Chapter regarding the truth of the testimony of the Apostles. The Jews are wrong to dispute the Ascension of Christ under the pretext that there were only eleven Apostles who saw him ascend; they who do not doubt the Ascension of Elijah, even though he had only Elisha as a witness.

III. One asks whether the ascension of Christ was foretold, just as his resurrection was.

I answer that many oracles of God foretold it. One may add Psalm 2:6: *Yet have I set my King upon Zion, the hill of my holiness,* and Psalm 68:19: *Thou hast ascended on high, thou hast led captivity captive: thou hast received gifts for men;* <note>The author provides Dutch translations of these verses; the English here follows the spirit of the text while matching familiar biblical phrasing.</note> words which clearly refer to the Messiah. But at the same time, one must note here that Christ ascended by his own power, and not by a foreign power, as did Enoch and Elijah.

CHRISTIAN THEOLOGY.

...that those who had been witnesses of his humiliation would also be witnesses of his exaltation, in order to strengthen their faith—which had been so greatly weakened and shaken by his suffering, but had begun to come alive through his resurrection—to make them see that he was the true Messiah and that his Kingdom was a spiritual Kingdom; to fill them with hope and to instill in them an unwavering courage to proclaim the Gospel.

2. The place from which Christ ascended was Bethany, located on the Mount of Olives, where the Garden of Gethsemane was; just as it was in this place that Christ had begun to suffer, it was also there that he began to be glorified.

<margin>Luke 24:50.</margin>
3. Christ, standing ready to part from his Disciples, lifted up his hands and blessed them. This was the precious pledge of his love that he left behind for them; and through this blessing, Heaven was opened to them, the earth was made subject to them, along with their enemies over whom they triumphed.

4. He was taken up in a cloud. One sees that God has used clouds in the most glorious workings of his providence. Elijah was taken up into Heaven in a fiery chariot; Christ on a cloud. It seems that God intended to show thereby the distinction between the service of the Law and that of the Gospel. The service of the Law is entirely of fire <note>referring to the dramatic, often fearful manifestations of God in the Old Testament, such as the fire on Mount Sinai</note>, and that of the Gospel, though much more glorious, is nevertheless gentle, which is well-portrayed by a cloud.

<margin>Claude <note>Likely Jean Claude (1619–1687), a prominent French Protestant theologian highly respected in the Dutch Republic.</note></margin>
5. It is noted that, while Christ ascended, his Disciples watched him with a steady gaze.
> "Such a rare sight," says a great man of this time, "filled their souls with an infinite number of thoughts. Amazement first ravished their spirit, but in a moment they saw all the riches of the Kingdom of Heaven; the Divinity of their Master, the purpose of his incarnation, the glory of his miracles, the mystery of his death, the incomprehensible wisdom of the Father, the unspeakable love of the Son, the salvation of the human race, the hope of the resurrection; all the great wonders of grace and of glory appeared before their eyes. In a moment they recognized the vanity

<column-break/>

> and the foolishness of human thoughts, the error of the Jews, who imagined for themselves a temporal Messiah, etc. In a moment, they worshipped the Lord Jesus in his triumph with a humbled heart. This act of worship was paired with the repentance they felt for the neglect of their duties during his stay with them on earth; this repentance immediately worked in them a sadness, which was increased upon seeing the departure of their Master, who left them like orphans in the midst of their enemies, and like sheep among wolves. Then their souls flew toward him, as if they had wanted to call him back, or follow him. In this rapture, faith came to their aid; it reminded them that they would always have him with them according to his promises through his spirit and grace, and that he would make them feel the effects of his protection."

6. The final circumstance is that two angels appeared before the Apostles to comfort them through the certain hope of his return; concerning which we must make this observation: that the angels, who serve God’s glory, also serve for the comfort of true believers.

### V. It is asked, for what reason did Christ ascend into Heaven?

<margin>Why Christ ascended into Heaven.</margin>
I answer, 1. That it was necessary for him to ascend into Heaven to enjoy the glory that was due to him. The earth is the valley of miseries, changes, and sins. Now the life that Christ had taken up through his resurrection had to be free from all these things, separated from all interaction with sinners, raised above the reach of all miseries and all worldly upheavals. It was then necessary that he climb to Heaven, which is a place of holiness, rest, and glory.

2. It was necessary that the human nature of Christ, which had united itself with the Divine, be taken up into the place where God had established his throne.

3. It was necessary that this Great High Priest enter into the Heavenly Sanctuary, and that he speak for us and prepare dwellings for us in that blessed place of residence. Just as the Old <term>High Priest</term> <note>Referring to the Jewish High Priest under the Mosaic Law, who performed rituals in the Temple that prefigured Christ's actions.</note>, after he had slaughtered the sacrifice outside
<margin>John 14:2.</margin>
the Sanctuary, with the...

6. If Christ had remained on earth / the Holy Spirit could not have been poured out over men / nor the Nations called to the knowledge of the true God.
> It is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Comforter <note>original: "Trooster", referring to the Paraclete or Holy Spirit</note> will not come to you, but if I go, I will send him to you. John 16.

<margin>John 7:39.</margin>
7. John says / that the Holy Spirit was not yet present, because Jesus was not yet glorified. John 7:39.

7. It was necessary / that Christ ascended to Heaven / to strengthen our faith. If Christ had remained below on earth / we could have imagined / that the reason / that kept him there / was / that something was lacking in the perfection of his sacrifice / and in the satisfaction <term>satisfaction: the theological concept that Christ’s death fully paid the debt of human sin to God's justice</term> / that he had undertaken to make for our sins.

8. He also had to ascend / to support our hope / and to assure us that we too shall be taken up into Heaven.

---

### VI.

<margin>Fruits of his Ascension.</margin>
From this one can easily discern / what the fruits <note>the spiritual benefits or results</note> are / that Christ's Ascension brings to us.

1. His Ascension assures us / that he has perfectly satisfied Divine justice through the power of his sacrifice: for entrance into heaven would otherwise not have been permitted to him.

2. The same is a proof / that he has earned entrance into Heaven for us / since he has gone to take possession of it.

3. It detaches our hearts and affections from earthly things / and lifts them up to heavenly ones.

4. It confirms the hope / that we have of one day being with the Lord in Paradise / for he has entered there / as our Head and our Forerunner.

<column-break/>

5. It fills us with joy / when we see our flesh and our blood / our dust and ashes reign / just as he rules above all Angels.

6. It comforts us against all persecutions / that we suffer for the sake of the Gospel / against the loss of our goods and temporal advantages / against every kind of adversity / and against death.

Upon the Ascension of Christ followed the descent of the Holy Spirit at the feast of Pentecost / who was poured out over the Apostles and first Christians. One cannot wonder enough at the happy progress of the service of these Evangelical Servants. In a very small number of years, they caused the Lord Christ / despite the power of Kings / the cruelty of authorities / the uprising of peoples / the eloquence of Orators / and the shrewdness of Philosophers / to reign over the entire world.

I will not dwell on refuting those / who deny Christ's Ascension / because of the great distance / that is between Heaven and earth; for they understand very little / how far God’s omnipotence reaches / and how swift glorified bodies are. Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher and famous critic of early Christianity</note>, although a sworn enemy of the Christians / says / that Christ was a pious and wise man; that he / after his death / entered into Heaven / and <margin>Eusebius, *Proof of the Gospel*, Book 3. <note>original: "Euseb. Dem. Evang l. 3."</note></margin> that one must be careful not to dishonor him, even though he has no pity for those who serve him. And in a treatise on Oracles, of which we have some remains / he says / that his own Gods declared / that the Lord Jesus was pious / that he became immortal after his death / and that his soul dwells in the heavenly abode of the saints and the pious.

I will also not recount the fables <note>original: "verdigtzelen", meaning fictional stories or legends</note> / that are told about the Ascension of Christ; for example / that as he ascended, he had pressed the marks of his feet into the earth / and that these had remained therein since that time / although the Christians took some of it away every day / and that Empress Helena <note>Mother of Constantine the Great, credited with finding many relics in the Holy Land</note>, having ordered the building of the magnificent Church of the Ascension / in the middle of which these footprints stood / could not pave this place or cover it with marble / like the others; and that one could also not close the vault / that was over these...

# DIVINE THEOLOGY. BOOK IX. CHAPTER XXIX.

<columns>

<margin>Suetonius, Life of Nero, ch. 13.</margin>
...that Nero seated Tiridates, King of Armenia, at his right hand. <note original="Suet. in Ner. c. 13">Suetonius was a Roman historian; here the author uses a secular Roman example to show that sitting at the "right hand" was a universal sign of the highest honor and shared authority.</note>
This expression includes many things.

I. When the Scripture says that God has placed his Son at his right hand, it intends to teach us that God has given him the governance of the World with supreme authority, and particularly that of his Church, of which he is the Head <margin>Matt. 28:18.</margin>. Therefore he says, in Matthew 28:18, *All power is given unto me in Heaven and on earth.* He testifies in John 17:2 <margin>John 17:2.</margin> that God has given him power over all flesh, so that he might bestow eternal life upon those who were given to him. For the same reason, he bears the Name of King of Kings, and <margin>1 Cor. 15:25.</margin> that of the Almighty. This causes Paul to say in 1 Corinthians 15:25, *For he must reign as King, until he has put all enemies under his feet.* Wherein one clearly sees that he considers sitting at the right hand and reigning to be one and the same thing.

To this, one must therefore attribute:

<margin>John 5:22.</margin>
1. The authority that God has given to his Son to judge the World: for he says himself that the Father judges no one, but that he has given judgment to the Son. He shall judge the living and the dead.

<margin>Matt. 18:18.</margin>
2. The authority to forgive sins; by virtue of the same, he said to his Disciples that whatever they should bind on earth would be bound in Heaven, and whatever they should loose on earth would be loosed in Heaven: for how could he have shared with the Apostles and Ministers of the New Testament the power to forgive sins in his Name, if he had not possessed it himself?

II. This expression also expresses the Supreme Glory and Majesty with which Christ has been clothed; Majesty and Glory worthy of the dignity of his Person and the Greatness of the work of Redemption. Now <margin>John 17:5.</margin> *glorify me, O Father,* he said in this regard in his High Priestly prayer, *with yourself, with the glory which I had with you <margin>Phil. 2:9, 10, 11.</margin> before the World was.* Paul says that God has highly exalted him and given him a name above every name.

->Part 4.<-

<column-break/>

<margin>Ps. 110:1.</margin>
III. Finally, this manner of speaking signifies the rest into which Christ entered after all his labor and strife. Therefore the Father says to him, *Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet,* as if the Father wished to take upon Himself what Christ still had to do to subdue the enemies of his name.

Now we must answer some difficulties.

<margin>When Christ sat at God's right hand.</margin>
1. It is asked, when did Christ sit at the right hand of the Father?
I answer, without recounting all the opinions of the Teachers <note>Referring to various church fathers and theologians.</note>, that Christ placed himself there after his Ascension, just as the scripture testifies in Ephesians 1:20, Mark 16:19, Hebrews 10:12, and 1 Peter 3:21, 22.

2. It is asked whether Christ—who is the true God, blessed with the Father for all eternity—did not have this dignity and glory before and during his <term>humiliation</term> <note>The "humiliation" refers to the period Christ spent on earth in human form, setting aside his divine glory.</note>: for if he did not have it, how could he be God? and if he did have it, how can one say that God gave it to him only after his resurrection?

I answer that one must consider Christ either as God or as <term>Mediator</term> <note>A "Mediator" is one who acts as a bridge between two parties; in theology, Christ bridges the gap between God and humanity.</note>. And the power and authority that he possesses as the Son of God is distinct from that which the Father gave him as the Son of Man—that is to say, insofar as he is Mediator. And this <margin>Daillé.</margin> power, as has been well noted <note original="Daille">Jean Daillé (1594–1670) was a prominent French Protestant theologian known for his writings on the early Church Fathers.</note>, is nothing other than the right and the authority with which he is clothed to save the World, to found the Church, to protect it against the powers of Hell, to raise and judge mankind, and subsequently to bring forth a new earth wherein righteousness and immortality shall dwell. Now, Christ only received this authority after his humiliation. Also, during the days of his flesh, he did not bear the signs of this glory—if I may be permitted to speak thus with a Great Man. He first assumed the same after his Resurrection and Ascension, which is the day of his coronation.

After Christ had finished and completed the work of Salvation, he received the new title of Savior, which he would not have had if he had not redeemed the World. See the Heavenly acclamations that arise concerning this in the Book of Revelation, Chapter 5:9, etc.

It distinguishes between Christ's eternal divine nature and the specific authority he earned as the Mediator following his earthly life and Ascension.</summary>

One must furthermore admit that, although Christ already possessed an infinite glory from all eternity, the same—with regard to its outward radiance—had been obscured by the weaknesses of the flesh in which he chose to reveal himself to the World. In this way, one can indeed say that he received a new glory when God drove away all the mists that covered it, and that he made him known to the World in a wonderful manner.

Regarding this Revelation, the Scripture says that the Father has glorified him; to bring this truth to light, a prominent Theologian <margin>Claude</margin> <note>Jean Claude (1619–1687) was a famous French Protestant pastor and theologian known for his clear explanations of doctrine.</note> uses this comparison.

> „ Imagine, he says, the Sun, which for a time illuminates no part of the earth, and which shoots all its rays upward toward Heaven. Next, imagine that the Sun turns toward the earth, and that it appears there surrounded by dark clouds, so that the part turned toward us is as if deprived of the rays of its light by the cover of the clouds that mist it over. Imagine finally, that all these clouds and mists disappear in an instant, and that we are thus irradiated by the light of the Sun. Look there, he adds, a Sketch of the dispensation <note original="huishouding">The "economy" or divine management of salvation history.</note> of the Savior. Before his incarnation, his glory was with the Father. He turned toward us and made himself known to the World, but under the darkness and the cover of the flesh. One saw him, but stripped of his radiance and luster. Finally, after his resurrection and Ascension, having cast off the cover of obscuration from himself, he showed himself to the eyes of the whole World in his full radiance.

# THE CHRISTIAN
### XXXI.

<margin>Isaiah 42:1; 49:3; 53:11.</margin>
...who has accomplished the work that God had given him to do. He is at once both servant and Lord; a Servant in respect to the Church over which he rules; whereas Moses was only a servant, both in respect to God and the Church, Jesus is Servant and Son over the house of God.

7. The name **Son of Man**, which is given to the Messiah in Daniel 7:13.

8. The name **Messenger of the Covenant**, <note>Original Dutch: *Engel des Verbonds*. While "Angel" is the literal translation, in 18th-century theology this refers to the "Messenger" or "Agent" of the covenant.</note> Malachi 3:1, by allusion to what is said in Exodus 23:20.

9. The name **Author and Captain of Salvation**, Hebrews 2:10, and of **Author and Finisher of faith**, Hebrews 12:2. **Captain of Salvation**, which is to say, the cause of Salvation and the Head of the saved. **Author and Finisher of faith**, that is, he who gives us faith, supports and perfects the same, our Head in all our struggles, and he who crowns our faith.

10. The name **Surety of the New Testament**, Hebrews 7:22. <note>A "Surety" is someone who takes legal responsibility for another's debt or obligations.</note>

11. The name **Mediator**, 1 Timothy 2:5, Hebrews 8:6, 9:15, 12:24.

Now we must consider in what sense Christ bears this last name.

One must not believe that Christ is a Mediator only in the same way as Moses is called a Mediator; for Moses was only a mere interpreter between God and the Israelites, a mutual envoy who brought the word of God to the people on God's behalf, and that of the people to God. He could do no more.

<margin>Deuteronomy 5:5.</margin>
Being himself a sinner and a finite creature, he was not capable of bringing about a true reconciliation between God and the people. One cannot say that God was moved—through love for Moses or out of consideration for his Person—to suspend his wrath against the Israelites for a time. Je-

<margin>1 Peter 1:18; Luke 1:18.</margin>
-sus is also not a Mediator solely because he established a new covenant with mankind in God's Name and explained God's will, although he is one in that sense too, since he has revealed the Counsel of God to us.

One must also not believe that he is our Mediator only in the sense in which one gives the name of "mediators" to arbiters who decide disputes, or like lawyers who plead and serve as advocates for one of the par-

<column-break/>

-ties, although it is true that he was the arbiter of the greatest dispute that ever existed, and the advocate who has pleaded our case. 1 John 2:1.

But he has been primarily our Mediator because he reconciles us with God and has made our peace with him through his blood.

<margin>Ephesians 2:13, 14.</margin>
It is therefore a great error to believe that Christ is our Mediator only because he has made known to us the way of Salvation, which consists in obedience to God's commandments; that he himself stepped onto that path and gave us a good example therein; and because he sealed his obedience with his blood.

<margin>Socinus, *On the Savior*, part 1, ch. 7; *Racovian Catechism*, ch. 1; *On the Prophetic Office of Christ*; Ostorodt, *Institutions*, ch. 37. <note>These references point to Socinianism, a 16th/17th-century theological movement that denied the divinity of Christ and viewed his death as an example of obedience rather than a sacrifice for sin.</note></margin>
One has only to consult the Scriptures to be convinced of the contrary. For (1) it says that Christ gave himself as a ransom for all, 1 Timothy 2:6. That he has become our peace through the blood of his cross, Colossians 1:20. Also, the shedding of his blood is joined to his covenant-making as Mediator, Hebrews 12:24.

<margin>Socinus, *On the Savior*, part 1, ch. 7.</margin>
It is without reason that some say the word "Mediator" in 1 Timothy 2:5 does not mean one who has made our peace because God's wrath is not mentioned in the preceding verses—as if the Scripture did not speak of the same in countless other places, as well as the necessity of our reconciliation with God.

They say that Christ is called the Mediator of the New Covenant in Hebrews 8:6, 9:15, 12:24, but that it does not follow from this that he has pacified God toward us.

I answer that this is the true reason why he bears this name. The necessity of our Salvation required that Christ be a Mediator in the sense in which we have explained it and shown elsewhere.

If Christ were only a Mediator because he revealed the way of Salvation to us through his teaching and example, one would have to place him in the rank of the Prophets and Apostles and other servants of God. We shall yet have the opportunity to treat this material more broadly.

# DIVINE THEOLOGY. IX. B. CHAPTER XXXI.

## CHAPTER XXXI.

->On the necessity of the<-
->Mediator; on the Qualities<-
->that he must have; and on the<-
->acts of his Mediation.<-

I will not expand upon the necessity of a Mediator, because the reasons which demonstrate the necessity of satisfaction <note>Theological "satisfaction" refers to the idea of making restitution or paying a debt for sin.</note> also prove this truth.

It is true that God was not bound to give this Mediator to mankind, because he could, if he so willed, have left them in a state of damnation; but, since he did not wish for the human race to perish, it was necessary to use a mediator, not only to moderate the rays of the infinite Majesty of God—which the sinner could not bear—but also to still the wrath of God and reconcile us with him, to bring us into his fellowship, and to earn for us the supernatural blessings of grace and glory.

Our Mediator had to possess six qualities.

I. He had to be independent and master of himself, and consequently God, in order to be able to do with his person as he pleased, and to satisfy an infinite justice. Therefore, neither Angels nor men could be our mediators.

II. He had to be capable of suffering, because he could not make satisfaction without suffering; thus the Mediator also had to be a creature, for only creatures can suffer.

III. He had to be able to undergo death, because we had deserved death. Therefore, our Mediator could not be an Angel.

IV. He had to have the same nature as the sinners. 1. So that sin might be borne and reconciled in the same nature in which it was committed. 2. So that we might have free access to him, to place our trust in him.

<margin>Hebrews 7:26.</margin>V. He had to be holy, innocent, undefiled, and separated from sinners, as the Apostle says: 1. So that he

<column-break/>

would be well-pleasing to God. 2. So that he would not need to make satisfaction for himself, as the ancient Priests did. 3. So that he could give us a perfect example. 4. So that he could be the source of the Spirit of sanctification. 5. So that he could break the kingdom of Satan. In a word, since he had to be God, it was impossible for him not to be holy.

VI. He had to be unable to sin. 1. So that the covenant he was to make would be an eternal covenant; for as soon as sin could take hold of someone who served as the foundation of our covenant with God, the covenant could not last forever. 2. So that he could impart to us a perfect holiness.

<margin>Romans 9:5. Hebrews 2:14. Hebrews 7:26.</margin>All these qualities met together in Christ. He is God over all, to be praised forever, with his Father; he is man, partaking of flesh and blood; He is Holy, freed from all sins and incapable of committing any.

It is a strange thing that, in order to defend the indifference of man's free will, some have dared to maintain that Christ could sin. How is it to be understood that one can say of a nature, which is united with the Divine in one person, that it can fall into sin?

If one now asks what the Mediator had to do, I answer:

I. That he had to make satisfaction to God for us, and reconcile us with him.

II. To bend the hearts of sinners, and extinguish the hatred they held toward God.

III. To cause all mistrust, which might exist between the two parties—God and men—to cease, and to be the surety for the one as well as for the other.

IV. To bring sinners into peace with the other creatures, who had become their enemies since the fall into sin.

V. To unite himself closely with us, so that we might be one body with him.

Jesus Christ has done all these things, for:

<margin>Romans 5:10.</margin>1. He has not only united the Divine nature with the human, but reconciled God with men. Paul teaches us this in several places, and primarily in Romans 5:10, where he says that we are reconciled to God through the death of his Son; and therefore Scripture calls him the Prince of Peace and our Peace.

THE CHRISTIAN

II. He has bent the hearts of men and extinguished the hatred they naturally held against God—not only through his Word, which provides us with powerful motives to love him, and not only through the example he gave us to follow, but also through his Spirit, which triumphs over our corruption and enables us to have fellowship with God.

III. Christ has been the guarantor <note>The original Dutch term "borg" refers to a legal surety or bondsman who takes responsibility for another's debt.</note> of God’s promises to men, and the guarantor of men’s promises to God. He was the guarantor of the Father’s promises because he was the Master and distributor of his treasures. And he was the guarantor of the promises of men because he made himself master of our spirit and soul through his Spirit, and through his blood he pardons the sins we commit against our promises.

<margin>Ephesians 1:10. Colossians 1:20. Matthew 10:34.</margin>
IV. He reconciled sinners with all creatures when he made our peace with the Creator. Paul teaches us this in the Epistles to the Ephesians and Colossians. It is true that Christ says he brought the sword and fire into the world and not peace, but this refers to the consequences that the Gospel produced by chance, due to the unbelief of those who defiantly reject his holy word and persecute the disciples of Christ. For otherwise, the natural end and the proper goal of the Gospel is to unite all people together.

Finally, he has united himself so closely with us that we are flesh of his flesh and bone of his bones. He is our Head, and we are his members. He is our Master, and we are his disciples. He is our King, and we are his subjects. He is our Vine, and we are his branches. He is our Bridegroom, and we are his Bride. This union is spiritual and hidden. The bond is faith on our part, and on the part of Christ, it is the Holy Spirit.

### CHAPTER XXXII.

->**Whether Christ was our Mediator in his two natures; whether he was the Mediator of the Angels; and when he obtained the office of Mediator.**<-

<margin>Peter Lombard, Book 3, Distinction question 19.9. Thomas Aquinas, part 3, question 26, article 1. Bellarmine, *Against* [Controversies], book 3, chapter 23. *Christ*, chapter 8. Becanus in *Manual*, Book 3, chapter 23. Stancarus.</margin>
The question is asked whether Christ was our Mediator with respect to his two natures, or of his human nature alone. (f)

I answer that if we search the Scriptures, we will find that they attribute the mediation of Christ to both the one and the other nature. Thus, it says that God obtained his Church through his blood (Acts 20:28) and that the Lord of Glory was crucified (1 Corinthians 2:8).

As man, he proclaimed the mysteries of the Gospel, but as God, he confirmed them and pressed them into the heart. It is true that Paul says there is one Mediator between God and men, the man Jesus Christ (1 Tim. 2:5). But, if one were to conclude from this that Christ is our Mediator only in regard to his human nature, one could also say it is written that God purchased his Church with his blood, and that the Lord of glory was crucified; therefore, it would be the Divine nature that shed its blood and was crucified. These names—Jesus, God, Jesus Christ man, Lord of glory—signify in the cited passages the *Person* of Christ, without actually defining to which nature belongs that which we attribute to him.

<margin>
Acts 20:28.
</margin>
<margin>
2 Cor. 2:8.

Therefore, from the name "man," which the Apostle gives to our Mediator, one can indeed deduce that the person who was clothed with this office was a man; but it does not follow from this that the Divine nature contributed nothing to the duties and ends of this great office. It was necessary that our Mediator was God to atone for our sins, to disarm the justice of God, to rule over the world, to found his Church and protect it against the attacks of the Devil, to raise men from the dead, and to receive believers into heaven. But Paul says here that Christ is man to confirm the truth of his human nature, and to make the terror which the Divinity of Christ could strike into us disappear (Heb. 4:15).

One will say that since God is the party with whom the Mediator must deal, the Mediator must be Mediator only in regard to his human nature.

I answer that if that were true, it would follow that our Mediator is then not God, which is a hideous blasphemy. But I add here that there is no harm in choosing a person from both

<column-break/>

parties as a Mediator in treaty negotiations. When in the common course of life a people is at odds with its Authority, one from that Authority—leaving aside his own interests—can enter into the Council of which he is a member as a Mediator between the two parties to reconcile them. When a Father and a Son, both Emperors, have been insulted by subjects or rebellious soldiers, who could prevent the Son from setting himself as Mediator between them to restore the subjects to the favor and grace of the King? Thereby he makes peace with himself, and he obtains the forgiveness of a debt by which he himself was wronged.

One will say that if Christ is our Mediator as God, then the Father and the Holy Spirit are also our Mediators.

I answer that to be Mediator, he had to be not only God, but also man, and that only the second Person of the Holy Trinity has united the two natures in himself.

One will say that a single act can only be the work of a single nature. One is mistaken: making a speech, for example, is an act of both our body and our soul.

One will say that the Mediator must hold the "middle-place" between the different parties, and that Christ, as a righteous man, held that place between God and sinners.

I answer that it is not necessary that the Mediator be of a different nature than those he wishes to unite: otherwise the Angels could be Mediators, whereas only one who was simultaneously God and man could be our Mediator.

It is said that Moses, who was only a man, was a Mediator.

Answer: that is true, but a symbolic <note>The original Dutch *voorbeeldig* refers to Moses as a "type" or "foreshadowing" of Christ in Reformed theology.</note> Mediator must be distinguished from the true Mediator.

It is asked whether Christ was the Mediator of the Angels?

We have already answered this question elsewhere and shown that Scripture says nothing of it. It says only that Christ is the Mediator between God and men. Why should he be the Mediator for the Angels, since there is no disagreement between God and these happy Spirits? If Adam had remained steadfast in the state of righteousness, he would have had no need of a Mediator. For what reason then would...

One asks, when was he appointed to this Office?

<margin>Ps. XLV. 8.</margin>
From his birth onward, he obtained the necessary gifts to serve this Office.

<margin>Isa. LXI. 1.</margin>

He exercised the same during his life and through his death, and he still exercises it since he ascended into Heaven.

I answer: 1. That it is not permitted for men to change the language of the Holy Spirit.

2. That, since the name of **Mediator** is given to Christ in particular, we must not attribute the same to any other.

3. That, if it were true that one must call "Mediators" all those who pray for others, one could say that all Christians and nations are Mediators, since they pray for one another—which until now no one has believed. In former times in the Roman Church, one could have said that the living believers were the Mediators of the deceased Saints, since there was a time and custom in which the living believers prayed for the dead Saints; we still have a prayer that was made every year for Pope Leo, in which it was prayed that the sacrifice <note>original: "offer"—referring here to the Mass or Eucharistic sacrifice</note> that was offered to God might serve to the benefit of the soul of Leo, His servant.

4. Furthermore, those who establish other Mediators besides Christ give them a ministry other than praying.

<margin>Book 1 on Indulgences, ch. 4.</margin>

# THE CHRISTIAN [THEOLOGY]

...is not, nor shall be, taken up into heaven / to pray for us as our advocate / except only our High Priest Jesus Christ / who is seated at the right hand of the Father / and prays for us.

Men will say that the merits of the Saints rest upon those of Christ. But however one turns or twists it / it will always follow / that one divides the honor of being Advocate between Christ and the Creature; for although it is claimed / that the merits of the Saints are founded upon those of Christ / and depend upon them / yet this does not prevent / one from viewing the merits of the Saints as their own merits / and extending them to the faithful / in order to obtain for them the grace / that they need. Thus a Christian / who owes the first and primary obligation for his Salvation <note>original: "Zaligheid," referring to the state of eternal grace and being saved</note> to Christ / would also be indebted for the same to the Saints.

Men will say / that someone / who requests the prayer of the Church / assumes that the same / being joined with his own prayers / will have more power / than if he prayed alone / and that consequently God, in the regard / which he has for the Church / finding a new motive to grant the grace / for which one prays / attributes the same to the merits of the Church.

I answer, that the prayer of the Church has more power with God than an individual prayer / not because there is any merit inherent in the church-prayer / for all merits come from Christ alone / but because many souls being gathered together create a more powerful desire / and a more notable request / to be heard by God.

Men will object / that / although it is commonly said / that there is but one God / who is good / and one master / one nevertheless generally also acknowledges / that there are many masters / and many good people; thus / when one says / that there is but one Mediator / one can say / that there are many.

I answer, that here a great distinction must be made; which the Scripture itself gives us to know: for it explains to us / in what sense it says / that there is but one Master and one good God / while it sometimes gives the name of "good" and of "Master" to men / whereas, on the contrary, it never applies the name of Mediator to them / and teaches nothing /

<column-break/>

from which one could conclude with any ground / that there are many Mediators. Among the things / that cannot be attributed to a creature / is the office of Mediator / as it is ascribed and proper to Christ.

Men will say / that *Moses* is called Mediator <note>Galatians 3:19</note> and *Timothy* a savior of himself and of others <note>1 Timothy 4:16</note>.

I answer, 1. that *Moses* is called Mediator only / because he made the will of God known to the people of *Israel* / and was their mouth before God. This cannot be said of any saints; besides, the issue here does not concern a Mediator like *Moses*, but like *Christ*. 2. It is testified of *Timothy* / that he would save himself and others / because he would bring men to Salvation through his preaching.

Men will say, that the Saints are our Mediators with *Christ* / and not with the Father.

I answer, that *Christ* / by calling us to himself / sufficiently indicates / that he needs no Mediator for us to come to him. He is our Advocate <term>Advocate: from the legal term "Voorspraak," a lawyer who pleads a case before a judge</term>. Who has ever heard that one needs Lawyers to go to a Lawyer to be heard? It is immediately through himself / that *Christ* leads us to the Father / and not through the intervention of *Peter* and of *Paul* with him.

To be a Mediator of intercession / one must know in particular all those / for whom one desires to speak and pray / and above all know whether they are children of God / and included in the number of the elect; one must be certain / that the grace / which one wishes to request for them / will be salutary to them / and that it will serve for God’s glory. <margin>Zech. 1:12</margin> 9. If an **Angel** prays for **Jerusalem** and for the cities of **Judah** in the book of **Zechariah**, one understands by this the **Angel of the Covenant**, the **Lord Jesus**, our only **Mediator**.

THEOLOGY. IX. B. CHAPTER XXXIV. 621

# CHAPTER XXXIV.

->Of the Three Offices of Christ.<-

The Mediatorial Office <note>The "Middelaar-Ampt" refers to the theological concept of Christ acting as the go-between for God and humanity.</note> is divided into three ministries that are inherently connected to and included within it: namely, those of **Prophet**, of **Priest**, and of **King**, all three of which **Christ** has exercised.

Holy Scripture frequently mentions these, and in particular, it indicates everywhere that our **Mediator** had to be **King**, **Priest**, and **Prophet**, specifically:

1. Firstly, in separate passages, such as **Deuteronomy 18:18**, where he is foretold as a **Prophet**; **Psalm 110:4** as a **Priest**; and **Psalm 2:6**, **110:1-2**, and **Isaiah 9:5** as a **King**.

2. Secondly, in some passages where all three of these ministries are presented together. Such as **Isaiah 61:1-2**: *The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me to bring good tidings to the humble.* Behold there his **Prophetic** ministry. *To proclaim liberty to the captives.* Behold there his **Royal** dignity. *To bind up the brokenhearted.* Behold there his **Priesthood**. **Zechariah 6:12-13**: *Behold a Man whose Name is the Branch, he shall grow up out of his place, and he shall build the Temple of the Lord, yes, he shall build the Temple of the Lord, and he shall bear the glory, and he shall sit and rule on his throne, and he shall be a Priest on his throne, and the counsel of peace shall be between them both.* Subsequently, he speaks of the calling of the **Gentiles**.

The same is also found in **Psalm 110**.

<margin>John 14:6</margin>
**Christ** also presented himself as being clothed with these three offices in the **Gospel**, when he says in **John 14:6**: *I am the way, the truth, and the life.* The **Way** through his **Priestly**, the **Truth** through his **Prophetic**, and the **Life** through his **Royal** Office.

<margin>1 Corinthians 1:30</margin>
**Paul** also joins these together in one passage, when he says in **1 Corinthians 1:30** that **Christ** has become to us from **God** our **Wisdom**, **Righteousness**, **Sanctification**, and **Redemption**. **Wisdom** as **Prophet**, **Righteousness** as **Priest**, **Sancti-**

<column-break/>

**-fication** and **Redemption** as **King**. **Wisdom** is the fruit of his **Prophetic** ministry, **Righteousness** is the work of his **Priestly** ministry, and **Sanctification** and **Redemption** are the effect of his **Royal** Ministry.

In the **Epistle to the Hebrews**, he likewise speaks of all three. He treats his **Prophetic Office**, in which regard he exalts him above all the **Prophets** and **Moses** himself. He describes his **Priesthood**, in which respect he places him above **Aaron** and **Levi**; he mentions his **Royal Office**, when he exalts him above **Joshua**, who had led the children of **Israel** into the land of **Canaan**; and he compares him to **Melchizedek** <note>A mysterious figure from Genesis who was both a king and a priest; he is considered a "type" or foreshadowing of Christ.</note>, who had been **King** and **Priest** at the same time.

The necessity of these three offices is easy to perceive. It was necessary that **Christ** be a **Prophet** to drive away the darkness of our ignorance; a **Priest** to deliver us from damnation and to acquire the **Peace** and **Love of God**; and a **King** to free us from the slavery of sin and death. He had to be a **Prophet** to make **Salvation** known to us; a **Priest** to obtain it; and a **King** to make it our own. As a **Prophet**, he had to teach us to know the **Divine** perfections; as a **Priest**, to reconcile us with **God**; and as a **King**, to subdue our enemies and his own. He had to be a **Prophet** to act toward us in **God’s** name; a **Priest** to be our advocate with **God**; and a **King** to make us free from our enemies.

The **Gentiles** <note>Meaning non-Jewish people or pagans in a historical context.</note> should not be surprised when we say that our **Mediator** had to perform these three ministries. They had their **Prophets** and **Soothsayers** to proclaim divine things, their **Priests** to reconcile their deities, and their **Kings** to rule them. All nations have shown—by the appointing, honoring, and choosing of their **Kings**, **Priests**, and **Prophets**—that they needed a true **Prophet**, a true **Priest**, and a true **King**; and thus they sought, as if groping with their hands, for the one whom they could not find in their darkness.

Regarding the **Jews**, they know that all the prominent offices and ministries that existed among them were images <note>In theology, "images" or "types" are Old Testament figures or events that prefigure something in the New Testament.</note> of those of the **Messiah**, and they were not ignorant that the an-

most visible dignities were those of Prophet, Priest, and King. They <note>The author is referring to the Jewish people.</note> therefore have no reason to be surprised that we, following the predictions of their Prophets, maintain that our Mediator must have three ministries; they must themselves accept our Jesus as the Messiah whom their Fathers expected, since he has been clothed with these three Offices.

No one had held them all together before him. Moses, who was the Head of the ancient Prophets, had neither the Priestly nor the Royal dignity. It is true that, as a Leader, he had the governance over the people of Israel; but properly speaking, Israel then had no other King than God. It is true that <margin>see Exodus 24.</margin> Moses sacrificed, see Exodus 24. But this was an extraordinary matter, for the consecration of Aaron and his inauguration into the Priesthood. Melchizedek was Priest and King, but not a Prophet. Aaron, to whom God had given the Priestly mitre, had no right to the Anointing of Kings and Prophets; and as for the Kings, God punished them severely when they stepped into the ministry of the Priests, as seen in the example of Uzziah <note>King Uzziah was struck with leprosy for attempting to burn incense in the Temple, a task reserved for priests.</note>. But Christ possessed all three Offices, and thus made known the infinite dignity of his person: for a mere creature could not exercise these three Offices.

The three Christian cardinal virtues correspond with these three Offices: **Faith**, which embraces the teaching of our Prophet; **Hope**, which rests upon the merits of our Priest; and **Love**, which submits itself to the Scepter of our King. Faith, which is an effect of his Prophetic Ministry, looks toward his Death (which is the principal part of his Priesthood) as well as his resurrection, ascension, and sitting at the right hand of God, which signifies nothing other than his Royal power.

Since we intend to deal with each of these ministries in particular, we shall further content ourselves with making some general remarks.

1. One must observe that these Offices of Christ were not to consist of physical and worldly things, but of spiritual and heavenly things: for

<column-break/>

the truth had to surpass all the shadows <note>In traditional theology, "shadows" refers to Old Testament rituals that prefigured or hinted at the "truth" found in Christ.</note>. Thus, it was not necessary that he, as a Priest, should offer animal sacrifices: but he had to slaughter an infinitely more glorious and worthy sacrifice; as King, he had to rule over the souls and minds of men, and as Prophet, he had to have his Throne in heaven and speak to us from there.

2. One must consider the order in which these Ministries must be arranged. It seems that the Priestly Office must be placed first, because he had to merit Salvation before he could proclaim it to us, apply it, and make it our own. It appears, however, that he began with the ministry of Prophet, continued with that of Priest, and ended with that of King.

There are those who believe that, although Christ taught on earth before he offered himself, one can nevertheless say that he did not fully reveal the will of his Father until after his sacrifice; and that it is properly through the pouring out of the Holy Spirit and the sending of his Apostles over the whole earth that he put the Prophetic Office into effect, and subsequently sat down as King at the right hand of the Father.

3. One must also observe that a single gift of grace can be attributed to Christ according to his three Offices. He preserves Salvation for us as King, but he also preserves it as Priest, who constantly prays for us, and as Prophet, who steadily teaches us our duty and presses his Law into our hearts. His death, which is the sacrificial offering of Christ, can also be viewed as a Battle which he, as King, engaged in to deliver his subjects.

Nothing now remains but to deal with the Anointing, by which Christ was consecrated into these three Offices, and which causes him to bear the name of **Christ**, which is to say, the Anointed One par excellence. To clarify this, one must know:

1. That under the Old Testament, three kinds of persons were anointed through an Anointing, the preparation of which is very accurately described in the Law-books of Moses. This Anointing was no simple or hollow ceremony; for, besides being the seal and mark of the Offices, it was an outward sign of the gifts of grace which
