DIVINITY. IX. B. CHAPTER XXXV.

God poured [His Spirit] upon those who were anointed, in order to make them fit for the duties of these honorable offices. These three types of persons were the **Prophets**, the **Priests**, and the **Kings**; the anointing of the Prophets is mentioned in 1 Kings 19:16, on the occasion of Elisha. It is not mentioned in other places; this caused some scholars to doubt the anointing of the Prophets: they are of the opinion that what is said of Elisha must be understood in a figurative sense. The anointing of the Priests is spoken of in Exodus 30; from this is taken that which gave the Holy Writer of the 133rd Psalm, verse 3, the inspiration to depict peace under the symbol of this precious oil poured out upon the head of Aaron. In 1 Kings 1:34, the anointing of Kings is mentioned, and it is said that Zadok and Nathan anointed Solomon. But one must carefully note that they only anointed the Kings who were not sons of Kings, or where the succession could be disputed, such as Solomon, who was anointed because of the rebellion of his brother Adonijah (1 Kings 1:5); Joash because of Athaliah (2 Chronicles 23:12); and Jehoahaz for the sake of his brother Jehoiakim (2 Kings 23:30).

<margin>Schickard</margin>
<note>Wilhelm Schickard was a 17th-century German polymath and Hebrew scholar.</note>
The Jewish Masters say that the Kings were anointed in a circle like an "O," or in the manner of a crown, and the Priests were anointed in the shape of a cross.

It is then no wonder that Jesus was anointed, since he had to be our Priest and our Prophet and our King; see Psalm 45:8.

II. But one must not imagine that the oil with which he was anointed was a material and earthly oil, like that which they used for anointing under the Old Testament. The anointing which Christ received was an entirely spiritual and heavenly oil, which, as it says in Psalm 45, was above that of his companions.

III. This signifies two things. 1. That Christ was consecrated into the office of **Mediator**. 2. That he received an abundance of grace to fulfill all his duties. Therefore he says himself through the mouth of Isaiah 61:1, *The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me.*

IV. If one asks, when was Christ anointed? The answer is easily given:

<column-break/>

1. He was anointed from his conception, being conceived of the Holy Spirit. 2. In his Baptism, when the Holy Spirit descended upon him; but above all after his ascension, when he became Lord and Christ (Acts 2:36).

<margin>Jean d'Espagne</margin>
<note>Jean d'Espagne was a prominent French Protestant theologian in the 17th century.</note>
I end this Chapter with an observation that some have made: namely, that when Holy Scripture speaks of Christ's suffering and death, it usually gives him the name **Christ**. *Christ has suffered, Christ has died. The Christ had to suffer all these things; the suffering of Christ,* etc. Possibly because this name includes that of Priest, which expresses the office he fulfilled when he offered himself to God on the cross. Paul says in Romans 6:8 and 10, that we have died with Christ, but shall also live in him. It is also noteworthy that when Paul describes the institution of the Holy Supper in 1 Corinthians 11, he always calls Jesus "Lord" and never "Christ." But perhaps one should not look for secrets in that.

### CHAPTER XXXV.

#### Of the Prophetic Office of Christ.

The first Office of Christ as **Mediator** is that of **Prophet**, in which he has revealed all the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven to mankind, as the **Supreme Teacher** of the Church.

There are those who would want to include the Prophetic Office under that of **King**, to whom it belongs to give laws, or under that of **Priest**, to whom God sometimes revealed the future and who gave answers on God's behalf. But those who hold this opinion do not explain themselves well: for, even if it were as they suggest, these three ministries nevertheless remain distinct from one another. The Prophets were raised up in an extraordinary manner, either to establish religion or to reform it. The Kings and Priests receive their commands with reverence. They were also called from another tribe, such as that of Levi, to whom the Priesthood belonged.

# CHRISTIAN
## THEOLOGY

One easily understands that it was necessary for us that Christ was our Prophet <note>The term "Prophet" here refers not just to one who predicts the future, but to a supreme teacher and messenger who reveals God’s will to humanity.</note>. Man can have no knowledge of God, nor of divine things, unless they are revealed to him. The natural man, says Paul in 1 Corinthians 2:14, does not understand the things of the Spirit of God. The Law and reason could not discover these mysteries; and no creature was capable of providing us any comfort against the feeling of sin, against death, against the miseries of the world, or against the terror of damnation. Christ alone could reveal to us those truths which we needed to know, and therefore it was <margin>Romans 10:27 <note>The text cites verse 27, though this famous passage about faith coming from hearing is found in Romans 10:17.</note></margin> necessary that he was our Prophet. Our salvation also required it, for there is no salvation without faith, and faith comes from hearing the word of God. There is no darker state than that of a person who lives in the darkness of ignorance and error, and who has no other leader or master than himself.

<margin>Deuteronomy 18:15, 16, 17, 18, 19.</margin> Moses had foretold that the Messiah would be a Prophet like him; in Deuteronomy 18:15, he says: *The Lord your God will raise up for you a Prophet from your midst, from your brothers, like me; to him you shall listen.* And in verses 18 and 19: *And I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him. And it shall come to pass, that whoever will not hear my words, which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him.* Peter also applies this oracle <margin>Acts 3:22; Isaiah 9:5.</margin> to Jesus in Acts 3:22. Isaiah speaks of the same office in chapters 42:1, 6; 49:6, 8; and 61:1, 2. Therefore, Christ is called in Matthew 23:8, etc., Counselor, Master, Teacher, and in Hebrews 3:1, the Apostle of our confession; and in Matthew 17:5, God says that we shall listen to him.

But, in order to well-comprehend that Christ alone was the Prophet whom we needed, one must observe the qualities that he had to possess.

1. Our Prophet had to have a perfect knowledge of all people, in order to give the necessary instructions, in whatever circumstances of time, place, and matters they might find themselves.

2. He had to have not only an infinite goodness, to teach us all that we needed to know, but also supreme authority over the conscience, and an absolute right over all the powers of our soul.

<column-break/>

3. He had to be infallible, incapable of misleading us, and of deceiving others or himself.

All these qualities are found in none other than the Son of God—God praised for all eternity <note>original: "God geprezen in alle eeuwigheid," likely translating the Latin "Deus benedictus in saecula."</note>. There is no one but He who is God who has an infinite knowledge, an unspeakable goodness, and an absolute authority over the Spirit and the conscience, along with the perfect privilege of infallibility. It was the Son alone, who is in the bosom of the Father, who could perfectly make known to us the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven.

The obedience that we owe to this supreme Prophet consists of true worship, as has been rightly noted, because we subject all our thoughts and reason to him, and must believe all that he teaches us. Since God alone must be worshipped, it follows that our Prophet must be God. In the governance of the soul and the conscience, neither Angel, nor man, nor any creature can be joined with God. After Christ had practiced this office—which he began at the age of twelve in the temple, in the midst of the Teachers—and was solemnly consecrated through his baptism, he was confirmed in it at the time of his glorification on the mountain by this voice from the high glory:

<margin>Matthew 17:5.</margin>
> This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him.

Christ has served this same office in various ways.

1. He explained the Law of Moses, and unfolded the true sense of the commandments against the false interpretations of the Pharisees and Scribes <note>The Pharisees and Scribes were religious leaders known for their strict, and sometimes legalistic, adherence to traditional interpretations of Jewish law.</note>. But he did not "improve" the Law, or add anything to it. We shall demonstrate this more broadly elsewhere.

2. He proclaimed the Gospel, which is therefore called the Gospel of Christ, and in this Gospel he has revealed: 1. all the essential perfections of the Godhead; 2. the incomprehensible mystery of the Trinity; 3. the secrets of God’s Will regarding the salvation of men, and his decree concerning the forgiveness of their sins, etc.; 4. all that belongs to our sanctification, the nature of sins, etc.; 5. all that could incite us to holiness; 6. the true objects of our hope and be-

<margin>Jean Claude, *Posthumous Works* <note>Jean Claude (1619–1687) was a renowned French Protestant theologian whose works were widely read in the Dutch Republic.</note></margin>
1. The Revelation of Christ occurred by means of words and instructions, whereas that of nature occurred by means of works—as has been very rightly observed. 2. The same things that are revealed in nature are infinitely clarified by the revelation of Christ. 3. Christ has made many things known to us of which no knowledge could be obtained through nature; furthermore, since the fall into sin, the Revelation of nature resembles a fallen palace, where one still sees some columns, arches, and capitals, but where one simultaneously perceives the marks of fire and destruction. It is a confused mixture of beauties and ruins. There is also a great distinction between the Revelation of the Law and that of the Lord Christ. The Law was a ministry of severity, a "Letter that killed" <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6, contrasting the strict requirements of the Mosaic Law with the life-giving Spirit of the Gospel.</note>. But the Revelation of Christ is a ministry of life, grace, and righteousness. The Law gave only the knowledge of sin, without a remedy. But the Revelation of Christ provides us, along with the knowledge of sin, the means to be delivered from it. The Law demanded an obedience without flaw or imperfection; Christ also requires the same obedience, but he simultaneously forgives its imperfection and deficiency, provided we have true repentance and take refuge in his fatherly mercy. The Law demanded perfect obedience, but it did not give the strength to fulfill it, while Christ accompanies his commands with the cooperating power of his Spirit. Christ has, moreover, pushed aside the veils under which the divine oracles were hidden and abolished the old church ceremonies. He has brought life and immortality to light, along with the resurrection of our bodies.

It required that He who created Heaven and earth should rule instead of the tyrant, Holiness instead of sin, and Truth instead of the lie.

### CHAPTER XXXVI.

->Of the Priesthood of Christ.<-

THE Second Office of Christ as <term>Mediator</term> <note>A go-between; in Christian theology, the one who reconciles God and humanity.</note> is his Priesthood.

It is not necessary for me to speak of the necessity of Christ’s Priesthood, because all the reasons that prove the necessity of his <term>satisfaction</term> <note>The legal payment or atonement for sin.</note> also demonstrate that of his Priestly office. I shall proceed to other observations.

<margin>
Psalm 110:4.
Hebrews 5:5 and 7:21.
</margin>
The Father has established the Son in this office, and indeed with an oath, in the most solemn manner. This oath shows the excellence of his Priesthood in two ways. First, because it shows the importance of the matter, for one does not swear an oath over small things. Second, because the oath makes this Priesthood irrevocable; it is also an eternal Priesthood. This eternity must not be viewed with respect to his sacrifice, which had a beginning and an end, for Christ offered himself only once; but its eternity consists in this: 1. That his Priesthood shall not make way for another; 2. That the effect and the power of the same extends into eternity.

<margin>
Smalcius, chapter 13.
*On the Divinity of Christ*.
Volkelius, book 3, chapter 37.
Racovian Catechism, *On the Office of Christ the Priest*.
<note>These references point to Socinian authors who argued that Christ was not a priest on earth but only became one in heaven.</note>
</margin>
The question is asked whether Christ was truly our Priest who began his Priesthood on earth, or whether he is called our Priest only in a figurative way and performed the duties of his office only in Heaven. In that view, his Priesthood would not differ from his Kingly office, except in so far as the office of King signifies the power to come to our aid, and that of Priest signifies the will to bring us his help. Thus, [according to that view] he did not bring about the reconciliation for our sins through his sacrifice on earth; but the reconciliation which he made after ascending to Heaven is our deliverance—either from sins, so that we should not give ourselves over to them, or from punishment, so that we should not suffer it.

# THEOLOGY. BOOK IX. CHAPTER XXXVI.

<margin>XI.</margin> This is the opinion of the <term>Socinians</term> <note>A rationalist Christian movement that denied the pre-existence of Christ and argued that his priesthood only began after his ascension into heaven.</note>.

<margin>XII.</margin> Our view is that Christ is truly and properly our Priest; that his Priesthood is a real Priesthood; that he began the same on the cross through the sacrifice of his body, and continues it without ceasing in Heaven through his intercession for us; that his sacrifice was a true reconciliation for our sins; and that according to his Priesthood, he is entirely distinct from his Kingly office, since his Priesthood comprises these two parts: the offering of his sacrifice and his intercession, whereas his Kingly office consists in the governing and protecting of the people whom he has purchased through his sacrifice. This is proven by:

1. The passages where he is named Priest, such as Psalm 110:4, and Hebrews 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, and where he is compared to the priests of old in Hebrews 5:1.

The word found in Psalm 110:4 must not be translated as "Prince," although it appears elsewhere in that sense (the Jews cite Genesis 41:45, Exodus 2:16 and 3:1, 2 Samuel 8:18, and 20:26 in support of this). For it is clearly stated there that he is a Priest after the order of Melchizedek. One must therefore take this word in the same sense regarding the Messiah as it is used regarding Melchizedek in Genesis 14:18-19, where the Hebrew word <note>original: "cohen"</note> must be translated as "Priest."

2. The passages in which the ministry of the Priesthood is attributed to him.

3. All the examples <note>These are "types" or historical figures/rituals believed to foreshadow Christ.</note> that have foreshadowed his Priesthood.

4. The passages that expressly report that he offered his sacrifice on the earth before he ascended to Heaven, as in Hebrews 1:3 and 9:11, 12.

5. The passages that say he offered a true sacrifice on the cross, in Hebrews 7:27 and 9:26, 28. For Paul argues there: 1. Concerning a Sacrifice which corresponds to those of the Old Testament through the slaughter and shedding of the blood of the sacrificial animal. 2. Concerning a Sacrifice that was performed once. 3. Which he accomplished in a visible manner. 4. And which had to precede his sitting at God’s right hand.

One might object using Hebrews 8:4, where Paul says that Christ would not be a Priest if he were on earth.

<column-break/>

Answer: The Apostle does not thereby deny that Christ was a Priest on earth; for he would then be contradicting himself (see Hebrews 7, 9, and 10). Rather, he is speaking of the second part of his Priesthood, namely his intercession with the Father, which he carries out in Heaven. The meaning of the words comes down to this: That if Christ were still present on earth today, he could not be a Priest because, after offering his sacrifice, he had to perform the same duty that the High Priests under the Law performed. These did not remain in the outer Court after they had slaughtered their sacrificial animal, but they entered into the Holy of Holies with the blood. If Christ had not also brought the blood of his sacrifice into the true Sanctuary, he would not have fulfilled all the parts of his Priestly office. From the aforementioned objection, it does not follow that Christ was not a true Priest on earth when he offered up his body; rather, it follows that he did not have to perform all the ministries of his Priesthood on earth. Just as the Priest under the Law was a true Priest before he entered the Holy of Holies with the blood, so likewise Christ was a true Priest before his entrance into the Heavenly Sanctuary.

One might object using Hebrews 5:5, where it is said that Christ did not glorify himself to become High Priest; but it was he who said to him: *You are my Son, today I have begotten you.* <note>original: "Gy zyt mijn Zoone, heden heb ik u gegenereert." A quote from Psalm 2:7 applied to Christ's appointment.</note>

I answer that Paul is not speaking here of the *time* in which Christ became High Priest, but of the *one* who appointed him to this office, in order to demonstrate not the timing, but the Divinity of this dignity.

One can draw no proof nor conclusion from this that Christ was only a Priest in Heaven. The misunderstanding arises from having a poor conception of the word "glorify," by which the Apostle intends to convey nothing other than that the one who conferred the honor of the Priesthood upon Christ and called him to it, is the same one who said to him, *You are my Son,* etc.

The Priesthood of Christ is foreshadowed by the <term>Levitical Priesthood</term> <note>The priesthood of the descendants of Levi in the Old Testament, who served in the Tabernacle and Temple.</note>.

CHRISTIAN THEOLOGY
<meta>Catchword: the</meta>

The Priesthood of Aaron was a model of Christ’s priesthood in several ways:

1. In the atonement for sins according to the way of the Law.
2. In a certain communion with God and the blessing that it brought upon the people.
3. In the appointment of Aaron to that office by God himself.
4. In the three parts that it likewise comprised, consisting of: 1. Offering sacrifices. 2. Entering into the Sanctuary. 3. Blessing the people.

It is easy to apply these four things to the Priesthood of Christ. Let us observe how his Priesthood excels above that of Levi.

1. The Levitical Priesthood had various imperfections which God saw fit to leave there, so that the people would certainly be prompted to seek another Priesthood and find true comfort in it.
2. The Priests of the Law were from the Tribe of Levi; Christ is from the Tribe of Judah (Hebrews 7:13, 14).
3. They were mere men, but Christ is God and man.
4. They were sinners and therefore had to offer sacrifices for themselves first; but Christ is the Holy of Holies <note>The author uses this title for Christ to emphasize his absolute purity compared to the high priest who only entered the physical "Holy of Holies."</note>, who has no need for a sacrifice for himself (Hebrews 7:26, 27).

<margin>Hebrews 9:14 etc., 10:14. Ephesians 5:2.</margin>
5. They were distinct from their offerings, and it was not their own blood, but that of another, through which they atoned for sin. Christ is Priest and Offering at the same time; he offered himself and shed his own blood for the forgiveness of sin.

6. They were many in number because one alone could not perform everything: Christ is the only High Priest, who has had neither successor nor deputy.

<margin>Hebrews 7:20, 21. Psalm 110.</margin>
7. The Priesthood of Christ was established with an oath, but that of Levi was not; which indicated that the latter would be abolished and the former would last forever.

<margin>Hebrews 7:16.</margin>
8. The Levitical Priesthood involved various fleshly <note>In this context, "fleshly" refers to physical rituals, ceremonies, and earthly regulations of the Old Covenant.</note> institutions and ceremonies: that of Christ has abolished and nullified them. Also, Christ was not appointed by virtue of the Law—which passed the Priesthood from the deceased priest to the living one—but by another Law that made him a Priest forever.

<column-break/>

<margin>Hebrews 9:13, 14. Law 10:3, 4 and 7:19. 1 John 1:7.</margin>
9. The Priesthood of Levi had no power to atone for sins and cleanse the conscience; likewise, the Law brought nothing to perfection. But the sacrifice of Christ has an infinite power, whether to justify us or to sanctify us.

<margin>Hebrews 10:11. Daniel 9:7. Hebrews 7:16.</margin>
10. The Levitical sacrifice had to be repeated every time because it was deficient: that of Christ is perfect and needs no repetition.

11. The Levitical Priesthood was to last only for a certain time and subsequently be abolished, and the priests were mortal men: but the Priesthood of Jesus is eternal because he is immortal.

12. The High Priest went into the Holy of Holies only once a year, and he came out again immediately: Christ has entered into Heaven forever, and if he must appear from there to judge the living and the dead, he shall return there again full of glory.

13. The Priesthood, among the children of Aaron, was not paired with the Royal Scepter. Christ is Priest and King at the same time. He is a Priest according to the order of Melchizedek.

It will not be necessary for us to discuss Melchizedek at length here. According to our view, he was neither Shem, nor Ham, nor the Holy Spirit, nor the Son of God: but was a King of Salem.

The correspondence of the Priesthood of Christ with that of Melchizedek consists:

1. In the Name of Melchizedek, which means "King of Peace": Christ is the Lord our Righteousness and our Prince of Peace. He has brought eternal righteousness and made peace with God, with the angels, with men (among both Jews and Gentiles), and the peace of man with his own conscience.

<margin>Hebrews 7:3.</margin>
2. In his genealogy. Paul says that Melchizedek was without father, without mother, and without genealogy. This does not mean that he actually had no father, nor mother, nor genealogy, nor predecessor, nor successor in his office; but that the Scripture mentions nothing of them, in order to more vividly depict the excellence of Christ’s Priesthood, which primarily consists in this: that he had neither predecessor nor successor in his ministry. 3. In the description that Paul makes of Melchizedek, whom he says was without beginning of days and end of life; not because his life truly had no beginning nor end, but because his birth and his death are entirely passed over in silence in the Holy Scriptures <note>Original: "H. Some believe that, just as Melchizedek offered bread and wine to Abraham, or, as they say, sacrificed it, the body and the blood of Christ are likewise offered in the Mass under the outward signs of bread and wine; and they are of the opinion that in this respect Christ has successors. <margin>

One must note here what we have already touched upon: that the Priests performed three things. 1. They sacrificed. 2. They prayed for the people, which especially belonged to the High Priest to do. 3. They blessed the same.

<column-break/>

Christ has exercised these three Priestly offices.

1. He offered himself to God for us on the cross. Isaiah 53:10. Heb. 10:10.

2. He has entered into the Heavens to pray for us.

3. He blesses us with heavenly <note>The original "overhemelsche" suggests blessings that are beyond or above the physical heavens.</note> blessings.

These three parts of Christ's Priesthood are of a great extent and are paired together. In vain would Christ have died for sinners to acquire Salvation for them if he did not apply the same to them through his intercession and give his blessing. Therefore John says (1 John 2:1, 2), after he has depicted Christ as our advocate with the Father, that he is our propitiation <note>Original: "verzoening," meaning atonement or reconciliation.</note>. Christ says himself (John 17:9) that he does not pray for the World, but for those whom the Father has given him, so that he might shed his blood for them.

To begin with the first of these offices of Christ's Priesthood, it is evident from what was said before that Christ did not offer a sacrifice of dumb animals, but himself through the eternal Spirit, as Paul expresses it (Heb. 9:14). He was delivered up for our sins (Rom. 4:25) and raised for our justification. The blood of animals could not atone for our sins: I will not involve myself further here, because I have already pressed this proof in another place. I shall only make the following observations on some passages of Scripture.

Eph. 5:25, 26, 27.

This Church consists of the true believers, who are the true members of the Church. Therefore it is said elsewhere (John 10:11) that Christ lays down his life for his sheep, and (Matt. 1:21) that he has come to save his people from their sins.

<margin>
John 17:2, 6.
John 6:39 and 15:3.
</margin>

Rom. 5:7, etc.
</margin>
3. Christ's sacrifice is the greatest sign of love that one can conceive.

4. Through his sacrifice, he has become the cause of Salvation for all who obey him. Heb. 5:9.

# CHAPTER XXXVII.
## On the Truth of the Satisfaction of Christ.

<margin>Socinus, *On the Saviour*, Book 1, Chapter 1. Crellius.</margin>
WE have said several times that Christ, through his death, has satisfied Divine justice. This matter deserves to be considered more closely. One must see whether Christ truly and properly satisfied [justice], and examine with all attention whether he is our Savior only because he made known to us God's will regarding our salvation; showed us the way that leads to Heaven by his teaching and example; and demonstrated through his resurrection and ascension that all who keep the same path as he did shall certainly be raised and taken up to Heaven, and according to the power the Father gave him, has obtained eternal life for all those who shall obey his commands; **or** whether he is our Savior through merits and through satisfaction to Divine justice for us and in our place. One must know clearly and distinctly whether he died only to confirm the New Covenant and the promises presented to us therein—to grant us the right to have a share in them, provided one fulfills the conditions attached thereto—to bring men to embrace and fulfill these conditions; and by the power he obtained, to forgive sins and carry out the promises regarding those who fulfill the covenant; **or** whether he died to suffer the punishments we had deserved, and through his death to earn the forgiveness of sins and eternal life. This is what we maintain against the Socinians <note>The Socinians were a group that denied the Trinity and the "satisfaction" theory of atonement, viewing Jesus primarily as a moral teacher and example.</note>.

One has only to read the Holy Scriptures to be convinced of the truth of our doctrine...

Who then will not marvel at the boldness of Socinus, who says that even if he found it ever so many times in the scripture that Christ has made satisfaction, he would never believe it should be understood in the sense in which we explain it.

Shall one say that Christ is a Mediator, just as Moses was? We have answered this in the preceding chapters, and we now add that it is nowhere testified of Moses that he gave himself over.

Shall one say that Christ is called a Redeemer, just as Moses bears the name of Redeemer of the people of Israel? Acts 7:35. We have shown the opposite when we explained the name of Redeemer, and we have proven that a true redemption is spoken of, since mention is made of a ransom. Matt. 20:28. 1 Cor. 6:20. 1 Pet. 1:18. Besides that, one must not judge a spiritual redemption, such as that of the Lord Christ, by a temporal redemption, such as that of Moses was.

One asks, to whom did Christ pay the ransom that he offered for us? This, it is said, cannot be the Devil, for that is unseemly to think; it also cannot be to God, it is added, because he did not hold us in slavery—on the contrary, he gave us Christ to redeem us. From which it is then concluded that Christ did not buy us free.

It is not difficult to answer that. Alcuin <note>Alcuin of York (c. 735–804), a scholar and advisor to Charlemagne.</note> mentions a Greek who appeared at the court of Charlemagne in his time and asserted that it was death that had received the ransom for our sins. Alcuin refutes this opinion (Letter to Charlemagne in Baluze's *Miscellanea*, Vol. 1, p. 365). Origen said that Satan had demanded the blood of Christ as a compensation for the freedom he had granted to men. These are ridiculous thoughts. 1. Therefore, I say that there is a great difference between the money that must be paid for a debtor and the crimes for which one must make satisfaction. The money given to be redeemed is paid to the person who has an interest in it. But in the case of crimes, it is not so. The punishment by which

<column-break/>

one is reconciled is not a thing that one possesses or can give. Meanwhile, it is said that someone who is punished pays the penalty or debt of his crime, but the payment is made to Justice and to the laws that demand it. 2. I answer that Christ paid our ransom to God, because He is the Sovereign Lord of the world, the protector of His rights, the upholder of justice; and as such, Christ presented the ransom to Him. The goodness He showed in giving us a Mediator and handing Him over to death for us does not deprive Him of His power as Sovereign, nor does it prevent Him from receiving the satisfaction of His justice from the hand of the <term>Surety: "Borg" in the original, a legal term for someone who takes responsibility for another person's debt or behavior.</term> whom He has given us, and as Sovereign to declare that the satisfaction is of sufficient value and that the rights of His justice are paid in the proper manner, upon which He can show His grace to mankind.

Shall one say that Christ has redeemed us from wrath by His life (Rom. 5:10), and consequently not by His death and the payment of any ransom for us, but through redemption from eternal death, which we shall obtain at the last day through His omnipotence? I answer that in reasoning thus, two things are mixed together: the acquisition of salvation, which is the first step of our redemption, which Christ earned for us by His blood and death; and the application of salvation, which Christ has arranged for us through His life and life-giving spirit.

Shall one say that, since we were sold without money—having thrown ourselves into the hands of the Devil—we were consequently also redeemed without money?

Answer: This conclusion does not hold. Do we not see every day that what was sold for a small price cannot be redeemed again except with much money and great cost? We had cowardly sold ourselves, but to buy us free from the curse we had deserved thereby, a great satisfaction was required.

Shall one say that when Scripture says we are reconciled with God through Christ, this reconciliation means our deliverance? This is said to be evident from the fact that it is said, not that God is reconciled with us, but that we are reconciled with God, in order

**Answer.** To reason in this way is to blind oneself. For: 1. Can one deny that the Scripture portrays God as having been our enemy, since it testifies that we were subject to His wrath and curse? 2. If our reconciliation meant only our conversion <note>The act of a person turning their heart toward God</note>, why is it that this reconciliation is attributed more to the death of Christ than to His life? Why does the Scripture describe our reconciliation as an effect of the infinite love of God, if it were true that all that was needed was for Him to make us stop hating Him? 3. It appears that Paul does not distinguish our reconciliation from our <term>justification</term> <note>justification: the legal act where God declares a sinner righteous</note>, as one can clearly conclude from Romans 5:9–10; for he uses these two expressions as synonymous: being "justified by the blood of Christ" and being "reconciled through His death." Certainly, <term>sanctification</term> <note>sanctification: the internal process of becoming holy</note> is not being spoken of there. People are thus confusing two reconciliations here: one that God made through Christ (2 Corinthians 5:18–19) and one that the Apostles exhort us to (verse 20). The first is the non-imputation of our sins, as Paul teaches us; but the second includes our conversion, which is brought about through faith and repentance.

Furthermore, it should be noted here that in the <note>original: "Siriſche vertaling"</note> Syriac translation of Romans 5:10, it says that God was reconciled with us.

One will say, that this satisfaction shows / that the one / for whom one satisfies / has not come to perform it himself / whereas / when one gives an example / it is presupposed / that it can be followed.

But one mixes satisfaction and suffering together. Christ, in satisfying, left no example to follow him / that is, to satisfy / for this is impossible: but suffering with patience / he taught us by his example to suffer with patience.

The first is / to satisfy Divine justice in truth / and to wipe away our sins : but this does not prevent / his also intending to give us a horror of sin / and to make us love righteousness. *Christ is given to us to be our righteousness and our sanctification.* His death was an atoning and merit-earning sacrifice ; an atoning sacrifice, which has reconciled our sin / and a merit-earning sacrifice, which has earned for us the gift of the Holy Spirit. But it appears clearly from all that the Scripture tells us / that Christ did not die only to make us holy. If his death had served only that purpose / it would only have been effective regarding men / whom it either convinces of unbelief through the proofs / which it contains of the truth ; or whose morals it improves through the examples of virtue / which it presents to them. But regarding God, it would have worked nothing other than this / that it would have been pleasing to him. Meanwhile, the Scripture sets as a firm Foundation / that his death had its chief effect in regard to God. Therefore it says so emphatically / that Christ <margin>Hebrews 5:1</margin> is our High Priest. *Now every High Priest is appointed for men, in things pertaining to God.* <note>The author argues that a priest's primary role is to act on behalf of humans toward God, rather than acting from God toward humans.</note>

2. It is ridiculous to say / that Christ died for our sins / because he died / to assure us of their forgiveness ; for who does not see the distinction / that exists between these two things; to die for our sins / and to die to assure us / that we have obtained the forgiveness of them.

3. Christ so truly died for our sins / that he became a curse and sin for us / because he subjected himself / to all the curses and punishments / which the Law pronounces against Sinners / <margin>Galatians 3:13. 2 Corinthians 5:21.</margin> and set himself as an atoning sacrifice for sin.

Will one say, that Christ did not undergo the curse / which we had deserved / because this curse was eternal death / which Christ could not have suffered / because it was necessary / that he rose from the dead.

This excuse is ridiculous / for Christ was a Divine Person / and his suffering / which not only has an infinite power / but was extremely heavy

<column-break/>

has been, in its way, an eternal death. The godless shall only bear a punishment / that will be infinite in duration / because they cannot withstand all the weight of God's wrath at once / as Christ has done. <note>This is a standard Reformed argument: because Christ is infinite (Divine), his finite time of suffering carries the weight of an eternity of human suffering.</note>

Will one say, that Paul wants to teach us nothing else / than that Christ suffered the death of the cross / which was cursed by God ; but that he was therefore not exposed to the curse / which we had deserved.

But, if this were the sense of the Apostle / would he say / that Christ has redeemed us from the curse of the Law / having become a curse for us? How could he have redeemed us from it / except by subjecting himself to the curse? The cross / to which Christ was nailed / was not the cause / for which it is said there / that he became a curse / but he suffered that cursed death / to show that he was subjected to all the weight of God's wrath. It is then untrue to say / that Christ was not subjected to it ; for / if he had not borne God's wrath / is it likely that he would have suffered such terrors / death-agonies / and soul-anxieties at the sight of the approach of death? <note>The author refers to Christ’s agony in the Garden of Gethsemane as proof he was facing more than just physical execution.</note>

It appears / that Paul speaks of the Heathen as well as of the Jews / for he adds there / that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Heathen in Jesus Christ. Galatians 3:14.

Will one say, that Christ is called sin / not / because he was a sacrifice for sin / but because he was treated exactly as if he were a Sinner? But one must note / that it does not only say that Christ became sin / but that God made him sin for us / which corresponds exactly to the saying of *Isaiah, that God caused the iniquity of us all to run upon him. Isaiah 53:6.*

# THEOLOGY. IX. B. CHAPTER XXXVII.

...confirmed throughout the whole 53rd Chapter of this Evangelical Prophet <note>Isaiah is often called the "Evangelical Prophet" in older theology because his prophecies of Christ are so detailed they resemble the Gospels (Evangelies).</note> / that we have already brought forward.

It is said, that one must not press this expression **to bear sin** too far: that this word often means **taking away** / and that it is in this sense / that it is written / that God bears the iniquity of men. Exodus 34:7. Numbers 14:18. to say that he forgives the same. Furthermore / that Christ is said to bear our sins / not because he has borne the punishments / which our sins deserved / but because he has healed our sicknesses and infirmities / just as Matthew explains these words. Chapter 8:16, 17. For / it is said, he did not bear the infirmities by taking them upon himself / but by healing them. It is true / that this expression means both **bearing** and **taking away** / and we acknowledge that Christ has done both; He has borne our sins and taken them away; He has released us from the punishment / which we deserved / by bearing the same for us / and he also takes away from our hearts through his spirit the failings / that are therein. However, it is certain / that in this place one must translate it as **bearing** / which is evident. 1. From what is added / *He has borne our sorrows*, see verse 4. and although the Prophet uses this manner of speaking once more in verse 11. after he had said / that the righteous servant of the Lord would justify many through his knowledge, and see the labor of his soul, one must nevertheless not believe / that Isaiah wants to teach us / that Christ bore our sorrows and iniquities after his resurrection / but he wants to show us the cause / and the foundation of the reward / which Christ was to receive / and of the justification / which he would merit; for how could he have justified / if he had not satisfied <note>The word "voldaan" here refers to "satisfaction," the legal payment or fulfillment of a debt of justice.</note>? 2. It also appears that one must translate **bearing the sins**, because the manner / in which Christ bore the same / is immediately added and explained there / by being **crushed** and **oppressed**, so that the punishment, which was upon him, has brought us peace. 3. It is fixed / that Christ has borne our sins / in the same way the atoning sacrifices bore them; also it is said / verse 10. that he has offered his soul as a **guilt offering**

<column-break/>

for sin, in allusion to the ancient atoning sacrifices / which were regarded as laden with the sins of the people / who therefore laid their hands on the head of the beasts / and made confession of their sins / to transfer the same, as it were, from themselves onto the sacrifice.

The Heathens / (as Herodotus notes of the Egyptians Book 2. Chapter 19. and Plutarch in his book *On Isis and Osiris*) also laid their hands on the head of the sacrificial animal with terrible curses / and in particular with this one / that all the disasters that were to happen to their people / in general or in particular / and especially to the one who offered the animal / might fall down upon its head.

One must therefore not compare what is said of God / that he bears the iniquities of his people / with what is testified of the Messiah: for it does not only say / that he has borne our sins / but that he has borne them **on the wood** <note>original: "op het hout" — a reference to the wooden cross, citing 1 Peter 2:24.</note>; that he was **oppressed, plagued, and crushed** for our transgressions / which is not said of God. Although Matthew, recounting the miracle-healings of Christ / says / that thereby was fulfilled / what is written in Isaiah / one must be careful not to believe / that this prophecy concerns only physical infirmities. But the Evangelist speaks thus. 1. Because the sicknesses of the body are the effects of sin / for whose sake Christ was crushed. 2. Because the healings / which Christ wrought in the days of his walking in Judea / were symbols of the grace / which he shows to our souls / whose sins he heals. 3. And that the sicknesses of the body presuppose those of the soul; therefore the Lord Christ said / healing the paralytic in body; *your sins are forgiven you.* Matthew 9:2.

It is said, that this manner of speaking is borrowed from the <term>Scapegoat [Hazazel]</term>, of which Leviticus 16 speaks; to which one cannot properly say / that the sins of the people were imputed / so that he bore them: but that this only means / that all the sins of the people were taken away in the same manner / as if this goat had loaded the same upon itself / but that for the rest one cannot say / that this goat for the people...

# THE CHRISTIAN <note>This header is likely part of a longer title like "The Christian Religion" or "The Christian Theology."</note>

...made satisfaction <note>This completes the thought from the previous page: even if a sacrifice was not killed in a specific way, it still fulfilled its purpose.</note> / since nothing is mentioned of its death.

But 1 / nothing obliges us to say / that this manner of speaking refers specifically to the goat *Azazel* <note>The "scapegoat" sent into the wilderness on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16).</note> / since nothing prevents us from believing / that the Prophet has his eye on all the Sin-offerings.

2. Although one must admit / that the sins of the people were not actually imputed to the goat *Azazel* / it does not follow from this / that it is the same with *Christ* as with this goat: for one must place a great distinction between the example and the truth / between the shadow and the body <note>A common theological distinction where Old Testament rituals are "shadows" pointing to the "body" or reality of Christ.</note>. Meanwhile one cannot deny / that this goat did in some way bear the sins / if one reads *Leviticus 16:20, 21* with some attention.

3. Regarding the excuse / that is sought by saying / that nothing is mentioned of the death of this goat. I answer, 1. That / if the Jews may be believed / this goat was thrown from a high precipice by the one who had led it into the Wilderness / and that it consequently fell down dead. They add to this / that / when it was perceived that the *Crimson* thread, which was fastened to the horns of the goat / became white / it was a sign that God was reconciled / for which they cite *Isaiah 1:18*. 2. I answer, that the sending away of this goat to the Wilderness / did not constitute the whole sin-offering. For another goat was slaughtered. *Leviticus 16:15, 16.* Thus one saw in these two goats an example of the true reconciliation for sin / which had to happen through the shedding of blood / and consequently the effect of this reconciliation / which takes away the sin from before God’s face.

It is said, that bearing sin does not always include a punishment in itself / but merely a suffering on the occasion of sins. Thus God threatens the *Israelites* / *Numbers 14:33* / that they shall bear the infidelities of their Fathers. *Lamentations 5:7.* They cry out / *Our Fathers have sinned, and we bear their iniquities*; one cannot say / it is added / that these places imply / that the *Jews* made satisfaction for the sins of their Fathers.

But I answer, 1. That it is not necessary / that the phrase / to bear sins, is always taken in one meaning / and that one must be blind / not to see / that the same is used regarding *Christ* in a special man-

<column-break/>

ner / since he suffered not merely on the occasion of sins / but in order to atone for sins. 2. One cannot deny / that the sense / which we give to this expression / is the most natural and the most proper sense. 3. It is certain / according to the ongoing testimony of the whole scripture / that *Christ* has suffered true pains and punishments / since it is said / that he has become a curse. The *Jews* sometimes call the *Messiah* the man / who must perform the reconciliation for sins / and the *Rabbis Judah* and *Simon* have said / that the *Messiah* would bear the sins.

The preposition *for*, when it is joined with suffering, commonly means the cause for which one suffers / or that which has deserved the punishment / as appears from *Leviticus 26:28, Deuteronomy 28:12, 2 Kings 23:26, Jeremiah 13:22*.

<margin>Crellius on Romans 4:25 <note>Johannes Crellius was a prominent Socinian theologian who argued against the traditional view of the atonement.</note></margin>
It is said, that one must interpret the first words of *Paul, He was delivered for our sins*, like the following / *He was raised for our justification*, that it signifies the end <note>The "end" here means the intended goal or result.</note> and not the cause.

<margin>Galatians 3:13. 2 Corinthians 5:21.</margin>
I answer, 1. That our justification is an end / that God has proposed for himself / but that one cannot say such a thing of sin. 2. And that our sins have been the true cause of *Christ's* death.

<margin>Crellius</margin>
Furthermore, one need only read the passage in *Galatians 3:19* / to see the distinction / that exists between this passage and that of *Romans 4:25* / besides that it is certain / that transgressions were the cause / that moved God to proclaim his law / to convict men of their iniquities. Finally, the *Socinians* <note>A group of 16th/17th-century Christians who rejected the Trinity and the idea that Christ died to satisfy divine justice.</note> themselves confess / that sins are the cause of *Christ's* death.

It is said as an excuse, that one must understand the words of the Apostle / *He was delivered for our sins* / like those of *1 Kings 14:16* / where it is said / that *Israel* was delivered up for the sins of *Jeroboam*.

But who does not see the distinction, that is between these two examples? *Israel* was not delivered up so that it would bear and take away the sins of *Jeroboam* / as is said of *Christ*; *Israel* was delivered up for its own improvement / and *Christ* was given over to death for our sins.

-># THEOLOGY. BOOK IX. CHAPTER XXXVII.<-

All these reasonings and answers to the presented objections are enough to prove the truth of Christ’s satisfaction <note>The theological doctrine that Christ’s suffering paid the "debt" humans owed to God's justice due to sin.</note> / and one can bring nothing substantial against it; we have already refuted the argument / that is taken from the idea / that anyone can waive his rights / that a creditor can forgive a debt / and that God can consequently step away from punishment / because he is regarded as the creditor. See Matthew 18. But so as to leave no objections unanswered / we shall present and resolve a few more.

1. It is objected, that one reads nowhere / that Christ has made satisfaction / and that he has borne for us the punishments / which we owed to Divine justice.

One can say nothing more absurd / for indeed the word satisfaction <note>original: "Satisfactio"</note> which is a Latin word / is not found in the Holy Scriptures / which were written in Hebrew and Greek. But the Scripture tells us the same thing in other words / when it testifies / that Christ has bought us / and has paid a ransom <term>ransom: a price paid to release a captive; here, Christ's life given to free humanity from sin</term> for us / that he became a curse for us / and is a reconciliation for our sins.

2. It is also said / that the doctrine of satisfaction conflicts with the Scripture / which says / that God forgives us our sins for free / and that where there is satisfaction / no forgiveness takes place.

<margin>
Socinus, book 
3: *On the 
Savior*, ch. 2. 
Crellius, ch. 
6. §. 14.
<note>References to Faustus Socinus and Johannes Crellius, 16th/17th-century theologians who rejected the traditional view of the Atonement.</note>
</margin>
But I answer, that these are not two contradictory things / to say that God forgives our sins / and that he receives a satisfaction for them / just as one will agree / when one considers / that there without the shedding of blood / that is without satisfaction / there is no forgiveness of sin; that we do not satisfy Divine justice / as it could demand / but that Christ has suffered for us; it says / Romans 3:24, 25. *that we are justified freely by the grace of God through the redemption that is in Christ, whom God has set forth to be a propitiation <note>A sacrifice that turns away divine wrath.</note> in his blood through faith.* God has shown us his love / by giving us his Son and forgiving our sins / and at the same time the love he had for his justice / by delivering his beloved Son up to it.

It will be objected, that one cannot

<column-break/>

say / that one forgives a debt to someone / when another has paid enough for him.

I answer, that this is true regarding monetary debts. It does not matter to the creditor / who pays him / but it is not so with crimes / which deserve death; God had the right to demand satisfaction from the humans themselves / as we have noted elsewhere / and to doom them to eternal punishment / but he did not do it. He contented himself with a surety <term>surety: a person who takes legal responsibility for another's debt or conduct</term> / and this surety he provided for us himself; is that not a clear proof of his infinite grace?

It is further said / that where there is no longer a debt / no forgiveness takes place and consequently / since our surety has loaded himself with our sins / one cannot say / that there is forgiveness.

I answer, that this reasoning would hold / if we had been required to bear the punishment ourselves: but / since God had the right to demand it from us / he shows us his grace by holding himself satisfied with what our surety has done.

3. It is said, that God forgave the sins of an Abel and of an Enoch / without looking to any satisfaction / but only to their faith / through which they believed that God is / and that he is a rewarder of all those who seek him. Hebrews 11:3, 6.

I answer, 1. That all the believers of the Old Testament were not saved / except through faith in the Messiah / who was to make satisfaction. 2. That in the cited passage it is indeed said / that he who comes to God / must believe that he is, etc. but that this does not include everything that one is required to believe. 3. That through this whole chapter it is evident / that the Patriarchs <note>The early fathers of the biblical faith, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.</note> were saved through faith in the Messiah / Hebrews 11:26, 9:15, Isaiah 53:6, 8. In short / it is certain / that one can seek God in no soul-saving way / except in Christ.

4. It is said, that it involves a contradiction / that Christ satisfies for us / since it would follow from this / that he has satisfied himself.

We have shown elsewhere / that nothing prevents Christ / although he was the offended Person / from being our Mediator; therefore, not dwelling further on that / I move to another objection.

5. It is said, that Christ did not suffer the eternal death / which we were meant to suffer / and that he consequently has not made satisfaction.

I answer, that it was enough that our Mediator suffered an infinite punishment / which through its weight <note>The author uses "weight" to mean the severity or intensity of the suffering, rather than its length in time.</note> equaled an eternal punishment.

6. It is said, that Christ did not suffer an infinite punishment / since his suffering lasted so short a time.

I answer, that Christ suffered a punishment of an infinite value / although it was not infinite in duration. The merits of the one suffering / cause the punishment to become infinite.

It is said, that / if it were true / that the infinity of the Person made the punishment infinite / it would follow from this / that Divine justice would have been satisfied / even if Christ had suffered only a light punishment / and shed a single drop of his blood / as Pope Clement VI <gloss>the sixth</gloss> (Extravagantes: *Unigenitus*) <note>A papal bull issued in 1343 concerning the "Treasury of Merit."</note> and Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Cardinal and influential defender of Catholic doctrine against the Reformation.</note> (*On Indulgences*, book 1, ch. 4) said.

I answer, that not all suffering / although borne by an infinite person / is satisfaction / but only that / which Divine justice demanded / which the Law required / and which corresponded to the greatness of the crimes committed.

It is further said / that the dignity of the Person adds nothing to the infinity of the punishment / because with God there is no acceptance of persons <term>acceptance of persons: a biblical phrase meaning partiality or favoritism based on status rather than facts</term>.

But the Scripture only means to say thereby / that God does not look at the outward qualities / which have nothing to do with the matter / at hand ; just as it is forbidden for a Judge to pardon a criminal / because he is rich / or a great Lord : but it does not follow from this / that God must pay no heed to the perfect merits of his adorable Son / in whom he has all his delight ; and that he must distinguish his counsel in an infinite manner from the suffering of all creatures / since he possesses the same Majesty / and the same perfections as his Father.

It is said, that this could take place / if Christ had suffered as God / but that his Humanity alone suffered.

I answer, that it is not necessary / for the punishment to be of an infinite power / that the Godhead suffer; it is enough / that the Person / who suffers / be Divine / although he suffers only in respect to the human nature / which he has personally united to himself.

It is said, that Christ / being God /

<column-break/>

could not bring to God that which God did not already possess.

**Answer.** I admit it / but / although everything belongs to God / nevertheless he desires that we offer him certain things / as if they belonged to us : thus he desired / that one slaughter sacrificial offerings for him ; and in this way Christ was able to sacrifice his own blood to him : for it depended on his will / whether to sacrifice the same or not. But in the same manner as we must bear the punishments / which Divine justice demands from Sinners / and the wicked suffer in hell / Christ was also able to bear the punishments / that we deserve.

It is said, that one could not sacrifice blood to God.

I answer, that this, however, does not prevent the shed blood from being able to satisfy Divine justice. Thus a Prince / who holds someone captive / can offer to release him / under the condition that he who seeks his freedom / exposes his life to his service.

7. It is said, that / if Christ had suffered the punishment / which we had deserved / and which the outcasts <note>The "reprobate" or those not chosen for salvation.</note> suffer / he would have fallen into despair / like the damned.

I answer, that despair is not the essence of the punishment / which we were bound to suffer ; and that / if the outcasts despair / such is a consequence of their corruption. Secondly, I do not know / whether one may well say / that Christ suffered the pains of the damned. One can read further what I have said about that in the treatise on Christ’s descent into hell.

8. It is objected, that it is impossible / that Christ has satisfied for men / because every Sinner / and even every sin deserving an infinite punishment / Christ would have been bound to suffer many deaths.

**Answer 1.** Those who make this objection / openly oppose the Scripture / which says / that God has caused the iniquities of us all to fall upon his Son ; Isaiah 53:4, 5, 6 <note>original: "Esa. LIII. 4. 5. 6."</note> and that he died for all, 2 Corinthians 5:15 <note>original: "2 Cor. V. 15."</note>.

**2.** One could add to this / that indeed / when several people owe a certain sum / for example a thousand rix-dollars <term>rix-dollar: a silver coin used across Northern Europe during this period</term> / one must pay a thousand rix-dollars for each person, head by head /

### DIVINITY. IX. Book. XXXVII. Chapter.

Part I. M m m m

<meta>Catchword: punishment</meta>

but that the punishment of one is sometimes enough for the debts of several; that the life of a King like David, was esteemed more than that of half of his army / 2 Sam. XVIII. 3. and that consequently the death of Christ could have been sufficient for the redemption of many.

3. But one must moreover observe / that the infinity of the Person of Christ is enough to satisfy for all men / although each of them deserves several infinite punishments.

9. It is said, that the forgiveness of sins is attributed to repentance and faith.

Answer. That is true / because those are the only conditions that God demands of us; but he demands <term>satisfaction: the legal payment or reparation for a debt or sin</term> from our <term>Surety: one who takes responsibility for another's debt or obligation; in this context, Christ</term>. Secondly, faith has as its object the Messiah / who has made the satisfaction.

10. It is said, that one cannot produce any Law / by which one can demand of an innocent person / that he suffer the punishment / which another deserves to bear in his body.

I answer, that the point here is not to know / whether there is some Law regarding this matter / but whether the Scripture does not clearly say / that Christ has borne our sins; the example of our Savior is extraordinary / but it is for that reason no less certain.

11. It is objected, that / if Christ had satisfied for us / we would be more obliged to him / than to his Heavenly Father.

Answer. This reasoning has no force / for the love of the Father / who has given us his Son / was an infinite love / just as well as the love of the Son / who delivered himself for us. Therefore, we have infinite obligations to these two adorable Persons. The Scripture also praises the love of the Father to us everywhere / 1 John III. 16. IV. 9. Rom. V. 8.

12. It is objected, that / if Christ has satisfied the Law for us / we are no longer bound to fulfill it.

But one is mistaken; this conclusion must not be drawn from it / but much rather these two.

1. That those / for whom Christ has died / are no longer subject to the curse of the Law. 2. That we must not keep the

<column-break/>

Law / as if we / through the keeping of the same / could satisfy God's justice; for we cannot fulfill the Law. Far from the doctrine of satisfaction releasing us from obedience to the Law / the Gospel draws a motive from it / which incites us to sanctification. It says / that God has redeemed us / so that we might serve him in holiness and in righteousness / Luke I. 74. and that Christ has borne our sins on the wood of the cross, so that we, having died to sin, might live to righteousness, 1 Pet. II. 24. Heb. IX. 14. 1 Thess. IV. Eph. II. 10. Tit. II. 14. 1 Pet. II. 9. 1 Cor. VI. 19. 20. 2 Cor. V. 15.

13. It is objected, that / if Christ had satisfied for us / and had died for us / the believers would not be necessitated to die.

I answer, that the death of believers is no punishment / but a blessed passage to eternal life.

14. It is objected, that the doctrine of satisfaction obscures the honor of God's omnipotence / as if God did not have the power to forgive us our sins without satisfaction.

But this is to deceive oneself. 1. It is not for a lack of power / that God could not forgive sin without satisfaction / but because his justice did not allow sin to go unpunished.

2. Far from the doctrine of Satisfaction obscuring the honor of God's omnipotence / it causes the same to shine forth with all its luster. It reveals to us his justice, which preferred not to spare God's own Son / rather than leave sin unpunished; his mercy, which has spared men / whom he / without delivering his Son to death / could not make blessed: his wisdom, which has combined the wonderful means of making his justice and mercy harmonize together: his omnipotence, which conquered the Devil and sin through the cross / and has drawn life out of death.

15. It is said, that our doctrine obscures the mercy of God / who demands no satisfaction; and his justice, which desires / that sin be punished in the sinners themselves.

I answer. 1. That mercy has not been wounded; God has demanded the satisfaction not from us / but from our Surety. 2. That justice demands nothing else / than that sin be punished.

Those who deny the Satisfaction <note>The "Satisfaction" is the legal payment or reparation made to God to answer for human sin.</note> tarnish God’s own honor. The Early Church has recognized the truth of the Satisfaction. Clement of Rome in his first Letter to the Corinthians / speaks thus: *Let us honor the Lord Jesus Christ, whose blood was shed for us.*

# THEOLOGY. IX. B. Chapter XXXVIII.

<margin>
Isaiah 43:25
44:22.
Micah 7:19.

Psalm 32.
Romans 4.
Isaiah 43:25

it is said that God blots out our transgressions, that he covers them with a cloud, that he casts them behind his back into the depths of the Sea, that he removes our transgressions from us as far as the East is from the West, that he does not reproach us for our sins, that he does not remember them; <note>The author is listing various biblical metaphors to emphasize that divine forgiveness is absolute and leaves no residue of guilt or punishment.</note> all the passages where it is said that Christ has blotted out and destroyed the "handwriting" of our sins <note>original: "hand-schrift onzer zonden," referring to a legal bond or debt-note.</note> which was against us: for it would not be destroyed at all if a portion of the debt—consisting of temporal punishment—were still in effect; finally, all the passages where it is said that we are justified freely. <note>original: "om niet," meaning by grace or without cost.</note>

It will be said that God forgives our debts and sins because he forgives the largest part of them; but 1. who has ever heard it said that a creditor remits the debts of his debtor if he still demands something from him? 2. Since the debt has such a connection with the punishment that there is no punishment where there is no debt, it is utterly ridiculous to say that God remits the debt but not the punishment.

<margin>Bellarmine, Book IV, *On Penance*, ch. 15.</margin>
It is said <note>referring to the arguments of Cardinal Robert Bellarmine, a leading Counter-Reformation theologian.</note> that there are things which would not happen if there were not certain causes, and which remain standing once they have happened even though the causes no longer exist; just as a building would not be completed if no one built it, yet the building remains even if the master builder is no longer present. But there is a very great difference between the analogy being brought forward and the matter in dispute: it is not necessary for a building to exist that the master who built it remains alive; but there is no man who can understand how God could demand punishment for a sin that he has already forgiven; once the builder is dead he works no more, and likewise the debt, once destroyed, can no longer bring punishments upon the sinners.

It is said that a King can forgive someone for their misdeeds, but at the same time demand that he give satisfaction to the party who was insulted; and that God can also forgive men their transgressions, yet still demand that they satisfy.

I answer that one is comparing two distinct things; a King can act in such a way because he is distinct from the insulted party, but here God is the insulted party.

3. This distinction harms the justice of God, for it suggests that God punishes that which he no longer judges to be guilty; it likewise contradicts the mercy of God as it is described to us in Scripture: for since it presents God to us as a Father of mercy, whose love far exceeds the tenderness of a Mother, how can one conceive that this merciful Father would still demand heavy satisfaction from those he has forgiven?

4. It is without basis that a distinction is made between sins committed before Baptism and sins committed after Baptism.

There are still some objections made which must necessarily be resolved.

<margin>Bellarmine, Book I, *On Indulgences*, ch. 3.</margin>
1. An objection is made from the passage of Paul in Colossians 1:24: *I now rejoice in my sufferings for you, and fill up in my flesh the remnants of the afflictions of Christ for his body, which is the church.* Two arguments are drawn from this. 1. That it must be that Christ left something that still remains to be done, since there is talk of the "remnants of the afflictions of Christ," and 2. That Paul testifies that he fulfills the remnants of these afflictions.

<margin>
Thomas Aquinas on this passage.
Contarini on this.
Justinian on this passage.
</margin>
To answer this, one must only make these two observations. The first observation is that by the "afflictions of Christ" one must not understand the suffering that Christ suffered in his own person during the days of his flesh, of which his death was the final part: for Paul speaks here of a suffering that was not yet ended, whereas it is certain that Christ suffered everything on the cross, and that nothing more was left for him to suffer for the reconciliation of our sins; one must then understand by these sufferings of Christ the sufferings that Christ imposes on each of his members who are in his communion: thus this expression is taken in 2 Corinthians 1:5, *as the sufferings of Christ abound in us,* says the Apostle, *so also through Christ our consolation abounds.* He calls it in other places the "affliction of the Gospel," the "bodily torment," the "dying and marks of the Lord Jesus." One can

# THE CHRISTIAN [THEOLOGY]

<columns>

[one] can easily give a reason for this way of speaking; it is because we endure this suffering for the love of Jesus and for the sake of his name, because there is such a close bond between Christ and his members <note>The "members" refers to the individual believers who make up the "body" of the Church.</note> that whatever the believers happen to suffer makes up a part of the sufferings of Christ, just as we name our wounds after the limbs in which we received them.

The second observation one must make is that God has assigned to every believer the share of suffering that he must endure for His name's sake, so that he might be conformed to His Son: this is what Paul wants to show us when he says that he "fills up what is lacking" of Christ’s afflictions; to teach us that he had already suffered a good portion of them, but that some still remained for him according to the counsel of God, as if he were saying: "Christ has suffered all that he had to suffer for our redemption; now I also, in my turn, am going to suffer everything to which he calls me for his glory and to advance his Kingdom, of which I have already suffered much." One can here compare the passage from 1 Peter 5:9.

2. Further, some passages are raised as objections, from which it is concluded that God, after he has forgiven the sins of believers, nevertheless chastises them in this life. For example: 1. What was said to David by Nathan, 2 Samuel 12:13, 14: *The Lord also has taken away your sin; you shall not die. Nevertheless, because by this deed you have given great occasion to the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme, the son also who is born to you shall surely die.* 2. That which one reads of David in 2 Samuel 24:10, 11, 12, who, although he had obtained mercy regarding the sin he committed in numbering the people, was nevertheless heavily punished. 3. That which is found in Exodus 32:10, 14, where it is said that although God forgave the children of Israel the sins of idolatry, he nevertheless caused a great part of them to perish in the wilderness. 4. The 14th Chapter of Numbers, verse 20, where it is shown that although God ceased to be further angry against the children of Israel who had murmured against him, he nevertheless caused almost all of them to fall in the wilderness. 5. That which one reads in Numbers 20:4, 25, and Deuteronomy 32:50, 51, of Aaron and Moses, who

<column-break/>

did not enter the promised land because of their unbelief; from all these passages it is concluded that although God forgives men their sin for the sake of the <term>satisfaction</term> <note>original: "voldoeninge." In this context, it refers to the theological belief that Christ's death paid the debt for sin.</note> of Christ, he nevertheless still demands some temporal punishment from man to give satisfaction to His justice.

But all those who make these objections here confuse fatherly chastisements with the actual punishments that God imposes to satisfy his justice. We readily grant that God often chastises his children for their improvement and conversion, but we deny that he demands "satisfactory" punishments from those whose sins he forgives. The chastisements of believers can indeed be called a "punishment" if one wishes to use this word improperly <note>In the sense of "figuratively" or "loosely."</note>: 1. either because they are, by their nature, the consequences and "stings" of sins; 2. or because they are painful to the flesh—but not everything that is painful to our nature is a punishment. When a sick person endures the iron and the fire <note>A reference to surgical tools and cauterization used in early modern medicine.</note>, he is not being punished. Because blood was drawn from a soldier who did not observe his duty among the Roman warriors, it does not follow that <term>blood-letting</term> <note>original: "aderlaaten." A common medical practice of the time; the author argues the act itself is medicinal, even if triggered by a mistake.</note> is a punishment. 3. or because believers sometimes view them as effects of God's wrath, and as if they were true punishments. 4. or because they are assigned by God just as punishments are pronounced by judges upon criminals. 

But one cannot give them this name in the same sense in which it is given to the judgments that God carries out over evildoers; and there is a very great difference between the chastisements with which God visits believers and the judgments he exercises over the godless: The one proceeds from a Father, who only chastises those whom he loves; the others are carried out by a strict Judge. The one is paired with a feeling of God's grace, and the other with a feeling of the wrath and the curse of God. The first last but a moment, and the second are forerunners of eternal punishments.

<margin>
Hebrews 12:6.
Proverbs 3:11.
Hebrews 12:8.
</margin>

When the Scripture speaks of the afflictions of believers, it says that they proceed from God's love; that those who are free from them are bastards <note>A reference to Hebrews 12:8, meaning they are not true children of God.</note>; that God sends the same for our improvement and to make us partakers of his holiness; that these are indeed trials, but that the...

# THEOLOGY. BOOK IX. CHAPTER XXXVIII.

[believers] have reason to be joyful about it.

If God wills that the child of David should die, it is not to satisfy his justice, but for the improvement of David, and to teach others not only to beware in the future of giving God's enemies cause to blaspheme the Lord, but also to strike the enemies of God with awe by letting them see that he does not leave sins unpunished. David's sin was the cause and the occasion why God caused David's child to die, but the death of the child was not the legal punishment for his sin. <note>In this context, the author distinguishes between "retributive punishment" (paying a debt of justice) and "chastisement" (a fatherly correction for the benefit of the child and others).</note>

It is said that it is clear enough that David did not view the death of his child as a remedy or a beneficial improvement, but as a very great evil and a punishment, since he wept, lamented, and fasted. This reasoning does not hold up, for everyone knows that the Saints pray to God that he might ward off all evil from them, even though they know that the evil must work together for their good; a sick person does not like bitter drinks, even though he hopes to be healed by them.

One must reason in much the same way regarding 2 Samuel 24. <note>This refers to the story where David conducts a census and God sends a plague upon Israel.</note>

What we read in Exodus 32:10, 14 does not provide a firm proof here, for although it is said there that God held back the heat of his anger so as not to utterly root out his people, it is not noted there that he forgave them; on the contrary, it is said that Moses still had to ask in verse 31 that this sin might be forgiven them. The slaughter by the Levites <note>After the incident of the Golden Calf, the Levites were ordered to kill those who had rebelled.</note> can indeed be called a true punishment regarding the evildoers who were killed; but if any believers were included in this slaughter, it was for them a chastisement that God wanted them to feel, to serve as an example to others, or for other reasons that he has not revealed to us. Moses acted then like a commander who punishes every tenth man of his regiments when they have caused a mutiny; one can say the same of Numbers 14.

Regarding Moses and Aaron, to whom God had granted forgiveness and who nonetheless died in the wilderness:

I answer, that it was not to satisfy his justice that God

<column-break/>

punished them so severely, but to give all the people a righteous terror, seeing that he did not even spare their leaders; to which one can add that the death of Moses and Aaron contained an indignation, and that God willed that they should die in the wilderness to teach us that it is not the Law—of which Moses was the servant—that gives us entrance into the heavenly Canaan, but Christ, who was prefigured by Joshua. <note>The author is using "typology," a common method of interpreting the Bible where Old Testament figures foreshadow New Testament truths. Moses represents the Law, which cannot save, while Joshua (whose name in Hebrew is the same as Jesus) represents the Savior who leads the people to the promised land.</note> One can apply the first answer to what is said in 1 Kings 13:2 <note>Likely referring to 1 Kings 13:24.</note> regarding a prophet who was torn apart by a lion.

3. It is further objected that Scripture often speaks of judgments that God exercises over his own children. Peter says in 1 Peter 4:17 that judgment begins at the House of God; now, whoever says "judgment" implies a punishment properly so called. But it is easy to answer that one should not press the word "judgment" too hard, for Paul teaches us in 1 Corinthians 11:32 that when we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord.

<margin>Oecumenius, Theophylact, Chrysostom on this passage. Claude Guillaud on this place.</margin> He does not say "we are punished," but "we are chastened," to show that these afflictions or judgments are not condemnations, but warnings; not death-penalties, but remedies; not punishments, but improvements; as a learned man of the Roman Church <note>Referring to Claude Guillaud, a 16th-century French theologian who, though Catholic, sometimes offered interpretations that Protestants found useful.</note> has noted with much discernment.

4. Other passages are also brought forward which seem to prove human "satisfactions"; Isaiah 1:16–17, where the Prophet promises the forgiveness of sins not only to those who are cleansed, but who are also practiced in works of mercy:

<margin>Bellarmin, Book 4 on Penance, chapter 3.</margin> Proverbs 16:6: *By mercy and truth iniquity is atoned for.* <note>original Latin: "Iniquitas expiatur."</note> Daniel 4:27: *Therefore, O King, let my counsel please you, and break off your sins by righteousness, and your iniquity by showing mercy to the poor.* Luke 11:41: *But give for alms those things which are within; and behold, everything is clean for you.* Matthew 3:8: *Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance.* 2 Corinthians 7:11, where mention is made of a "vengeance" that sinners exercise upon themselves. 2 Chronicles 7:14: *If my people, upon whom my name is called, shall humble themselves and pray and seek my face and turn from their evil ways, then I will hear from heaven and...*

<meta>This page continues the author’s systematic refutation of the Roman Catholic doctrine of "satisfaction"—the idea that human works or penance can satisfy God's justice for the temporal punishment of sin.
