Both the one and the other Dispensation had the same <term>Mediator</term> <note>A go-between; in Christian theology, Jesus Christ is the sole bridge between God and humanity.</note>, the seed of the woman, the seed of Abraham who is Christ, by whose grace the Fathers were Saved just as we are, according to the testimony of Peter in Acts 15:10, 11. There is no other name given to men by which they may be Saved. He alone is the way, the truth, and the life. He is the same yesterday and today, and shall be forever. Heb. 13:8.

It is said that Paul speaks of the doctrine in this place. But if the Doctrine is eternal, then the covenant which is presented therein is also eternal.

<column-break/>

It is said that "yesterday" signifies the days that preceded Christ's ascension, and "today" those that followed it. But it appears that Paul's aim is to exhort the believers to steadfastness, considering that the Doctrine of the Gospel which he proclaimed to them was the same as that which was formerly taught to their Fathers.

It is said that these expressions "yesterday" and "today" only signify a recent matter that has not arisen for a long time, as can be seen in Job 8:9. But one only has to compare this passage of Job with that of Paul to see that there is a great difference between the two.

Regarding Acts 15:11, where Peter says *that we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they*, it is said that this refers to the Apostles compared with the believing Gentiles, and not the Apostles compared with the Fathers of the Old Testament. But: 1. Peter had just spoken of these Fathers. 2. His aim is to prove that the yoke of the <term>Ceremonial Law</term> <note>The religious rituals and dietary laws of the Old Testament, which many early Christians believed were no longer binding.</note> should not be laid upon the Gentiles, because the Fathers had not been able to bear it; to which he adds that one is not Saved except through the grace of the Lord Jesus, who had already Saved these Fathers, who otherwise could not have been Saved by the keeping of a Law they could not bear. If the Apostles had wanted to join themselves here with the believing Gentiles, Peter would have said, *they believe to be saved, even as we.*

Against Acts 4:12, where it is said that there is no other Name under Heaven given by which one can be Saved than that of Jesus, it is brought in that it speaks of the time following the appearance of Christ in the flesh. But it is clear that all times are considered. There is no Salvation without a Mediator, and there is no Mediator but Jesus Christ.

<margin>
Ps. 63:9.
Mal. 3:1.
Isa. 53:5.
1 Tim. 2:5.
</margin>
The same conditions are prescribed under the Old as under the New Dispensation.

The same Promises are made under both, Acts 13:32, 3:25, 26, Gal. 3:8, 9, 14, 18, Gen. 15:6, Ps. 32:1, Jer. 31:33, Isa. 43:25, Acts 10, Heb. 10, 8:6.

<margin>Genesis 15:6. Romans 4:11. Galatians 3:6, 7, 8. Psalm 116:10. 2 Corinthians 4:13. Hebrews 11. Romans 9:4. Hebrews 9:15. Isaiah 9:5. Genesis 49:18.</margin>
John 10:43. Deuteronomy 30:6. Ezekiel 36:26. Matthew 22. Hebrews 9:15. One also sees that the Believers possessed the same hope. Job 19:25. Psalm 16:11. Psalm 22:5. Daniel 12:2.

It will be argued that the promises were given *to* and not *for* the Fathers <note>The "Fathers" refers to the Old Testament patriarchs such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.</note>, for the benefit of the believers of the New Testament, just as the promises of the calling of the Gentiles were made to the Old Fathers but only intended for the times of the New Testament.

I answer that it is absurd to say that the Prophets would have given such promises to the believers of their time and that they would have understood them without applying them to themselves, especially since they had to struggle with the same miseries and had need of the same remedy.

2. Paul says that the adoption as children, the glory, the covenants, and the promises belonged to the Israelites, and that Christ paid for the transgressions committed under the first Testament.

<margin>Isaiah 9:5. Genesis 49:18.</margin>
3. It is evident that the promises belonged to them, since they applied them to themselves. "A child is born to us," they say through the mouth of Isaiah, "a Son is given to us." "For your salvation," said Jacob, "I wait, O Lord."

4. What is brought up regarding the calling of the Gentiles is not relevant. For the calling of the Gentiles does nothing for the salvation of the Jews. But it was not so with the coming of the Messiah.

It is said that the promise, which occurs so often in the Scriptures of the Old Testament, in which God declares that he is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, was very obscure and could not be understood by the believers, or that it was a special promise only for the Patriarchs.

Answer: Since this promise was made for the comfort of the Fathers, it is not probable that they would have understood nothing of it.

<margin>Hebrews 11:10, etc.</margin>
It is said that they expected the city which has foundations, namely heaven, not because this city was promised to them, but because it was suited to their desire, and that it was believable that God would give it to them.

I answer that the Fathers would not have hoped for heaven unless

<column-break/>

their hope had been built upon some promise. Paul says that the Fathers died in faith: and faith presupposes a revelation and a promise.

<margin>Verse 14, 16.</margin>
One can read neither Job nor David without being convinced that they both had a firm hope of eternal happiness. "I know," says the former, "that my Redeemer lives, and he shall stand at last over the dust; and after my skin has been thus destroyed, yet in my flesh shall I see God." "I will," says David, "behold your face in righteousness, and be satisfied with your likeness."
<margin>Job 19:25, 26. Psalm 17:15.</margin>

Finally, it appears that the covenant seals <note>The "covenant seals" refers to sacraments like circumcision in the Old Testament and baptism in the New.</note> under the Old and New Testament signified the same grace. "Brothers," says Paul, "I do not want you to be ignorant that our Fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and that they all ate the same spiritual food, and drank the same spiritual drink." 1 Corinthians 10:1, 3, 4.

One must not say that the Ancients ate the same food among themselves, but not with us. That would contradict Paul, whose purpose is to compare the Ancients with the Christians, and who clearly says that Christ, in whom the Ancients believed, was the rock that followed them.

Furthermore, the promises made to Abraham and his seed show that he was convinced of the immortality of his soul and of another life; and we shall prove in another place that these two chief doctrines were revealed under the Old Testament.

It will be said that the promises made to Abraham are temporal, and for the most part concern only his descendants, and that consequently he could have received them even if he believed he would be killed.

The answer is: 1. That it would be quite rare that God, who made his covenant with Abraham and wished to favor him more than other mortals, would have been content with making him promises whose fulfillment he would not enjoy. 2. That it is a great pleasure for a Father to know that his offspring will be happy after his death, but that this would nonetheless not prevent the Father, for his own person, from...

Finally, that Paul proves that the promised **seed**, the origin of all promised blessings, is the **Messiah**.

Several other objections are also raised, which we must not leave unresolved.

<margin>Romans 16:25.</margin>
I. It is objected that Paul says in Romans 16:25 that the Gospel was kept secret for all ages.

**Answer.** The Apostle does not say absolutely that the mystery of the Gospel was kept secret for all times, but by comparison to the present revelation: therefore he immediately adds, *but is now revealed and made known through the Prophetic writings.* It appears then: 1. That this mystery was kept secret in regard to the <term>Gentiles<note>The original Dutch uses 'Heidenen' (Heathens), referring to non-Jewish nations.</note></term>, whom God allowed to walk in their own ways. 2. Because the same was not revealed as clearly to the Fathers as it is now to the believers of the New Testament.

<margin>1 Peter 1:12.</margin>
II. It is said that it was revealed to the Prophets, as Peter remarks, that it was *not for them, but for us* that they ministered these things.

<column-break/>

**Answer:** This means nothing other than that the Prophets knew by revelation that the matters they predicted would not be fulfilled in their own time. Therefore, his meaning is by no means to say that those things belonged to us alone.

III. The question is asked: how could the death of Christ on the cross have been of any fruit for the believers under the Old Testament, since He did not suffer the same in their time, having only come into the world many centuries after their passing?

I answer that Christ’s suffering from the beginning of the world has had as much power to atone for sins as if He had truly endured it from the beginning of the world; because it was certain and fixed that He would undergo it one day, and that God, who is all-knowing, knew that Christ would certainly suffer, and as our <term>surety<note>original: "borge" – a legal or financial guarantor who takes responsibility for another's debt.</note></term> would fulfill His <term>suretyship<note>original: "borgtogt"</note></term> for us in His time, just as a prisoner is set free even though his ransom is not yet actually paid, as long as there is certainty that the one whose prisoner he is is satisfied with the word of his guarantor. <term>Natural causes<note>Physical events that require a present action to produce an effect.</note></term> cannot work unless they essentially exist in nature, just as a medicine does not cure a sick person when it is not prepared and taken; but it is not so with <term>moral causes<note>Interpretive note: Here, a 'moral cause' refers to a legal or spiritual agreement where the promise of a future act is legally valid in the present.</note></term>; it is enough that one is assured that they will one day exist, and that the one with whom they will count is convinced of it.

<margin>2 Timothy 1:9, 10.</margin>

But the words of the Apostle do not have this meaning.

1. One could say that Paul wants to make known to us that grace and eternal life were unknown to the Gentiles, of whom he had called himself the Minister. (verse 11).

2. But one can simply answer that Paul’s aim is to show that grace was placed in a full light in the <term>fullness of time<note>A biblical concept referring to the era of Christ's birth and ministry.</note></term>, in comparison with the state of the Fathers, who by no means had such a clear revelation of it; they had the shadows, and

This page systematically addresses counter-arguments (objections V through XII) often raised by Socinian theologians who claimed the Old Testament only offered earthly benefits.</meta>

...seen examples of this; Christ has made the same disappear and allowed us to behold without a veil that which they had seen only very obscurely.

V. It is said that in the places where the promises of the Law are spoken of—Leviticus 26:3, 4; Deuteronomy 27:2—no mention is made of eternal life.

I answer: 1. That although no explicit mention is made there, it does not follow that the same was not promised. In general, God had promised life to those who would keep His Law (Leviticus 18:5). He had promised them the forgiveness of sins, which goes hand in hand with eternal life.

2. It is certain that under the veil of the temporal goods that were promised to the Israelites, spiritual goods were included.

3. One does not doubt that the ancients who lived godlessly had to fear eternal punishment and death; yet no mention is made of it in Leviticus 26 or Deuteronomy 27.

VI. It is objected that Paul says in Hebrews 2:3 that <term>Salvation</term> <note>The Dutch "Zaligheid" refers to both the state of being saved and the eternal happiness of heaven.</note> began to be proclaimed by the Lord.

Answer: This is said in contrast to the Apostles; for Salvation had at the very least already been proclaimed by John the Baptist, who was the forerunner of Christ.

<margin>Smalcius <note>Valentinus Smalcius (1572–1622), a prominent Socinian theologian often at odds with orthodox Protestantism.</note> against Franz <note>Wolfgang Franz (1564–1628), a Lutheran theologian.</note></margin>
VII. It is objected from Galatians 3:23, where it is said that before faith came, we were kept under the Law, etc. From which one concludes that at that time, people did not yet believe in eternal life.

Answer: Who does not see that this only means that before the Gospel—which is the Doctrine of Faith—was preached by the Apostles under the <term>New Dispensation</term> <note>The "New Huishouding" or New Covenant era following the arrival of Christ.</note>, the believers of the Old Law were under a schoolmaster? This certainly did not prevent them from having faith, as one can clearly see they did from various places cited by the Apostles: Romans 1:17, 4:3, 5, 9, 11, 12; 2 Corinthians 4:13; Galatians 3:6, 7, 8; Hebrews 11.

<margin>Volkelius <note>Johannes Volkelius (d. 1618), a Polish theologian who argued that the Old Testament lacked the promise of eternal life.</note></margin>
VIII. It is objected that John says that eternal life has been revealed (1 John 1:2).

Answer: By "eternal life" in this place, one must understand Jesus Himself, who was from the beginning.

<column-break/>

IX. It is objected that Paul says in Romans 3:21 that the righteousness of God has been revealed without the Law.

Answer: The Apostle means nothing other than that the righteousness of faith—that is, the manner in which one is justified through faith in Christ—is not revealed by the <term>Moral Law</term> <note>The "Zedelyke Wet," referring to the Ten Commandments and ethical requirements of the Torah.</note>; from which it follows that our justification through faith was not revealed under the Old Testament. Paul also says that the Law and the Prophets bear witness to this righteousness.

<margin>Socinus <note>Faustus Socinus (1539–1604), the Italian theologian whose followers denied Christ's divinity and the continuity of the Old and New Covenants.</note> in the book *Whether the Kingdom of Poland*, chapter 7, against Palaeologus, part IV; Ostorodt, *Institutes*, chapter 5 <note>Christoph Ostorodt (d. 1611), a German Socinian.</note>.</margin>
X. It is objected that it is said in Hebrews 8:6 that Christ is a <term>Mediator</term> <note>A go-between; here, the one who negotiates the relationship between God and humanity.</note> of a much better covenant, which is established on better promises.

Answer: That the promises proposed under the Gospel are called "better promises" not because they are more glorious than those made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (for that cannot be); therefore, they bear this name only regarding the manner of their presentation and the extent that they have with respect to other nations.

XI. It is objected from Hebrews 9:8, where one reads that the way into the Holy of Holies was not yet revealed while the first Tabernacle still stood.

I answer that these words do not mean that the believers under the Old Testament were not taken up into Heaven. The example of Enoch and Elijah proves the contrary. But they indicate: 1. That the sacrifice of Christ, through which the Heavens are opened, was not yet actually offered then. 2. That the legal ceremonies, which are signified here by the Tabernacle, could not by themselves bring about entry into Heaven. 3. That the way to Heaven was not yet as clearly revealed under the Old Dispensation as it has been under the New, because the power of Christ’s sacrifice was covered with many veils. It is then not because the ancient believers did not know that their spirit returned to God and was taken up into a place of rest, but because their knowledge is not to be compared with that which we have after we have seen Christ enter into Heaven.

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of the "Covenant of Grace" being present in the Old Testament. Following previous objections, the author now addresses the interpretation of specific New Testament verses that seem to suggest the promises of God were only fulfilled or revealed with the coming of Christ. The author argues for a continuity of grace from the beginning of the world, even if the "management" or "economy" of that grace changed with the New Testament.</meta>

# THEOLOGY. IX. B. CHAPTER XLVII.

...having received a testimony through faith, they did not obtain the promise: *God having provided something better for us, so that they should not be made perfect without us.* <note>Original: Hebrews 11:39-40. The author is responding to the argument that Old Testament believers did not receive the "perfection" of salvation.</note>

**Answer.** Most interpreters understand this "promise" to be that of the coming of Christ in the flesh to complete the work of our salvation; and they say that God, having postponed this coming until the times of the New Testament, the ancient Fathers did not reach Perfection without us, because Perfection consists in the actual reconciliation of sins through the sacrifice of Christ. One cannot indeed deny that the Apostle in this Letter uses the term "perfection" to mean the actual and essential reconciliation of sins, contrasted with that of the Law.

But, in my judgment, it is better to understand by these promises the highest degree of the fulfillment of the promises made to the Fathers through the second coming of Christ, and especially through the glorious resurrection from the dead. This is evident: 1. By the purpose of the Apostle, which is not to comfort the Hebrews against the feeling of their sins (which he had done in the preceding chapters), but to comfort them against the miseries of the present life, so that they might endure the persecutions to which they were called. Now, there was nothing that could provide them more comfort than to set before their eyes the fulfillment of God’s great promises on the Last Day, in which their perseverance would be crowned. 2. Because in the preceding chapter he had said, *You have need of patience, so that, having done the will of God, you might carry away the promise.* Now, that refers not to the first, but to the second coming of Christ. 3. Because Paul clearly makes the hope of the persecuted Christians consist in the Resurrection. They, he says, escaped the edge of the sword, etc., etc., so that they might obtain a better resurrection.

The Fathers therefore did not obtain the promises because they had not yet risen, so that they would not be made perfect without us; that is to say, so that they would not obtain perfect blessedness without us. And thus God has provided something better for

<column-break/>

us, because it is under the New Covenant, under which we live, that this resurrection has been postponed. There are many places where the resurrection is called the "promise" made to the Fathers. Paul, in Acts 26:6, 7, 8, says that he was brought before the Court for the hope of the promise that God had made to the Fathers; and he adds to this, *Why do you consider it an incredible thing that God raises the dead?* It is for the sake of the hope of Israel, he says in Acts 24 and 28, that I am surrounded by these chains, and now I stand and am judged for the hope of the promise made by God to the Fathers.

->Some other objections are also raised.<-

1. It is objected from Mark 1:1 that the beginning of the Gospel was only in the time of John the Baptist; from which one concludes that the Gospel was previously unknown. But one does not understand that Mark, by the "Gospel," means the <term>New Dispensation</term> <note>Original: "Nieuwe Huishouding." This refers to the specific era or "house-management" of God's plan, rather than the underlying message of salvation itself.</note> and not the doctrine of grace. The New Dispensation began with John the Baptist, but the doctrine of grace has been proclaimed from the beginning of the world.

2. It is objected from Matthew 11:13, where it is said that all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John.

But from this one can conclude nothing else than that the dispensation of the Law lasted until John, which does not prevent the covenant and the doctrine of grace from having had a place beforehand.

3. It is objected from Jeremiah 31:31, etc., where God speaks thus: *Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel.* This covenant, it is said, is the covenant of grace. That is true; but it does not follow that the same had not already been made: for it is the same covenant that was made with Abraham. Here, then, it is only a matter of the renewal of the covenant of grace, which had to be renewed in such a way that it would be entirely different under the new Dispensation than it had been under the old.

4. But, it is said, was the covenant not abolished? I answer 1. That the covenant of works, which God had entered into with Adam, was indeed abolished.

<meta>This page continues the author's argument that the Old Testament was not merely a set of earthly rules, but was fundamentally part of the same "Covenant of Grace" found in the New Testament. The author is refuting contemporary scholars who claimed that ancient Israelites had no concept of eternal life or spiritual salvation.</meta>

# THE CHRISTIAN GOD

...been. 2. That what is called the Old **Dispensation** <note>Dutch: *Huishouding*. This term refers to the "management" or "economy" of God's relationship with humanity in a specific era.</note> has also been abolished regarding the ceremonies that were celebrated within it. However, the same doctrine of grace that is proclaimed under the New Dispensation was taught under the Old, and the **Covenant of Grace**—which began after the fall of Adam—has existed and shall exist for eternity.

5. It is said that the faith of the Fathers consisted only in believing in the future coming of the *Messiah*. But this is a mistake: their faith consisted in fixing that same faith upon the *Messiah* who was to come, and in placing all their trust in him.

6. It is said that their faith was very weak and their knowledge very small. I admit that their knowledge and faith were not as great as those of believers under the *New Testament*, and it is difficult to determine exactly how far their faith extended. But it is hard to believe that those who lived in the times of *Isaiah*, *Daniel*, and *Zechariah* would have paid no heed to the **divine oracles** <note>Dutch: *Godspraaken*, referring to prophetic revelations.</note> that these Prophets proclaimed; or that the ancient Fathers in general could have imagined that the sacrifices they saw offered every day meant nothing and yet still reconciled their sins—something even the wise **pagans** <note>Dutch: *Heidenen*.</note> did not believe regarding their own sacrifices.

7. It is objected that it appears the two Disciples who went to *Emmaus*, as well as the Apostles, expected a **fleshly and temporal kingdom**. This is clearly seen from *Luke 24:21* and from the words of *Peter*, who advised *Christ* against suffering (*Matthew 16:22*). But one must not believe that all the Jews who lived before the coming of *Christ* held this view; it is certain that those who did hold it could have overcome their prejudices by reading the Prophets. We also see that *Christ* earnestly rebuked his Disciples for this (*Matthew 16:21, 22; Luke 24:25, 26*).

8. It is said that all the promises made to Israel are temporal <note>Meaning "temporary" or "earthly," rather than eternal.</note>.

I Answer, 1. that this is not generally true; there are many promises that are entirely spiritual. One may read *Exodus 34:6, 7; Leviticus 27:12, 41, 42; Deuteronomy 18:15; 30:2, 3, 11, 12; Isaiah 45:17; Daniel 12:2; etc.* 2. Secondly,

<column-break/>

is it to be thought—as has been very well noted—that God proclaimed his law directly from Heaven and prescribed religion with all its circumstances, only for the entire religion to be limited and bound to the earth? 3. Furthermore, the promises given to the people of Israel are contained and expressed in such words that they could not possibly have had their fulfillment in this life alone. 4. Finally, if the Law given to the Jews had not included the promises of **Salvation** <note>Dutch: *Zaligheid*.</note> in the life to come, the state of this people who served the true God would have been far more miserable than that of a great portion of the pagans, who remained at peace in their religions.

9. It is objected that the *Holy Spirit* was promised as a special gift of the *New Covenant*.

I answer that this only means the Spirit would be poured out in greater abundance (*John 7:39*); for the Fathers of the *Old Covenant* participated in the Spirit (see *Psalm 51:11; 143:10; Isaiah 44:3; 59:21; Ezekiel 36:27; 39:29; Haggai 2:5*).

<margin>Smalcius, *On the Divinity of Christ*, chapter 7, in the excerpts.</margin>
10. It is said that the Jews themselves confess that no promise of eternal life is to be found in the *Old Testament*. But 1. This is untrue. One only has to read **Menasseh Ben Israel** <note>Original: *Menasse Ben Israël*. A famous Sephardic rabbi and scholar in Amsterdam (1604–1657) who argued for the immortality of the soul from Jewish scripture.</note> in his four books on the immortality of the soul, and in his first book on the resurrection (chapters 1 and 10). One could also bring other testimonies that refute what **Smalcius** <note>Valentinus Smalcius (1572–1622), a Socinian theologian known for questioning traditional interpretations of Christ and the Old Testament.</note> says of the Jews. 2. Even if modern Jews had said this, it is certain that the ancient Jews never said such a thing.

<margin>Cocceius, *Gemara Sanhedrin*, p. 318. <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a prominent Dutch theologian known for "Covenant Theology."</note></margin>
Everyone knows the opinion of the **Pharisees** against the **Sadducees** <note>The Pharisees believed in the resurrection and afterlife, while the Sadducees famously denied them.</note>.

<margin>Smalcius, against Franz, disputation 7, *On Good Works*.</margin>
It is said that because the Covenant of Grace is called the *New* and a *Better Covenant*, it follows that under a better and new Covenant there is also a new doctrine, namely that of eternal life.

But we have seen that there are other and more profound reasons why the new is called a better Covenant.

Meanwhile, as we see, there have been two Dispensations, although there is only one Covenant of Grace. The one is sometimes called the *Old*, the other the *New Covenant*.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "Covenant of Grace," explaining why God revealed His plan for salvation in stages throughout history, moving from the strict "Old Dispensation" of Moses to the "New Dispensation" of Christ.</meta>

# DIVINITY. IX. B. XLVII. CHAPTER.

One must not be surprised that God presented the **covenant of grace** in various ways. His Wisdom shines through in this: that He did not wish to complete His work all at once, nor to spread the great light—which He caused to shine in these last days—all at one time. Instead, He did so by steps and degrees, just as the Sun climbs by degrees until it reaches its noon-day height.

It was fitting that the Church in its maturity should possess more advantages than in its infancy, and that the closer the *Messiah* <note>The promised Savior.</note> approached, the clearer the prophecies of His coming would become.

<margin>Gen. III. 15.</margin>
The covenant of grace can be contained within four periods. 1. From Adam to Abraham, for the first promise was made to Adam.
<margin>Gen. XII. 3. XXII. 18. XXVI 4.</margin>
2. From Abraham to Moses, for the same promise, though in different words, was repeated to Abraham. 3. From Moses to Christ. 4. From Christ's first coming to His last.

But here, a few more observations must be made.

<margin>2. Cor. III. 6. Col. II. 14.</margin>
**I.** The Mosaic **Dispensation** <note>Dutch: *Huishouding*, meaning God's "household management" or theological era.</note> can be considered either in terms of the outward aspects of the legal discipline—which was very strict, as was evident at the proclamation of the Law—and in this respect, the Law is called a **Letter that kills**, a handwriting that was against us. Or, it can be considered in terms of the **Evangelical promises** <note>Promises related to the Gospel or "Good News" of salvation.</note> which some already understood in this dispensation, and the truth that lay hidden under the shadows. In this respect, this Dispensation was gentler, because it held the example of future goods; and from this, the believers—who paid heed to this hidden truth and had received the light of the Holy Spirit—drew all their comfort. Thus, in the Old Dispensation, there was a mixture of the Law and the Gospel. That which it had of the Law terrified the Sinner. That which it had of the Gospel lifted up tender souls and comforted them. See Exodus XIX. 12, and XXIV. 5. &c. In the first of these Chapters, we see that God, wishing to proclaim His Law, commanded that boundaries be set around the mountain to keep the people back, while He allowed no one to approach Him but Moses alone. In the second, we read how the covenant was established through the blood of beasts, and how the elders of the people, being

<sig>I. Part. Errr</sig>

<column-break/>

called and admitted onto the mountain with Moses, enjoyed God’s presence.

**II.** It must be noted that the Old Dispensation had several distinguishing marks.

1. In it, God gave to men the promises of the coming *Messiah*.

2. The mysteries were taught obscurely therein. Therefore, the time of the Old Testament is compared to the night, and its ceremonies are called a veil. 2. Cor. III. 13.

<margin>Rom. VIII. 15.</margin>
3. The Spirit that was communicated was a **Spirit of bondage** <note>Meaning a spirit of slavery or fear rather than the freedom of children.</note>, and those who lived under this Dispensation differed in no way from slaves.

<margin>Gal: IV. 1. V. 1.</margin>
4. The Old Dispensation was strict and punitive; Moses almost always had the rod in his hand, and the Prophets thundered at nearly every moment by proclaiming curses.

5. It had to come to an end, just as it has indeed ended.

<margin>Hebr. IX. 9. 10; Acts XIII. 39: Rom: IV. 7. Ps. XXXII. Rom. IX. 4. Gal. IV. 2. Lev. XXVI. Isa. XLIV. Zech. XII. John. XVI. 13: 1. John. II. 20.</margin>
In the meantime, the believers who lived under it obtained the forgiveness of their sins, adoption as children, sanctification, the gifts of the spirit, and eternal life.

**III.** Upon this Old Dispensation, the New has followed, under which all things are made new. The expected *Messiah* has come, and the ceremonies are abolished. The Spirit has been poured out in greater measure; the church has also reached its maturity. More knowledge, holiness, faith, hope, comfort, and joy have arisen; eternal life has been brought to light through Christ, and this Dispensation shall last until it makes way for heavenly Glory.

**IV.** Thus one sees how the Old Testament differed from the New.

<margin>Heb VIII. 11.</margin>
1. That the one proclaimed the coming *Messiah*, and the other offers Him as having already come.

<margin>2. Cor. III. 18.</margin>
2. In the one, the mysteries are covered with many veils. In the other, we behold with an uncovered head the Glory of the Lord as in the mirror of the Gospel.

<margin>Heb. X. 1.</margin>
3. The first was full of shadows; the second has the living image of the things themselves. The Saving grace has appeared to all men and has made the shadows disappear through its radiant light.

# THE CHRISTIAN

4. There was much more to observe in the service of the Old than in that of the New Testament; the ceremonial duties alone already constituted an unbearable yoke, whereas the yoke—that is, the service of Christ—is light and gentle (Matthew 11:30).

5. Under the Old Testament, the Spirit of servitude prevailed over the Spirit of adoption as children, if I may put it that way; and the curses of the Law thundered more than the promises of the Gospel were heard. But we do not have the Spirit of servitude to live in dread and fear again; rather, we have the Spirit of adoption as children, which constantly makes us cry out: *Abba, Father* <note>A phrase from Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:6, signifying a close, personal relationship with God.</note>.

<margin>
Psalm 147:19, 20.

John 4:23, 24.
1 Timothy 2:8.
Ephesians 2:14.
</margin>

Under the Old **Dispensation** <term>Huishouding: A theological era or "household management" of God's plan.</term> there was only one people that was favored by God and possessed His laws; but under the New, the Name of God resounds from the East to the West. In all places, all those who serve Him in spirit and in truth are pleasing to Him. The middle wall of partition between nation and nation is broken down and shall not be built up again.

7. Finally, the Old Dispensation has ended, but the New shall last as long as Heaven and Earth endure.

### XLVIII. CHAPTER.

->Whether the Moral Law is abolished in the<-
->New Dispensation.<-

Before we finish this book, it is necessary to examine some questions.

The first is whether, under the New Dispensation, the Moral Law <note>The "Moral Law" refers to the eternal ethical standards, primarily summarized in the Ten Commandments, as opposed to ceremonial or civil laws of ancient Israel.</note> still has a place?

<margin>
Romans 3:20.
Galatians 3:10.
</margin>
I answer: 1. That the Moral Law no longer has the same use that it had in the state of uprightness <note>The "state of uprightness" refers to the condition of humanity before the Fall of Adam.</note>; for we have shown in another place that no flesh can be justified by the works of the Law, and that all those who are under the Law lie under the curse.

<margin>
Galatians 3:13.
</margin>
2. That believers are no longer under the curse which the Law pronounced against transgressors, because Christ has freed us from the curse, having Himself become a curse for us.

<column-break/>

3. But that we are, nevertheless, always under the governance of the Law of God; that it is the rule for our conduct in life, and that we are obliged to keep its commandments. It serves us then not only as a bridle to restrain our passions in a certain way, or as a mirror in which we discover our flaws, but it also governs our life and shows us our duties in a perfect manner.

It also appears from Scripture that Christ and His Apostles recommend to us the keeping of this Law; they prescribe to us the practice of all the commandments; one need only read Christ's moral sermons on the mount <note>The Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5-7).</note> to be convinced of this.

<margin>
Matthew 5, 6, 7; 22:36, 37.
Romans 13:8, 9.
Hebrews 11, 12.
</margin>
The Savior commands us above all to love God with our whole heart, and our neighbor as ourselves; His Apostles urge in all places the fulfillment of these commandments. If they say that without faith one cannot please God, they also say that without **sanctification** <note>The process of being made holy or living a godly life.</note> no one shall see God.

But, to be fully assured that the Moral Law has no contradiction with the **covenant of grace**, one must observe:

1. That in this covenant we promise to be His people, and consequently to obey His laws.

2. That in this covenant God desires us to show Him perfect obedience, as to our Father and our Lord.

3. That if Christ acts in this covenant as a Surety who fulfills the Law for us, He also appears therein as our Head, who through His Spirit fulfills the Law in us and for us.

4. That if He has delivered us by His death from the punishment with which the Law threatened us, He has also given us in His life an example of virtues that we must follow.

5. That the Holy Spirit, whom we receive through this covenant, is not only a Spirit of comfort, but also of sanctification, who incites us to the observation of the Law and the practice of good works.

6. That if the saving grace has appeared to us, it is so that we should live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present world.

I shall say no more of it now...

1. It is said that we are no longer under

it is only for the Wicked that the

otherwise, the commandments of the Law

7. It is said that a Law that
provokes and increases sin should
have no place under the New Testament.
<margin>Rom. 5:20. etc.</margin>
I answer that it is only by accident
that the Law stirs up and increases
sin, because the corruption of
men is so great that what
is forbidden to them becomes much more pleasant:
permission breeds distaste, and
difficulty ignites desire. Thus it
happens that the Law, far from curbing
the lusts of men,
ignites them—not because the Law
properly produces this effect:
for far be it from us that we should in any way
reject this holy Law and illustrious
revelation of God's will, which gives us
the precept for our life.

I answer that a Law given to the
Jews as Jews does not indeed
concern Christians: but that a
Law given to the Jews as being
the people of God, concerns all
who are also the people of God;
and it is in this manner that we must
speak of the moral Law.

## CHAPTER XLIX.
### Whether the Churchly or Ceremonial Law has been abolished.

We must not reason regarding the Ceremonial Law in the same way as we have done regarding the Moral Law <note>The Moral Law refers to the Ten Commandments, which the author previously argued remain in effect as a rule of conduct, whereas the "Ceremonial Law" refers to the specific religious rituals of ancient Israel.</note>: for although we can make very great use of it—considering it as the pattern that not only foreshadowed everything the Messiah would do, but contains a singular correspondence between the pattern and the truth represented by it (which serves in no small way to strengthen our faith and prove the truth of the Christian Religion)—and although we find therein symbols of the Divine mercy that God requires of us, nevertheless we do not doubt that the same has been abolished, so that Christians are no longer obligated to observe it.

<margin>Gal. IV. 2.</margin>
<margin>Eph. II. 14.</margin>
<margin>Col. II. 14.</margin>
I. This Law was a **tutor**, which brought man to Christ and kept him in expectation of the coming goods until the time appointed by the Father; but we no longer need a tutor to lead us to the Savior, since He has come and the church has reached its majority <note>The author uses a legal metaphor: just as a child outgrows a guardian upon reaching adulthood, the church outgrew the need for the Old Testament rituals upon the arrival of Christ.</note>: This Law was given to distinguish the Jews from the Gentiles, therefore it is also called a **partition wall**: but Christ has taken away this wall, and in Him there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, Scythian and Barbarian: This Law was a **handwritten bond** <note>original: "hand-schrift." This refers to Colossians 2:14, depicting the law as a debt or legal document that stood against humanity.</note> that was written against us, but Christ has torn it and nailed it to the cross: This Law was a **shadow** of the things to come; but the shadow disappeared at the coming of the **Sun of Righteousness**, why then should we still hold fast to the shadow? Since we now have the body itself: This Law was a **veil** that covered the mysteries, but that veil is broken, just as it was torn at the death of Christ.

<margin>Jeremiah XXXI. 31. 32.</margin>
<margin>Dan. IX. 27, 24.</margin>
<margin>Heb. VII. 12.</margin>
II. The annulment of this Law was foretold: God testifies through the Prophet

<column-break/>

Jeremiah, that he would establish a new covenant with the house of Israel, "not," He says, "according to the Covenant that I had made with their fathers": Daniel had foretold that the Messiah would cause the sacrifice and grain offering to cease, and that he would seal up the vision and the prophecy; David promises a new High Priest in the 110th Psalm; now according to Paul, when the Priesthood is changed, it is necessary that a change occurs in the Law: some add to this what Jeremiah III. 16 says; that there would be no more **ark**; "in those days," says the Lord, "they shall say no more, The ark of the Covenant of the Lord," etc. Others prove it by Psalm L. 13. There are also some who believe that Hagar, being cast out by Abraham, was a symbol of what was to happen regarding the Law of ceremonies <note>Referring to the allegory in Galatians 4, where Hagar represents the Old Covenant of Sinai and Sarah represents the New Covenant of Grace.</note>.

III. This Law was given only for the Jews, for as long as they should be separated from the other nations; the same can therefore no longer have a place today, since all nations know the true God: how would it be possible for people from all corners of the world to journey to Jerusalem three times every year? Where would one find enough sacrificial beasts to be offered? From where would one fetch all the incense that would have to be burned?

IV. The destruction of Jerusalem was a proof that God wished to destroy this Law, which required that one come to offer sacrifices to God in Jerusalem every year; the confusion of the tribes is further proof of this, for today one can no longer distinguish the tribe of Levi <note>The "tribe of Levi" was the only group authorized to perform priestly duties. The author argues that because Jewish genealogical records were lost, the ritual law can no longer be legally practiced.</note>.

V. When one reads the Prophets, it appears clearly that the primary intent of God in instituting the offerings was not to signify that it was a matter that was pleasing to Him in and of itself, or consistent with His nature, but that He had seen fit to act so as to accommodate the Jewish people; it is in this sense that some understand what God says in Ezekiel XX. 25, "Therefore I also gave them statutes that were not good." But hear what God says through Jeremiah, Chapter VII. 22, 23: "For I did not speak to your fathers, on the day—"

It must be noted that this service was abolished because the truth has followed the type <note>In theology, a "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow something in the New Testament.</note>, and the body followed the shadow; we no longer have circumcision in the flesh, but we have circumcision in the Spirit; we no longer offer animal sacrifices, but we offer our bodies as a sacrifice. Christ, our Passover Lamb, has been slaughtered for us; we no longer have a High Priest who offers lambs and goats, but we have Jesus the Supreme High Priest, who, after offering himself through the eternal Spirit, entered into Heaven so that he might be an intercessor for us there, and we have all become priests, etc.

I cannot neglect to make some remarks here on the decree of the Apostles in the Council of Jerusalem; in this decree, one finds the commandments that are called the Noachide Laws <note>The "Laws of Noah" are seven moral imperatives that, according to the Talmud, were given by God as a binding set of laws for all of humanity.</note>.

The question is asked whether the prohibition against eating blood or strangled meat flows from natural law, such that it would still obligate Christians today?

**Answer 1.** It is known to everyone that the Jews believe one must entirely abstain from blood, whether they believe that this prohibition is one of those they say were given to Noah, or whether they are of the opinion that the Ceremonial Law has not been abolished. <margin>Buxtorf, *The Jewish Synagogue*, page 403. Babylonian *Gemara* on the Title *Sanhedrin*, Chapter VII, and in *Genesis Rabbah*, Section 34. Maimonides in *The Laws of Kings*, Chapter 9. **2.** Everyone also knows that Muhammad similarly prohibited the use of blood. <margin>Surah II of the *Quran*. Elmacin in *History of the Saracens*, Book I, Chapter 1. Jaime Bleda, *Defense of the Faith in the Cause of the Moriscos*, Chapter 8.</margin>

**3.** Many among the Early Church Fathers held the same thoughts, as did many Church Councils.

**4.** The Greeks abstain from blood to this very day.

**5.** Among the Christians, Curcellaeus (a Remonstrant) <note>The Remonstrants were a Dutch Protestant group who followed the teachings of Jacobus Arminius.</note>, and among the orthodox, Becman and Salmasius, along with some

<column-break/>

others, have also been of the opinion that one must abstain from blood.

But other Christians are of different thoughts and believe that the prohibition of the Apostles obligates no one anymore today.

Those who maintain that one must still abstain from blood make several objections.

**First objection.** It is said that it was forbidden in the state of uprightness <note>The "state of uprightness" refers to the period before the Fall of Man in Eden.</note> and consequently flows from natural law.

**Answer.** Without wishing to decide whether it was forbidden before sin was committed, I deny the conclusions one wishes to draw from that: did the prohibition God gave not to eat from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil also flow from natural law?

**2nd Objection.** It is said that God only permitted the eating of meat after the Deluge (Genesis 9:3).

**Answer.** It is not probable that God gave more freedom to men after the Deluge than before it.

**3rd Objection.** It is said that it appears God forbade men from eating meat with its blood after the Deluge (Genesis 9:4).

**Answer.** This is granted, but this Law was purely ceremonial, obligating no more than the other ceremonies; it is the same with the prohibition made by the Law.

**4th Objection.** It is said that what was prescribed to Noah, as the restorer of the human race, obligates all men.

**Answer.** This is denied, for then one would also be obligated to offer sacrifices, just as Noah did.

**5th Objection.** It is said that a commandment based on a rational reason, which corresponds with the Sixth Commandment—*Thou shalt not kill*—is moral.

**Answer.** If that were so, then the majority of the Ceremonial Laws would be moral; for why did God require so many purifications? It was to teach us that He loves holiness above all—that is a moral reason; however, the laws regarding those sanctifications were ceremonial.

### 6th Objection.
It is said that a commandment accompanied by promises and terrible threats is moral in nature, and that the prohibition against eating blood is paired with such things in Deuteronomy 12:23, 24, 25 and Leviticus 17:10.

**Answer.** I deny this; otherwise, circumcision would be a **Moral Law**, for God issues a terrible threat against those who were not circumcised in Genesis 17:14. In the same way, one could argue regarding the prohibition of eating unleavened bread during the Passover feast in Exodus 12:15, and the prohibition of eating fat in Leviticus 7:25. One may further examine Leviticus 26:14, 15, 16 for similar threats. <note>The author argues that just because a law has a harsh penalty doesn't mean it is a "moral law" (a universal rule of right and wrong); ritual laws also carried heavy penalties in the Old Testament.</note>

### 7th Objection.
It is said that strangers were forbidden from eating blood in Leviticus 17:10. Now, it is added that the strangers who were inhabitants were only bound to observe the **Moral Laws**, or those given to Noah; but they were not permitted to keep the Ceremonial Laws, such as the Passover, as seen in Exodus 12:43.

The answer is: 1. That Leviticus 17 speaks of strangers who were circumcised and obligated to keep all the commandments; this is evident from the fact that uncircumcised strangers were not forbidden from eating an animal that died of itself <note>original: "dood aas"</note> in Deuteronomy 14:21.

2. That the same strangers are discussed in the 10th verse as in the 8th and 9th.

### 8th Objection.
It is said that the Apostles clearly forbade the eating of blood and of strangled meat in the Church Assembly <note>The Council of Jerusalem, described in Acts 15.</note> at Jerusalem.

I answer that this is certain, but it is also certain:

1. That the Ceremonial Law was abolished by Christ, according to Ephesians 2:15.

2. That Christ, arguing with the Pharisees, teaches that nothing which enters the mouth defiles a man. Matthew 15:1, 2, 15.

3. That Paul, in Romans 14:14, 17, declares that nothing is unclean in itself, except when someone considers it to be unclean; for the Kingdom of God does not consist of food and drink.

4. That he says in 1 Corinthians 10:25 that one may eat anything sold in the meat market <note>original: "vleesch-huis"</note>: Now, it is believed that this letter was written after the Church Assem-

<column-break/>

bly of Jerusalem.

5. That he does not want anyone to judge us regarding food or drink, Colossians 2:16, 17, this being a letter written approximately 15 years after the Jerusalem Church Assembly.

6. That he declares in Titus 1:15 that all things are pure to those who are pure, and that it is the teaching of **Devils** to forbid eating foods that God has created.

7. That the prohibition of the Apostles in the Church Assembly of Jerusalem was for a time, intended for the Jews who were not yet firm in the teaching of the Apostles, and who could not yet be convinced that all things are pure for those who are pure; and who knows if the prohibition of this Council even affected all the Churches?

### 9th Objection.
It is said that we must receive all the commandments of God as if they will always remain in effect until God makes it known to us that they have been abolished.

I answer: 1. That the commandment to abstain from blood lasted until the coming of the Messiah, at which time God made it known that all the ceremonies had come to an end. 2. That this commandment can take place when one fears giving offense. This was the motive of the Church Assembly of Jerusalem: Thus, the observance of the Apostolic prohibition would still continue if we were in the same circumstances of time as the Apostles were. <note>This refers to the "law of love," where a Christian might choose to give up a right to avoid upsetting someone with a more sensitive conscience.</note>

### 10th Objection.
It is said that if this prohibition is binding as long as there are "weak" people, it remains binding today because many are still offended when they see blood being eaten, such as the Greeks and the Jews.

I answer: 1. That if one abstains from blood for the sake of weak brothers, it does not bring any detriment to the *right* we have to eat it, but only affects the *exercise* of that right. 2. That one must distinguish the times of the Apostles from the present. In the beginning of Christianity, it was impossible for many Jews not to be offended by the eating of blood by the Gentiles: thus, it was a duty of love to have compassion for their weakness; but today’s Christians ought to be instructed in the will of God, so that one should not...

**11. Objection.** That this Church decree <note>Referring to the Council of Jerusalem, where the Apostles met to decide which Jewish laws applied to Gentile converts.</note> was made through the power of the Holy Spirit, that the Apostles declare these things are necessary, and that they place the prohibition of blood and strangled meat alongside sexual immorality.

**12. Objection.** One raises the opinion of many Church Fathers <note>The influential early Christian theologians of the first few centuries.</note> against this.

**I answer:** 1. That there were many Church Fathers with different opinions, such as Augustine in *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, book 32, chapter 13. 2. That some Church Fathers did not well understand what the reason for the Council of Jerusalem was. 3. That there could have been many reasons that may have obliged Tertullian and others to abstain from blood, such as the fear they had that the Pagans might accuse the Christians of not following the Apostles' commands. 4. That there are Church Fathers who condemned the eating of blood because it offended the weak. 5. That many group strangled meat with blood, and yet even the greatest enemies of eating blood confess that it is permitted to eat strangled meat. One can look further into this matter in the treatise by Mr. Heidegger, the famous theologian in Zurich. <note>Johann Heinrich Heidegger (1633–1698), a Swiss Reformed theologian.</note>

Some further objections are made to show that the Ceremonial law must remain in force. However, these are also easily answered.

**1.** It is said that it is not our place to abolish God's laws. That is true: But God himself has abolished them by sending us the one whom they foreshadowed. <note>Referring to Jesus Christ as the fulfillment of the Old Testament "shadows" or rituals.</note>

<column-break/>

**2.** It is said that God’s immutability <note>The theological concept that God does not change.</note> does not allow Him to change what He has once instituted.

But one is mistaken; when God has instituted a matter only for a time, He can set it aside without being accused of inconstancy.

<margin>Genesis 17:7, 13</margin>
**3.** It is said that circumcision is called an **eternal Covenant**. I answer that it is named thus because it had to endure until the coming of the Messiah. The root word <note>The Hebrew word *olam*.</note> does not always signify eternity, but rather a long duration. 
<margin>Exodus 21:6</margin>
The servant who bound himself to serve until the **Jubilee year** <note>A year of emancipation and restoration held every 50 years in ancient Israel.</note> is said to serve "forever" or "always." Add to this that circumcision is called an eternal Covenant because it was a sign of a Covenant that would last forever.

**4.** It is said that the Ceremonial law is more perfect than the Moral law, since God gave it after He had proclaimed the **Ten Words** <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>.

But one has only to use their reason to see that the **Moral Law**, which is grounded in natural right, is much more glorious than the **Ceremonial Law**, which rests on mere arbitrary will.

<margin>Deut. 30:2, 4, 5. Ezekiel 37:24, 25; 40, 41, 42.</margin>
**5.** Some point to certain prophecies <note>original: "Godspraaken"</note> that seem to foretell the restoration of Jerusalem, the rebuilding of the Temple, and the return of the Ten Tribes.

But, besides the fact that the prophecies cited can be understood and explained as the true return of the Jews from the Babylonian captivity, etc., it is certain that the Spirit of God has hidden spiritual promises beneath these temporal ones.

The Jerusalem that must be rebuilt is the **Church**, and not the earthly Jerusalem. The religion that shall be instituted there is a spiritual religion. The incense that shall be burned there consists of and from the prayers and thanksgivings of the Saints. One must not be surprised that God describes the service of the **New Covenant** through words that express the service of the old; it was fitting that God, who desired that His people should observe the Ceremonial Law, indicated He intended to relieve His people of it, for fear that they might throw off this yoke from their necks themselves because of the unbearable burden attached to it.

# THEOLOGY. IX. B. Chapter 50.

<margin>Acts 18:18.</margin>
6. ¶ One might object using what the Apostles at times have done to win over the Jews and to accommodate their weakness.

But it is evident from what has been said that what they did in that regard was only for a time, in order to bring the weak brothers to Christ. <note>The author refers to "weak brothers" as those early Jewish Christians who still felt bound by old customs; the Apostles accommodated them temporarily to avoid unnecessary conflict while they grew in faith.</note>

7. Finally, it is said that one must abolish all kinds of external ceremonies in the Church.

I answer that this conclusion does not follow. Some ceremonies are necessary for the sake of order, as long as one does not seek to gain merit from them, nor imagines that they are so necessary that those who do not observe them sin greatly—provided they act without despising the Church that prescribed them and without giving offense.

One must also be careful not to multiply these ceremonies so much that they become an unbearable burden.

There is a great difference between the ceremonies of the Old and those of the New Testament. The former are no longer in use because they prefigured the Messiah, who has come. The latter serve for the maintenance of good order in the Church. The former constituted the primary part of the religious service; the latter are merely aids to it.

---

### CHAPTER L.

->Whether the Civil Law is abolished.<-

REngarding the Civil Law, <note>In this context, "Civil Law" refers to the judicial and political laws given specifically to the nation of Israel in the Old Testament, distinct from the Ten Commandments (Moral Law).</note> one can consider it in two ways.

1. One can consider it as that which separated the people of Israel from all other nations, and as a Law that prefigured the Kingdom of Christ. In that respect, it is <margin>Gal. 2:28. Eph. 2:14.</margin> abolished; for there is no longer any distinction between Jew and Gentile in Christ. The middle wall of separation is broken down. Christ having come, we no longer need the symbols that formerly foreshadowed Him. The Jews themselves no longer constitute a commonwealth. They are subject to the powers and authorities under which they are scattered. One can also consider this Law as containing various statutes that concerned none but the 

<column-break/>

Jews in particular, or which were shadows of things that were to happen; such as, for example, the Law of divorce, the firstborn, the <term>cities of refuge</term> <note>Specified towns where someone who committed accidental manslaughter could claim asylum from blood vengeance.</note>, the jubilee years, the <term>waters of jealousy</term> <note>A ritual ordeal described in Numbers 5 used to determine if a wife had been unfaithful.</note>, the manner in which one had to sow both <note>Likely referring to the prohibition against sowing a field with two different types of seed.</note>, and the division of the Land of Canaan. In this respect, the Civil Law is also annulled.

2. But one can consider it under another respect, as containing some laws which are based on the Law of nature—sound and common to all men—which serve as explanations of the ten commandments and can be observed by all nations. In this respect, it is not abolished; thus, nothing prevents the maintenance of laws that punish the guilty, prescribe the maintenance of order, protect widows and orphans, etc. The most civilized nations have observed these, and their fulfillment is strictly recommended to us in the New Testament.

One can consider the children of Jacob <note>The Israelites.</note> either as a people in general or as the Jewish people in particular; all the Laws that suit the children of Jacob, when considered as a people in general, can be common to other nations. But all those given to them specifically as the descendants of Jacob no longer suit us any more than those of the Assyrians, Persians, and Greeks.

One might say that it were to be wished that all nations conformed to the Jewish Civil laws. But this is impossible, because the maintenance of those laws depends on certain circumstances that are not found among other nations. God, who made these laws primarily for the Jews and did not place other nations in the state in which they were, has also not subjected them to the same. If it then happens that Christians prefer certain laws of the old Roman Emperors over the Civil laws that God made for the Jews, it is only because the former better suit their state than the latter.

One might say that if Christ had wanted the Civil law to be abolished, he would have put another in its place. When he was on earth, he never wanted to involve himself in the settling of disputes. Luke 12:13, 14.
